wrong intention associated with wrong view, and all other wrong intentions not associated with it, as well as factors associated with wrong view—these are called wrong view that is not wrong intention.

The answer is:
wrong view associated with wrong intention, and all other factors associated with wrong intention that are not associated with wrong view—this is called wrong intention that is not wrong view.

The answer is:
excluding the wrong intention that is associated with wrong view, all other factors associated with both wrong view and wrong intention are called wrong view associated with wrong intention.

The answer is:

wrong intention not associated with wrong view, wrong view not associated with wrong intention, and all other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—this is called that which is neither wrong view nor wrong intention.

wrong effort dissociated from wrong view, as well as all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*). Regarding the three fetters up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*): among those three fetters, how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
The answer is:
First, there is the indeterminate; second, there is that which requires further analysis.
Precepts, stealing, and doubt are unwholesome when they exist in the desire realm, but they are indeterminate when they exist in the form and formless realms.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are definitely unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Among the outflows (*āsrava*), one is neutral (*avyākṛta*) and two are to be analyzed.
The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is either unwholesome or neutral.
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
shamelessness (*ahrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anottappa*), and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) associated with them—this is called unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate?
The answer is:
the outflow of desire that is dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread; this is called the indeterminate.
The outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsava) is either unwholesome (akuśala) or indeterminate (avyākṛta).
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
The outflow of ignorance associated with lack of shame and lack of dread is called unwholesome.
What is indeterminate?
The answer is:
The outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava) that is dissociated from lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya) is called indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Among the floods (ogha), one is indeterminate and three should be analyzed.
The flood of sensual desire (kāma-ogha) is either unwholesome (akuśala) or indeterminate.
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
the flood of desire associated with shamelessness and lack of dread; this is called unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate?
The answer is:
the outflow of desire that is dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread; this is called the indeterminate.
The outflow of ignorance is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
The outflow of ignorance associated with lack of shame and lack of dread is called unwholesome.
What is indeterminate?
The answer is:
The flood of ignorance that is dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread is called indeterminate.
The flood of views is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
What is unwholesome?
Answer: The three views of the desire realm are called unwholesome.
What are the indeterminate ones?
Answer: The two views of the desire realm and the five views of the form and formless realms are called indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The same applies to the yokes (*yoga*).
Among the types of feeling (*vedanā*), one is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and three should be analyzed.
Sensual feeling (*kāma-vedanā*) is either unwholesome (*akuśala*) or indeterminate.
What is unwholesome?
Answer: Shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anottappa*), together with the desire associated with them, are called unwholesome (*akuśala*).
What is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Answer: Receptivity to desire that is dissociated from shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) is called indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Receptivity to precepts (*śīla-samādāna*) is either unwholesome (*akuśala*) or indeterminate.
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
that which exists within the desire realm is called unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate?
The answer is:
that which exists in the realms of form and formlessness is called the indeterminate.
Feeling is seen as either unwholesome or indeterminate.
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
The two views within the desire realm are called unwholesome.
What is indeterminate?
The answer is:
The two views of the desire realm and the four views of the form and formless realms are called indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Among the fetters (*bandhana*), two are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and two should be analyzed.
The fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-bandhana*) and the fetter of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-bandhana*) are unwholesome when they exist in the desire realm.
In the form and formless realms, these are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), as well as the fetters of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), and envy (*īrṣyā*), are definitely unwholesome (*akuśala*).
The fetter of craving (*anunaya*) and the fetter of pride (*māna*) are unwholesome when they exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In the form and formless realms, these are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Among the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), two are unwholesome (*akuśala*), one is indeterminate, and two are to be analyzed.

Precept-attachment (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are unwholesome in the desire realm, but they are indeterminate in the form and formless realms.
Among the views, two are indeterminate and three should be analyzed.
False view, adherence to views, and adherence to precepts and rituals are unwholesome when in the desire realm, but they are indeterminate when in the form and formless realms.
Among the six types of craving for the body (*kāyatanatṛṣṇā*), two are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and four should be analyzed.
Craving arising from eye-contact and ear-contact is unwholesome when in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) when in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The craving for mental contact (*manosaṃsparśatṛṣṇā*) is unwholesome (*akuśala*) when it exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) when it exists in the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), two are unwholesome, one is indeterminate, and four are to be analyzed.

The underlying tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*) and the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) are unwholesome (*akuśala*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*).
The underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
the latent tendency of ignorance associated with shamelessness and lack of dread; this is called unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate?
The answer is:
the latent tendency of ignorance that is dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread; this is called the indeterminate.
The fetter of views is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
The three views of the desire realm are called unwholesome.
What is indeterminate?
The answer is:
The two views of the desire realm and the five views of the form and formless realms are called indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), three are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and six should be analyzed as being either unwholesome or indeterminate.

The fetter of craving, the fetter of pride, the fetter of wrong resolve, and the fetter of doubt are unwholesome when they exist in the desire realm, and indeterminate when they exist in the form and formless realms.
The fetter of ignorance is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
the fetter of ignorance associated with shamelessness and lack of dread; this is called unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate?
The answer is:
the fetter of ignorance that is dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread; this is called the indeterminate.
The fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) is either unwholesome (akuśala) or indeterminate (avyākṛta). What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
One type of view in the desire realm is called unwholesome.
What is indeterminate?
The answer is:
The two views of the desire realm and the three views of the form and formless realms are called indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), thirty-three are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and sixty-four are indeterminate; one [proclivity] should be analyzed separately.

The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) in the desire realm is either unwholesome (*akuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
The latent tendency of ignorance associated with lack of shame and lack of dread is called unwholesome.
What is indeterminate?
The answer is:
The latent tendency of ignorance that is dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread is called the "indeterminate single-gate" [category]. This concludes the section on the unwholesome.
Regarding these three fetters, how many have retribution and how many are without retribution?
Answer: All unwholesome states have retribution; all indeterminate states are without retribution.
This extends even to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*); how many among them have retribution, and how many are without retribution?
Answer: All unwholesome states have retribution; all indeterminate states are without retribution. [The two gates on retribution and non-retribution are concluded.
Regarding these three fetters, how many are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), and how many are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Answer: The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is abandoned through the vision of the truths (darśana).
The first two types are either abandoned through the vision of the truths or abandoned through both vision and cultivation (darśana-bhāvanā-heya).
What is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*)?
The answer is:

if it is the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), or the fetters (*saṃyojana*), which are abandoned by the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) for those who practice through firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) or firm dharma (*dharmānusārin*), this is called abandoned through the vision of the truths.

As for the remaining [factors]: if they are abandoned by ordinary persons through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they resemble the faculty of mind (*manas*) that is cultivated through progressive training;

if abandoned by the disciples of the World-Honored One, they are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*). This applies to the perversion of regarding precepts and vows as supreme (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), which are abandoned through the vision of the truths.
The first two types are either abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned through both the vision of the truths and cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through the vision of the truths?
The answer is:

If it is the view of precept-and-vow (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), pride (māna), hatred (pratigha), or attachment (anunaya), and these are abandoned through the patience associated with the practice of firm faith and firm dharma—this is called abandonment through the vision of the truths (satyadarśana-prahātavya).
As for the remainder: if it is abandoned by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
if it is abandoned by the disciples of the World-Honored One (*śrāvaka*), it is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*).
Greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) are abandoned through cultivation.
The first two types are either abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) or abandoned through both seeing the truths and cultivation.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
The answer is:
If it is abandoned through cultivation by one who has attained the vision of the traces [of the path], this is called abandonment through cultivation.
As for the remainder: if abandoned by an ordinary person, it is abandonment through cultivation;
if abandoned by a disciple of the World-Honored One, it is abandonment through the vision of the truths.
The outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), when viewed from the perspective of the truths (*satya*), consist of the first three types:
they are either abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), or abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or abandoned by both seeing the truths and cultivation.
What is abandoned through the vision of the truths? Answer:

If there are the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), the *nivṛtti* and *jñāna-āsravas*, or the fetters (*saṃyojana*), which are abandoned by the patience (*kṣānti*) of those who practice through firm faith and firm dharma—this is called abandonment through the vision of the truths.
What is abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
The answer is:
if that which is abandoned by one who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) and is still in training (*śaikṣa*) is abandoned through cultivation, this is called abandonment through cultivation.
As for the remaining [fetters]: those severed by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
those severed by the disciples of the World-Honored One (*śrāvaka*) are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*).
Among the floods (*ogha*), the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) is abandoned through cultivation.
The first two types—the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)—are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satya-darśana*).
The first three types—the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*)—are abandoned through the vision of the truths.
The first two types of yokes (*yoga*) are likewise.
Among the [five] clingings (*upādāna*), the clinging to sensual pleasures is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The first two types of clinging to precepts and views are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
The first two types of clinging to self are abandoned through the vision of the truths.
Among the three kinds of bonds, the bond of attachment to sensual desire and the bond of ill will are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The first two kinds of bonds—the bond of clinging to precepts and observances and the bond of the view of self—are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana*).
Among the first two types of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), covetousness, ill-will, drowsiness, and restlessness are abandoned through reflection (*vicaya*).
The first two types of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) are definitely abandoned through reflection.
The hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*) is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*),
but is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*) by the disciples of the World-Honored One (*śrāvaka*).
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) is abandoned through cultivation.
The first two types of fetters—craving and conceit—are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
The first three types of fetters—envy and stinginess—are definitely abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Among the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), sensual desire and ill-will are abandoned through cultivation.
The first two types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, *śīlavrataparāmarśa*, doubt (*vicikitsā*), and the five views are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*).

Among the six types of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), the first two types and the five types of craving for the aggregates (*pañca-upādānaskandha-rāga*) are definitely abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The craving for mental objects (*manosaṃcetanā*) is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).

Among the first three types of the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and the tendency of ill will (*pratigha*) are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The first two types—the tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), the tendency of pride (*māna*), and the tendency of ignorance (*avidyā*)—are abandoned through the vision of the truths.
The first three types of view-fetters (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) and the doubt-fetter (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the first two types of resentment-fetter (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The first two types of attachment-fetter (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), pride-fetter (*māna-saṃyojana*), and ignorance-fetter (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) are abandoned through the vision of the truths.

The first three kinds of fetters—namely, the fetter of views, the fetter of attachment to precepts and rituals, and the fetter of doubt—are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
The first two kinds of fetters—namely, the fetter of envy and the fetter of avarice—are definitely abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), twenty-eight are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*) and ten are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
As for the remainder: if abandoned by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they are abandoned through cultivation;
if abandoned by a disciple of the World-Honored One (*śrāvaka*), they are abandoned through the vision of the truths. This concludes the three gates regarding the vision of the truths.

Regarding these three fetters: how many are abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), how many are abandoned through the vision of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path (*samudaya-nirodha-mārga-satya*), and how many are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?
The answer is:
the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
The attachment to precepts has two modes of activity: it is either abandoned through the vision of suffering or abandoned through the vision of the path.
Doubt has four modes of activity: it is either abandoned through the vision of suffering, or abandoned through the vision of the origin, cessation, or the path.

Greed, hatred, delusion, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*), the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*) consist of four modes.
The yokes (*yoga*) are also like this.

Among the clingings (*upādāna*), the clinging to sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*) and the clinging to self (*ātmanopādāna*) consist of five courses; the clinging to precepts (*śīlavratopādāna*) consists of two courses; and the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*) consists of four courses.

Among the fetters (*bandhana*), the bodily fetter of sensual craving (*kāmacchanda-bandhana*) and the bodily fetter of ill will (*vyāpāda-bandhana*) consist of five courses; the bodily fetter of the misapprehension of precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-bandhana*) consists of two courses; and the bodily fetter of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi-bandhana*) consists of four courses.

Regarding the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*): the hindrance of sensual desire, ill will, sloth-and-torpor, and restlessness-and-agitation are abandoned through five modes of practice; the hindrance of regret is abandoned through concentration and reflection; and the hindrance of doubt is abandoned through four modes of practice.

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of craving (*anunaya*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha*), and the fetter of conceit (*māna*) belong to five modes of practice; the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*) and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya*) are definitely abandoned through the mode of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Among the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) belong to five modes; the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*); the clinging to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) belongs to two modes; and doubt (*vicikitsā*) belongs to four modes.

Among the views (*dṛṣṭi*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*). False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) are [abandoned] by four modes of activity (*ākāra*); the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is [abandoned] by two modes of activity.

Among the cravings for existence (*tṛṣṇā*), five cravings for the body (*kāyatṛṣṇā*) are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), while the craving for mental contact (*manasparśatṛṣṇā*) is [abandoned] by five modes of activity.

Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of sensual desire, the underlying tendency of ill will, the underlying tendency of craving for existence, the underlying tendency of pride, and the underlying tendency of ignorance consist of five modes; the underlying tendency of views and the underlying tendency of doubt consist of four modes.

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of craving (*anunaya*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha*), the fetter of pride (*māna*), and the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā*) belong to five modes of cultivation; the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi*), the fetter of adherence to precepts and vows (*parāmarśa*), and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*) belong to four modes of cultivation; while the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*) and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya*) are definitely abandoned through the cultivation of reflection (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), twenty-eight are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), nineteen through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), nineteen through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), and twenty-two through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*); ten are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). This concludes the four gates regarding the Truth of Suffering.
Of these three fetters, how many are views and how many are non-views?
The answer is:
two are views, and one is a non-view.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are not [fully] seen.
Among the outflows (*āsrava*), one is not seen, while two should be analyzed.
The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is either seen or not seen.
What is "view"?
The answer is:
the five views of the desire realm; these are called "views."
What is "not seeing"? Answer:
With the exception of the five views of the desire realm, all other outflows of desire are called "not seeing."
Regarding the outflows (āsrava), they are either seen or not seen.
How are they seen?
The answer is:
The five views of the form and formless realms are called "views.
What is not a view? Answer:
Excluding the five views of the form and formless realms, all other outflows (āsrava) are called "not seeing.
Among the floods (ogha), one is seeing and three are not seeing.
The same applies to the yokes (yoga).
Among the sensations (*vedanā*), two are views and two are not views.
Among the fetters (*bandhana*), two are views and two are not views.
The hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and the knots (*grantha*) are not views.
Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), two are views (*dṛṣṭi*) and three are non-views (*adṛṣṭi*).
That which is a view is indeed a view;
attachment to the body (*kāyāsneha*) is a non-view.
Among the *anuśayas*, one is associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*) and six are not.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), two are associated with views and seven are not.
Among the ninety-eight *anuśayas*, thirty-six are associated with views and sixty-two are not. [The section on the five gates of views is concluded.]
Regarding these three fetters, how many are with vitarka and vicāra, how many are without vitarka but with vicāra, and how many are without both vitarka and vicāra?
The answer is:
all three types of formations may be with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka but with vicāra, or without both vitarka and vicāra.
Greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of sensual desire are accompanied by both applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra).

As for the remaining three types of action, they may be accompanied by both applied and sustained thought, or by sustained thought alone without applied thought, or be without both applied and sustained thought.
Among the floods (*ogha*), the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*) is with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*);

the remaining three types of action may be with applied and sustained thought, or without applied thought but with sustained thought, or without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*).
The yokes are also like this.
Among the clingings, the clinging to sensual desire has both applied thought and sustained thought;
the remaining three modes of conduct may have both applied and sustained thought, may have no applied thought but only sustained thought, or may have neither applied nor sustained thought.

Among the bonds (*bandhana*), the bond of sensual desire for the body (*kāmarāga-kāyabandhana*) and the bond of ill will (*vyāpāda-kāyabandhana*) possess both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

As for the remaining three types of conduct (*carita*), they may possess both applied and sustained thought, or lack applied thought while possessing sustained thought, or lack both applied and sustained thought.

The fetters of covetousness, ill-will, envy, and avarice are accompanied by both applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra). As for the remaining three modes of activity, they may be with applied and sustained thought, or without applied thought but with sustained thought, or without both applied and sustained thought.
Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), sensual desire and ill will possess both initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*);

the remaining factors and the three types of views may possess both initial and sustained application, or lack initial application but possess sustained application, or lack both initial and sustained application.

Among the five types of craving for the body, four involve both initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*). Craving for mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa-tṛṣṇā*) belongs to three categories: it may involve both initial and sustained application, it may involve no initial application but only sustained application, or it may involve neither initial nor sustained application.

Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and the underlying tendency of ill will (*vyāpāda*) are accompanied by both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
As for the remaining three underlying tendencies, they may be accompanied by both applied and sustained thought, or by sustained thought alone, or be without both applied and sustained thought.

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*), and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya*) possess both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

As for the remaining three types of fetters, they may possess both applied and sustained thought, or lack applied thought while possessing sustained thought, or lack both applied and sustained thought.
Among the ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*), those of the desire realm possess both initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*).

Those of the form realm have three modes of activity: some possess both initial and sustained application, some possess no initial application but have sustained application, and some possess neither initial nor sustained application.
In the formless realm, there is neither initial nor sustained application. This concludes the six gates concerning initial and sustained application.

Of these three fetters, how many are associated with the faculty of pleasure, how many with the faculty of pain, how many with the faculty of joy, how many with the faculty of grief, and how many with the faculty of equanimity?

Answer: The three [fetters] of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) exclude the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) excludes four [faculties], namely, the faculty of suffering.
Greed consists of three [faculties], excluding the faculty of suffering and the faculty of sorrow.
Hostility consists of three, excluding the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy.
Delusion, as well as the outflow of desire and the outflow of ignorance, consist of five.
Regarding the three *āsravas* (outflows), they exclude the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Among the *oghās* (floods), the flood of desire (*kāmaugha*) and the flood of ignorance (*avidyaugha*) consist of five [faculties].
Regarding the *bhavaugha* (flood of existence), it consists of three, excluding the faculty of pain and the faculty of grief.
The four floods (*ogha*) exclude the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
The yokes (*yoga*) are likewise.
Among the graspings (*upādāna*), there are five in the grasping of sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*).

The three fetters of the precept-obsession (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) and the self-obsession (*attavāda*) exclude the faculty of physical pain (*dukkhindriya*) and the faculty of mental distress (*domanassindriya*).
The four views (*diṭṭhi*) exclude the faculty of physical pain.

Among the bonds (*gantha*), the bond of ill-will (*vyāpādagantha*) and the bond of attachment to the body (*kāyagantha*) exclude the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*).
The remaining three fetters exclude the faculty of suffering and the faculty of grief.
Among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of sensual desire excludes the faculty of suffering and the faculty of grief;
the hindrance of ill will excludes the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy.
The five factors—drowsiness (*middha*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—are associated with three faculties, excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*).
Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are associated with two faculties: the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) consists of three [roots], excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).

The fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*) consist of three [roots], excluding the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) are associated with two faculties: the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Among the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), the three [beginning with sensual desire] exclude the faculty of physical pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The three [fetters] of ill-will exclude the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy.
The three [fetters] of personality-belief and attachment to precepts and rituals exclude the faculty of pain and the faculty of grief.
Doubt excludes four [faculties], namely, the faculty of pain.
Among the views (*dṛṣṭi*), the four types of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are associated with [all] except the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
The remaining three views are associated with all except the faculty of suffering and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Among the bodily cravings (*kāyānuśaya*), the five bodily cravings are associated with two faculties: the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
The three [types of craving] associated with the mind exclude the faculty of pain and the faculty of grief.

Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the three—namely, the tendency of sensual desire, the tendency of craving for existence, and the tendency of pride—exclude the faculty of pain and the faculty of grief.
The latent tendency of hatred (*pratighānuśaya*) consists of three [faculties], excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*) consists of five.
The latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*) and doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*) consist of four, excluding the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*).

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) consists of three [faculties], excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).

The fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) consist of three [faculties], excluding the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) is associated with five [faculties].
The fetters of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) and doubt (vicikitsā-saṃyojana) are associated with four, excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkha-indriya).

The fetters of envy (īrṣyā-saṃyojana) and avarice (mātsarya-saṃyojana) are associated with two faculties: the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasya-indriya) and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣā-indriya).

Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the misapprehension of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the misapprehension of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and those abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*)—namely, desire and pride—are associated with two faculties: the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Doubt and hatred abandoned through the vision of the truths are associated with two faculties: the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
False view and ignorance abandoned through the vision of the truths are associated with three [faculties], excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*).
The three types of greed abandoned through contemplation are associated with the faculties excluding the faculty of suffering and the faculty of grief.
Hatred is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy.
Pride is associated with two faculties: the faculty of joy and the faculty of equanimity.
The latent tendency of ignorance consists of five [factors].
In the form realm, there are three, excluding the faculty of physical pain and the faculty of grief.
In the formless realm, there is one, associated with the faculty of equanimity. Thus concludes the seventh section, the Section on the Faculties.
Regarding these three fetters, how many are bound to the desire realm, how many are bound to the form realm, and how many are bound to the formless realm?
The answer is:
all three have three modes of activity; they may be bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
Greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*) are bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*);
the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) is either bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*);
the remaining three modes of conduct (*trivṛtti*) are either bound to the realm of desire, bound to the realm of form, or bound to the formless realm.
Among the floods (*ogha*), the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) is bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*);
the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) is either bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*);
the remaining three modes of conduct (*carita*) are either bound to the realm of desire or bound to the realms of form and formlessness.
The yokes (*yoga*) are also like this.
Among the clingings (*upādāna*), the clinging to sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*) is bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The clinging to self (*ātmopādāna*) is either bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) or bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The remaining three modes of conduct are either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form and formless realms.
Among the bonds (*bandhana*), the bond of sensual craving (*kāmarāga-bandhana*) and the bond of ill-will (*vyāpāda-bandhana*) are bound to the desire realm;
the remaining three modes of conduct are either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form and formless realms.
The five hindrances, as well as the fetter of ill-will, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice, are bound to the desire realm;
the remaining three modes of conduct are either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form and formless realms.
Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), sensual desire and ill-will are bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*);

the remaining [fetters], as well as the five views and three modes of conduct, are either bound to the realm of desire or bound to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Among the cravings for the body, the craving for nose-contact and the craving for tongue-contact are bound to the realm of desire;
the craving for eye-contact and the craving for ear- and body-contact are either bound to the realm of desire or bound to the realm of form;
the three types of craving for mind-contact are either bound to the realm of desire, or bound to the realms of form or formlessness.
Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and the underlying tendency of ill will (*pratigha*) are bound to the desire realm;
the underlying tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) is either bound to the form realm or the formless realm;
the remaining three modes of activity are either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form and formless realms.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*), and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya*) are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
the remaining three types of conduct are either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).

Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), thirty-six are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), thirty-one are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and thirty-one are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*). This concludes the section on the eight gates of bondage.
Regarding all fetters and latent tendencies that belong to the desire realm: do those fetters and latent tendencies exist within the desire realm?
Answer: Some are fetters and latent tendencies of the desire realm, yet those fetters and latent tendencies do not exist within the desire realm.
What are the fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*) of the desire realm that do not reside in the desire realm?
The answer is:

Māra Pāpīyān, though entangled by fetters and proclivities, dwells in the Brahma Heaven; likewise, the Tathāgata’s speech is also entangled by fetters and proclivities when, having passed away from the form realm, he manifests the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the desire realm. These are called the fetters and proclivities of the desire realm that do not reside in the desire realm.
What are the fetters that exist in the desire realm, yet those fetters do not belong to the desire realm?
The answer is:
one who is bound by fetters passes away from the desire realm and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm.

Furthermore, there are all those fetters (saṃyojana) belonging to the form and formless realms that, while residing in the desire realm, manifest before one; these are called "fetters in the desire realm" even though those fetters themselves do not belong to the desire realm.
What are the fetters and proclivities of the desire realm, and how do those fetters also exist within the desire realm?
The answer is:
one who is entangled by these fetters passes away from the desire realm and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) within the desire realm.

Furthermore, those fetters and proclivities that exist in the desire realm and manifest while abiding in the desire realm—these are called the fetters that are of the desire realm, and those fetters also exist in the desire realm.
How can it be that they are neither the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm, nor do those fetters exist in the desire realm?

The answer is: when one is bound by various fetters, one passes away from the form realm and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) within the form realm.

Dying from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to be born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); dying from the formless realm to be born in the formless realm; and dying from the formless realm to be born in the form realm.

Furthermore, whatever fetters (*saṃyojana*) exist in the form and formless realms that, while residing in the form realm, become manifest; and whatever fetters exist in the formless realm that, while residing in the formless realm, become manifest—these are called fetters that do not belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), nor do those fetters reside in the desire realm.
Regarding all those fetters (saṃyojana) that belong to the form realm (rūpadhātu), do those fetters exist within the form realm?
Answer: There may be fetters that belong to the form realm, yet those fetters do not exist within the form realm.
What are the fetters that belong to the form realm, yet those fetters do not exist within the form realm?
The answer is:
one who is bound by fetters passes away from the desire realm and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm.

Furthermore, there are fetters belonging to the form realm that, while residing in the desire realm, manifest in the present; these are called fetters of the form realm whose corresponding fetters do not reside in the form realm.
Question: How can it be that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) exist in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), yet those fetters do not belong to the form realm? Answer:

Māra Pāpīyān, though entangled by various fetters, dwells in the Brahma Heaven; likewise, the Tathāgata’s speech is also entangled by fetters, as he passes away from the form realm and manifests the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, there are fetters belonging to the formless realm that, while residing in the form realm, manifest in the present; these are called fetters residing in the form realm, yet those fetters do not belong to the form realm.
What are the fetters and proclivities of the form realm, and how do those fetters also exist in the form realm?
The answer is:

one who is entangled by various fetters and proclivities passes away from the form realm and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) within the form realm.

Furthermore, all fetters (saṃyojana) that belong to the form realm, which abide in the form realm and manifest before one—these are called fetters of the form realm, and those fetters also exist within the form realm.
What are the fetters that do not belong to the form realm, yet those fetters also do not exist in the form realm?

Answer: Those who are bound by various fetters, having passed away from the desire realm, bring about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) within the desire realm.

One passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm; one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm; and one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm.
Furthermore, whatever fetters and afflictions exist in the formless realm may manifest while one is dwelling in the desire realm.

Furthermore, all fetters (saṃyojana) that exist in the formless realm, which abide in the formless realm and manifest before one—these are called fetters that do not belong to the form realm, nor do those fetters exist in the form realm.
It is likewise for the non-afflictions (*asamyojana*).
Regarding all those fetters (*saṃyojana*) that belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), do those fetters exist within the formless realm?
Answer: Yes.
Thus, whatever fetters (saṃyojana) exist in the formless realm, those fetters belong to the formless realm.
Is it possible that there are fetters belonging to the formless realm, yet those fetters do not reside in the formless realm?
Answer: Yes, there are.

There are all those fetters (*saṃyojana*) and proclivities (*anuśaya*) that belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which, while residing in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), manifest before one.
Are there any fetters and proclivities that do not belong to the formless realm, yet those fetters and proclivities also do not exist in the formless realm?
The answer is: It is so.
Whatever fetters (saṃyojana) there are that do not belong to the formless realm, those fetters likewise do not exist in the formless realm.
Is it possible that there are fetters which do not exist in the formless realm, yet those fetters are not such that they do not belong to the formless realm?
Answer: Yes.

All fetters (*saṃyojana*) belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), having resided in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), have now been completed through the nine gates.
Is a disciple of the Blessed One who has attained the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), yet whose form [existence] is not yet exhausted, bound by form?
The answer is: It is so.
If one is bound by form, is form not yet exhausted?
He replied: "It is so.
If suffering is not yet exhausted, is one bound by suffering?"
Answer: It is so;
when suffering is not yet exhausted, one is bound by suffering.
Is it possible, however, to be bound by suffering while suffering is not yet exhausted?
Answer: There are.

For a *sakṛdāgāmin* who has attained the stage of "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*), having exhausted the fetters to be abandoned through superior and medium levels of cultivation regarding the bonds of the desire realm, they remain bound by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with those corresponding feelings (*vedanā*) and the lower fetters.
The same applies to perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This concludes the ten gates.
Regarding a disciple of the Blessed One who has accomplished the vision of the truths: if form has already been exhausted, is that person liberated from form?
Answer: Yes.
It is so. If form is not bound, is that form exhausted?
Answer: Yes.
Thus it is.
If feeling has already ceased, is that feeling not bound?
Answer: Yes.
It is so. If a feeling is not bound, is that feeling exhausted?
Is there perhaps a case where a feeling is exhausted, yet that feeling is not unbound?
Answer:

There are those who, as *kulaṃkula* or *sakṛdāgāmin*, have exhausted the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through superior and medium cultivation regarding the bonds of the desire realm; yet they remain bound by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the lower fetters within their corresponding sensations (*vedanā*).
The same applies to perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This concludes the eleven gates.

There are five types of persons: those of steadfast faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those of steadfast Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those liberated through faith (*śraddhāvimukta*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
Regarding these three fetters, how many does a person of firm conviction possess and how many does he not possess?
Answer: As long as the "knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering" (duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna) has not yet arisen, he possesses them all.
When the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāta-jñāna*) arises, two are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
Regarding greed, hatred, delusion, and sensual craving, if these are not yet exhausted, all are accomplished.
When sensual craving has been exhausted, nothing is accomplished.
Among the outflows (*āsrava*), when sensual craving has not been exhausted, everything is accomplished;
when sensual craving has been exhausted, two are accomplished and one is not.
Among the floods (*ogha*), if desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*) is not yet exhausted, all are accomplished;
if desire-attachment is already exhausted, three are accomplished and one is not.
The same applies to the yokes (*yoga*) and the graspings (*upādāna*).
Regarding the fetters (*bandhana*): if sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) has not yet been exhausted, all are accomplished;
if sensual desire has already been exhausted, two are accomplished and two are not.
Regarding the coverings (*nīvaraṇa*): if sensual desire has not yet been exhausted and the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all are accomplished.
If sensual desire is not yet exhausted and the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path has arisen, four are accomplished and one is not accomplished;
if sensual desire is already exhausted, none are accomplished.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), if sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) has not yet been exhausted, all are accomplished;
if sensual desire has already been exhausted, two are accomplished and three are not.

Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), if sensual desire has not yet been exhausted and the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all are accomplished.
If sensual desire is not yet exhausted and the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering has arisen, four are accomplished and one is not accomplished;
if sensual desire is already exhausted but the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering has not yet arisen, three are accomplished and two are not accomplished;
if sensual desire is already exhausted and the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering has arisen, two are accomplished and three are not accomplished.
Regarding the [knowledge] of the middle [truth], when the subsequent knowledge of suffering has not yet arisen, all are accomplished;
when the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen, three are accomplished and two are not accomplished.
Among the attachments to the body (*kāyatanha*), if attachment to sensual desire (*kāmataṇhā*) has not been exhausted, all [factors] are accomplished;
if attachment to sensual desire has been exhausted but attachment to the Brahma-world (*brahmataṇhā*) has not been exhausted, four are accomplished and two are not;
if attachment to the Brahma-world has been exhausted, one is accomplished and five are not.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), if sensual desire is not yet exhausted, all are accomplished;
if sensual desire is already exhausted, five are accomplished and two are not.
Among the knots (*grantha*), if sensual desire is not yet exhausted, all are accomplished.
When sensual craving has already been exhausted, six are accomplished and three are not.
Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), when sensual craving is not yet exhausted and the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all are accomplished.

When the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvayajñāna) has not yet arisen, one does not possess [the abandonment of] that which is to be abandoned through the truth of suffering in the desire realm; all other [abandonments] are possessed.

When the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen but the dharma-knowledge of origin (samudaya-dharmajñāna) has not yet arisen, one does not possess [the abandonment of] that which is to be abandoned through the truth of suffering in the three realms; all other [abandonments] are possessed.

When the knowledge of the dharma regarding the origin (samudaya-dharmajñāna) has arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the origin (samudaya-anvayajñāna) has not yet arisen, one does not possess [the abandonment of] those factors to be abandoned by the truth of suffering in the three realms; however, one still possesses the remainder of those factors to be abandoned by the truth of the origin in the desire realm.

When the knowledge of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*kṣayadharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen, one does not possess the [defilements] to be abandoned through the truths of suffering and origin in the three realms; the remainder is possessed.

When the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the destruction (*kṣayānvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, one does not possess those [defilements] to be abandoned through the truths of suffering and origin in the three realms, as well as the remainder of those to be abandoned through the truth of cessation in the desire realm; the remainder is possessed.

When the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*) has arisen but the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, one does not possess the [defilements] to be abandoned by the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation within the three realms; however, one possesses the remainder.

When the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) arises, one does not possess the [defilements] to be abandoned by the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation within the three realms; furthermore, one possesses the remainder of those to be abandoned by the truth of the path within the desire realm.

When craving for the desire realm has been exhausted but craving for the form realm has not yet been exhausted, and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, one does not possess any [defilements] of the desire realm, while possessing the remainder.

When the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering has arisen, but the knowledge of the unknown regarding origination has not yet arisen, one does not possess any [defilements] of the desire realm; furthermore, one possesses the remaining [defilements] of the truth of suffering to be abandoned that pertain to the form and formless realms.

When the knowledge of the unknown regarding cultivation (*anvaya-anājñāta-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation (*nirodha-anājñāta-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, one does not possess any [defilements] of the desire realm; furthermore, one possesses the remaining [defilements] of the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned by the truths of suffering and its origin.

When the knowledge of the exhaustion of the unknown (*ājñāta-ājñāna*) arises, one no longer possesses any [defilements] of the desire realm; however, one still possesses the remaining [defilements] of the truth of suffering, the truth of origin, and the truth of cessation that are to be abandoned in the form and formless realms.

When craving for the realm of form has been exhausted, but craving for the formless realm is not yet exhausted, and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen, one does not possess any [fetters] belonging to the realms of desire and form; the remainder are possessed.

When the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāta-jñāna*) has arisen, but the knowledge of the unknown regarding origination (*samudaya-ajñāta-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, one does not possess any [defilements] of the desire or form realms; furthermore, one possesses the remaining [defilements] of the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the truth of suffering.

When the knowledge of the unknown regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-ajñāta-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation (*nirodha-ajñāta-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, one does not possess any [defilements] of the desire or form realms; furthermore, one possesses the remaining [defilements] of the formless realm that are to be abandoned through the truths of suffering and origin.

When the knowledge of the exhaustion of the unknown (kṣayajñāna) arises, one no longer possesses anything pertaining to the desire realm or the form realm; however, one still possesses the remaining [defilements] of the formless realm that are to be abandoned through the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation.
The same applies to those established in the Dharma (*dharmasthita*).
For a person liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), how many of these three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are accomplished and how many are not accomplished? Answer:
Nothing is accomplished.
When greed, hatred, delusion, and sensual craving have not been exhausted, everything is accomplished;
when sensual craving has been exhausted, nothing is accomplished.
Among the outflows with taints (*sāsrava*), if desire-love (*kāmarāga*) is not yet exhausted, all are accomplished;
if desire-love is already exhausted, two are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
Among the floods (*ogha*), if desire-love is not yet exhausted, three are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
When sensual craving has been exhausted, two are accomplished and two are not accomplished.
It is the same for the yokes (*yoga*).
Among the graspings (*upādāna*), when sensual craving has not yet been exhausted, two are accomplished and two are not accomplished.
When sensual craving has been exhausted, one is accomplished in one [bond] and unaccomplished in three.
Among the fetters (*bandhana*), when sensual craving has not yet been exhausted, one is accomplished in two and unaccomplished in two;
when sensual craving has been exhausted, one is unaccomplished in all.
Regarding the "coverings" (*nīvaraṇa*): if desire and lust have not been exhausted, four are accomplished and one is not;
if desire and lust have been exhausted, none are accomplished.
Regarding the "fetters" (*saṃyojana*): if desire and lust have not been exhausted, all are accomplished.
When sensual desire is already exhausted, two are accomplished and three are not.
Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), when sensual desire is not yet exhausted, two are accomplished and three are not;
when sensual desire is already exhausted, none are accomplished at all.
Regarding the view of non-attainment (*avidyā-dṛṣṭi*):
among the attachments to the body (*kāya-tṛṣṇā*), if desire-attachment (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*) is not yet exhausted, all are attained;
if desire-attachment is already exhausted but attachment to the Brahma-heaven (*brahmā-loka-tṛṣṇā*) is not yet exhausted, four are attained and two are not.
In the case of Brahmā, when craving has been exhausted, one is accomplished and five are not accomplished.
Among the proclivities (*anuśaya*), if craving for the desire realm has not yet been exhausted, five are accomplished and two are not accomplished;
if craving for the desire realm has already been exhausted, three are accomplished and four are not accomplished.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), if desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*) is not yet exhausted, six are accomplished and three are not;
if desire-attachment is already exhausted, three are accomplished and six are not.
Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*): when desire-love (*kāmarāga*) is not yet exhausted, ten are accomplished and eighty-eight are not accomplished;
when desire-love is already exhausted but form-love (*rūparāga*) is not yet exhausted, six are accomplished and ninety-two are not accomplished;
when form-love is already exhausted but formless-love (*ārūpyarāga*) is not yet exhausted, three are accomplished and ninety-five are not accomplished.
The same applies to one who has attained vision.
Regarding a person who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*), how many of these three fetters do they possess and how many do they not possess? Answer:
Nothing is accomplished.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are not accomplished.
Among the outflows (āsrava), two are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
Among the floods (*ogha*), two are accomplished and two are not accomplished.
It is the same for the yokes (*yoga*).
Among the clingings (*upādāna*), one is accomplished and three are not accomplished.
The bonds (*bandhana*) are not accomplished;
the hindrances (*nivaraṇa*) are not accomplished.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), two are accomplished and three are not accomplished.
The lower fetters are not accomplished.
Views are not accomplished.
Among the attachments to the body, one is accomplished and five are not accomplished.
Among the *anuśayas*, three are established and four are not established.
Among the *saṃyojanas*, three are established and six are not established.
Among the ninety-eight *anuśayas*, three are established and ninety-five are not established. The twelve gates are concluded.
Regarding the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), by how many conditions is that view of a self conditioned?
Answer: It may be by four, three, two, or one.
What are the four?
The answer is:

when a view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises in succession to another view of self, and one contemplates that very [view] as preceding and succeeding, it constitutes the cause, the immediate condition, the object condition, and the predominant condition; these are called the four.
Who are the three?
The answer is:

when a view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises immediately after another view of self, that [subsequent one] does not reflect upon the preceding or succeeding [moments]; it is thus a cause, a sequence-condition (anantara-pratyaya), and a dominant-condition (adhipati-pratyaya), but lacks an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).

Just as the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises in succession from various states of mind, and that very view, when contemplating its own prior and subsequent births, has no sequence in terms of cause, condition, or predominance—this is called the third [type].
What are the two?
The answer is:

when, following the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), several moments of mind arise and then the view of a self arises again, one does not reflect upon their prior and subsequent arising; they are related as cause and predominant condition—these are called the two.
Who is the one?
The answer is:
for that which arises later, the preceding [moment] is its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
If it does not provide conditions, there is one predominance condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
For those in the future, past, and present, if they provide conditions, there are both object and predominance conditions;
if they do not provide conditions, there is one predominance condition.
Regarding the future, present, and past: if they provide conditions, they serve as object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
if they do not provide conditions, they serve as one [predominant condition].
For those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), there is one [predominant condition].

Regarding those bound to the form realm and those bound to the desire realm: if they follow in immediate succession, there is both the condition of succession (*anantara-pratyaya*) and the condition of predominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
if they do not follow in immediate succession, there is only the single condition of predominance.
Regarding those bound to the desire realm and those bound to the formless realm, there is only the single condition of predominance.

Regarding those bound to the formless realm and those bound to the desire realm: if they follow in immediate succession, there is both the condition of succession (*anantara-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
if they do not follow in immediate succession, there is only the predominant condition.
Regarding those bound to the form realm and those bound to the formless realm, there is only the predominant condition.
Regarding those bound to the formless realm and those bound to the form realm: if they follow in immediate succession, they are both the conditions of succession and dominance;
if they do not follow in immediate succession, there is only the condition of dominance.

As it is with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), so it is for all such views—whether they are not universal (*asarvatraga*) or universal (*sarvatraga*). They are either not universal or universal.
How many objects (ālambana) do the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the clinging to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa) have? Answer:
They may have four, three, two, or one.
What are the four?
The answer is:

when, following the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the grasping of precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) arises, and one contemplates that very [view] as preceding and succeeding, it is the cause, the immediate condition, the object-condition, and the predominant condition; these are called the four.
Who are the three?
The answer is:

when, for example, the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises immediately after [another state], and one does not reflect upon that which arose before or that which arises after, there is the condition of cause (*hetu*), the condition of immediate succession (*anantara*), and the condition of predominance (*adhipati*), but no object-condition (*ālambana*).

Just as the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises in succession and gives rise to various thoughts of the grasping of precepts and vows (śīlavrataparāmarśa), when one contemplates those very [thoughts] in terms of their prior and subsequent arising, their causes, conditions, and predominant influences, there is no fixed succession; this is called the third [category].
What are the two?
The answer is:

For example, when a certain number of moments of consciousness arise in succession to the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and a grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) arises immediately thereafter, one does not reflect upon the preceding and succeeding moments as being cause and dominant condition; these are called the two.
Who is the one?
The answer is:
that which arises later with respect to that which arose earlier acts as a condition, specifically as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If it does not provide an object-condition, it is one [condition], namely the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
For those in the future, past, and present, if they provide an object-condition, they are both object-conditions and predominant conditions;
if they do not provide an object-condition, they are one [condition], namely the predominant condition.
Regarding the future, present, and past: if they provide conditions, they are both object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
if they do not provide conditions, they are solely dominant conditions.
For those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), there is only one [type of] dominant condition.
Regarding those bound to the realm of form and those bound to the desire realm: if they are in sequence but lack an object-condition, they function as sequence-condition and predominance-condition;
if they have an object-condition but are not in sequence, they function as object-condition and predominance-condition;
if they are both in sequence and have an object-condition, they function as sequence-condition, object-condition, and predominance-condition.
If they do not constitute sequential or objective conditions, there is one predominance condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Those bound to the desire realm and those bound to the formless realm [condition each other] through one predominance condition.
Those bound to the formless realm and those bound to the desire realm, if they do not constitute sequential or objective conditions, [function as] sequential and predominance conditions.
If it provides an object-condition but not a sequential condition, it is an object-condition and a predominance-condition;
if it provides both a sequential condition and an object-condition, it is a sequential-condition, an object-condition, and a predominance-condition;
if it provides neither a sequential condition nor an object-condition, it is a single predominance-condition.
Those bound to the form realm and those bound to the formless realm [act as] one [type of] predominance (*adhipati*).
Those bound to the formless realm and those bound to the form realm: if there is sequence (*anupūrvi*) but no object-condition (*ālambana*), there is sequence and predominance;
if there is an object-condition but no sequence, there is object-condition and predominance.
If it provides the condition of sequence (*anantara*) and the condition of object (*ālambana*), it is [a condition] by way of sequence, object, and predominance (*adhipati*);
if it does not provide the condition of sequence and the condition of object, it is one [condition], namely predominance.
As with the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), so it is with the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
"Not all-pervasive" and "all-pervasive," "all-pervasive" and "not all-pervasive.

This concludes the ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Unwholesome, of the Abhidharma; it consists of six hundred and two ślokas in the Sanskrit original, which corresponds to fourteen characters in the Qin translation.
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle Four;
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra and Zhu Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty.

Chapter Two: The Section on the Single Path (Ekāyana-varga). Part One of the Second Sub-section of the Section on the Single Path. The single path traverses the six [realms]; there are the seven small and the seven great; inclusion; the chain; existence; by what concentration are the fetters (saṃyojana) extinguished? The various paths, the knowledges of abandonment, and the eight persons.
The nine fetters (*saṃyojana*):

the fetter of craving (*anunaya*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha*), the fetter of pride (*māna*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi*), the fetter of dogmatic adherence (*parāmarśa*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*), the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya*), and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*).
If one is bound by the fetter of craving within the body, does one also have the fetter of ill-will?
If one is bound by the fetter of ill-will, does one also have the fetter of craving?
If one is bound by the fetter of craving within the body, are there also the fetters of conceit, ignorance, views, wrong resolve, doubt, avarice, and envy?
If one is bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), is one also bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*)?
Within the body, up to being bound by the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), is one also bound by the fetter of envy?
If there is the fetter of envy, is there also the fetter of stinginess? [End of the first section.]
If there is a bond of past craving within the body, is there also one in the future?
If there is one in the future, is there also one in the past?
If there is one in the past, is there also one in the present?
1. If there is the present, is there also the past? 2.
If there is the future, is there also the present?
3. If there is the present, is there also the future?
If there is the past, is there also the future and the present?
If there is the future and the present, is there also the past?
If there is the future, are there also the past and the present?
1. If there is the past and the present, is there also the future? 2. If there is the present, are there also the past and the future?
3. If there is the past and the future, is there also the present? 4. If there is the past and the present, is there also the future?
5. If there is the present, are there also the past and the future? 6. If there is the past and the future, is there also the present?
The same applies even to stinginess and envy.
If there is a bond of past attachment within the body, is there also a bond of past ill-will?
If there is a bond of past ill-will, is there also a bond of past attachment?
If there is a bond of past craving within the body, is there also a bond of future ill-will?
And if there is a bond of future ill-will, is there also a bond of past craving? II.
If within this body there is the bond of past craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), is there also the bond of present ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
And if there is the bond of present ill-will, is there also the bond of past craving? III.
If within one's continuum there is the bond of past craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), is there also the bond of past and present ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
If there are bonds of past and present ill-will, is there also the bond of past craving? (4)
If within one's continuum there is the bond of past craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*), is there also the bond of future and present aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
And if there is the bond of future and present aversion, is there also the bond of past craving? (5)
If within a person there is the bond of past craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*), is there also the bond of past and future aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
And if there are bonds of past and future aversion, is there also the bond of past craving? (6)
If within a person there is the bond of past craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), is there also the bond of past, future, and present ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
And if there are bonds of past, future, and present ill-will, is there also the bond of past craving? [End of the seven items.]

Past attachment, past ill-will, and past pride constitute one; future [attachment, ill-will, and pride] constitute two; present [attachment, ill-will, and pride] constitute three; past and present [attachment, ill-will, and pride] constitute four; future and present [attachment, ill-will, and pride] constitute five; past and future [attachment, ill-will, and pride] constitute six; and past, future, and present pride constitutes seven. This same pattern applies up to stinginess and envy, thus completing the great set of seven.
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are included within the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?

How many underlying tendencies are included within the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and so on, up to the ignorance (*avidyā*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm? [End of the section on the doors.]

Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*): do the three fetters encompass the three unwholesome roots, or do the three unwholesome roots encompass the three fetters?

Regarding the three fetters up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*): do the three fetters encompass the ninety-eight proclivities, or do the ninety-eight proclivities encompass the three fetters?

Up to the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) and ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*): do the nine fetters encompass the ninety-eight proclivities, and do the ninety-eight proclivities encompass the nine fetters? This concludes the section on the fetters (*saṃyojana-dvāra*).

Of these three fetters, how many lead to rebirth in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), how many lead to rebirth in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and how many lead to rebirth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?

This continues up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*); how many lead to rebirth in the realm of desire, and how many lead to rebirth in the realms of form and the formless? [End of the Section on the Doors.]
By which samādhi is the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) exhausted?

By which samādhi are the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), and even the latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyānuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm exhausted? [Thus ends the section on the gates of samādhi.]
If a fetter is past, has that fetter already bound?
If that fetter has already bound, is it a past fetter?
If a fetter is future, will that fetter bind?
If those fetters are to be bound, are they future fetters?
If those fetters are currently binding now, are they present fetters?
If they are binding now, are those fetters present? [End of the section on the three periods of time regarding fetters.]
If one uses a path to extinguish the fetters of the desire realm, and subsequently falls away from that path, does one become bound by those fetters or not?

If one uses a path to extinguish the fetters of the form and formless realms, and subsequently falls away from that path, does one become bound by those fetters or not? [End of the section on falling away from the path.]
There are nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*):
the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the truths of suffering and origin within the desire realm constitutes one knowledge of abandonment;
