when the previously arisen bond of craving has not yet been exhausted, and furthermore, the bond of views within that body has not yet been exhausted but does not manifest in the present—this is called having the bond of past craving and the bonds of past and future views within the body, without the present [bond].
What is meant by the presence within a person of the past fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) as well as the past, future, and present fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
The answer is:

when the fetter of craving within that person has previously arisen and not yet been exhausted, and furthermore, the fetter of views within that same person manifests in the present—this is called the presence within a person of the past fetter of craving as well as the past, future, and present fetter of views.
If there is bondage by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) pertaining to the past, future, and present, is there also bondage by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) pertaining to the past?
Answer: If it has previously arisen and not yet been exhausted, then there is bondage.
If that which has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen has ceased, then one is no longer bound by views regarding these seven matters.
The same applies to the loss of aspiration and doubt.

Regarding past attachment, past aversion, and past pride: there is one [type] for the past; two for the future; three for the present; four for the past and present; five for the future and present; six for the past and future; and seven for the past, future, and present pride. This applies likewise up to stinginess and envy.

The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) includes three underlying tendencies (anuśaya); the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) includes six; doubt (vicikitsā) includes twelve; greed (rāga) includes five; hatred (pratigha) includes five; and ignorance (avidyā) includes four—one underlying tendency enters into it only slightly.

Among the five outflows (*āsrava*), there are thirty-one of the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), fifty-two of the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and fifteen of the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

Among the floods (*ogha*), there are nineteen of the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), twenty-eight of the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), fifteen of the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*), and thirty-six of the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*).
The yokes (*yoga*) are also like this.

Among the clingings (*upādāna*), there are twenty-four of sensual clinging (*kāmopādāna*), six of precept-and-vow clinging (*śīlavratopādāna*), thirty of view-clinging (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*), and thirty-eight of self-clinging (*ātmavādopādāna*).

Among the fetters (*bandhana*), there are five of the bodily fetter of sensual craving (*kāmacchanda-bandhana*), five of the bodily fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda-bandhana*), six of the bodily fetter of the misapprehension of precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-bandhana*), and twelve of the bodily fetter of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi-bandhana*).

Regarding the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*): within the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), there are five; within the hindrance of ill will (*vyāpāda*), there are five; lethargy (*styāna*), torpor (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and remorse (*kaukṛtya*) do not mutually include one another among the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*); and within the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā*), there are four.

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), there are five of the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*); the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) each have fifteen; the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) are not mutually included within the other fetters.

Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), there are five for sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), five for ill-will (*vyāpāda*), three for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), six for the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and twelve for doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Among the views (*dṛṣṭi*), there are three each for the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), twelve each for false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and six for the clinging to precepts and rituals.

Among the cravings of the body (*kāyatanhā*), the craving for nose-contact (*ghānasamphassatanhā*) and the craving for tongue-contact (*jivhāsamphassatanhā*) are included within one latent tendency (*anusaya*) by way of a minor portion.

The cravings for eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact (*kāyasamphassatanhā*) are included within two latent tendencies by way of a minor portion. The craving for mind-contact (*manosamphassatanhā*) is included within thirteen latent tendencies, and it is also included within two latent tendencies by way of a minor portion.

Regarding the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): the underlying tendency of sensual desire consists of five; the underlying tendency of aversion consists of five; the underlying tendency of craving for existence consists of ten; the underlying tendencies of pride and ignorance each consist of fifteen; the underlying tendency of views consists of thirty-six; and the underlying tendency of doubt consists of twelve.

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), there are five for the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*); fifteen each for the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*); eighteen each for the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of dogmatic adherence (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*); twelve for the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*); and the fetters of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) and envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) are not included among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of the desire realm is mutually included within the view of a self-identity of the desire realm; likewise, the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) [of the desire realm] are [included], up to the proclivity of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm being mutually included within the proclivity of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm. This concludes the section on the gate of mutual inclusion and subsumption.
Regarding the three fetters and the three unwholesome roots: do the three fetters include the three unwholesome roots, or do the three unwholesome roots include the three fetters?
Answer: Each does not include the other.

Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the three outflows (*āsrava*): the three fetters are included within a portion of two outflows, and a portion of those two outflows is included within the three fetters; as for the remaining factors, they are each mutually non-inclusive.

Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the four floods (*ogha*): the three fetters are included within a portion of the three floods, and a portion of the three floods is included within the three fetters; as for the remaining factors, they are each mutually non-inclusive.
The same applies to the yokes (*yoga*).

Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the four graspings (*upādāna*): one fetter and one grasping are mutually inclusive; two fetters and [one] grasping are partially included in three graspings; three graspings are partially included in two fetters; and the remaining factors are each not mutually inclusive.
Regarding the three fetters (saṃyojana) and the four bonds (bandhana): are the three fetters included within the four bonds?
Answer: Some are fetters but not bonds.
What are fetters that are not bonds?
The answer is:
two fetters are called fetters that are not bonds.
What are those that are bonds but not fetters?
The answer is:
the three bonds are what are called bonds but not fetters.
What is bondage?
The answer is:
a single fetter is called bondage.
What is neither a fetter nor a bond?
Answer: It is all things except those mentioned above.

Among the three fetters and the five hindrances, a portion of one fetter is included within one hindrance, and a small portion of one hindrance is included within a portion of one fetter; the remaining factors are each mutually exclusive and do not include one another.
Regarding the three fetters and the five fetters: do the three fetters include the five fetters, or do the five fetters include the three fetters?
Answer: Each does not include the other.

Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*): are the three fetters included within the five lower fetters, or are the five lower fetters included within the three fetters?
Answer: The five include the three, but the three do not include the five.
What is not included in feeling?
The answer is:
sensual desire and ill will.
Regarding the three fetters and the five views: are the three fetters subsumed within the five views?
The answer is:
some fetters are not views.
What is a fetter that is not a view?
The answer is:
one fetter is called a fetter that is not a view.
What are views that are not fetters?
The answer is:
the three views are what are called views that are not fetters.
What is the fetter of views?
The answer is:
two fetters are called the fetter of views.
What is neither a fetter nor a view?
The answer is:
excluding the aforementioned instances.

Regarding the three fetters and the sixfold attachment to the body: do the three fetters include the sixfold attachment to the body, or does the sixfold attachment to the body include the three fetters?
The answer is:
each is not included within the other.

Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): one fetter is included within one underlying tendency; two fetters are included within a portion of one underlying tendency; a portion of one underlying tendency is included within two fetters; and the remaining factors are each mutually non-inclusive.

Of the three fetters and the nine fetters, one fetter is included within one fetter; two fetters are partially included within two fetters; two fetters are partially included within two fetters; and the remaining ones are each mutually non-inclusive.

Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*): the three fetters encompass twenty-one proclivities, and those twenty-one proclivities encompass the three fetters; as for the remaining [proclivities], they do not mutually encompass one another.

Regarding the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*): do the nine fetters include the ninety-eight proclivities, or do the ninety-eight proclivities include the nine fetters?
Answer: Nine times nine is eighty-one; it is not ninety-eight times nine.
What is it that is not received or entered?
The answer is:
stinginess and envy. This concludes the section on the "Gate of the Chain."

Regarding these three fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many pertain to existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and how many to existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Answer: All of them pertain to at least some portion [of these existences].
There is that which enters into the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), that which enters into the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and that which enters into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*), as well as the outflows of existence in the realm of desire (*kāmabhava*) and the realms of form and formlessness—these enter into the remaining spheres of entry: those entering into the realm of desire, those entering into the realm of form, and those entering into the formless realm.

Among the floods (*ogha*), the flood of desire (*kāmāsrava*) leads to existence in the realm of desire; the flood of existence (*bhavāsrava*) leads to entry into the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); and the remaining [floods] lead to entry into the realm of desire, as well as entry into the realms of form and the formless.
The yokes (*yoga*) are also like this.

Among the clingings (*upādāna*), the clinging to sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*) leads to rebirth in the realm of sensual desire; the clinging to self-theories (*ātmavādopādāna*) leads to rebirth in the realms of form and formlessness; and the remaining clingings lead to rebirth in the realms of sensual desire, form, and formlessness.

Among the bonds (*bandhana*), the bond of attachment to sensual desire (*kāmarāga-kāyabandhana*) and the bond of ill-will (*vyāpāda-kāyabandhana*) lead to rebirth in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); as for the remaining [bonds], they lead to entry into the realms of desire, form, and the formless (*rūpa-arūpyadhātu*).

The coverings (*nīvaraṇa*), along with ill-will (*vyāpāda*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), and envy (*īrṣyā*), lead to existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhava*); the remaining factors lead to what enters [the desire realm], as well as to what enters the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will lead to existence in the desire realm; the remaining factors and views (*dṛṣṭi*) lead to what enters [the desire realm], as well as to what enters the realms of form and formlessness.

Within the craving for the body, the craving for nose-contact and tongue-contact experiences the sphere of sensual existence; the craving for eye-, ear-, and body-contact enters into the sphere of sensual existence and enters into the sphere of form.
The objects of entry for the craving for mental existence (*manosaṃyojana-taṇhā*) are the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) and the underlying tendency of ill will (*pratighānuśaya*) pertain to the existence of desire (*kāma-bhava*); the underlying tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*) pertains to the existence of form (*rūpa-bhava*) and the existence of the formless (*ārūpya-bhava*). As for the remaining [underlying tendencies], their objects of entry are the existence of desire, the existence of form, and the existence of the formless.

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*), the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) lead to rebirth in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); the remaining ones lead to rebirth in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).

Of the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), thirty-six proclivities pertain to the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu*), thirty-one pertain to the existence of form (*rūpadhātu*), and thirty-one pertain to the existence of the formless (*ārūpyadhātu*). This concludes the third section on the gates of existence.
By which samādhi is the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) extinguished?
The answer is:
either by relying on the four [dhyānas] or by relying on the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) depend either on the four [dhyānas] or on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), delusion (*moha*), and the outflow of sensuality (*kāma-āsrava*) depend on the threshold concentration.
The outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) depend either on the seven [stages] or on the threshold concentration.
Among the floods (*ogha*), the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) relies on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*) rely either on seven [stages] or on the threshold concentration.
The flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*) relies either on four [stages] or on the threshold concentration.
The yokes (*yoga*) are also like this.
Among the clingings (*upādāna*), the clinging to sensual pleasure (*kāmopādāna*) relies on the *anāgamya* stage.
The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*) and the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*) rely either on the four dhyānas or on the *anāgamya*.
Regarding my reception [of these fetters], they may depend on either the seven [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage.
Among the fetters (*bandhana*), the fetter of sensual desire for the body (*kāmarāga-bandhana*) and the fetter of ill will (*pratigha-bandhana*) depend on the *anāgamya*.
The fetter of attachment to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-bandhana*) and the fetter of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-bandhana*) depend on either the four [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya*.

The fetters of covetousness (*abhidhyā*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), avarice (*mātsarya*), and envy (*īrṣyā*) depend on one of the six factors of the *anāgamya* (preliminary) dhyāna; the remaining [fetters] depend either on the seven stages—the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments—or on the *anāgamya*.
Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), sensual desire and ill-will depend on the *anāgamya* stage.
The remaining [fetters] and the views depend either on the four dhyānas or on the *anāgamya*.
Among the attachments to the body (*kāmarāga*), the attachment to the sense-faculties of nose and tongue depends on the *anāgamya*.
The craving associated with eye, ear, and body contact relies either on the first dhyāna or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The craving associated with mental contact relies either on the seven [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration.
Among the underlying tendencies (anuśaya), the tendency of sensual desire and the tendency of ill-will rely on the threshold concentration.
The latent tendency of craving, the latent tendency of pride, and the latent tendency of ignorance either depend on the seven [stages] or on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The latent tendency of views and the latent tendency of doubt either depend on the four [dhyānas] or on the threshold concentration.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha*), the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya*), and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*) depend on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the fetter of pride (*māna*), and the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā*) either depend on seven [stages] or depend on the threshold concentration.

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), the fetter of envy (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) are based either on the four dhyānas or on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage.
Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), those of the desire realm are based on the *anāgamya*.

The [defilements] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are abandoned through the vision of the Four Truths (*catur-āryasatya*) are based either on the four dhyānas or on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).

Those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm are based either on the seven [stages] or on the threshold concentration; these are the three-gate meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
Are all past fetters already bound by those fetters?
Answer: It is so;
all past fetters are already bound by those fetters.
Is it possible that one is already bound by fetters, yet these fetters are not past?
Answer: Yes;
there are those who are bound by future and present fetters.
Are all future fetters destined to be bound by those fetters?
Answer: There are some future fetters that are not destined to be bound by those fetters.
What is meant by "future fetters that do not constitute being bound by fetters"?
The answer is:

those future fetters that are forever exhausted without remainder, already ceased and already vomited out, and from which one is certain never to fall back—this is called future fetters that do not constitute being bound by fetters.
How can one be bound by fetters that are not future?
The answer is:

when all past fetters have been exhausted without remainder, having been eliminated and vomited out, yet one definitely falls away from that state of the exhaustion of those fetters—this is called being bound by fetters that are not future.
What is meant by "future fetters that will become bound by fetters"?
The answer is:

when all future fetters have been forever exhausted without remainder, already ceased and already vomited out, yet one definitively falls away from that state of the exhaustion of those fetters; this is called future fetters that will become bound by fetters.
What is it that is neither a future fetter nor subject to being bound by a fetter?
The answer is:

those fetters of the past that have been forever exhausted without remainder, already ceased, and already vomited out; as well as the certainty of non-retrogression regarding the exhaustion of those fetters and the fetters of the present—this is called that which is neither a future fetter nor subject to being bound by a fetter.
Are all fetters that are present currently bound by those fetters?
Answer: It is so;
all fetters that are present are currently bound by those fetters.
Is there a case where one is currently bound by fetters, yet those fetters are not present?
Answer: There is;
this concludes the section on being bound by past and future fetters.
Regarding the path by which one severs the fetters of the desire realm: if one falls away from that path, will one again be bound by those fetters or not?
The answer is:
one will again be bound by those fetters.
Regarding the path by which one severs the fetters of the form and formless realms: if one falls away from that path, does one again become bound by those fetters or not?
Answer: One again becomes bound by the fetters; this concludes the section on the point of falling away from the path.
The nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*):
the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the truths of suffering and origin within the desire realm is the first knowledge of abandonment;
the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the truths of suffering and origin within the form and formless realms is the second knowledge of abandonment.
The exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the truth of cessation in the desire realm is the third knowledge of abandonment;
the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the truth of cessation in the form and formless realms is the fourth knowledge of abandonment;
the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the truth of the path in the desire realm is the fifth knowledge of abandonment.
The exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned by the Path Truth in the realms of form and formlessness constitutes six knowledges of abandonment;
the exhaustion of the five lower fetters constitutes seven knowledges of abandonment;
and the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form constitutes eight knowledges of abandonment.
When all fetters are exhausted, there are nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
Are the nine knowledges of abandonment included within all knowledges of abandonment, or are all knowledges of abandonment included within the nine knowledges of abandonment?
Answer: All nine are not all nine.
What is it that is not included?
Answer:

A disciple of the Blessed One who has realized the truths (dṛṣṭiprāpta), though not yet having exhausted craving for the desire realm, has exhausted the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanāheya) in the desire realm; such a person does not undergo rebirth, and while traversing the two paths, they do not receive the designation of "one who possesses seven knowledges of abandonment" (saptajñānaprahāṇa).

When sensual desire has been exhausted but desire for the form realm has not yet been exhausted, the fetters of the form realm to be abandoned through cultivation are exhausted; however, one does not enter into the nine knowledges of abandonment (*navabijñāna-parijñā*).

When desire for the form realm has been exhausted but desire for the formless realm has not yet been exhausted, the fetters of the formless realm to be abandoned through cultivation are exhausted; however, one does not enter into the nine knowledges of abandonment. This concludes the nine knowledges of abandonment.
There are eight persons:

those entering the stream (srotāpanna-pratipannaka), those who have realized the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phalastha); those entering the stage of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka), those who have realized the fruit of once-returning; those entering the stage of non-returning (anāgāmi-pratipannaka), those who have realized the fruit of non-returning; those entering the stage of arhatship (arhat-pratipannaka), and those who have realized the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phalastha).
Regarding one who is proceeding toward the realization of *srotāpanna*, how many of these nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) do they possess, and how many do they not possess?
Answer: They may not possess any, or they may possess one, two, three, four, or five.

What is it that is not accomplished? The answer is: the non-accomplishment of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*); the non-accomplishment of the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*); the non-accomplishment of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*); and the non-accomplishment of the knowledge regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*). The non-accomplishment of the patience regarding the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) constitutes one [category]. The patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) constitute two. The patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) constitute three. The patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) constitute four. The patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) constitute five. Upon attaining the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*), one becomes a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and accomplishes the sixth stage of the realization of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
Regarding the realization of the Sakṛdāgāmin: how many of these nine knowledges of abandonment (prahāṇajñāna) does he accomplish, and how many does he not accomplish?
The answer is:

if one who has exhausted double the [remaining] desires attains realization by skipping stages (vyutkrāntaka), obtaining the fruit of the Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) all at once—hence the term "double"—then he may either not accomplish any of them, or he may accomplish one, two, three, four, five, or six.

What is it that is not accomplished? The answer is: the receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is not accomplished; the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is not accomplished; the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) is not accomplished; the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is not accomplished. The receptivity to the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) constitute one [instance]. The receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) constitute two. The receptivity to the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) constitute three. The receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) constitute four. The receptivity to the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) constitute five. If, through the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*), one attains the realization of a stream-winner (*srotāpanna*) and proceeds toward the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), these constitute six. Upon attaining the fruit of a once-returner, one accomplishes the six knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
Regarding one who attains the realization of an Anāgāmin: how many of these nine knowledges of abandonment (prahāṇajñāna) does he accomplish, and how many does he not accomplish? Answer:
If he attains realization by transcending the stages through the exhaustion of sensual desire, he may accomplish none, or one, two, three, four, five, or six.

What is it that is not accomplished? The answer is: the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* is not accomplished; the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* is not accomplished; the *duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti* is not accomplished; the *duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna* is not accomplished. (1) The *samudaya-dharma-kṣānti* is not accomplished; the *samudaya-dharma-jñāna* is not accomplished. (2) The *samudaya-anvaya-kṣānti* and the *samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*. (3) The *nirodha-dharma-kṣānti* and the *nirodha-dharma-jñāna*. (4) The *nirodha-anvaya-kṣānti* and the *nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*. (5) The *mārga-dharma-kṣānti* and the *mārga-dharma-jñāna*. (6) The *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*; if one has attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* and is progressing toward the fruit of *anāgāmin*, these two paths are counted as such.
An Anāgāmin achieves one knowledge of abandonment—the knowledge of the abandonment of the five lower fetters.
For one who is proceeding toward the realization of Arhatship, how many of these nine knowledges of abandonment are achieved and how many are not achieved?
Answer: Either one or two.

If craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) is not yet exhausted, one accomplishes one knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), namely the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīyasaṃyojana*).
When craving for form (*rūparāga*) has been exhausted, one accomplishes two knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*):
the knowledge of the abandonment of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīyasaṃyojana*), and the knowledge of the abandonment of the exhaustion of craving for form.
Upon attaining arhatship, one accomplishes one knowledge of abandonment: the knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanaparyādāna*).

The Second Chapter on the Single Path in the Section on Fetters (*Saṃyojana-varga*) is completed. In the Sanskrit original it consists of one thousand and forty *ślokas*; in the Qin [translation] it comprises eleven thousand nine hundred and twenty-two words.
Abhidharma Ekottarika-varga.
Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra, Volume Six.
Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra, Volume Seven.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīr during the Fu Qin dynasty.
There are five [categories] regarding the two types of elements (*dhātu*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and the fruits (*phala*); there are ninety-five fetters together with the three types of fetters.
This gateway extensively explains the fruits; within this gateway, there are those with desire and the eight persons who should train.
Through the threefold restraint of the body, one undergoes birth and death and receives existence; having died, one does not [immediately] take birth, while those with desire remain behind.
There are two kinds of bases for the body:
two in the desire realm, two in the form realm, and two in the formless realm.
Is it possible for the fetters of the desire realm to be bound all at once, and to be unbound all at once?
Is there gradual attainment of bondage and gradual non-attainment of bondage?
Is it possible for the fetters of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to be attained simultaneously and simultaneously not attained?
Is there gradual attainment of bondage and gradual non-attainment of bondage?
Is it possible for the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) to be bound all at once and not bound all at once?
Or are they bound gradually and not bound gradually?
When the fetters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned by the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*) are exhausted, by which fruit (*phala*) are they subsumed?

The exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, abandoned through seeing the truths in the form realm, abandoned through cultivation in the form realm, abandoned through seeing the truths in the formless realm, and abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—by which fruit (phala) are these subsumed?
There are five categories of fetters (*saṃyojana-varga*):

the category of fetters to be abandoned by the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and the categories of fetters to be abandoned by the vision of the truths of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*), as well as by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
When the category of fetters to be abandoned by the vision of the truth of suffering is abandoned, to which fruit does it belong?

The abandonment of the seeds of fetters (*saṃyojana-bīja*) abandoned through the contemplation of the Truth of Origination, the Truth of Cessation, and the Truth of the Path—by what fruit is this subsumed?
There are nine types of seeds of fetters:

those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*), those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), and the seeds of fetters abandoned through contemplation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The exhaustion of the seeds of fetters abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna)—in what fruit is this comprised?

The exhaustion of the seeds of fetters abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvayajñāna), abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of origin (samudaya-dharmajñāna), abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvayajñāna), abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (nirodha-dharmajñāna), abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvayajñāna), abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of the path (mārga-dharmajñāna), abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvayajñāna), and abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā)—in what fruit is this comprised?

The fifteen types of fetters (*saṃyojana-bīja*): the types of fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering in the desire realm; the types of fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, and through cultivation, in the desire realm; the types of fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering in the form realm; the types of fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, and through cultivation, in the form realm; and the types of fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering in the formless realm; the types of fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, and through cultivation, in the formless realm.
The exhaustion of the seeds of fetters (saṃyojana-bīja) to be abandoned through the vision of the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) in the desire realm—by which fruit is this comprised?

The exhaustion of the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the Truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm—by which fruit are these comprised?

To which fruit does the exhaustion of the seeds of fetters abandoned through the truth of suffering in the form realm belong? To which fruit does the exhaustion of the seeds of fetters abandoned through the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation, in the form realm belong?
The exhaustion of the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): by which fruit is this subsumed?

The exhaustion of the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the truths of origin (*samudayasatya*), cessation (*nirodhasatya*), the path (*mārgasatya*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the formless realm: by which fruit is this subsumed?
The exhaustion of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi)—of what fruit is it comprised?

The exhaustion of the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), and even up to the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—of what fruit is it comprised?

When a disciple of the Blessed One who has realized the truths has not yet exhausted sensual desire, but has exhausted the fetters of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation—of what fruit is this comprised?

When sensual desire is already exhausted but desire for the form realm is not yet exhausted, and the fetters of the form realm to be abandoned by cultivation are exhausted—of what fruit is this comprised?

When craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) has been exhausted, but craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) has not yet been exhausted, the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm—of what fruit is this comprised?
There are eight persons:

one who is entering the realization of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka*) and one who has attained stream-entry; one who is entering the realization of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala-pratipannaka*) and one who has attained once-returning; one who is entering the realization of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala-pratipannaka*) and one who has attained non-returning; and one who is entering the realization of arhatship (*arhat-phala-pratipannaka*) and one who has attained arhatship.
The exhaustion of the fetters (*āsravakṣaya*) realized by one who is entering the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala-pratipannaka*)—by which fruit is it subsumed?

The exhaustion of the fetters realized by one who has attained stream-entry, up to and including one who is entering the realization of arhatship and attaining the exhaustion of the fetters of an arhat (*arhatphala-pratipannaka*)—by which fruit is each subsumed?
If one who has attained the state of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) is accomplished in the various factors of training (śaikṣadharma), does the stream-enterer encompass those factors?
And if those factors are encompassed by the stream-enterer, are they factors of training?
The same applies to the Sakṛdāgāmin and the Anāgāmin.
Regarding the various dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that constitute an Arhat: does the Arhat encompass those dharmas?
If those factors are subsumed under the category of Arhat, are they the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma)?
Are the untainted dharmas (anāsravadharma) accomplished by a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry?
If those factors are subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), are they untainted (anāsrava) factors?
The same applies to the fruits of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), and arhatship (arhat).
Regarding those dharmas accomplished by a stream-enterer (srotāpanna): are those dharmas subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry?
If those dharmas are subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry, does the stream-enterer accomplish those dharmas?
The same applies to the Sakṛdāgāmin, the Anāgāmin, and the Arhat.
When those who have passed away from the desire realm are reborn again in the desire realm, do they all undergo existence within the desire realm?
If one experiences existence in the desire realm and exhausts that existence there, does one die in the desire realm and return to be born again in the desire realm?
If one dies in the form realm and returns to be born in the form realm, does one exhaust all existence in the form realm?
If one undergoes existence in the form realm and passes away from there, is one reborn back in the form realm?
If one passes away from the formless realm, is one reborn back in the formless realm, having fully undergone existence in the formless realm?
If one receives existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and, having exhausted it, passes away from the formless realm to be reborn again in the formless realm;

or if one passes away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be reborn again in the desire realm—how many types of persons are there in such cases? By how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are they driven? And by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are they bound?

When one dies in the form realm and is reborn again in the form realm, how many [types of] persons are there; by how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are they bound; and by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are they bound?
When one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm, how many [types of] persons are there; by how many latent dispositions are they bound; and by how many fetters are they bound?
If one does not pass away from the desire realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, is it the case that they will never again undergo existence in the desire realm?
If they do not undergo existence in the desire realm, is it the case that they have never passed away from the desire realm nor been reborn in the desire realm?
If one does not pass away from the form realm and is not reborn in the form realm, is it the case that they have entirely ceased to undergo existence in the form realm?
If they have entirely ceased to undergo existence in the form realm, is it the case that they have entirely neither passed away from the form realm nor been reborn in the form realm?
Is it the case that one who does not die in the formless realm and is not reborn in the formless realm has entirely ceased to undergo existence in the formless realm?
And if one has entirely ceased to undergo existence in the formless realm, has one entirely ceased to die in the formless realm and not be reborn in the formless realm?

If one does not die in the desire realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, how many [factors] does this person possess, by how many latent tendencies (anuśaya) is he bound, and by how many fetters (saṃyojana) is he bound?
If one does not die in the form realm and is not reborn in the form realm, how many [factors] does this person possess, by how many latent tendencies is he bound, and by how many fetters is he bound?

One does not die in the formless realm and is not reborn in the formless realm; how many persons are there, by how many latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are they driven, and by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are they bound?
Is it possible for one to die in the desire realm and not be reborn in the desire realm?
Is there anyone who, passing away from the desire realm, is not reborn in the form or formless realms?
Is there anyone who, passing away from the form realm, is not reborn in the form realm?
Is there anyone who, passing away from the form realm, is not reborn in the desire or formless realms?
Is it possible to pass away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and not be reborn in the formless realm?
Is it possible to pass away from the formless realm and not be reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?

If one passes away from the desire realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, how many types of persons are there; by how many latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are they bound; and by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are they bound?

If one dies in the desire realm and is not reborn in the form or formless realms, how many [factors] does this person possess, by how many latent tendencies (anuśaya) is he bound, and by how many fetters (saṃyojana) is he tied?
If one dies in the form realm and is not reborn in the form realm, how many [factors] does this person possess, by how many latent tendencies is he bound, and by how many fetters is he tied?

If one passes away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is not reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how many [factors] does this person possess, by how many latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is he driven, and by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) is he bound?

If one passes away from the formless realm and is not reborn in the formless realm, how many [factors] does this person possess, by how many latent tendencies is he driven, and by how many fetters is he bound?
Is there anyone who, passing away from the desire realm, is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm?
Is there anyone who, passing away from the form realm, is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm?
Is there anyone who, passing away from the formless realm, is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm?

If one passes away from the desire realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, how many persons are there; by how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) are they bound; and by how many fetters (saṃyojana) are they bound?

If one passes away from the form realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, how many persons are there; by how many latent dispositions are they bound; and by how many fetters are they bound?

If one dies in the formless realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, how many *pudgalas* (persons) are there; by how many *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) are they driven; and by how many *saṃyojanas* (fetters) are they bound?
Is it possible for one whose craving for the desire realm (*kāmarāga*) is not yet exhausted to die and not be reborn in the desire realm?
Is there anyone who, having not yet exhausted craving for form, passes away and is not reborn in the desire realm or the form realm?
Is there anyone who, having not yet exhausted craving for the formless, passes away and is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm?

If one dies with sensual craving (*kāmarāga*) not yet exhausted and is not reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how many [factors] does this person possess, by how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is he driven, and by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) is he bound?

If one dies with craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) not yet exhausted and is not reborn in either the desire realm or the form realm, how many [factors] does this person possess, by how many underlying tendencies is he driven, and by how many fetters is he bound?

If one dies with craving for the formless realm not yet exhausted, and is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, how many persons are there? By how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) is such a person driven? And by how many fetters (saṃyojana) is he bound?
I wish to explain fully the meaning of this chapter:

the two types of the desire realm, the two types of the form realm, and the two types of the formless realm; namely, the categories of fetters abandoned through the realization of the Four Noble Truths and the categories of fetters abandoned through cultivation.
Is it possible for the fetters of the desire realm to be bound all at once?
Answer: Yes;
this occurs when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) falls away from detachment from the desire realm, or when one dies in the form or formless realms and is reborn in the desire realm.
"Can it not be bound at one time?
He replied: "It can;
an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) attains freedom from craving for the desire realm."
"Can it be bound gradually?
He replied,
"It cannot."
"Is it possible to gradually attain the state of being unbound?
He replied:
"Yes, World-Honored One. A disciple of the World-Honored One first extinguishes the fetters abandoned through the vision of the Four Truths, and subsequently those abandoned through cultivation."
Is it possible for the fetters of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to be bound all at once?
Answer: Yes.

This occurs when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), having fallen away from detachment from the form realm, dies from a higher plane and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or in the Brahma heavens.
"Is it possible to attain non-attachment all at once?
He replied:
"It is possible; an ordinary person may attain non-craving for the realm of form."
"Can one gradually attain that which is subject to fetters? He replied, "No."
Is it possible to gradually attain the state of being unbound?
He replied:
Yes, World-Honored One; a disciple of the Buddha first extinguishes the fetters abandoned through the vision of the Four Truths, and subsequently [extinguishes those] abandoned through cultivation.
Is it possible for the fetters of the formless realm to be bound all at once?
Answer: It is not possible.
"Is it possible to attain non-attachment all at once? He replied, "It is not."
Can one gradually attain fettering? Answer: No.
"Is it possible to gradually attain the state of being unbound?
He replied: "It is possible;

the disciples of the World-Honored One first extinguish the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the Four Truths, and subsequently [extinguish those] to be abandoned through cultivation—thus concluding the two types of realms."
When the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through the realization of the Four Truths in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are exhausted, by which fruit (phala) are they subsumed?
Answer: They are subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or they have no specific location.
Those abandoned through contemplation in the desire realm are either the fruit of *anāgāmin* or *arhat*, or they have no specific location.
Those abandoned through the four truths in the form realm are the four fruits of the *śrāmaṇya*, or they have no specific location.
Those abandoned through cultivation in the form realm are either [attained by] an Arhat or have no fixed location.
Those abandoned through the four truths in the formless realm belong to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Those abandoned through contemplation are the Arhat.
There are five types of fetters:
the type of fetter abandoned through the truth of suffering, and the types of fetters abandoned through the truths of origin, cessation, the path, and contemplation.
When the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering are exhausted, by which fruit are they subsumed?
The answer is:
they are subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or they have no specific location.
Those abandoned by the Truth of Origination and the Truth of Cessation belong to four of the fruits of śrāmaṇya, or they have no fixed location.
Those abandoned by the Truth of the Path belong to four of the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Those abandoned by cultivation complete the five types of arhats.
The nine types of fetters (*saṃyojana*):

the types of fetters abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*), those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), and the types of fetters abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
When the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) are exhausted, in which fruit are they included? Answer:
They are included in the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or else in the fruit of the path not yet entered at the stage of "no-fixed-location" (*anāgamya*).

Those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*), those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), and those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*)—these pertain to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or they have no fixed location.
Those abandoned by the knowledge of the unknown of the Path constitute four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Those abandoned by cultivation [are abandoned] by the ninefold gate of the arhat.
There are fifteen kinds of fetters:

The seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the truth of suffering in the desire realm; the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation, in the desire realm; the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the truth of suffering in the form realm; the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation, in the form realm; and the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the truth of suffering in the formless realm; the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation, in the formless realm.

When the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are exhausted, by which fruit (*phala*) are they subsumed?
Answer: They are subsumed under the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), or they have no specific location.
Those [defilements] of the desire realm abandoned through the truths of origin, cessation, and the path are included in four fruits of the śramaṇa, or they have no fixed location.
Those of the desire realm abandoned through cultivation are included in the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of arhatship, or they have no fixed location.
Those abandoned through the truth of suffering in the form realm belong to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or have no fixed location.
Those abandoned through the truths of origin, cessation, and the path in the form realm belong to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or have no fixed location.
Those abandoned through cultivation in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) pertain to the fruit of arhatship, or have no specific location.
Those abandoned through the truth of suffering in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) pertain to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or have no specific location.
Those abandoned by the truth of the cessation of the habitual tendencies of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) pertain to four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or they have no fixed location.
Those abandoned by the truth of the path (mārgasatya) of the formless realm pertain to four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The [defilements] abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm; the fifteen types [of defilements] of the Arhat are thus completed.
When the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is exhausted, by which fruit is it subsumed? Answer:
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or none at all.
The view of self-identity (sīlabbataparāmāsa) and doubt (vicikicchā) pertain to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of desire (kāmāsava) pertain either to the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala), or none at all.
The outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) pertain to Arhats.
Among the floods (*ogha*), the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) pertains to those in the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmin*) or Arhats, or it may have no specific locus.
The outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) pertain to the Arhat.
The outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) pertains to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The same applies to the yokes (*yoga*).
Among the [five] clingings, the clinging to sensual pleasures is either the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala), or it has no fixed location.
The clinging to precepts and observances and the clinging to views are the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
I have realized the fruit of arhatship.
Among the fetters, the bodily fetter of sensual desire and the bodily fetter of ill will are either absent in the fruit of non-returning or in the fruit of arhatship.

The fetters of the body consisting of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the fetter of the body consisting of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) [are abandoned] through the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.

Among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), sloth-and-torpor (*styānamiddha*), and restlessness-and-regret (*auddhatyakaukṛtya*) [are abandoned] through the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) and the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), or they have no fixed location [for abandonment].
The hindrance of doubt does not find a place within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
as for the fetters of ill-will, stinginess, and envy among the fetters, they do not find a place within either the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of arhatship.
The fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*) [are abandoned] at the fruit of arhatship.

Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) [are abandoned] at the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) or the fruit of arhatship, or they have no specific location [for abandonment].
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) pertains to four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it has no fixed location.
The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) pertain to four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Among the views, the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) pertain to four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or they have no fixed location.
Regarding wrong view, the clinging to views, and the clinging to precepts, there are four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Within the attachment to the body, the attachment to olfactory contact and gustatory contact pertains to the fruit of anāgāmin and the fruit of arhat, or it may have no fixed location.
The craving for contact through the eye, ear, and body pertains to the fruit of Arhatship, or it has no fixed location.
The craving for contact through the mind pertains to the fruit of Arhatship.

Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the tendency of sensual desire and the tendency of ill-will pertain to the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) and the fruit of Arhatship, or they have no fixed location.
The latent tendencies of craving (*rāgānuśaya*), conceit (*mānānuśaya*), and ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*) are abandoned at the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*).
The latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*) and doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*) are abandoned at the four fruits of śramaṇaship (*catur-śrāmaṇyaphala*).

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratighasaṃyojana*), the fetter of avarice (*mātsaryasaṃyojana*), and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyāsaṃyojana*) are abandoned at the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) or the fruit of arhatship; or they may have no specific locus [of abandonment].
The fetters of craving (*rāga*), conceit (*māna*), pride (*mada*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) are abandoned at the fruit of arhatship.
The fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi*), regret (*parāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are abandoned at the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.

Regarding the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*): those abandoned through the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path in the desire realm are abandoned at the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or they have no specific location [of abandonment].
Those abandoned through contemplation in the desire realm [are included in] the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of arhatship, or they have no fixed location.
Those abandoned by the two paths [of seeing and cultivation] have no fixed location.
Those abandoned by the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path in the form realm [are included in] the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or they have no fixed location.
Those abandoned through contemplation in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) pertain to the fruit of arhatship, or have no specific location.
Those abandoned through the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) pertain to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or have no specific location.
Those abandoned by the Path of Truth (mārgasatya) in the formless realm are included in four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Those abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā) in the formless realm are included in the fruit of arhatship. The section on the gates of inclusion is concluded.

When a disciple of the Blessed One who has realized the truths has not yet exhausted the craving of the desire realm, but has exhausted the fetters of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation, in which fruit is this comprised?
Answer: It is the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin, or there is no specific location [for it].

When sensual craving has been exhausted but craving for the form realm has not yet been exhausted, the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through contemplation in the form realm—of what fruit is this comprised?
Answer: It is not included in any [fruit].

When craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) has been exhausted, but craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-tṛṣṇā*) has not yet been exhausted, the exhaustion of those [defilements] of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—in what fruit is this included?
Answer: There is no such place; thus ends the section on the gate of non-desire.
The eight persons:

one who is entering the realization of stream-entry and one who has attained stream-entry; one who is entering the realization of once-returning and one who has attained once-returning; one who is entering the realization of non-returning and one who has attained non-returning; one who is entering the realization of arhatship and one who has attained arhatship.
Regarding those who have attained the realization of *srotāpanna* and whose fetters are exhausted, by which fruit are they subsumed?
The answer is:
there is no specific location [for such a classification].
If one attains the stage of *srotāpanna*, they are simply a *srotāpanna*.
As for the attainment of the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* through the realization of the exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana-kṣaya*), by which fruit is it subsumed?
The answer is:
The fruit of *srotāpanna* may have no fixed location.
One who attains the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* is simply a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
When one proceeds toward *anāgāmin* and realizes the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), by which fruit is this subsumed?
Answer: The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin may have no fixed location.
Upon attaining the state of an Anāgāmin, one is immediately an Anāgāmin.
To which fruit is the realization of the exhaustion of fetters by one proceeding toward arhatship subsumed?
The answer is:
it is subsumed under the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), or there is no specific location [for its inclusion].
Having attained arhatship, one completes the eight types of persons who are arhats.
Regarding those who have accomplished the dharmas of training and are srotāpannas: are these dharmas subsumed within the fruit of srotāpatti?
Answer: It is sometimes included and sometimes not included.
How is it included?
Answer: When the conditioned fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) is attained and not lost, this is called "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*).
What is "non-comprehension"?

Answer: The stream-enterer (srotāpanna) increases and further attains various sublime, untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya); having attained them, his fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted and he realizes [the fruit]. This is called "not being included.
If all dharmas are included within the fruit of stream-entry, are they the dharmas of one in training (śaikṣa-dharma)?
Answer: It is either *śaikṣa* (in training) or neither *śaikṣa* nor *aśaikṣa* (beyond training).
What is *śaikṣa*?
Answer: The conditioned fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) is called "in training" (śaikṣa).
What is that which is neither in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa)?
Answer: The unconditioned fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) is called neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
The same applies to the fruits of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and non-returner (anāgāmin).
"One who has attained the qualities of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) achieves arhatship; does the arhat encompass those qualities?
Answer: "It is so."
If one posits that the dharmas subsumed under arhatship are those of an arhat, are they the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma)?
The answer is:
some are the dharmas of one beyond training, while others are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣadharma).
What is the state of no-more-learning? Answer:
The conditioned Arhat is called one who has attained no-more-learning.
What is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
The answer is:
the unconditioned arhat is called neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Regarding those untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) possessed by a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), are those dharmas included within the category of the stream-enterer?
Answer: They are either included or not included.
What is meant by "retention"?
The answer is:
having attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) and not losing it—this is called retention.
What is meant by "not included"?
The answer is:

when a *srotāpanna* increases and further attains the subtle, untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), and having attained them, exhausts the fetters and realizes the fruit—yet this is not the accomplishment of a *srotāpanna* through the cessation not due to counting [the moments]—this is called "not included."
If all dharmas are subsumed under the stage of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), are they untainted (anāsrava) dharmas?
Answer: Yes, they are.
The same applies to the Sakṛdāgāmin and the Anāgāmin.
Regarding those untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma) that constitute an Arhat, are those dharmas subsumed within the Arhat?
Answer: It is sometimes included and sometimes not included.
How is it included?
Answer: To attain the fruit of arhatship and not lose it is called "comprehension" (saṃgraha).
What is "non-comprehension"?
Answer: One who has attained the cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) while being an Arhat is said to be "not included.
Furthermore, if various phenomena are included by an Arhat, are those phenomena untainted (anāsrava)?
Answer: It is so.
Are those dharmas that constitute a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) subsumed within the state of being a stream-enterer?
Answer: There may be dharmas that a srotāpanna has accomplished, yet those dharmas are not included within the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
What are these dharmas that a srotāpanna has accomplished, which are not included within the fruit of stream-entry?
Answer:

A *srotāpanna* increases and further attains the subtle, untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). Having attained them, they exhaust the fetters and realize the fruit; furthermore, they accomplish the *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation) and the *srotāpanna* [status] itself, as well as the tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) that constitute a *srotāpanna*. These are called the phenomena accomplished by a *srotāpanna*, and these phenomena are not subsumed within the fruit of *srotāpatti*.
What are those dharmas subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) that do not constitute the attainment of stream-entry?
The answer is:

those dharmas which one has not yet attained as the fruit of stream-entry, or which one has attained and then lost—these are called the dharmas subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry that do not constitute the attainment of stream-entry.
What are the dharmas that constitute the attainment of a srotāpanna, and which dharmas are subsumed under the fruit of srotāpattiphala?
The answer is:

to have attained the fruit of srotāpattiphala and not lose it—these are called the dharmas that constitute the attainment of a srotāpanna, and these are the dharmas subsumed under the fruit of srotāpattiphala.
What are those dharmas that do not constitute a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and are not included within the fruits of stream-entry?
Answer: With the exception of the aforementioned matters.
The same applies to the Sakṛdāgāmin and the Anāgāmin.
Are all dharmas that constitute an Arhat included within what is called an "Arhat"?
The answer is: No.
There may be certain dharmas that constitute an Arhat, yet these dharmas are not subsumed under the category of "Arhat.
How is it that there are certain dharmas which constitute an Arhat, yet these dharmas are not subsumed under the dharmas of an Arhat?
The answer is:

It is neither the attainment of cessation through deliberation nor the possession of out-flowing (sāsrava) dharmas that constitutes an Arhat’s possession of dharmas; these dharmas are not included within the category of an Arhat.
What are those phenomena (dharmas) comprised within an arhat, yet which do not constitute the accomplishment of an arhat?
The answer is:
if one has not yet attained arhatship, or having attained it, one immediately loses it—these are called the phenomena comprised within an arhat that do not constitute the accomplishment of an arhat.
What are the dharmas that constitute the attainment of arhatship, and which dharmas are comprised within the state of an arhat?
The answer is:
the attainment of arhatship without loss—these are called the dharmas that constitute the attainment of arhatship and the dharmas comprised within the state of an arhat.
What are those dharmas that do not constitute an Arhat, yet are also not subsumed under the category of an Arhat?
Answer: Excluding the aforementioned matters; thus ends the second section on subsumption.
If one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm, does one necessarily undergo existence within the desire realm?
Answer: There are cases where one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm, yet does not undergo existence within the desire realm.
What is meant by passing away from the desire realm and being reborn again in the desire realm without undergoing existence in the desire realm?
The answer is:

one passes away from the desire realm and accomplishes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm; this is called passing away from the desire realm and being reborn again in the desire realm without undergoing existence in the desire realm.
What is meant by "experiencing existence in the desire realm without having died from the desire realm and without being reborn in the desire realm"? Answer:

If one dies in the form realm and manifests an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for the desire realm, this is called experiencing existence in the desire realm without having died from the desire realm and without being reborn in the desire realm.
What is meant by "passing away from the desire realm and being reborn again in the desire realm, experiencing existence within the desire realm"?
The answer is:

passing away from the desire realm and bringing about the intermediate state (antarābhava) and the birth-state (upapattibhava) within the desire realm—this is called passing away from the desire realm and being reborn again in the desire realm, experiencing existence within the desire realm.
What is meant by "not passing away from the desire realm, not being reborn in the desire realm, and not undergoing existence in the desire realm"?
The answer is:

one who passes away from the form realm and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*) within the form realm; one who passes away from the form realm and is reborn in the formless realm; one who passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm; and one who passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm. This is called "not passing away from the desire realm, not being reborn in the desire realm, and not undergoing existence in the desire realm."
If one dies in the form realm and is reborn again in the form realm, does one necessarily undergo existence in the form realm?
Answer: There are cases where one dies in the form realm and is reborn again in the form realm without undergoing existence in the form realm.
What is meant by "passing away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and being reborn in the form realm, yet not receiving existence in the form realm"?
The answer is:

passing away from the form realm and manifesting the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—this is called passing away from the form realm and being reborn in the form realm, yet not receiving existence in the form realm.
What is meant by "one who undergoes existence in the form realm, dies in the non-form realm, and is not reborn in the form realm"?
The answer is:

one who passes away from the desire realm and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm; this is called undergoing existence in the form realm, dying in the non-form realm, and not being reborn in the form realm.
What is meant by passing away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and being reborn again in the form realm, thereby undergoing existence in the form realm?
The answer is:

passing away from the form realm and bringing about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*) within the form realm—this is called passing away from the form realm and being reborn again in the form realm, thereby undergoing existence in the form realm.
What is meant by "not passing away from the form realm, not being born in the form realm, and not receiving existence in the form realm"? The answer is:

one who passes away from the desire realm and undergoes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the birth-state (*upapattibhava*) within the desire realm; one who passes away from the desire realm and is born in the formless realm; one who passes away from the formless realm and is born in the formless realm; and one who passes away from the formless realm and is born in the desire realm. This is called "not passing away from the form realm, not being born in the form realm, and not receiving existence in the form realm."
When one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm, does one necessarily undergo existence in the formless realm?
Answer: It is so;
when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm, one necessarily undergoes existence in the formless realm.
Is there anyone who, having received existence in the formless realm, passes away from the formless realm and is born again in the formless realm?
Answer: There is.
If one dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or dies in the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm,
there are four such persons:
ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) of the desire realm, and ordinary beings and noble ones of the form realm.
Those who pass away from the form realm and are reborn again in the form realm are of three types:
ordinary persons of the desire realm, ordinary persons of the form realm, and noble ones.
Those who pass away from the formless realm and are reborn again in the formless realm are of two types:
There are ordinary persons and noble ones in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), ordinary persons are driven by ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and bound by nine fetters (*saṃyojana*);
noble ones are driven by ten latent tendencies and bound by six fetters.
Ordinary persons in the realm of form are driven by sixty-two latent tendencies (anuśaya) and bound by six fetters (saṃyojana);
noble ones (ārya) are driven by six latent tendencies and bound by three fetters.
Ordinary persons in the formless realm are driven by thirty-one proclivities and bound by six fetters;
noble ones are driven by three proclivities and bound by three fetters. This concludes the section on the places of death and rebirth.
If one does not die in the desire realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, is it the case that they will entirely not undergo existence in the desire realm?
Answer: There are cases where one does not die in the desire realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, yet it is not that they do not undergo existence in the desire realm.
What is it to not die in the desire realm and not be reborn in the desire realm, yet not be without the existence (bhava) of the desire realm?
The answer is:

one who dies from the form realm and brings about the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the desire realm; this is called not dying in the desire realm and not being reborn in the desire realm, yet not being without the existence of the desire realm.
What is meant by "not receiving existence in the desire realm, yet not passing away from the desire realm, and not being born in the desire realm"?
The answer is:

when one passes away from the desire realm and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm—this is called "not receiving existence in the desire realm, yet not passing away from the desire realm, and not being born in the desire realm."
What is meant by "not passing away from the desire realm, not being reborn in the desire realm, and not undergoing existence in the desire realm"?
