The answer is: passing away from the form realm and manifesting the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth within the form realm; passing away from the form realm and being reborn in the formless realm; passing away from the formless realm and being reborn in the formless realm; and passing away from the formless realm and being reborn in the form realm. This is called not passing away from the desire realm, not being reborn in the desire realm, and not undergoing existence in the desire realm.
What is meant by "neither passing away from the realm of desire, nor being born in the realm of desire, yet not not receiving existence in the realm of desire"?
The answer is:

one who passes away from the realm of desire and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*) within the realm of desire; this is called neither passing away from the realm of desire, nor not being born in the realm of desire, nor not receiving existence in the realm of desire.
Is it the case that one who does not pass away from the form realm and is not reborn in the form realm does not, in every instance, fail to undergo existence in the form realm? Answer:
It may be that one does not pass away from the form realm and is not reborn in the form realm, yet it is not the case that they do not undergo existence in the form realm.
What is meant by "not passing away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and not being reborn in the form realm, yet not not experiencing existence in the form realm"?
The answer is:

one who passes away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm—this is called "not passing away from the form realm and not being reborn in the form realm, yet not not experiencing existence in the form realm."
What is meant by "not receiving existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu-bhava*), yet not having died from the form realm, and not being born in the form realm"?
The answer is:

one who dies from the form realm and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—this is called not receiving existence in the form realm, yet not having died from the form realm, and not being born in the form realm.
What is meant by "not passing away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), not being reborn in the form realm, and not undergoing existence in the form realm"? Answer:

One who passes away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and undergoes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth within the desire realm; one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); one who passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm; and one who passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm—these are called those who do not pass away from the form realm, are not reborn in the form realm, and do not undergo existence in the form realm.
What is meant by "neither not passing away from the form realm, nor not being reborn in the form realm, nor not receiving existence in the form realm"?
The answer is:

one who passes away from the form realm and brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*) within the form realm; this is called neither not passing away from the form realm, nor not being reborn in the form realm, nor not receiving existence in the form realm.
Is it not the case that one who does not pass away from the formless realm and is not reborn in the formless realm will, in their entirety, not undergo existence in the formless realm?
Answer: It is so;
one who does not pass away from the formless realm and is not reborn in the formless realm will, in their entirety, not undergo existence in the formless realm.
Is there one who does not receive existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-bhava*), yet is not one who has not died from the formless realm and will not be born in the formless realm?
Answer: There is.

For example, one who dies in the formless realm and is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), but is not one who dies in the desire realm and will not be born in the desire realm.
There are five such persons:
ordinary beings of the desire realm, ordinary beings and noble ones of the form realm, and ordinary beings and noble ones of the formless realm.
There are six such persons who do not die in the form realm and are not reborn in the form realm:
Ordinary persons and noble ones of the desire realm; ordinary persons and noble ones of the form realm; ordinary persons and noble ones of the formless realm.
There are four types of persons who do not die in the formless realm and are not reborn in the formless realm:
ordinary persons and noble ones of the desire realm, and ordinary persons and noble ones of the form realm.
Having been driven by the objects of the senses and bound by the fetters, one reaches the state where there is neither birth nor death.
Is it possible that one who dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is not reborn in the desire realm?
Answer: Yes.

Not being reborn, one completes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm and the intermediate state of the form realm; having been born into the birth-state (*upapattibhava*) of the formless realm, one attains *parinirvāṇa*.
Is it possible that one who passes away from the desire realm is not reborn in the form realm?
Answer:

There is no birth [in the form realm]. Having completed the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm and completed the intermediate state of the desire realm, one is born in the formless realm and attains parinirvāṇa.
Is there anyone who, at the end of life in the desire realm, is not born in the formless realm?

Answer: One is not reborn [in the desire realm] when one completes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire or form realms, or when one attains parinirvāṇa in the birth-state (*upapattibhava*).
Is it possible that one who dies in the form realm is not reborn in the form realm?
Answer: One is not reborn;

having completed the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the intermediate state of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and attains parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible that one who passes away from the form realm is not reborn in the desire realm?
Answer: One is not reborn;
having completed the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm and the intermediate state of the form realm, one is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and attains parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible that one who passes away from the form realm is not reborn in the formless realm?
Answer: No, they do not arise.
Having completed the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they enter parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible that one who passes away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not reborn in the formless realm?
Answer: One is not reborn [there] if one completes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm or the form realm, or if one attains parinirvāṇa in the birth-state (*upapattibhava*).
Is it possible that one who dies in the formless realm is not reborn in the desire realm?
Answer: One is not reborn;
having completed the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm and the intermediate state of the form realm, one is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and attains parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible that one who passes away from the formless realm is not reborn in the form realm?
The answer is:

they do not take birth. Having completed the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the intermediate state of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they take birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and attain *parinirvāṇa*.
If one dies in the desire realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, there are six such persons:
Ordinary persons and noble ones of the desire realm; ordinary persons and noble ones of the form realm; ordinary persons and noble ones of the formless realm.
If one dies in the desire realm and is not reborn in the form realm, there are six such persons:
ordinary persons and noble ones of the desire realm; ordinary persons and noble ones of the form realm; and ordinary persons and noble ones of the formless realm.
If one dies in the desire realm and is not reborn in the formless realm, there are four such persons:
ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire realm, and ordinary beings and noble ones of the form realm.
There are five types of persons who, at the end of life in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), are not reborn in the realm of form:
ordinary beings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*) of the realm of form, and ordinary beings and noble ones of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are five types of persons who, at the end of life in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), are not reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
ordinary beings of the desire realm, ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*) of the form realm, and ordinary beings and noble ones of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are three types of persons who, at the end of life in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), are not reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):
ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), ordinary beings of the form realm, and noble ones (*ārya*).
There are two types of persons who, at the end of life in the formless realm, are not reborn in the formless realm: [ordinary beings of the formless realm and noble ones].
Ordinary beings of the desire realm and ordinary beings of the form realm.
There are four types of persons who, at the end of life in the formless realm, are not reborn in the desire realm:
ordinary beings of the desire realm, ordinary beings of the form realm, ordinary beings of the formless realm, and noble ones.
There are four types of persons who, upon the end of life in the formless realm, are not reborn in the form realm:
ordinary beings of the desire realm, ordinary beings of the form realm, ordinary beings of the formless realm, and noble ones.
[This concludes] the section on not being born in a place where one is driven by the objects of the senses and bound by the fetters.
Is it possible that one who dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Answer: Yes.
Not being reborn, one accomplishes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or attains parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible that, having passed away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Answer: Yes.
Not being reborn, one accomplishes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm or the form realm, or attains parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible that, having ended one's life in the formless realm, one is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm?
Answer: They are not reborn, having either completed the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or attained parinirvāṇa.
If one dies in the desire realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are four such persons:
Ordinary persons and noble ones of the desire realm; ordinary persons and noble ones of the form realm.
If one dies in the form realm and is not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, such a person belongs to three categories:
an ordinary person of the desire realm, an ordinary person of the form realm, or a noble one of the form realm.
There are two types of persons who, at the end of life in the formless realm, are not reborn in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm:
ordinary beings of the desire realm and ordinary beings of the form realm.
They are driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*). This concludes the third place of non-rebirth.
Is it possible that one who has not yet exhausted craving for the realm of desire dies and is not reborn in the realm of desire?
Answer: No, they are not reborn [there], as they have already completed the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the realm of desire.
Is it possible that one who has not yet exhausted craving for form dies and is not reborn in the realm of desire or the realm of form?
Answer: It is not so;
such a person does not fail to produce the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the realm of desire or the realm of form.
Is it possible that one who has not yet exhausted craving for the formless realm dies and is not reborn in the desire, form, or formless realms?
Answer: It is not so;
such a person brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the desire or form realms.
If one dies with craving for the desire realm (*kāmarāga*) not yet exhausted, yet is not reborn in the desire realm, such persons are of two types:
ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) of the desire realm.
If one dies with craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) not yet exhausted, yet is not reborn in either the desire or form realms, such persons are of four types:
Ordinary persons and noble ones of the desire realm; ordinary persons and noble ones of the form realm.
If one dies with craving for the formless realm not yet exhausted, such that they are not reborn in the desire, form, or formless realms, there are four such persons:
ordinary persons and noble ones of the desire realm, and ordinary persons and noble ones of the form realm.
Ordinary persons in the desire realm are driven by ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and bound by nine fetters (*saṃyojana*);
noble ones (*ārya*) are driven by ten underlying tendencies and bound by six fetters.
Ordinary persons in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) are driven by sixty-two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and bound by six fetters (saṃyojana);
noble ones (ārya) are driven by six underlying tendencies and bound by three fetters.
Ordinary persons in the formless realm are driven by thirty-one proclivities and bound by six fetters;
noble ones are driven by three proclivities and bound by three fetters.

The third *varga* of the *Abhidharma* masters is completed. In the Sanskrit original, it consists of four hundred and sixty-seven *ślokas*; in the Qin translation, it consists of six thousand one hundred and fifty-three words.
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Volume Seven.
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Volume Eight.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīr during the Fu Qin dynasty, with the assistance of several others;
including the two conditions, there is sequential cognition.
The faculties that are associated [with the path] are also accomplished;
if they are not yet accomplished, one realizes them through the knowledge of abandonment, pervading all ten doors.

The twenty-two faculties (indriya), the eighteen bases (āyatana), the twelve sense-spheres (dhātu), the five aggregates (skandha), the five aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandha), the six elements (dhātu);
material phenomena (rūpadharma) and immaterial phenomena (arūpadharma); visible phenomena (sanidarśanadharma) and invisible phenomena (anidarśanadharma);

resistant phenomena (sapratighadharma) and non-resistant phenomena (apratighadharma); tainted phenomena (sāsravadharma) and untainted phenomena (anāsravadharma); conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma).
Regarding phenomena (*dharma*): past phenomena, future phenomena, and present phenomena; wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, and indeterminate phenomena;
phenomena bound to the desire realm, phenomena bound to the form realm, and phenomena bound to the formless realm;

phenomena of those in training (*śaikṣa*), phenomena of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and phenomena of neither training nor beyond training; and those to be abandoned by the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*).
Dharmas, dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation, and dharmas not to be abandoned; the four truths, the four dhyānas,
the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery,
the ten totalities, the eight knowledges, the three samādhis, the three fetters, the three unwholesome roots, the three outflows, the four floods, and so forth.
The four yokes, the four graspings, the four bonds; the five hindrances, the five fetters, the five lower fetters, the five views;
the six cravings for the body, the seven latent tendencies, the nine fetters, and the ninety-eight latent tendencies.
By how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) influenced? ...

[and so on] ... by how many underlying tendencies is the ignorance-underlying-tendency (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) influenced? [This concludes] one section.
By how many underlying tendencies is the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) influenced?

Regarding the two gates: how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) underlie the object-conditioned consciousness (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna) of the ignorance-tendency (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
And how many underlying tendencies underlie the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya) as its object-conditioned consciousness?

Regarding the three gates: how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) are bound by the object-conditioned consciousness associated with the ignorance-latent-disposition that is abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm?
Following the mental faculty (manas-indriya), how many moments of mind arise in succession?

Regarding the sequence of how many moments of mind arise from the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation within the formless realm— this being the first of four gateways—

is it to be said that this latent tendency associated with the eye faculty is accompanied by both applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), without applied but with sustained thought (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), or without either applied or sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*)?

Regarding the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which are themselves subject to other latent tendencies—should these latent tendencies be said to be with vitarka and with vicāra, without vitarka but with vicāra, or without vitarka and without vicāra? [The answer is: They belong to all five categories.
The eye faculty is driven by various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). With how many faculties are these latent dispositions associated?

Up to the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), with how many faculties are these latent dispositions associated? [Explain] according to the six gates.
Who possesses the eye-faculty?
Up to: who possesses the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm across the seven gates?
Who does not possess the eye-faculty?
Furthermore, who does not possess the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm?
At the time of the knowledge of abandonment regarding the eye-faculty, how many latent tendencies and how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned through that knowledge?

Up to the point of the knowledge of abandonment regarding the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—how many latent tendencies and how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned and known through this ninefold gate?
When the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*) is realized as exhausted, how many latent tendencies and how many fetters are realized as exhausted?

When one realizes the exhaustion of the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how many latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are realized as exhausted?
I wish for the meaning of this chapter to be fully expounded according to the ten gates.
By how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) is the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya) influenced?
By those that pertain to all [categories] in the desire realm and the form realm, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties.
The mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) is associated with all [categories].
The male faculty (*puruṣa-indriya*) and female faculty (*strī-indriya*) are associated with all [categories] of the desire realm as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*) is associated with all [categories] of the three realms as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) pertains to all [factors] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as well as to those that are universal and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) pertains to those that are universal and those to be abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm.

The faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*) comprises everything in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and everything in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), with the exception of the doubt in the desire realm that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated therewith.
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) comprises everything in the desire realm.
The faculty of guarding is associated with all [defilements].
The faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are associated with all [defilements] throughout the three realms as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya), and the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātāvīndriya) do not exist [in this context].

The eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base; the form-base, sound-base, and tangible-object-base; and the eye-consciousness-base, ear-consciousness-base, and body-consciousness-base belong to both the desire realm and the form realm, and are to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
The odor-base, taste-base, nose-consciousness-base, and tongue-consciousness-base belong to the desire realm, are common to all [categories], and are to be abandoned by cultivation.
The mind-base, mental-object-base, and mind-consciousness-base belong to all [realms and categories].

The sense-bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, as well as the sense-bases of visible forms, sounds, and tangibles, pertain to both the pervasive categories and those to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire and form realms.
The sense-bases of odors and tastes pertain to both the pervasive categories and those to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.
The mind-base (manāyatana) and the phenomena-base (dharmāyatana) comprise all [factors].

As for the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), it comprises all factors pertaining to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu), as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanāprahātavya).
The aggregates of sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) comprise all [factors].
The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) pertains to all [factors] common to the desire and form realms (kāma-rūpadhātu) as well as those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
The aggregates of sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) pertain to all [factors].
The earth element (pṛthivī-dhātu) up to the space element (ākāśa-dhātu) pertain to all [factors] common to the desire and form realms as well as those abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the seeds of consciousness: all [factors].
Regarding material phenomena (*rūpadharma*): those pertaining to the desire realm and the form realm, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding immaterial phenomena (*arūpadharma*): all [factors].
Visible phenomena and phenomena with resistance belong to all categories within the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.
Invisible phenomena and non-resistant phenomena belong to all categories.
All contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma).
None of the uncontaminated phenomena (anāsrava-dharma).
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma).
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) do not exist [as objects of clinging]. All phenomena of the past, future, and present;
all wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*); those common to all three realms (*traidhātuka-sarvatraga*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Unwholesome factors (*akuśala-dharma*) comprise all those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Neutral factors (*avyākṛta-dharma*) comprise all those of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*), as well as two types from the desire realm.
Those abandoned through the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*) in the desire realm pertain to all [factors].
All phenomena bound to the desire realm are bound to the desire realm.
All phenomena bound to the form realm are bound to the form realm.
All phenomena bound to the formless realm are bound to the formless realm.
Dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) do not exist [in this context].
All dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training [are included].
Dharmas to be abandoned by the vision of the truths (*darśana-prahātavya*) are all [to be abandoned] by the vision of the truths.

Dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation are abandoned by cultivation; this applies to all [such dharmas] and to those that pervade all. There are no [dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation] among the dharmas that are not to be abandoned.
Regarding the truth of suffering and the truth of origination, it applies to all.
The Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path do not exist [within the formless realm].
Within the dhyānas, all factors of the form realm are present.
The four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni) belong to the form realm, pertain to all [categories], and are abandoned through cultivation.
Within the formless realm, all [factors] of the formless realm are present;

these include the first, second, and third liberations, the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), as well as those factors of the form realm that are universal and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The remaining liberations (*vimokṣa*) and all bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are [associated with] the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the universal [factors], and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
There are none associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is [associated with] the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the universal [factors], and those to be abandoned by cultivation.
Conventional knowledge (samvṛti-jñāna) encompasses all [objects], except for those associated with vision that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object.
Suffering-knowledge, origination-knowledge, cessation-knowledge, and path-knowledge, as well as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, do not exist [as objects].

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) includes everything abandoned by the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and everything that is pervasive and abandoned by the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).

The clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) includes everything abandoned by the truth of suffering and everything that is pervasive and abandoned by the truth of origination. Doubt (*vicikitsā*) includes everything abandoned by the truths of origination, cessation, and the path (*mārgasatya*), as well as everything abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and everything pervasive. It also includes all doubt associated with ignorance (*avidyā*) that takes contaminated objects as its condition (*sāsravālambana*), and the ignorance associated with doubt that takes uncontaminated objects as its condition (*anāsravālambana*).
Among the unwholesome roots, greed and hatred have as their objects the outflows (*āsrava*) of the desire realm.
Ignorance has as its objects everything in the desire realm, excluding the ignorance of the desire realm that has the outflows-free (*anāsrava*) as its object.
Among the outflows (*āsrava*), the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) comprises everything in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) comprises everything in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).
The outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) comprises everything, except for that ignorance which has the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.
Among the floods (*ogha*), the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) comprises everything in the realm of desire;
the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) comprises everything in the realms of form and formlessness;
and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*) comprises everything, with the exception of ignorance that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.

Regarding the outflows of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*): those with outflow that are to be abandoned by the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*) have outflow as their object; likewise, the ignorance associated with views that has no outflow as its object [is also included].
The same applies to the yokes (*yoga*).
Among the graspings (*upādāna*), the grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*) comprises everything belonging to the desire realm.

Regarding the aggregate of precepts (*śīla-skandha*): it includes everything abandoned by the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), everything common to what is abandoned by the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), and that which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and has as its object the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

Regarding the aggregate of views (*dṛṣṭi-skandha*): it includes that which is associated with outflows and has as its object the Truths of Seeing (*darśana-satya*), as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with views that has as its object the untainted (*anāsrava*).
I receive all [fetters] of the form and formless realms.

Among the fetters (*bandhana*), the bodily fetter of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-bandhana*) and the bodily fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda-bandhana*) have as their objects the outflows (*āsrava*) of the desire realm.

The bodily fetter of attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-bandhana*) consists of everything abandoned by the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), everything common to that which is abandoned by the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), and that which has outflows and is abandoned by the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
I see that the fetters of the body (*kāyabandhana*) are those with outflows (*sāsrava*) conditioned by the truths (*satyālambana*), which are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*dṛṣṭiheya*).
Among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) have outflows conditioned by the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Drowsiness (*styāna*), torpor (*middha*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) pertain to everything in the realm of desire.
The hindrance of restlessness (auddhatya-middha) pertains to the desire realm and is abandoned through both universal application and cultivation.

The hindrance of doubt (vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa) pertains to the desire realm and is abandoned through the vision of the truths; it has out-flowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana) when associated with doubt, and non-out-flowing objects (anāsrava-ālambana) when associated with ignorance (avidyā).
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) has as its object the outflows (*āsrava*) of the desire realm.
The fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) have as their object the outflows of the three realms.

The fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) pertain to the desire realm and are abandoned through both universal objects and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill will (*vyāpāda*) have as their objects the outflows (*āsrava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) consists of everything abandoned by the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and that which is abandoned by the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) when it is pervasive.

The view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists of all [factors] abandoned by the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), those abandoned by the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*) that are pervasive, and those with outflow-objects (*sāsravālambana*) abandoned by the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) consists of those with outflow-objects abandoned by the truths of vision (*darśanasatya*), as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt that has non-outflow-objects (*anāsravālambana*).

Among the views, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are entirely abandoned through the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), as well as those [factors] common to all that are abandoned through the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).

Regarding false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), those with outflowing objects (*sāsravālambana*) are abandoned through the truths of vision (*darśanasatya*), as are the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with false views that has non-outflowing objects (*anāsravālambana*).
The view of grasping at [wrong] views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) has as its objects the outflows (*sāsrava*) abandoned through the vision of the truths.

The view of grasping at precepts and rituals (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*) has as its objects everything abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), everything abandoned through the vision of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) that is universal, and those abandoned through the vision of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) that have outflows as their objects.
The craving for the nose and tongue among the cravings for the body pertains to the desire realm and is common to all [categories] as well as being abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The craving for the eye, ear, and body pertains to both the desire and form realms and is common to all as well as being abandoned through cultivation.
The craving for mental objects (*manosaṃcetanā-taṇhā*) has as its object the outflows (*sāsrava*) of the three realms.

Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the tendency of sensual greed (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*) and the tendency of ill-will (*pratigha-anuśaya*) have as their object the outflows of the desire realm.
The tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāga-anuśaya*) has as its object the outflows of the form and formless realms.
The latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*) has as its object the outflows (*sāsrava*) of the three realms.
The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) pertains to all [objects], except for that ignorance which has the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as its object.

The latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) consists of those outflows to be abandoned by the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*), as well as that ignorance associated with views which has the outflow-free as its object.

The proclivity of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) consists of that which has outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and is abandoned by the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with doubt that has non-outflow-objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) has outflow-objects belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) have as their objects the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the three realms.
The fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) has as its objects all [phenomena], except for that ignorance which has untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena as its object.

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) has as its objects the outflow-tainted phenomena abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*), as well as the ignorance associated with those views that has untainted phenomena as its object.
The fetter of wrong resolve (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) has outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*).

The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) has outflowing objects and is abandoned through the vision of the truths; furthermore, the ignorance associated with doubt (*vicikitsā-samprayukta-avidyā*) has non-outflowing objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).
The fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) pertain to the entire realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), those abandoned through the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) in the realm of desire include all [tendencies] abandoned through the truth of suffering in the realm of desire, as well as all [tendencies] abandoned through the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*) in the realm of desire that pertain to the universal [categories].

That which is abandoned by the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*) in the desire realm includes everything abandoned by the truth of origin in the desire realm, as well as everything common to all [categories] abandoned by the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) in the desire realm.

That which is abandoned by the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) in the desire realm includes everything abandoned by the truth of cessation in the desire realm, as well as everything common to all [categories].

That which is abandoned by the path-truth of the desire realm includes everything abandoned by the path-truth of the desire realm, as well as that which is common to all [factors] of the desire realm.
That which is abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm includes everything abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm, as well as that which is common to all [factors] of the desire realm.
The same applies to the realms of form and formlessness. This concludes the section on the "gates of latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*). Regarding the question:
"How many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bind the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object?
The answer is:
In the desire and form realms, there are three types; in the formless realm, they pertain to all [objects] as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the consciousness that takes objects as its objects (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*), when the two gates are combined, there are four types; within the Four Noble Truths, excluding the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), these include both [those abandoned by seeing] and those abandoned through cultivation.
The faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body are likewise.
As for the mental faculty (*manas*), its object-consciousness has conditioned things as its object;
its object-of-object-consciousness also has conditioned things as its object.

Regarding the male faculty and female faculty: as for the consciousness that takes them as objects, they are associated with the three types [of afflictions]—those to be abandoned by the contemplation of suffering and origination—in the desire realm; and with those that pervade all [categories] and those to be abandoned by contemplation in the form realm.

As for the consciousness that takes the object of that [primary] consciousness as its object, they are associated with the four types in the desire realm, the three types in the form realm, and those that pervade all [categories] and those to be abandoned by contemplation in the formless realm.
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya), as a condition for consciousness, consists of three types in the three realms;
as a condition for object-conditioned consciousness (ālambanapratyaya-vijñāna), it consists of four types.

The pleasure-faculty (sukhendriya), as a condition for consciousness, consists of four types in the desire realm, the conditioned objects of the form realm, and two types along with those universal to all [realms] in the formless realm.
Regarding the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*): in the desire realm and the formless realm, there are four types;

in the form realm, it has conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*). Regarding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*): as for the consciousness that takes it as its object, there are three types in the desire realm; in the form realm, it includes all [types] and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

As for the object-conditioned consciousness: in the desire realm, there are four types; in the form realm, there are three types; in the formless realm, it includes all [types] and those to be abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*): the consciousness that takes it as its object has conditioned things of the desire and form realms as its conditions, and two types [of consciousness] of the formless realm as well as those that pervade all;
the consciousness that takes the object of that object as its condition has conditioned things of the desire and form realms as its conditions, and four types of consciousness of the formless realm.

The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness, consists of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) objects of the desire realm, and those common to all [categories] and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the form realm;

as the object-object-condition (*ālambanālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness, it consists of the conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya*) of the desire realm, the three types [of objects] of the form realm, and those common to all and those to be abandoned by cultivation of the formless realm.
The faculty of guarding (rakkhita-indriya), as a condition for consciousness, has conditioned things as its object;
as a condition for the object-conditioned consciousness, it has conditioned things as its object.

For the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, there are four types of conditions for consciousness, and four types of conditions for the object-conditioned consciousness.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*): with respect to the consciousness that takes them as objects, they are of two types and pervade all [realms]; with respect to the consciousness that takes those objects as its own objects, they are of four types.

The eye-base (*cakṣur-dhātu*), the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-bases, and the visible-form-base (*rūpa-dhātu*), sound-, and tangible-base (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*): with respect to the consciousness that takes them as objects, they belong to three types in the desire and form realms, and to all types and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm;
with respect to the consciousness that takes those objects as its own objects, they are of four types.
The eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and body-consciousness-appropriating consciousnesses take as their object three types [of consciousness] in the desire and form realms;
the object-of-object consciousness takes as its object four types in the desire and form realms, two types in the formless realm, and those that pervade all.

The possession of the nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness by means of the objects of smell and taste consists of three types in the desire realm, and those that pertain to all [categories] and those to be abandoned by cultivation in the form realm;

as for the consciousness that takes these as its object (ālambanālambana-vijñāna), it consists of four types in the desire realm, three types in the form realm, and those that pertain to all [categories] and those to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm.
The mind-base (manāyatana) and the mind-consciousness-base (manovijñānāyatana): as object-conditioned consciousness, they have conditioned objects;
as object-of-object-conditioned consciousness, they have conditioned objects.
The mental-object-base (dharmāyatana): as object-conditioned consciousness, it has all [objects].
Regarding the consciousness that takes objects as its conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), it has conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as its object.

For the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and the bases of ear, nose, tongue, and body, as well as the bases of visible form, sound, and tangibles, the consciousness that takes them as objects consists of three types belonging to the desire and form realms, and those pertaining to all [categories] and those to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm;
the consciousness that takes these as its objects as conditions consists of four types.

Regarding the mind-consciousness element associated with the odor-base and the taste-base: the consciousness that takes these as its object consists of three types in the desire realm, and all types in the form realm as well as those abandoned by cultivation;

the consciousness that takes these as its object-of-object consists of four types in the desire realm, three types in the form realm, and all types in the formless realm as well as those abandoned by cultivation.
The mind-base (manāyatana): consciousness conditioned by it has conditioned objects;
consciousness conditioned by the object-conditioned [consciousness] has conditioned objects.
The mental-object-base (dharmāyatana): consciousness conditioned by it has all things as its objects.
Regarding the consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition (ālambana-pratyaya), it has conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) as its object.

As for the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha): regarding the consciousness that takes it as its condition, it is of four kinds in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu), two kinds in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), and also common to all;
regarding the consciousness that takes [it] as its condition through its own object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), it is of four kinds.

Regarding the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness: as for the consciousness that takes them as objects, it has conditioned things as its object; as for the consciousness that takes the object of that [first] consciousness as its object, it also has conditioned things as its object.

Regarding the aggregate of form: as for the consciousness that takes it as an object, it belongs to the three types in the desire and form realms, and in the formless realm, it pertains to all [types] as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna), there are four types:
the aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; as for the condition-consciousness (pratyaya-vijñāna), it has outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana);
as for the object-condition consciousness, it has conditioned objects (saṃskṛta-ālambana).

Regarding the elements from the earth element up to the space element, the consciousness that takes them as objects consists of three types [of afflictions] in the desire and form realms, and those pervasive in the formless realm as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation;
the consciousness that takes these objects as its own objects consists of all four types.

Regarding the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*): as a condition for consciousness, it is an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for that which has outflows (*sāsrava*); as a condition for the object-condition of consciousness, it is a condition for that which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Regarding the form-element (*rūpa-dharma*): as a condition for consciousness, it is of four kinds in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), of two kinds in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and [it also serves as] a universal condition for all.
Regarding consciousness as object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), there are four types.
Regarding formless phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*), consciousness as object-condition takes all [phenomena] as its object;
consciousness as object-condition takes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as its object.

Regarding visible phenomena (*dṛśya-dharma*) and resistant phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*), the consciousness that takes them as objects consists of three types from the desire and form realms, and those from the formless realm that pertain to all [categories] and are abandoned by cultivation;
the consciousness that takes the object of that object (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) consists of four types.

Regarding invisible phenomena (*anidarśana*) and non-obstructive phenomena (*apratigha*): the consciousness that takes them as objects (*ālambana-vijñāna*) consists of all [consciousnesses] associated with the contemplation of the Four Truths (*catur-āryasatya-cintā*) throughout the three realms;
the consciousness that takes those objects as its own objects (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) has conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as its objects.
Regarding contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*): the consciousness that takes them as an object has contaminated objects;
the consciousness that takes the object of that [first] consciousness as its object has conditioned objects.

Regarding uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*): the consciousness that takes them as an object consists of the three kinds [of paths], the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and those that pervade all [objects].
Object-condition consciousness has conditioned objects.
Conditioned phenomena are object-conditions for consciousness;
object-condition consciousness also has conditioned objects.
Regarding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), they are objects of consciousness through two types [of consciousness] and all pervasive mental applications (*sarvatraga-manasikāra*).
Regarding the object-conditions of consciousness, they are conditioned objects.
Regarding past, future, and present phenomena, they are objects of consciousness as conditioned objects.
Regarding the consciousness that takes objects as its condition (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna), it has conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) as its object-condition.
Regarding wholesome dharmas: the consciousness that takes them as its object (ālambana-vijñāna) has all things as its object;
the consciousness that takes objects as its condition (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna) has conditioned phenomena as its object-condition.

Regarding unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*): the consciousness that takes them as object consists of the outflow-bound objects of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those common to all [objects] and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The consciousness that takes the object of that object as its own object consists of the conditioned objects of the desire realm, the three types [of objects] of the form realm, and those common to all and those to be abandoned by cultivation of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding indeterminate dharmas: the consciousness that takes them as objects consists of the three types of the desire realm and the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) objects of the form and formless realms;
the consciousness that takes those objects as its further objects consists of the four types of the desire realm and the conditioned objects of the form and formless realms.

Regarding dharmas bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the consciousness that takes them as an object consists of the outflow-bound objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) of the desire realm, those common to all [categories] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the consciousness that takes the object of that [first] consciousness as its object (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*), it consists of the conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*) of the desire realm, the three types [of objects] of the form realm, and those common to all [categories] of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and those abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding consciousnesses that take phenomena bound to the form realm as their objects: those belonging to the desire realm are of three kinds; those belonging to the form realm are the outflow-bound (sāsrava) objects; and those belonging to the formless realm are all four kinds, including those abandoned by contemplation (bhāvanā-heya). Regarding consciousnesses that take the objects-of-objects (ālambana-ālambana) as their objects:
those belonging to the desire realm are of three kinds; those belonging to the form realm are the conditioned (saṃskṛta) objects; and those belonging to the formless realm are all four kinds.

Regarding the consciousness that takes as its object the factors associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*): it consists of three types from the desire and form realms, and the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) of the formless realm.

Regarding the consciousness that takes as its object the object of that [preceding] consciousness: it consists of three types from the desire realm, four types from the form realm, and the conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*) of the formless realm.

Regarding the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): as objects of consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*), they are of two kinds and also pervade all [consciousnesses];
as objects of the object-consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*), they are of four kinds.

Regarding the dharmas that are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*): as objects of consciousness, they are of four kinds—namely, those with outflows (*sāsrava*) that are to be abandoned by the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), it has conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya*).
Regarding dharmas abandoned by the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya-dharma*), the object-condition consciousness has outflowing objects (*sāsrava-pratyaya*);
the object-of-object-condition consciousness (*ālambanālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*) has conditioned objects.
Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the consciousness that takes them as objects consists of three types in the three realms;
the consciousness that takes those objects as its objects consists of four types.
Regarding the dharmas not subject to abandonment (*aheya*), the consciousness that takes them as objects consists of three types and those that are universal to all.
Regarding the consciousness that takes objects as its conditions (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna), it has conditioned things (saṃskṛta) as its object-condition.
Regarding the truths of suffering (duḥkha-satya) and origination (samudaya-satya), the consciousness that takes them as its conditions has out-flowing things (sāsrava) as its object-condition;
the consciousness that takes those as its object-conditions has conditioned things as its object-condition.
Regarding the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*): as a condition for consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*), it consists of two types—contemplation of cessation and that which is universal;
as a condition for the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*), it has conditioned things as its objects.
Regarding the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*): as a condition for consciousness, it consists of two types and that which is universal.
Regarding the consciousness that takes objects as its conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), there are four types:

for the dhyānas, the consciousness that takes objects consists of the four types of the desire realm, the conditioned objects of the form realm, and the two types of the formless realm along with those that pervade all;
the consciousness that takes objects as its conditions consists of the four types of the desire and formless realms, and the conditioned objects of the form realm.

Among the four immeasurables, compassion (*karuṇā*) and protection (*anukampā*) take as their objects the three types [of consciousness] in the desire and form realms, and those that pertain to all [consciousnesses] and those to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm;
as for the consciousness taking that object (*ālambana-ālambana-vijñāna*), they take the three types in the desire realm and the four types in the form and formless realms.
After the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*), the four subsequent bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are likewise.
Regarding *joy* (*prīti*): its object-consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) consists of three types from the desire and form realms;

its object-object-consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) consists of three types from the desire realm, four types from the form realm, two types from the formless realm, and those that pervade all.
The first and second liberations, as well as the first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), are likewise.

Regarding the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, and the base of nothingness: the consciousness that takes them as objects consists of three types from the desire realm, four types from the form realm, and the conditioned objects of the formless realm;
the consciousness that takes those objects as its objects likewise consists of three types from the desire realm, four types from the form realm, and the conditioned objects of the formless realm.

Regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the consciousness that takes it as its object consists of three types from the desire and form realms, and the contaminated (*sāsrava*) objects of the formless realm;

the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object consists of three types from the desire realm, four types from the form realm, and the conditioned objects (*saṃskṛtālambana*) of the formless realm.

Regarding the liberations of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness within the deliverances: they take consciousness as their object—three types from the desire realm and four types from the form and formless realms;
taking that which takes consciousness as its object as their object—three types from the desire realm and four types from the form and formless realms.
The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the liberation of cessation have consciousness as their object: three types in the three realms;
having the object of that object-consciousness as their object: three types in the desire realm and four types in the form and formless realms.
The entry into the sphere of infinite space and the entry into the sphere of infinite consciousness are likewise so; as for formless states, they share the same antidotes as those with form.

Regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*): when taking consciousness as its object, it pertains to two types in the desire realm—those common to all and those abandoned through cultivation—and to all types in the form realm and those abandoned through cultivation.

When taking the object of consciousness as its object, it pertains to four types in the desire realm, three types in the form realm, and all types in the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*): its object-consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) consists of two types from the form and formless realms, those that pervade all [categories] of the form and formless realms, and those from the desire realm that pervade all and are abandoned through cultivation;
its object-object-consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) consists of three types from the desire realm and four types from the form and formless realms.
The knowledge of others' minds has four types as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) within the desire and form realms, two types within the formless realm, and those that pervade all;
its object-object-condition (*ālambanālambana-pratyaya*) consists of the four types.

Conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*), as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness, has outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*); as the object-object-condition (*ālambanālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness, it has conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*).

Knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and the knowledges of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*), as the object-condition for consciousness, pertain to two categories as well as to all-pervading [categories].
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), there are four types.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), as for the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*): its object-condition consciousness consists of three types across the three realms;
its object-condition-of-object-condition consciousness consists of four types.

Regarding the view of misapprehension of precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): as a conditioning consciousness, it consists of the three types belonging to the three realms and those with outflows (*sāsrava*) to be abandoned by the Truth of the Path;
as a conditionally conditioned consciousness, it consists of the four types.
Regarding doubt (*vicikitsā*): as a conditioning consciousness, it consists of those with outflows.
Regarding the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), it has conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*).

Regarding greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the object-consciousness has objects that are the outflows of the desire realm; for the form realm, it includes those that are universal (*sarvatraga*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the object-conditioned consciousness, it has conditioned objects of the desire realm; for the form realm, it consists of three types; and for the formless realm, it includes those that are universal and those to be abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the consciousness that takes outflows as its object: it consists of the three types [of consciousness] of the desire realm and the outflow-associated [consciousness] of the form and formless realms.

Regarding the consciousness that takes the object of that [previous] consciousness as its object: it consists of the three types [of consciousness] of the desire realm and the conditioned-object-associated [consciousness] of the form and formless realms.

The outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) has consciousness as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and is conditioned by the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*). Its object-object-condition (*ālambanālambana-pratyaya*) is conditioned by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Among the floods (*ogha*), the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) has consciousness as its object-condition; it is conditioned by the outflows of existence in the desire realm, and by those [factors] in the form realm that are common to all and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the consciousness that takes [objects] as its conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*): in the desire realm, it has conditioned objects; in the form realm, it has three types of objects; and in the formless realm, it has all objects as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Regarding the outflowing consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*):

as for the consciousness that takes [objects] as its conditions, in the desire realm it has three types of objects; in the form and formless realms, it has outflowing objects. Regarding the consciousness that takes [objects] as its conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*):
in the desire realm it has three types of objects; in the form and formless realms, it has conditioned objects.
The remainder: the consciousness that takes [them] as an object has outflowing objects;
the consciousness that takes [the object of] that object as its object has conditioned objects.
The same applies to the yokes (*yoga*).

Within the [five] grasps (*upādāna*), regarding the grasp of sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*): the consciousness that takes it as its object consists of the outflow-tainted objects of the desire realm, and those of the form realm that are universal and abandoned through cultivation;

the consciousness that takes that object as its object consists of the conditioned objects of the desire realm, the three types of objects of the form realm, and those of the formless realm that are universal and abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding the consciousness that takes precept-reception as its object, it consists of three types from the three realms, as well as those with outflow-objects to be abandoned by the Truth of the Path;

regarding the consciousness that takes the object of that [previously mentioned] consciousness as its object, it consists of four types. Regarding the consciousness that takes the view of self-reception as its object, it consists of those with outflow-objects.
Regarding the consciousness that takes objects as its condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it has conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) as its object.

Regarding my feeling (*vedanā*), the consciousness that takes it as its condition has three types [of objects] in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) objects in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the consciousness that takes objects as its condition, it has three types [of objects] in the desire realm and conditioned things in the form and formless realms.

Among the bonds (*bandhana*), regarding the bond of sensual desire for the body (*kāma-rāga-kāya-bandhana*) and the bond of ill-will (*pratigha-kāya-bandhana*): the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) has as its objects the outflows (*sāsrava*) of the desire realm and, in the form realm, those that are universal (*sarvatraga*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The object-of-object-condition consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) has as its objects the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) factors of the desire realm, the three types [of factors] in the form realm, and in the formless realm, those that are universal and those to be abandoned by cultivation.

The bodily fetter of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists of three types [of consciousness] in the three realms as object-conditioning consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*), and those with outflows conditioned by the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) as object-conditioning consciousness;
as object-of-object-conditioning consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*), it consists of four types.
The bodily fetter of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) consists of [consciousnesses] conditioned by that which has outflows (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the consciousness that takes [objects] as its conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), it has conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) as its objects.

Within the "coverings" (*nīvaraṇa*), desire, ill-will, torpor, drowsiness, restlessness, and frivolity: their consciousness that takes [objects] as conditions has the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) objects of the desire realm; for the form realm, they pertain to all [categories] and to those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Their consciousness that takes [objects] as conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*) has the conditioned objects of the desire realm; for the form realm, they are of three kinds; for the formless realm, they pertain to all [categories] and to those abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*): in the desire realm, there are three types; in the form realm, it is associated with all [factors] as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the object-condition consciousness: in the desire realm, there are four types; in the form realm, there are three types; and in the formless realm, it is associated with all [factors] as well as those abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) among the fetters: the consciousness that takes it as its object consists of the outflow-tainted objects of the desire realm, and those common to all [categories] and those to be abandoned by cultivation in the form realm;

the consciousness that takes that object as its object consists of the conditioned objects of the desire realm, the three types [of objects] in the form realm, and those common to all and those to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm.

Regarding the fetters of stinginess and envy: as for the consciousness that takes them as objects, they consist of three types in the desire realm, and all pervasive types as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation in the form realm;

as for the consciousness that takes the objects of those objects, they consist of four types in the desire realm, three types in the form realm, and all pervasive types as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm.

As for the remainder: the consciousness that takes [the lower fetters] as its object has outflowing objects as its condition; the consciousness that takes the object of that object as its condition has conditioned phenomena as its condition.

Within the lower fetters, sensual desire and ill-will: the consciousness that takes them as its object has outflowing objects of the desire realm as its condition, and [objects] of the form realm that are common to all [fetters] as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the consciousness that takes [objects] as its conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*): for the desire realm, it has conditioned objects; for the form realm, it has three types; and for the formless realm, it pervades all [categories] as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): as the consciousness that takes [it] as its condition, it has three types in the three realms;
as the consciousness that takes [objects] as its conditions, it has four types.

Regarding the view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): as a conditioning consciousness, it consists of the three types of the three realms and those with outflows conditioned by the truth of the path;
as a conditionally-conditioning consciousness, it consists of the four types.
Regarding doubt (*vicikitsā*): as a conditioning consciousness, it consists of those with outflows conditioned by [the truths].
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), it has conditioned phenomena as its object.
Among the views, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*): for the object-consciousness, there are three types across the three realms;
for the object-object-consciousness, there are four types.

Regarding the view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): as a condition for consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*), it consists of the three types belonging to the three realms (*dhātu*) and those with outflows (*sāsrava*) conditioned by the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*);

as a condition for the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*), it consists of all four types. As for the remaining [factors], as a condition for consciousness, they consist of those with outflows.
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), it has conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*).

Within the "body of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-kāya*), for the craving of nose and tongue contact, the object-condition consciousness consists of three types from the desire realm, and all [types] and those to be abandoned by cultivation from the form realm;

the object-conditioned-object-condition consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) consists of four types from the desire realm, three types from the form realm, and all [types] and those to be abandoned by cultivation from the formless realm.
Regarding the craving for contact of the eye, ear, and body: with respect to the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*), there are three kinds in the desire realm and the form realm;

with respect to the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*), there are four kinds in the desire and form realms, two kinds in the formless realm, and those that pervade all [realms].

The craving for mental contact (*manosaṃsparśatṛṣṇā*) has, as its object, consciousness that is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and conditioned by objects; having consciousness as its object of object (*ālambanālambana*), it is conditioned by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the underlying tendencies of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) have, as their object, consciousness associated with outflows in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); they are common to all [categories] in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Object-condition consciousness;
conditioned by the conditioned of the desire realm;
three kinds in the form realm.
In the formless realm, there are the underlying tendencies of craving for existence (bhavarāgānuśaya) that pertain to all [objects] and are to be abandoned through cultivation;
these take consciousness as their object.
The consciousness that takes objects consists of three types in the desire realm; it consists of the outflow-tainted [consciousness] conditioned by the form and formless realms;
and the consciousness that takes objects of objects consists of three types in the desire realm and the conditioned-conditioned [consciousness] in the form and formless realms.

As for the remaining [fetters], the consciousness that takes them as objects has outflowing (sāsrava) objects; the consciousness that takes those objects as its own objects has conditioned (saṃskṛta) objects.

Among the fetters, the fetter of ill-will (pratigha-saṃyojana), as the consciousness that takes it as an object, has objects that are outflowing in the desire realm, and [objects] in the form realm that are common to all [fetters] as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

Regarding the consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*): for the desire realm, it has conditioned objects; for the form realm, it has three types; and for the formless realm, it encompasses all [objects] as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the fetters of stinginess (*mātsarya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*): for the consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition, they have three types in the desire realm, and for the form realm, they encompass all [objects] as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation;

for the consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), they have four types in the desire realm, three types in the form realm, and for the formless realm, they encompass all [objects] as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

As for the remaining [factors], the consciousness that takes them as objects has outflowing (sāsrava) objects; the consciousness that takes those objects as its own objects has conditioned (saṃskṛta) objects.

Regarding the ninety-eight proclivities (anuśaya), those proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of the truth of suffering in the desire realm, as objects of consciousness, consist of the three types [of proclivities] in the desire realm—those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, by the vision of origin, and by cultivation—as well as those that pervade all [categories] and those to be abandoned by cultivation in the form realm.

Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*): it consists of four types from the desire realm (excluding that which is abandoned by the truth of cessation), three types from the form realm, and all [types] from the formless realm, as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The same applies to those abandoned by the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) and those abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) in the desire realm: as for the consciousness that takes them as objects, there are three types from the desire realm, as well as those with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) to be abandoned by the truth of cessation in the desire realm; from the form realm, those that are universal (*sarvatraga*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

As for the consciousness that takes these as its object-of-objects (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*): from the desire realm, those with conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*); from the form realm, the three types; and from the formless realm, those that are universal and those to be abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): as for the consciousness that takes them as objects, there are three types from the desire realm, as well as those with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) to be abandoned by the Truth of the Path in the desire realm; and those that pertain to all [categories] and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

As for the consciousness that takes the object-of-the-object (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*), there are four types from the desire realm, three types from the form realm, and those that pertain to all [categories] and those to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
