Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) in the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*): as for the consciousness that takes them as objects, there are three types from the desire and form realms, and those from the formless realm that are universal as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As for the consciousness that takes those objects as its own objects (*ālambana-ālambana-vijñāna*), there are three types from the desire realm, and four types from the form and formless realms.
The same applies to those [defilements] abandoned through the contemplation of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) in the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*): the consciousness that takes them as objects consists of three types from the Desire and Form Realms, as well as the contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the Truth of Cessation in the Form Realm; for the Formless Realm, it consists of those that pertain to all [categories] and those abandoned through contemplation. As for the consciousness that takes these objects as its own objects (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*):
in the Desire Realm, there are three types; in the Form Realm, there are those with conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*); and in the Formless Realm, there are four types.

Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the Path Truth (*mārgasatya*) of the Form Realm: as for the consciousness that takes them as objects, there are three types in the Desire and Form Realms; [there are] those with outflow-objects (*sāsravālambana*) to be abandoned by the Path Truth of the Form Realm; and those common to all categories and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the Formless Realm.
As for the consciousness that takes the object-of-object (*ālambanālambana*), there are three types in the Desire Realm, and four types in the Form and Formless Realms.

Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): the consciousness that takes them as objects consists of three types from the three realms;
the consciousness that takes those objects as its objects consists of three types from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and four types from the form and formless realms.
The same applies to those [defilements] abandoned through the contemplation of the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*).

Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*): the object-conditioning consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) consists of the three types belonging to the three realms, as well as the outflow-conditioned (*sāsrava-ālambana*) [proclivities] abandoned through the truth of cessation in the formless realm;

the object-of-object-conditioning consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) consists of the three types of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the four types of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the conditioned-object (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*) [proclivities] of the formless realm.

Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the Path Truth (*mārgasatya*) in the Formless Realm: the consciousness that takes them as objects consists of the three types [of proclivities] in the three realms, as well as those with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) to be abandoned by the Path Truth in the Formless Realm;
the consciousness that takes those objects as its objects consists of the three types in the Desire Realm and the four types in the Form and Formless Realms. [The three gates are concluded.]
The mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) successively gives rise to fifteen states of mind.
The pleasure-faculty (*sukhendriya*) successively gives rise to eleven states of mind: five from the desire realm, five from the two dhyānas, and one from the formless realm.
The joy-faculty (*saumanasyendriya*) successively gives rise to ten states of mind: five from the desire realm and five from the second dhyāna.
The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) and the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya) sequentially give rise to five moments of mind.

The faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya), the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya), and the faculties of energy (vīrya), mindfulness (smṛti), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā) sequentially give rise to fifteen moments of mind.
Regarding the faculty of "I do not yet know" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), there is no further text concerning the sequential non-arising of fifteen minds.
Regarding the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), three minds arise sequentially.

The support of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and body-consciousness successively gives rise to ten minds: five of the desire realm and five of the first dhyāna, which are associated with the cultivation of the truths.
The support of nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness successively gives rise to five minds: those of the desire realm.

The mind-base (manāyatana), the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), and the mind-consciousness-base (manovijñānāyatana); the mind-entry (manāyatanamukha), the dharma-entry (dharmāyatanamukha); the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; the aggregates of the predominance of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; the element of consciousness; formless dharmas (arūpadharma); invisible dharmas (anidarśanadharma); non-resistant dharmas (apratighadharma); tainted dharmas (sāsravadharma); and conditioned dharmas (saṃskṛtadharma)—these sequentially give rise to fifteen states of mind.
Untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) sequentially give rise to three types of thought: those involving the contemplation of the three realms.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) do not sequentially give rise to thought.
Past phenomena sequentially give rise to two types of thought: those involving the contemplation of the two time periods of future and present.
Future dharmas do not give rise to minds in succession.
Present dharmas—whether wholesome, indeterminate, or bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—give rise to fifteen minds in succession.
Unwholesome dharmas successively give rise to five types of consciousness.
Learner (śaikṣa) and non-learner (aśaikṣa) dharmas successively give rise to three types of consciousness.

Dharmas that are neither learner nor non-learner, dharmas abandoned through the vision of the truths (darśana-heya), and dharmas abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) successively give rise to fifteen types of consciousness.
Regarding the dharmas that are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*), three moments of mind arise in succession.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), fifteen moments of mind arise in succession.
Regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), no moments of mind arise in succession.
The Truth of the Path sequentially gives rise to three minds.
Dhyāna sequentially gives rise to fifteen minds.
The Four Immeasurables sequentially give rise to six minds: one from the desire realm and five from the form realm.
The formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) successively produce fifteen states of mind.
The first and second liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the first four bases of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*) successively produce six states of mind.

The pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*), the latter four bases of mastery, and the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) successively produce five states of mind: the four [pure] form-elements and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

The liberation of the sphere of infinite space, the entry into the sphere of infinite space, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the entry into the sphere of infinite consciousness arise in succession as six minds: four formless and one form.
The liberation of the sphere of nothingness and the liberation of neither-perception-nor-non-perception give rise to five successive moments of mind;
the liberation of cessation does not give rise to successive moments of mind.
Dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) successively gives rise to two moments of consciousness.
Subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) successively gives rise to three moments of consciousness.
Knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) successively gives rise to six moments of consciousness: five pertaining to form and one pertaining to the five sensual desires.
The conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) successively gives rise to fifteen moments of mind.

The knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), as well as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*), successively give rise to three moments of mind.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) successively give rise to fifteen moments of mind.
From greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), five minds arise in succession;
for the remaining [outflows], fifteen minds arise.
Among the floods (*ogha*), from the flood of desire, five minds arise in succession.
The remaining fifteen minds are likewise.
The same applies to the yokes (*yoga*).
Among the sensations (*vedanā*), the sensation of desire (*kāma-vedanā*) successively gives rise to five minds;
Regarding the remaining [fetters], there are fifteen moments of mind.
Among the fetters (*bandhana*), the bodily fetter of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-bandhana*) and the bodily fetter of ill will (*vyāpāda-bandhana*) sequentially give rise to five moments of mind;
for the remaining [fetters], there are fifteen.
Regarding the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and the fetters of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), and envy (*īrṣyā*), five minds arise in succession;
for the remaining ten [fetters], ten [minds] arise.
Among the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), greed (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) give rise to five minds in succession.
The remaining [afflictions] and the five views give rise to fifteen types of mind.
Within the craving for the body (*kāyatanā*), the craving for nose and tongue contact gives rise to five types of mind in succession;
the craving for eye, ear, and body contact gives rise to ten types of mind in succession.
From the latent tendency of craving for mental objects (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*), fifteen states of mind arise in succession.
Among the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), those of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*pratigha*) give rise to five states of mind in succession;
the remaining [latent tendencies] give rise to fifteen states of mind.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetters of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), and envy (*īrṣyā*) successively give rise to five minds;
the remaining fifteen [fetters] do likewise.

Regarding the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), those of the desire realm successively give rise to five minds, those of the form realm to ten minds, and those of the formless realm to fifteen minds—this concludes the section on the sequential gate (*krama-mukha*).

The male faculty, the female faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of grief are driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); these tendencies possess both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) are without applied thought or sustained thought.
As for the remaining faculties, they belong to three categories of activity.
The eye-consciousness-element, the ear-consciousness-element, and the body-consciousness-element are either with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra.
The fragrance-element, the flavor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, and the tongue-consciousness-element are with vitarka and vicāra;
the remaining elements belong to the three modes of activity.

The sense-sphere of odor and the sense-sphere of taste are accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); the remaining sense-spheres belong to the three types of mental application (*tri-ākāra*).

The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*), visible phenomena (*sanidarśana-dharma*), invisible phenomena (*anidarśana-dharma*), resistant phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*), non-resistant phenomena (*apratigha-dharma*), tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), past, future, and present phenomena, wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*), indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*), and phenomena bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) belong to the three types of mental application.
Unwholesome dharmas and dharmas bound to the desire realm possess both vitarka and vicāra.
Dharmas bound to the formless realm possess neither vitarka nor vicāra.
There are none among the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, and the dharmas to be abandoned through the contemplation of the Four Truths, consist of three modes of practice.
There are none that are not to be abandoned.
The Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination consist of three modes of practice.
In the truth of cessation and the truth of the path, there is none.
Among the dhyānas, in the first dhyāna, there may be both vitarka and vicāra, or no vitarka and only vicāra;
in the remaining dhyānas, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.
The four immeasurables and the three types of cultivation.
The formless attainments are without vitarka and vicāra.
The first two liberations and the first four bases of mastery involve all three types of cultivation.
The remaining liberations (*vimokṣa*), spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā*).
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) do not exist [therein].
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) consist of three modes of activity.

The knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness; and the view of a self-identity, the clinging to rules and rituals, and doubt—these are associated with the three modes of activity (trivipāka).
Greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of desire are accompanied by both initial application and sustained application (savitarka-savicāra);
the remaining factors are associated with the three modes of activity.
Among the floods (*ogha*), the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) is with initial application and sustained application (*savitarka-savicāra*);
the remaining three [floods] possess the other three modes of activity (*tri-ākāra*).
The yokes (*yoga*) are also thus.
Among the *upādānas*, the *kāma-upādāna* is accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra;

the remaining three types of *upādāna* possess the three modes of activity (*tri-ākāra*). Among the *bandhanas*, the *kāma-rāga-bandhana* and the *pratigha-bandhana* are accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra.
The remaining three modes of activity;
the five hindrances, as well as the fetters of ill-will, stinginess, and envy, possess both applied thought and sustained thought;
the remaining three modes of activity.
Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), sensual desire and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) are accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*);
the remaining [fetters], as well as the five views and the three modes of conduct (*trivṛtti*), are likewise.
Among the attachments to the body (*kāyagredha*), the attachment to the sense-bases of nose and tongue is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought.
The craving for contact of the eye, ear, and body is either with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra;
the craving for contact of the mind belongs to all three modes of activity.
Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the tendencies of sensual desire and ill-will are with vitarka and vicāra.
The remaining three modes of conduct:
among the fetters, the fetters of ill-will, stinginess, and envy are accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra;
the remaining three modes of conduct are as follows.

Regarding the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*): those of the desire realm are accompanied by both initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*); those of the form realm belong to the three modes of activity; and those of the formless realm are without initial application or sustained application.

This concludes the examination of the five doors. As for the eye-faculty, it is bound by various proclivities; these proclivities are associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*).
The faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body are likewise.
The mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) has five;
the male and female faculties have three, excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
The faculty of suffering and the life-faculty each consist of four [factors], excluding the faculty of suffering.
The faculty of pleasure consists of four, excluding the faculty of suffering.
The faculty of suffering consists of four, excluding the faculty of pleasure.

The faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*), the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*), and three others—excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*)—are associated with these.
The faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*) and the four faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom (*paññindriya*)—excluding the faculty of pain—are associated with them.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) are not bound by any underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana), the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness bases (manovijñāna-dhātu) consist of four [faculties], excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya);
the remaining bases consist of five.
The eye-sphere (cakṣur-āyatana), the ear, nose, tongue, body, and body-spheres consist of four, excluding the faculty of suffering.

The remaining [factors] enter into five categories: the aggregates (*skandha*) and the seeds of the aggregates; material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) and immaterial phenomena (*arūpadharma*); visible phenomena (*sanidarśanadharma*) and invisible phenomena (*anidarśanadharma*); resistant phenomena (*sapratighadharma*) and non-resistant phenomena (*apratighadharma*); outflowing phenomena (*sāsravadharma*); and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). These are the five.
There are no untainted (anāsrava) dharmas or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas.
There are five [categories] of past, future, and present dharmas; wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas; and dharmas bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
There are three factors bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
There is one factor bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
There are none that are bound to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), nor among the factors of training (*śaikṣadharma*), nor among the factors beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*).
There are five [factors] that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner dharmas;
four [factors] that are dharmas to be abandoned by the vision of the Four Truths;
and five [factors] that are dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation.
There is no [factor] that is not subject to cessation.
There are five [factors] for the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination.
For the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path, there are none.
Within the dhyānas, there are three factors in the first dhyāna, excluding the faculty of suffering and the faculty of grief.
There are two in the second dhyāna: the faculty of joy and the faculty of equanimity.
There are two in the third dhyāna: the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of equanimity.
In the first dhyāna of the four dhyānas, there is one faculty:

the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). Among the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), compassion (*karuṇā*), pity (*maitrī*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) exclude three faculties: the faculty of physical pain (*duḥkhendriya*), the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*), and [the faculty of joy].
Joy (*muditā*) consists of two faculties: the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
The one formless attainment (ārūpya-samāpatti) is associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
The first and second liberations (vimokṣa), and the first four bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), are associated with two faculties: the faculty of joy (sukhendriya) and the faculty of equanimity.
The remaining liberations, bases of mastery, and all bases of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are associated with one faculty: the faculty of equanimity.
In the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), there are none.
In the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are three, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
In conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), there are five.
The knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path; emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness—these are absent [in these cases].

Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and greed (*rāga*), there are four [factors], excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Regarding ill-will (*vyāpāda*), there are four [factors], excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
The five [factors]—dullness, ignorance, the outflow of desire, and the outflow of ignorance;
the three [factors] of the outflow of existence, excluding the faculty of pain and the faculty of grief.
Among the floods (ogha), the flood of desire and the flood of ignorance consist of these five.
The outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) are three, excluding the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*);
the outflows of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*) are four, excluding the faculty of pain.
The yokes (*yoga*) are likewise.
Among the feelings, there are five in the feeling of sensual desire;
four in the feeling of attachment to precepts and the feeling of views, excluding the faculty of suffering;
and three in the feeling of self-identity, excluding the faculties of suffering and grief.
Among the bonds (*bandhana*), the bond of ill-will (*vyāpāda-bandhana*) consists of four [faculties], excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*);
the remaining bonds consist of four [faculties], excluding the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*).
Among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) consists of four [faculties], excluding the faculty of pain.
The four [hindrances] of ill-will exclude the faculty of pleasure;
drowsiness and restlessness are five [faculties];
sleep, frivolity, and doubt are three [faculties], excluding the faculties of pleasure and pain.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda*) consists of four [faculties], excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*);
the fetter of craving (*anunaya*) and the fetter of conceit (*māna*) consist of four, excluding the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*);
the fetters of stinginess (*mātsarya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*) consist of three, excluding the faculties of pleasure and pain.
Among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), sensual desire consists of four [faculties], excluding the faculty of suffering;
ill will consists of four, excluding the faculty of pleasure;

the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the five views, and the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ tṛṣṇākāyāḥ*) consist of four, excluding the faculty of suffering.
The latent tendencies of sensual desire, pride, views, and doubt—these four—are dissociated from the faculty of physical pain;
the latent tendency of ill will—these four—are dissociated from the faculty of pleasure;
the latent tendency of craving for existence—these three—are dissociated from the faculties of physical pain and mental grief.
The latent tendency of ignorance consists of five [faculties].
Among the fetters, the fetter of ill-will consists of four, excluding the faculty of pleasure;
the fetter of craving, the fetter of pride, the fetter of views, the fetter of wrong resolve, and the fetter of doubt each consist of four, excluding the faculty of pain.
The fetter of ignorance consists of five [roots];
the fetters of stinginess and envy consist of three, excluding the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of pain.
Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), those abandoned through the vision of the truths in the desire realm consist of three, excluding the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of pain.
The four types of craving abandoned through contemplation exclude the faculty of suffering.
The four types of ill-will exclude the faculty of pleasure.
The three types of pride exclude the faculties of pleasure and suffering.
Ignorance has five [roots].
In the form realm, there are three, excluding the faculty of pain and the faculty of grief.
In the formless realm, there is one. This concludes the sixth section, the Gate of the Faculties, concerning the faculty of equanimity.
Who accomplishes the eye faculty?
The answer is:
those in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) who have acquired it and do not lose it.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, and tongue.
Who possesses the faculty of the body?
The answer is:
Regarding the desire realm and the form realm:
who possesses the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*)?
The answer is:
Among all sentient beings,
who possesses the male faculty and the female faculty? Answer:
If one has attained and not lost [the faculties] in the desire realm,
who possesses the life-faculty? Answer:
Among all sentient beings,
who is endowed with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?
The answer is:
Regarding the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven: whether one is born below the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven or is a noble being (ārya) born above it, who possesses the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya)?
The answer is: [None].
Regarding the desire realm:
who possesses the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)? Answer:
Regarding the Ābhāsvara Heaven: whether one has descended from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, or if a noble being (ārya) is born above it—who among these possesses the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)?
Answer: [They do.]
If sensual desire has not yet been exhausted,
who possesses the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
The answer is:
Among all sentient beings,
who is accomplished in the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom?
The answer is:
One does not sever the roots of goodness.
Who possesses the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya), and the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātāvīndriya)? Answer:
If they are obtained and not lost,
who possesses the eye-āyatana and the āyatanas of ear, nose, and tongue?
The answer is:
If one has attained and not lost [the faculties] of the form realm or the desire realm,
who possesses the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) and the bases of visible form, sound,
and tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*)? Answer:
Regarding the desire realm and the form realm:
who possesses the eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and body-consciousness?
The answer is:
Regarding the Brahmakāyika devas, whether they have descended from the Brahmakāyika realm or are born in a higher realm and currently manifest there:
who possesses the faculties of smell (*ghrāṇa-dhātu*), taste (*jihvā-dhātu*), olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇa-vijñāna-dhātu*), and gustatory consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna-dhātu*)?
Answer: It is one for whom craving in the desire realm has not been exhausted.
Who possesses the mental faculty (manas-dhātu), the dharma-faculty (dharma-dhātu), and the mental-consciousness faculty (mano-vijñāna-dhātu)?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the eye-base and the bases of ear, nose, and tongue?
Answer: Those in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) who have attained [these faculties] and not lost them.
Who possesses the sense-base of the body (kāyāyatana) and the sense-bases of visible form, sound, and tangibles (rūpa-, śabda-, spraṣṭavyāyatana)?
Answer: The desire realm and the form realm.
Who possesses the sense-sphere of odor and the sense-sphere of taste?
Answer: The desire realm.
Who accomplishes the sense-base of mind and the sense-base of mental phenomena?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who is it that accomplishes the aggregate of form?
Answer: In the desire and form realms, or when a noble being is born into the formless realm as a dharma-body,
who accomplishes the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the aggregate of the predominance of form?
Answer: [They are] those in the desire realm and the form realm.
Who accomplishes the aggregates (skandhas) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the earth element, up to and including the space element?
Answer: Those in the desire realm and the form realm.
Who possesses the seed of consciousness?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the dharma of form?
Answer: Those in the desire realm and the form realm, or noble ones born in the formless realm—
who among them possess formless dharmas?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the visible dharmas and the resistant dharmas?
Answer: [Those in] the desire realm and the form realm.
Who accomplishes the invisible and non-obstructive dharmas?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes outflowing (sāsrava) and non-outflowing (anāsrava) dharmas, conditioned (saṃskṛta) and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas, and past, future, and present dharmas?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes wholesome dharmas?
Answer: One who has not severed the roots of goodness.
Who accomplishes unwholesome dharmas?
Answer: It is one for whom sensual craving has not yet been exhausted.
Who accomplishes indeterminate dharmas?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the dharmas bound to the desire realm?
Answer: The desire realm and the form realm.
Who accomplishes the factors bound to the form realm?
Answer: [Those belonging to] the desire realm and the form realm.
Who accomplishes the factors associated with the formless realm?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the dharmas of training and the dharmas beyond training?
Answer: If one has attained them and does not lose them,
who is it that accomplishes the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the factors to be abandoned by the vision of the truths?
Answer: It is one who has not yet produced the path-knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna).
Who accomplishes the dharmas abandoned by cultivation, the dharmas that are not to be abandoned, and the truths of suffering and its origin?
Answer: All sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the truth of cessation?
Answer: If it is attained and not lost,
who is it that accomplishes the Truth of the Path?
Answer: If it is attained,
who among those in dhyāna accomplishes the first dhyāna?
Answer: It is the Brahmakāyika devas, or those below the Brahmakāyikas, or noble beings born in the higher realms—
these are the ones who accomplish the second dhyāna.
Answer: It is the Ābhāsvara devas, or those who have descended from the Ābhāsvara realm, or noble beings born in the higher realms.
Who accomplishes the third dhyāna?
Answer: It is the Śubhakṛtsna devas, or those born below the Śubhakṛtsna level, or noble ones born above it—
who accomplishes the fourth dhyāna?
Answer: Regarding the Fruit-Bearing Heaven (Phala-deva), whether it be those who have descended from the Fruit-Bearing Heaven or noble ones born in the higher realms—
who among them accomplishes the four immeasurables?
Answer: If one has attained it and does not lose it.
Among those in the formless realm, who accomplishes the sphere of infinite space?
Answer: Regarding those born in the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), whether they are below that sphere or are noble ones (ārya) born above it—
who among them accomplishes the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana)?
Answer: Regarding those born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana), whether they descend from that sphere or are noble ones (ārya) born in a higher realm,
who would achieve the "unestablished" state?
Answer:

Those born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) include those who have descended from that sphere, as well as undefiled persons (anāsrava-pudgala) and all superior noble ones (ārya) who are born above.
Who accomplishes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
The answer is:
all sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the liberations (vimokṣa), the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana)?
Answer: Whoever has attained them and does not lose them.
Who accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: Whoever has attained them.
Who achieves the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: One who has attained it and does not lose it.
Who accomplishes conventional knowledge?
The answer is:
all sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path, as well as emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness?
Answer: Whoever has attained them.
Regarding the fetters, who possesses the view of a self-identity?
The answer is:
those in whom the knowledge of the unknown has not yet arisen.
Who accomplishes the adherence to precepts and the doubt? Answer:
One for whom the knowledge of the path of non-arising has not yet arisen.
Who accomplishes lust, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of desire?
Answer: One whose craving for the realm of desire is not yet exhausted.
Who accomplishes the outflow of existence and the outflow of ignorance?
The answer is:
one whose craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has not yet been exhausted.
Among those in the flow, who accomplishes the flow of desire?
Answer: One whose craving for desire is not yet exhausted.
Who accomplishes the outflow of existence (bhava-āsrava) and the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava)? Answer:
One whose craving for the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is not yet exhausted.
Who accomplishes the outflow of views? Answer:
One for whom the knowledge of the path of non-arising has not yet arisen.
The same applies to the yokes (*yoga*).
Among the graspings (*upādāna*), who possesses the grasping of desire?
The answer is:
If sensual desire has not been exhausted,
who accomplishes the acquisition of precepts and the acquisition of views?
The answer is:
When the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen and the knowledge of the unknown has not yet arisen,
who possesses the acquisition of self?
The answer is:
When craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has not yet been exhausted,
among the fetters (*bandhana*), who is bound by the bodily-fetter of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-bandhana*) and the bodily-fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-bandhana*)? Answer:
If sensual desire has not yet been exhausted,
who is bound by the fetter of attachment to precepts and vows and the fetter of the view of self-identity?
The answer is:
When the knowledge of the path (mārga-anājñāta-jñāna) has not yet arisen,

among the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), who possesses the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill will (vyāpāda), sloth and torpor (styānamiddha), or restlessness and remorse (auddhatyakaukṛtya)? Answer:
If sensual desire has not been exhausted,
who possesses the hindrance of doubt?
The answer is:
If sensual desire has not yet been exhausted and the knowledge of the path regarding phenomena (mārga-dharma-jñāna) has not yet arisen,
among the fetters (saṃyojana), who is possessed of the fetters of ill-will, stinginess,
and envy? Answer:
If sensual desire is not yet exhausted,
who possesses the fetter of craving and the fetter of conceit?
The answer is:
Regarding those who have not yet exhausted their craving for the formless realm:
among the lower fetters, who possesses sensual desire and ill will?
The answer is:
Sensual craving has not yet been exhausted.
Who possesses the view of a self-identity?
The answer is:
Who possesses the perversion of precepts and the doubt when the "knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering" (duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna) has not yet arisen? Answer:
Regarding those for whom the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
among those in the stage of seeing, who possesses the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi)?
The answer is:

When the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkhe ’jñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, who possesses false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)? Answer: [The one who has not yet produced that knowledge].
When the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
among the attachments to the body (*kāyatanānuśaya*), who possesses the attachment to the contact of the nose and the tongue? Answer:
If sensual desire has not yet been exhausted,
who possesses craving for eye-contact, ear-contact,
and body-contact? Answer:
If craving for the Brahma-heaven has not yet been exhausted, who is it that accomplishes "having already exhausted craving"?
Answer: [It is one who has attained the fruit of non-returning.]
Regarding those whose craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not yet exhausted:
among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), who possesses the underlying tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and the underlying tendency of ill-will (*pratigha*)?
The answer is:
If sensual craving has not yet been exhausted,
who possesses the underlying tendencies of craving for existence, conceit, and ignorance?
The answer is:
Who, while not yet having exhausted craving for the formless realm,
possesses the latent tendency of views and the latent tendency of doubt?
The answer is:
When the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, among the fetters (saṃyojana), which ones does one possess:
the fetter of ill-will (pratigha), the fetter of stinginess (mātsarya), or the fetter of envy (īrṣyā)? Answer:
If sensual craving has not been exhausted,
who is bound by the fetters of craving, pride, and ignorance?
The answer is:
Who, while not yet having exhausted craving for the formless realm,
possesses the fetter of views along with the fetters of envy and doubt? Answer:
When the knowledge of the path and the knowledge of what was previously unknown have not yet arisen,
among the ninety-eight *anuśayas*, which ones are possessed by one who has abandoned the *anuśayas* of the suffering-truth (*duḥkha-satya*) of the desire realm? Answer:

If sensual craving has not yet been exhausted, and the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) has not yet arisen—then who possesses the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the truth of origin (samudaya-satya) in the desire realm?
Answer: [Such a person].
If sensual craving has not yet been exhausted and the cultivation of dharma-knowledge has not yet arisen,
who is endowed with the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the truth of cessation in the desire realm? Answer:
If sensual craving has not been exhausted, and the dharma-knowledge of exhaustion has not yet arisen,
who is endowed with the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the Path Truth (mārgasatya) of the desire realm? Answer:
If sensual craving has not yet been exhausted, and the knowledge of the path regarding phenomena (mārga-dharma-jñāna) has not yet arisen,
who possesses the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm?
The answer is:
If sensual desire has not yet been exhausted,
who is endowed with the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering in the realm of form? Answer:

If craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) has not been exhausted, and if the knowledge of the suffering of the realm of form (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, who possesses the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*) in the realm of form?
Answer: [Such a person].

If craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) has not been exhausted, and if the knowledge of the unknown (*anvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen through practice—who then possesses the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) in the realm of form?
Answer: [Such a person].

If craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) is not yet exhausted, or if it has been exhausted but the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) has not yet arisen—whom does this constitute as being possessed of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the Path Truth (*mārgasatya*) of the form realm? Answer: [Those who have not yet abandoned them].

If craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) has not been exhausted, and if the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) has not yet arisen, who possesses the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the form realm?
Answer: [Such a person].
If craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) has not been exhausted,
who possesses the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)? Answer:
When the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering has not yet arisen,
who possesses the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the truth of origin within the formless realm?
The answer is:
The knowledge of the unknown has not yet arisen.
Who possesses the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the truth of cessation within the formless realm? Answer:
When the knowledge of the unknown (*ajñāta-jñāna*) has not yet arisen,
who is possessed of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the Path Truth (*mārga-satya*) of the formless realm? Answer:
When the knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen,
who is possessed of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the formless realm? Answer:
The seventh section is concluded: those who have not yet exhausted their craving for the formless realm do not possess [it].
Who does not possess the eye faculty?
The answer is:
In the formless realm, the faculties of the desire realm—whether not yet attained or having been attained and then lost—are absent.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, and tongue.
Who does not possess the faculty of the body?
Answer: There is no one who does not possess the mental faculty (manas-indriya) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Who, then, does not possess the male faculty (puruṣendriya) or the female faculty (strīndriya)?
Answer: In the form and formless realms, [the life-faculty] has not been attained; in the desire realm, it may not have been attained, or if attained, it is lost.
There is no case where the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not fully accomplished.
Who does not possess the faculty of pleasure?
The answer is:
ordinary persons born in the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna).
Who does not possess the faculty of suffering?
The answer is:
those in the realms of form and formlessness.
Who does not possess the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)?
The answer is:
ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Who does not possess the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*)?
Answer: One for whom sensual craving (*kāmarāga*) has been exhausted.
The faculties of guarding are not unaccomplished.
Who does not accomplish the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom?
The answer is:
The roots of goodness are severed.
Who does not possess the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known"? Answer:
Whether they have not yet obtained them, or having obtained them they have lost them—
who does not possess the eye-base (cakṣur-dhātu) and the bases of the ear, nose, and tongue?
The answer is:
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), these do not exist; in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), they have either not yet been attained or, having been attained, have been lost.
Who does not possess the possession of the body (kāyadhāraṇa) and the possessions of visible form, sound, and tangibles (rūpa-śabda-spraṣṭavyadhāraṇa)? Answer:
The Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Who does not possess the possession of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and body-consciousness? Answer:
For one born in the Brahma Heaven, these do not manifest before them.
Who does not possess the acquisition of odor, the acquisition of taste, the acquisition of nose-consciousness, and the acquisition of tongue-consciousness? Answer:
In the realms of form and formlessness,
there is no one who does not achieve the possession of the mind-base (*manāyatana*), the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), and the mental-consciousness-base (*manovijñānāyatana*).
Who does not achieve the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*) and the bases of the ear, nose, and tongue?
Answer: In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), [these are absent]; in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), they are either not yet attained or, having been attained, are lost.
Who does not possess the sense-base of body (kāyāyatana) and the sense-bases of visible form, sound, and tangibles (rūpa-śabda-spraṣṭavyāyatana)?
Answer: The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Who does not possess the acquisition of odors and tastes?
Answer: In the realms of form and formlessness,
there is no sense-base of mind (manāyatana) or sense-base of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is not accomplished.
Who does not achieve the aggregate of form? Answer:
Ordinary persons born in the formless realm.
The aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all fully accomplished.
Who does not fully accomplish the aggregate of the predominance of form? Answer:
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
there is no aggregate of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that is not fully accomplished.
Who is it that does not accomplish the earth element, up to and including the space element?
Answer: In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
there is no seed of consciousness that is not fully accomplished.
Who does not achieve the dharmas of form?
The answer is:
ordinary beings born in the formless realm.
There is no formless dharma that is not accomplished.
Who does not accomplish visible dharmas and obstructive dharmas? Answer:
In the formless realm,
there is no dharma that is invisible, non-obstructive, or not fully accomplished.
There is no dharma— whether outflowing or non-outflowing, conditioned or unconditioned, past, future, or present— that is not fully accomplished.
Who does not accomplish wholesome dharmas?
The answer is:
one whose roots of goodness are severed.
Who does not accomplish unwholesome dharmas?
The answer is:
one for whom sensual craving has been exhausted.
There is no indeterminate dharma that is not accomplished.
Who does not accomplish the dharmas bound to the desire realm? Answer:
The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Who does not possess the factors associated with the form realm (rūpadhātu)? Answer:
Regarding the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):
there is no dharma bound to the formless realm that is not accomplished.
Who does not accomplish the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Answer: Whether they have not yet been attained or, having been attained, are lost;
there are no dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner which one does not possess.
Who does not accomplish the dharmas to be abandoned by the vision of the truths?
Answer: One in whom the subsequent knowledge of the path has arisen.
Regarding those things abandoned through reflection, there is no dharma of cessation; the truth of suffering and the truth of origination are not unaccomplished.
Who does not accomplish the truth of cessation?
The answer is:
Whether they have not yet attained it, or having attained it they lose it—
who would not be established in the Truth of the Path?
The answer is:
"Not yet attained.
[Question: Among those in dhyāna, who does not achieve the first dhyāna?
[Answer: It is said:
When ordinary beings are born in the Brahma Heaven,
who does not achieve the second dhyāna?
The answer is:
When ordinary beings are born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
who would not be accomplished in the third dhyāna?
The answer is:
When ordinary worldlings are born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven,
who would not possess the fourth dhyāna?
The answer is:
Regarding the statement that ordinary beings are born in the formless realm, the translator notes that this is how the original scripture reads.
Who would not be accomplished in the four immeasurables?
The answer is as follows:
Whether they have not yet attained it, or having attained it have lost it—
among those in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), who does not possess the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana)?
The answer is:
When ordinary worldlings are born in the sphere of infinite space,
who does not achieve the sphere of infinite consciousness?
The answer is:
When ordinary persons are born in the sphere of consciousness (vijñānasthiti),
who does not achieve the station of non-activity?
The answer is:

When ordinary persons are born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), there is nothing they do not achieve regarding the spheres of liberation (vimokṣa), the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana). Who would fail to achieve these? None.
Answer: Whether they have not yet attained it, or having attained it they lose it—
who would not fail to accomplish the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
Answer: Not yet.
Who does not possess the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: Whether it has not yet been attained or, having been attained, is lost— in all such cases,
conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is not unaccomplished.
Who does not accomplish the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path, as well as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
Answer: Those who have not yet attained them.
Among the fetters, who does not possess the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi)?
Answer: One in whom the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (duḥkhe ’jñāsyāmīti-jñāna) has arisen.
Who does not accomplish the adherence to precepts and doubt?
Answer: When the knowledge of the path of non-arising has arisen.
Who does not accomplish greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of sensual desire?
Answer: One for whom sensual craving has been exhausted.
Who does not possess the outflow of the taints and the outflow of ignorance?
Answer: One for whom craving for the formless realm has been exhausted.
Among those in the stream, who does not possess the flow of desire?
The answer is:
one for whom sensual craving has been exhausted.
Who does not accomplish the outflow of existence and the outflow of ignorance?
Answer: One for whom craving for the formless realm has been exhausted.
Who does not accomplish the outflow of views?
Answer: One in whom the subsequent knowledge of the path has arisen.
The yoke is also like this.
Regarding the sensations (*vedanā*), who does not possess the sensation of desire (*kāma-vedanā*)?
The answer is:
When sensual craving has already been exhausted,
who does not possess the acceptance of precepts and the acceptance of views?
The answer is:
When the knowledge of the unknown regarding the Path arises,
who does not possess the acquisition of self?
The answer is:
When craving for the formless realm has been exhausted,
among the fetters, who does not possess the bodily fetter of sensual desire and the bodily fetter of ill will? Answer:
Sensual craving has already been exhausted.
Who does not possess the fetter of attachment to precepts and rituals and the fetter of the view of self?
The answer is:

When the knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) arises, among the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), who does not possess sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill will (vyāpāda), sloth-and-torpor (styāna-middha), and restlessness-and-regret (auddhatya-kaukṛtya)?
Answer: [None].
When sensual craving has already been exhausted,
who does not possess the hindrance of doubt?
The answer is:
When sensual craving has already been exhausted, or when sensual craving has not yet been exhausted and the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) has arisen—
among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), who does not possess the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya*), and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*)? Answer:
When sensual craving has already been exhausted, who does not possess the fetter of craving and the fetter of conceit?
Answer: [No one].
The craving for the formless realm has already been exhausted.
Among those with lower fetters, who does not possess sensual desire and ill will? Answer:
Sensual desire has already been exhausted.
Who does not possess the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)? Answer:
When the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering arises,
who does not possess the view of self-righteousness (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*)? Answer:
When the knowledge of the unknown regarding the Path arises,
among those who have seen [the truths], who does not possess the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi)? Answer:

When the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) arises, who does not possess false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?
Answer: [None].
When the knowledge of the path of non-arising arises, who among those possessing craving for the body does not possess craving for nose-contact and tongue-contact?
Answer: [None].
Sensual craving has already been exhausted.
Who does not possess eye-contact-craving, ear-contact-craving, and body-contact-craving? Answer:
The craving for the Brahma heavens has been exhausted.
Who would not be endowed with craving for mental volition?
The answer is:
Attachment to the formless realm has been exhausted.
Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), who does not possess the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and ill will? Answer:

When sensual craving has already been exhausted, who does not possess the latent tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*), the latent tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*), and the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*)?
The answer is: [no one].
The craving for the formless realm has already been exhausted.
Who does not possess the latent tendency of views and the latent tendency of doubt? Answer:
The path-knowledge of the unknown arises.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), who does not possess the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya*), and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*)? Answer:
When sensual craving has already been exhausted, who does not possess the fetter of craving, the fetter of conceit, and the fetter of ignorance?
The answer is: [no one].
When craving for the formless realm has been exhausted, who does not possess the fetters of views, transgression of precepts, and doubt?
Answer: [None].
The path-knowledge of the unknown arises.

Regarding the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), which ones are not possessed by one who has abandoned the proclivities to be severed through the vision of the truth of suffering in the desire realm?
Answer:

When craving for sensual desire has already been exhausted, if craving for sensual desire has not yet been exhausted and the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises:
who does not possess the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*) of the desire realm? Answer:
When craving for sensual desire has already been exhausted, if craving for sensual desire has not yet been exhausted, the knowledge of the dharma regarding the origin of suffering arises.
Who does not possess the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the truth of the cessation of suffering within the desire realm?
Answer: [The following].

When craving for sensual desire has already been exhausted, or when craving for sensual desire has not yet been exhausted but the knowledge of the exhaustion of phenomena (kṣayajñāna) has arisen—whom does this not constitute as having abandoned the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the Path Truth of the Desire Realm?
Answer: [The Arhat].
When sensual craving has already been exhausted, if sensual craving has not yet been exhausted, the path-knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) arises.
Who does not possess the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm? Answer: [The one for whom sensual craving has already been exhausted.]
Sensual craving has already been exhausted.
Who does not possess the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering within the form realm? Answer:

If craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) has already been exhausted, or if craving for the realm of form has not yet been exhausted when the knowledge of the suffering of the unknown (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) arises—who does not possess the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*) of the realm of form? Answer: [The one who has already exhausted craving for the realm of form.]
When craving for form has been exhausted, if craving for form has not yet been exhausted, the knowledge of the subsequent realization (anvaya-jñāna) arises.
Who does not possess the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the truth of cessation within the realm of form? Answer: [The one who has not yet exhausted craving for form.]
When craving for form has been exhausted, if craving for form has not yet been exhausted, the knowledge of the exhaustion of the unknown arises.
Who does not possess the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the Path Truth of the Form Realm? Answer: [The one who has not yet exhausted craving for form.]

When craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) has been exhausted, or when craving for the form realm has not yet been exhausted and the knowledge of the path of non-arising (*anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen—who does not possess the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the form realm?
Answer: [Such a person].
Craving for the realm of form has already been exhausted.
Who does not possess the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering in the formless realm? Answer:
The knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering has arisen.
Who does not possess the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the truth of origin within the formless realm? Answer:
The knowledge of the unknown (anvaya-jñāna) has arisen.
Who does not possess the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the truth of cessation within the formless realm? Answer:
The knowledge of the exhaustion of the unknown (ājñātāvyajñāna) has arisen.
Who does not possess the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the Path Truth of the formless realm? Answer:
The path of knowledge of the unknown arises.
Who does not possess the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm?
Answer: [As follows].
The craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is already exhausted; the eight gates [of non-attainment] are thus concluded.

Regarding the faculty of the eye (*cakṣurindriya*), at the time of the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*): for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has reached the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*), thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) have the knowledge of their abandonment, yet the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not entirely exhausted; for a noble one (*ārya*), three underlying tendencies of the form realm have the knowledge of their abandonment, yet the fetters are not entirely exhausted.

As with the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties; the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), ear, nose, tongue, and body bases; the form, sound, and tangibility bases; the eye-sphere (*cakṣur-dhātu*), ear, nose, tongue, and body spheres; the form, sound, and tangibility spheres; the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the aggregate of predominance over form (*rūpādhipati-skandha*); the earth element up to the space element; form-phenomena, visible phenomena, and resistant phenomena; phenomena bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*); the fourth dhyāna; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the liberations (*vimokṣa*); the latter four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*); and the knowledge of others' minds. At the time of abandoning knowledge, for an ordinary person who has reached the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form, thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through knowledge, yet the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not entirely exhausted; for a noble one (*ārya*), three underlying tendencies are abandoned through knowledge, yet the fetters are not entirely exhausted.

When the faculty of mind (manendriya) attains the knowledge of abandonment, one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); three acquisitions (prāpti) are abandoned through this knowledge, and the three fetters (saṃyojana) are forever exhausted.
As it is with the faculty of mind, so it is with the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya), the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
the mental base (manāyatana), the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), and the mental-consciousness base (manovijñānāyatana); and the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness; the element of consciousness;
formless phenomena; invisible phenomena; non-obstructive phenomena; phenomena with outflows; conditioned phenomena; past, future, and present phenomena;
wholesome phenomena and indeterminate phenomena; phenomena bound to the formless realm; and phenomena that are neither in training nor beyond training.

When one realizes through the knowledge of equanimity and the knowledge of abandonment the states abandoned by reflection, the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of Origination, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the liberation of cessation, one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm;
three underlying tendencies are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters are eternally exhausted.

Regarding the male faculty and the female faculty: at the time of their abandonment through knowledge, for an ordinary person who has reached the exhaustion of sensual desire, thirty-six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters (saṃyojana) are eternally exhausted; for a noble one, four underlying tendencies are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters are eternally exhausted.

As with the male faculty and the female faculty, so it is with the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), the odor-base (*gandhāyatana*) and taste-base (*rasāyatana*), the nose-consciousness-base (*ghrāṇavijñānāyatana*) and tongue-consciousness-base (*jihvāvijñānāyatana*), the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*) and taste-element (*rasadhātu*), unwholesome phenomena (*akuśaladharma*), and phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātupratisaṃyuktadharma*). At the time of abandoning and knowing these, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has reached the exhaustion of desire for the sense realm, thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned and known, and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eternally exhausted; for a noble one (*ārya*), four underlying tendencies are abandoned and known, and the three fetters are eternally exhausted.

Regarding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), at the time of its abandonment through knowledge, one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the Subhakṛtsna Heaven; yet, even when that faculty of pleasure is abandoned through knowledge, the fetters and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not entirely exhausted.

Regarding the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), at the time of its abandonment through knowledge, one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the Ābhāsvara Heaven; yet, even when that faculty of joy is abandoned through knowledge, the fetters and underlying tendencies are not entirely exhausted.

Regarding the maintenance of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and body-consciousness: at the time of the knowledge of abandonment when one reaches the exhaustion of craving in the Brahma-heavens, although there is the knowledge of abandonment regarding the maintenance of those three consciousnesses, the fetters and underlying tendencies are not entirely exhausted.

When the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) regarding the dharmas to be abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśanaheya*) is attained: if desire for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) is not yet exhausted and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is present before one, fourteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eternally exhausted;

if desire for the realm of form is already exhausted and the subsequent knowledge of the path is present before one, seven underlying tendencies are abandoned and the three fetters are eternally exhausted.

Regarding the first dhyāna among the meditative absorptions: at the time of the knowledge of abandonment, although one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the first dhyāna, the fetters and underlying tendencies associated with that knowledge of abandonment of the first dhyāna are not yet entirely exhausted.

Regarding the second dhyāna: at the time of the knowledge of abandonment, although one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of the second dhyāna, the fetters and underlying tendencies associated with that knowledge of abandonment of the second dhyāna are not yet entirely exhausted.
As with the second dhyāna, so it is with joy (*prīti*), the first and second liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Regarding the third dhyāna, at the time of the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the third dhyāna; yet, by that very knowledge of abandonment of the third dhyāna, the fetters and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not entirely exhausted.

Regarding the sphere of infinite space within the formless realm: at the time of attaining the knowledge of abandonment, one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of infinite space; yet, through that very knowledge of abandonment of the sphere of infinite space, the fetters and underlying tendencies are not entirely exhausted.
The same applies to the liberation of the sphere of infinite space and the entry into the sphere of infinite space.

Regarding the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*): at the time of the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of consciousness; yet, regarding that very sphere of consciousness, the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not entirely exhausted.
The same applies to liberation from the sphere of consciousness and entry into the sphere of consciousness.

Regarding the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*): at the time when the knowledge of abandonment reaches the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of nothingness, although that knowledge of abandonment regarding the sphere of nothingness exists, the fetters and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not entirely exhausted.
The same applies to liberation from the sphere of nothingness.

Regarding the fetter of the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): at the time of abandoning through knowledge, when craving for the form realm has not yet been exhausted and the "unknown-to-be-known" knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) is present, eighteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through knowledge, but the fetters are not entirely exhausted.

When craving for the form realm has already been exhausted and the "unknown-to-be-known" knowledge of suffering is present, nine underlying tendencies are abandoned through knowledge, but the fetters are not entirely exhausted.

As with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), so it is with the view of a self among the lower fetters (avarabhāgīya) and the view of a self among the views (dṛṣṭi). At the time of abandoning through knowledge, when craving for the form realm has not yet been exhausted and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna) is present, eighteen proclivities (anuśaya) are abandoned through knowledge, yet the fetters (saṃyojana) are not entirely exhausted.

When craving for the form realm has already been exhausted and the subsequent knowledge of suffering is present, nine proclivities are abandoned through knowledge, yet the fetters are not entirely exhausted.

Regarding the abandonment through knowledge of the view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*): when the desire for the form realm (*rūparāga*) has not yet been exhausted and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is present, fourteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eternally exhausted;

when the desire for the form realm has already been exhausted and the subsequent knowledge of the path is present, seven underlying tendencies are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters are eternally exhausted.

As with the underlying tendency of attachment to precepts (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*), so it is with the influx of views (*diṭṭhāsava*), the yoke of views (*diṭṭhiyoga*), the clinging to precepts (*sīlabbatupādāna*), the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), the bodily fetter of attachment to precepts (*sīlabbataparāmāsakāyagandha*), the bodily fetter of the view of self (*attānudiṭṭhikāyagandha*), attachment to precepts and doubt among the lower fetters (*orambhāgiya*), wrong view, the clinging to views, and attachment to precepts among the views, the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) and the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) among the proclivities (*anusaya*), and the fetter of views, the fetter of resentment, and the fetter of doubt among the fetters (*saṃyojana*). At the time of the knowledge of abandonment (*pahāṇañāṇa*), when the craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) has not yet been exhausted and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*maggānvayāñāṇa*) is present, there is the abandonment of fourteen underlying tendencies and the permanent exhaustion of three fetters.

When the craving for the form realm has already been exhausted and the subsequent knowledge of the path is present, there is the abandonment of seven underlying tendencies and the permanent exhaustion of three fetters.

When greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) are abandoned through knowledge, for an ordinary person who has reached the exhaustion of sensual craving, thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are forever exhausted; for a noble one (*ārya*), four underlying tendencies are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters are forever exhausted.

Thus, when there is the abandonment through knowledge (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) of the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the yoke of desire (*kāma-yoga*), the grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*), the bodily fetters of desire-lust (*kāmacchanda-kāya-bandhana*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda-kāya-bandhana*), among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*)—namely sensual desire, ill-will, sloth-torpor, and restlessness-and-worry; among the fetters (*saṃyojana*)—namely the fetters of ill-will, avarice, and envy; among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*)—namely sensual desire and ill-will; among the attachments to the body (*kāmarāga-śarīra*)—namely the attachment to odors and tastes; among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)—namely the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and ill-will; and among the fetters (*saṃyojana*)—namely the fetters of ill-will, avarice, and envy: at that time of abandonment through knowledge, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has reached the exhaustion of desire-lust, thirty-six underlying tendencies are abandoned through knowledge and three fetters are eternally exhausted; for a noble one (*ārya*), four underlying tendencies are abandoned through knowledge and three fetters are eternally exhausted.

Regarding the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*): at the time of the knowledge of abandonment, when craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is exhausted, three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through knowledge and three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eternally eliminated.

Likewise, regarding the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*), the yoke of existence (*bhava-yoga*), the yoke of ignorance (*avidyā-yoga*), the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*), the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), the craving for mental contact (*manasikāra-tṛṣṇā*), the underlying tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*), the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*), the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*): at the time of the knowledge of abandonment, when craving for the formless realm is exhausted, three underlying tendencies are abandoned through knowledge and three fetters are eternally eliminated.

Regarding the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*): at the time of the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*), when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) reaches the exhaustion of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-kṣaya*), thirty-six latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are forever exhausted; however, when a noble one (*ārya*) brings the knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) into presence, eight latent tendencies are abandoned through knowledge, yet the fetters are not entirely exhausted.

Regarding the craving associated with eye, ear, and body-contact: at the time of abandoning through knowledge, one reaches the exhaustion of craving up to the Brahma-heaven; yet, for those three types of craving, the underlying fetters (*anuśaya*) are not entirely exhausted by that abandonment through knowledge.

Among the ninety-eight underlying fetters, when the underlying fetters to be abandoned by the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) in the desire realm are abandoned through knowledge, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) reaches the exhaustion of desire for the desire realm, whereby thirty-six underlying fetters are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eternally exhausted. For a noble one (*ārya*), when the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is present before them, ten underlying fetters are abandoned through knowledge, yet the fetters are not entirely exhausted.

Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the knowledge of the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*) within the desire realm: at the time of their abandonment through knowledge, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) reaches the exhaustion of desire for the desire realm, thirty-six proclivities are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eternally exhausted; however, when a noble one (*ārya*) brings the knowledge of the dharma regarding origin (*samudayadharmajñāna*) into presence, seven proclivities are abandoned through knowledge, yet the fetters are not entirely exhausted.
The same applies to those [defilements] abandoned through the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

When one attains the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) in the desire realm, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has reached the exhaustion of sensual craving abandons thirty-six proclivities through the knowledge of abandonment and brings the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) to permanent end; whereas for a noble one (*ārya*), when the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) is present before them, they abandon eight proclivities through the knowledge of abandonment, yet the fetters are not entirely exhausted.

Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*): at the time of their abandonment through knowledge, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has reached the exhaustion of desire, thirty-six proclivities are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eternally exhausted; for a noble one (*ārya*), four proclivities are abandoned through knowledge and the three fetters are eternally exhausted.
