Composed by Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīr together with Zhu Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty.
Section Three: The Chapter on Knowledge (Jñāna-vastu). Third, the Verse Summary of the Five Sub-chapters:
The eightfold [knowledge] has five locations;
the knowledge of others' minds, if one can practice this knowledge, is most excellent when associated [with the others].
Among the eighty kinds of knowledge, discernment is always foremost; all associated awakenings—
The world perceives the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"There are eight kinds of those who have attained the path of training (*śaikṣa*), and ten kinds of Arhats who have exhausted all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)."
Regarding the eight types of trainees (*śaikṣa*), how many are accomplished in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
Regarding the ten types of *arhats* whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*), how many are accomplished in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
What is view? What is knowledge? What is wisdom?
If it is vision, is it knowledge?
If it is knowledge, is it vision?
If it is vision, is it wisdom?
If it is wisdom (*prajñā*), is it vision (*darśana*)?
If it is knowledge (*jñāna*), is it wisdom?
And if it is wisdom, is it knowledge?
Is vision subsumed by knowledge, or is knowledge subsumed by vision?
Is vision subsumed by wisdom, or is wisdom subsumed by vision?
Is knowledge subsumed by wisdom, or is wisdom subsumed by knowledge?
If one is accomplished in view, is one also accomplished in knowledge?
If one is accomplished in knowledge, is one also accomplished in view?
If one is accomplished in view, is one also accomplished in wisdom?
If one possesses wisdom (*paññā*), does that person possess vision (*diṭṭhi*)?
If one possesses knowledge (*ñāṇa*), does that person possess wisdom?
And if one possesses wisdom, does that person possess knowledge?
If a view has already ceased without remainder, is that [cessation] wisdom?
If wisdom has already ceased without remainder, is that [cessation] a view?
If a view has already ceased without remainder, is that [cessation] discernment (*prajñā*)?
If wisdom (*prajñā*) has been extinguished without remainder, is that [state] view (*dṛṣṭi*)?
If knowledge (*jñāna*) has been extinguished without remainder, is that wisdom?
If wisdom has been extinguished without remainder, is that knowledge?
Question: Regarding determination, inclusion, accomplishment, and cessation:
Is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
And if it is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena, is it right view?
Is that which is called conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Conversely, is that which is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena conventional knowledge?
When the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present before one, how many awakening factors and how many elements of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are present?

When the awakening factors of energy (*vīrya*), joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), right speech (*samyagvāc*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) manifest, how many awakening factors and how many path constituents (*mārgāṅga*) manifest?
If various phenomena are associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness, are they also associated with the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena?
Conversely, if various phenomena are associated with the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena, are they also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness?

Are all phenomena associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness, as well as the awakening factors of energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity; and with right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration?
If various phenomena are associated with right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), are they also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
And if various phenomena are associated with everything up to right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), are they also associated with right concentration?
Furthermore, if various phenomena are associated with right concentration, are they also associated with right mindfulness?
What is mundane right view?
What is mundane right knowledge?
If it is mundane right view, is it also mundane right knowledge?
If it is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-samprajanya*), is it conventional view (*saṃvṛti-dṛṣṭi*)?
Is conventional view subsumed under conventional knowledge?
And if it is conventional knowledge, is it subsumed under conventional view?
If one possesses the mundane right view (*laukika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), does one also possess mundane right knowledge (*laukika-samyagjñāna*)?
Conversely, if one possesses mundane right knowledge, does one also possess mundane right view?
If worldly views (*laukikadṛṣṭi*) and so forth have been extinguished without remainder, are worldly knowledges (*laukikajñāna*) and so forth also extinguished?
Conversely, if worldly knowledges and so forth have been extinguished without remainder, are worldly views and so forth also extinguished?
Question: Regarding determination, inclusion, accomplishment, and cessation:
what is untainted right view?
What is untainted right knowledge?
If it is an outflow-free (anāsrava) view and so forth, is it an outflow-free wisdom (jñāna) and so forth?
Conversely, if it is an outflow-free wisdom and so forth, is it an outflow-free view and so forth?
Are outflow-free views and so forth subsumed within outflow-free wisdom and so forth?
If one possesses untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and so forth, is it necessarily subsumed under untainted vision (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*)?
If one is endowed with untainted vision and so forth, does one also possess untainted knowledge and so forth?
Furthermore, if one is endowed with untainted knowledge and so forth, does one also possess untainted vision and so forth?
Regarding the questions, the established principles, the inclusion, and the accomplishment—
may the meaning of this chapter be fully expounded.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
There are eight types of those who have attained the path of training (*śaikṣa*) and ten types of Arhats whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*).
Regarding these eight types of those on the path of training: how many are accomplished in the past, how many are accomplished in the future, and how many are accomplished in the present?
Answer:

If, based on the samādhi with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), the first vision of one in training (*śaikṣa*) manifests before him, he possesses eight types [of knowledges] in the future and eight types in the present, but none in the past; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

If, relying on the samādhi with directed thought and sustained thought, the training in vision manifests before one, one accomplishes eight types [of knowledges] in the past, eight in the future, and eight in the present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

If, relying on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra, one brings to presence the training in vision, then eight [factors] are past, eight are future, and seven are present—excluding right intention; and once these have ceased, they are not lost.

If one practices the training while relying on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and brings the vision [of the truths] into manifestation, then eight [factors] are past, eight are future, and four are present—excluding right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), right speech (*samyag-vāk*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), because these do not pertain to the formless realm. Once these have ceased, they are not lost.

If one enters the samādhi of cessation or if a mundane mind manifests before one, those eight [factors] are past and eight are future; there are none in the present that possess both vitarka and vicāra. End of section on "possessing both vitarka and vicāra."

If, relying on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra, the training of the first vision manifests before one, that [person] has none in the past, eight in the future, and seven in the present; once it has ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the training in vision manifests based on the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra, there are seven past [dharmas], eight future, and seven present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

If, relying on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the training in vision (*dṛṣṭiśikṣā*) manifests before one, there are seven past, eight future, and four present [factors]; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

If one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and a conventional mind (*lokasamvṛti-citta*) manifests before them, there are seven [kinds of knowledge] in the past, eight in the future, and none in the present; once that [attainment] has ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the training in vision (*dṛṣṭi*) manifests based on the samādhi with directed thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), there are seven past [dharmas], eight future, and eight present; this concludes the section on those without directed thought and sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*).

If, relying on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the first vision manifests for one in training (*śaikṣa*), he possesses none of the past, eight of the future, and four of the present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when one relies on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and the training in vision (*dṛṣṭiśikṣā*) manifests before them, there are four past [factors], eight future, and four present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and a conventional mind (*lokasamvṛti-citta*) manifests before them, there are four [types] in the past, eight in the future, and none in the present; provided that, once ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the training in vision (*dṛṣṭi*) manifests based on the *samādhi* with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), there are four [factors] in the past, eight in the future, and eight in the present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when one relies on the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra, and the training in vision manifests before them, there are four past [factors], eight future, and seven present; this concludes the section on the trainees (śaikṣa).
Regarding the ten types of Arhats who have exhausted the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), how many are accomplished in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?

Answer: If, relying on the concentration with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*), the first knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) manifests before them, then for that person: there is none in the past; ten are accomplished in the future; and nine are accomplished in the present—excluding right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Once that [knowledge] has ceased, it is not lost.

Furthermore, when the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests in dependence on the samādhi with directed thought and sustained evaluation (savitarka-savicāra), nine [knowledges] are past, ten are future, and nine are present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

If, based on the concentration without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*), the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*) manifests, then nine [factors] exist in the past, ten in the future, and eight in the present—excluding right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Once these have ceased, they are not lost.

If, based on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-jñāna*) manifests, then nine [factors] are past, ten are future, and five are present; there is no initial higher restraint (*adhiśīla*), and once that has ceased, it is not lost.

If one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and a conventional mind (*lokasamvṛti-citta*) manifests, for that person there are nine [knowledges] in the past, ten in the future, and none in the present; once that [attainment] has ceased, they are not lost.

If, based on the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, the first vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests, then nine [dharmas] are past, ten are future, and nine are present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the wisdom or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests in dependence on the samādhi with directed thought and sustained thought (savitarka-savicāra), ten [factors] are past and future, and nine are present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when either wisdom or vision of the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests in dependence on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra, ten [factors] are past and future, and eight are present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the wisdom or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests based on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), ten [factors] are past and future, and five are present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the conventional mind (*lokasamvṛti-citta*) manifests; therein, ten [factors] exist in the past and future, while vitarka and vicāra do not exist in the present.

If, relying on the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra, the first vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) manifests, there are none in the past, ten in the future, and eight in the present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests in dependence on the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra, eight [paths] are past, ten are future, and eight are present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi) manifests based on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), eight [factors] are past, ten are future, and five are present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and a conventional mind (*lokasamvṛti-citta*) manifests before them, eight [types of knowledge] are past, ten are future, and none are present; once that [attainment] has ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) arises in dependence on the samādhi with directed thought and sustained thought (savitarka-savicāra), eight past, ten future, and nine present visions have been completed; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the first vision of the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) based on the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra manifests before one, there are eight past [dharmas], ten future, and eight present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when either knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests in dependence on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra, nine [factors] are past, ten are future, and eight are present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) based on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) is present, there are nine [knowledges] in the past, ten in the future, and five in the present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, upon entering the samādhi of cessation, the mundane mind manifests before him; for him, nine [types of minds] exist in the past, ten in the future, and none in the present. Once that [samādhi] has ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) associated with the samādhi that possesses both vitarka and vicāra manifests, nine [factors] are past, ten are future, and nine are present; this concludes the section on those without vitarka and vicāra.
If, based on the formless attainments, the first vision of one beyond training manifests, he possesses ten past and future [factors] and five present ones; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests based on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), there are five past [factors], ten future, and five present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

If one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and a conventional mind (*laukikacitta*) manifests, there are five past [factors], ten future [factors], and none present; once that [attainment] has ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests in dependence on the samādhi with directed thought and sustained thought (savitarka-savicāra), there are five past [factors], ten future, and nine present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests based on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra, those five past, ten future, and eight present [factors] are completed; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the first vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) based on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) manifests, there are five past, ten future, and five present [factors]; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) based on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) is present, there are six past [factors], ten future, and five present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, upon entering the samādhi of cessation, the conventional mind manifests before one; therein, six [dharmas] are past, ten are future, and none are present. Once that [samādhi] has ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) manifests in dependence on the concentration with directed thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*), six [factors] are past, ten are future, and nine are present; once they have ceased, they are not lost.

Furthermore, when the wisdom or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests in dependence on the concentration without directed thought and sustained investigation (avitarkāvicāra-samādhi), there are six past [factors], ten future, and eight present [factors] for the True Person (āryapudgala). Thus ends the section on the True Persons.
What is view (*dṛṣṭi*), what is knowledge (*jñāna*), and what is wisdom (*prajñā*)? What is view?
The answer is:
The eye-faculty consists of the five views, mundane view, the view of one in training, and the view of one beyond training.
What is wisdom?
The answer is:

Excluding the wisdom associated with the consciousness-body that corresponds to the practice of patience, it includes all other wisdoms associated with the consciousness-bodies, as well as the wisdom associated with the five consciousness-bodies, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is wisdom?
The answer is:

wisdom associated with the group of mental consciousnesses, as well as wisdom associated with the group of the five sensory consciousnesses; this concludes the inquiry regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Are all views cognitions?
Answer: Some are views but not cognitions.
What is seeing that is not knowledge?
The answer is:
the patience (kṣānti) practiced by means of the eye-faculty; this is called seeing that is not knowledge.
What is knowledge that is not vision?
The answer is:

excluding the five views and worldly conventional views, all other outflow-tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness aggregate, as well as the wisdom associated with the five consciousness aggregates, and the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising—these are called knowledge that is not vision.
What is knowledge-and-vision (*ñāṇadassana*)?
The answer is:

with the exception of the patience (*khanti*) practiced during cultivation, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), all other untainted wisdoms (*anāsravaprajñā*), the five views (*pañcadṛṣṭi*), and mundane views (*laukikadṛṣṭi*)—these are called knowledge-and-vision.
What is neither knowledge nor vision?
Answer: It is everything except for the aforementioned matters.
Regarding what is called "view" (dṛṣṭi), is it wisdom (prajñā)?
The answer is:
some views are not wisdom. [Note: In the Sanskrit tradition, "view" is one of the ten knowledges (*daśa-jñāna*), specifically referred to as *vidyā* or "clear knowledge."]
What is that which is vision but not wisdom?
The answer is:
the eye-faculty; this is called vision but not wisdom.
What is wisdom that is not vision?
The answer is:

excluding the five views and mundane right view, all other tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness aggregate, the wisdom associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)—these are called wisdom that is not vision.
What is the wisdom that is vision?
The answer is:

with the exception of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), all other untainted wisdoms (*anāsravaprajñā*), as well as the five views and mundane views (*laukikadṛṣṭi*), are called the wisdom that is vision.
What is neither view nor wisdom?
The answer is:
excluding the aforementioned instances.
Are all forms of knowledge (jñāna) wisdom (prajñā)?
Answer: It is so;
knowledge is indeed wisdom.
Is there any wisdom that is not knowledge?
The answer is:
there is that which has been cultivated through patience and finalized through deliberation.
Regarding what is called "view" (dṛṣṭi), is it subsumed under "knowledge" (jñāna)? Answer:
Some views are not knowledge.
What is seeing that is not knowledge?
The answer is:
the patience (kṣānti) practiced by means of the eye-faculty; this is called seeing that is not knowledge.
What is knowledge that is not vision?
The answer is:

excluding the five views and mundane view (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*), all other outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) associated with the mental consciousness aggregate, the wisdom associated with the five consciousness aggregates, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)—these are called knowledge that is not vision.
What is "view-cognition" (*dṛṣṭi-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

excluding the patience that is being cultivated (*bhāvyamānā kṣānti*), as well as the cognition of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the cognition of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), all other untainted wisdoms (*anāsravā prajñā*), the five views (*pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ*), and conventional views (*saṃvṛti-dṛṣṭi*), etc., are called view-cognition.
What is neither knowledge nor vision?
Answer: It is everything except for those aforementioned matters.
Regarding what is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), is it subsumed under wisdom (*prajñā*)?
Answer: Some views are not wisdom.
What is seeing that is not wisdom?
The answer is:
the eye-faculty; this is called seeing that is not wisdom.
What is wisdom that is not vision?
The answer is:

excluding the five views and mundane views (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*), all other tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) associated with the group of mental consciousnesses, the wisdom associated with the group of the five sensory consciousnesses, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)—these are called wisdom that is not vision.
What is the wisdom that is vision (*dṛṣṭi-prajñā*)?
The answer is:

with the exception of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), all other untainted wisdoms (*anāsrava-prajñā*), the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*), and mundane views (*laukika-dṛṣṭi*), etc., are called the wisdom that is vision.
What is neither view nor wisdom?
Answer: It is that which remains after excluding the aforementioned matters.
Does wisdom (jñāna) encompass discernment (prajñā), or does discernment encompass wisdom?
The answer is:
discernment encompasses wisdom, but wisdom does not encompass discernment.
What is not included?
The answer is:
regarding the patience practiced and the knowledge of patience, one does not attain wisdom.
The same applies to accomplishment (*samanvāgama*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
[These are]: inquiry (*paripṛcchā*), determination (*vyavasthāna*), inclusion (*saṃgraha*), accomplishment, and cessation.
That is to say: is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: There may be right view that is not the factor-of-enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is right view that is not the factor-of-enlightenment of investigation of phenomena?
Answer: Worldly right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) is what is called right view that is not the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
What is the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena that is not right view?

Answer: Knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are called the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that is not right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
What, then, is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena that is right view?
Answer:

With the exception of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), all other untainted wisdoms (*anāsravaprajñā*) are called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is neither right view nor the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena?
Answer: Excluding the aforementioned matters.
That is to say, is equal wisdom (samatājñāna) the awakening factor of the investigation of dharmas (dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga)?
Answer: Sometimes conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is not the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
What is conventional knowledge that is not the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena?
Answer: Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and so forth are called conventional knowledge that is not the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena that is not conventional knowledge?
Answer: The patience practiced during cultivation is called the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is not conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
What, then, is conventional knowledge that is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena?

Answer: With the exception of the patience (kṣānti) that is being practiced, all other untainted wisdoms (anāsravaprajñā) are called conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) and the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
What is neither conventional knowledge nor the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena?
Answer: Excluding the aforementioned cases.
When the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) manifests before one, how many awakening factors and how many elements of the path (*mārgāṅga*) manifest?
Answer:

If, relying on the future *savitarka-savicāra* samādhi, the learner’s (*śaikṣa*) awakening factor of mindfulness manifests, then six awakening factors and eight factors of the path manifest; for the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), six awakening factors and nine factors of the path manifest.

If, relying on the first dhyāna, the training-stage awakening factor of mindfulness manifests, then seven awakening factors and eight path-factors manifest; for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven awakening factors and nine path-factors manifest.

If, relying on the intermediate dhyāna, one brings the training of the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) into presence, then six awakening factors and seven factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present; for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six awakening factors and eight factors of the path are present.

If, relying on the second dhyāna, the training stage of the awakening factor of mindfulness manifests, then seven awakening factors and seven factors of the path manifest; for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven awakening factors and eight factors of the path manifest.

If, relying on the third or fourth dhyāna, the training of the awakening factor of mindfulness manifests before one, then six awakening factors and seven factors of the path manifest; for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six awakening factors and eight factors of the path manifest.

If one, relying on the formless attainments, brings the training of the awakening-factor of mindfulness into presence, then six awakening-factors and four modes of the path are present; for one beyond training, six awakening-factors and five modes of the path are present.

The awakening factors of dharma, energy, tranquility, and concentration, as well as the guarding of the mind, and likewise right view, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, are also thus.
When the awakening factor of joy (*pītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) manifests, how many awakening factors and how many path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) manifest?
The answer is:

if a learner (*śaikṣa*) relies on the first dhyāna and the awakening factor of joy manifests, then seven awakening factors and eight path-factors manifest; for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), seven awakening factors and nine path-factors manifest.

If, relying on the second dhyāna, the training-stage factor of enlightenment of joy (prītisambodhyaṅga) manifests, then seven factors of enlightenment and seven limbs of the path manifest; for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven factors of enlightenment and eight limbs of the path manifest.
When the right intention (samyak-saṃkalpa) manifests, how many factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and how many factors of the path (mārgāṅga) manifest? Answer:

If, relying on the future concentration with applied and sustained thought (savitarka-savicāra-samādhi), the right intention of one in training (śaikṣa) manifests, then six factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path manifest; for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path manifest. Knowledge and vision do not coexist simultaneously.

If, relying on the first dhyāna, the learner’s (śaikṣa) right intention manifests, then seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path manifest; for the one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path manifest.
When such speech as this comes before one, how many factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and how many limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are present?
The answer is:

if, relying on the future *samādhi* with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), the speech of a trainee (*śaikṣa*) comes before one, then six factors of enlightenment and eight limbs of the path are present; for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), six factors of enlightenment and nine limbs of the path are present.

If, relying on the first dhyāna, the learner’s [path of] right speech manifests, then for him the seven factors of enlightenment and eight limbs of the path manifest; for the one beyond training (aśaikṣa), the seven factors of enlightenment and nine limbs of the path manifest.

If, based on the intermediate dhyāna, the trainee’s [paths] such as the "equal" speech manifest, then for him the six factors of enlightenment and seven factors of the path manifest; for the non-trainee, the six factors of enlightenment without joy manifest along with eight factors of the path.

If, relying on the second dhyāna, the training [stage] brings forth the "equal speech" (samyagvāc), then the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and the seven limbs of the path (mārgāṅga) excluding right intention (samyaksaṃkalpa) are present; for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), the seven factors of enlightenment and the eight limbs of the path are present.

If, relying on the third or fourth dhyāna, the training [factors] such as right speech manifest, then six factors of enlightenment and seven factors of the path manifest; for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path manifest.
It is the same for right action and right livelihood.
Regarding those factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness, are they also the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena?
The answer is:
The awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena—this is called the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena.
What is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena that is not the awakening factor of mindfulness? Answer:
The awakening factor of mindfulness: this is called the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena, not the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness and the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena? Answer:

Excluding the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), all other factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) are called both the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness and the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena.
What are those that are neither the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness nor the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena?
Answer:

All other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called neither the awakening factor of mindfulness nor the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena.

The factors of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*) and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), are likewise.
Regarding all phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), are they also associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: There are cases where there is the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) but not the awakening factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
What is the case where there is the awakening factor of mindfulness but not the awakening factor of joy?
Answer:

The factor of awakening that is joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), as well as those factors associated with the factor of awakening that is mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) but not associated with the factor of awakening that is joy—these are called the factor of awakening that is mindfulness but not the factor of awakening that is joy.
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness? Answer:

The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy; this is called the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
What are the awakening factor of mindfulness and the awakening factor of joy? Answer:

With the exception of the awakening factor of mindfulness itself, all other factors associated with the awakening factor of joy are called the awakening factor of mindfulness and the awakening factor of joy.
What is that which is neither the awakening factor of mindfulness nor the awakening factor of joy? Answer:

The awakening factor of mindfulness that is dissociated from the awakening factor of joy, as well as other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—this is called that which is neither the awakening factor of mindfulness nor the awakening factor of joy.
The same applies to right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).
Regarding those factors that are associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*), are they all [themselves] mindfulness?
The answer is: no.
Thus it is.
If various dharmas are associated with mindfulness, are they the awakening factor of mindfulness?
The answer is: Yes.
Thus it is.
If the factor of dharma-discernment is associated with the awakening-factor of dharma-discernment, is it also associated with the awakening-factor of energy?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena that is not the awakening factor of energy.
What is the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena that is not the awakening factor of energy? Answer:
The awakening factor of energy: this is called the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, not the awakening factor of energy.
What is the awakening factor of energy that is not the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena? Answer:

The awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (dharma-pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) is called the awakening factor of energy (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is not the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena.
What is the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena that is also the awakening factor of energy?
The answer is:

Excluding the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), all other factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) are called both the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena and the factor of enlightenment of energy.
What are those that are neither the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena nor the factor of enlightenment of energy?
Answer:

All other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are said to be neither the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena nor the awakening factor of energy.

The same applies to the awakening factors of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*).

Regarding all phenomena associated with the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*): are they also associated with the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: There are cases where there is the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (dharmavicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) but not the awakening factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
What is the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena that is not the awakening factor of joy?
Answer:

The factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) itself, as well as those factors associated with the factor of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) that are not associated with the factor of joy—these are called the factor of investigation of phenomena that is not the factor of joy.
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena? Answer:

The factor of investigation of phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy; this is called the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena.
What are the factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:

With the exception of the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena itself, all other factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy are called the factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena and joy.
What is that which is neither the factor-of-enlightenment of investigation-of-phenomena (dharmapravicaya-sambodhyaṅga) nor the factor-of-enlightenment of joy (prīti-sambodhyaṅga)? Answer:

The factor-of-enlightenment of investigation-of-phenomena that is not associated with the factor-of-enlightenment of joy, as well as other mind, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—this is called that which is neither the factor-of-enlightenment of investigation-of-phenomena nor the factor-of-enlightenment of joy.
The same applies to equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Are those factors that are associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) also associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: Yes.
In this way, all dharmas associated with right view are that factor-of-enlightenment which is the investigation of dharmas (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Is there any factor-of-enlightenment which is the investigation of dharmas that is not associated with right view?
Answer: Yes.
There are factors of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that are not subsumed by right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Regarding those factors associated with the enlightenment factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), do they possess the enlightenment factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is the awakening factor of energy that is not the awakening factor of joy.
What is the awakening factor of energy that is not the awakening factor of joy?
The answer is:

The factor of joy-enlightenment, as well as those factors associated with the enlightenment-factor of energy that are not associated with the enlightenment-factor of joy—these are called the enlightenment-factor of energy that is not the enlightenment-factor of joy.
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga) that is not the factor of enlightenment of energy (vīryasaṃbodhyaṅga)? Answer:
The factor of enlightenment of energy associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy; this is called the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not the factor of enlightenment of energy.
What are the factors of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:
With the exception of the factor of enlightenment of energy itself, all other factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy are called the factors of enlightenment of energy and joy.
What is that which is neither the awakening-factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) nor the awakening-factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:

The awakening-factor of energy that is not associated with the awakening-factor of joy, as well as all other mental states (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*). This is called that which is neither the awakening-factor of energy nor the awakening-factor of joy.
The same applies to right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).
Regarding those factors associated with the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), are they also associated with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
The answer is:
Or, there is the awakening factor of energy that is not the awakening factor of tranquility.
What is the awakening factor of energy that is not the awakening factor of tranquility? Answer:
The awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)—this is called the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that is not the awakening factor of tranquility.
What is the awakening factor of tranquility that is not the awakening factor of energy? Answer:
The awakening factor of energy is called the awakening factor of tranquility but not the awakening factor of energy.
What is the awakening factor of energy that is also the awakening factor of tranquility?
The answer is:

Excluding the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*), all other factors associated with the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) are called both the awakening factor of energy and the awakening factor of equanimity.
What is neither the awakening factor of energy nor the awakening factor of equanimity?

Answer: All other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are said to be neither the awakening factor of diligence nor the awakening factor of tranquility.
It is the same for concentration, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, equanimity, and the awakening factor of concentration.
Are all those factors associated with the awakening factor of energy also associated with the application of energy?
Answer: It is so.
If all dharmas are associated with skillful means, are they the factor of enlightenment of diligence?
Answer: It is so.
If the various dharmas are associated with the awakening factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*), are they also associated with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Sometimes the factor of enlightenment of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga) is not the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (praśrabdhisaṃbodhyaṅga).
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not the factor of enlightenment of tranquility?

Answer: The factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)—this is called the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
What is the factor of enlightenment of tranquility that is not the factor of enlightenment of joy?
Answer:

The factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) itself, as well as those factors associated with the factor of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) that are not associated with the factor of joy—these are called the factor of tranquility but not the factor of joy.
What are the factors of enlightenment of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) and tranquility (*praśrabdhisambodhyaṅga*)? Answer:

With the exception of the factor of enlightenment of tranquility itself, all other factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy are called the factors of enlightenment of joy and tranquility.
What is that which is neither the factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) nor the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhisaṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:

The factor of tranquility that is not associated with the factor of joy, as well as all other mind, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are said to be neither the factor of joy nor the factor of tranquility.
The same applies to concentration, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Are all those factors associated with the awakening factor of joy also associated with right view?
Answer: Sometimes the factor of awakening of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga) is not right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
What is the factor of awakening of joy that is not right view?
Answer:

The factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that are also associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), as well as other factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy that are not associated with right view—these are called "the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not right view."
What is right view that is not associated with the awakening factor of joy? Answer:

The awakening factor of joy associated with right view, as well as all other factors associated with right view but not associated with the awakening factor of joy—this is called right view that is not the awakening factor of joy.
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga) associated with right view (samyagdṛṣṭi)? Answer:

With the exception of the right view associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy, all other factors associated with both the factor of enlightenment of joy and right view are called the factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy and right view.
What is neither the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) nor right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
The answer is:

right view that is not associated with the factor of joy, the factor of joy that is not associated with right view, and all other remaining minds (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*). These are called those that are neither the factor of joy nor right view.
The same applies to equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding those factors associated with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), are they also the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
The answer is:
Or, there is the awakening factor of pliancy that is not the awakening factor of concentration.
What is the awakening factor of pliancy that is not the awakening factor of concentration?
The answer is:

Regarding the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), this refers to the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that is not the awakening factor of concentration.
What is the awakening factor of concentration that is not the awakening factor of tranquility? Answer:
Regarding the awakening factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), this is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that is not the awakening factor of pliancy.
What is the awakening factor of pliancy that is also the awakening factor of concentration? Answer:
Excluding the awakening factor of concentration, all other factors associated with the awakening factor of tranquility—these are called the awakening factors of tranquility and concentration.
What are those that are neither the awakening factor of tranquility nor the awakening factor of concentration?
Answer:

All other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called neither the awakening factor of tranquility nor the awakening factor of concentration.
The same applies to the awakening factor of vigilance, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Are those factors associated with the awakening factor of tranquility also associated with right view?
Answer: Sometimes the awakening factor of tranquility is not right view.
What is the awakening factor of tranquility that is not right view?

Answer: Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), as well as those factors associated with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that are not associated with right view—these are called the awakening factor of tranquility that is not right view.
What is right view that is not the awakening factor of tranquility?
Answer: The factor of enlightenment of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) associated with right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) is called "right view but not the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
What is the factor of enlightenment of tranquility that is [associated with] right view?

Answer: With the exception of the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), all other factors associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) are called "the factor of enlightenment of tranquility associated with right view.
What is neither the factor of enlightenment of tranquility nor right view?
Answer:

The factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that is not associated with right view, as well as other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*)—these are said to be neither the factor of enlightenment of tranquility nor right view.
The same applies to equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding those factors that are associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), are they also associated with the awakening factor of vigilance (*apramāda-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is the factor of concentration-enlightenment (samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is not the factor of vigilance-enlightenment (apramāda-saṃbodhyaṅga).
What is the factor of concentration-enlightenment that is not the factor of vigilance-enlightenment? Answer:
Regarding the awakening factor of vigilance (*prahāṇa-saṃbodhyaṅga*), this refers to the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that is not the awakening factor of vigilance.
What is the awakening factor of vigilance that is not the awakening factor of concentration? Answer:
The awakening factor of concentration—this is called the awakening factor of vigilance that is not the awakening factor of concentration.
What is the awakening factor of concentration that is also the awakening factor of vigilance?
The answer is:

Excluding the factor of enlightenment of vigilance (*samprajanya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), all other factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) are called both the factor of enlightenment of concentration and the factor of enlightenment of vigilance.
What are those that are neither the factor of enlightenment of concentration nor the factor of enlightenment of vigilance?
Answer:

All other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called neither the awakening factor of concentration nor the awakening factor of equanimity.

Regarding those factors that are associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), are they also [associated with] right view?
The answer is: Yes.

What is right view that is not the awakening factor of concentration?
Answer: The factor of enlightenment of concentration associated with right view—this is called right view that is not the factor of enlightenment of concentration.
What is the factor of enlightenment of concentration that is right view?

What is neither the concentration factor of enlightenment nor right view?
Answer:

The concentration associated with right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) but not associated with the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), as well as all other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are said to be neither concentration associated with the factors of enlightenment nor right view.

Regarding those factors that are associated with the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), are they also concentration?
The answer is:
Thus it is.

Are those factors associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) also views?

Or, there is the factor of enlightenment of vigilance (prahāṇasaṃbodhyaṅga) that is not right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
What is the factor of enlightenment of vigilance that is not right view? Answer:

Right view, as well as those factors associated with the awakening factor of vigilance (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) that are not associated with right view—these are called the awakening factor of vigilance but not right view.
What is right view but not the awakening factor of vigilance?
Answer: Right view associated with the awakening factor of vigilance—this is called right view that is not the awakening factor of vigilance.
What is the awakening factor of vigilance that is right view?

Answer: With the exception of the factor of awakening that is vigilance (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), all other factors associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) are called "the factor of awakening that is vigilance together with right view.
What is neither the factor of awakening that is vigilance nor right view?
Answer:

Those factors dissociated from right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) that are associated with the awakening factor of vigilance (*samprajanya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), as well as all other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are said to be neither the awakening factor of vigilance nor right view.
The same applies to equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Are all factors associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) also associated with the application of energy (*vīrya-saṃskāra*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is the factor of enlightenment of vigilance (saṃprajanya-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is not the application of energy (vīrya-saṃskāra).
What is the factor of enlightenment of vigilance that is not the application of energy? Answer:
What is right effort that is not the awakening factor of vigilance?
Answer: [The following:]
Regarding the awakening factor of protection (*rakkha-sambojjhaṅga*), this is called the application of mindfulness that is not the awakening factor of protection.
What is the application of mindfulness that is the awakening factor of protection?
The answer is:

Excluding the preliminary applications (*parikarman*), all other factors associated with the awakening factor of vigilance (*samprajanya-sambodhyanga*) are called the preliminary applications of the awakening factor of vigilance.
What are those that are neither the awakening factor of vigilance nor the preliminary applications?
Answer:
All other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called neither the awakening factor of vigilance nor right effort.
The same applies to equanimity of mindfulness (samānasmṛti) and equanimity of concentration (samānasamādhi).
Are those factors associated with right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) also associated with right intention (samyaksaṃkalpa)?
Answer: No.
There are those who possess right view but do not possess right intention.
What is meant by possessing right view but not right intention?
The answer is:
Right view associated with right intention, as well as those factors associated with right view but not associated with right intention—these are called right view that is not right intention.
What is right intention that is not right view?
Answer:

Those factors associated with right intention (samyak-saṃkalpa) that are also associated with right view (samyag-dṛṣṭi), as well as those factors associated with right intention that are not associated with right view—these are called "associated with right intention but not associated with right view."
What is right view and right intention?
The answer is:

excluding those factors associated with right intention that are themselves associated with right view, all other factors associated with both right view and right intention are called right view and right intention.
What is that which is neither right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) nor right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*)? Answer:

Right intention not associated with right view, right view not associated with right intention, and all other mind, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called that which is neither right view nor right intention.
Are all dharmas associated with right view also associated with right effort?
Answer: Some are associated with right view but not with right effort.
What is right view that is not associated with right effort?
The answer is:
right view that is associated with right effort; this is called right view that is not right effort.
What is right effort that is not right view?
The answer is:
right view itself, as well as those factors associated with right effort that are not associated with right view—this is called right effort that is not right view.
What is right view with right effort?
The answer is:
with the exception of right effort itself, all other factors associated with right view are called right view with right effort.
What is that which is neither right view nor right effort?
The answer is:

right effort dissociated from right view, as well as all other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called that which is neither right view nor right effort.
The same applies to equanimity of mindfulness (samānasmṛti) and equanimity of concentration (samānasamādhi).
If various dharmas are associated with equanimity of intention (samānāśaya), are they also associated with equanimity of application (samānopāya)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is right intention that is not right effort.
What is right intention that is not right effort?
The answer is:
When there is association with right intention but not with right effort, this is called right intention that is not right effort.
What is right effort that is not right intention? Answer:

Right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), as well as those factors associated with right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) that are not associated with right intention—these are called "right effort that is not right intention.
What is both right intention and right effort?
Answer: With the exception of right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*), all other factors associated with right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) are called "right intention and right effort.
What is neither right intention nor right effort?
Answer:

Those factors that are not associated with right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) and are not right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*), namely all other minds (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*); these are called neither right intention nor right effort.
The same applies to equanimity of mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti*) and equanimity of concentration (*samādhi*).
If various dharmas are associated with skillful means (*upāya*), are they also associated with equanimity of mindfulness?
The answer is: [Yes].
Or, there may be equal application of effort (samyak-pradhāna) but not equal mindfulness (samyak-smṛti).
What is meant by equal application of effort but not equal mindfulness?
The answer is:
Equanimity of mindfulness—this is called equanimity of application of energy that is not equanimity of mindfulness.
What is equanimity of mindfulness that is not equanimity of application of energy? Answer:
This is called equanimity of mindfulness without equanimity of application.
What is equanimity of application with equanimity of mindfulness?
The answer is:
Excluding right mindfulness, all other factors associated with right effort are called right effort and right mindfulness.
What are those that are neither right effort nor right mindfulness?
Answer:
All other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called neither equal application nor equal mindfulness.
The same applies to "equanimity" (*samādhi*).
If various dharmas are associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*), are they also equanimity?
The answer is: No.
Or, there is equal mindfulness that is not equal concentration.
What is equal mindfulness that is not equal concentration?
The answer is:
Equilibrium of concentration, this is called equilibrium of mindfulness that is not equilibrium of concentration.
What is equilibrium of concentration that is not equilibrium of mindfulness?
The answer is:
"Equal mindfulness, yet not equal concentration": this is called "equal mindfulness, not equal concentration.
What is meant by "equal mindfulness and equal concentration"?
Answer: With the exception of right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), all other factors associated with right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) are called right mindfulness and right concentration.
What are those that are neither right mindfulness nor right concentration?
Answer:
All other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called "neither equal mindfulness nor equal concentration."
What is mundane right view (*laukika-samyagdṛṣṭi*)? What is mundane right knowledge (*laukika-samyagjñāna*)?
And what is mundane right view?
The answer is:
What is mundane conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that is associated with the group of mental consciousness (*manovijñānakāya*) and is wholesome yet contaminated (*sāsrava*)?
The answer is:
Is the wholesome, out-flowing wisdom associated with the mental consciousness aggregate, as well as the wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousness aggregates,
and the conventional view (sāmayikī dṛṣṭi), the same as conventional knowledge (sāmayikī prajñā)?
Answer: It is so;
if one possesses conventional right view, one possesses conventional right knowledge.
However, can there be conventional right knowledge that is not conventional right view?
Answer: Yes, there is wholesome wisdom associated with the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya-saṃprayukta-kuśala-prajñā*).
Does mundane right view (*laukika-samyagdṛṣṭi*) subsume mundane right knowledge (*laukika-samyagjñāna*), or does mundane right knowledge subsume mundane right view?
Answer:
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) subsumes conventional view (*saṃvṛti-dṛṣṭi*), but conventional view does not subsume conventional knowledge.
What is not subsumed?
Answer: It is wholesome wisdom associated with the five groups of consciousness.
Its acquisition and its cessation are likewise so.
Question: Determination, definition, inclusion, accomplishment, and cessation.
What is untainted right view (*anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi*)? What is untainted right knowledge (*anāsrava-samyajñāna*)?
And what is untainted right view?
Answer: The wisdom of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) do not include untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*).
What, then, is untainted equal-wisdom (*anāsravasamantajñāna*)?
Answer: It is all other untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) excluding the patience (*kṣānti*) that has been cultivated.
If it is untainted right view (*anāsravasamyagdṛṣṭi*), is it untainted right knowledge (*anāsravasamyagjñāna*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there are instances where the untainted view (anāsravā dṛṣṭi) is not the untainted knowledge (anāsravā prajñā).
What is the untainted view that is not the untainted knowledge?
The answer is:
The patience practiced is called untainted right view (*anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi*), but it is not untainted right knowledge (*anāsrava-samyagjñāna*).
What is untainted right knowledge that is not untainted right view?
The answer is:

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*): these are called untainted right knowledge (*anāsrava-samyagjñāna*), but not untainted right view (*anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
What is untainted right view that is also untainted right knowledge?
Answer:

With the exception of the patience cultivated through practice (*pratipannaka-kṣānti*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), all other untainted wisdoms (*anāsravaprajñā*) are called untainted right view (*anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi*) and untainted right knowledge (*anāsrava-samyagjñāna*).
What is that which is neither non-outflow view nor non-outflow knowledge?
Answer: It is everything except for those aforementioned matters.
Does the untainted right view (anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi) subsume the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna)? Answer:
Sometimes the untainted right view is not the untainted knowledge.
What is that which is untainted right view (anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi) but not untainted right knowledge (anāsrava-samyagjñāna)? Answer:
The patience (kṣānti) practiced during cultivation; this is called untainted right view but not untainted right knowledge.
What is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that is not untainted vision (*anāsrava-darśana*)?
The answer is:
the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*); these are called untainted knowledge that is not untainted vision.
What is untainted right view (anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi) that is also untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna)? Answer:

With the exception of the patience during the course of practice (pratipannaka-kṣānti), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), all other untainted knowledges are called untainted right view that is also untainted knowledge.
What is that which is neither non-outflow view nor non-outflow knowledge?
Answer: It is everything except for the aforementioned cases.
If one accomplishes untainted right view (anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi), does one also accomplish untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna)?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes untainted knowledge, one also accomplishes untainted right view.
Is there one who possesses the untainted right view but does not possess untainted knowledge?
Answer: Yes;
for example, when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is present before one.

wrong view, extreme view, and the views opposed [to them];

If it is neither a view of one in training nor a view of one beyond training, is it non-training-and-non-beyond-training knowledge?
Conversely, if it is non-training-and-non-beyond-training knowledge, is it a non-training-and-non-beyond-training view?
If it is neither a view of one in training nor a view of one beyond training, is it wisdom that is neither of training nor beyond training?
Conversely, if it is wisdom that is neither of training nor beyond training, is it a view that is neither of training nor beyond training?

Conversely, if it is wisdom that is neither of the learner nor of one beyond learning, is it knowledge that is neither of the learner nor of one beyond learning?

Or if it is neither-learner-nor-non-learner knowledge, is it subsumed by neither-learner-nor-non-learner vision?

among these five views, what kind of view is it?

that an Arhat is liberated from doubt and attains Arhatship through the knowledge of others.
Among these five views, what kind of view is each?

What is wrong view and what is wrong knowledge?
What is wrong view?
The answer is:
The five views do not have a fixed meaning; all five views are, in essence, false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
If they are fixed, that which is called "this view" is: there is no giving, no retribution, and no teaching—this is what is termed a false view.
What is wrong knowledge?
The answer is:
defiled wisdom associated with the group of mental consciousnesses and defiled wisdom associated with the group of the five sensory consciousnesses; this is called wrong knowledge.
If it is wrong view, is it wrong knowledge?
Answer: It is so;
wrong view is wrong knowledge.
Is there any wrong knowledge that is not wrong view?
Answer: There is.

Excluding the five views, it includes all other defiled wisdom associated with the group of mental consciousnesses, as well as defiled wisdom associated with the group of the five sensory consciousnesses.
Does wrong view include wrong knowledge, or does wrong knowledge include wrong view?
Answer:
Wrong knowledge includes wrong view, but wrong view does not include wrong knowledge.
What is not included?
The answer is:

with the exception of the five views, all other defiled wisdom associated with the group of mental consciousnesses, as well as defiled wisdom associated with the group of the five sensory consciousnesses.
If one is possessed of wrong view, is one also possessed of wrong knowledge?
Answer: It is so;
if one is possessed of wrong view, one is also possessed of wrong knowledge.
Is there one who possesses wrong knowledge but does not possess wrong view?
Answer: There is;
namely, those in training who have seen the tracks.
If wrong view has been extinguished without remainder, is that wrong knowledge?
Answer: It is so;
if wrong knowledge has been extinguished without remainder, that is wrong view.
Is there a case where wrong views have been extinguished without remainder, yet it is not wrong knowledge?
Answer: Yes; for example, one who has attained the vision of the tracks of training (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta).
The questions are: fixed principles, inclusion, accomplishment, and cessation.
What is equal vision? What is equal knowledge?
And what is equal vision?
Answer: The wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness aggregate is not included within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What, then, is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
Answer:

Excluding the patience (kṣānti) that is being cultivated, it refers to all other wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness-body and the wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousness-bodies.
Is right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) identical to conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: There are cases where there is right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) but not right knowledge (samyagjñāna).
What is meant by right view that is not right knowledge?
Answer: The patience practiced is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), not right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
What is right knowledge that is not right view?
Answer:

The wholesome wisdom associated with the five bodies of consciousness, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), are called equal wisdom (*samatājñāna*) but not equal view (*samatādṛṣṭi*).
What, then, is equal wisdom that is also equal view?
Answer:

With the exception of the patience practiced during cultivation, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising, all other wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness aggregate is called conventional knowledge and conventional view.
What is neither right view nor right knowledge?
The answer is:
all things except those mentioned above.
Does right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) subsume right knowledge (samyagjñāna)? Answer:
Some right views do not subsume right knowledge.
What is right view that is not conventional knowledge?
The answer is:
the patience (kṣānti) practiced during cultivation; this is called right view that is not conventional knowledge.
What is equal knowledge (sammā-ñāṇa) that is not equal view (sammā-diṭṭhi)?
The answer is:

wholesome wisdom associated with the five groups of consciousness, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna); these are called equal knowledge that is not equal view.
What is right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) that is also conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
The answer is:

with the exception of the patience during the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārge kṣānti), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), all other wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness aggregate (manovijñānakāya) is called right view that is also conventional knowledge.
What is neither right view nor right knowledge?
The answer is:
with the exception of those aforementioned matters.
Accomplishment (*samudāgama*), cessation (*nirodha*), and likewise [the others].
These are the inquiry (*praśna*), the determination of principles (*sthāpanā*), inclusion (*saṃgraha*), accomplishment, and cessation.
Are all inverted wisdoms (*viparīta-prajñā*) fetters (*saṃyojana*)?
Answer: Some are contrary wisdom but not fetters.
What is contrary wisdom that is not a fetter?
Answer: With the exception of the two fetters—view and the resolve for non-existence—all other defiled wisdoms are called "adverse wisdom" that is not a fetter.
What is a fetter that is not adverse wisdom?
Answer: The seven fetters (saṃyojana) are called fetters that are not contrary to wisdom (prajñā).
What are those that are contrary to wisdom and are also fetters?
Answer: Two fetters are called the fetter that is contrary to wisdom.
What is neither contrary to wisdom nor a fetter?
Answer: Excluding the aforementioned matters.
What is the vision of training (śaikṣa-darśana), what is the knowledge of training (śaikṣa-jñāna), and what is the wisdom of training (śaikṣa-prajñā)?
What is the vision of one in training?
The answer is:
the wisdom of one in training.
What is the knowledge of those in training?
The answer is:
the eight knowledges of those in training.
What is the wisdom of one in training?
The answer is:
it refers to the vision of one in training, the knowledge of one in training, and the wisdom of one in training. This is what is meant.
If one studies vision, does one study knowledge?
Answer: It is so;
that which is the study of knowledge is the study of vision.
Is there any instance where there is the vision of one in training (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭi) that is not the knowledge of one in training (śaikṣa-jñāna)?
Answer: There is;
namely, the patience (kṣānti) being practiced.
If one studies vision, is this the study of wisdom?
The answer is: Yes.
If one trains in wisdom, does one train in vision?
The answer is: Yes.
If one trains in knowledge, does one train in wisdom?
Answer: It is so;
if one trains in knowledge, one trains in wisdom.
Is there that which is the wisdom of one in training (śaikṣa-jñāna) but not the knowledge of one in training (śaikṣa-jñāna)? Answer:
Yes; namely, the patience (kṣānti) being practiced.
Does the training in vision encompass the training in knowledge, and does the training in knowledge encompass the training in vision? Answer:
The training in vision encompasses the training in knowledge, but the training in knowledge does not encompass the training in vision.
What is not included?
The answer is:
the patience that is being practiced.
Is the training in vision subsumed by the training in wisdom?
Answer: It is so.
Does the training in wisdom include the training in view?
Answer: It is so.
Does the wisdom of training encompass the insight of training, or does the insight of training encompass the wisdom of training? Answer:
The insight of training encompasses the wisdom of training, but the wisdom of training does not encompass the insight of training.
What is not included?
The answer is:
the patience that is being practiced.
If one accomplishes the vision of training, does that person accomplish the knowledge of training?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes the knowledge of training, one accomplishes the vision of training.
Is there one who possesses the vision of a trainee (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭi) but does not possess the knowledge of a trainee (śaikṣa-jñāna)?
Answer: Yes;
for example, when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharmakṣānti) is present before one.
If one has accomplished the vision of a trainee, does that person possess the wisdom of a trainee?
Answer: It is so.
If one achieves the wisdom of training (śaikṣa-prajñā), does that person possess the vision of training (śaikṣa-darśana)?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the wisdom of a trainee (śaikṣa-jñāna), does that person possess the insight of a trainee (śaikṣa-prajñā)?
