Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes the wisdom of a trainee, that person possesses the insight of a trainee.
Is there one who possesses the wisdom of training (śaikṣa-prajñā) but does not possess the knowledge of training (śaikṣa-jñāna)?
Answer: Yes;
for example, when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) is present before one.
Question: Determination, definition, inclusion, and accomplishment.
What is the vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadṛṣṭi*), what is the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*), and what is the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣaprajñā*)?
What is the vision of one beyond training?
Answer: The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) do not include all untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*).
What, then, is the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*)?
Answer: It consists of the eight knowledges of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the wisdom of one beyond training?
Answer:
It refers to the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi), the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna), and the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣaprajñā).
Is the vision of one beyond training the same as the knowledge of one beyond training?
Answer: It is so;
that which is the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is the knowledge of one beyond training.
Is there, however, any knowledge of one beyond training that is not the vision of one beyond training?
Answer: Yes;
it is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Is the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*) the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣaprajñā*)?
Answer: It is so.
Is the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) the knowledge of one beyond training?
Answer: It is so.

Does the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi) include the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna), and does the knowledge of one beyond training include the vision of one beyond training?
Answer:

The knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) subsumes the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi), but the vision of one beyond training does not subsume the knowledge of one beyond training.
What is not subsumed?
Answer: The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Does the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi) subsume the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣaprajñā), and does the wisdom of one beyond training subsume the vision of one beyond training?
Answer: Unlearned wisdom (aśaikṣī prajñā) subsumes unlearned vision (aśaikṣī dṛṣṭi), but unlearned vision does not subsume unlearned wisdom.
What is not subsumed?
Answer: The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Does the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣaprajñā*) subsume the knowledge of one beyond training?
Answer: It is so.
Does the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-prajñā) subsume the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
Attainment is likewise so.
Question: Definition, determination, inclusion, and accomplishment.
What is non-learner and non-non-learner view? What is non-learner and non-non-learner knowledge? What is non-learner and non-non-learner wisdom?
What is the view that is neither of one in training nor of one beyond training?
The answer is:
the eye faculty, the five views, and mundane views.
What is knowledge that is neither of training nor beyond training?
The answer is:
it is the tainted wisdom associated with the group of mental consciousnesses and the wisdom associated with the group of the five sensory consciousnesses.
What is wisdom that is neither of the learner nor of the adept?
The answer is:
tainted wisdom associated with the group of mental consciousnesses, and wisdom associated with the group of the five sensory consciousnesses.
If it is neither the vision of one in training nor the vision of one beyond training, is it the knowledge of one who is neither in training nor beyond training?
Answer: It may be vision that is not knowledge.
What is seeing that is not knowledge?
The answer is:
the eye-faculty; this is called seeing that is not knowledge.
What is knowledge that is not vision?
The answer is:

excluding the five views and mundane right view, all other outflow-tainted wisdom associated with the group of mental consciousnesses and the wisdom associated with the group of the five sensory consciousnesses—this is called knowledge that is not vision.
What is the knowledge of views?
The answer is:
the five views and mundane right view; these are called the knowledge of views.
What is neither view nor knowledge?
Answer: It is all things except for those mentioned above.
Is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner view also non-learner-nor-non-learner wisdom?
Answer: Some are view but not wisdom.
What is seeing that is not wisdom?
The answer is:
the eye-faculty; this is called seeing that is not wisdom.
What is wisdom that is not view?
The answer is:

excluding the five views and worldly conventional views, all other tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness aggregate and the wisdom associated with the five consciousness aggregates—this is called wisdom that is not view.
What is the wisdom of views?
The answer is:
the five views and mundane views such as these are called the wisdom of views.
What is neither view nor wisdom?
The answer is:
excluding the aforementioned instances.
Is that which is neither training nor beyond-training knowledge (jñāna) also that which is neither training nor beyond-training wisdom (prajñā)?
Answer: It is so.
If it is wisdom that is neither of the learner nor of the adept, is it knowledge that is neither of the learner nor of the adept?
Answer: It is so.
Is that which is comprised by neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee view also comprised by neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee knowledge?
Answer: It may be view but not knowledge.
What is seeing that is not knowledge?
The answer is:
the eye-faculty; this is called seeing that is not knowledge.
What is knowledge that is not vision?
The answer is:

excluding the five views and mundane right view, all other tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness aggregate and the wisdom associated with the five consciousness aggregates—this is called knowledge that is not vision.
What is the knowledge of views?
The answer is:
the five views and mundane right view; these are called the knowledge of views.
What is neither view nor knowledge?
The answer is:
excluding the aforementioned matters.
Is that which is comprised by neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee view also comprised by neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee wisdom?
Answer: It may be view but not wisdom.
What is seeing that is not wisdom?
The answer is:
the eye-faculty; this is called seeing that is not wisdom.
What is wisdom that is not vision?
The answer is:

excluding the five views and worldly conventional views, all other tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness aggregate and the wisdom associated with the five consciousness aggregates—this is called wisdom that is not vision.
What is the wisdom of views?
The answer is:
the five views and mundane views (sāṃvṛtijñāna), these are called the wisdom of views.
What is neither view nor wisdom?
The answer is:
excluding the aforementioned instances.
Is that which is comprised by knowledge that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner also comprised by wisdom that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: It is so.
Is non-learner and non-non-learner wisdom subsumed by non-learner and non-non-learner knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
Accomplishment, cessation, and likewise [the others] are also thus.
These are: inquiry, establishment of principles, inclusion, accomplishment, and cessation.
As that Brahmā made this statement:

Regarding this Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Sovereign, I have falsely claimed the inferior dharma as supreme; this is the view-delusion (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which is to be abandoned through the vision of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

Regarding the Creator, I claim that what was not created was created; this is the precept-and-vow-delusion (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is to be abandoned through the vision of the Truth of Suffering.

To speak of "sublime" while using inferior dharmas to falsely claim them as supreme is the view-grasping (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), which is abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya).

To create sentient beings where none exist and to falsely claim such acts were performed is the precept-and-vow-grasping (śīlavrataparāmarśa), which is abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering.
Just as those Brahmakāyika devas speak thus:

"This Brahmā is the Great Brahmā, the Sovereign, the Wealthy One," falsely claiming the inferior to be supreme—this is the "thief-like view" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), which is to be abandoned through the vision of the Truth of Suffering.
To claim that one creates the various classes of sentient beings when there is no such creator is the "theft of precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering.
To call something "sublime" while stealing base dharmas and claiming them to be supreme is the "theft of views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering.

To claim that sentient beings are created, or to speak of creation where there is no creator, is the theft of precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is to be abandoned through the realization of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
For example, as that brahmin Dīrghanakha spoke these words:
"Everything, Gautama!"
I cannot bear it.
This is included within the extreme view of annihilationism and is to be abandoned through the realization of the Truth of Suffering.
All of this, Gautama!
I accept this;
it is included within the extreme view of eternalism and is to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering. Regarding "I have what I accept and what I do not accept":
[this refers to] the distinction between what is accepted and what is not accepted.
That which exists as "endurance" is subsumed under the extreme view of eternalism and is to be abandoned through the realization of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
That which exists as "non-endurance" is subsumed under the extreme view of annihilationism and is to be abandoned through the realization of the truth of suffering.
This refers to the view that an Arhat emits impurity, and that his physical form is like that of a *kāmāvacara* deva or a spirit.

To claim that an Arhat emits impurity and defiles his bedding and mats—asserting what was not done as having been done—is the "theft of precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is to be abandoned through the realization of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
This so-called view that an Arhat is liberated by himself alone and lacks further knowledge—
claiming that an Arhat does not possess this wisdom— is a false and heterodox view, to be abandoned through the Truth of the Path.
This refers to the view that an arhat is liberated from doubt;
yet the arhat has already transcended doubt. This is a false and deviant view, abandoned through the Truth of the Path.
The view that one has attained arhatship through the knowledge of others—
that an arhat is not known by others— is a false and erroneous view, abandoned through the realization of the Truth of the Path.

This view, which claims that what is called the "path to suffering" is indeed the "path to suffering," and asserts that there is no action where there is action—this is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering. This concludes the fifth section, named after this chapter.

The fourteenth chapter, the Fivefold Section (Pañcaka-varga) of the Abhidharma, is completed. It consists of two hundred ślokas of fourteen syllables each in the Sanskrit original, and three thousand five hundred and forty-nine words in the Qin translation.
The knowledge of others' minds has four aspects, and craving likewise has five;
clearly understanding and extinguishing inversions, one practices the path of samādhi.
What is the knowledge of others' minds? What is the knowledge of recollecting past lives?
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, does one thereby know the minds of others?
Conversely, if one knows the minds of others, does one possess the knowledge of others' minds?
If one possesses the knowledge of recollecting past lives, does one thereby recollect past lives?
If one possesses the knowledge of recollecting past lives, is that the "knowledge of recollecting past lives"?
If it is the knowledge of recollecting past lives, does that person know the mental states and thoughts of others in the past?
If one knows the mental states and thoughts of others in the past, is that the knowledge of recollecting past lives?
What is equanimity-liberation of mind (*samacittavimukti*)? What is liberation of mind free from doubt (*aniścitacittavimukti*)?
For what reason is equanimity-liberation of mind called "love" (*prema*)?
Are all liberations of mind associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
If they are associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), are they all liberated through the resolve of equanimity (sāmayikī vimukti)?
And as for those who are liberated through the resolve of being free from doubt (akopyā vimukti), are they all associated with the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna)?
If one is associated with the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), is all such a person liberated through the resolve free from doubt (*akopya-dṛṣṭi-vimukti*)?
What is the clear vision (*vidyā*) of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and what is the knowledge (*jñāna*) of the learner?
What is the clear vision of the adept (*aśaikṣa*) and what is the knowledge of the adept?
When practicing the Dharma, what kind of faith is first attained: faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha?
Regarding these four perversions, how many are extinguished and how many are not extinguished by a Srotāpanna?
Regarding these three samādhis, how many does a srotāpanna accomplish in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
If a path is past, has that entire path been cultivated and relied upon?
If a path has been cultivated and relied upon, is that entire path past?
If a path is future, is that entire path neither cultivated nor relied upon?
If a path is neither cultivated nor relied upon, is that entire path future?
If a path is present, is that entire path to be cultivated?
If a path is to be cultivated, is that entire path present?
I wish to explain in full the meaning of this chapter:
What is the knowledge of others' minds? What is the knowledge of recollecting past lives?
And what is the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer:

If, through the wisdom cultivated and its fruit, one recollects what has been cultivated, and having attained it without loss, the applicable wisdom manifests before one; and regarding the perceptions, observations, and activities of other sentient beings and others, one knows their mental states as they truly are—this is called the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*)?
The answer is:

it is that wisdom which is cultivated and its fruit; when the wisdom that can be employed—having recollected what was cultivated and attained without loss—is present before one, one cognizes past lives according to their characteristics in countless births. This is called the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, does one thereby know the minds of others?
Answer: There are cases where one possesses the knowledge of others' minds but does not know the minds of others.
What is meant by "the knowledge of others' minds" being "not the knowledge of others' minds"?
The answer is:
if the knowledge of others' minds pertains to the past or the future, this is called "knowledge of others' minds" which is "not the knowledge of others' minds."
What is meant by "knowing another's mind" without it being the "knowledge of another's mind"?
The answer is:
when one knows another's mind by observing their physical signs or hearing their words, this is called knowing another's mind without it being the knowledge of another's mind.
What is the knowledge that knows the minds of others, and how does it know the minds of others?
The answer is:

if there is a wisdom that is cultivated and the fruit of such cultivation, which—having recollected what was cultivated—is an attained and non-forgettable wisdom that manifests before one; and if, regarding the perceptions, observations, and activities of other beings and other persons, one knows their mental states as they truly are, this is called the knowledge that knows the minds of others, and it is by this that one knows the minds of others.
What is meant by not possessing the knowledge of others' minds and also not knowing the minds of others?
Answer: It refers to all cases except those mentioned above.
If one possesses the knowledge of recollecting past lives, does that mean one actually recollects past lives?
The answer is:
there are cases where one possesses the knowledge of recollecting past lives but does not actually recollect past lives.
How is it that the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) does not itself recollect past lives?
The answer is:
if the knowledge of recollecting past lives pertains to the past and the future, this is called the knowledge of recollecting past lives that does not recollect past lives.
What is the recollection of past lives that is not the knowledge of recollecting past lives?
The answer is:

as one is born with the recollection of past lives, if one attains this knowledge through birth such that it recognizes the forms and appearances of those past lives, this is called the recollection of past lives that is not the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
What is the knowledge of recollecting past lives?
Does that [knowledge] itself recollect past lives? Answer:

If, through the wisdom cultivated and its fruit, one recollects what was cultivated and, having attained it without loss, brings forth the applicable wisdom that is present before one, such that one knows past lives according to their characteristics throughout countless births—this is called the knowledge of recollecting past lives, by which one recollects past lives.
What is it that is neither the knowledge of recollecting past lives nor the failure to recollect past lives?
The answer is:
excluding the aforementioned matters.
If one possesses the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), does that person know the mental states and dharmas thought by others in the past?
Answer: There are cases where one possesses the knowledge of recollecting past lives but does not know the mental states and dharmas thought by others in the past.
What is the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna) such that one does not know the mental states of others in the past?
The answer is:

if the knowledge cultivated and its fruit—the knowledge that has been cultivated, attained, and not lost, which is brought into presence—knows the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and mind experienced by oneself during past births, this is called the knowledge of recollecting past lives such that one does not know the mental states of others in the past.
What is meant by knowing the mental states of others in the past that is not the knowledge of recollecting former existences (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

if there is a wisdom that is cultivated and its fruit, which—having recollected what was cultivated—is a wisdom already attained and not lost, and which is currently present and functional; and if, regarding this life, there is a knowledge of the minds of other sentient beings that has grasped the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and mind of those others in the past—this is called knowing the mental states of others in the past that is not the knowledge of recollecting former existences.
How does the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna) also know the mental states and dharmas contemplated by others in the past?
The answer is:

when there is a wisdom that is cultivated and its fruit, which—having recollected what was cultivated—is a wisdom already attained and not lost, and which is currently present and functional; and when this wisdom perceives the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and mind of other sentient beings and other persons during their past lives, as maintained by their own cognition—this is called the knowledge of recollecting past lives that also knows the mental states and dharmas contemplated by others in the past.
What is the case where there is no knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and one also does not know the mental states of others in the past?
The answer is:

if there is a wisdom that is cultivated and the fruit of such cultivation, wherein the memory of what was cultivated is attained and not lost, and this applicable wisdom manifests in the present, such that one knows within this life the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and mind with which one personally interacted in the past—this is called having neither the knowledge of past lives nor knowing the mental states of others in the past.
What is liberation through equanimity of mind (*samacittavimukti*), and what is liberation through freedom from doubt (*aniścitacittavimukti*)?
What is meant by liberation through equanimity of mind?
The answer is:

The mind that is associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) of an Arhat liberated through equanimity—whether it has already been liberated, is being liberated, or will be liberated—is called "liberation through equanimity."
What is the liberation through the mind characterized by the absence of doubt?
The answer is:

it is the mind—whether already liberated, currently being liberated, or yet to be liberated—that is associated with the Arhat’s knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) regarding the dharmas that are free from doubt; this is called the liberation through the mind characterized by the absence of doubt.
For what reason is "equanimity-liberation" (samacittavimukti) referred to as "love" (prema)?
The answer is:
the Arhat who possesses equanimity-liberation protects this dharma; he cherishes and treasures that equanimity-liberation for himself.
The Arhat well protects himself, cherishing the storehouse of the self, thinking: "May I not fall away from this Dharma.
It is just as a woman who has an only son, who loves him so dearly that she never takes her eyes off him.

Just as that mother nurtures, protects, covers, and shelters [her child], so that it is neither cold nor hot, neither hungry nor thirsty, and free from all afflictions—so too, these Arhats liberated by mind protect, take up, and store this Dharma within themselves;
those Arhats liberated by mind well protect, take up, and store [it], thinking: "May I not fall away from this Dharma."
For this reason, the term "equanimity-liberation" (sāmayikī-kṣānti-vimukti) refers to "love" (maitrī).
Are all equanimity-liberations associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna)?
Answer: No.
Or, there is equanimity-liberation that is not associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
What is this equanimity-liberation that is not associated with the knowledge of exhaustion?
The answer is:

The mind of an Arhat who is liberated through equanimity (sāmayikī-vimukti), being associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi), is liberated, has been liberated, or will be liberated throughout the three periods of time; this is called liberation through equanimity that is not associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
What is that which is associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) but is not liberation through equanimity of mind (*sāmayikī cetovimukti*)?
The answer is:

for an Arhat free from doubt (*akopyadharman*), the mind that is associated with the knowledge of exhaustion—whether it has been liberated, is being liberated, or will be liberated—is called that which is associated with the knowledge of exhaustion but is not liberation through equanimity of mind.
What is meant by "equanimity-liberation associated with the knowledge of exhaustion"?
The answer is:

the equanimity-liberation of an Arhat associated with the knowledge of exhaustion refers to the mind that has been liberated, is being liberated, or will be liberated; this is called equanimity-liberation associated with the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is meant by "not associated with equanimity-liberation and not associated with the knowledge of exhaustion"?
The answer is:

the mind of an Arhat free from doubt—whether it is currently liberated, already liberated, or will be liberated—which is associated with the knowledge of non-arising and the right view of one beyond training; this is called "not associated with equanimity-liberation and not associated with the knowledge of exhaustion."

Are all those associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) associated with the liberation through the absence of doubt (*aniścitavimukti*)?
Answer: It is so;
all that is associated with the knowledge of non-arising is associated with the liberation through the absence of doubt.
Is there any liberation through the resolution of doubt that is not associated with the knowledge of non-arising?
Answer: Yes.

There is the mind associated with the knowledge of exhaustion and the right view of one who is an Arhat of the dharma of being without doubt, which has been liberated, is being liberated, or will be liberated.
What is training in clear vision (*vidyā*)? What is training in knowledge (*jñāna*)?
And what is training in clear vision?
The answer is:
It is the training in wisdom (*prajñā*).
What is the training in knowledge (*jñāna*)?
The answer is:
This concerns the training in the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).
What is the clear vision (*vidyā*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and what is the knowledge (*jñāna*) of one beyond training?
What is the clear vision of one beyond training?
Answer: It is the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna).
What is the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna)?
Answer: It is the eight knowledges of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
When practicing the Dharma, what kind of faith is first attained: faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha?
The answer is:

The cultivation of the dharma of suffering, the cultivation of the dharma of its origin, the cultivation of the dharma of its cessation, and the cultivation of the dharma of the path—these are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Regarding these four inversions, how many are extinguished and how many remain unextinguished for a *srotāpanna*?
The answer is:
all are extinguished.
Regarding these three samādhis, how many does a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) accomplish in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
The answer is:
they all accomplish them in the future; those that have already ceased but are not lost are accomplished in the past; and if they are manifest before one, they are accomplished in the present.
If a path is past, has all that path already been cultivated and relied upon?
Answer: It is so;
if a path is past, all that path has already been cultivated and relied upon.
Is there a path that has been cultivated and relied upon, yet is not of the past?
Answer: Yes;
it is the future path that has been cultivated and relied upon.
If one asks: "Is every path that is future neither yet cultivated nor yet relied upon?
The answer is:
"There may be paths that are future which are neither not-yet-cultivated nor not-yet-relied-upon."
What is the path that is future, yet this path is neither unpracticed nor unattended?
The answer is:
the future path has already been practiced and already attended; this is called the path that is future, yet this path is neither unpracticed nor unattended.
What is it that is neither cultivated nor relied upon, yet this path is not future?
The answer is:
when a path never before attained manifests in the present, this is what is neither cultivated nor relied upon, and this path is not future.
What is the path that is future, yet this path has not been cultivated and has not been relied upon?
The answer is:
if the path is future and has not been cultivated and has not been relied upon, this is called the path that is future, yet this path has not been cultivated and has not been relied upon.
What is the path that is not future, yet this path is neither unpracticed nor unattended? Answer:
When a past path, previously attained, manifests in the present, this is called the path that is not future, yet this path is neither unpracticed nor unattended.
If a path is present before one, is that entire path cultivated with tranquility?
The answer is:
Yes; if a path is present before one, that entire path is cultivated with tranquility.
Is it possible that one cultivates this path, yet this path does not manifest before one?
The answer is:
Yes. For example, when the path has not yet been attained, the remaining paths of the future which are cultivated through those seeds do not manifest.

The third chapter, "The Section on the Knowledge of Others' Minds" (*Paracittajñāna-varga*), in the *Abhidharma* is hereby concluded. In the Sanskrit original it consists of one hundred and thirty-two *ślokas*; in the Qin translation it comprises two thousand seventy-four words, totaling thirteen thousand one hundred and sixty-nine words.
The Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra, Volume Ten;
The Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra, Volume Eleven.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra.
Compiled by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Fu Qin dynasty:
The wisdom that realizes the cessation of conditions is also the mindfulness of impermanence;
it is the final among the seven stations.

Regarding the eight knowledges— namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna), knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)— how many knowledges are subsumed under the knowledge of phenomena, and so on, up to how many knowledges are subsumed under the knowledge of the path?

If one has attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), how many of these eight knowledges does one possess and how many does one not possess? Likewise, up to the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), how many of these eight knowledges does one possess and how many does one not possess?
If one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), does one cultivate the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
Conversely, if one cultivates the subsequent knowledge, is there the knowledge of phenomena?

When one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena, are there the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path?
If one cultivates the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), does one possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
If, up to and including the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), does one possess the knowledge of the path?
If one cultivates the knowledge of the path, does one possess the knowledge of exhaustion?
Is there any dharma that is both *dharma-jñāna* and has *dharma-jñāna* as its object?
Is there any *dharma-jñāna* that has as its objects *paracitta-jñāna*, *saṃvṛti-jñāna*, *duḥkha-jñāna*, *samudaya-jñāna*, *nirodha-jñāna*, or *mārga-jñāna*?
Is there any *mārga-jñāna* that has *mārga-jñāna* as its object?

Are path-knowledge, dharma-knowledge, subsequent-knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, conventional-knowledge, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, and knowledge of cessation objects [of consciousness]?
How many objects does dharma-knowledge take as its object?

How many objects do dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, and knowledge of the path take as their objects?
How many conditions does path-knowledge (maggañāṇa) condition?

How many conditions do dhamma-knowledge (dhammañāṇa), subsequent knowledge (anvayañāṇa), knowledge of others' minds (paracittañāṇa), conventional knowledge (sammutiñāṇa), knowledge of suffering (dukkhañāṇa), knowledge of origin (samudayañāṇa), and knowledge of cessation (nirodhañāṇa) condition?
If various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are those fetters extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
Conversely, if fetters are extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena, are they fetters bound to the desire realm?
As for those fetters bound to the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), are those fetters extinguished by the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
If those fetters are extinguished by the knowledge of the unknown (anājñāta-ājñāna-jñāna), are they fetters bound to the form and formless realms?
Are all those fetters that are to be abandoned by the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)?
If those fetters are abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), are those fetters abandoned by the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*)?

Are those fetters abandoned by the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) which are abandoned by the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*)?
If those fetters are abandoned by the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), are those fetters abandoned by the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*)?
Are those fetters which are extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) fully realized as exhausted by that knowledge of phenomena?
If those fetters are proven to be exhausted through the attainment of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), does the knowledge of phenomena extinguish those fetters?
And regarding those fetters that are to be extinguished by the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), is there proof of their exhaustion through that subsequent knowledge?
If those fetters are realized as being exhausted through the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), does that knowledge of the unknown extinguish those fetters?

Regarding those fetters extinguished by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*): does the knowledge of the path realize the exhaustion of those fetters?
If one attains the realization of the exhaustion of those fetters through the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), does that knowledge of the path extinguish those fetters?

By how many knowledges is the faculty of the eye (*cakṣurindriya*) known, and so on, up to: by how many knowledges is the ignorance (*avidyā*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) known?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:

"By cultivating, practicing, and widely disseminating the perception of impermanence, one exhausts sensual desire, exhausts desire for the realm of form, and exhausts desire for the formless realm; one exhausts restlessness, exhausts conceit, and exhausts ignorance. This perception should be said to be associated with dharma-knowledge."

Regarding the knowledge of the unknown, the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of its origin, the knowledge of its cessation, and the knowledge of the path: should these be said to be with vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka and with vicāra, or without vitarka and without vicāra?
Should it be said that it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), or associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
Should it be said to be empty (*śūnya*), signless (*animitta*), and wishless (*apraṇihita*)?

Should it be said to have objects belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-ālambana*), or objects belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-ālambana*), or objects that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta-ālambana*)?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:

"A bhikṣu who is skilled in the seven points and has mastered the meaning of the three contemplations regarding this Dharma attains the exhaustion of all outflows. He discriminates form as suffering, the origin of form, the cessation of form, and the path leading to the cessation of form; he knows, as they truly are, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form."
Should this wisdom be called "dharma-wisdom" (*dharmajñāna*),
or should it be called "path-wisdom" (*mārgajñāna*)?
The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
What is the exhaustion of form?
What is the relinquishment and emergence from form?
What is the distinction between the exhaustion of form and the relinquishment and emergence from form?
What are feeling, perception, and formations? What is the exhaustion of consciousness?
What is the relinquishment of consciousness?
What is the difference between the exhaustion of consciousness and the relinquishment of consciousness?
I wish to expound fully the meaning of this chapter.
There are eight knowledges:

the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) subsumes dharma-knowledge itself, while five other knowledges enter into it to a small degree:
the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
The knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) subsumes the knowledge of the unknown; five knowledges enter into it to a small degree:
the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
The knowledge of others' minds is subsumed by the knowledge of others' minds; four knowledges partially enter into it:
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Conventional knowledge (samvṛtijñāna) subsumes conventional knowledge; one type of knowledge enters into it slightly:
the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
Suffering-knowledge (duḥkhajñāna) subsumes suffering-knowledge; two types of knowledge enter into it slightly:
Dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are [included].
Knowledge of origination and knowledge of cessation are likewise.
Path-knowledge subsumes path-knowledge, while three knowledges enter into it to a small degree:
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)—this concludes the section on the single-inclusion gate.
If one has attained the knowledge of phenomena, how many of these eight knowledges does one possess, and how many does one not possess?
Answer: It may be three, four, five, six, seven, or eight.
What are the three?
Answer:

In the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are three factors—the [three] truths such as suffering; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are four, being the aforementioned three plus that one.

In the subsequent patience regarding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayakṣānti*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there are three; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are four.

In the subsequent knowledge of the unknown suffering (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), there are four [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and five if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds; this remains as before for the subsequent [stages].
In the patience regarding the dharma of cultivation (*dharmajñānakṣānti*), there are four if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and five if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the stage of the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-anvaya-jñāna*), if one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are five; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are six.

In the stage of the subsequent patience toward phenomena (*dharmajñāna-anvaya-kṣānti*), the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-anvaya-jñāna*), and the patience regarding the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharmajñāna-kṣānti*), if one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, there are five; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are six.
In the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*kṣayadharma-jñāna*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there are six; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are seven.

In the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of destruction (*kṣayānvaya-kṣānti*), in the subsequent knowledge of destruction (*kṣayānvaya-jñāna*), and in the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārgadharma-kṣānti*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there are six; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are seven.

In the path-knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*), there are seven [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), there are seven if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), how many of these eight knowledges does one accomplish and how many does one not accomplish?
Answer: Either four, five, six, seven, or eight.
What are the four?
The answer is:

when there is the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāta-jñāna*) but no knowledge of others' minds, there are four factors, namely suffering and so forth; when there is knowledge of others' minds, there are five.
In the stage of the patience of the dharma of practice (*dharmakṣānti*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there are four; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are five.
In the stage of the dharma-knowledge of practice (*dharmajñāna*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there are five; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are six.

In the stage of the patience of the knowledge of the unknown regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), there are five [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); there are six if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the stage of the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), there are six if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds; there are seven if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the case of the patience regarding the full knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*), the full knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāta-jñāna*), and the dharma-patience regarding the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), there are six [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*); there are seven if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
In the case of the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), there are seven if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds; there are eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the case of the patience regarding the unknown of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the unknown of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are seven;

if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are eight. If one is endowed with the knowledge of others' minds, how many of these eight knowledges does one possess, and how many does one not possess?
Answer: It may be two, four, five, six, seven, or eight.
What are the two?

Answer: For ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), there are two types of knowledge: conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). For those free from outflows (*anāsrava*), when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is present, there are two.

When the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) is present, there are four. When the subsequent patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*) is present, there are four.
In the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāta-jñāna*), there are five; in the patience regarding the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*), five.

In the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), six; in the patience regarding the unknown regarding origination (*samudaya-ajñāta-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the unknown regarding origination (*samudaya-ajñāta-jñāna*), as well as in the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*), there are six.

In the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), seven; in the patience regarding the unknown regarding cessation (*nirodha-ajñāta-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation (*nirodha-ajñāta-jñāna*), as well as in the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), there are seven.
Regarding the eight [knowledges] of the path-dharma-knowledge (mārga-dharma-jñāna), the path-subsequent-forbearance (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti), and the path-subsequent-knowledge (mārga-anvaya-jñāna):
if one possesses conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), how many of these eight knowledges does one possess and how many does one not possess?
Answer:
It may be one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight.
What is meant by "one"?
Answer:

For an ordinary person who lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there is one; for a stainless person when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is present before them, there is one.
For an ordinary person who possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are two; for a stainless person when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering is present before them, there are two.

In the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), there are three [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*), and four if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
In the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-kṣānti*), there are three if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and four if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), there are four [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and five if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the patience regarding the dharma of origination (*samudaye dharmajñānakṣānti*), there are four if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and five if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the stage of the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-anvaya-jñāna*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there are five; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are six.

In the stage of the subsequent patience regarding phenomena (*dharmajñāna-anvaya-kṣānti*), in the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-anvaya-jñāna*), and in the patience regarding the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharmajñāna-kṣānti*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there are five; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are six.

In the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*kṣayadharma-jñāna*), there are six [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and seven if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the patience regarding the unknown of destruction (*kṣayānvaya-kṣānti*), in the knowledge of the unknown of destruction (*kṣayānvaya-jñāna*), and in the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārgadharma-kṣānti*), there are six if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and seven if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the path-knowledge of dharma (*mārga-dharmajñāna*), there are seven [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), there are seven if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), how many of these eight knowledges does one possess and how many does one not possess?
Answer: It may be three, four, five, six, seven, or eight.
What are the three?
The answer is:

when one possesses the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) but lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are three; when one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are four.

In the stage of the patience regarding the unknown of suffering (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*), there are three knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and four if one possesses it.
In the stage of the knowledge regarding the unknown of suffering (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), there are four knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and five if one possesses it.

In the stage of the patience of dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñānakṣānti), there are four knowledges when one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and five knowledges when one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
In the stage of dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), there are five knowledges when one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and six knowledges when one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the stage of the patience of the knowledge of the unknown regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), there are five [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds; there are six if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the stage of the knowledge of the dharma of exhaustion (*kṣayadharma-jñāna*), there are six if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds; there are seven if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the case of the patience regarding the full knowledge of the unknown (*ājñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*), the full knowledge of the unknown (*ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), and the dharma-patience regarding the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), there are six [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); there are seven if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
In the case of the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), there are seven if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds; there are eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the path of patience regarding the unknown (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the path of knowledge regarding the unknown (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), there are seven knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
If one has attained the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanā-jñāna*), how many of these eight knowledges does one possess, and how many does one not possess?
Answer: It may be five, six, seven, or eight.
What are the five?

Answer: During the cultivation of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), there are five knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and six if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

During the subsequent patience (*anvayakṣānti*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the patience regarding the knowledge of cessation (*kṣayajñānakṣānti*), there are five knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and six if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
In the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*kṣayajñāna*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there are six; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are seven.

In the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of destruction (*kṣayānvayakṣānti*), in the subsequent knowledge of destruction (*kṣayānvayajñāna*), and in the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārgadharmakṣānti*), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there are six; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are seven.
In the path-knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*), there are seven [knowledges] when the knowledge of others' minds is absent, and eight when the knowledge of others' minds is present.

In the patience regarding the path of subsequent knowledge (*mārgānvayakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), there are seven when the knowledge of others' minds is absent, and eight when the knowledge of others' minds is present.
If one has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), how many of these eight knowledges does one possess and how many does one not possess?
Answer: Either six, seven, or eight.
What are the six?
The answer is:

when there is the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of the dharma (dharmajñāna), but no knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), there are six; if there is knowledge of others' minds, there are seven.

In the stage of the patience regarding the full knowledge of the unknown (*ājñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*), the full knowledge of the unknown (*ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), and the dharma-patience regarding the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), there are six knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and seven if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
In the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), there are seven knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the path-knowledge-of-the-unknown-forbearance (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the path-knowledge-of-the-unknown (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), there are seven knowledges when the knowledge of others' minds is absent, and eight knowledges when the knowledge of others' minds is present.
If one has attained the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), how many of these eight knowledges does one possess, and how many does one not possess?
Answer: Sometimes seven, sometimes eight.
What are the seven?

Answer: In the path-knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), there are seven knowledges if one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), there are seven knowledges if one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, and eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds. This concludes the two sections on the gates of accomplishment.
If one is cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), is that the knowledge of what is not yet known (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: One may be cultivating the knowledge of phenomena without it being the knowledge of what is not yet known.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and not the knowledge of what is not yet known (*anājñātajñāna*)? Answer:

When one practices the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering, the knowledge of phenomena regarding the origin, the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation, or the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path; or when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings to presence a previously acquired knowledge of phenomena—this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena and not the knowledge of what is not yet known.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of what is not yet known (anājñāta-ājñāna-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of the dharma (dharma-jñāna)?
The answer is:

when one cultivates the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering, the knowledge of the unknown regarding the origin, or the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation; or when a learner who has seen the path, or an arhat, brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of the unknown—this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of what is not yet known that is not the knowledge of the dharma.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when practicing the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), whether one is a seeker who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat; or when, having not previously attained untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), mundane knowledge (*laukikajñāna*) manifests before them—at such times, one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge. This is called cultivating the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge.
What is meant by not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and not cultivating the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
The answer is:

for one who has attained the vision of the tracks (śaikṣa-darśanamārga-pratilabdha), such as an Arhat, when the previously acquired conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is present before them, or when conventional knowledge not previously acquired is present before them, at that time they do not cultivate the knowledge of phenomena or the subsequent knowledge.

In all ordinary persons with defiled minds or neutral minds, when entering the concentration of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*) or the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*), in the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), and when all stages of patience (*kṣānti*) are present, one does not cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of what is yet to be known (*anvaya-jñāna*). This is called not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena and not cultivating the knowledge of what is yet to be known.
If one is cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one possess the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: One may cultivate the knowledge of phenomena without possessing the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) without the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one cultivates the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), or the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) without possessing the knowledge of others' minds; or when one cultivates the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvayajñāna*)—whether as a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat—and the previously acquired knowledge of phenomena manifests before them, yet that is not the knowledge of others' minds.
If one has not previously attained untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) and it now manifests before one, at that time one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds;

if one has not previously attained conventional wisdom (saṃvṛti-jñāna) and it now manifests before one, at that time one cultivates the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), but not the knowledge of others' minds.
This is called cultivating the knowledge of dharma but not the knowledge of others' minds.
What is meant by cultivating the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of dharma?
The answer is:

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*): when either previously acquired or previously unacquired knowledge of others' minds manifests, or when previously unacquired conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) manifests—and this is not itself the knowledge of others' minds—at that time, one who is training (*śaikṣa*), having seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*), or an Arhat, cultivates the knowledge of others' minds; or when previously acquired knowledge of others' minds manifests, this is not the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). This is called cultivating the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of phenomena.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)? Answer:

When one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds is practicing the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), whether they be a learner on the track of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat, and the previously attained knowledge of phenomena manifests before them, they cultivate that [knowledge]; this is the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds.

If one has not previously attained the manifestation of untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna), at the time of its attainment, one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna);

if one has not previously attained the manifestation of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), at the time of its attainment, one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of others' minds.
This is called cultivating the knowledge of dharma and the knowledge of others' minds.
What is it to neither cultivate the knowledge of dharma nor the knowledge of others' minds? Answer:

When one who is practicing the unknown-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāta-jñāna*), the unknown-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-ajñāta-jñāna*), or the unknown-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-ajñāta-jñāna*), or a learner on the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) or an Arhat brings to presence the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) previously acquired—that is not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) consisting of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*).
If one brings to presence the worldly knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*) previously acquired, that is not the knowledge of others' minds;
if one brings to presence the worldly knowledge not previously acquired, at that time one cannot cultivate either dharma-knowledge or the knowledge of others' minds.

In all cases of ignorance, the knowledge of others' minds, the defiled mind, and the indeterminate mind of ordinary persons; when entering the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*; in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*); and when all stages of receptivity (*kṣānti*) are present—these do not cultivate the knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*) nor the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of dharma and not possessing the knowledge of others' minds.
If one is cultivating the knowledge of dharma at that time, does one possess the conventional knowledge?
Answer: Yes.
Or, one may cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) but not conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena but not conventional knowledge?
The answer is:

When practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering, the dharma-knowledge of origination, the dharma-knowledge of cessation, or the dharma-knowledge of the path; when practicing the subsequent knowledge of the path; or when a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat brings to presence the dharma-knowledge previously attained, or brings to presence an untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) not previously attained—at such times, one cultivates dharma-knowledge but not conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna). This is called cultivating dharma-knowledge but not conventional knowledge.
What is the cultivation of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) that is not dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna)?
The answer is:
when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), whether having previously attained it or not, brings conventional knowledge into manifestation.

When one who is practicing the limit of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*), the limit of the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaye 'nvayajñāna*), or the limit of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe 'nvayajñāna*), whether they be a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat, brings to presence a conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) previously acquired or not previously acquired, they cannot at that time cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). This is called cultivating conventional knowledge and not the knowledge of phenomena.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
The answer is:

when a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada) or an arhat brings to presence a previously unobtained outflow-free knowledge (anāsravajñāna), at that time they cultivate conventional knowledge.
If one has not previously attained mundane knowledge and brings it into manifestation, and at that time attains the cultivation of untainted knowledge,
this is called the cultivation of dharma-knowledge and conventional knowledge.
What is the non-cultivation of dharma-knowledge and conventional knowledge?
Answer:

For one who has entered the path of vision (śaikṣa-darśanamārga), for an arhat, or when the previously attained untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) manifests before them—yet that is not the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna);

during all defiled or neutral states of mind; upon entering the samādhi of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) or the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); in the heaven of non-conception (asaṃjñi-deva); and when any of the receptive patiences (kṣānti) manifest—one does not cultivate dharma-knowledge or conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
If one is cultivating the knowledge of phenomena at that time, is it the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)?
The answer is:
Or, one may cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) but not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena but not the knowledge of suffering?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the path of the knowledge of the dharma of the exhaustion of outflows—whether a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat—brings to presence the dharma-knowledge previously acquired that is not the knowledge of suffering, this is called cultivating the dharma-knowledge but not the knowledge of suffering.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)? Answer:

When one who is practicing the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna)—whether a learner on the path of vision (darśana-mārga) or an arhat—brings to presence the knowledge of suffering previously acquired, which is not the knowledge of phenomena; this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering that is not the knowledge of phenomena.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?
The answer is:

when the knowledge of phenomena regarding the cultivation of suffering and the knowledge of the path (mārga-anvayajñāna) regarding the cultivation [of the truths] are present—whether for a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣadṛṣṭiprāpta) or for an Arhat—and the previously acquired knowledge of phenomena manifests before them, this is the knowledge of suffering.

If, when one has not previously attained either untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) or conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), these now manifest, and at that time one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*),
this is called cultivating the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of suffering.
What is meant by not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the cultivation of the knowledge of arising (samudayajñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), or the knowledge of the unknown (anvayajñāna)—whether they be a seeker who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-darśanamārga-pratipanna) or an arhat—brings to presence a previously acquired untainted knowledge (anāsravajñāna) that is neither the knowledge of phenomena nor the knowledge of suffering; this is what is meant.

Whether it be worldly knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that is presently manifest, at such times one does not cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) or the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).

Furthermore, when all ordinary persons possess a defiled or neutral mind; when they enter the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*; in the Heaven of No Perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*); or when any of the "acceptances" (*kṣānti*) are presently manifest—one does not cultivate the knowledge of phenomena or the knowledge of suffering.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).
If one is cultivating the knowledge of phenomena at that time, is one also cultivating the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*)?
Answer: No.
Or, one may cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) but not the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena but not the knowledge of origination?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering, the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation, or the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path—whether they be a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat—brings to presence the dharma-knowledge previously acquired, which is not the knowledge of cultivation; this is called cultivating the knowledge of dharma and not the knowledge of cultivation.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of practice (*bhāvanājñāna*) that is not the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the knowledge of the subsequent realization (*anvayajñāna*)—whether a learner on the path of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of practice, this is not the knowledge of phenomena; this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of practice that is not the knowledge of phenomena.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena regarding cultivation; when one cultivates the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*); or when, for a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or for an arhat, the previously attained knowledge of phenomena manifests before them—these are the knowledge of cultivation.

If one has not previously attained untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna), or if mundane knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) is present before one, at that time one cultivates and practices the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
This is called the cultivation of dharma-jñāna and anvaya-jñāna.
What is meant by not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the path of the subsequent knowledge of the exhaustion of suffering (*duḥkhakṣayānvayajñāna*), whether they be a learner on the track of vision (*śaikṣa-darśanamārgastha*) or an arhat, brings to presence an originally attained untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) that is neither the knowledge of phenomena nor the knowledge of origination; this is what is meant.

Whether it be worldly knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that manifests in the present, one cannot at that time cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

Furthermore, when all ordinary persons possess a defiled or neutral mind; when entering the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*; in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*); or when any of the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) manifest—one does not cultivate the knowledge of phenomena or the subsequent knowledge.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
If one is cultivating the knowledge of phenomena at that time, is it also the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)?
The answer is:
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) but not the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena but not the knowledge of exhaustion?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, the knowledge of the dharma of origination, or the knowledge of the dharma of the path—whether as a learner who has seen the tracks or as an arhat—brings to presence the dharma-knowledge previously acquired, which is not the knowledge of exhaustion; this is called cultivating the knowledge of dharma and not the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that is not the knowledge of non-arising (*anvayajñāna*)? Answer:

When one who is practicing the knowledge of the unknown regarding exhaustion (*kṣayājñātājñānajñāna*), whether they be a learner on the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) or an arhat, brings to presence the previously attained knowledge of exhaustion which is not the knowledge of non-arising—this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion that is not the knowledge of non-arising.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the knowledge of the phenomena of exhaustion, or one who is practicing the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), being either a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat, brings to presence the knowledge of phenomena previously acquired—this is the knowledge of exhaustion.

If one has not previously attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) or if untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) is present before one, at that time one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
This is called the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is meant by not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudayānvayajñāna*), or a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the path], or an arhat, brings to presence a previously acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) that is neither the knowledge of phenomena nor the knowledge of exhaustion; this is what is meant.

Whether it be mundane knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that is currently manifest, one cannot at that time cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) or the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

This is also the case for all ordinary persons when their minds are defiled or neutral, when they have entered the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*, in the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), and when all moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*) are manifest; in these states, one does not cultivate the knowledge of phenomena or the knowledge of exhaustion.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna).
If one is cultivating the knowledge of phenomena at that time, is one also cultivating the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)?
Answer: No.
Or, one may cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) but not the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena but not the knowledge of the path?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, the knowledge of the dharma of origination, or the knowledge of the dharma of cessation—whether they be a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat—and brings to presence the dharma-knowledge previously acquired, which is not path-knowledge, this is called "practicing dharma-knowledge, not path-knowledge."
What is the cultivation of path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*) that is not dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings to presence a path-knowledge previously acquired, which is not dharma-knowledge—this is called the cultivation of path-knowledge that is not dharma-knowledge.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)?
The answer is:

when one who is training in the traces of vision or an Arhat brings to presence the dharma-knowledge of the path that was previously attained during the cultivation of the path—this is the knowledge of the path.

If one has not previously attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) or if untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) is present before one, at that time one cultivates dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*).
This is called the cultivation of dharma-knowledge and path-knowledge.
What is meant by not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
The answer is:
