when one who is practicing the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaye 'nvayajñāna*), or the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe 'nvayajñāna*), or when a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the truths] or an arhat brings to presence a previously acquired outflow-free knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) that is neither the knowledge of phenomena nor the knowledge of the path; this is what is meant by not cultivating them.

Whether one has previously attained it or not previously attained it, when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is present, one cannot at that time cultivate dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) or path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*).

Furthermore, for all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) during states of defiled or neutral mind, upon entering the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or *nirodha-samādhi*, in the Heaven of No Perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), and when any of the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) are present, one does not cultivate dharma-knowledge or path-knowledge.
This is called the completion of not cultivating dharma-knowledge and path-knowledge.
When one cultivates unknown-knowledge (anājñāta-ājñāna-jñāna), does one then possess the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of the unknown (anājñāta-ājñāna-jñāna) but not the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of the unknown but not the knowledge of others' minds? Answer:

When one practices the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge of origin and cessation (*samudaye-nirodhe 'nvaya-jñāna*), there is no knowledge of others' minds;

when one practices the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge 'nvaya-jñāna*), whether as a seeker who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-darśana-mārga*) or as an arhat, if the previously attained subsequent knowledge manifests, this is not knowledge of others' minds;

or if, at a time when previously unattained outflow-free knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) manifests, one attains and cultivates the subsequent knowledge at that moment, it is not knowledge of others' minds.

If one does not previously possess mundane knowledge (*lokasamvṛtijñāna*) and it now manifests, at that time one cultivates the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) but not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
This is called cultivating the knowledge of the unknown but not the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds that is not the knowledge of the unknown?
Answer: It is the knowledge of others' minds belonging to ordinary persons (pṛthagjana).

Whether it be one who has previously attained it or one who has not previously attained it, when the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) manifests before them; or when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that was not previously attained manifests before them—this is not the knowledge of others' minds—at that time, one who is a trainee on the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) or an Arhat cultivates the knowledge of others' minds. When the knowledge of others' minds that was previously attained manifests before them, this is not the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*).
This is called cultivating the knowledge of others' minds, not the knowledge of what is yet unknown.
What is meant by cultivating the knowledge of what is yet unknown and the knowledge of others' minds?
The answer is:

When one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds practices the path of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), whether as a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has entered the stream of vision or as an Arhat, if the previously acquired knowledge of the unknown manifests before them, this is the knowledge of others' minds;

or, if the previously unacquired untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) or conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) manifests before them, at that time one cultivates both the knowledge of the unknown and the knowledge of others' minds.
This is called cultivating the knowledge of the unknown and the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of the unknown and the knowledge of others' minds?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering, the dharma-knowledge of origination, cessation, or the path—whether they be a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat—brings to presence an originally acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), this is neither the knowledge of what is not yet known (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) nor the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
If they bring to presence an originally acquired mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), this is not the knowledge of others' minds.
If they bring to presence a mundane knowledge that was not previously acquired, at that time they do not cultivate the knowledge of what is not yet known nor the knowledge of others' minds.

In all cases of ignorance, the knowledge of others' minds, the defiled mind, and the indeterminate mind of ordinary persons; when entering the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*; in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*); and when all forms of patience (*kṣānti*) are present—one does not cultivate the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of others' minds.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
If one cultivates the knowledge of the unknown, does one also cultivate those [other] knowledges?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of what is not yet known (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) but not conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of what is not yet known but not conventional knowledge?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the path of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), whether they be a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat, brings to presence the previously attained knowledge of the unknown, or brings to presence an untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) not previously attained—at that time, they cultivate the knowledge of the unknown and not conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). This is called cultivating the knowledge of the unknown and not conventional knowledge.
What is the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*) but not the cultivation of the knowledge of what is not yet known (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person brings to presence either a conventional knowledge previously attained or one not previously attained; or when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*), or an arhat, brings to presence either a conventional knowledge previously attained or one not previously attained—at such times, they do not cultivate the knowledge of what is not yet known. This is called the cultivation of conventional knowledge but not the cultivation of the knowledge of what is not yet known.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who has cultivated the limit of the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), or the limits of the knowledge of the unknown regarding origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*), or a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the path] or an arhat, brings to presence a conventional knowledge not previously attained, at that time they cultivate the knowledge of the unknown.
If, when the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) that was previously unattained manifests in the present, one attains the cultivation of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) at that time—
this is called the cultivation of both the knowledge of the unknown (ajñāta-ājñāna-jñāna) and conventional knowledge.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of the unknown and conventional knowledge?
Answer:

When one is practicing the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), or the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination, cessation, and the path (*samudaya-nirodha-mārga-dharmajñāna*); or when a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an Arhat brings to presence the previously attained untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), this is not the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñāta-ājñāna*).

Furthermore, during all defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*) and neutral minds (*avyākṛta-citta*), upon entering the concentration of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*) or the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*), in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), and when all patiences (*kṣānti*) are present—one does not cultivate the knowledge of the unknown or conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of the unknown at that time, is it also the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) but not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of the unknown but not the knowledge of suffering?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the path of training—whether a seeker who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-darśanamārga-pratipannaka) or an arhat—is cultivating the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna) or the knowledge of the exhaustion of the unknown (ājñātāvī-jñāna), and this previously attained knowledge of the unknown manifests before them, it is not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna). This is called cultivating the knowledge of the unknown without the knowledge of suffering.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) that is not the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñāta-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*)—whether a learner on the path of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat—brings to presence the knowledge of suffering previously acquired, this is not the knowledge of the unknown; this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering that is not the knowledge of the unknown.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of suffering through the knowledge of the unknown?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering, or practicing the knowledge of the unknown regarding the path—whether a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of the unknown, this is the knowledge of suffering.

If one has not previously attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), or if untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) is present before one, at that time one attains and cultivates subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).
This is called the cultivation of subsequent knowledge and the knowledge of suffering.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the cultivation of the dharma-knowledge of origination, cessation, or the path; or a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the noble ones], or an arhat, brings to presence a previously acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) which was not, at that time, the knowledge of the unknown or the knowledge of suffering.

Whether it be mundane knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that manifests in the present, at that time one does not cultivate the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).

Furthermore, for all ordinary persons with defiled or neutral minds, when entering the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*, in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), and when all moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*) manifest, one does not cultivate the knowledge of the unknown nor the knowledge of suffering.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of the unknown at that time, does one also cultivate the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*)?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of what is not yet known (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) but not the knowledge of cultivation (kṣaya-jñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of what is not yet known but not the knowledge of cultivation?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāta-jñāna*) or the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation (*nirodha-ajñāta-jñāna*), whether they be a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat, brings to presence the previously attained knowledge of the unknown (*ajñāta-jñāna*) which is not the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*); this is called cultivating the knowledge of the unknown and not the knowledge of cultivation.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*) that is not the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the knowledge of cultivation regarding phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), whether a learner on the path of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat, brings to presence the knowledge of cultivation previously acquired—this is not the knowledge of the unknown; this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of cultivation that is not the knowledge of the unknown.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of what is not yet known (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna) and the knowledge of what has been known (ājñāta-jñāna)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the path of the knowledge of what is not yet known and the knowledge of what has been known—whether a learner who has seen the tracks (dṛṣṭapada) or an arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of what is not yet known, this is the knowledge of what has been known.

If one has not previously attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), or if untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) is present before one, at that time one attains and cultivates the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of what has been known (*ājñātāvī-jñāna*).
This is called the cultivation of the knowledge of the unknown and the knowledge of what has been known.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of what has been known (*ājñātāvī-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), or the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*)—whether as a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or as an arhat—brings to presence the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) previously acquired, this is neither the knowledge of the unknown nor the knowledge of what has been known.

Whether it be worldly knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that is now manifest, at that time one does not cultivate the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of what has been known (*ājñātāvī-jñāna*).

Furthermore, for all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) when their minds are defiled or neutral, when they have entered the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*, in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), and when any of the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) are manifest, one does not cultivate the knowledge of the unknown nor the knowledge of what has been known.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) and the knowledge of cultivation (kṣaya-jñāna).
If one is cultivating the knowledge of the unknown, is that the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of what is not yet known (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) but not the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of what is not yet known but not the knowledge of exhaustion? Answer:

When one who is practicing the path—whether a trainee who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-darśanamārga-pratipanna) or an arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), this is not the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna). This is called cultivating the knowledge of the unknown, but not the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that is not the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*)? Answer:

When one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of exhaustion—whether a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of exhaustion, this is not the knowledge of the unknown; this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion that is not the knowledge of the unknown.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the path of the knowledge of the unknown regarding exhaustion (*kṣayānājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna-mārga-anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), whether a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat, brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of the unknown, this is the knowledge of exhaustion.

If one has not previously attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), or if untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) is present before one, at that time one attains and cultivates the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
This is called the cultivation of the knowledge of the unknown and the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is meant by not cultivating the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), or the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*)—whether they be a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat—brings to presence the untainted knowledge previously acquired, this is neither the knowledge of the unknown nor the knowledge of exhaustion.

Whether it be mundane knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that is manifested in the present, at that time one does not cultivate the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

Furthermore, for all ordinary persons when their minds are defiled or neutral, when they have entered the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*, in the Heaven of No Perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), and when any of the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) are manifested, one does not cultivate the knowledge of the unknown nor the knowledge of exhaustion.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) at the time when one cultivates the knowledge of the unknown, does one [also] cultivate the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) but not the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of the unknown but not the knowledge of the path?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaye 'nvaya-jñāna*), or the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe 'nvaya-jñāna*)—whether as a seeker established in the vision of the path (*śaikṣa-darśana-mārga-stha*) or an Arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired subsequent knowledge that is not the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), this is called the cultivation of subsequent knowledge and not the knowledge of the path.
What is the cultivation of path-knowledge that is not unknown-knowledge?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the cultivation of the knowledge of the dharma of the path—whether a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat—brings to presence the path-knowledge previously acquired, this is not unknown-knowledge; this is called the cultivation of path-knowledge that is not unknown-knowledge.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) through the knowledge of what is not yet known (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna)?
The answer is:

when a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada) or an arhat cultivates the knowledge of the path through the knowledge of what is not yet known, and the previously attained knowledge of what is not yet known manifests before them—this is the knowledge of the path.

If one has not previously attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) or if untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) is present before one, at that time one attains the cultivation of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñājñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
This is called the cultivation of the knowledge of the unknown and the knowledge of the path.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), or the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), or a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings to presence a previously acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that is neither the knowledge of the unknown nor the knowledge of the path; [this is the non-cultivation thereof].

Whether it be worldly knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that manifests in the present, at that time one does not cultivate the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

Furthermore, for all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) when their minds are defiled or indeterminate, when they enter the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*, in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), and when all moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*) manifest, one does not cultivate the knowledge of the unknown nor the knowledge of the path.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
When one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), is that the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds but not conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of others' minds but not conventional knowledge? Answer:

When one who has attained the path through the knowledge of others' minds—whether a trainee (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks or an Arhat—brings to presence a previously acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), this is the knowledge of others' minds;
or, when bringing to presence an untainted knowledge not previously acquired, at that time one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds, but not conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
This is called cultivating the knowledge of others' minds but not conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
What is meant by cultivating conventional knowledge but not the knowledge of others' minds?
The answer is:
For an ordinary person who lacks the knowledge of others' minds, either the mundane knowledge previously acquired or that not previously acquired manifests in the present;

or for a learner on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) regarding the edge of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*), or an arhat, when the mundane knowledge previously acquired manifests in the present—this is not the knowledge of others' minds;
or when the mundane knowledge not previously acquired manifests in the present—at such times, one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds.
This is called cultivating the knowledge of equality (samatājñāna) but not the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
What is the cultivation of both the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of equality?
The answer is:

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when the knowledge of others' minds—whether previously attained or not previously attained—is manifested before them, or when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) not previously attained is manifested before them (which is not itself the knowledge of others' minds), at that time they cultivate the knowledge of others' minds.

For one who has entered the path of vision (*śaikṣa-darśanamārga*) or an Arhat, when the previously attained knowledge of others' minds is manifested before them, this is equalized knowledge (*samatājñāna*);
or when conventional knowledge not previously attained is manifested before them, at that time they cultivate the knowledge of others' minds.

If, when the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that was previously unattained manifests before one, one attains at that time the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge?
The answer is:

when one practices the dharma-knowledge of suffering, the dharma-knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path; when one lacks the knowledge of others' minds while practicing the subsequent knowledge of the path; and when a learner who has seen the tracks (the stream-enterer) or an arhat brings to presence the originally acquired untainted knowledge—this is not the knowledge of others' minds.

If one has not previously attained the manifestation of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), at that time one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) or conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

Furthermore, in all cases where there is no knowledge of others' minds—such as when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) possesses a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) or an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), or when one has entered the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*, or in the Heaven of No Perception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), or when any stage of receptivity (*kṣānti*) is manifest—one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds or conventional knowledge.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
When one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds, is that the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of suffering.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of suffering?
The answer is:

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*): whether it is a knowledge of others' minds previously acquired or not previously acquired that now manifests, or if it is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) not previously acquired that now manifests—this is not the knowledge of others' minds.

At the time this [conventional knowledge] is attained, one who is a trainee (*śaikṣa*) following the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) or an Arhat cultivates the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of others' minds previously acquired manifests.
This is called cultivating the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of suffering.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering but not the knowledge of others' minds? Answer:

When practicing the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*), and when lacking the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); or when practicing the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), whether one is a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat; and when either the previously attained knowledge of suffering manifests before them, or an unconditioned knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) not previously attained manifests before them—at these times, one cannot cultivate the knowledge of others' minds.
If a conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) not previously attained manifests before them, at that time one may cultivate the knowledge of suffering, but not the knowledge of others' minds.
This is called cultivating the knowledge of suffering, but not the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the cultivation of both the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of suffering?
The answer is:

When one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds is practicing the path of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), whether as a trainee (*śaikṣa*) who has entered the stream of vision or as an Arhat, and when either previously unattained outflow-free knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) or conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is present before them, at that time they attain and cultivate both the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*). This is called the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of suffering.
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle Eleven [and] Fascicle Twelve.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra and Zhu Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty.

From the remainder of the *Citta-bhāvanā-varga* (Chapter on the Cultivation of Mind) within the fourth section of the *Jñāna-skandha* (Book of Knowledge): What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of suffering?
Answer:

When one is practicing the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), or the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), and either a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat brings to presence the originally acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), this is not the knowledge of others' minds nor is it the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
Furthermore, when one brings to presence the originally acquired conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), this is not the knowledge of others' minds.

If one has not previously attained mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and it does not manifest at present, then at that time one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) or the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).

Furthermore, in all cases where there is no knowledge of others' minds—such as when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) possesses a defiled mind (*kliṣṭacitta*) or an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛtacitta*), when entering the meditative absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamādhi*) or the absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*), in the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñideva*), or when any of the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) are manifest—one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds or the knowledge of suffering.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of suffering.
When one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds, does one also cultivate that [knowledge of] the habitual?
Answer: Yes.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of cultivation.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of cultivation?
The answer is:

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), whether they have previously attained it or not, when the knowledge of others' minds manifests before them; or when they have previously not attained it, and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) manifests before them—which is not itself the knowledge of others' minds—at that time they cultivate the knowledge of others' minds.
For one in training who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣadṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an Arhat, the knowledge of others' minds which they have previously attained manifests before them.
This is called cultivating the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of practice.
What is meant by cultivating the knowledge of practice but not the knowledge of others' minds? Answer:

When one practices and cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (*anvayajñāna*), or the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); or when practicing and cultivating the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)—whether as a seeker who has entered the stream of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or as an Arhat—if the previously acquired knowledge of phenomena is manifested, or if an unconditioned knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) not previously acquired is manifested, at that time one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds.
If a conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) not previously acquired is manifested, at that time one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena but not the knowledge of others' minds.
This is called the cultivation of the knowledge of wisdom, but not the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the cultivation of both the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of wisdom? Answer:

When one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds is practicing the path of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), whether as a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has entered the stream of vision or as an arhat, and when mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*) or untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) not previously attained manifests before them, at that time they attain and cultivate the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of cultivation (*vairāgya-jñāna*). This is called cultivating the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of cultivation.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the practice?
The answer is:

when one is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering, the subsequent knowledge of suffering, the dharma-knowledge of cessation, the subsequent knowledge of cessation, or the dharma-knowledge of the path; or when a learner who has seen the tracks [of the path] or an arhat brings to presence the originally acquired untainted knowledge, this is not the knowledge of others' minds.

If one has not previously attained mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and it does not manifest at present, then at that time one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) or the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*).

Furthermore, in all cases where there is no knowledge of others' minds—such as when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) possesses a defiled mind (*kliṣṭacitta*) or an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛtacitta*), when entering the *asaṃjñisamādhi* or the *nirodhasamādhi*, in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), or when any moment of receptivity (*kṣānti*) manifests—one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds or the knowledge of cultivation.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of cultivation.
If one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds at that time, is it the knowledge of exhaustion?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of exhaustion.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of exhaustion? Answer:

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), whether they previously attained it or not, when the knowledge of others' minds manifests before them, or when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that was not previously attained manifests before them—though this is not itself the knowledge of others' minds—at that time they cultivate the knowledge of others' minds;
likewise, for one who has entered the path of vision (*śaikṣa-darśanamārga*) or an Arhat, the knowledge of others' minds that was previously attained manifests before them.
This is called cultivating the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
What is meant by cultivating the knowledge of exhaustion but not the knowledge of others' minds?
The answer is:

When practicing the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-kṣayajñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge of the destruction (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣayajñāna*), one does not practice the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). This applies to those who have entered the path of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or to Arhats, when the previously attained knowledge of destruction manifests before them, or when an unconditioned knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) not previously attained manifests before them; at such times, they do not practice the knowledge of others' minds.

Furthermore, if a conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) not previously attained manifests before them, at that time they practice the knowledge of destruction, but not the knowledge of others' minds.
This is called cultivating the knowledge of the destruction [of the outflows] (kṣayajñāna) but not the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
What is the cultivation of both the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the destruction? Answer:

When one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds is practicing the path of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), whether as a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has entered the stream of vision or as an arhat, and when mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*) or untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that was previously unattained manifests before them, they attain at that time the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*). This is called the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of exhaustion?
The answer is:

when one is practicing the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, the subsequent knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the dharma of origination, the subsequent knowledge of origination, or the knowledge of the dharma of the path; or when a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat brings to presence the originally acquired untainted knowledge—this is neither the knowledge of others' minds nor the knowledge of exhaustion.
If one who has previously attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) brings it into manifestation, this is not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);

if one who has not previously attained conventional knowledge brings it into manifestation, at that time one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds or the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

Furthermore, for all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who lack the knowledge of others' minds—during states of defiled or neutral mind, upon entering the meditative absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamādhi*) or the absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*), in the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñideva*), and when any of the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) are manifest—one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds or the knowledge of exhaustion.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of exhaustion.
If one is cultivating the knowledge of others' minds, is that the knowledge of the path?
Answer: Yes.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of the path.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of the path?
The answer is:

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), whether they have previously attained it or not, when the knowledge of others' minds manifests before them—or when mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that was not previously attained manifests before them—this is not [the path of] the knowledge of others' minds; yet at that time, one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds.

For a trainee (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the path] or an Arhat, when the previously attained knowledge of others' minds manifests before them, this is not the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
This is called cultivating the knowledge of others' minds but not the knowledge of the path.
What is cultivating the knowledge of the path but not the knowledge of others' minds? Answer:

Regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path practiced, there is no knowledge of others' minds; regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path practiced, whether it be a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat, when the dharma-knowledge previously attained manifests before them, this is not knowledge of others' minds.
If the untainted knowledge previously unattained manifests before them, one cannot at that time cultivate the knowledge of others' minds.
If the conventional knowledge previously unattained manifests before them, one can at that time cultivate the dharma-knowledge of the path, but not the knowledge of others' minds.
This is called the cultivation of the knowledge of the path, but not the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the cultivation of both the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the path?
The answer is:

When one who has attained the path through the knowledge of others' minds—whether a trainee on the path of vision or an Arhat—attains the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), this is the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) regarding the previously acquired knowledge of others' minds. Whether it be conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) or untainted knowledge (anāsravajñāna) that was not previously attained now manifests before them, at that time they cultivate both the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the path.
This is called cultivating the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the path.
What is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the path?
The answer is:

When practicing the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of the dharma of origin (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvayajñāna*), or the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvayajñāna*), for one who has entered the stream of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an Arhat, if the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) previously acquired manifests before them, this is not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) nor the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
If the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) previously acquired manifests before them, this is not the knowledge of others' minds.
If the conventional knowledge not previously acquired manifests before them, at that time one cannot cultivate the knowledge of others' minds nor the knowledge of the path.

In all cases of ignorance, when an ordinary person possesses a defiled mind or an indeterminate mind, when entering the samādhi of non-perception or the samādhi of cessation, in the heaven of non-perception, and when all moments of receptivity (kṣānti) are present, one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds or the knowledge of the path.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the path.
When one cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), is that the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) but not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).
How does one cultivate conventional knowledge but not the knowledge of suffering?
The answer is:
When an ordinary person brings to presence either previously acquired or previously unacquired conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);

or when a learner who has entered the path of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat brings to presence either previously acquired or previously unacquired conventional knowledge during the cultivation of the practice of the subsequent knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they cannot at that time cultivate the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).
This is called cultivating the knowledge of equality (samata-jñāna) but not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).
What is meant by cultivating the knowledge of suffering but not the knowledge of equality?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering—whether a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat—brings to presence the previously attained knowledge of suffering, or brings to presence an untainted knowledge not previously attained, they cannot at that time cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). This is called cultivating the knowledge of suffering but not conventional knowledge.
What is the cultivation of both conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*), being either a learner on the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) or an arhat, brings to presence a conventional knowledge or an outflow-free knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) that was previously unobtained, at that time one cultivates both conventional knowledge and knowledge of suffering; this is called the cultivation of conventional knowledge and knowledge of suffering.
What is the non-cultivation of conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the cultivation of the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudayadharmanirvedhabhāgīya*), the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhadharmanirvedhabhāgīya*), or the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārgadharmanirvedhabhāgīya*), or a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings to presence the previously acquired outflow-free knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), this is not the knowledge of suffering.

In all defiled minds and indeterminate minds, upon entering the samādhi of non-perception or the samādhi of cessation, in the heaven of non-perception, and when all forms of patience (*kṣānti*) are present, one does not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) or the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of equanimity (*upekṣājñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of equanimity, does one also cultivate the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*)?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) but not the knowledge of practice (anvayajñāna).
How does one cultivate conventional knowledge but not the knowledge of practice?
The answer is:
When a worldling brings to presence either a conventional knowledge previously acquired or one not previously acquired;

or when a learner who has entered the path of vision, or an arhat, brings to presence a conventional knowledge previously acquired or one not previously acquired at the conclusion of the subsequent knowledge of suffering or the subsequent knowledge of cessation—during these times, they do not cultivate the knowledge of cultivation.
This is called cultivating conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) but not analytical knowledge (pratisaṃkhyā-jñāna).
What is the cultivation of analytical knowledge but not conventional knowledge?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the path of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)—whether they be a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat—either brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of phenomena or brings to presence an unconditioned knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) not previously acquired, at that time they do not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). This is called cultivating the knowledge of phenomena but not conventional knowledge.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*) and the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the knowledge of the path of origination (*samudayānvayajñāna*), or a learner who has entered the stream of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), or an arhat, brings to presence either mundane knowledge (*laukikajñāna*) not previously attained or untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), at that time they cultivate the knowledge of equality and the knowledge of origination; this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of equality and the knowledge of origination.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*) and the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), or the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*)—whether they be a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat—brings to presence the originally acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), this is not the knowledge of cultivation.

In all defiled minds and neutral minds; when entering the concentration of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*) or the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*); in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*); and when all stages of receptivity (*kṣānti*) are present—therein one does not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) or the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanā-jñāna*).
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of equality (samatājñāna) and the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
If one is cultivating the knowledge of equality, is that the knowledge of exhaustion?
The answer is: No.
Or, one cultivates conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) but not the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
How does one cultivate conventional knowledge but not the knowledge of exhaustion?
The answer is:
When a worldling brings to presence either a conventional knowledge previously acquired or one not previously acquired;

or when a learner who has entered the path of vision, or an arhat, brings to presence either a conventional knowledge previously acquired or one not previously acquired at the conclusion of the subsequent knowledge of suffering or the subsequent knowledge of origin—on such occasions, they do not cultivate the knowledge of exhaustion.
This is called cultivating conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) but not the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
What is meant by cultivating the knowledge of exhaustion but not conventional knowledge? Answer:

When one who is practicing the path of the knowledge of the destruction of outflows (kṣayajñāna-mārga-ājñājñāna) is a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat, and either the previously attained knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) manifests before them, or an unconditioned knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) not previously attained manifests before them—at that time, they do not cultivate conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna). This is called cultivating the knowledge of destruction but not conventional knowledge.
What is the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the limit of the subsequent knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayānvaya-jñāna*), whether as a learner who has entered the path of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat, brings either previously unobtained conventional knowledge or untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) into manifestation; at that time, one cultivates conventional knowledge and the knowledge of exhaustion. This is called the cultivation of conventional knowledge and the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the non-cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*), or the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*), or a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings to presence the originally acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), this is not the knowledge of exhaustion.

In all defiled minds and indeterminate minds, upon entering the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), in the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), and when all moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*) are present, one does not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) or the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of equality, is that the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) but not the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
How does one cultivate conventional knowledge but not the knowledge of the path? Answer:
When an ordinary person brings to presence either a mundane knowledge previously acquired or one not previously acquired;

or when a practitioner on the path of seeing suffering, at the limit of the subsequent knowledge of suffering, or at the limits of the subsequent knowledge of origin or cessation; or when a learner who has seen the tracks, or an arhat, brings to presence either a mundane knowledge previously acquired or one not previously acquired—at these times, they do not cultivate the knowledge of the path.
This is called cultivating conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) and not path knowledge (mārgajñāna).
What is the cultivation of path knowledge and not conventional knowledge? Answer:

When practicing the path, whether it be the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) or the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna), for one who is a learner (śaikṣa) who has seen the tracks (dṛṣṭi-pratipanna) or an Arhat, when the path-knowledge previously attained manifests, or when an untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) not previously attained manifests—at such times, one does not cultivate conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna). This is called cultivating path-knowledge and not conventional knowledge.
How does one cultivate both conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat brings to presence either conventional knowledge or untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) that was previously unobtained, at that time they cultivate both conventional knowledge and the knowledge of the path; this is called cultivating conventional knowledge and the knowledge of the path.
What is the non-cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and path knowledge (*mārgajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*), or the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), or a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings to presence the originally acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), this is not path knowledge.

In all defiled minds and indeterminate minds, upon entering the concentration of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*) or the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*), in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), and when all moments of patience (*kṣānti*) are present, one does not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
This is called not cultivating the path-knowledge (mārga-jñāna) that is equal-knowledge (samatā-jñāna).
If one cultivates the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), does one [also] cultivate the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna)?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of suffering but not the knowledge of origination.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of suffering but not the knowledge of origination?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering or the subsequent knowledge of suffering—whether they be a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of suffering, this is called cultivating the knowledge of suffering and not the knowledge of origin.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of origination (samudaya-dharmajñāna) or the subsequent knowledge of origination (samudaya-anvayajñāna)—whether they be a learner on the path of vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat—brings to presence the knowledge of origination previously acquired, this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of origination that is not the knowledge of suffering.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), a learner on the track of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), or an arhat, brings to presence either mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*) not previously attained or untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), at that time they cultivate the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination; this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination?
The answer is:

when one practices the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the subsequent unknown-knowledge of cessation, or the dharma-knowledge of the path; or when a learner who has seen the tracks [of the noble path] or an arhat brings to presence the untainted knowledge previously acquired—this is not the knowledge of suffering nor the knowledge of origination.

If mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), whether previously acquired or not previously acquired, is present before one, it is impossible at that time to cultivate the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).

This refers to all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) whose minds are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*), as well as those who have entered the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*, those in the Heaven of No Perception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), and when any of the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) are present before them; in these cases, they do not cultivate the knowledge of suffering or the knowledge of origination.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination.
If one is cultivating the knowledge of suffering, is that the knowledge of cessation?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of suffering but not the knowledge of exhaustion.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of suffering but not the knowledge of exhaustion?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna) or the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvayajñāna)—whether as a seeker who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of suffering, this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering, not the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that is not the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayadharman*) or the subsequent knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayānvayajñāna*)—whether they be a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of exhaustion, this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion that is not the knowledge of suffering.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the path of the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*), whether a learner on the track of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat, brings to presence either previously unobtained mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*) or untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), at that time one cultivates the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of exhaustion; this is called cultivating the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is meant by not cultivating the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanā-dharmajñāna*), the subsequent unknown-knowledge of cultivation (*anvaya-anājñāta-jñāna*), or the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*)—whether a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat—brings to presence the originally acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that is neither the knowledge of suffering nor the knowledge of exhaustion; this is what is meant.

Whether it be worldly knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that is manifest, one cannot at that time cultivate the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

Furthermore, for all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) with defiled or neutral minds, when entering the samādhi of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the samādhi of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or for those in the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), and when any moment of receptivity (*kṣānti*) is manifest, one does not cultivate the knowledge of suffering or the knowledge of exhaustion.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of exhaustion.
If one is cultivating the knowledge of suffering, is that the knowledge of the path?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of suffering but not the knowledge of the path.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of suffering but not the knowledge of the path?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna) or the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvayajñāna)—whether as a seeker who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of suffering, this is called cultivating the knowledge of suffering and not the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) that is not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)? Answer:

When one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of the path—whether a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat—brings to presence the knowledge of the path previously acquired, this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of the path that is not the knowledge of suffering.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)? Answer:

When one who is practicing the knowledge of the unknown regarding the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna)—whether a learner on the track of vision (dṛṣṭi-patta) or an arhat—brings to presence either previously unobtained outflow-free knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) or conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), at that time one cultivates the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the path; this is called cultivating the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the path.
What is meant by not cultivating the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one is practicing the knowledge of the dharma of cultivation (*bhāvanā-dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanā-anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), or the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*); or when a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings to presence a previously attained outflow-free knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that is neither the knowledge of suffering nor the knowledge of the path.

Whether it be mundane knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that is currently manifest, one cannot at that time cultivate the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

This is because all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), when their minds are defiled or neutral, when they have entered the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*, in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), or when any of the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) are currently manifest, do not cultivate the knowledge of suffering or the knowledge of the path.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the path.
If one is cultivating the knowledge of cessation, is that the knowledge of exhaustion?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of cultivation (bhāvanājñāna) but not the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
What is the case of cultivating the knowledge of cultivation but not the knowledge of exhaustion?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the path—whether a learner on the track of vision or an arhat—manifests the previously acquired knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*), this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of cultivation, not the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) but not the knowledge of arising (*anvayajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayadharmajñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayānvayajñāna*), whether as a seeker who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or as an arhat, brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of exhaustion, this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion but not the knowledge of arising.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) through the knowledge of practice (mārgajñāna)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the path of the knowledge of the unknown (anvayajñāna)—whether a learner on the track of vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat—brings to presence either mundane knowledge (laukikajñāna) not previously attained or untainted knowledge (anāsravajñāna), at that time one cultivates the knowledge of practice and the knowledge of exhaustion; this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion through the knowledge of practice.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna*), or the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*)—whether as a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or as an arhat—brings to presence the originally acquired untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), this is not the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion.

Whether it be conventional knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that is manifest, at that time one cannot cultivate the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*) or the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

For all ordinary persons with defiled minds or neutral minds, when entering the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*, in the Heaven of No Perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), and when any of the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) are manifest, one does not cultivate the knowledge of cultivation or the knowledge of exhaustion.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
If one is cultivating the knowledge [of the path], is that the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of cultivation (bhāvanājñāna) but not the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
What is meant by cultivating the knowledge of cultivation but not the knowledge of the path?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing, training, or has seen the tracks—whether a learner or an Arhat—brings to presence the previously acquired knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*), this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of cultivation, not the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of the path that is not the knowledge of practice?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of the path—whether a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat—brings to presence the knowledge of the path previously attained, this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of the path that is not the knowledge of practice.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) by means of the knowledge [of the path] (jñāna)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the knowledge of the unknown regarding the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna)—whether a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat—brings to presence either a previously unobtained outflow-free knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) or conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), at that time one cultivates the knowledge of the path by means of the knowledge; this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of the path by means of the knowledge.
What is the non-cultivation of the knowledge of cultivation and the knowledge of the path?
The answer is:

when one who has practiced the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, the subsequent knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the dharma of cessation, or the subsequent knowledge of cessation—whether as a learner who has seen the tracks or as an arhat—brings to presence the originally acquired untainted knowledge, this is not the cultivation of the knowledge of cultivation and the knowledge of the path.

Whether it be one who has originally attained it or one who has not originally attained it, when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is present before them, they cannot at that time cultivate the knowledge of practice (*bhāvanājñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

Furthermore, for all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) with afflicted minds or neutral minds; when entering the *asaṃjñi-samādhi* or the *nirodha-samādhi*; in the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*); and when all moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*) are present before them—they do not cultivate the knowledge of practice or the knowledge of the path.
This is called not cultivating the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
If one is cultivating the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), is that the knowledge of the path?
Answer: No.
Or, one cultivates the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) but not the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
How does one cultivate the knowledge of exhaustion but not the knowledge of the path?
The answer is:

When one who is practicing the path—whether a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat—brings to presence the previously attained knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), this is called cultivating the knowledge of exhaustion and not the knowledge of the path.
What is the cultivation of the knowledge of the path that is not the knowledge of exhaustion?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the dharma-knowledge of the path—whether a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat—brings to presence the knowledge of the path previously attained, this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of the path that is not the knowledge of exhaustion.
How does one cultivate the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the knowledge of the unknown regarding the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)—whether a learner on the track of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat—brings to presence either worldly knowledge (*laukikajñāna*) not previously attained or untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), at that time one cultivates the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path; this is called the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path.
What is meant by not cultivating the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
The answer is:

when one who is practicing the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*), or the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvayajñāna*)—whether as a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat—the originally attained untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) manifests before them, yet this is neither the knowledge of exhaustion nor the knowledge of the path.

Whether it be a mundane knowledge previously acquired or not previously acquired that is presently manifest, one cannot at that time cultivate the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) or the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).

This is also the case for all ordinary persons with defiled or neutral minds, when entering the samādhi of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) or the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), in the heaven of non-conception (asaṃjñisattva), and when any of the "acceptances" (kṣānti) are presently manifest; in these states, one does not cultivate the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of the path.

This concludes the section on the three doors of cultivation regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*).
Is there any dharma that is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the knowledge of dharmas (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: Yes.

There is [a case where] it exists; there is no [case where] unknown-knowledge (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) exists as its object. There is [a case where] it exists with other remaining objects as its condition.
Is there perhaps a case where unknown-knowledge has unknown-knowledge as its object?
The answer is: Yes.
There is. The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has no object; the remaining [knowledges] have objects.
Is it possible for the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) to know another's mind by taking that other's mind as its object?
Answer: Yes.
There is; there is a remainder that has an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Is it possible for conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) to have conventional knowledge as its object?
Answer: Yes.
There is; there is a remainder that serves as a condition.
Is it possible for the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) to have the knowledge of suffering as its object?
Answer: Yes.
There are none.
The knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge have objects; the remaining [knowledges] have no objects.
The same applies to the knowledge of cultivation.
Is there any knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) that takes knowledge of exhaustion as its object?
Answer: No;
nor does any other remaining [knowledge] take it as its object.
Is there path-knowledge that takes path-knowledge as its object?
Answer: Yes.

Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has no such objects; the remaining [knowledges] do have objects. Regarding the four conditions in the gateway of dependent origination, for that dharma-knowledge, it is the cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya), the immediate-condition (anantara-pratyaya), the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), and the predominant-condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna) has [other states] as its cause, immediate antecedent, and predominance, but lacks an object-condition.
Knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) has [other states] as its cause, immediate antecedent, object, and predominance.
Conventional knowledge (samvṛti-jñāna) has [other knowledges] as its immediate, object, and predominant conditions, but it has no cause-condition.

Knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna), and knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) have [other knowledges] as their cause, immediate, and predominant conditions, but they have no object-condition.
Path-knowledge is the cause, the immediate antecedent, the object-condition, and the predominant condition for subsequent knowledge.
Subsequent knowledge is the cause, the immediate antecedent, the object-condition, and the predominant condition for that very subsequent knowledge.
The knowledge of others' minds has [the preceding state as its] cause, immediate, object, and predominance conditions.
Conventional knowledge has [the preceding state as its] immediate, object, and predominance conditions, but no cause condition.
The knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, and the knowledge of cessation have [the conditions of] cause, sequence, and predominance, but lack the object-condition (*ālambana*).
The knowledge of the path has [the conditions of] cause, sequence, object, and predominance; it is largely similar to the fourfold origination-knowledge.
Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has [other dharmas] as its cause, immediate antecedent, and predominance condition, but it has no object-condition.
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna), that knowledge of others' minds has [other dharmas] as its cause, immediate antecedent, object-condition, and predominance condition.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is related [to itself] by way of cause, immediate succession, object-condition, and predominance.
Suffering-knowledge (duḥkhajñāna) and origin-knowledge (samudayajñāna) are related [to conventional knowledge] by way of cause, immediate succession, object-condition, and predominance;
however, there are cases where there is a cause but no object-condition, and cases where there is an object-condition but no cause.
The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is a cause, a sequence-condition (anantara), and a predominance-condition (adhipati), but it has no object-condition (ālambana).

The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), and the knowledge of what is not yet known (anvayajñāna) are [for it] a cause, a sequence-condition, an object-condition, and a predominance-condition.
Equal-knowledge (samata-jñāna) is the cause, immediate antecedent, condition, and predominance for that same equal-knowledge.
Suffering-knowledge (duḥkha-jñāna) and origination-knowledge (samudaya-jñāna) are the immediate antecedent, condition, and predominance for it, but not its cause.
