The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) are sequential conditions (anantara-pratyaya), predominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya), but lack causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya) and objective conditions (ālambana-pratyaya).
The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledge of the unknown (anvayajñāna) are sequential conditions, objective conditions, and predominant conditions, but lack causal conditions.
The knowledge of others' minds is [related to itself] by way of cause, immediate succession, object, and predominance.
As for the knowledge of suffering, that knowledge of suffering is related to it by way of cause, immediate succession, and predominance, but not by way of object.
The knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanā-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*khaya-ñāṇa*) [act as] cause, immediate, and predominant conditions, but not as object conditions.

Path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*), dharma-knowledge (*dhamma-ñāṇa*), subsequent-knowledge (*anvaya-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*parassa-citta-ñāṇa*) [act as] cause, immediate, object, and predominant conditions.

Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) has [other knowledges] as its cause, immediate antecedent, object-condition (ālambana), and predominance-condition (adhipati), but it has no [simultaneous] cause.
The same applies to the knowledge of cultivation (bhāvanājñāna) and the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
As for the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), that path-knowledge has itself as its cause, immediate antecedent, object-condition, and predominance-condition.
Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and knowledge of others' minds are [related to] the cause, immediate, object, and predominant conditions.
Conventional knowledge is related to the immediate, object, and predominant conditions, but lacks the cause condition.
The knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, and the knowledge of cessation have the conditions of cause, sequence, and predominance, but they lack an object-condition (*ālambana*).
Regarding those fetters (*saṃyojana*) bound to the desire realm: are those fetters extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: There are fetters bound to the desire realm that are not extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).
How is it that there are fetters bound to the desire realm which are not extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena?
Answer:

Those fetters bound to the desire realm that are extinguished by patience (*kṣānti*), as well as those not extinguished by other forms of knowledge (*jñāna*), are called "fetters bound to the desire realm whose extinction is not by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)."
What are those fetters that are extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), yet these fetters are not bound to the desire realm? Answer:

Those fetters bound to the form and formless realms that are extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena—these are called fetters extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena that are not bound to the desire realm.
What are the fetters bound to the desire realm that are extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)? Answer:

Those fetters bound to the desire realm which are extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena—these are called the fetters bound to the desire realm that are extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena.
What are those fetters bound to the realm of desire that are not extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

those fetters bound to the realms of form and formlessness that are extinguished by patience (*kṣānti*), as well as those not extinguished by other forms of knowledge—these are called the fetters bound to the realm of desire that are not extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena.
Regarding those fetters bound to the form and formless realms, are those fetters extinguished by the knowledge of the unknown?
Answer: It is so;
those fetters extinguished by the knowledge of the unknown are fetters bound to the form and formless realms.
Are there fetters bound to the form and formless realms that are not abandoned by the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*)? Answer:

There are certain fetters bound to the form and formless realms that are abandoned by patience (*kṣānti*), as well as others that are abandoned by other types of knowledge, and yet others that are not abandoned at all.
Regarding those fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), are those fetters extinguished by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)?
Answer: Those fetters are not extinguished by the knowledge of suffering; those fetters are extinguished by patience (*kṣānti*).
If the various fetters are extinguished through the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), are those fetters abandoned by the vision of suffering (*darśana-prahātavya*)? Answer:
Those fetters are not abandoned by the vision of suffering; those fetters are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Regarding those fetters that are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*): are those fetters extinguished by the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)?
Answer: Those fetters are not abandoned by the knowledge of the path; those fetters are extinguished by receptivity (*kṣānti*).
If the various fetters are extinguished through the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), are those fetters abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)? Answer:
Those fetters are not abandoned by the path of seeing; those fetters are extinguished through cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—this is the sixth gateway of extinction (*nirodhadharmamukha*).
If various fetters are extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), are those fetters fully realized as exhausted by that same knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: It is so;
if various fetters are extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena, those fetters are fully realized as exhausted by that same knowledge of phenomena.
Is it the case that there are fetters for which one realizes the exhaustion through the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), yet those fetters are not extinguished by the knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: Yes;
there are fetters that are extinguished by the receptivities (*kṣānti*) and other knowledges, yet for which one realizes the exhaustion through the knowledge of phenomena.
If various fetters are extinguished through the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāna-jñāna*), are those fetters realized as being exhausted through that same knowledge of the unknown?
Answer: It is so;
if various fetters are extinguished through the knowledge of the unknown, those fetters are realized as being exhausted through that knowledge of the unknown.
Is there any fetter that is both fully realized through the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and yet is not extinguished by the knowledge of exhaustion?
Answer: Yes;
there are those fetters which are extinguished by patience (*kṣānti*) as well as by other knowledges, and which are fully realized through the knowledge of exhaustion.

If the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are extinguished through the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path, are those fetters fully realized as exhausted through the knowledge of the path?
Answer: It is so;
if the various fetters are extinguished through the knowledge of the path, those fetters are fully realized as exhausted through the knowledge of the path.
Is there a case where one fully realizes the exhaustion of certain fetters through the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), yet those fetters are not extinguished by the knowledge of the path?
Answer: Yes.

There are fetters that are extinguished by patience (*kṣānti*) as well as by other knowledges; those fetters are fully realized as exhausted through the knowledge of the path, which is the seventh door of correct extinction.
The eye-faculty is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties.
The faculty of mind (*manendriya*) is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

The same applies to the faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), joy (*saumanasyendriya*), equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), as well as the faculties of faith (*śraddhendriya*), energy (*vīryendriya*), mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

The male faculty and the female faculty are known by six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The life faculty is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.

The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) and the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (ājñendriya), and the faculty of "one who has already known" (ājñātāvīndriya) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna), the knowledge of origin (samudayajñāna), and the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).

The eye-base, the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and the form-base, sound-base, and tangible-object-base are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.

The eye-consciousness element, the ear-consciousness element, and the body-consciousness element are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

The nose-consciousness element and the tongue-consciousness element are known by six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The nose-consciousness-element and the tongue-consciousness-element are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion.
The *dharmadhātu* is known by the ten knowledges (*jñāna*).

The sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, as well as the sense bases of visible form, sound, and tangibles, are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.

The odor-base (*ghānāyatana*) and the taste-base (*jivhāyatana*) are known by six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
The mind-base (*manāyatana*) is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion.
The dharma-base (dharmāyatana) is known by ten knowledges.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) and the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
The aggregates of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion.
The aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).

The aggregates of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path.
The earth element, up to and including the space element, are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The consciousness element is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path.
Material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*) are known by ten knowledges.

Visible phenomena (*sanidarśana-dharma*) and resistant phenomena (*sapratigha-dharma*) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Unseen phenomena (*anidassana-dhamma*) and non-obstructive phenomena (*appaṭigha-dhamma*) are known by ten knowledges (*ñāṇa*).
Contaminated phenomena (*sāsava-dhamma*) are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*khaya-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*).
Uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsava-dhamma*) are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering (*dukkha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-ñāṇa*).
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are known by six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Dharmas of the past, future, and present are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Wholesome dharmas are known by ten knowledges.
Unwholesome dharmas are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*) are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

Phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.

Dharmas bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

Dharmas bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are known by six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.

The dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation.
The dharmas that are neither of those in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa) are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the path.
The dharmas to be abandoned by seeing the truths and the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path.
The dharmas not to be abandoned are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the origin.
The Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path.
The Truth of Cessation is known by six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, and the knowledge of the path.
The Truth of the Path is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation.
The dhyānas are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation.
The four immeasurables are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.

The base of infinite space and the base of infinite consciousness within the formless realm are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is known by six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

The first, second, and third liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the eight bases of totality are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).

The liberation of the sphere of infinite space, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the liberation of the sphere of nothingness are known by seven types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

The liberation of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the liberation of cessation are known by six types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
The sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness are also like this.

The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) knows six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*), and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).

The knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*) is known by six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation.
Conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*) is known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

The knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path are each known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of exhaustion.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

Greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The outflows (*āsrava*) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
The remaining [outflows] are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path.

Within the floods (*ogha*), the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*) is known by seven knowledges, excluding the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The outflows (*āsrava*) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
The remaining [outflows] are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path.
The yokes (*yoga*) are also thus.

Among the sensations, the sensation of desire (*kāma-vedanā*) is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñāta-ājñāna-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
The sensation of "I" (*ātma-vedanā*) is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The remaining eight knowledges (jñāna) know [the fetters], excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).

Among the fetters, the bodily fetter of sensual desire (kāmarāga-kāyagrantha) and the bodily fetter of ill-will (vyāpāda-kāyagrantha) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (anvayajñāna), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The remaining eight knowledges (jñāna) know them, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).

The hindrances (nīvaraṇa), as well as the fetter of ill-will (pratighasaṃyojana), the fetter of stinginess (mātsaryasaṃyojana), and the fetter of envy (īrṣyāsaṃyojana), are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmītijñāna), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The remaining eight knowledges (jñāna) know [these objects], excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).

Among the lower fetters (avarabhāgīya), desire (kāmarāga) and ill-will (vyāpāda) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown (anvayajñāna), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The remaining [cravings] and the five views are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

Among the cravings for the body, the cravings for nose and tongue are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.
The remaining eight knowledges know [these], excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path.

Among the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of sensual desire and the underlying tendency of ill-will are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the unknown, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.

The latent tendency of craving (*rāgānuśaya*) is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
The remaining [latent tendencies] are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path.

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*), the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) are known by seven knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
The remaining [fetters] are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path.

The ninety-eight proclivities (anuśaya) are known by seven knowledges in the desire realm—excluding the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
They are known by seven knowledges in the form realm—excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of the path.

The formless realm is known by six knowledges; it is known through the gateway of eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"By cultivating, practicing, and extensively disseminating the perception of impermanence, one exhausts sensual desire."
Should this perception be said to be associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) or associated with the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?
Should it be said to be accompanied by applied thought (savitarka) and sustained thought (savīcāra)?
Should it be said to be associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya)?
Should it be said that this is associated with the wishless (*apranihita*)?

Should it be said that its object is the exhaustion of the fetters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)? Should this perception be said to be associated with the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) or associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)?
Is it with applied thought and sustained thought, or without applied thought but with sustained thought, or without applied thought and without sustained thought?
Is it associated with the faculty of pleasure, or associated with the faculty of joy, or associated with the faculty of equanimity?
Should it be said that this is associated with the wishless (apraṇihita)?

Should it be said that its object is the exhaustion of the fetters of the form realm (rūpadhātu) and the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)? Should this perception be said to be associated with the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna) or associated with the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)?
Is it with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka but with vicāra, or without both vitarka and vicāra?
Is it associated with the faculty of pleasure, or associated with the faculty of joy or the faculty of equanimity?
Should it be said that it is associated with wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)?
Should it be said that its object is the exhaustion of the fetters belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?

Regarding the exhaustion of pride and ignorance, is this perception associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), or associated with the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), or associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
Is it with applied thought and sustained thought, or without applied thought but with sustained thought, or without applied thought and without sustained thought?
Is it associated with the faculty of pleasure, or associated with the faculty of joy or the faculty of equanimity?

Should it be said that they are associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*), or that they have objects belonging to the desire realm, or that they have objects belonging to the form and formless realms? [This applies] to all nine doors of the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:

A bhikkhu who is skilled in the seven bases and has mastered the meaning of the threefold contemplation attains the exhaustion of the outflows regarding these phenomena, knowing the suffering of form through four knowledges:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of suffering, and conventional knowledge.
There are four knowledges regarding the arising of form:
knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of arising (samudaya-jñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
There are four knowledges regarding the cessation of form:
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of the unknown (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding the path leading to the cessation of form, there are four knowledges:
the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of the unknown, the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and conventional knowledge.
The four knowledges regarding the gratification of form are:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of origination, and conventional knowledge.
The four knowledges regarding the peril of form are: [the same four].
Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of suffering, and conventional knowledge.
The transcendence of form consists of four knowledges:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of exhaustion, and conventional knowledge.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
What is the exhaustion of form? What is the relinquishing and emerging from form?
What is meant by the exhaustion of form?
The answer is:
If craving for form is present and it is extinguished, this is called the exhaustion of form (*rūpa-kṣaya*).
If other forms that serve as conditions for craving are extinguished, this is called the relinquishment and emergence from form (*rūpa-pratinisarga*).
Furthermore, when the defiled forms are extinguished, this is called the "exhaustion of form" (*rūpa-kṣaya*).
When the remaining conditions for defiled forms are extinguished, this is called the "rejection and emergence from form" (*rūpa-niḥsaraṇa*).
Furthermore, if craving or defilement regarding form is present, and that [craving or defilement] is extinguished, this is called the exhaustion of form (*rūpa-kṣaya*).
If other conditions for form—whether craving or defilement—are present, and they are extinguished, this is called the relinquishment of form (*rūpa-pratinisarga*).
The exhaustion of form and the relinquishment of form—this is called their distinction.
The exhaustion of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is called their distinction.

The Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda-śāstra, Chapter Four: The Cultivation of Knowledge, ends here. In the Sanskrit original it consists of nine hundred and thirty ślokas; in the Qin translation it consists of fifteen thousand nine hundred and seventy-two words.
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle 12;
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle 13.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra.
Sengqie Tipo (Saṃghadeva), Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra during the Fu Qin dynasty, possessed the faculties of human wisdom and samādhi. His awakening-mind was in accord with the Path;
he cultivated two kinds of knowledge, one practice, six minor [knowledges], and seven major [knowledges].

The seven persons, eight knowledges, three samādhis, three faculties, seven factors of enlightenment, and eight factors of the path are associated with knowledge; furthermore, two types of knowledge and one type of practice proceed through six, two, and seven [categories] respectively.
The seven persons:
one of firm faith, one of firm Dharma, one liberated through faith, one who has attained vision, one who has realized through the body, one liberated by wisdom, and one liberated both ways.
The eight knowledges:

The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
The three samādhis:
emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*).
The three faculties:
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known.
The seven factors of enlightenment:

The awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity.
The eight factors of the path:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; together with the types of knowledge:
forty-four types of knowledge and seventy-seven types of knowledge; the single practice, the six, the seven, and the great seven.
The seven persons:
one of firm faith, one of firm Dharma, one liberated through faith, one who has attained vision, one with bodily realization, one liberated through wisdom, and one liberated both ways.
The eight knowledges:
Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin, knowledge of cessation, and knowledge of the path.

Regarding these eight knowledges, how many does a person of firm conviction (śraddhādhimukta) possess and how many does he not possess? Up to and including a person liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), how many of these eight knowledges do they possess and how many do they not possess?

Regarding these eight knowledges, how many does a person of firm conviction (śraddhādhimukta) possess in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present? Furthermore, regarding these eight knowledges, how many does one liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) possess in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?

When the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) is present before a person of firm conviction (*śraddhādhimukta*), how many knowledges are present? Up to when the path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*) is present, how many knowledges are present?
Furthermore, when the dharma-knowledge is present before a person of both-fold liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), how many knowledges are present?
When the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) is present, how many knowledges are present?

Regarding these three samādhis, how many does a person of firm faith (śraddhādhimukta) possess and how many does he not possess? Furthermore, regarding these three samādhis, how many does a person liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) possess and how many does he not possess?

Regarding these three samādhis, how many does a person of firm faith accomplish in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present? Furthermore, regarding these three samādhis, how many does one liberated both ways accomplish in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
When the samādhi of the firm conviction in the emptiness of persons manifests before one, how many knowledges manifest?
When the wishless and signless samādhis manifest before one, how many knowledges manifest?
Furthermore, when the emptiness samādhi manifests for one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), how many knowledges (*jñāna*) manifest?
When the wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*) samādhis manifest, how many knowledges manifest?
When the faculty of "one of firm conviction" (*śraddhādhimukta*) is present, how many knowledges (*jñāna*) are present?
It is the same for the "one of dharma-nature" (*dharmānusārin*).
When the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is present for one liberated through both parts (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), how many knowledges are present?
The same applies to one who has attained realization through the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
When a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) brings the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) into manifestation, how many knowledges (*jñāna*) are manifested?
The same applies to one who is liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
When the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present for one of firm conviction, how many knowledges (*jñāna*) are present?
... up to when the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present, how many knowledges are present?
Up to the point when the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present before one who is liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), how many knowledges (*jñāna*) are present?
Up to the point when the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present before him, how many knowledges are present?
When the vision of those with firm faith (śraddhādhimukta) and others manifests, how many knowledges (jñāna) manifest?
Up to when the equipoise of those who are "equal" (samayavimukta) manifests, how many knowledges manifest?
And up to when the vision of those who are "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) and others manifests, how many knowledges manifest?
Furthermore, when the "equality" concentration (*samatā-samādhi*) manifests, how many knowledges (*jñāna*) manifest?
Are those phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) also associated with the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
And if those phenomena are associated with the subsequent knowledge, are they also associated with the knowledge of phenomena?

Are all dharmas associated with the knowledge of dharmas (*dharmajñāna*) also associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), signlessness (*animitta*), the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of investigation of dharmas (*dharmavicayasambodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of energy (*vīryasambodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of joy (*prītisambodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhisambodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣāsambodhyaṅga*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*)?
If various phenomena are associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*), are they associated with knowledge (*jñāna*)?
Are all phenomena, up to and including those associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*), associated with equanimity?
If various phenomena are associated with equanimity, are they associated with mindfulness?
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"The forty-four kinds of knowledge should be taught:

the knowledge of the suffering of old age and death, the knowledge of the origin of old age and death, the knowledge of the cessation of old age and death, and the knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of old age and death."
Should this wisdom be called the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), or even the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
The same applies to the knowledge of birth, existence, and so forth, up to the knowledge of formations (*saṃskārajñāna*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
One should explain seventy-seven kinds of knowledge:
the knowledge that understands aging and death as conditioned by birth, and the knowledge that understands aging and death as not conditioned by anything else;
the knowledge that understands aging and death as conditioned by birth in the distant past, and the knowledge that understands aging and death as not conditioned by anything else in the distant past.

One possesses the knowledge that understands aging and death conditioned by birth in the distant future; one does not possess knowledge that understands aging and death conditioned by birth through any other cause.

This is the knowledge abiding in the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*): it is impermanent, conditioned, produced by causes and conditions, subject to exhaustion, subject to transformation, free from desire, subject to cessation, subject to dispersal, and a phenomenon to be severed by wisdom.
Should this knowledge be called dharma-knowledge, up to and including path-knowledge?
This applies likewise to the knowledge that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations.
If one possesses dharma-knowledge, does one also possess subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
If one possesses the knowledge of the unknown (anājñāta-ājñāna), does one possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?

If one possesses the knowledge of phenomena, does one possess the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path?
If one has attained the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), has one also attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)? ...
up to ... if one has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), has one also attained the knowledge of the path?
If one has attained the knowledge of the path, has one also attained the knowledge of exhaustion? [End of the first section.]
If one has attained the knowledge of phenomena regarding the past, has one also attained it regarding the future?
If one has attained it regarding the future, has one also attained it regarding the past?
If one has attained it regarding the past, has one also attained it regarding the present?
If it is present, is it also past?
If it is future, is it also present?
And if it is present, is it also future?
If something is past, is it also future and present?
If something is future and present, is it also past?
If something is future, is it also past and present?
If one possesses [defilements] in the past and present, does one possess them in the future?
If one possesses them in the present, does one possess them in the past and future?
If one possesses them in the past and future, does one possess them in the present? Thus concludes the survey of the six periods.
The same applies up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
If one possesses past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), does one possess past unknown-knowledge (*anājñātajñāna*)?
Conversely, if one possesses past unknown-knowledge, does one possess past dharma-knowledge?
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also have future unknown-knowledge?
Conversely, if one has future unknown-knowledge, does one also have past dharma-knowledge?
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess present unknown-knowledge?
Conversely, if one possesses present unknown-knowledge, does one also possess past dharma-knowledge?
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also have past and present unknown-knowledge?
Conversely, if one has past and present unknown-knowledge, does one also have past dharma-knowledge?
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), does one also possess future and present unknown-knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
Conversely, if one possesses future and present unknown-knowledge, does one also possess past dharma-knowledge?
If one has accomplished the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also have the past and future knowledge of the unknown (anvayajñāna)?
Conversely, if one has the past and future knowledge of the unknown, does one also have the past knowledge of phenomena?
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also have past, future, and present unknown-knowledge?
Conversely, if one has past, future, and present unknown-knowledge, does one also have past dharma-knowledge?
Up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), it is likewise; this concludes the seven [knowledges].
Past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), past unknown-knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and past knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) constitute one [category].

The second is regarding the future; the third is regarding the present; the fourth is regarding the past and present; the fifth is regarding the future and present; the sixth is regarding the past and future; and the seventh is the knowledge of others' minds regarding the past, future, and present. This applies likewise up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
I wish to expound fully the meaning of this chapter.
There are seven types of persons:

those of firm faith (śraddhādhimukta), those of firm dharma (dharmānusārin), those liberated through faith (śraddhāvimukta), those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), those with bodily realization (kāyasākṣin), those liberated through wisdom (prajñāvimukta), and those liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
There are eight knowledges:

the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
Regarding these eight knowledges, how many does a person of firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) possess, and how many does he not possess?
Answer:
It may be one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight.
What is meant by "one"?

Answer: In the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), there is one [moment] when the knowledge of others' minds is absent, and two when the knowledge of others' minds is present.
In the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), there are three when the knowledge of others' minds is absent, and four when the knowledge of others' minds is present.

In the patience regarding the unknown of suffering (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*), there are three knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and four if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the subsequent knowledge regarding the unknown of suffering (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), there are four knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and five if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the stage of the patience of the dharma of cultivation (*dharma-kṣānti*), there are four knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and five knowledges if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the stage of the dharma-knowledge of cultivation (*dharma-jñāna*), there are five knowledges if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and six knowledges if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the stage of the patience regarding the knowledge of the unknown of cultivation (*bhāvanā-ajñāta-jñāna-kṣānti*), there are five knowledges when the knowledge of others' minds is absent, and six knowledges when the knowledge of others' minds is present.

In the stage of the knowledge of the dharma of exhaustion (*kṣaya-dharma-jñāna*), there are six knowledges when the knowledge of others' minds is absent, and seven knowledges when the knowledge of others' minds is present.

In the case of the patience of the full knowledge of the unknown (*ājñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*), the knowledge of the full knowledge of the unknown (*ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), and the patience regarding the factors of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), there are six [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and seven if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds. In the case of the knowledge of the factors of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), there are seven if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, and eight if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.

In the case of the patience regarding the unknown of the path (*mārga-ajñāna-kṣānti*), there are seven knowledges when one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and eight when one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
It is the same for the stage of the steadfast dharma (*dharmābhisamaya*).
Regarding these eight knowledges, how many does a person liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) possess, and how many does he not possess?
Answer: Either seven or eight.
If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, there are seven; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are eight.
The same applies to vision (*darśana*).

Regarding the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*), the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), and the one doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)—once all these have been accomplished, they are fully perfected.
As for the person of firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), regarding these eight knowledges (*jñāna*), how many are accomplished in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
Answer:

In the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti), there is no knowledge of others' minds; thus, there is one [type] in the past and future, and none in the present.
In the case of the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), there are two [types] in the past and future, and none in the present.

When there is the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) but no knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), there is one in the past, three in the future, and two in the present;
when there is the knowledge of others' minds, there are two in the past, four in the future, and two in the present.

In the *duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-kṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of suffering), there is no knowledge of others' minds; thus, there are three [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.
In the *paracittajñāna* (knowledge of others' minds), there are four [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.
When there is the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'jñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) but no knowledge of others' minds, there are three in the past, four in the future, and two in the present;
when there is knowledge of others' minds, there are four in the past, five in the future, and two in the present.
In the stage of patience regarding the dharma of practice (*dharmakṣānti*), there is no knowledge of others' minds; there are four [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.
In the stage of knowledge of others' minds, there are five [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.
When practicing the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) without the knowledge of others' minds, there are four past, five future, and two present [knowledges];
when practicing the knowledge of others' minds, there are five past, six future, and two present [knowledges].
In the stage of the patience of the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), there is no knowledge of others' minds; five [knowledges] exist in the past and future, and none in the present.
In the stage of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), six [knowledges] exist in the past and future, and none in the present.
When practicing the knowledge of the unknown (anvaya-jñāna) without the knowledge of others' minds, there are five in the past and future, and two in the present;
when practicing the knowledge of others' minds, there are six in the past and future, and two in the present.

In the stage of the patience of the exhaustion of phenomena (*kṣayadharman*), there is no knowledge of others' minds; for the past and future, there are five [knowledges], and for the present, there are none.
In the stage of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), for the past and future, there are six [knowledges], and for the present, there are none.

When the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*kṣayajñāna*) is present but the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is absent, there are five past, six future, and two present knowledges;
when the knowledge of others' minds is present, there are six past, seven future, and two present knowledges.
In the stage of the patience of the knowledge of the unknown (*ajñāta-jñāna-kṣānti*), there is no knowledge of others' minds; for the past and future, there are six, and for the present, none.
In the stage of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), for the past and future, there are seven, and for the present, none.
In the case of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) when the knowledge of others' minds is absent, there are six [knowledges] in the past and future, and two in the present;
when the knowledge of others' minds is present, there are seven in the past and future, and two in the present.
In the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), there is no knowledge of others' minds; thus, there are six in the past and future, and none in the present.
In the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), there are seven in the past and future, and none in the present.
In the knowledge of the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna), if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), there are six past, seven future, and two present [knowledges];
if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are seven past, eight future, and two present [knowledges].

In the case of the patience regarding the unknown of the path (*mārga-ajñāna-kṣānti*), there is no knowledge of others' minds; seven [knowledges] exist in the past and future, but none in the present.
In the case of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), eight [knowledges] exist in the past and future, but none in the present.
The same applies to those of steadfast dharma (*dharmābhisamaya*).
Regarding these eight knowledges (*jñāna*), how many does a person liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) possess in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
Answer:

One who lacks the knowledge of others' minds accomplishes seven [knowledges] in the future; those that have already ceased but are not lost are accomplished in the past, and those currently present are accomplished in the present.

One who possesses the knowledge of others' minds accomplishes eight [knowledges] in the future; those that have been exhausted but are not lost are accomplished in the past, and those currently present are accomplished in the present.
The same applies to the vision [of the truths].

Regarding those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*), those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), and those liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*): they all fully accomplish the future [attainments]; if they have already been exhausted and not lost, they accomplish the past; and whatever is currently manifest before them, they accomplish the present. Thus ends the section on the three times.
When the knowledge of dharma pertaining to the person (pudgala-dharmajñāna) is present before one who possesses firm faith, how many knowledges are present?
Answer: Two.

There are two [knowledges] when dharma-knowledge and suffering-knowledge are present; two when dharma-knowledge and origination-knowledge are present; two when dharma-knowledge and cessation-knowledge are present; and two when dharma-knowledge and path-knowledge are present.
When unknown-to-be-known knowledge (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) manifests, how many knowledges manifest?
The answer is:

two. [Namely,] the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) make two; the knowledge of the unknown and the knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) make two; the knowledge of the unknown and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) make two.
When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) is present, how many knowledges are present?
Answer: Two.
The knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) are two; the knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) are two.
It is the same for the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
When the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) is present, how many knowledges are present?
Answer: Two. They are the knowledge of the path and the knowledge of phenomena.
The same applies to the person of steadfast dharma (*dharmasthita*).
When the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) manifests for a person liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), how many knowledges manifest? Answer:
There are either two or three:
the two consisting of dharma-knowledge and knowledge of suffering; the two consisting of dharma-knowledge and knowledge of origin; the two consisting of dharma-knowledge and knowledge of cessation;
or, when there is no knowledge of others' minds, the two consisting of dharma-knowledge and knowledge of the path; or, when there is knowledge of others' minds, the three.
When the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) is present, how many knowledges are present? Answer:
Either two or three.
The two [knowledges] of unknown-knowledge and suffering-knowledge; the two of unknown-knowledge and origination-knowledge; the two of unknown-knowledge and cessation-knowledge;
the two of unknown-knowledge and path-knowledge when lacking the knowledge of others' minds; and the three when possessing the knowledge of others' minds.
When the knowledge of others' minds is present before one, how many knowledges are present?
Answer: Either two or three.
When the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is present, there are two knowledges if it is not the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), or three if it is the knowledge of the path.
When conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is manifested, how many knowledges are manifested? Answer:
Either one or two.
When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is present, if it lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there is one; if it possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are two.
When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) is manifested, how many knowledges are manifested?
Answer: Two. [They are] both the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), and both the knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
The same applies to the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
When the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is present before one, how many knowledges are present? Answer:
There are either two or three.

When there is path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*) and dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) but no knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), there are two; if there is knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
When there is path-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) but no knowledge of others' minds, there are two; if there is knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
The same applies to those who have attained vision and those who have realized it through the body.
When a person liberated by wisdom brings the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) into manifestation, how many knowledges are manifested? Answer:
There are either two or three:

if there is dharma-knowledge and knowledge of suffering, there are two—either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising; if there is the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, there are three.

If there is dharma-knowledge and knowledge of origin, there are two—either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising; if there is the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, there are three.

If there is dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) and knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), there are two [knowledges] when knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) and knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) are absent; if there is knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of non-arising, there are three.

If there is dharma-knowledge and knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), there are two when knowledge of non-arising and knowledge of others' minds are absent; if there is knowledge of exhaustion, knowledge of non-arising, and knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
When the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) is present, how many knowledges are present? Answer:
Either two or three.

The knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) are two [types] when there is neither the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*); they are three [types] if there is the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.

The knowledge of the unknown and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) are two [types] when there is neither the knowledge of exhaustion nor the knowledge of non-arising; they are three [types] if there is the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.

If there is knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna) and knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), there are two: either knowledge of non-exhaustion (akṣaya-jñāna) or knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).

If there is knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of non-arising, there are three. If there is knowledge of the unknown and knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), there are two: either knowledge of non-exhaustion or knowledge of non-arising, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna). If there is knowledge of exhaustion, knowledge of non-arising, and knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
When the knowledge of others' minds is present, how many knowledges are present?
Answer: Either two or three.
When the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is present, there are two knowledges if it is not the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), or three if it is the knowledge of the path.
When conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is manifested, how many knowledges are manifested? Answer:
Either one or two.

When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is present, there is one if it does not include knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and there are two if it includes knowledge of others' minds.
When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) is manifested, how many knowledges are manifested?
Answer: Either two or three.

If it consists of the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), there are two, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). If it includes the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, there are three.

The knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of what is yet to be known (*anvaya-jñāna*) constitute two [knowledges] when they are neither the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*); if they are the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, they constitute three.
It is the same for the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion.
When the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) is present, how many knowledges are present?
Answer: Either two or three.

The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) are two [knowledges] when they are devoid of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), and the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna); if they include the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of others' minds, they are three.

The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) and the knowledge of what is not yet known (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna) are associated with two types of knowledge: the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) and either the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) or the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna). If they are associated with both the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising along with the knowledge of others' minds, they are associated with three types of knowledge.
The same applies to the one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). This concludes the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).
Regarding these three samādhis, how many does the person of firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) accomplish, and how many does he not accomplish? Answer:
Whether there are two or three,
as long as the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*kṣayadharmanirvedhabhāgīya*) has not yet arisen, one accomplishes two and does not accomplish one;
once the patience regarding the dharma of cessation has arisen, all are accomplished.
It is the same for one of firm nature (*dharmānusārī*).

One who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), one who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*), one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), and one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)—all of these achieve [the fruits] in their entirety.
Regarding these three samādhis, how many does a person of firm conviction accomplish in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
Answer:
If, relying on the samādhi of emptiness, one attains realization by skipping stages and reaches the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*, there is none in the past, two in the future, and one in the present.

Regarding the past, the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) consists of one [application of mindfulness], emptiness (śūnyatā); regarding the future, it consists of two, namely emptiness and wishlessness (apraṇihita); regarding the present, it consists of one, namely emptiness.

Regarding the subsequent patience toward the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñānakṣānti), the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna), and the dharma-patience toward the origin of suffering (samudaye dharma-kṣānti), there is one in the past, two in the future, and one in the present, which is wishlessness.
Regarding the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*): there are two in the past and future, and one in the present.
Regarding the subsequent patience toward the knowledge of phenomena (*anvayakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (*anvayajñāna*):
there are two in the past and future, and one in the present, as above.
In the *kṣānti* of the knowledge of the exhaustion of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*), there are two past, three future, and one present instances of the signless (*animitta*).
In the *jñāna* of the knowledge of the exhaustion of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), there are three past and future, and one present.

In the case of the patience regarding the full knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñānājñānti*), the knowledge of the exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the dharma-patience regarding the path (*mārgadharmakṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*), and the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgājñānti*), there are three types in the past and future, and one type in the present, which is the wishless (*apraṇihita*).

If one attains realization by skipping stages (vyutkrāntaka) based on the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*), regarding the patience toward the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), there are none in the past, two in the future, and one in the present.
Regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), there is one in the past, two in the future, and one in the present.

Regarding the patience of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*), the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), the patience regarding the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*), the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), the patience of the unknown regarding origination (*samudaya-ajñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*), and the knowledge of the unknown regarding origination (*samudaya-ajñāsyāmīti-jñāna*): there is one in the past, two in the future (emptiness and wishlessness), and one in the present (wishlessness).

In the *kṣānti* of the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*), there are two [aspects] of the past: emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); three of the future; and one of the present: signlessness (*animitta*).

In the *jñāna* of the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), there are two [aspects] of the past: wishlessness and signlessness; three of the future; and one of the present: signlessness.

Exhaustion-of-the-unknown-patience (kṣayānvaya-kṣānti), exhaustion-of-the-unknown-knowledge (kṣayānvaya-jñāna), dharma-patience regarding the path (mārga-dharma-kṣānti), dharma-knowledge regarding the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna), and subsequent-patience regarding the path (mārgānvaya-kṣānti) [are associated with] three wishless (apraṇihita) and three signless (animitta) concentrations in the past; three wishless and three signless in the future; and one wishless concentration in the present.
The same applies to the steadfast dharma (dharmābhiśraddha).

For those who are liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), those who have realized through the body (kāyasākṣin), those liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta), and those liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), all [factors] are accomplished in the future; if they have already been exhausted but not lost, they are accomplished in the past; and if they are currently manifesting, they are accomplished in the present.
When the samādhi of the firm conviction in the emptiness of persons manifests, how many knowledges manifest?
Answer: Either two or none.
There are two [knowledges] when the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of phenomena are present: the knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
There are none during the moments of patience (kṣānti). When the wishless samādhi (apraṇihita-samādhi) is manifested, how many knowledges are manifested?

Answer: Either two or none. [In the case of] the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), there are two; [in the case of] the knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), there are two; [in the case of] the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena, there are two; [in the case of] the knowledge of origin and the subsequent knowledge, there are two; [in the case of] the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena, there are two. In the case of the receptivities (kṣānti), there are none.
When the signless samādhi manifests before one, how many knowledges manifest?
Answer: Either two or none.

Regarding the two—knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)—and the two—knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of the unknown (*anvayajñāna*)—there is none [of these] during the moments of patience (*kṣānti*).
It is the same for those firmly established in the Dharma (*dharmaniyata*).
When a person liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) brings the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) into manifestation, how many knowledges are manifested?
Answer: Two.
[They are] both the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of phenomena; both the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the unknown.
When the wishless samādhi (apraṇihita-samādhi) is present before one, how many knowledges (jñāna) are present?
Answer: Either two or three.

The knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) constitute two; the knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) constitute two; the knowledge of origin and the knowledge of phenomena constitute two; the knowledge of origin and the subsequent knowledge constitute two;
the knowledge of the path and the knowledge of phenomena, when lacking the knowledge of others' minds, constitute two, but if possessing the knowledge of others' minds, they constitute three;
the knowledge of the path and the subsequent knowledge, when lacking the knowledge of others' minds, constitute two, but if possessing the knowledge of others' minds, they constitute three.
When the signless samādhi is present before one, how many knowledges are present?
Answer: Two.
The two—knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)—and the two—knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of the unknown (*anvayajñāna*).
It is the same for those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and those who are body-witnesses (*kāyasākṣin*).
When a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) brings the emptiness concentration (*śūnyatāsamādhi*) to presence, how many knowledges are present?
Answer: Two.
[They are] both the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of phenomena; both the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the unknown.
When the wishless samādhi (apraṇihita-samādhi) is present before one, how many knowledges (jñāna) are present?
Answer: Either two or three.

The knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) constitute two [knowledges] when they are neither the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) nor the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna); if they are the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, they constitute three.

The knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the unknown (anvaya-jñāna) constitute two when they are neither the knowledge of exhaustion nor the knowledge of non-arising; if they are the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, they constitute three.

If one possesses the knowledge of cultivation (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), there are two [knowledges]—the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)—or three, if the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are both present.

If one possesses the knowledge of cultivation and the knowledge of the unknown (*anvayajñāna*), there are two—the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising—or three, if the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are both present.

The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) are two when they are without the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), or the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna); if they include the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of others' minds, they are three.

Path-knowledge and knowledge of the unknown constitute two [knowledges] when they are devoid of the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of others' minds; if they include the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of others' minds, they constitute three.
When the signless samādhi manifests before one, how many knowledges manifest?
Answer: Either two or three.

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) constitute two [knowledges] when there is neither the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) nor the knowledge of exhaustion; they constitute three if there is both the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.

The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of what is not yet known (*anvayajñāna*) constitute two when there is neither the knowledge of non-arising nor the knowledge of exhaustion; they constitute three if there is both the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
The same applies to those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). This concludes the three types of samādhi.
When the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) manifests for one of firm conviction (*śraddhādhimukta*), how many knowledges (*jñāna*) manifest? Answer:
Either two or none. [The pairings are as follows:

Suffering-knowledge and Dharma-knowledge; Suffering-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge; Origination-knowledge and Dharma-knowledge; Origination-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge; Cessation-knowledge and Dharma-knowledge; Cessation-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge; Path-knowledge and Dharma-knowledge. There is no [pairing] with Patience (*kṣānti*).
The seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path are also like this.
The person of firm dharma is also like this.
When the faculty of "already-known" (*ājñātendriya*) manifests for a person liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), how many knowledges (*jñāna*) manifest?

The answer is: either two or three. [These are: the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna); the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the unknown (anvaya-jñāna); the knowledge of origination and the knowledge of phenomena; the knowledge of origination and the knowledge of the unknown; the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of phenomena; and the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the unknown.

If one possesses path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*) and dharma-knowledge (*dhammañāṇa*) but lacks knowledge of others' minds (*paracittañāṇa*), there are two; if one possesses knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
If one possesses path-knowledge and unknown-knowledge (*anattañāṇa*) but lacks knowledge of others' minds, there are two; if one possesses knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
The seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path are also like this.
The same applies to the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and the one who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
When the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) is present before a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), how many knowledges (*jñāna*) are present?
Answer: Either two or three.

If it consists of the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), there are two, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna). If it includes the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, there are three.

The knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the unknown (anvaya-jñāna), together with either the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) or the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), constitute two; if both the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are present, they constitute three.

The knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), together with either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, constitute two; if both the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are present, they constitute three.

If one possesses the knowledge of cultivation (*śikṣā-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñāta-ājñāna-jñāna*), there are two [knowledges]—the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)—or three, if the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are both present.

If one possesses the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), there are two [knowledges]—the knowledge of non-exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising—or three, if the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are both present.
