If there is knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), there are two; if there is knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of non-arising, there are three.

If there is knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), there are two; if there is knowledge of exhaustion, knowledge of non-arising, and knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are three.

The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) and the knowledge of what is not yet known (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna) are associated with two [knowledges]: the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna). If the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of others' minds are present, they are associated with three.
The seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path are also like this.
When right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) is present before one, how many knowledges (*jñāna*) are present?
The answer is:

Either two or three: the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) constitute two; the knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) constitute two; the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena constitute two; the knowledge of origin and the subsequent knowledge constitute two; the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena constitute two; the knowledge of cessation and the subsequent knowledge constitute two;

the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena constitute two—if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), there are two; if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are three.

In the case of path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), there are two [knowledges] if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*); there are three if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
The same applies to those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*). This concludes the section on the three faculties (*indriya*).

Regarding those phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), they are not the knowledge of what is yet to be known (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*). Are they the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
Answer: Some phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena are not the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) that is not the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)? Answer:

Those factors associated with the knowledge of phenomena that are not included within the knowledge of others' minds; this is called the knowledge of phenomena that is not the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the knowledge of others' minds that is not the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
The answer is:

those factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not included within the knowledge of phenomena; this is called the knowledge of others' minds that is not the knowledge of phenomena.
What is the knowledge of others' minds through the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)? Answer:

It is the inclusion within the knowledge of phenomena of those factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds; this is called the knowledge of others' minds through the knowledge of phenomena.
What is that which is neither the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) nor the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)? Answer:

It refers to all other instances of the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of others' minds that are not included within them and are not associated with them, as well as the remaining mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*). This is called that which is neither the knowledge of phenomena nor the knowledge of others' minds.
The same applies to the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of its origin, the knowledge of its cessation, and the knowledge of the path, as well as to right view.

Regarding those phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), they are not the knowledge of equality (*samatā-jñāna*); are they the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)?
Answer: There are cases where there is dharma-knowledge that is not the emptiness samādhi.
What is dharma-knowledge that is not the emptiness samādhi?
Answer:

The dharmas associated with the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) that are associated with the emptiness-trance (śūnyatā-samādhi), as well as all other dharmas associated with dharma-knowledge that are not associated with the emptiness-trance—these are called "dharma-knowledge that is not the emptiness-trance."
What is the emptiness samādhi that is not the dharma-knowledge? Answer:

It refers to those factors associated with the emptiness samādhi that are associated with the dharma-knowledge, as well as other factors associated with the emptiness samādhi that are not associated with the dharma-knowledge; these are called the emptiness samādhi that is not the dharma-knowledge.
What is the concentration on emptiness associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-śūnyatā-samādhi*)?
The answer is:

excluding the concentration on emptiness that is associated with the knowledge of phenomena itself, all other factors associated with the concentration on emptiness associated with the knowledge of phenomena—these are called the concentration on emptiness associated with the knowledge of phenomena.
What is that which is neither dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) nor the emptiness-concentration (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)?
The answer is:

the emptiness-concentration not associated with dharma-knowledge, the dharma-knowledge not associated with the emptiness-concentration, as well as other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*). This is called that which is neither dharma-knowledge nor the emptiness-concentration.
The same applies to wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), signlessness (*animitta*), the awakening factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding those phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), are they the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is dharma-knowledge that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
What is dharma-knowledge that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
The answer is:

Those factors associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) that are not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*): these are called the knowledge of phenomena that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not the knowledge of phenomena? Answer:

Those phenomena associated with the faculty of "I do not yet know" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) that are not included among the other dharma-knowledges (dharma-jñāna) and are not associated with them—these are said to be associated with the faculty of "I do not yet know" but are not dharma-knowledge.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)? Answer:

Those factors subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena; these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" associated with the knowledge of phenomena.
What is that which is neither the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) nor the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
The answer is:

the knowledge of phenomena not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; all phenomena not included within the knowledge of phenomena or the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and not associated with them; and furthermore, other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called that which is neither the knowledge of phenomena nor the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
The same applies to the faculty of "I-have-known" (ājñātāvīndriya) and the faculty of "I-am-knowing" (ājñendriya).
Regarding all phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), are they also associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛtisambodhyaṅga)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is dharma-knowledge that is not the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
What is dharma-knowledge that is not the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness?
The answer is:
The awakening factor of mindfulness associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is called "knowledge of phenomena but not the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not the knowledge of phenomena? Answer:

Those factors that are associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) but are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), as well as all other factors associated with the knowledge of phenomena—these are called the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not the knowledge of phenomena.
What is the knowledge of phenomena that is the awakening factor of mindfulness?

Answer: Excluding the factor of mindfulness-enlightenment-factor (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), all other factors associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) are called "the knowledge of phenomena and the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor.
What is neither the knowledge of phenomena nor the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor?
Answer:

The factors dissociated from the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) that constitute the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga), as well as other mind, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called neither the knowledge of phenomena nor the awakening factor of mindfulness.

The factors of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as right effort (*samyakpradhāna*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), are also like this.
Regarding all phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), are they the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: It is so;
those dharmas that are associated with the knowledge of dharmas (*dharmajñāna*) are the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Is there, however, that which is associated with the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of dharmas but is not the knowledge of dharmas?
Answer: There are.
This concludes the section on the dharmas associated with the factor-of-enlightenment of investigation-into-dharmas that are not subsumed by dharma-knowledge.
The same applies to the gateway of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Regarding those phenomena associated with the knowledge of others' minds, are they that knowledge?
Answer: Some are the knowledge of others' minds, but not conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
What is the knowledge of others' minds that is not conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)? Answer:
Those factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not subsumed under conventional knowledge; this is called the knowledge of others' minds that is not conventional knowledge.
What is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that is not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)? Answer:
Those factors associated with conventional knowledge that are not included within the knowledge of others' minds; this is called conventional knowledge that is not the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the knowledge of others' minds that is also conventional knowledge? Answer:
The factors associated with conventional knowledge that are subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds—this is called the knowledge of others' minds that is also conventional knowledge.
What is that which is neither the knowledge of others' minds nor conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
The answer is:

the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge; those things not included in and dissociated from the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge; and all other mind, mental factors (*caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*). This is called that which is neither the knowledge of others' minds nor conventional knowledge.
The same applies to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), the factor of awakening of investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Regarding those factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): they are not the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), or the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); they are not the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) or the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*). Are they then the wishless [samādhi] (*apraṇihita*)?
Answer: There is the knowledge of others' minds that is not associated with the wishless (*apranihita*).
What is this knowledge of others' minds that is not associated with the wishless?
Answer:

The factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are associated with the wishless, as well as those factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not associated with the wishless—these are called the knowledge of others' minds that is not wishless.
What is the absence of aspiration that is not the knowledge of others' minds? Answer:

The knowledge of others' minds associated with the absence of aspiration, and all factors associated with the absence of aspiration but dissociated from the knowledge of others' minds—this is called the absence of aspiration that is not the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the knowledge of others' minds associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*)? Answer:

With the exception of the wishless associated with the knowledge of others' minds, all other factors associated with the wishless that constitute the knowledge of others' minds—this is called the knowledge of others' minds associated with the wishless.
What is that which is neither the knowledge of others' minds nor wishlessness?
The answer is:

wishlessness dissociated from the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of others' minds dissociated from wishlessness, as well as other mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*). This is called that which is neither the knowledge of others' minds nor wishlessness.
The awakening factor of mindfulness, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity; likewise for right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

Regarding those dharmas associated with the knowledge of others' minds, are they not the faculty of "I do not yet know" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), but rather the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*)?
Answer: Some instances of the knowledge of others' minds are not the faculty of "having known."
What is the knowledge of others' minds that is not the faculty of one who has already known? Answer:

Those factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known—this is called the knowledge of others' minds that is not the faculty of one who has already known.
What is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*) that is not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)? Answer:

It refers to those factors associated with the faculty of one who has already known which are included within the knowledge of others' minds, as well as all factors associated with the faculty of one who has already known that are not included within the knowledge of others' minds and are not conjoined with it; these are called the faculty of one who has already known that is not the knowledge of others' minds.
What is the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātendriya) in relation to the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)? Answer:

The factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are subsumed within the faculty of one who has already known; this is called the faculty of one who has already known in relation to the knowledge of others' minds.
What is that which is neither the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) nor the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*)? Answer:

That which is not included within the faculty of one who has already known and is the knowledge of others' minds; furthermore, all other instances of the knowledge of others' minds that are not included within or associated with the faculty of one who has already known; as well as other minds, mental factors (*citta-caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*). These are called that which is neither the knowledge of others' minds nor the faculty of one who has already known.
The faculty of ignorance (*ajñāna-indriya*) is also like this.

Those dharmas associated with the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*), those not associated with the aforementioned [knowledges], and those associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)—are they not associated with the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), nor with the signless (*animitta*)? Are they the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)?
Answer: Sometimes the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) is not the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi).
What is the knowledge of suffering that is not the emptiness samādhi?
Answer:

The factors associated with the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) that are associated with the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi), as well as those factors associated with the knowledge of suffering that are not associated with any other emptiness samādhis—these are called the knowledge of suffering that is not the emptiness samādhi.
What is the emptiness samādhi that is not the knowledge of suffering?
The answer is:

the knowledge of suffering associated with the emptiness samādhi, and those factors associated with the emptiness samādhi that are not associated with the various knowledges of suffering—this is called the emptiness samādhi that is not the knowledge of suffering.
What is the emptiness samādhi associated with the knowledge of suffering? Answer:

With the exception of the emptiness samādhi that is associated with the knowledge of suffering itself, all dharmas associated with the emptiness samādhi of the knowledge of suffering are called the emptiness samādhi of the knowledge of suffering.
What is that which is neither the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) nor the emptiness concentration (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)?
The answer is:

the emptiness concentration not associated with the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of suffering not associated with the emptiness concentration, as well as other mental states (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), form (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*). This is called that which is neither the knowledge of suffering nor the emptiness concentration.
The same applies to the knowledge of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-jñāna*). As for the remaining cases, they are as in the case of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).

Regarding those factors associated with the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), are they not the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and are they not empty (*śūnya*) or signless (*animitta*), yet are they wishless?
Answer: Sometimes there is knowledge of cultivation (bhāvanājñāna) that is not associated with the wishless (apraṇihita).
What is knowledge of cultivation that is not associated with the wishless?
Answer: That which is associated with the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) and is wishless (*apraṇihita*), this is called "the knowledge of origination but not the wishless.
What is the wishless but not the knowledge of origination?

Answer: The knowledge of cultivation (bhāvanājñāna) and those other factors associated with the knowledge of cultivation that are not associated with the wishless (apraṇihita), these are called "wishless but not the knowledge of cultivation.
What is both the knowledge of cultivation and the wishless?

Answer: With the exception of the wishless (*apranihita*), all other factors associated with the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) are called the "knowledge of origination associated with the wishless.
What is neither the knowledge of origination nor the wishless?
Answer:

That which is dissociated from the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*), as well as other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called "not cultivation."
Knowledge is not without aspiration (*apraṇihita*).
The remainder is as in the case of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).

Regarding those factors associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), are they not the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), empty (*śūnya*), and without aspiration (*apraṇihita*), and are they signless (*animitta*)?
Answer: Sometimes the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is not signless (animitta).
What is the knowledge of exhaustion that is not signless?
Answer: That which is associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and is signless (animitta) is called "the knowledge of exhaustion but not the signless.
What is the signless but not the knowledge of exhaustion?

Answer: All other factors associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that are not themselves the knowledge of exhaustion, as well as those factors associated with the signless (*animitta*), are called "signless but not the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion that is signless?
Answer: With the exception of the signless (animitta), all other factors associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) are called the signless associated with the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is neither the knowledge of exhaustion nor the signless?
Answer:

That which is dissociated from the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and is signless (*animitta*), as well as other minds (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), form (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*)—these are called "neither the knowledge of exhaustion nor the signless."
The remainder is as in the case of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).

Regarding those factors associated with path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*), are they not associated with the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*), yet are they associated with the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, path-knowledge may not be the wishless concentration.
What is path-knowledge that is not the wishless concentration? Answer:
When path-knowledge is associated with wishlessness, this is called path-knowledge that is not wishlessness.
What is wishlessness that is not path-knowledge? Answer:

The knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and those factors associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) that are not associated with the various knowledges of the path—these are called "wishless but not the knowledge of the path.
What is the knowledge of the path that is wishless? Answer:
Excluding those associated with the wishless, all factors associated with the knowledge of the path—these are called the knowledge of the path associated with the wishless.
What is neither the knowledge of the path nor the wishless? Answer: [The factors associated with other knowledges and dissociated factors.]

The wishless that is dissociated from the knowledge of the path, as well as other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are said to be neither the knowledge of the path nor the wishless.
The remainder is as in the case of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).

Regarding those factors associated with the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), are they not associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and the signless (*animitta*), and are they the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is the emptiness samādhi that is not the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown.
What is the emptiness samādhi that is not the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown"? Answer:

Those factors associated with the emptiness samādhi that are not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) are called "emptiness samādhi but not the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not the emptiness samādhi?
Answer:

The factors comprised by the faculty of "I do not yet know" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) that are included within the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi), as well as those factors associated with the faculty of "I do not yet know" that are not comprised by and are not associated with the various emptiness samādhis—these are called the faculty of "I do not yet know" that is not the emptiness samādhi.
What is the emptiness samādhi associated with the faculty of "I do not yet know"? Answer:
Those factors associated with the emptiness samādhi that are subsumed under the faculty of "I do not yet know" are called the emptiness samādhi associated with the faculty of "I do not yet know."
What is that which is neither the emptiness samādhi nor the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
The answer is:

the emptiness samādhi not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; all emptiness samādhis not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and dissociated from it; and furthermore, other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called that which is neither the emptiness samādhi nor the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
The same applies to the faculty of "I already know" (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Regarding all phenomena associated with the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), are they also associated with the factor of awakening of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is the concentration on emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi) that is not the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
What is the concentration on emptiness that is not the awakening factor of mindfulness? Answer:
The mindfulness factor of enlightenment associated with the emptiness samādhi—this is called "emptiness samādhi but not the mindfulness factor of enlightenment.
What is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment that is not the emptiness samādhi? Answer:

The factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are associated with the remaining samādhis of emptiness, but are not associated with the samādhi of emptiness itself—these are called the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not the samādhi of emptiness.
What is the samādhi of emptiness associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness?
Answer: Excluding the awakening factor of mindfulness, all other factors associated with the emptiness samādhi are called the emptiness samādhi and the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is neither the emptiness samādhi nor the awakening factor of mindfulness?
Answer:

The factors dissociated from the emptiness samādhi—namely, the awakening factor of mindfulness and other mental states, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—are called those that are neither the emptiness samādhi nor the awakening factor of mindfulness.

The factors of awakening of investigation of phenomena (*dharma-vicaya*), energy (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), right effort (*samyak-prahāṇa*), and right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), are likewise [associated with emptiness].
Are those factors associated with the emptiness samādhi also associated with the factor of awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Sometimes the emptiness samādhi is not the joy factor of enlightenment.
How is it that the emptiness samādhi is not the joy factor of enlightenment?
Answer:

The factor of awakening of joy associated with the concentration of emptiness, and those factors associated with the concentration of emptiness that are not associated with the factor of awakening of joy—these are called the concentration of emptiness that is not the factor of awakening of joy.
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy (muditā-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is not associated with the concentration of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi)? Answer:

It refers to the factors associated with the concentration of emptiness that are associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy, as well as those factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy that are not associated with any concentrations of emptiness; these are called the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not the concentration of emptiness.
What is the awakening factor of joy associated with the concentration of emptiness?
The answer is:

excluding those factors of the awakening factor of joy that are not associated with the concentration of emptiness, all factors associated with both the concentration of emptiness and the awakening factor of joy are called the awakening factor of joy associated with the concentration of emptiness.
What is neither the emptiness concentration (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) nor the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:

The factor of enlightenment of joy not associated with the emptiness concentration, the emptiness concentration not associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy, and furthermore, other mind, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called neither the emptiness concentration nor the factor of enlightenment of joy.
The same applies to equanimity (*upekṣā*).
If all phenomena are associated with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), are they also the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Yes.
Thus, if all dharmas are associated with the emptiness samādhi, they are the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*).
Is it possible that there are dharmas associated with the awakening factor of concentration that are not associated with the emptiness samādhi?
Answer: There are;
there are factors associated with the awakening factor of concentration that are not subsumed by the emptiness samādhi.
It is the same for the samādhi of equanimity as well.
If all phenomena are associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*), are they not signless (*animitta*) and are they the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
Answer: Some are wishless but are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is the wishless (apraṇihita) that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)? Answer:

Those factors associated with the wishless that are not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"—this is called the wishless that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) that is not associated with the wishless (apraṇihita)? Answer:

It refers to those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" which are subsumed by the wishless, as well as all factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are not subsumed by the wishless; these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not the wishless.
What is the faculty of "I do not yet know" associated with the wishless? Answer:
The factors associated with the wishless that are subsumed under the faculty of "I do not yet know" are called the faculty of "I do not yet know" associated with the wishless.
What is that which is neither the *apranihita* (wishless) faculty nor the *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya* (faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown")?
The answer is:

those things not included within the *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya* that are associated with the *apranihita* faculty; those things associated with the *apranihita* faculty that are not included within the *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya* and are dissociated from it; and all other mind, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind. These are called that which is neither the *apranihita* faculty nor the *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*.
The same applies to the faculty of "I have known" (ājñātāvīndriya) and the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñendriya).
Regarding all phenomena associated with wishlessness (apraṇihita), are they also associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛtisambodhyaṅga)?
The answer is: No.
Or, there may be the wishless (appanihita) that is not the awakening factor of mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga).
What is the wishless that is not the awakening factor of mindfulness?
The answer is:
The awakening factor of mindfulness associated with wishlessness—this is called "wishlessness but not the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not wishlessness? Answer:
Those factors that are wishless, yet dissociated from the wishless and associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness—these are called the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not wishless.
What is the wishless awakening factor of mindfulness?
Answer: Excluding the awakening factor of mindfulness, all other factors associated with wishlessness are called the wishless awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is neither wishless nor the awakening factor of mindfulness?
Answer:

The awakening factor of mindfulness that is not associated with the wishless, as well as other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called "neither wishless nor the awakening factor of mindfulness."

The awakening factors of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), energy (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as right effort (*samyakpradhāna*) and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), are likewise [to be understood].
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirteenth.
