translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīr together with Zhu Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty.

The remainder of the fifth section, the *Saṃprayukta-varga*, within the *Jñāna-skandha*: "Are all phenomena associated with wishlessness also associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?"
Answer: There are cases where there is the wishless (*apraṇihita*) but not the factor-of-enlightenment of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is the case where there is the wishless but not the factor-of-enlightenment of joy?
Answer:

The factors associated with the wishless that are associated with the awakening factor of joy, as well as all other factors associated with the wishless that are not associated with the awakening factor of joy—these are called "associated with the wishless but not the awakening factor of joy."
What is the factor of awakening of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga) that is not associated with the wishless (apraṇihita)? Answer:

It refers to the wishless associated with the factor of awakening of joy, and those factors associated with the factor of awakening of joy that are not associated with the wishless; this is called the factor of awakening of joy that is not the wishless.
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*)? Answer:

With the exception of the factor of enlightenment of joy that is itself associated with the wishless, all factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy associated with the wishless are called the factor of enlightenment of joy associated with the wishless.
What is that which is neither the wishless (*apraṇihita*) nor the factor of enlightenment consisting of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:

The factor of enlightenment consisting of joy that is not associated with the wishless, the wishless that is not associated with the factor of enlightenment consisting of joy, and furthermore, other mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), form (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*). This is called that which is neither the wishless nor the factor of enlightenment consisting of joy.
The same applies to right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).
Regarding those phenomena associated with wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), are they the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*)?
The answer is: yes.
Thus, those dharmas associated with wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) are that concentration factor of enlightenment (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*).
Is it possible that there are dharmas associated with the concentration factor of enlightenment that are not associated with wishlessness?
Answer: There are;
there are factors associated with the awakening factor of concentration that are not subsumed by the wishless [samādhi].
The same applies to the even-concentration (*sāmayika-samādhi*).
The same applies to the gate of signlessness (*animitta-mukha*).

Regarding those phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), they are neither the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) nor the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Are they the factor of mindfulness-enlightenment (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Sometimes the faculty of "I do not yet know" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) is not the factor of mindfulness-enlightenment (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
What is the faculty of "I do not yet know" that is not the factor of mindfulness-enlightenment?

Answer: When the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) subsumes the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga), this is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?

Answer: Those factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are not subsumed under the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) are called the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown.
What is the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" that is the awakening factor of mindfulness?

Answer: Those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
What is neither the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness?
Answer:

The factors not included within the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)—namely, the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga), as well as other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta), matter (rūpa), the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra)—are said to be neither the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know" nor the awakening factor of mindfulness.

The factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharma-pravicaya*), energy (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*), as well as right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), right effort (*samyak-prahāṇa*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), are likewise.
Are those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) also associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Sometimes the faculty of "I do not yet know" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) is not the factor of joy in enlightenment (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga).
What is the faculty of "I do not yet know" that is not the factor of joy in enlightenment?
Answer:

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that subsumes the awakening-factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*), as well as those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are not subsumed by the awakening-factors of joy and are not conjoined with them—these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not the awakening-factor of joy.
What is the factor of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga) that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)? Answer:

Those factors associated with the factor of joy that are not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"—this is called the factor of joy that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) associated with the factor of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga)? Answer:

Those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are subsumed within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" associated with the factor of joy.
What is that which is neither the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) nor the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:

That which is not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" while being the factor of enlightenment of joy; those things not included within either the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" or the factor of enlightenment of joy, being dissociated from them; and furthermore, all other minds (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*). This is called that which is neither the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor the factor of enlightenment of joy.
Regarding those phenomena associated with the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), are they also the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Some are associated with the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know" but are not the awakening factor of tranquility.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) that is not the awakening factor of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga)? Answer:

The awakening factor of tranquility associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"—this is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not the awakening factor of tranquility.
What is the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)? Answer:

Those factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of tranquility that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"—this is called the factor of enlightenment of tranquility that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is the faculty of "I do not yet know" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) associated with the awakening factor of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga)? Answer:

Those factors that are associated with the faculty of "I do not yet know" and associated with the awakening factor of tranquility—these are called the faculty of "I do not yet know" associated with the awakening factor of tranquility.
What is neither the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) nor the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:

The factor of enlightenment of tranquility that is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," as well as other mind, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called neither the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
The same applies to the awakening factor of vigilance (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Regarding those phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), are they also associated with the faculty of resolve (*adhimokṣendriya*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) that is not the faculty of "right intention" (samyak-saṃkalpa).
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not the faculty of "right intention"? Answer:

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) associated with right intention (samyak-saṃkalpa), and those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are not associated with right intention—these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not right intention.
What is meant by "equanimity of intention" (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) that is not the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
The answer is:

those factors associated with equanimity of intention that are dissociated from the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know"—this is called equanimity of intention that is not the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know."
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) associated with the mental application (saṃkalpa)?
The answer is:

those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and associated with the mental application—these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" associated with the mental application.
What is that which is neither the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) nor right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*)?
The answer is:

right intention not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," all [factors] not associated with both the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and right intention, as well as other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—this is called that which is neither the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor right intention.
It should be understood that the sense-bases (*indriya-mukha*) are likewise.
Regarding those phenomena associated with the faculty of ignorance (*ajñāna-indriya*), are they also associated with the factor of mindfulness-enlightenment (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
The answer is: No.
Or, there is the faculty of ignorance that is not the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is the faculty of ignorance that is not the awakening factor of mindfulness? Answer:

When the faculty of ignorance (*ajñendriya*) includes the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), this is called "the faculty of ignorance that is not the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not the faculty of ignorance? Answer:

Those factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are not subsumed by the faculty of ignorance—these are called the awakening factor of mindfulness that is not the faculty of ignorance.
What is the faculty of ignorance associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness?

Answer: Those factors associated with the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) are called the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" and the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is neither the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" nor the awakening factor of mindfulness?
Answer:

Those factors not included within the faculty of "I do not know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya)—namely, the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛtisambodhyaṅga), as well as other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitasika), matter (rūpa), the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra)—are called "neither the faculty of 'I do not know' nor the awakening factor of mindfulness."
The same applies to the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and concentration, as well as to right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Regarding all phenomena associated with the faculty of equanimity: are they also associated with the awakening factor of joy?
Answer: Sometimes the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is not the factor of joy in awakening (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga).
How is it that the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is not the factor of joy in awakening?
Answer:

Those factors included within the faculty of ignorance (*ajñendriya*) that are associated with the awakening factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*), as well as those factors associated with the faculty of ignorance that are not included within the awakening factor of joy and are not concomitant with it—these are called "the faculty of ignorance that is not the awakening factor of joy."
What is the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya)? Answer:

Those factors associated with the factor of joy that are not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"—this is called the factor of joy that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga)? Answer:

Those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are subsumed within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy.
What is that which is neither the faculty of ignorance (*ajñānendriya*) nor the factor of joy in enlightenment (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:

That which is not included within the faculty of ignorance but includes the factor of joy in enlightenment; those things not included within the faculty of ignorance or the factor of joy in enlightenment that are dissociated from them; and all other mind, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are said to be neither the faculty of ignorance nor the factor of joy in enlightenment.
The same applies to right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Regarding those dharmas that are associated with the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*), are they also associated with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is the faculty of ignorance that is not the awakening factor of equanimity.
What is the faculty of ignorance that is not the awakening factor of equanimity? Answer:

The factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) associated with the faculty of ignorance (*ajñāna-indriya*): this is called the faculty of ignorance that is not the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
What is the factor of enlightenment of tranquility that is not the faculty of ignorance? Answer:

Those factors that are dissociated from the faculty of ignorance (*avidyā-indriya*) but associated with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): these are called the awakening factor of tranquility that is not the faculty of ignorance.
What is the faculty of ignorance that is the awakening factor of tranquility?

Answer: Those factors associated with the faculty of "I do not know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and associated with the factor of equanimity (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) are called the faculty of "I do not know" and the factor of equanimity.
What are those that are neither the faculty of "I do not know" nor the factor of equanimity?
Answer:

The factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that is dissociated from the faculty of "I do not know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), as well as other mind, mental factors, form, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are said to be neither the faculty of "I do not know" nor the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
The same applies to the awakening factor of vigilance (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Regarding those factors that are associated with the faculty of "I do not know" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), are they also associated with the faculty of resolve (*adhimokṣendriya*)?
The answer is: [Yes].
Or, there is the faculty of ignorance that is not the faculty of equanimity.
What is the faculty of ignorance that is not the faculty of equanimity? Answer:

The faculty of ignorance (avidyendriya) associated with equanimity (upekṣā), and those factors associated with the faculty of ignorance that are not associated with equanimity—these are called the faculty of ignorance that is not equanimity.
What is equanimity (upekṣā) that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya)?
The answer is:

those factors associated with equanimity that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"—this is called equanimity that is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is the equanimity associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"? Answer:

The factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are also associated with equanimity—this is called the equanimity associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is that which is neither the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) nor the faculty of "equanimity" (*upekṣendriya*)?
The answer is:

the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not associated with equanimity, all instances of equanimity that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and furthermore, other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind; these are called that which is neither the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor the faculty of equanimity.
The remaining [details] correspond as above. This concludes the section on the gates of correspondence.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"I shall now explain forty-four kinds of knowledge."
The knowledge of the suffering of old age and death consists of four knowledges:

dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of suffering, and conventional knowledge. The knowledge of the origin of old age and death consists of four knowledges: [dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of origin, and conventional knowledge].
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of the unknown (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The four knowledges regarding the knowledge of the exhaustion of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇakṣayajñāna*) are:
the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of the unknown, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and conventional knowledge.
The knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of aging and death consists of four knowledges:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, path-knowledge, and conventional knowledge.
The same applies to the knowledges of birth, existence, and so forth, down to the knowledges of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). Thus ends the section on the forty-four doors of knowledge.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"I shall now declare seventy-seven kinds of knowledge.
Regarding the knowledge that birth is the condition for aging and death, there are four knowledges:"
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The knowledge that knows old age and death by not taking other births as its object consists of four knowledges:
the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of the unknown, the knowledge of origination, and conventional knowledge.
The four knowledges that know the past, long-distant origination-conditioned aging-and-death are:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and analytical knowledge.
There are no other four knowledges that know the past, long-distant origination-conditioned aging-and-death.
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of the unknown (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding the knowledge that knows old age and death conditioned by birth over a long period in the future, there are four knowledges:
the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of the unknown, the knowledge of origination, and conventional knowledge.
The knowledge that does not take other future, long-distant births as conditions for aging and death consists of four knowledges:
dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and analytical knowledge (*paricchedajñāna*).

Just as with the knowledge abiding in the dharma-realm—namely, the knowledge that [birth] is impermanent, conditioned, mind-dependent, arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to change, and subject to cessation—this knowledge is one: analytical knowledge. This applies even up to the knowledge of the conditionality of ignorance leading to formations; thus ends the seventy-seven doors of knowledge.
If one has accomplished dharma-knowledge, does one also have subsequent knowledge?
Answer: If one has attained it.
If one has attained the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), has one also attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)? Answer: Yes.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), does one also possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)? Answer:
If one has attained it and not lost it, then one accomplishes it; if one has not attained it, or if having attained it one loses it, then one does not accomplish it.
If one has attained the knowledge of others' minds, does one possess that dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has been acquired.
If one has accomplished the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), does one possess that conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna)? Answer: It is so.
If one achieves conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), does one also achieve dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna)?
Answer: If it has been attained.
If one has accomplished the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one have the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)? Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), has one also attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)? Answer: Yes.

If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), does one also possess the knowledge of origination (anvaya-jñāna), the knowledge of cessation (kṣaya-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)?
Answer: If they have been attained.
If one has attained the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), has one also attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
This concludes the section on the knowledge of phenomena.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of the unknown (anājñāta-ājñāna-jñāna), does one also accomplish the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna)? Answer:
If it has been attained and not lost, then one accomplishes it; if it has not been attained, or if it was attained but then lost, then one does not accomplish it.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, does that person possess the knowledge of what is not yet known?
Answer: If they have attained it.
If one is accomplished in the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), is one also accomplished in conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna)? Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), does one also accomplish subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: If one has attained it.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), does one possess the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)? Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), has one also attained the knowledge of the unknown (anājñāta-jñāna)?
Answer: If it has been acquired.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), does one also possess the knowledge of the origin, cessation, and the path (samudaya-kṣaya-mārga-jñāna)?
Answer: If they have been attained.
If one has attained the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), has one also attained the knowledge of what is not yet known (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna)?
Answer: It is so;
this concludes the section on the knowledge of what is not yet known.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds, does one possess that knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*), does one also possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)? Answer:
If it has been attained and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been attained, or if it was attained but subsequently lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path?
Answer: If one has attained them.
If one has attained the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), does one possess the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)? Answer:

If it has been attained and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been attained, or if it was attained but subsequently lost, then one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds. [End of section on the knowledge of others' minds.]
If one accomplishes conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), does one thereby possess the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path?
Answer: If one has attained them.
If one has attained the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), has one also attained those knowledges? Answer: Yes.
If one has accomplished the knowledge of suffering, does one also possess the knowledge of origination, cessation, and the path?
Answer: If one has attained them.
If one has attained the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), has one also attained the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one has accomplished the knowledge of cultivation (vāsanājñāna), does one also possess the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of the path (kṣayamārgajñāna)?
Answer: If one has attained them.
If one has attained the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (kṣayajñāna), has that person also attained the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)? Answer: Yes.
If one has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), does one possess the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)?
Answer: If one has acquired it.
If one has attained the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), does one also have the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna)?
Answer: It is the same;
this concludes the single contemplation.
If one has accomplished the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), has one also accomplished it in the future? Answer: Yes.
If one possesses that in the future, does one possess it in the past?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted but not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted and then lost, then one does not possess it.
If it is past, is it also present?
Answer: It is so if it is currently manifest.
If one possesses it in the present, does one possess it in the past? Answer:
If it has been exhausted but not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it has been exhausted and then lost, then one does not possess it.
If that [dharma] is future, is it also present?
Answer: It is so if it is manifested before one.
If it exists in the present, does it exist in the future?
Answer: It is so.
If one has that in the past, does one have it in the future and the present?
The answer is:
one achieves it in the future, and in the present if it is currently manifest.
If those [dharmas] are future or present, are they also past?
The answer is:
if they have been exhausted but not lost, then they are accomplished; if they have not been exhausted, or if they were exhausted but then lost, then they are not accomplished.
If something is future, is it also past and present?
The answer is:

there may be that which is future but lacks the past and present; or that which has the past but lacks the present; or that which has the present but lacks the past; or that which has both the past and the present.
What is meant by "future, but not past or present"?
The answer is:

if one has attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) but has not yet exhausted it, or if, having exhausted it, one has lost it and it does not manifest before one, this is called "future, but not past or present."
What is meant by "future and past, but not present"?
The answer is:
if a dharma-knowledge has already been exhausted and has not been lost, yet this dharma-knowledge does not manifest before one, this is called being future and past, but not present.
What is meant by "future and present [dharmas] are not past"?
The answer is:
if a dharma-knowledge manifests in the present and is not exhausted, or even if it were exhausted, it is immediately lost; this is called being future and present, but not past.
What is meant by "future and past and present"?
The answer is:
if a dharma-knowledge has already been exhausted but not lost, and furthermore this dharma-knowledge is manifest in the present, this is called "future and past and present."
If they are past and present, are they also future?
The answer is: Yes.
If one possesses [the dharma] in the present, does one also possess it in the past and future? Answer:

One possesses it in the future. Regarding the past, if it has been exhausted but not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted and then lost, then one does not possess it.
If those [dharmas] are past or future, are they also present? Answer:
If the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) is currently manifest, it passes through six [moments].
The same applies to the knowledge of the unknown, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
If one possesses the past knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess it in the future?
He replied: "It is so.
If that [dharma] is future, is it also past?"
Answer: If it is exhausted yet not lost, then it is accomplished; if it is not exhausted, or if it is exhausted and then lost, it is not accomplished.
If that [dharma] is past, is it also present?
Answer: If it is present before one.
Suppose it is present; is it also past?
He replied: "It is so.
If that is future, is it also present?"
Answer: If it is present before one,
then if that [state] is present, is that [state] also future?
Answer: It is so.
If that [dharma] is past, is it also future and present?
Answer: It is accomplished in the future; if it is present, it is so when it manifests before one.
If it exists in the future and the present, does it also exist in the past?
Answer: It is so.
If it is future, is it also past and present?
Answer: Sometimes the future lacks the past and present; sometimes the past lacks the present; and [sometimes] both the past and present [are absent].
What does it mean for the future to lack the past and present?
Answer:

If one knows the knowledge of others' minds and does not lose it, or if it is not yet exhausted, but should it be exhausted it is then lost and does not manifest before one—this is called having no past or present [of that knowledge] in the future.
What is meant by "future and past, but not present"?
The answer is:

if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds that has already ceased but has not been lost, and this knowledge of others' minds is not currently manifest before one, this is called "future and past, but not present."
What is meant by "the future together with the past and present"?
The answer is:

if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds that has already ceased but is not lost, and furthermore, this knowledge of others' minds is currently manifest before one, this is called "the future together with the past and present."
If they are past or present, are they also future?
The answer is: Yes.
If something exists in the present, does it also exist in the past and the future?
Answer: It is so.
If those [knowledges] are past or future, are they also present?
The answer is:
if they are present before one, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) proceeds through six [stages].
If one has attained the knowledge of the past and so forth, has one also attained it in the future?
The answer is: Yes.
If that [dharma] is future, is it also past? Answer: Yes.
If something is past, is it also present?
Answer: It is, provided it is currently manifest.
If one exists in the present, does one exist in the past?
Answer: It is so.
If something is future, is it also present?
Answer: It is so if it is currently manifest.
If it exists in the present, does it also exist in the future?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses that in the past, does one also possess it in the future and the present? Answer:
One accomplishes it in the future; as for the present, it is accomplished if it manifests before one.
If they are future or present, are they also past?
The answer is: Yes.
If one possesses that in the future, does one also possess it in the past and present? Answer:
One accomplishes it in the past; as for the present, one possesses it if it is currently manifest.
If they are past or present, are they also future?
He replied: "It is so."
If it is present, is it also past and future?
Answer: It is so.
If those [dharmas] are past or future, are they also present?
The answer is:
if they are currently manifesting, [they are present]. (The sixth section concludes.)
If one has attained past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), has one also attained past unknown-knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)? Answer:
If it is exhausted and not lost, then one has attained it; if it is not exhausted, or if it is exhausted but then lost, then one has not attained it.
If one has attained past unknown-knowledge (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), does one also possess past dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: If it is exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it is not exhausted, or if it is exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess the future knowledge of the unknown (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: If it has been attained.
If one has attained the future knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), has one also attained the past knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)? Answer:
If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one has attained it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one has not attained it.
If one has attained past dharma-knowledge, has one also present unknown-knowledge?
Answer: If it is manifest at the present moment.
If one has attained present *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*, has one also attained past *dharmajñāna*?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted and not lost, then one has attained it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one has not attained it.
If one accomplishes the past dharma-knowledge, does one also accomplish the past and present unknown-knowledge?
Answer:

One may accomplish the past dharma-knowledge without possessing the past and present unknown-knowledge; or possess the past [unknown-knowledge] without the present; or possess the present [unknown-knowledge] without the past; or possess both the past and present unknown-knowledge.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena) but does not possess past or present *anvayajñāna* (subsequent knowledge)? Answer:

If *dharmajñāna* has already been exhausted but not lost, and furthermore, this *anvayajñāna* has not been exhausted—or even if it were exhausted, it has been lost and does not manifest before one—this is called accomplishing past *dharmajñāna* while not possessing past or present *anvayajñāna*.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharmajñāna* and past *anvayajñāna*, yet they are not present? Answer:

If *dharmajñāna* and *anvayajñāna* have already been exhausted and are not lost, and furthermore this *anvayajñāna* is not present, this is called accomplishing past *dharmajñāna* and past *anvayajñāna*, but not as present.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharma-jñāna* and present *anājñāta-ājñāsyāmīndriya*, but not the past?
The answer is:

if *dharma-jñāna* has already been exhausted and is not lost, and this *anājñāta-ājñāsyāmīndriya* is present before one; or if it has not yet been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost—this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* and present *anājñāta-ājñāsyāmīndriya*, but not the past.
How does one accomplish past *dharma-jñāna* as well as past and present *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*?
The answer is:

if *dharma-jñāna* and *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna* have already been exhausted and not lost, and furthermore this *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna* is present before one, this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* as well as past and present *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*.
If one has attained past and present unknown-knowledge (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*), does one also possess past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the future and present knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna)? Answer:
One may accomplish the past knowledge of phenomena without accomplishing the future and present knowledge of the unknown.
Regarding the future [knowledge] and the absence of present and future unknown-knowledge (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna):
how is it that one accomplishes past dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) but not future and present unknown-knowledge?
Answer:

If the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already been exhausted and not lost, and furthermore, this [person] has not yet attained the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), this is called "accomplishing past dharmajñāna but not future or present anvayajñāna."
How is it that one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the future knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātamājñāsyāmī-jñāna*), but not the present? Answer:

If the knowledge of phenomena has already been exhausted and not lost, and furthermore, this [attainment of] the knowledge of the unknown has been acquired but does not manifest before one, this is called accomplishing the past knowledge of phenomena and the future knowledge of the unknown, but not the present.
How does one accomplish past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) as well as future and present unknown-knowledge (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

if dharma-knowledge has already been exhausted and not lost, and this unknown-knowledge is present before one, this is called accomplishing past dharma-knowledge as well as future and present unknown-knowledge.
If one accomplishes the future and present knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), does one also accomplish the past knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one accomplishes it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not accomplish it.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the past and future knowledge of the unknown (anvayajñāna)? Answer:

One may accomplish the past knowledge of phenomena without accomplishing the past and future knowledge of the unknown; or one may accomplish the future [knowledge of the unknown] but not the past; or one may accomplish both the past and future knowledge of the unknown.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharma-jñāna* but does not accomplish past or future *anvaya-jñāna*? Answer:
If *dharma-jñāna* has already been exhausted and is not lost, yet this person has not attained *anvaya-jñāna*, this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* but not past or future *anvaya-jñāna*.
How is it that one accomplishes the past *dharmajñāna* and the future *anvayajñāna*, but not the past?
The answer is:

if the *dharmajñāna* has already been exhausted and is not lost, and furthermore, this person attains the *anvayajñāna*—whether it has not yet been exhausted, or even if it has been exhausted, it is immediately lost—this is called accomplishing the past *dharmajñāna* and the future *anvayajñāna*, but not the past.
How does one accomplish past dharma-knowledge as well as past and future unknown-knowledge?
The answer is:
if dharma-knowledge and unknown-knowledge have been exhausted and are not lost, this is called accomplishing past dharma-knowledge as well as past and future unknown-knowledge.
If one has attained the knowledge of the unknown regarding the past and future, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena regarding the past?
Answer: If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes past *dharma-jñāna*, does one also accomplish past, future, and present *anājñāta-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*?
The answer is:

one may accomplish past *dharma-jñāna* without accomplishing past, future, or present *anājñāta-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*; or [accomplish] the future [but] not the past or present; or [accomplish] the past and future [but] not the present; or [accomplish] the future and present [but] not the past; or [accomplish] the past, future, and present *anājñāta-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena) but does not accomplish past, future, or present *anvayajñāna* (subsequent knowledge)? Answer:

If *dharmajñāna* has already been exhausted and is not lost, yet one has not attained *anvayajñāna*, this is called accomplishing past *dharmajñāna* but not accomplishing past, future, or present *anvayajñāna*.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharma-jñāna* and future *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*, but not the past or present? Answer:

If *dharma-jñāna* has already been exhausted but not lost, and one has acquired this future *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*; or if it has not been exhausted; or even if it was exhausted, it has been lost and does not manifest—this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* and future *anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*, but not the past or present.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharma-jñāna* and past and future *anvaya-jñāna*, but not the present? Answer:

If *dharma-jñāna* and *anvaya-jñāna* have already been exhausted and are not lost, yet this *anvaya-jñāna* does not manifest before one, this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* and past and future *anvaya-jñāna*, but not the present.
How is it that one achieves past *dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of phenomena) and future and present *anājñāta-ājñāsyāmīndriya* (the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"), but not the past?
The answer is:

if *dharma-jñāna* has already been exhausted and is not lost, and this *anājñāta-ājñāsyāmīndriya* is present before one, yet [if] it has not been exhausted, or even if it were exhausted, it has been lost; this is called achieving past *dharma-jñāna* and future and present *anājñāta-ājñāsyāmīndriya*, but not the past.
How does one accomplish past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) as well as past, future, and present unknown-knowledge (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

if dharma-knowledge and unknown-knowledge have already been exhausted and not lost, and furthermore this unknown-knowledge is present before one, this is called accomplishing past dharma-knowledge as well as past, future, and present unknown-knowledge.

If one has attained the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*) regarding the past, present, and future, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding the past?

Answer: If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess the knowledge of phenomena or the knowledge of the unknown. (End of section seven.)
If one has attained the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess the past knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)? Answer:
If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained the knowledge of others' minds in the past, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) in the past?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess the future knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)? Answer:
If it has been attained and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been attained, or if it was attained but subsequently lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses the future knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)? Answer:
If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess the present knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: If it is manifest in the present.
If one has attained the present knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does that person also accomplish past and present knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)? Answer:

One may accomplish past knowledge of phenomena but not past and present knowledge of others' minds; or [accomplish] the past but not the present; or [accomplish] both past and present knowledge of others' minds.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharma-jñāna* but does not accomplish past or present *paracitta-jñāna*? Answer:

If *dharma-jñāna* has already been exhausted but is not lost, and this *paracitta-jñāna* has not yet been exhausted—or even if it has been exhausted, it is lost and does not manifest before one—this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* but not accomplishing past or present *paracitta-jñāna*.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharma-jñāna* and past knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*), but not the present? Answer:

If the *dharma-jñāna* and the knowledge of others' minds have already ceased but are not lost, and furthermore this knowledge of others' minds does not manifest before one, this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* and past knowledge of others' minds, but not the present.
How does one accomplish the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) as well as the past and present knowledge of others' minds?
The answer is:

if the knowledge of phenomena has already been exhausted and not lost, and furthermore this knowledge of others' minds is present before one, this is called accomplishing the past knowledge of phenomena as well as the past and present knowledge of others' minds.
If one has attained the knowledge of others' minds regarding the past and present, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) regarding the past?
The answer is:
if it is exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it is not exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the future and present knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)? Answer:

One may accomplish the past knowledge of phenomena without accomplishing the future and present knowledge of others' minds; or accomplish it in the future without accomplishing it in the present; or accomplish it in both the future and the present as the knowledge of others' minds.
How is it that one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) of the past but not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) of the future or present? Answer:

If the knowledge of phenomena has already been exhausted and is not lost, yet this person has not attained the knowledge of others' minds—or if having attained it, they have lost it—this is called accomplishing the past knowledge of phenomena without the future or present knowledge of others' minds.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharma-jñāna* and future *paracitta-jñāna*, but not the present?
The answer is:

if *dharma-jñāna* has already been exhausted and is not lost, and furthermore, this *paracitta-jñāna* is known and is not lost but does not manifest before one, this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* and future *paracitta-jñāna*, but not the present.
How does one accomplish past *dharma-jñāna* as well as future and present *paracitta-jñāna*?
The answer is:

if this *dharma-jñāna* has already been exhausted but not lost, and furthermore, this *paracitta-jñāna* is manifest before one, this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* as well as future and present *paracitta-jñāna*.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) in the future and present, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) in the past?
Answer: If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does that person also possess the past and future knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)? Answer:
There are cases where one has accomplished the past knowledge of phenomena but lacks the past and future knowledge of others' minds.
And [the case where one possesses] the future [knowledge] but not the past:
and [the case where one possesses] the knowledge of others' minds regarding the past and the future.
How is it that one accomplishes the past *dharmajñāna* but does not accomplish the knowledge of others' minds regarding the past and the future?
Answer:

If the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already been exhausted but not lost, and one has not yet attained the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), or if having attained it one has subsequently lost it, this is called "accomplishing past dharmajñāna but not past or future paracittajñāna."
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharmajñāna* and future *paracittajñāna*, but not the past?
The answer is:

if *dharmajñāna* has already been exhausted and is not lost, and furthermore, this *paracittajñāna* is known and is not lost; yet [the latter] is not exhausted, or even if exhausted, is lost—this is called accomplishing past *dharmajñāna* and future *paracittajñāna*, but not the past.
How does one accomplish both past *dharma-jñāna* and past and future *paracitta-jñāna*?
The answer is:
if *dharma-jñāna* and *paracitta-jñāna* have already ceased but are not lost, this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* as well as past and future *paracitta-jñāna*.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) pertaining to the past and future, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) pertaining to the past? Answer:
If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but subsequently lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), does one also possess the past, future, or present knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)? Answer:

One may accomplish the past knowledge of phenomena without possessing the past, future, or present knowledge of others' minds; or possess the future [knowledge of others' minds] without the past or present; or possess the past and future [knowledge of others' minds] without the present; or possess the past, future, and present knowledge of others' minds.
What is meant by one who has accomplished past *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena) but has not accomplished past, future, or present *paracittajñāna* (knowledge of others' minds)?
The answer is:

if *dharmajñāna* has already been exhausted and is not lost, yet this person has not attained *paracittajñāna*, or if having attained it, he has lost it—this is called accomplishing past *dharmajñāna* but not accomplishing past, future, or present *paracittajñāna*.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharma-jñāna* and future *para-citta-jñāna*, yet lacks [the accomplishment of] past or present [knowledge]?
The answer is:

if *dharma-jñāna* has already been exhausted and not lost, and furthermore, this *para-citta-jñāna* is known and not lost; yet if it is not exhausted, or even if it were exhausted it is lost and does not manifest before one—this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* and future *para-citta-jñāna*, but not [accomplishing] the past or present.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharma-jñāna* as well as past and future *paracitta-jñāna*, but not the present?
The answer is:

if *dharma-jñāna* and *paracitta-jñāna* have already ceased but are not lost, and furthermore this *paracitta-jñāna* does not manifest before one, this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* and past and future *paracitta-jñāna*, but not the present.
How does one accomplish the knowledge of dharmas (dharmajñāna) of the past, as well as the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) regarding the past, future, and present?
The answer is:

if the knowledge of dharmas has already been exhausted but not lost, and this knowledge of others' minds is manifest in the present, this is called accomplishing the knowledge of dharmas of the past, as well as the knowledge of others' minds regarding the past, future, and present.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) pertaining to the past, future, and present, does one possess that [knowledge] regarding past phenomena?

Answer: If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds. (End of section seven.)
If one has attained the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), has one also attained the past conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one achieves the knowledge of past [dharmas] and so forth, does one also achieve the knowledge of past dharmas?
Answer: If it is exhausted and not lost, then one achieves it; if it is not exhausted, or if it is exhausted but then lost, then one does not achieve it.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, has one also accomplished future conventional knowledge? Answer: Yes.
If one achieves the future conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*), does one also achieve the past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted and not lost, then one achieves it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not achieve it.
If one has attained past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess present conventional knowledge?
Answer: If it is present before one.
If one has attained present conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), has one also attained past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted and not lost, then one has attained it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one has not attained it.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one possess past and present conventional knowledge?
Answer: One possesses the past; as for the present, it is possessed if it is currently manifest.
If one has attained the knowledge of past and present and so forth, does one possess the knowledge of past phenomena?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess future and present conventional knowledge (samvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: One possesses it in the future; as for the present, one possesses it if it is currently manifest.
If one achieves the future and present *samvṛtijñāna* (conventional knowledge), does one also achieve the past *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena)? Answer:
If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one achieves it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not achieve it.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, has one also accomplished past and future conventional knowledge? Answer: Yes.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of the past and future, etc., does one also accomplish the knowledge of past phenomena?
Answer: If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one accomplishes it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not accomplish it.
If one has accomplished past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess past, future, and present conventional knowledge (samvṛtijñāna)?
The answer is:
one possesses it in the past and future; as for the present, one possesses it if it is currently manifest.
If one has attained the knowledge of the past, future, and present, does one possess the knowledge of past phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it. [The seven knowledges are concluded.]
If one has accomplished the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess the past knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)? Answer:
If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) of the past, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) of the past?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), has one also accomplished the future knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)? Answer: Yes.
If one has attained the knowledge of future suffering, does one also possess the knowledge of past phenomena? Answer:
If it is exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it is not exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one possess present knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?
Answer: If it is manifested in the present.
If one has attained present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), has one also attained past knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?
The answer is:
if it is exhausted and not lost, then one has attained it; if it is not exhausted, or if it is exhausted but then lost, then one has not attained it.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the past and present knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)? Answer:

One may accomplish the past knowledge of phenomena without accomplishing the past and present knowledge of suffering; or accomplish the past [knowledge of suffering] without the present; or accomplish the present [knowledge of suffering] without the past; or accomplish both the past and present knowledge of suffering.
How is it that one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) but does not accomplish the past or present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
The answer is:

if the knowledge of phenomena has already been exhausted and is not lost, yet this knowledge of suffering has not been exhausted—or even if it was exhausted, it has been lost and does not manifest—this is called accomplishing the past knowledge of phenomena but not the past or present knowledge of suffering.
What is meant by one who has accomplished past *dharma-jñāna* and past *duḥkha-jñāna*, but not the present?
The answer is:

if *dharma-jñāna* and *duḥkha-jñāna* have already been exhausted and are not lost, yet this *duḥkha-jñāna* does not manifest before one, this is called having accomplished past *dharma-jñāna* and past *duḥkha-jñāna*, but not the present.
How is it that one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), but not the past?
The answer is:

if the knowledge of phenomena has already been exhausted but not lost, and this knowledge of suffering is present before one, yet [the former] is not exhausted—or if it were exhausted, it has been lost—this is called accomplishing the past knowledge of phenomena and the present knowledge of suffering, but not the past.
How does one accomplish both past *dharmajñāna* and past and present *duḥkhajñāna*?
The answer is:

if *dharmajñāna* and *duḥkhajñāna* have already been exhausted and are not lost, and furthermore this *duḥkhajñāna* is present before one, this is called accomplishing both past *dharmajñāna* and past and present *duḥkhajñāna*.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) regarding the past and present, does one also possess that knowledge regarding past phenomena (*dharma*)?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess future and present knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?
Answer: One possesses it in the future; as for the present, one possesses it if it is currently manifest.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) regarding the future and the present, does that person also possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) regarding the past?
The answer is:
if it has been exhausted and not lost, then they possess it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then they do not possess it.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), has one also accomplished past and future knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)? Answer:

One has accomplished it in the future; as for the past, one has accomplished it if it has been exhausted and not lost, but if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted and then lost, one has not accomplished it.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering regarding the past and future, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena regarding the past?
The answer is:
if it is exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it is not exhausted, or if it is exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes past *dharmajñāna*, does one also accomplish past, future, and present *duḥkhajñāna*?
The answer is:

one may accomplish past *dharmajñāna* and future *duḥkhajñāna* but not past or present; or past and future but not present; or future and present but not past; or past, future, and present *duḥkhajñāna*.
How is it that one accomplishes the past *dharma-jñāna* and the future *duḥkha-jñāna*, but not the past or present?
The answer is:

if the *dharma-jñāna* has already been exhausted and is not lost, and furthermore, this *duḥkha-jñāna* has not yet been attained; or if it has been attained but is not yet exhausted, or even if exhausted, it is lost and does not manifest before one—this is called accomplishing the past *dharma-jñāna* and the future *duḥkha-jñāna*, but not the past or present.
How is it that one accomplishes past *dharmajñāna* as well as past and future *duḥkhajñāna*, but not the present?
The answer is:

if *dharmajñāna* and *duḥkhajñāna* have already been exhausted and are not lost, yet this *duḥkhajñāna* does not manifest before one, this is called accomplishing past *dharmajñāna* and past and future *duḥkhajñāna*, but not the present.
How is it that one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) of the past, as well as the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) of the future and present, but not of the past?
The answer is:

if the knowledge of phenomena has already been exhausted and is not lost, and this knowledge of suffering is present before one, yet [the knowledge of suffering] is not exhausted, or even if exhausted, is lost; this is called accomplishing the knowledge of phenomena of the past, as well as the knowledge of suffering of the future and present, but not of the past.
How does one accomplish past *dharma-jñāna* as well as past, future, and present *duḥkha-jñāna*?
The answer is:

if *dharma-jñāna* and *duḥkha-jñāna* have already been exhausted and are not lost, and furthermore this *duḥkha-jñāna* is present before one, this is called accomplishing past *dharma-jñāna* as well as past, future, and present *duḥkha-jñāna*.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) pertaining to the past, future, and present, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) pertaining to the past?

Answer: If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one possesses it; if it has not been exhausted, or if it was exhausted but then lost, then one does not possess the knowledge of suffering. (End of Section 7.)
The knowledge of the path leading to the exhaustion of the habitual tendencies (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*) is also like this;

thus ends the small set of seven. Regarding the past *dhamma*-knowledge (*dhamma-ñāṇa*): there is one [type] for knowing the past, future, and others' minds; two for the future; three for the present; four for the past and present; five for the future and present; six for the past and future; and seven for the past, future, and present.
The knowledge of others' minds consists of seven [factors], and so it is for the knowledge of the path; thus ends the Great Seven.

This concludes the fifth chapter, "The Chapter on the Association of Knowledge. In the Sanskrit original, this consists of one hundred and forty-three *ślokas*; in the Qin translation, it comprises fifteen thousand one hundred and nine words.
The Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra, Volume Fourteen;
The Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra, Volume Fifteen.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra.
Sanghadeva, the Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra during the Fu Qin dynasty, [stated]:
"Evil conduct and false speech [arise from] sentient beings and life; the body has no instruction, for one's own actions follow behind."
I wish to explain fully the meaning of this chapter:

regarding the three types of misconduct and the three unwholesome roots, do the three types of misconduct encompass the three unwholesome roots, or do the three unwholesome roots encompass the three types of misconduct?

Regarding the three types of wholesome conduct and the three roots of goodness: do the three types of wholesome conduct encompass the three roots of goodness, or do the three roots of goodness encompass the three types of wholesome conduct?

Regarding the three types of unwholesome conduct and the ten courses of unwholesome action: do the three types of unwholesome conduct encompass the ten courses of unwholesome action, or do the ten courses of unwholesome action encompass the three types of unwholesome conduct?

Regarding the three types of wholesome conduct and the ten courses of wholesome action: do the three types of wholesome conduct encompass the ten courses of wholesome action, or do the ten courses of wholesome action encompass the three types of wholesome conduct?

Regarding the three types of action and the ten courses of action: do the three types of action encompass the ten courses of action, or do the ten courses of action encompass the three types of action?
Regarding the three types of action and the four types of action—

namely, black action with black retribution, white action with white retribution, black-and-white action with black-and-white retribution, and neither-black-nor-white action which is without retribution and leads to the exhaustion of action— is it the case that the three types of action subsume the four types of action, or that the four types of action subsume the three types of action?

Furthermore, regarding the three types of action—those with results in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*), those with results in the next life (*upapadyavipāka*), and those with results in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavipāka*); those with pleasant results, painful results, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant results; those of the past, future, and present; the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; those of the learner (*śaikṣa*), the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and neither-learner-nor-non-learner; and those abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-prahātavya*), those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and those not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)—does the former subsume the latter, or does the latter subsume the former?

Regarding the four types of action—black with black retribution, white with white retribution, black-and-white with black-and-white retribution, and neither-black-nor-white which is without retribution and leads to the exhaustion of action—and the three types of action—those with retribution in the present life, those with retribution upon rebirth, and those with retribution in subsequent lives;

those with pleasant retribution, those with painful retribution, and those with neither-painful-nor-pleasant retribution; those of the past, future, and present; those that are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; those of the trainee (*śaikṣa*), the non-trainee (*aśaikṣa*), and neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee; and those to be abandoned by seeing the truths, those to be abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned: do the four types of action subsume the three types of action, or do the three types of action subsume the four types of action?

Regarding the three types of action—those with retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*), those with retribution in the next birth (*upapadyavipāka*), and those with retribution in subsequent births (*aparaparyāyavipāka*); furthermore, the three types of action—those with pleasant retribution (*sukhavipāka*), those with painful retribution (*duḥkhavipāka*), and those with neither-painful-nor-pleasant retribution (*aduḥkhāsukhavipāka*); as well as those that are past, future, or present; wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the form or formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*); those of the learner (*śaikṣa*), the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), or neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*); and those to be abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or those not to be abandoned (*aheya*)—does the former subsume the latter, or does the latter subsume the former?

Regarding the three types of action—those with pleasant retribution, those with painful retribution, and those with neither-painful-nor-pleasant retribution—and furthermore, the three types of action—past, future, and present; wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; bound to the desire realm, bound to the form and formless realms; trainee, non-trainee, and neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee; and those to be abandoned by seeing the truths, those to be abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned: does the former subsume the latter, or does the latter subsume the former?

Regarding the three types of formations—past, future, and present; furthermore, the three types of formations—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; those of the learner (*śaikṣa*), the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and neither-learner-nor-non-learner; and those to be abandoned by vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*), those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and those not to be abandoned (*aheya*)—does the former subsume the latter, or does the latter subsume the former?

Regarding the three types of formations—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—and furthermore, the three types of formations bound to the desire realm, the form and formless realms; those of the learner (*śaikṣa*), the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and neither-learner-nor-non-learner; and those abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and not to be abandoned (*aheya*): does the former include the latter, or does the latter include the former?

The three types of formations are those bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form and formless realms; furthermore, there are the three types of formations that are in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those that are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*); as well as those abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-prahātavya*), those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and those not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*). Do the former include the latter, or do the latter include the former?

Regarding the three types of conduct—those of the learner (*śaikṣa*), those of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and those that are neither learner nor non-learner—and furthermore, the three types of conduct—those to be abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and those that are not to be abandoned (*aheya*)—does the former subsume the latter, or does the latter subsume the former?
Is there any karma that, when its retribution is experienced, results in physical pain being experienced but not mental?

"Neither posterior nor anterior, neither anterior nor posterior.

false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha; by the retribution of this action, one undergoes a lifespan of one kalpa in the Avīci Great Hell.

The answer is:

there is a first type of volitional action associated with meditative absorption (*samādhi-saṃskāra*), the retribution of which is a lifespan of eighty thousand *kalpas* in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaṃjñi-asaṃjñin*).
