Answer: Right livelihood constitutes the three types of wholesome bodily conduct; this is called right action and right livelihood.
What is not right action and not right livelihood?
Answer:
Excluding right livelihood and the four types of verbal sublime conduct, all other verbal sublime conduct is called non-right-action; this concludes the section on right livelihood.
The three unwholesome actions, the three crookednesses, and the three stains are as follows:

Curvature of the body, impurity of the body, and turbidity of the body; curvature of speech, impurity of speech, and turbidity of speech; curvature of the mind, impurity of the mind, and turbidity of the mind.
What is meant by curvature of the body?
The answer is:
Deceit is the manifestation of bodily conduct.
What is meant by "bodily impurity"?
The answer is:
What is bodily turbidity when the conduct of the body is dominated by hatred?
The answer is:
What is the bodily conduct of one whose lust is excessive and whose speech is crooked?
The answer is:
Regarding the flourishing of hypocrisy and verbal conduct:
what is meant by "impurity of speech"?
The answer is:
What is verbal turbidity when the conduct of speech is dominated by intense hatred?
The answer is:
What is meant by "excessive lustfulness," "verbal conduct," and "mental crookedness"?
The answer is:
What is the defilement of the mind that constitutes the practice of hypocrisy? Answer:
What is the turbidity of the mind when the conduct of the mind is dominated by intense ill-will? Answer:
Regarding the three unwholesome courses of action—sexual misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct—are the three crookednesses, corruptions, and turbidities subsumed within them?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there are unwholesome actions that are neither crooked (*vaṅka*), nor corrupt (*doṣa*), nor turbid (*kaṣāya*).
What are unwholesome actions that are neither crooked, nor corrupt, nor turbid?
The answer is:

Excluding those unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind characterized by the abundance of deceitful desire and anger associated with the realm of desire, all other unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are called unwholesome conduct that is neither crooked, nor corrupt, nor turbid.
What are crookedness, corruption, and turbidity that are not unwholesome conduct?
The answer is:

the deceptive bodily, verbal, and mental actions associated with the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the intense mental actions associated with craving in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); these are called crookedness, corruption, and turbidity that are not unwholesome conduct.
What are the crookedness, corruption, and turbidity of unwholesome conduct?
The answer is:

the unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind—characterized by the abundance of deceitful desire and hatred bound to the realm of desire—is called the crookedness, corruption, and turbidity of unwholesome conduct.
What are those that are neither unwholesome conduct nor crooked, corrupt, and turbid?
The answer is:
excluding the aforementioned matters.

Regarding the three types of wholesome conduct (*sucarita*) and the three purities (*pariśuddhi*): do the three types of wholesome conduct subsume the three purities, or do the three purities subsume the three types of wholesome conduct?
Answer: They subsume one another according to their respective categories.
Regarding the three types of wholesome conduct (*sucarita*) and the three fulfillments (*paripūri*): do the three types of wholesome conduct subsume the three fulfillments?
Answer: Some are wholesome conduct but not fulfillments.
What is wholesome conduct that is not fulfilled?
The answer is:

with the exception of the untrained (aśaikṣa) wholesome conduct of body and speech, all other wholesome conduct of body and speech, as well as all wholesome conduct of mind—this is called wholesome conduct that is not fulfilled.
What is that which is fulfilled but not a wholesome course of action?
The answer is:
the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa); this is called that which is fulfilled but not a wholesome course of action.
What is the fulfillment of sublime conduct?
The answer is:
the sublime conduct of body and speech belonging to one beyond training (aśaikṣa); this is called the fulfillment of sublime conduct.
What is the non-fulfillment of sublime conduct?
The answer is:
excluding the aforementioned matters.
Regarding the three purities and the three fulfillments: do the three purities encompass the three fulfillments?
The answer is:
some are pure but not fulfilled.
What is purity that is not fulfillment?
The answer is:
with the exception of the purity of body and speech belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), all other purities of body, speech, and mind are called purity that is not fulfillment.
What is that which is fulfilled but not purified?
The answer is:
the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣacitta); this is called fulfilled but not purified.
What is meant by "purity and fulfillment"?
The answer is:
the purity of the body and speech of one beyond training (aśaikṣa); this is called purity and fulfillment.
What is meant by "not being fulfilled through purification"?
The answer is:
excluding all those aforementioned matters already concluded as fulfilled.
Are all bodily misconducts exclusively unskillful bodily actions?
Answer: Yes;
all bodily misconducts are exclusively unskillful bodily actions.
Is there a bodily action that lacks skillful means (*kauśalya*) which is yet not a bodily misconduct (*kāyaduścarita*)?
Answer: Yes;
namely, obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) bodily action and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) bodily action lacking skillful means.
Are all unwholesome verbal actions necessarily unskillful verbal actions?
Answer: Yes;
all unwholesome verbal actions are necessarily unskillful verbal actions.
Is there a case where one has verbal conduct lacking in skillful means, yet that is not verbal misconduct?
Answer: Yes;
there is verbal conduct that is obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), as well as verbal conduct that is unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and lacks skillful means.
Are all those unwholesome mental actions necessarily unskillful mental actions?
Answer: Some unwholesome mental actions are not unskillful mental actions.
What is unwholesome mental conduct that is not unskillful mental activity?
The answer is:
the three types of unwholesome mental conduct; these are called unwholesome mental conduct that is not unskillful mental activity.
What is that which is an unskillful mental formation but not an unwholesome mental action? Answer:
Concealed indeterminate volition (*cetanā*) and unconcealed indeterminate unskillful volition; this is called an unskillful mental formation that is not an unwholesome mental action.
What is unwholesome mental conduct that is also unskillful mental activity?
It is answered:
Unwholesome volition (*cetanā*)—this is called unwholesome mental conduct that is also unskillful mental activity.
What is that which is not unwholesome mental conduct, yet is not without skillful means in mental conduct?
Answer: It is the exclusion of all such aforementioned instances of unwholesome conduct.
Are all instances of excellent bodily conduct necessarily instances of skillful bodily conduct?
Answer: It is so;
all instances of excellent bodily conduct are indeed instances of skillful bodily conduct.
Is there any skillful bodily action that is not a sublime bodily action?
Answer: Yes;
namely, skillful bodily action that is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Are all wholesome verbal actions skillful verbal actions?
Answer: Yes;
all wholesome verbal actions are indeed skillful verbal actions.
Is there that which is a skillful verbal formation but is not a virtuous verbal formation?
Answer: There is;
namely, skillful verbal formations that are non-obscured and neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Are all instances of excellent mental conduct necessarily instances of skillful mental conduct?
Answer: Some instances of excellent mental conduct are not instances of skillful mental conduct.
What is wholesome mental conduct that is not skillful mental conduct?
Answer: The three types of wholesome mental conduct; these are called wholesome mental conduct that is not skillful mental conduct.
What is skillful mental activity that is not wholesome mental activity?
The answer is:
non-obscured indeterminate skillful volition; this is called skillful mental activity that is not wholesome mental activity.
What is wholesome mental conduct that is also skillful mental conduct?
The answer is:
wholesome volition; this is called wholesome mental conduct that is also skillful mental conduct.
What is that which is neither a sublime mental action nor a skillful mental action?
Answer: It is everything except for those aforementioned sublime mental actions.
If various dharmas are obtained through volitional action (*saṃskāra*), should those dharmas be described as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
The answer is:
regarding the meaning of retribution (*vipāka*), those dharmas obtained through volitional action should be described as indeterminate.
If it is asked: "Are those dharmas which are acquired through the practice of such retributive meanings indeterminate?
The answer is: "It is so."
If one were to say:
"Originally, the Tathāgata had no virtuous mind, yet he spoke gentle words, wonderful words, and soft, beautiful words; are these words virtuous?
The answer is: Yes.

It is so. Listen to what I say: regarding the meaning of retribution, if various dharmas are acquired through volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and those dharmas are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), one should not make such a statement as:
"Originally there was no wholesome mind in the Tathāgata; he spoke gentle words, exquisite words, soft and beautiful words—this speech was wholesome."
Although such words have been spoken, this matter is not so.
If one were to say:
"Originally there was no virtuous mind in the Tathāgata; he spoke gentle words, exquisite words, and soft, beautiful words—these words were virtuous," [this would be incorrect].
One should not speak thus:
"Dharmas that have the sense of retribution are indeterminate because they are obtained through formative action (saṃskāra);
dharmas that have the sense of retribution are indeterminate because they are obtained through formative action."
This is not so. One should speak thus: "Originally there was no Tathāgata;

rather, during a previous life, he performed wholesome deeds and received their retribution. When that retribution manifested in the present, he obtained the four great elements of the throat by virtue of those causes and conditions."
When the four great elements act and the four great elements produce sound, that sound is not a karmic retribution.
Can past action have a past retribution, or can it have a future or present retribution?
He replied: "It is so.
Is it possible for future formations to have a future retribution?"
Answer: There are [karmas], but none that are past or present.
Is there perhaps a present karma that has a present retribution?
Answer: There is.
In the past there is none; in the future there are three; thus the three times are concluded.
Is it possible that while bodily action receives retribution, such is not the case for vocal and mental actions?
Answer: There is.
For example, when the body is impure but the speech is pure, at that time there may be a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind;
likewise, when the body is pure but the speech is impure, at that time there may be an unwholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
This is called the case where bodily action receives its retribution, while vocal and mental actions do not.
Is there a case where vocal action receives its retribution, while bodily and mental actions do not?
The answer is: Yes.
There are cases where the body is pure while the speech is impure; at that time, there may be either a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
There are also cases where the body is impure while the speech is pure; at that time, there may be either an unwholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
This is called the case where the verbal formation receives its retribution, whereas the bodily and mental formations do not.
Is there a case where the mental formation receives its retribution, while the bodily and verbal formations do not?
Answer: Yes.
There are cases where, for instance, while the body is impure and the speech is impure, at that very moment there is a wholesome mind;
or where, while the body is pure and the speech is pure, at that very moment there is an unwholesome mind.
This is called the volitional action of the mind receiving its retribution, whereas the bodily and verbal actions do not.
Is it possible that the bodily and verbal actions receive their retribution while the mental action does not?
Answer: There is.
For example, when the body is impure and the speech is impure, at that time there may be a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind;
likewise, when the body is pure and the speech is pure, at that time there may be an unwholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
This is called the case where bodily conduct and verbal conduct receive retribution, while mental conduct does not.
Is there perhaps a case where bodily conduct and mental conduct receive retribution, while verbal conduct does not?
The answer is: There is.
For example, when the body is impure but the mouth is pure, at that time there may be an unwholesome mind;
or when the body is pure but the mouth is impure, at that time there may be a wholesome mind.
This is called the case where bodily action and mental action receive their retribution, while vocal action does not.
Is there perhaps a case where vocal action and mental action receive their retribution, while bodily action does not?
Answer: There is.
For example, when the body is pure but the speech is impure, at that time there is an unwholesome mind;
or when the body is impure but the speech is pure, at that time there is a wholesome mind.
This is called the way in which verbal and mental actions receive their retribution, whereas bodily action does not.
Is it possible that just as bodily and verbal actions receive retribution, so too do mental actions?
Answer: There is.
For example, when the body is impure and the speech is impure, at that time there is an unwholesome mind;
when the body is pure and the speech is pure, at that time there is a wholesome mind.
This is called how bodily actions and verbal actions receive their retribution; mental actions are likewise.
Is it possible that bodily, verbal, and mental actions do not receive retribution and yet receive retribution?
Answer: Yes, there are:

the various formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), matter that is the ripening of karma (*vipāka-rūpa*), the mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), and formations dissociated from mind.

Is it possible for these three types of formations to receive their retribution neither before nor after one another—namely, as retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*), retribution upon rebirth (*upapadya-vedanīya*), or retribution in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*)?

Answer: Receiving retribution consists of: present-life retribution for form (*rūpa*); birth-time retribution for mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*); and subsequent-rebirth retribution for formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, there is present-life retribution for mind and mental factors; birth-time retribution for form; and subsequent-rebirth retribution for formations dissociated from mind.

Furthermore, there are formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra) that have their retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*), which give rise to mind, mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), and matter that has its retribution in a future birth (*upapadyavipāka*). This concludes the third section on matter with subsequent retribution (*aparaparyāyavipāka*).
The same applies to those with a pleasant retribution, a painful retribution, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant retribution.
Matter bound to the desire realm; mind and mental factors bound to the form realm; formations dissociated from the mind bound to the formless realm.
Furthermore, mind and mental factors bound to the desire realm; matter bound to the form realm; and formations dissociated from the mind bound to the formless realm.

Furthermore, there are formations dissociated from the mind bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), matter bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the mental states and mental factors bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This concludes the three realms.
Is it possible for two types of formations—wholesome and unwholesome—to receive their retribution neither simultaneously nor sequentially?
Answer:
[The factors] that receive retribution are wholesome form, unwholesome mind and mental concomitants, and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Furthermore, wholesome mind and mental concomitants, and formations dissociated from mind; unwholesome form; and both wholesome and unwholesome—these two categories are concluded.
The same applies to those [defilements] abandoned through seeing the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

This concludes the second chapter, "On False Speech" (*mithyāvāk*), of the Abhidharma, consisting of two hundred and forty-five *śloka* in the Sanskrit original and five thousand one hundred words in the Qin translation.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra and Zhu Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty. Chapter Three:

The Section on the Categories of Harming Sentient Beings (Sattvavadha-varga), Part Three. Is it possible that one harms sentient beings yet does not exhaustively harm them? Or is it possible that one does not harm sentient beings yet exhaustively harms them?
Is it possible that while some sentient beings have been harmed and all have been harmed, other sentient beings have not been harmed and none have been harmed?
And if some sentient beings have not been harmed and none have been harmed, would one who acts in such a way necessarily be reborn in hell as a result of their retribution?
Is it possible that one performs unwholesome and painful actions that have not yet ripened, such that upon first receiving their retribution, his mind is necessarily defiled?
Furthermore, if one takes the life of a sentient being and subsequently does not receive the precepts, can it be said that he is pure among all sentient beings?
If one is pure among all sentient beings, has one received the precepts among all sentient beings?
Conversely, if one has received the precepts among all sentient beings, is one pure among all sentient beings?
If one is endowed with the body, does one possess bodily formations?
Conversely, if one possesses bodily formations, does one have a body?
If one is endowed with the body, does one possess verbal formations?
If one accomplishes verbal formations, does that person possess bodily [form]?
If one accomplishes bodily [form], does that person possess mental formations?
If one accomplishes mental formations, does that person possess bodily [form]?
If one is endowed with the body, does one possess bodily formations and verbal formations?
Conversely, if one possesses bodily and verbal formations, does one possess the body?
If one is endowed with the body, does one possess bodily formations and mental formations?
If one accomplishes bodily action and mental action, does that person possess a body?
If one accomplishes the body, does that person possess vocal action and mental action?
Furthermore, if one accomplishes vocal action and mental action, does that person possess a body?
If one is endowed with the body, does that person possess bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations?
Conversely, if one is endowed with bodily, verbal, and mental formations, does that person possess the body? [End of section on the body.]
If one accomplishes bodily formations, does one also have verbal formations?
If one accomplishes verbal formations, does one also have bodily formations? If one accomplishes bodily formations, does one also have mental formations?
If one accomplishes mental formations (*manas-karman*), does he possess bodily formations (*kāya-karman*)?
If one accomplishes bodily formations, does he possess vocal and mental formations?
If one accomplishes vocal and mental formations, does he possess bodily formations? [End of section on bodily formations.]
If one is accomplished in verbal formations, does one also possess mental formations?
Conversely, if one is accomplished in mental formations, does one also possess verbal formations?
If the craving for formations has not been exhausted, has the retribution for those formations also not been exhausted?
If the desire for retribution (*vipākakāma*) is not yet exhausted, is the desire for action (*kriyākāma*) also not yet exhausted?
If the desire for action is exhausted, is the desire for retribution also exhausted?
If the desire for retribution is exhausted, is the desire for action also exhausted?
If an action has a result, does that action necessarily have a retribution?
Conversely, if an action has a retribution, does that action necessarily have a result?
And if an action has no result, does that action necessarily have no retribution?
If an action is without retribution, is that action entirely without fruit?
If an action is unwholesome, is that action entirely inverted?
If an action is inverted, is that action entirely unwholesome?
If an action is not unwholesome, is that action necessarily non-perverted?
Conversely, if an action is non-perverted, is that action necessarily not unwholesome?
If one accomplishes unwholesome conduct, does one also accomplish conduct pertaining to the form and formless realms?
Conversely, if one accomplishes conduct pertaining to the form and formless realms, does one also accomplish unwholesome conduct?
If one accomplishes wholesome conduct of the desire realm, does that person accomplish wholesome conduct of the form and formless realms?
Conversely, if one accomplishes wholesome conduct of the form and formless realms, does that person accomplish wholesome conduct of the desire realm?
If one accomplishes the formations of the desire realm, does one also accomplish the formations of the form realm?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the formations of the form realm, does one also accomplish the formations of the desire realm?
If one accomplishes the formations of the desire realm, does one also accomplish the formations of the formless realm?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the formations of the formless realm, does one also accomplish the formations of the desire realm?
If one accomplishes the formations of the desire realm, does that person accomplish the formations of the form realm and the untainted (anāsrava) formations?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the formations of the form realm and the untainted formations, does that person accomplish the formations of the desire realm?
If one accomplishes the formations of the desire realm, does one also accomplish the formations of the formless realm and the untainted formations?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the formless realm and untainted formations, does one also accomplish the formations of the desire realm?
If one accomplishes the formations of the form realm, does one also accomplish the formations of the formless realm and the untainted formations?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the formations of the formless realm and the untainted formations, does one also accomplish the formations of the form realm?
If one accomplishes the formations of the formless realm, does one also accomplish the untainted (anāsrava) formations?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the untainted formations, does one also accomplish the formations of the formless realm?
If one accomplishes the formations of the desire realm, the formations of the form and formless realms, and untainted (anāsrava) formations, where will they be reborn after the end of their life?
I pray that you will fully expound the meaning of this chapter.
Is it possible that one harms sentient beings, yet the harming of sentient beings is not exhausted?
The answer is:
Yes; for example, when one cuts off the life of a sentient being, yet does not cease seeking through skillful means.
Is it possible that one does not harm sentient beings, yet the harming of sentient beings is completely exhausted?
The answer is:
Yes; for example, when one does not take the lives of sentient beings and employs skillful means to cease seeking [harm].
Is it the case that when one harms sentient beings, all sentient beings are harmed?
The answer is:
Yes; for example, when one takes the life of a sentient being, the means [of harm] cease seeking further victims.
Is there a case where a sentient being does not harm others, yet the harming of sentient beings is not exhausted?
Answer: Yes;
for example, when one does not take the lives of sentient beings, yet does not cease from seeking them through skillful means.
Is there one who does not harm sentient beings, yet because their harming of sentient beings is not exhausted, they will certainly be born in hell as a result of those various actions?
Answer: Yes;
for example, one who employs means to bring about the destruction of others without providing rescue, should their life end in the interim.
Is it possible that one performs unwholesome and painful actions that have not yet matured, such that upon first receiving the retribution for those actions, his mind is necessarily defiled?
Answer: Yes;
for example, when one performs an act of despair, he first receives the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in hell.
If one has harmed the lives of sentient beings and subsequently does not receive the precepts, can it be said that they are pure among all sentient beings?
The answer is:

Yes. For example, one who intended to harm sentient beings through skillful means but encountered the Dharma in the interim; or one who has attained the vision of the truths (satyadarśin) regarding all sentient beings.
"Is one purified among all sentient beings by receiving the precepts, or is one's past transformed by receiving the precepts?
The answer is:
"One may be pure among all sentient beings, yet not have received the precepts among all sentient beings. This statement is concise; the translator intended to demonstrate this point.
What is meant by "purifying among all sentient beings while not receiving the precepts among all sentient beings"?
The answer is:
as when one does not receive the precepts, yet encounters the Dharma in the interim; this is called purifying among all sentient beings while not receiving the precepts among all sentient beings.
What is meant by "receiving the precepts among all sentient beings, yet not being pure among all sentient beings"?
The answer is:
as when one receives the precepts and then transgresses them; this is called receiving the precepts among all sentient beings while not being pure among all sentient beings.
What is meant by purifying oneself among all sentient beings while receiving the precepts among all sentient beings?
The answer is:
as when one receives the precepts and does not transgress them; this is called purifying oneself among all sentient beings while receiving the precepts among all sentient beings.
Question: Why is it that among all sentient beings one purifies them, yet among those who are not all sentient beings one receives the precepts?
Answer: It is by excluding the aforementioned matters.
If one is endowed with the body, does that person possess bodily formations?
Answer: There are cases where one is endowed with the body but not with bodily formations.
What is meant by "possessing the body but not bodily formations"?
The answer is:

an ordinary person within the thickening membrane of the egg or dwelling in the mother’s womb; or one born in the desire realm who possesses neither deportment nor non-deportment, whose body lacks informative intimation (*vijñapti*), or if such intimation exists, it is immediately lost. This is called possessing the body but not bodily formations.
What is it to accomplish bodily formations but not the body?
The answer is:
when a person free from defilements is born into the formless realm, this is called accomplishing bodily formations but not the body.
What is the accomplishment of the body and bodily formations?
The answer is:

a person free from defilements who is in the womb, whether the egg-membrane has thickened or not; or one born in the desire realm, whether abiding in formal deportment or not abiding in formal deportment.

Neither being in a state of non-decorum nor not being in a state of decorum, having bodily intimation, or if such intimation exists and is not lost, or if one is born in the form realm—this is called being endowed with both body and bodily formations.
What is meant by not possessing the body and not possessing bodily formations?
The answer is:
ordinary persons born in the formless realm; this is called not possessing the body and not possessing bodily formations.
If one is endowed with the body, does that person possess verbal formations?
Answer: There are cases where one is endowed with the body but not with verbal formations.
What is meant by "accomplishing bodily action but not verbal action"? Answer:

It refers to an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) within the thickening membrane of an egg or dwelling in the mother’s womb; or one born in the desire realm who is neither in a state of decorum nor in a state of non-decorum, whose verbal informative intimation (vijñapti) is absent, or if such intimation exists, it has already been lost. This is called accomplishing bodily action but not verbal action.
How is it that one accomplishes verbal formations but not bodily ones? Answer:
When a stainless person is born in the formless realm, this is called accomplishing verbal formations but not bodily ones.
What is meant by "accomplishing bodily and vocal conduct"?
The answer is:

a person free from defilement who, while in the womb at the stage when the membranes have gradually thickened, is born in the desire realm—whether abiding in deportment, not abiding in deportment, or neither abiding nor not abiding in deportment—and possesses verbal instruction, or having possessed it does not lose it; or if born in the form realm. This is called accomplishing bodily and vocal conduct.
What is meant by not accomplishing the body but not the verbal formations?
The answer is:
ordinary persons born in the formless realm; this is called not accomplishing the body but not the verbal formations.
If one is endowed with the body, is one also endowed with mental formations?
Answer: It is so;
if one is endowed with the body, one is also endowed with mental formations.
Is there one who accomplishes mental formations but not bodily formations?
Answer: There is;
namely, those born in the formless realm.
If one is endowed with the body, does that person possess bodily and verbal formations?
The answer is:

there are cases where one is endowed with the body but not with bodily and verbal formations; or with bodily formations but not verbal formations; or with verbal formations but not bodily formations; or with both bodily and verbal formations.
What is meant by "possessing bodily action but not vocal or mental action"?
The answer is:

an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) dwelling within the thickening membrane of the egg or in the mother’s womb; or one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who is neither in a state of deportment (*airyāpathika*) nor in a state that is not deportment, and whose bodily and vocal actions are without informative intimation (*avijñapti*), or if such intimation existed, it has already been lost. This is called possessing bodily action but not vocal or mental action.
What is meant by one who accomplishes the body and bodily formations, but not vocal formations?
The answer is:

if one is born in the desire realm, neither in a state of deportment nor in a state that is not deportment, possesses bodily informative action (*vijñapti*) or, even if possessing it, does not lose it; yet lacks vocal informative action or, even if possessing it, loses it immediately—this is called accomplishing the body and bodily formations, but not vocal formations.
What is it to accomplish bodily and verbal formations but not bodily formations?
The answer is:

if one is born in the desire realm, neither abiding in deportment nor not abiding in deportment, such that there is verbal intimation—or if there was verbal intimation—it is not lost; whereas there is no bodily intimation—or if there was bodily intimation—it is immediately lost. This is called accomplishing bodily and verbal formations but not bodily formations.
What is it to be endowed with the body and the activities of body and speech?
The answer is:

a person free from defilements who is in the stage of the *kalala* or *arbuda* within the mother’s womb; or one born in the desire realm who abides in deportment, or does not abide in deportment, or abides neither in deportment nor in non-deportment, and whose bodily and verbal actions possess informative intimation (*vijñapti*), or if such intimation exists, it is not lost; or one born in the form realm. This is called being endowed with the body and the activities of body and speech.
If one accomplishes the conduct of body and speech, does that person accomplish the body?
Answer: Either they accomplish it, or they do not.
How is it accomplished?
The answer is:
that which was explained above is called accomplishment.
What is it that is not accomplished?
The answer is:
when a person free from defilements is born in the formless realm, this is called "not accomplished."
If one accomplishes the body, does that person accomplish bodily action and mental action? Answer:
There are cases where one accomplishes the body and mental action but not bodily action, as well as cases where one accomplishes both bodily and mental action.
What is it to be endowed with bodily and mental formations, but not with bodily formations?
The answer is:

an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) dwelling within the thickening membrane of the egg or in the mother’s womb; or one born in the desire realm who is neither in a state of decorum nor in a state of non-decorum, whose body lacks informative intimation (vijñapti), or if such intimation exists, it has already been lost. This is called being endowed with bodily and mental formations, but not with bodily formations.
What is it to be endowed with the body, bodily formations, and mental formations?
The answer is:

a person free from defilement who is in the womb during the stage when the egg-membrane has thickened; or one born in the desire realm who abides in deportment, or does not abide in deportment, or abides neither in deportment nor in non-deportment, such that they possess bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) or, if they have possessed it, do not lose it; or one born in the form realm—this is called being endowed with the body, bodily formations, and mental formations.
If one accomplishes bodily formations and mental formations, does that person accomplish the body?
The answer is:
they may accomplish it, or they may not.
How is it accomplished?
The answer is:
that which was explained above is called accomplishment.
What is meant by "not accomplishing"?
The answer is:
when a person free from defilements (*vimala*) is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called "not accomplishing."
If one accomplishes the body, does one also accomplish verbal and mental conduct? Answer:
One may accomplish the body and mental conduct but not verbal conduct, or one may accomplish both verbal and mental conduct.
What is it to accomplish bodily and mental formations, but not vocal formations?
The answer is:

an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) dwelling within the thickening membrane of the egg or in the mother’s womb; or one born in the desire realm who is neither in a state of formal deportment nor in a state of non-deportment, whose vocal intimation is absent, or if present, is immediately lost—this is called accomplishing bodily and mental formations, but not vocal formations.
What is it to accomplish bodily action, verbal action, and mental action?
The answer is:

a person free from defilement who is in the womb at the stage when the egg-membrane has thickened; or one born in the desire realm who abides in deportment, or does not abide in deportment, or abides in neither deportment nor non-deportment; and whose speech is instructive, or if there is instruction, it is not lost; or one born in the form realm—this is called accomplishing bodily action, verbal action, and mental action.
If one accomplishes the conduct of speech and mind, does one also accomplish that of the body?
Answer: One may accomplish it, or one may not.
How is it accomplished?
The answer is:
that which was explained above is called accomplishment.
What is meant by "not accomplishing"?
The answer is:
when a stainless person (*vimala*) is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called not accomplishing.
If one is endowed with the body, does that person possess bodily, vocal, and mental formations?
The answer is:

there are cases where one is endowed with the body and mental formations but not with bodily or vocal formations; cases where one is endowed with the body and mental formations but not with vocal formations; cases where one is endowed with vocal and mental formations but not with bodily formations; and cases where one is endowed with bodily, vocal, and mental formations.
What is it to accomplish bodily and mental formations, but not bodily and vocal formations?
The answer is:

an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) in the thickening stages of the egg-membrane or dwelling in the mother’s womb; or one born in the desire realm who is neither in a state of decorum nor in a state of non-decorum, whose body and speech lack informative intimation (vijñapti), or who, even if such intimation existed, has lost it. This is called accomplishing bodily and mental formations, but not bodily and vocal formations.
What is it to be endowed with the body and the bodily and mental activities, but not the vocal activity?
The answer is:

if one is born in the desire realm, neither abiding in the formal deportment nor not abiding in the formal deportment, such that there is bodily intimation (*vijñapti*)—or if there was bodily intimation—it is not lost; whereas there is no vocal intimation—or if there was vocal intimation—it is immediately lost. This is called being endowed with the body and the bodily and mental activities, but not the vocal activity.
What is it to accomplish bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, yet not accomplish bodily conduct?
The answer is:

if one is born in the desire realm, neither abiding in the *airyāpathika* (postures) nor in the *anairyāpathika* (non-postures), such that there is verbal informative action (*vijñapti*), or if having had such action, one does not lose it; whereas there is no bodily informative action, or if having had such action, one immediately loses it—this is called accomplishing bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, yet not accomplishing bodily conduct.
What is it to be endowed with the body and the activities of body, speech, and mind?
The answer is:

a person free from defilement who is in the womb at a stage where the egg-membrane is gradually thickening; or one born in the desire realm who abides in deportment, or does not abide in deportment, or neither abides nor does not abide in deportment, such that there is instruction regarding body and speech, or if there is instruction, it is not lost; or one born in the form realm—this is called being endowed with the body and the activities of body, speech, and mind.
If one accomplishes the conduct of body, speech, and mind, does that person accomplish the body?
Answer: Either they accomplish it or they do not.
How is it accomplished?
The answer is:
that which was explained above is called accomplishment.
What is it that is not accomplished?
The answer is:
when a stainless person (vimala-pudgala) is born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), this is called the non-accomplishment of the body. Thus ends [the section on] the body.
If one accomplishes bodily formations, does one also accomplish verbal formations?
Answer: There are cases where one accomplishes bodily formations but not verbal formations.
What is meant by "accomplishing bodily formations but not verbal formations"? Answer:

If one is born in the desire realm, neither abiding in deportment nor not abiding in deportment, possesses bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)—or even if such intimation was previously present—it is not lost; yet lacks verbal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*)—or even if such intimation was previously present—it is immediately lost. This is called accomplishing bodily formations but not verbal formations.
What is it to accomplish verbal formations but not bodily formations?
The answer is:

if one is born in the desire realm, neither in a state of deportment nor in a state of non-deportment, possesses verbal informative action (*vijñapti*)—or, if such action existed, does not lose it—and lacks bodily informative action—or, if such action existed, loses it immediately—this is called accomplishing verbal formations but not bodily formations.
What is meant by "accomplishing bodily and verbal conduct"? The answer is:

a person free from defilements (*anāsrava*) who is in the womb during the stage when the egg-membrane is thickening; or one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who abides in deportment, or does not abide in deportment, or abides neither in deportment nor in non-deportment, and whose bodily and verbal actions possess informative intimation (*vijñapti*), or even if they possess informative intimation, they do not lose it; or one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); or a person free from defilements born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This is called accomplishing bodily and verbal conduct.
What is meant by not accomplishing bodily and verbal conduct?
The answer is:

an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) dwelling in the mother’s womb during the stages when the egg-membrane is gradually thickening; or one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who is neither in a state of decorum (*airyāpathika*) nor in a state of non-decorum, whose bodily and verbal informative acts (*vijñapti*) are absent, or if present, are immediately lost; or an ordinary person born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). These are said to be those who do not accomplish bodily and verbal conduct.
If one accomplishes bodily formations, does one also accomplish mental formations?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes bodily formations, one accomplishes mental formations.
Is there one who accomplishes mental formations but does not accomplish bodily formations?
Answer: There is.

This refers to an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) dwelling within the thickening membrane of the egg or in the mother’s womb; or one born in the desire realm who is neither in a state of decorum nor in a state of non-decorum, whose body lacks informative intimation (vijñapti), or whose informative intimation, if present, has already been lost; or an ordinary person born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
If one accomplishes bodily action, does one also accomplish verbal and mental actions? Answer:
One may accomplish bodily and mental actions but not verbal action, or one may accomplish verbal and mental actions.
What is it to accomplish bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*) and mental formations (*manas-saṃskāra*), but not vocal formations (*vāk-saṃskāra*)?
The answer is:

if one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), neither in a state of formal deportment (*airyāpathika*) nor in a state that is not formal deportment, such that one possesses bodily informative action (*vijñapti*) or, having possessed it, does not lose it; yet one lacks vocal informative action or, having possessed it, loses it—this is called accomplishing bodily and mental formations, but not vocal formations.
What is meant by accomplishing bodily action as well as vocal and mental actions?
The answer is:

a person free from impurities who is in the thickening membrane of the egg or in the mother’s womb; or one born in the desire realm who abides in deportment, does not abide in deportment, or neither abides nor does not abide in deportment, such that they possess bodily and vocal informative acts (*vijñapti*), or even if possessing them, do not lose them; or one born in the form realm; or a person free from impurities born in the formless realm—this is called accomplishing bodily action as well as vocal and mental actions.
If one accomplishes the conduct of speech and mind, does that person accomplish the conduct of body?
Answer: Either they accomplish it, or they do not accomplish it.
How is it accomplished?
The answer is:
that which was explained above is called accomplishment.
What is meant by "not accomplishing"?
The answer is:

if one is born in the desire realm, neither abiding in the deportment nor not abiding in the deportment; if there is no bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), or if such intimation exists it is immediately lost; yet there is verbal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*), or if such intimation exists it is not lost—this is called "not accomplishing."
If one accomplishes verbal formations, does one also accomplish mental formations?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes verbal formations, one accomplishes mental formations.
Is there one who accomplishes mental formations but not verbal formations?
Answer: Yes.

This includes ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) dwelling within the thickening membrane of the egg or in the mother’s womb; or those born in the desire realm who are neither in a state of deportment nor in a state of non-deportment, whose verbal informative action (*vijñapti*) is absent, or whose verbal informative action, if present, has already been lost; as well as ordinary persons born in the formless realm.
If sexual misconduct has not been exhausted, is its retribution for sexual misconduct also not exhausted?
Answer: It is so;
if sexual misconduct has not been exhausted, its retribution for sexual misconduct is also not exhausted.
Is there a case where the retribution for sexual misconduct has not been exhausted, yet one is no longer engaged in such conduct?
The answer is:

Yes. For example, a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) who has exhausted the conduct of sexual misconduct abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), yet whose retribution for that sexual misconduct has not yet been exhausted.
If the conduct of lust is exhausted, is the retribution for lust also exhausted?
Answer: It is so;
if the retribution for lust is exhausted, then the conduct of lust is exhausted.
Is there any case where sexual misconduct has been completely exhausted, yet its retribution has not?
Answer: Yes.

For example, in the case of a Srotāpanna, sexual misconduct that was to be abandoned through the vision of the truths has been completely exhausted, yet the retribution for that sexual misconduct remains unexhausted.
If a formation has a fruit, does that formation necessarily have an exhausted retribution?
Answer: It is so;
if a formation has a retribution, this formation necessarily has an exhausted fruit.
Is there any action that has a fruit but no retribution?
Answer: Yes;
namely, indeterminate and untainted actions.
If an action is without fruit, is that action entirely without retribution?
Answer: There is no action that does not have a fruit.
Is there any action that is without retribution?
The answer is:
Yes, namely, indeterminate and untainted actions.
If one performs unwholesome actions, are all such actions inverted?
Answer: Some unwholesome actions are not inverted.
How is it that one who practices what is unwholesome does not practice with perversion?
The answer is:
suppose there is someone who perceives the fruit of their actions, and thus sees and speaks as follows:
There are actions and there are the fruits of action:
namely, bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.

It is just as if there were someone who does not see but has the perception of seeing; who does not hear, does not distinguish, and does not cognize, yet has the perception of cognizing. He does not, by virtue of that perception, that acceptance, that view, that desire, or that wisdom, claim: "I do not see, I do not hear, I do not distinguish, and I do not cognize."

It is as if there were someone who sees but has the perception of not seeing, or hears, distinguishes, and cognizes but has the perception of not hearing, distinguishing, or cognizing; he does not, by means of this perception, this acceptance, this view, this desire, or this wisdom, claim: "I see, hear, distinguish, and cognize."
This is called practicing what is unwholesome while that practice is not inverted.
What is practicing what is inverted while this practice is not unwholesome?
The answer is:
It is just as if there were someone who holds no views and has no realization of the fruits, yet speaks thus:
"There is no volitional action, nor is there any fruit of volitional action";
yet that person performs excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind.

It is as if there were someone who, though not seeing, has the perception of seeing; though not hearing, not distinguishing, and not cognizing, has the perception of cognizing; and by means of that perception, that acceptance, that view, that desire, and that wisdom, [claims]: "I see, hear, distinguish, and cognize."

It is as if there were someone who, having seen, perceives it as not seen; having heard, distinguished, or cognized, perceives it as not heard, distinguished, or cognized. By means of this perception, this acceptance, this view, this desire, and this wisdom, he thinks: "I have not seen, heard, distinguished, or cognized."
This is called practicing perversely while that practice is not unwholesome.
What is practicing unwholesomely while that practice is perverse? Answer:
It is just as if there were someone who holds the view that there is no seeing and no fruit of action, and who speaks thus:
"There is no volitional formation, nor is there any fruit of volitional formation";
yet such a person engages in misconduct of body, speech, and mind.

It is as if there were someone who does not see and has no perception of seeing, does not hear, does not distinguish, and does not cognize, yet has no perception of not cognizing; he does not, by means of that perception, that acceptance, that view, that desire, or that wisdom, claim: "I see, hear, distinguish, and cognize."

It is as if there were someone who sees and has the perception of seeing, hears, differentiates, and cognizes and has the perception of cognizing; yet, by means of that perception, that acceptance, that view, that desire, or that wisdom, he does not think: "I do not see, I do not hear, I do not differentiate, and I do not cognize."
This is called practicing what is unwholesome and practicing perversely.
What is practicing what is not unwholesome and practicing non-perversely? Answer:
It is just as if there were someone who perceives that there are fruits, and who thus perceives and thus speaks:
"There are volitional formations; there is the fruit and result of volitional formations;
there are bodily wholesome actions, and verbal and mental wholesome actions."

It is as if there were someone who does not see and has the perception of not seeing, does not hear, does not distinguish, and does not cognize and has the perception of not cognizing; by means of this perception, this acceptance, this view, this desire, and this wisdom, he thinks: "I do not see, I do not hear, I do not distinguish, and I do not cognize."

It is as if there were someone who, having seen, has the perception of having seen; having heard, distinguished, or cognized, has the perception of having heard, distinguished, or cognized. By means of this perception, this acceptance, this view, this desire, and this wisdom, he thinks: "I have seen, heard, distinguished, and cognized."
This is called practicing what is not unwholesome; this practice is not inverted.
It is likewise for what is not [unwholesome].
If one accomplishes unwholesome practice, does that person accomplish practice belonging to the form and formless realms?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes unwholesome conduct, one accomplishes the conduct of the form and formless realms.
Is it possible to accomplish the conduct of the form and formless realms without accomplishing unwholesome conduct?
Answer: Yes.
This applies to one who is born in the desire realm and has exhausted desire for it, or to one who is born in the form realm.
If one accomplishes wholesome conduct of the desire realm, does that person accomplish wholesome conduct of the form and formless realms?
Answer: One may accomplish wholesome karma of the desire realm but not wholesome karma of the form or formless realms.
How does one accomplish wholesome karma of the desire realm but not wholesome karma of the form or formless realms?
Answer:

If one is born in the desire realm and has not severed the roots of goodness, yet does not attain wholesome states of mind belonging to the form or formless realms, this is called "accomplishing wholesome conduct of the desire realm but not wholesome conduct of the form or formless realms."
What is it to accomplish wholesome conduct of the form and formless realms but not wholesome conduct of the desire realm?
The answer is:

if one is born in the form realm and attains a wholesome mind of the formless realm, this is called accomplishing wholesome conduct of the form and formless realms but not wholesome conduct of the desire realm.
How does one accomplish wholesome courses of action of the desire realm as well as wholesome courses of action of the form and formless realms?
The answer is:

if one is born in the desire realm and attains wholesome minds of the form and formless realms, this is called accomplishing wholesome courses of action of the desire realm as well as wholesome courses of action of the form and formless realms.
What is it to not accomplish wholesome conduct of the desire realm while not failing to accomplish wholesome conduct of the form and formless realms?
The answer is:
one whose roots of wholesomeness are severed; this is called not accomplishing wholesome conduct of the desire realm while not failing to accomplish wholesome conduct of the form and formless realms.
If one accomplishes the formations of the desire realm, does one also accomplish the formations of the form realm? Answer: Yes.
If one achieves the formations of the form realm, does one achieve the formations of the desire realm? Answer: Yes.
If one accomplishes the formations of the desire realm, does one accomplish the formations of the formless realm?
Answer: Yes;
if one accomplishes the formations of the desire realm, one accomplishes the formations of the formless realm.
Is it possible that one who possesses formations of the formless realm does not possess formations of the desire realm?
Answer: Yes;
for example, one who is born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes the formations of the desire realm, does one also accomplish the untainted (anāsrava) formations? Answer:
One may accomplish the formations of the desire realm without accomplishing the untainted formations.
What is it to accomplish activities of the desire realm but not untainted (anāsrava) activities?
The answer is:
if an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is born in the desire or form realms, this is called accomplishing activities of the desire realm but not untainted activities.
What is it to accomplish untainted (*anāsrava*) formations but not formations of the desire realm?
The answer is:
when a stainless person (*vimala-pudgala*) is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called accomplishing untainted formations but not formations of the desire realm.
How does one accomplish both the formations of the desire realm and the untainted (anāsrava) formations?
The answer is:
when a person free from defilement (vimala) is born in either the desire realm or the form realm, this is called accomplishing both the formations of the desire realm and the untainted formations.
What is meant by not accomplishing both the conditioned formations of the desire realm and the untainted formations?
The answer is:
when an ordinary person is born in the formless realm, this is called not accomplishing the conditioned formations of the desire realm and the untainted formations.
If one accomplishes the formations of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-saṃskāra*), does one also accomplish the formations of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-saṃskāra*)?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes the formations of the form realm, one accomplishes the formations of the formless realm.
Is there one who accomplishes the formations of the formless realm but does not accomplish the formations of the form realm?
Answer: Yes, one who is born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes the formations of the form realm, does one also accomplish the untainted (anāsrava) formations?
Answer: One may accomplish the formations of the form realm without accomplishing the untainted formations.
What is it to accomplish the formations of the form realm but not the untainted formations?
The answer is:
ordinary persons born in the desire realm or the form realm; this is called accomplishing the formations of the form realm but not the untainted formations.
What is it to accomplish untainted (*anāsrava*) formations but not form-realm (*rūpadhātu*) formations?
The answer is:
when one who is free from defilement (*vimala*) is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called accomplishing untainted formations but not form-realm formations.
How does one accomplish both the practices of the form realm and the untainted practices?
The answer is:
when a stainless person is born into the desire realm or the form realm, this is called accomplishing both the practices of the form realm and the untainted practices.
What is meant by not accomplishing both the form-realm practices and the untainted practices?
The answer is:
an ordinary person born in the formless realm; this is called not accomplishing the form-realm practices and the untainted practices.
If one accomplishes the formations of the formless realm, does one accomplish the untainted formations?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes the untainted formations, one accomplishes the formations of the formless realm.
Is there one who accomplishes the formations of the formless realm but not the untainted formations?
Answer: Yes, the ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
If one accomplishes formations of the desire realm, or formless and form realms, or untainted (anāsrava) formations, where will they be reborn after the end of this life?
Answer: Either in the desire realm, or the form realm, or the formless realm, or in no specific location.

The third chapter, "On the Harm to Sentient Beings" (*Sattvavadha-varga*), in the *Abhidharma* concludes here. The Sanskrit original consists of three hundred and nine *ślokas* and four thousand six hundred and thirty-one words.
