Composed by Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīr during the Fu Qin dynasty:
There are informative and non-informative [forms]; all conditioned phenomena are the fruits thereof.
Or there are those who are learners with outflows (*sāsrava-śaikṣa*); they contemplate the precepts last.
If one accomplishes bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does he also accomplish non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Conversely, if he accomplishes non-intimation, does he also accomplish intimation?
If one accomplishes wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, or non-obscured-unspecified bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does that person also accomplish the non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the non-intimation, does that person also accomplish the intimation?
If one accomplishes past bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does one also accomplish the non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Conversely, if one accomplishes the non-intimation, does one also accomplish the intimation?
If one accomplishes past wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, or unobscured-unspecified bodily intimations, does one also accomplish the non-intimation?
If one accomplishes non-informative matter (avijñapti), does one also accomplish informative matter (vijñapti)?
If one accomplishes future bodily informative matter, does one also accomplish non-informative matter?
If one accomplishes non-informative matter, does one also accomplish informative matter?
If one accomplishes future bodily intimation that is wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, or unobscured-unspecified, does that person also accomplish non-intimation?
Conversely, if one accomplishes non-intimation, does that person also accomplish bodily intimation?
If one accomplishes present bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does one also accomplish non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Conversely, if one accomplishes non-intimation, does one also accomplish intimation?
If one accomplishes present wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, or unobscured-unspecified bodily intimation, does one also accomplish non-intimation?
If one achieves non-informative action (avijñapti), does one also achieve informative action (vijñapti)?
The same applies to verbal informative action.
Regarding all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-vipāka), are those phenomena results bound to the desire realm?
If a formation produces a fruit bound to the desire realm, is that formation itself bound to the desire realm?
Regarding all formations bound to the form realm, do those formations produce a fruit bound to the form realm?
If a formation produces a fruit bound to the form realm, is that formation itself bound to the form realm?
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have results bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), are those phenomena themselves bound to the formless realm?
Conversely, if conditioned phenomena are bound to the formless realm, do they have results bound to the formless realm?
Are all untainted formations (anāsrava-saṃskāra) results of untainted formations?
Conversely, if a formation is a result of an untainted formation, is that formation itself untainted?
Are all formations that do not belong to the realm of desire (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) results of formations that do not belong to the realm of desire?
If a formation is not the fruit of the desire realm, is that formation not of the desire realm?
If formations are not of the form realm, are those formations not the fruit of the form realm?
If a formation is not the fruit of the form realm, is that formation not of the form realm?
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) do not belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), are those phenomena not the fruits of the formless realm?
Conversely, if conditioned phenomena are not the fruits of the formless realm, do those phenomena not belong to the formless realm?
If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not untainted (*anāsrava*), are those phenomena not the fruit of the untainted?
Conversely, if a phenomenon is not the fruit of the untainted, is that phenomenon not untainted?
Furthermore, can there be tainted phenomena with tainted fruits; tainted phenomena with untainted fruits; or tainted phenomena with both tainted and untainted fruits?

Is there an outflow-free action that has an outflow-free fruit? Is there an outflow-free action that has an outflow-possessing fruit? Is there an outflow-free action that has both outflow-possessing and outflow-free fruits?
Furthermore, is there an action—whether outflow-possessing or outflow-free—that has both outflow-possessing and outflow-free fruits?
Do contaminated and uncontaminated formations have contaminated fruits?
Do contaminated and uncontaminated formations have uncontaminated fruits?

Is it possible for training (śaikṣa) formations to have the fruit of training, for training formations to have the fruit of beyond-training (aśaikṣa), or for training formations to have the fruit of neither-training-nor-beyond-training?

Is there a case where a path of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-caryā) has a fruit of one beyond training? Is there a case where a path of one beyond training has a fruit of one in training (śaikṣa)? Is there a case where a path of one beyond training has a fruit that is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training?

Is there a case where a path that is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training has a fruit that is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training? Is there a case where a path that is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training has a fruit of one in training? Is there a case where a path that is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training has a fruit of one beyond training?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"One does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate ethical discipline, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom.
What is meant by not cultivating the body, not cultivating ethical discipline, not cultivating the mind, and not cultivating wisdom?
If one does not cultivate the body, does that person not cultivate morality, not cultivate the mind, and not cultivate wisdom?
Conversely, if one does not cultivate wisdom, does that person not cultivate the body?
If one does not cultivate morality, does that person not cultivate the mind and not cultivate wisdom?
If one does not cultivate wisdom, does one not cultivate ethical discipline?
If one does not cultivate the mind, does one not cultivate wisdom?
And if one does not cultivate wisdom, does one not cultivate the mind?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"Cultivate the body, cultivate morality, cultivate the mind, and cultivate wisdom.
What is meant by cultivating the body, cultivating morality, cultivating the mind, and cultivating wisdom?
If one cultivates the body, does one also cultivate morality, the mind, and wisdom?
Conversely, if one cultivates wisdom, does one also cultivate the body?
If one cultivates morality, does one also cultivate the mind and wisdom?
If one cultivates wisdom, does one cultivate ethical discipline?
If one cultivates the mind, does one cultivate wisdom?
If one cultivates wisdom, does one cultivate the mind?

Is it possible to accomplish past ethical discipline (*śīla*) without accomplishing this same kind in the future or present; or to accomplish it in the future without accomplishing it in the present; or to accomplish it in the present without accomplishing it in the future; or to accomplish it in both the future and the present?

Is there one who possesses future morality but not this kind of past or present; or one who possesses past but not present; or one who possesses present but not past; or one who possesses both past and present of this kind?

Is there one who accomplishes present morality, but not this kind of past or future; or one who accomplishes the past but not the future; or one who accomplishes the future but not the past; or one who accomplishes both the past and the future of this kind?
I wish to expound fully upon the meaning of this chapter.
If one accomplishes bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti*), does one also accomplish non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
The answer is:
There are cases where there is informative action (vijñapti) but no non-informative action (avijñapti). What is informative action that is not non-informative action?
The answer is:

One born in the desire realm who is neither in a state of formal restraint nor in a state of non-restraint may possess bodily informative action (*vijñapti*) but not obtain non-informative action (*avijñapti*); or, having previously possessed informative action which has not been lost, they do not obtain non-informative action. This is called "informative action but not non-informative action."
What is non-informative [action] that is not informative?
The answer is:

when a stainless person is in the mother’s womb during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana; or when one born in the desire realm abides in restraint but has not yet acquired the restraint of the precepts, such that the body lacks informative action, or having previously possessed informative action, it has been lost, and they thereby acquire non-informative action.
If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and lacks informative intimation (vijñapti),
or if an undefiled person (anāsrava-pudgala) is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), this is called non-informative intimation (avijñapti) that is not informative intimation.
What is informative intimation and non-informative intimation?
Answer:
One born in the desire realm who does not obtain the restraint of the precepts possesses informative action (*vijñapti*) of the body and obtains non-informative action (*avijñapti*);
or, having previously possessed informative action without losing it, one obtains non-informative action.

In the state of abiding by the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*), in the state of not abiding by the restraint of the precepts, and also in the state of neither restraint nor non-restraint, there is bodily informative action (*vijñapti*) and one acquires non-informative action (*avijñapti*); or, having previously possessed informative action without losing it, one acquires non-informative action;
or, if born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is bodily informative action—this is called informative and non-informative action.
What is non-informative action that is neither informative nor non-informative?
The answer is:

an ordinary person dwelling in the mother’s womb during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana; or one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state that is neither disciplined nor undisciplined, whose body lacks informative action, or whose previously existing informative action has been lost, yet who does not acquire non-informative action.
Ordinary persons born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are said to possess neither informative action (vijñapti) nor non-informative action (avijñapti).
If one accomplishes wholesome informative bodily action, does that person also accomplish non-informative action?
Answer: Sometimes there is informative action (vijñapti) that is not non-informative action (avijñapti).
What is informative action that is not non-informative action?
Answer:

One born in the desire realm in a state of non-restraint possesses informative bodily action (*vijñapti-kāya-karman*) but does not possess non-informative action (*avijñapti*); because they have not lost the original informative action, they do not possess non-informative action.
Likewise, one who is neither in a state of restraint nor in a state of non-restraint possesses informative bodily action but does not possess non-informative action.
When one possesses manifest action (vijñapti) but does not possess non-manifest action (avijñapti), this is called "manifest action but not non-manifest action.
What is "non-manifest action but not manifest action"? Answer:

When a person free from outflows (vimala) dwells in the mother’s womb or within the thickening layers of the egg-membrane; or when one born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) who abides in a state of restraint does not acquire the restraint of the precepts, such that they possess no informative bodily action (vijñapti-kāya-avijñapti), or have lost their original informative action and acquired non-informative action;
or when one born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) possesses no informative bodily action;
or when a person free from outflows is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)—this is called non-informative action (avijñapti) without informative action (vijñapti).
What is informative action and non-informative action?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm in a state where restraint is possible, yet who has not obtained the restraint of the precepts, possesses informative action of the body and obtains non-informative action therein.
If one does not lose the informative action (*vijñapti*) previously possessed and acquires its non-informative action (*avijñapti*);

or if, in the state of moral discipline (*saṃvara*), or in the state of non-discipline (*asaṃvara*), or in the state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, one possesses a wholesome bodily informative action and acquires its non-informative action;
or if, having been born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one possesses a wholesome bodily informative action—these are called informative and non-informative actions.
What is neither informative nor non-informative?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person is in the mother’s womb during the stages of the embryo and the thickening of the membranes; or when one is born in the desire realm in a state of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), such that they possess no informative bodily action, have lost any previously existing informative action, and do not acquire non-informative action.

In a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, there is no informative bodily action (*vijñapti*), and any previously existing informative action has been lost; furthermore, such a person does not acquire non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
This refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which is called "neither informative nor non-informative."
If one accomplishes unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), does one also accomplish the non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes the non-intimation, one also accomplishes the intimation.
Is there one who possesses informative action (vijñapti) but not non-informative action (avijñapti)?
Answer: Yes.

For example, one born in the desire realm in a state of restraint (saṃvara), who possesses unwholesome bodily informative action but does not acquire non-informative action; or one who previously possessed informative action and has not lost it, yet does not acquire non-informative action.

In the state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, there is unwholesome bodily informative intimation (*vijñapti*), yet one does not acquire non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*); because the previously existing informative intimation is not lost, one does not acquire non-informative intimation.
If one accomplishes the bodily intimation that is obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), does he also accomplish the non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There is no one who accomplishes the non-intimation.
Is there anyone who accomplishes bodily intimation?
Answer: There is;
namely, one born in the form realm who possesses obscured-unspecified bodily intimation.
If one accomplishes non-obscured neutral bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does that person accomplish the non-informative (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There is no such case where one accomplishes the non-informative.
Is there anyone who possesses informative action (*vijñapti*)?
Answer: Yes.

One born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) who possesses non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) bodily informative action. [The discussion on] informative action is concluded.
If one accomplishes past bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does that person also accomplish non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There are cases where there is intimation but not non-intimation.
What is meant by "informative action" (vijñapti) but not "non-informative action" (avijñapti)?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who abides in a state that is neither formal discipline nor non-discipline, and whose original informative action has not been lost but who does not possess non-informative action—this is called informative action but not non-informative action.
What is non-informative action (avijñapti) that is not informative action (vijñapti)?
The answer is:

when a stainless person (anāsrava-pudgala) is in the womb with the fetal membranes gradually thickening; or if one is born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) in a state of restraint (saṃvara) but does not obtain the restraint of the precepts (śīla-saṃvara), such that they possess no prior informative action and any existing informative action has been lost; or if one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) and possesses no prior informative action; or if one is a learner (śaikṣa) born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)—this is called non-informative action that is not informative action.
What is informative action (vijñapti) and non-informative action (avijñapti)?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm in a state of restraint who has not obtained the restraint of the precepts, yet possesses the original informative action without losing it—such a person obtains non-informative action.

In the case of the restraint of the precepts, the non-restraint, and the state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint, if one possesses the manifest action (*vijñapti*) of the body and does not lose it, one acquires the unmanifest action (*avijñapti*);
if one is born in the form realm and possesses the manifest action of the body without losing it, this is called both manifest and unmanifest action.
What is that which is neither informative nor non-informative?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person is in the mother’s womb during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana; or when one is born in the desire realm in a state where one has neither attained restraint (saṃvara) nor non-restraint (asaṃvara); or when one originally lacks informative action (vijñapti), or if such action was present, it has already been lost.
Arhats and ordinary persons born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are said to possess neither informative action (vijñapti) nor non-informative action (avijñapti).
If one accomplishes past wholesome bodily informative action, does that person also accomplish non-informative action?
Answer: Sometimes there is informative action (vijñapti) but no non-informative action (avijñapti).
What is informative action that is not non-informative action?
Answer:

One born in the Desire Realm in a state of non-restraint possesses the informative act (*vijñapti*) of an originally wholesome body without losing it, yet does not possess the non-informative act (*avijñapti*);

likewise, one in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint possesses the informative act of an originally wholesome body without losing it, yet does not possess the non-informative act—this is called "informative act but not non-informative act."
What is non-informative (avijñapti) that is not informative (vijñapti)?
The answer is:

for a stainless person (vimala-pudgala) dwelling in the mother’s womb or within the successive layers of the egg-membrane; or, if born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), residing in a state of restraint (saṃvara-stha) yet not having obtained the restraint of the precepts (śīla-saṃvara); or when there is no original informative action of the body, or if such informative action has been lost.
If one is born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one's original wholesome bodily non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is absent;
if one is born in the realm of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called non-informative action that is not informative action (*vijñapti*).
What is informative action and non-informative action?
Answer:

One born in the desire realm who dwells in a state of restraint does not obtain the restraint of the precepts; yet, if their original wholesome bodily informative action (*vijñapti*) is not lost, they obtain its non-informative action (*avijñapti*).

One who dwells in a state of restraint, a state of non-restraint, or a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint, if their original wholesome bodily informative action is not lost, they obtain its non-informative action.

If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) and has not lost the informative intimation (vijñapti) of the original wholesome bodily action, this is called "informative intimation and non-informative intimation" (vijñapti-avijñapti).
What is "neither informative intimation nor non-informative intimation"? Answer:

When ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are in the mother’s womb or within the thickening layers of the egg-membrane; or when they are born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in a state of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), such that their wholesome bodily action originally lacks informative intimation (*vijñapti*) or, if it had informative intimation, it has not been lost;

or when they are in a state of neither restraint nor non-restraint, such that their original wholesome bodily action lacks informative intimation or, if it had informative intimation, it has been lost;
or when Arhats and ordinary persons are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): these are called those who possess neither informative intimation nor non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*).
If one accomplishes past unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does he also accomplish the non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: It is so;
if he accomplishes the non-intimation, he also accomplishes the intimation.
Is there one who possesses informative action (*vijñapti*) but not non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: Yes.

For example, one born in the desire realm in a state where restraint (*saṃvara*) is possible, who has not lost the original unwholesome bodily informative action but has not yet acquired non-informative action.

In the state of being neither-disciplined-nor-undisciplined, one possesses the manifest action (*vijñapti*) of an originally unwholesome body which is not lost, yet one does not possess its non-manifest action (*avijñapti*).
If one accomplishes past manifest bodily action that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) or unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), does one also accomplish its non-manifest action?
Answer: There is no one who has accomplished the past informative act (*vijñapti*) without having accomplished the non-informative act (*avijñapti*).
If one accomplishes the future bodily informative act, does he also accomplish the non-informative act?
Answer: There is no one who accomplishes informative action (vijñapti).
Is there anyone who accomplishes non-informative action (avijñapti)?
Answer: There are.

For example, when an undefiled person (*vimala*) is in the mother’s womb within the stages of the embryo and the thickening membranes; or when one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) attains a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); or when an undefiled person born in the form realm is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If one accomplishes the future wholesome bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does that person also accomplish the non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There is no such accomplishment of the intimation.
Is there anyone who possesses non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)?
The answer is: Yes.

There are those who are undefiled (*anāsrava*) while remaining within the womb as the fetal membranes gradually thicken; those born in the desire realm who attain a wholesome mind of the form realm and thus produce a form-realm [non-informative matter]; and undefiled persons born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes future unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, or unobscured-unspecified bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does that person accomplish non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There is no case where one accomplishes intimation but not non-intimation, [this applies] up to the end of the future.
If one accomplishes present bodily informative action (*vijñapti-karman*), does one also accomplish the non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There are cases where there is informative action but no non-informative action.
What is meant by "having informative action but not non-informative action"?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm in a place where restraint is possible, yet does not obtain the restraint of the precepts; such a person possesses informative action of the body but does not obtain non-informative action; or, having previously possessed informative action which has not been lost, they do not obtain non-informative action.

In a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, one possesses bodily informative action (*vijñapti*) but does not possess non-informative action (*avijñapti*); or, having previously possessed informative action which has not been lost, one does not possess non-informative action;
or, if born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one possesses bodily informative action—this is called informative action without non-informative action.
What is non-informative matter (avijñapti) that is not informative matter (vijñapti)?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who abides in the restraint of the precepts (śīla-saṃvara), yet has not acquired the restraint; whether entering meditative concentration or not, their body possesses no informative matter, and they have lost the informative matter previously possessed, thereby acquiring non-informative matter.

In the case of the precepts, the non-precepts, and that which is neither precept nor non-precept, there is no manifest action (*vijñapti*) of the body; or, having previously possessed manifest action, it is lost, and one acquires non-manifest action (*avijñapti*);
or, if one is born in the form realm and enters meditative concentration—this is called non-manifest action without manifest action.
What is informative action (vijñapti) and non-informative action (avijñapti)?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state of discipline but has not obtained the formal precepts possesses informative action of the body and obtains non-informative action; or, having previously possessed informative action without losing it, one obtains non-informative action.

In the sphere of the precepts, as well as in the spheres of neither-discipline-nor-non-discipline, when there is bodily intimation (*vijñapti*) and one acquires non-intimation (*avijñapti*), and when there is original intimation that is not lost and one acquires non-intimation—this is called "intimation and non-intimation."
What is neither informative nor non-informative?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person is in the mother’s womb within the stages of the ovum and the thickening membrane; or when born in the desire realm, abiding in a state of non-restraint, not having obtained the restraint of the precepts, and not having entered meditative concentration—such that the body possesses no informative action, any previously existing informative action has been lost, and they have not acquired non-informative action.

In the state of being neither disciplined nor undisciplined, there is no bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*); if one previously possessed bodily intimation but has lost it, one does not acquire non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
Furthermore, if one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) without having entered meditative concentration, there is no bodily intimation;
and if one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called "neither intimation nor non-intimation."
If one accomplishes the present bodily informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of a wholesome nature, does that person also accomplish the non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There are cases where one accomplishes the informative intimation but not the non-informative intimation.
What is meant by "informative action exists, but non-informative action does not"?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who abides in the discipline but has not obtained the precepts; such a person possesses informative action of the wholesome body but does not possess non-informative action; or, having previously possessed informative action which has not been lost, they do not possess non-informative action.

In a state that is neither unwholesome nor non-unwholesome, there is wholesome bodily informative action (*vijñapti*) but no non-informative action (*avijñapti*); or, having previously possessed informative action which has not been lost, one does not possess non-informative action;
or, if born in the form realm, there is wholesome bodily informative action—this is called informative action without non-informative action.
What is non-informative action that is not informative action?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who abides in the state of restraint but has not obtained the precepts, whether entering or not entering meditative concentration, possesses a wholesome bodily non-informative action; or, having possessed informative action previously, it is lost, and they obtain non-informative action.

In the case of the precepts, the non-precepts, and that which is neither precept nor non-precept, when there is no manifest bodily action (*vijñapti*) of the wholesome, or when an original manifest action has been lost and one acquires its non-manifest counterpart (*avijñapti*),
or when one is born in the form realm and enters meditative concentration— this is called non-manifest action that is not manifest action.
What is informative action (vijñapti) and non-informative action (avijñapti)?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who abides in the discipline but has not obtained the formal precepts possesses informative action of a wholesome body and obtains non-informative action; or, having previously possessed informative action without losing it, one obtains non-informative action.

In the sphere of morality, in the sphere of immorality, and in the sphere that is neither moral nor immoral, when there is a wholesome bodily informative act (*vijñapti*) and one acquires its non-informative counterpart (*avijñapti*), or when there is an original informative act that is not lost and one acquires its non-informative counterpart—this is called informative and non-informative action.
What is non-informative action that is neither informative nor non-informative?
The answer is:

one who is dwelling in the mother’s womb or within the successive layers of the fetal membrane; or one born in the desire realm who abides in the discipline but has not yet obtained the precepts and does not enter meditative concentration; such a person possesses no informative action of the body, and having lost any previously existing informative action, they do not possess non-informative action.

In states that are neither unwholesome nor wholesome, when there is no manifest bodily action, or when a previously existing manifest action has been lost and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is not acquired;
or when one is born in the form realm and does not enter meditative concentration, such that there is no manifest bodily action;
or when one is born in the formless realm—these are called "neither manifest nor non-manifest."
If one accomplishes present unwholesome bodily intimation (*vijñapti*), does that person also accomplish non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There are cases where there is intimation but not non-intimation.
What is the case where there is informative action (*vijñapti*) but no non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in a state of moral discipline (*śīla*), who possesses unwholesome bodily informative action but does not possess non-informative action; or one who, having previously possessed informative action, has not lost it, yet does not possess non-informative action.

In a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, there is an unwholesome bodily intimation (*vijñapti*), yet one does not obtain the non-intimation (*avijñapti*); or, having previously possessed an intimation that has not been lost, one does not obtain the non-intimation—this is called "intimation, but not non-intimation."
What is non-informative action that is not informative action?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who abides in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*) possesses non-informative action; this occurs when there is no unwholesome bodily informative action, or when previously existing informative action has been lost, and one thereby acquires that non-informative action.

In a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, when there is no unwholesome bodily informative intimation (*vijñapti*), or when an original informative intimation has been lost, and one acquires non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*), this is called "non-informative intimation without informative intimation."
What is informative and non-informative action?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who abides in the discipline possesses informative bodily action and acquires its non-informative counterpart; having previously possessed informative action, they do not lose it and thus acquire its non-informative counterpart.

In a state that is neither formal discipline nor non-discipline, when there is an unwholesome bodily informative act (*vijñapti*) by which one acquires its non-informative counterpart (*avijñapti*), or when there is a previously existing informative act that is not lost by which one acquires its non-informative counterpart—this is called informative and non-informative action.
What is the case of neither informative nor non-informative action?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person is in the mother’s womb during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana; or when one is born in the desire realm and abides in a state of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), such that there is no unwholesome bodily informative action, and any previously existing informative action has been lost, and one does not acquire non-informative action.

In the state of being neither disciplined nor undisciplined, there is no unwholesome bodily informative intimation (*vijñapti*), and any previously existing informative intimation has been lost, such that one does not possess non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*);
or, if one is born in the form or formless realms—this is called "neither informative nor non-informative."
If one accomplishes a present bodily intimation that is obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), does he also accomplish the non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There is no one who accomplishes the non-intimation.
Is there anyone who possesses informative action (*vijñapti*)?
The answer is:
Yes; there is one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) who possesses obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) bodily informative action.
If one accomplishes present non-obscured neutral bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does that person accomplish the non-informative (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There is no such accomplishment of the non-informative.
Is there anyone who accomplishes informative action?
Answer: There is.
One born in the desire realm, or one born in the form realm whose non-obscured neutral bodily informative action is currently present at the end [of its duration].
The same applies to oral instruction.
Regarding those formations that belong to the desire realm, do those formations have results that belong to the desire realm?
Answer: Yes.
Thus, those formations that belong to the desire realm have their fruit in the desire realm.
Is it possible for there to be formations whose fruit is in the desire realm, yet those formations themselves do not belong to the desire realm?
The answer is: Yes.
There is; for example, when one on a path belonging to the form realm manifests a transformation in the desire realm and utters speech of the desire realm.
If various formations belong to the form realm, do those formations have results that belong to the form realm?
Answer: Yes.
In this way, those formations that have the form realm as their fruit are formations of the form realm.
Is it possible for there to be formations of the form realm that do not have the form realm as their fruit?
The answer is: Yes.

Yes. For example, when a path belonging to the form realm produces a transformation-body in the desire realm and causes it to speak the language of the desire realm, or when a path belonging to the form realm severs fetters and attains realization.
Regarding those formations that belong to the formless realm, do those formations have results that belong to the formless realm?
Answer: It is so:
if those formations have a fruit in the formless realm, do those formations belong to the formless realm?
Is there any formation that belongs to the formless realm, yet whose fruit does not belong to the formless realm?
Answer: There is;
for example, when one abandons fetters through the path of the formless realm and attains realization.
Are all those formations that are outflow-free (anāsrava) necessarily formations that have an outflow-free fruit?
Answer: It is so;
those formations that are untainted have untainted fruits.
Is it possible for there to be formations that have untainted fruits, yet those formations themselves are not untainted?
Answer: There are.
For example, the paths of the form and formless realms sever the fetters and lead to realization.
Are all formations that do not belong to the desire realm necessarily not the fruits of the desire realm?
Answer: It is so;
those formations that are not the fruit of the desire realm are themselves not of the desire realm.
Is there any formation that is not of the desire realm, yet is not itself the non-fruit of the desire realm?
Answer: Yes.
For example, when one on a path belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) manifests a transformation (*nirmāṇa*) in the desire realm and produces speech of the desire realm.
Are those formations (*saṃskāra*) not of the form realm, and are those formations not the fruit of the form realm?
Answer: It is so;
those formations that do not belong to the form realm are not the fruit of the form realm.
Is it possible that there are formations which are not the fruit of the form realm, yet those formations are not non-form-realm?
Answer: There is.

For example, as one on the path of the form realm manifests a transformation in the desire realm and produces speech of the desire realm; likewise, as one on the path of the form realm severs the fetters and proceeds toward realization.
If various formations do not belong to the formless realm, do those formations not have the formless realm as their fruit?
Answer: It is so;
if various formations do not belong to the formless realm, those formations do not have the formless realm as their fruit.
Is there an action that does not have the formless realm as its fruit, yet that action is not such that it does not belong to the formless realm?
Answer: Yes;
for example, when one severs the fetters through the path of the formless realm and attains realization.
If various formations (*saṃskāra*) are not untainted (*anāsrava*), are those formations not the fruit of the untainted?
Answer: It is so;
if various formations are not the fruit of the untainted, those formations are not untainted.
Is there a case where an action is not untainted (anāsrava), yet that action does not have an untainted fruit?
Answer: Yes;
for example, when one attains the realization of the path that severs the fetters belonging to the realm of form and the formless realm.
Is there any contaminated action that has a contaminated fruit?
The answer is:
Yes; namely, the fruit of dependence (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).
Is there a case where a contaminated action has an uncontaminated fruit? Answer:
Yes, namely, the fruit of liberation.
Is there a case where a contaminated action has both a contaminated and an uncontaminated fruit?
Answer: Yes;
namely, the fruit of reliance (*niṣyanda-phala*), the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*), and the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*). This concludes the section on contaminated [actions].
Is there any untainted action that has an untainted fruit?
Answer: Yes;
namely, the fruit of support and the fruit of liberation.
Is there any untainted action that has a tainted fruit? Answer: No.
Is there any untainted action that has both tainted and untainted results? Answer: No.
Is there any contaminated action that has both contaminated and uncontaminated results? Answer: No.
Is there any case where tainted and untainted formations have a tainted fruit? Answer: No.
Is there any contaminated or uncontaminated action that has an uncontaminated fruit?
Answer: Yes;
the fruit of liberation is both contaminated and uncontaminated.
Is there perhaps a fruit of training for one who trains?
He replied:
Yes, there is; it is the fruit of the basis.
Is there a fruit of the learner (śaikṣa) or the non-learner (aśaikṣa)? Answer:
Yes, namely, the fruit of the basis (āśrayaphala).
Is there perhaps a fruit that belongs neither to the learner (*śaikṣa*) nor to the one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*)?
Answer: Yes, there is;
it is the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*) at the conclusion of the training (*śaikṣa*).
Is there an action of one beyond training that has a fruit of one beyond training?
Answer: Yes, namely, the fruit of its basis (*āśrayaphala*).
Is there any practice of one beyond training that constitutes the fruit of training? Answer: No.
Is there perhaps an action of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) that has neither-training-nor-beyond-training as its fruit?
Answer: Yes;
it is the fruit of liberation at the conclusion of the stage of one beyond training.
Is there that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner action with a result that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: Yes;
namely, the fruit of support, the fruit of retribution, and the fruit of liberation.
Is there any conduct that is neither of the learner nor of the non-learner which constitutes the fruit of the learner? Answer: No.
Is there any conduct that is neither of the learner nor of the non-learner, yet has the fruit of the non-learner? Answer: No.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"One does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate precepts, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom.
What is meant by "not cultivating the body"?
Answer:
It is because bodily desire is not yet exhausted, greed is not yet exhausted, mindfulness is not yet exhausted, and thirst is not yet exhausted.
Furthermore, although one has exhausted craving for form by means of the path of non-obstruction, one has neither cultivated nor relied upon that path.
Thus one does not cultivate the body; the same applies to not cultivating ethical discipline.
What is meant by "not cultivating the mind"?
The answer is:
The desire of the mind is not yet exhausted, greed is not yet exhausted, craving is not yet exhausted, and thirst is not yet exhausted.
Furthermore, by means of the path of non-obstruction, one exhausts the attachment to the formless realm, yet that path is neither cultivated nor relied upon.
If one does not cultivate the mind, it is the same for not cultivating wisdom.
If one does not cultivate the body, does that person not cultivate precepts? Answer:
It is so. If one does not cultivate morality, does that person not cultivate the body?
Answer: Yes.
Thus it is.
If one does not cultivate the body, does one also not cultivate the mind?
The answer is:
Thus, if one does not cultivate the body, one does not cultivate the mind.
Is it possible that one does not cultivate the mind but does not fail to cultivate the body?
Answer: Yes.
There is [the case where] craving for form is exhausted, but craving for what is above it is not yet exhausted.
If one does not cultivate the body, does one also not cultivate wisdom?
Answer: Yes.
Thus, if one does not cultivate the body, one does not cultivate wisdom.
Is it possible that one does not cultivate wisdom but does not fail to cultivate the body?
The answer is: Yes.
There is [a case where] craving for form has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
If one does not cultivate virtue (*śīla*), does one also not cultivate the mind (*citta*)?
The answer is: Yes.
Thus, if one does not cultivate morality, one does not cultivate the mind.
Is it possible that one does not cultivate the mind but does not fail to cultivate morality?
The answer is: Yes.
There is [one for whom] craving for form is exhausted, but craving for what is above it is not yet exhausted.
If one does not cultivate morality, does that person not cultivate wisdom?
Answer: Yes.
In this way, if one does not cultivate ethical discipline (*śīla*), one does not cultivate wisdom (*prajñā*).
Is it possible that one does not cultivate wisdom but does not fail to cultivate ethical discipline?
Answer: Yes.
There is [the case where] craving for form has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
If one does not cultivate the mind, does one also not cultivate wisdom?
Answer: Yes.
It is so. If one does not cultivate wisdom, does that person not cultivate the mind?
He replied:
Thus it is.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"Cultivate the body, cultivate ethical discipline, cultivate the mind, and cultivate wisdom."
What is the cultivation of the body?
The answer is:
the exhaustion of attachment to the body, the exhaustion of craving for the body, the exhaustion of mindfulness [of the body], and the exhaustion of thirst for the body.
Furthermore, by means of the path of non-obstruction, one exhausts craving for form; that path is cultivated with tranquility.
Thus one cultivates the body; precepts are likewise cultivated.
How does one cultivate the mind?
The answer is:
the exhaustion of mental affection, the exhaustion of craving, the exhaustion of longing, and the exhaustion of thirst.
Furthermore, by means of the path of non-obstruction, one exhausts attachment to the formless realm; that path is cultivated with tranquility.
The cultivation of the mind is thus; the cultivation of wisdom is likewise.
If one cultivates the body, does one also cultivate the precepts?
The answer is:
Thus it is.
If one cultivates morality, does one also cultivate the body?
The answer is:
It is so. If one cultivates the body, does one cultivate the mind?
Answer: Yes.
It is so. If one cultivates the mind, does one cultivate the body?
Is it possible to cultivate the body without cultivating the mind?
Answer: There is.
For one who has exhausted craving for form but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher [realms], if they cultivate the body, do they also cultivate wisdom?
Answer: It is so.
If one cultivates wisdom, does one also cultivate the body?
Is there one who cultivates the body but does not cultivate wisdom?
Answer: There is;
for example, one who has exhausted craving for the realm of form but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms.
If one cultivates ethical discipline, does one also cultivate the mind?
Answer: It is so.
If one cultivates the mind, does one cultivate the precepts?
Is it possible to cultivate the precepts without cultivating the mind? Answer:
There is [a case where] craving for form is exhausted, but craving for what is above it is not yet exhausted.
If one cultivates ethical discipline (*śīla*), does that person cultivate wisdom (*prajñā*)?
Answer: Yes.
Thus it is.
If one cultivates wisdom, one cultivates ethical discipline; however, is there a case where one cultivates ethical discipline but does not cultivate wisdom?
The answer is: Yes.
There is [a case where] craving for form is exhausted, but craving for what is above it is not yet exhausted.
If one cultivates the mind, does one cultivate wisdom?
Answer: Yes.
Thus it is.
If one cultivates wisdom, does one also cultivate the mind?
He replied:
Thus it is.
Is it possible to possess past ethical discipline (*śīla*) without possessing this same kind in the future or the present?
The answer is: Yes.
Is there a case where the precepts have been received and are not lost, yet this seed does not manifest?
And is it the case that this seed exists in the future but is not present here?
The answer is: Yes.

There are cases where the precepts associated with the Path (*mārga-samprayukta-śīla*) and the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samprayukta-śīla*) have been exhausted but are not lost, yet this seed does not manifest before one.
Is it also the case that this seed is present but not future?
The answer is: Yes.
If there is a case where the precepts have been fully received and not lost, and this seed manifests in the present, does that seed also manifest in the future?
The answer is: Yes.

There are cases where the precepts associated with the Path (*mārga-sahagata*) and those associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahagata*) have been exhausted but are not yet lost; such seeds have manifested in the present and have passed away.
Is it possible to possess future precepts without possessing them in the past or the present, such that these seeds [do not exist] in those times?
Answer: Yes, there are Arhats born in the formless realm;
and are these past, rather than present?
Answer: Yes.

When the precepts associated with the Path (*mārga-samprayukta-śīla*) and the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samprayukta-śīla*) have ceased but are not lost, these seeds do not manifest before one.
And is it the case that this seed is present rather than past?
Answer: Yes, there is.
Is it that one first attains the untainted discipline (*anāsrava-śīla*) in the past, present, or this [present] life?
Answer: Yes.

There are cases where the precepts associated with the Path (*mārga-samprayukta-śīla*) and the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samprayukta-śīla*) have been exhausted but are not lost;
these seeds are present and extend into the future. Is it possible to possess present precepts without possessing those seeds of the past or future?
Answer: Yes, there is.
It refers to the initial acquisition of the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Is this type [of restraint] past rather than future?
Answer: Yes.
When the teachings and precepts are fully maintained without loss, this seed manifests in the present;
and does this seed also exist in the future, but not in the past?
Answer: Yes, there is.
It is the initial attainment of the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara).
Does this also apply to past and future instances of this kind?
Answer: Yes.

The precepts associated with the Path (*mārga-samprayukta-śīla*) and the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samprayukta-śīla*), having been exhausted, are not lost; rather, this seed manifests in the present.

This concludes the fourth chapter on the "Exposition of the Taught and the Unmanifest" (*savijñapti-avijñapti-varga*) in the *Abhidharma*. It consists of three hundred and seventy-three *śloka*s in the Sanskrit original, and four thousand nine hundred and fifty-four words in the Qin translation.
5. The Fifth Chapter on Self-Practice from the Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda: What is self-practice?
For what reason is there self-practice?
Regarding those actions that one performs by oneself, should those actions be said to belong to the past, the future, or the present?
Regarding those actions that one performs by oneself, are those actions accomplished?
If a practice is accomplished, is that practice self-practice?
Is it the case that what can be practiced is not self-practice, and thus that practice is not accomplished?
If a practice is not accomplished, is that practice not self-practice?
If an action is performed by oneself, must that action necessarily result in retribution?
Conversely, if an action necessarily results in retribution, is that action performed by oneself?
If an action is not performed by oneself, does that action necessarily not result in retribution?
If an action will certainly not result in retribution, is that action not one performed by oneself?
If an action is accomplished through its application, will that action necessarily result in retribution?
If an action will necessarily result in retribution, is that action accomplished?
If an action that ought to be performed is not accomplished, will that action necessarily not receive its retribution?
Conversely, if an action necessarily does not receive its retribution, is that action not accomplished?
For example, when a *srotāpanna* has unwholesome actions whose painful retribution has not yet matured, by what means do they obstruct the paths of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:

"This is called a disciple of the World-Honored One who has exhausted the realms of hell, exhausted the realm of animals, and exhausted the realm of hungry ghosts, and does not fall into the evil destinies.

Does a stream-enterer possess this knowledge—namely, the realization: "I have exhausted hell, exhausted the animal realm, and exhausted the hungry ghost realm; I shall never again fall into the evil destinies"—or does he not realize this for himself?
What is the training in harmful intent?
Is all training the fruit of harmful intent?
What is the maintenance of the life-force, and what is the relinquishing of the life-force?
What is mental distraction?
By association with which fetters (*paryavasthāna*) are dharmas entirely unwholesome?
What is the Buddha’s word? And what constitutes the Buddha’s word?
Should these be called wholesome or indeterminate?
What kind of dharma is the word of the Buddha?
What dharmas are termed sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhutadharma, and upadeśa?
What dharma is called "seal" (mudrā)?
What dharma is called "number" (saṃkhyā)?
What dharma is called "calculation" (gaṇanā)?
What kind of phenomena are called "books"?
What kind of phenomena are called "verses"?
And what kind of phenomena are called "various arts and crafts"?
If one is accomplished in the training of the precepts, is that person accomplished in the precepts that are neither of the trainee nor of the non-trainee?
Conversely, if one is accomplished in the precepts that are neither of the trainee nor of the non-trainee, is that person accomplished in the training of the precepts?
If one possesses the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), does that person possess the precepts that are neither of one in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa)?
Conversely, if one possesses the precepts that are neither of one in training nor beyond training, does that person possess the precepts of one beyond training?
I wish to expound fully upon the meaning of this chapter.
What is "one's own practice"?
The answer is:

If the retribution of an action is received in this very life, it is called "attainment in the present. When there is an action here that gives rise to the experience of its retribution there, this is called "action performed by oneself.
By what kind of action performed by oneself?
The answer is:
This action is its own fruit, its own support, and its own retribution;
furthermore, when this action undergoes retribution, it is this very mind that receives it and no other. For this reason, one performs the action oneself.
Regarding the practice that one employs for one's own cultivation, should this practice be said to belong to the past, the future, or the present?
The answer is:
that practice belongs to the past.
If one practices a practice that is to be practiced by oneself, is that practice accomplished?
Answer: There are cases where one practices a practice that is to be practiced by oneself, yet this practice is not accomplished.
What is meant by "a karma is performed, yet that karma is not accomplished"?
The answer is:

when the retribution for a performed action is obtained in the present, and while that action is still producing its retribution, it ceases—that is called "a karma is performed, yet that karma is not accomplished."
What is meant by "the karma is accomplished, yet this karma is not one's own action"?
The answer is:

when the retribution for an action is not obtained in the present life, such that this action does not receive its retribution upon arising while that [corresponding] action is not lost—this is called "the karma is accomplished, yet this karma is not one's own action."
What is meant by "performing an action oneself and that action being accomplished"?
The answer is:

when the retribution for an action is obtained in the present, and that action produces its retribution such that it is not lost—this is called performing an action oneself and that action being accomplished.
What is meant by "a formation is not one's own formation and that formation is not accomplished"?
The answer is:

when the retribution of a formation is not obtained in the present, and that formation arises without receiving its retribution or is lost, this is called "a formation is not one's own formation and that formation is not accomplished."
It is likewise for that which is not [wholesome].
If one performs an action by means of a particular conduct, will that conduct necessarily result in retribution?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there are actions performed by oneself that will certainly not yield retribution.
What are these actions performed by oneself that will certainly not yield retribution?
The answer is:

Karma has its retribution obtained in this very life; that karma produces a retribution in the present life, and that karma produces a retribution in a future life—this is called "karma of one's own making. Furthermore, there is karma whose retribution is necessarily not experienced.
What is meant by "there is karma that will inevitably be experienced as retribution, yet that karma is not currently being performed"? Answer:

It refers to karma whose retribution is not to be obtained in the present life; that karma has arisen but its retribution is not yet being experienced because its maturation has not yet ripened. This is called "there is karma that will inevitably be experienced as retribution, yet that karma is not currently being performed."
What is meant by "performing an action that is self-performing, and for which that action will necessarily receive its retribution"?
The answer is:

when the retribution for an action is obtained in the present life—that is, the action arises and receives its retribution, and that action does not have retribution in a future life—this is called performing an action that is self-performing, and for which that action will necessarily receive its retribution.
What is meant by "there is karma that is not self-performed, yet that karma will certainly not receive its retribution"?
The answer is:

there is karma whose retribution is not obtained in the present; that karma arises without receiving retribution while its retribution matures. This is called "karma that is not self-performed, yet that karma will certainly not receive its retribution."
It is likewise for that which is non-virtuous.
If an action is accomplished through its performance, must that action necessarily receive its retribution?
Answer: Yes.
There are actions that are accomplished, yet those actions will certainly not result in retribution.
What are these actions that are accomplished, yet will certainly not result in retribution?
The answer is:
Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are past—whether unwholesome or, if wholesome, tainted (*sāsrava*)—their retribution has matured, yet those formations are not lost.

Regarding all conditioned phenomena that are future—whether unwholesome or, if wholesome, tainted—they will certainly not arise; or if one possesses neutral (*avyākṛta*) or untainted (*anāsrava*) formations, this is called "possessing formations" such that those formations will certainly not receive their retribution.
What are those actions that are certain to yield retribution, yet for which that retribution is not realized?
The answer is:
those past actions that are unwholesome, or even wholesome but with outflows (*sāsrava*), whose retribution has not yet matured and which have been lost.

If various formations (*saṃskāra*) are unwholesome in the future, or even wholesome yet tainted (*sāsrava*), and they cannot necessarily arise, these are called formations that will certainly receive retribution, yet those formations are not accomplished.
What are formations that are accomplished and which will certainly receive retribution?
Answer: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are past—whether unwholesome or, if wholesome, tainted (*sāsrava*)—have not yet ripened as retribution, yet those formations are not lost;
all conditioned phenomena that are future—whether unwholesome or, if wholesome, tainted—will necessarily arise once they are acquired.

If various formations are currently unwholesome, or if they are wholesome but with outflows (*sāsrava*), these are called formations that are accomplished and for which one must necessarily experience retribution.
What are formations that are not accomplished and for which one does not necessarily experience retribution?
The answer is:
Those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are past—whether unwholesome or, if wholesome, tainted (*sāsrava*)—have already ripened as retribution and those phenomena have ceased;
those conditioned phenomena that are future—whether unwholesome or, if wholesome, tainted—have not yet been attained and will certainly not arise.

If one does not possess indeterminate or untainted formations (*avyākṛta-anāsrava-saṃskāra*), this is called "not possessing those formations," and such formations will certainly not receive retribution.
Is it not also the same [for other cases]?

If there is a *srotāpanna* whose unwholesome formations (*akuśala-saṃskāra*) resulting in painful retribution have not yet matured, by what means does he obstruct the paths of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts?
Answer: There are two kinds of fetters that bind and constrain, through which one will inevitably fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts:
the fetters to be abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) and the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

That stream-enterer has exhausted the fetters abandoned through the vision of the truths, but has not yet exhausted those abandoned through cultivation; because he possesses these [factors] unevenly, he does not go to the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
For example, just as a chariot with two wheels that are not damaged can reach its destination, whereas if one wheel is damaged it cannot reach its destination,
so too are beings bound by the two kinds of fetters that lead to rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts:
the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the truths and the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation.

That stream-enterer has exhausted the fetters abandoned through the vision of the truths, though not yet exhausted the fetters abandoned through cultivation; being thus partially endowed [with these qualities], he does not go to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
For example, just as a hawk with both wings intact can fly into the sky, but cannot reach the sky if one wing is broken;

so too, those bound by the two types of fetters fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. However, for that *srotāpanna*, the fetters abandoned through seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) are exhausted, while the fetters abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are not yet exhausted. Because these are present in such an uneven distribution, he does not go to the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has said:
"This is called a disciple of the World-Honored One who has exhausted rebirth in hell, exhausted rebirth as an animal or a hungry ghost, and has completely ceased falling into the evil realms.

Does a *srotāpanna* possess this knowledge, awakening to the fact that "hell is exhausted for me, animals and hungry ghosts are exhausted, and I have completely ceased falling into the evil realms," or does he not awaken to it himself?
Answer: It is not self-awakened.
How can this be known?
Answer: One goes forth with faith in the World-Honored One.
As the World-Honored One has said:

Those who self-reflect upon these four dharmas will diligently advance themselves, thinking: "My time in hell is exhausted; my time as an animal or a hungry ghost is exhausted; I shall never again fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, a stream-enterer possesses four kinds of knowledge:

knowledge of suffering, knowledge of its origin, knowledge of its cessation, and knowledge of the path. A stream-enterer does not yet possess the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
What is the training in malice?
The answer is:

as when one who trains has not yet exhausted desire, and being struck by another with hands, stones, knives, or clubs, being oppressed by that pain, gives rise to the thought to cause that person severe agony or to cause that person’s wife to be childless; such is the training in malice.

Suppose one who has trained to the point of exhausting sexual desire is beaten with hands, stones, knives, or clubs; being oppressed by that pain, he regresses from his state of freedom from desire. Having regressed, he gives rise to this thought:
"May he suffer such cruel agony! May his wife remain childless!"
If one trains in this way, does one train in all that constitutes the fruit of what is contrived?
The answer is: No.
"No, it is not so. If sentient beings possess great power and perform their actions, those [actions] will not bear fruit.
What is the practice of maintaining life?
The answer is:"
Suppose an Arhat were to give his robes, alms bowl, door keys, sandals, needle case, and other personal requisites to the Sangha or to an individual, and then resolve:
"By virtue of this karmic retribution, may my lifespan be increased."
Having made this vow, he enters the fourth dhyāna of the "summit" (mūrdhan). The retribution of that object of focus then becomes the retribution of life-span, and thus he dwells with that life-span.
How does he relinquish his life-span? Answer:
For example, when an Arhat gives his robes, alms bowl, door keys, sandals, needle case, or other requisites to the Sangha or to an individual, he then resolves:
"The lifespan and karmic rewards I have attained shall become the reward for this gift."
Having made this vow, he enters the fourth dhyāna of the Peak (mūrdhan). His retribution of lifespan then becomes the retribution of his giving, and in this manner he relinquishes his life.
What is mental distraction?
The answer is:
The mind becomes disturbed by four things:
seeing non-humans in the form of mad elephants, horses, wild goats, or wild oxen, one becomes terrified and the mind becomes disturbed;
or if a non-human, out of anger, strikes the limbs and joints, one suffers excruciating pain and the mind becomes disturbed.
Or, there are those whose minds are deranged due to various major errors,
or whose minds are deranged as a result of the retribution for past actions.
By association with which fetters (*paryavasthāna*) are all phenomena unwholesome?
Answer: Lack of shame and lack of remorse.
What does the Buddha’s teaching say about this?
Answer: The ten types of speech in the ten regions of India are all considered "speech"; this is what is called the Buddha’s speech.
Should one say that the Buddha’s speech is wholesome (*kuśala*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*)?
Answer: The Buddha’s words are either wholesome or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
Answer: A virtuous mind refers to what the Tathāgata has taught in the ten matters mentioned above; this is called "virtuous.
What is "indeterminate"?
Answer: The indeterminate mind as spoken of by the Tathāgata regarding the ten matters mentioned above is called "indeterminate.
What dharma is designated by the term "Buddha's word"?
Answer: The collections of names (nāmakāya), phrases (padakāya), and syllables (vyañjanakāya) abide in succession.
The interlocutor replied:
The sets of names (nāmakāya), phrases (padakāya), and phonemes (vyañjanakāya) abide in succession.
What dharma is designated by the term "seal" (mudrā)?
The answer is:
What dharma is designated by the name "the wisdom attained through the bodily formations produced by skill"?
The answer is:
What dharma is designated as "the knowledge acquired through skillful verbal formations"?
The answer is:
Regarding the wisdom attained through the mental formations produced by skill:
what dharma is designated as "writing"? The answer is: [it is the dharma of] the marks of letters.
Regarding the bodily formations produced by skillful means and the wisdom realized thereby—
what dharma is designated by this verse?
The answer is:
Regarding the verbal formations produced by skillful means and the wisdom they engender—
what dharma is designated as these various modes of engraving?
The answer is:
Wisdom is primary, yet it is disturbed by skillful means; these are the various knowledges that are thereby realized.
If one achieves the morality of a learner (*śaikṣa*), does one thereby achieve the morality that is neither of a learner nor of one beyond learning (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Answer: There are cases where one who is in training (śaikṣa) is accomplished in the precepts, but not in the precepts that are neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (naiva-śaikṣa-na-aśaikṣa).
What is meant by being accomplished in the precepts as one in training, but not in the precepts that are neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training?

Answer: A trainee (śaikṣa) who is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is said to be one who has achieved the precepts of training (śaikṣa-śīla), but not the precepts that are neither-training-nor-non-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-śīla).
How is it that one achieves the precepts that are neither-training-nor-non-training, yet is not a trainee?
Answer: Arhats and ordinary persons born in the realm of desire or the realm of form are said to possess precepts that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
How does a learner possess precepts that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: When a trainee (śaikṣa) is in the desire realm or the form realm, this is called the accomplishment of the morality of a trainee that is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
What is the accomplishment of morality that is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee?

Answer: An Arhat or an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is said to neither possess the precepts of one in training (śaikṣa) nor the precepts of one who is neither in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
If one possesses the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), does that person also possess the precepts of one who is neither in training nor beyond training?
Answer: There are cases where one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa) possesses precepts that are neither of the stage of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
How is it that one who is beyond training possesses precepts that are neither of the stage of training nor beyond training?

Answer: An Arhat who is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is said to be accomplished in the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), but not in those that are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
How is one accomplished in the precepts that are neither of training nor beyond training, but not in those of one beyond training?
Answer:

When a learner (śaikṣa) or an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is born into the desire realm or the form realm, this is called being endowed with neither-learner-nor-non-learner morality (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-śīla), but not with non-learner morality.
How is one endowed with non-learner morality and neither-learner-nor-non-learner morality?

Answer: When an Arhat is born in the realm of desire or the realm of form, this is called being accomplished in the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), yet not in those of one in training or one beyond training.
What is meant by being accomplished in the precepts of one beyond training, yet not in those of one in training or one beyond training?
Answer:

When a learner (śaikṣa) or an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), this is called neither possessing the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-śīla) nor possessing those that are neither of a learner nor of one beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).

This concludes the fifth section on the eight channels of practice; in the Sanskrit original it consists of one hundred eighty-five ślokas, and in the Qin translation it comprises two thousand three hundred seventy-eight words.
The Fourth Chapter on Practice (Caryā-vastu) is completed.

The Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra, Volume Eighteen.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Fu Qin dynasty.
"The four great elements are what is produced"—this is called the condition (*pratyaya*); it is the accomplishment of the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).

[The section on] "Derived from the Four Great Elements" follows below. Chapter One: The Chapter on the Purification of the Faculties (*Indriya-varga*). Regarding the elements derived from the four great elements: how many are visible (*sanidarśana*) and how many are invisible (*anidarśana*); how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and how many are without resistance (*apratigha*); how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*); how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and how many are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); how many are past (*atīta*), how many are future (*anāgata*), and how many are present (*pratyutpanna*); how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*); how many are of those in training (*śaikṣa*), how many are of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither of those in training nor beyond training; and how many are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and how many are not to be abandoned? [End of the section on the elements.]
If one achieves the four great elements, does one achieve derived matter?
Conversely, if one achieves derived matter, does one achieve the four great elements?
If one does not achieve the four great elements, does one not achieve derived matter?
If one does not accomplish derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), does one also not accomplish the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)? [End of section on derived matter.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish wholesome matter (*kuśala-rūpa*)?
If one accomplishes wholesome form, does one also accomplish the four great elements?
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish unwholesome form?
If one accomplishes unwholesome form, does one also accomplish the four great elements?
If one is endowed with the four great elements, is one also endowed with obscured-unspecified form?
Conversely, if one is endowed with obscured-unspecified form, is one also endowed with the four great elements?
If one achieves the four great elements, does one achieve non-obscured neutral matter?
Conversely, if one achieves non-obscured neutral matter, does one achieve the four great elements? [The Single Gate is concluded.]
If one is endowed with the four great elements, is one also endowed with wholesome and unwholesome form?
Conversely, if one is endowed with wholesome and unwholesome form, is one also endowed with the four great elements?
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish wholesome and obscured-unspecified matter?
Conversely, if one accomplishes wholesome and obscured-unspecified matter, does one also accomplish the four great elements?
If one possesses the four great elements, does one also possess wholesome and non-obscured neutral matter?
Conversely, if one possesses wholesome and non-obscured neutral matter, does one also possess the four great elements?
If one is endowed with the four great elements, is one also endowed with unwholesome and obscured-unspecified form?
Conversely, if one is endowed with unwholesome and obscured-unspecified form, is one also endowed with the four great elements?
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish unwholesome and non-obscured-neutral matter?
Conversely, if one accomplishes unwholesome and non-obscured-neutral matter, does one also accomplish the four great elements?
If one is endowed with the four great elements, is one also endowed with obscured-unspecified and non-obscured-unspecified matter?
Conversely, if one is endowed with obscured-unspecified and non-obscured-unspecified matter, is one also endowed with the four great elements? (End of the paired section.)
If one is endowed with the four great elements, is one also endowed with wholesome, unwholesome, and obscured-unspecified matter?
Conversely, if one is endowed with wholesome, unwholesome, and obscured-unspecified matter, is one also endowed with the four great elements?
If one is endowed with the four great elements, is one also endowed with wholesome, unwholesome, and non-obscured-neutral matter?
Conversely, if one is endowed with wholesome, unwholesome, and non-obscured-neutral matter, is one also endowed with the four great elements?
If one is endowed with the four great elements, is one also endowed with wholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified matter?
Conversely, if one is endowed with wholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified matter, is one also endowed with the four great elements?

If one accomplishes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), does one also accomplish unwholesome (*akuśala*), obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) form?
Conversely, if one accomplishes unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified form, does one also accomplish the four great elements? (End of Section Three)
If one possesses the four great elements, does one also possess wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified matter?

Conversely, if one possesses wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified matter, does one also possess the four great elements? [End of section on the four great elements.]
If one accomplishes wholesome form, does one also accomplish unwholesome form?
Conversely, if one accomplishes unwholesome form, does one also accomplish wholesome form?
If one accomplishes wholesome form, does one also accomplish obscured-unspecified form?
If one accomplishes obscured neutral form, does one accomplish wholesome form?
