If one accomplishes wholesome form, does one accomplish non-obscured neutral form?
If one accomplishes non-obscured neutral form, does that person accomplish wholesome form?
Conversely, if one accomplishes wholesome form, does that person accomplish unwholesome or obscured neutral form?
If one accomplishes unwholesome or obscured-unspecified form, does that person accomplish wholesome form?
If one accomplishes wholesome form, does that person accomplish unwholesome or non-obscured-unspecified form?
If one accomplishes unwholesome and non-obscured neutral form, does that person accomplish wholesome form?
If one accomplishes wholesome form, does that person accomplish obscured neutral and non-obscured neutral form?
If one achieves both obscured-neutral and unobscured-neutral matter, does one achieve wholesome matter? [End of the "Double" section.
If one achieves wholesome matter, does one achieve unwholesome, obscured-neutral, or unobscured-neutral matter?
If one accomplishes unwholesome matter and obscured-unspecified or non-obscured-unspecified matter, does that person accomplish wholesome matter? [End of section on wholesome matter.
If one accomplishes unwholesome matter, does that person accomplish obscured-unspecified matter?
If one possesses obscured indeterminate matter, does one possess unwholesome matter?
If one possesses unwholesome matter, does one possess non-obscured indeterminate matter?
If one possesses non-obscured neutral matter, does one possess unwholesome matter?
If one possesses unwholesome matter, does one possess obscured neutral and non-obscured neutral matter?

If one possesses obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) form, does that person possess unwholesome (*akuśala*) form? [End of section on the unwholesome.
Furthermore, if one possesses obscured-unspecified form, does that person possess non-obscured-unspecified form?
If one accomplishes non-obscured neutral matter (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*), does one also accomplish obscured neutral matter (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*)?
By which meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) extinguished?

By which meditative absorption are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), contact with resistance (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*), initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*), the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the nutriment of physical food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*), the nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*), and the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) extinguished?
When the four great elements have been exhausted without remainder, what result should it be said to produce?

Regarding derived matter, ill-will, contact through resistance, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; as well as the food of morsels, the food of contact, the food of mental volition, and the food of consciousness—by which samādhi are these extinguished?
When the four great elements have been exhausted without remainder, what fruit should it be said to produce?
I pray that you will fully expound the meaning of this chapter.
How many of the derived bases (upādāya-rūpa) among the four great elements are visible?
Answer: One. How many are invisible?
Answer: Eight [elements] and two partially included.
How many are with resistance (*sapratigha*)?
Answer: Nine [elements] and a small portion of one.
How many are non-obstructive?
Answer: One part enters slightly.
How many are with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
Answer: Nine [factors] and two partial entries.
How many are untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: One minor category.
How many are conditioned?
Answer: Nine [factors] and a small portion of two.
How many are past?
Answer: Eleven minor entrances.
How many are in the future?
Answer: Eleven minor entrances.
How many are present?
Answer: Eleven minor entries (*anupraveśa*).
How many are wholesome?
Answer: Three are minor entries.
How many are unwholesome?
Answer: Three minor entries.
How many are indeterminate?
Answer: Seven;
three partially enter.
How many are bound to the desire realm?
Answer: Two [factors] and a portion of nine [factors] are included.
How many are bound to the form realm?
Answer: Nine are partially included.
How many are unconditioned?
Answer: One minor entry.
How many are trainings?
Answer: One minor entry.
How many are beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
Answer: One minor category.
How many are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: Nine [factors] and a small portion of two [factors].
How many are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
Answer: Nine, with a partial inclusion of two.
How many are not abandoned?
Answer: One part has been completed.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish derived matter?
Answer: It is so;
if one is endowed with the four great elements, one is endowed with derived matter.
Is it possible, however, to be endowed with derived matter without being endowed with the four great elements?
Answer: There is;
it is when an immaculate person (*vimala-pudgala*) is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If one does not possess the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), does one also not possess derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)?
Answer: It is so;
if one does not achieve derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), one does not achieve the four great elements (mahābhūta).
Is there anyone who does not achieve the four great elements but is not non-achieved of derived matter?
Answer: Yes, there is;
for instance, when an immaculate person (vimala-pudgala) is born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and has completed their actions.
If one is endowed with the four great elements (mahābhūta), is one also endowed with wholesome matter (kuśala-rūpa)?
Answer: One may accomplish the four great elements but not wholesome form.
How does one accomplish the four great elements but not wholesome form?
The answer is:

When an ordinary person is in the mother’s womb within the layers of the egg-membrane, or if they are born in the desire realm in a state of non-restraint, they lack the informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of wholesome bodily and vocal actions, or they lose the informative intimation previously possessed;

likewise, in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint, they lack the informative intimation of wholesome bodily and vocal actions, or they lose the informative intimation previously possessed. This is called being endowed with the four great elements but not with wholesome form (*rūpa*).
How is it that one accomplishes wholesome form (*rūpa*) but not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)?
The answer is:
when a stainless person (*vimalapudgala*) is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called accomplishing wholesome form but not the four great elements.
What is meant by "accomplishing the four great elements and wholesome form"?
The answer is:

when a stainless person is in the mother’s womb within the stages of the membrane and the thickening of the chorion; or when one is born in the desire realm—whether in a state of moral discipline, a state of non-discipline, or a state that is neither disciplined nor undisciplined—and possesses wholesome informative acts of body and speech, or does not lose the informative acts previously possessed; or when one is born in the form realm. This is called accomplishing the four great elements and wholesome form.
What is it that neither accomplishes the four great elements nor wholesome form?
The answer is:
an ordinary person born in the formless realm; this is called neither accomplishing the four great elements nor wholesome form.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one accomplish unwholesome form?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes unwholesome form, one accomplishes the four great elements.
Is there anyone who possesses the four great elements but does not possess unwholesome matter?
Answer: Yes.

There are those in the womb or within the stages of the egg and membrane; those born in the desire realm who abide in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*) but lack the non-informative (*avijñapti*) expression of unwholesome bodily or vocal action, or have lost the informative expression they previously possessed; those who abide in neither the state of moral discipline nor the state of non-discipline and lack the non-informative expression of unwholesome bodily or vocal action, or have lost the informative expression they previously possessed; and those born in the form realm.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one accomplish obscured-unspecified form?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes obscured-unspecified form, one accomplishes the four great elements.
Is there one who possesses the four great elements but not the non-obscured indeterminate form?
Answer: Yes.
For example, one born in the desire realm, or one born in the form realm who lacks the unmanifest (avijñapti) bodily and vocal actions that are obscured-indeterminate.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish non-obscured neutral matter?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes non-obscured neutral matter, does one also accomplish the four great elements?
Answer: It is so.
(End of the single-section.)
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish wholesome and unwholesome form?
The answer is:

there are cases where one accomplishes the four great elements but not wholesome or unwholesome form; cases where one accomplishes wholesome form but not unwholesome form; cases where one accomplishes unwholesome form but not wholesome form; and cases where one accomplishes both wholesome and unwholesome form.
What is it to be endowed with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) but not with wholesome or unwholesome matter?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is in the mother’s womb within the thickening layers of the membrane, or when born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in a state that is neither governed by discipline (*saṃvara*) nor non-discipline (*asaṃvara*), such that there is no informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of wholesome or unwholesome bodily or vocal action, or where previously existing informative intimation has been lost—this is called being endowed with the four great elements but not with wholesome or unwholesome matter.
What is it to possess the four great elements and wholesome form, but not unwholesome form?
The answer is:

an undefiled person while remaining in the mother’s womb during the stages of the membrane and the thickening of the chorion; or one born in the desire realm who abides in the precepts, such that there is no manifest expression of unwholesome bodily or vocal action, or any prior manifest expression has been lost.

Furthermore, in a state that is neither characterized by restraint nor non-restraint, there is wholesome informative action (*vijñapti*) of body and speech, and original informative action is not lost; there is unwholesome non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of body and speech, and original informative action is lost.
If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), this is called being endowed with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and wholesome matter (*rūpa*), but not unwholesome matter.
What is it to be endowed with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as well as wholesome and unwholesome form (*rūpa*)?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who dwells in a state of non-restraint, such that there is no manifest intimation (*vijñapti*) of wholesome bodily or vocal action, or where manifest intimation previously possessed has been lost; or one who dwells in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint, such that there is manifest intimation of unwholesome bodily or vocal action, or manifest intimation previously possessed has not been lost, while there is no manifest intimation of wholesome bodily or vocal action, or manifest intimation previously possessed has been lost—this is called being endowed with the four great elements as well as wholesome and unwholesome form.
How does one accomplish the four great elements as well as wholesome and unwholesome matter?
The answer is:

being born in the desire realm in a state of moral discipline (*śīla*), one possesses unwholesome bodily and vocal informative acts (*vijñapti*) that are either currently manifest or were previously manifest and have not been lost.
In a state that is neither of moral discipline nor non-discipline, there is wholesome instruction of body and speech, and the original instruction is not lost;

likewise, in a state that is neither of moral discipline nor non-discipline, there is wholesome and unwholesome instruction of body and speech, and the original instruction is not lost—this is called being endowed with the four great elements and wholesome and unwholesome form.
If one accomplishes wholesome or unwholesome form, does one also accomplish the four great elements?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish wholesome, obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter? Answer:

One may accomplish the four great elements but not wholesome or obscured-unspecified matter; or wholesome matter but not obscured-unspecified matter; or both wholesome and obscured-unspecified matter.
How does one accomplish the four great elements and non-virtuous, obscured-unspecified matter?
The answer is:

an ordinary person dwelling in the mother’s womb during the stages of the ovum and the thickening membrane; or, having been born into the desire realm in a state lacking moral discipline, possessing no informative intimation of virtuous bodily or vocal action, or having lost the informative intimation previously possessed.

Furthermore, in a state that is neither governed by precepts nor contrary to precepts, there is no manifest intimation (vijñapti) of wholesome bodily or vocal action; or, where there was previously such intimation, it has been lost. This is called being endowed with the four great elements and unwholesome, obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) matter.
How does one accomplish the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and wholesome form (*kuśala-rūpa*), but not non-obscured neutral form (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*)?
The answer is:

an undefiled person (*vimala-pudgala*) while in the mother’s womb during the stages of the embryo and the thickening of the membranes; or, having been born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whether abiding in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*), in the state of non-discipline (*aśīla*), or in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, such that there is wholesome informative action (*vijñapti*) of body and speech, or the original informative action has not been lost.

If one born in the realm of form possesses obscured-unspecified bodily and vocal non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), this is called being endowed with the four great elements and wholesome form, but not obscured-unspecified form.
How is one endowed with the four great elements and both wholesome and obscured-unspecified form?
Answer:

One born in the Form Realm who possesses the manifest bodily and vocal intimation that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) is said to be endowed with the four great elements and wholesome as well as obscured-unspecified matter.
If one is endowed with wholesome and obscured-unspecified matter, is he also endowed with the four great elements?
Answer: It is so.
If one is endowed with the four great elements, is one also endowed with wholesome and non-obscured neutral matter?
Answer:
One may possess the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) form, but not wholesome (*kuśala*) form; or one may possess wholesome and non-obscured neutral form.
How does one possess the four great elements and non-obscured neutral form, but not wholesome form?
Answer:

When an ordinary person is in the mother’s womb, within the layers of the egg and membrane; or when born in the desire realm in a state lacking moral discipline (*aśīla*), such that there is no informative intimation (*avijñapti*) of wholesome bodily or vocal action, or any pre-existing informative intimation has been lost;

or likewise in a state that is neither moral discipline nor non-discipline, such that there is no informative intimation of wholesome bodily or vocal action, or any pre-existing informative intimation has been lost—this is called being endowed with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and non-obscured neutral form (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*), but not wholesome form.
How does one accomplish the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as well as wholesome and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter?
The answer is:

an undefiled person (*vimalapudgala*) while dwelling in the mother’s womb during the stages of the embryo and the thickening of the membranes; or, if born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whether abiding in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*), in the state of non-discipline (*aśīla*), or in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, such that they possess wholesome informative acts (*vijñapti*) of body and speech, or have not lost the informative acts previously possessed.
If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), this is called being endowed with the four great elements (mahābhūta) as well as wholesome and non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) matter.
If one is endowed with wholesome and non-obscured neutral matter, is that person also endowed with the four great elements?
Answer: It is so.
If one is endowed with the four great elements, is one also endowed with unwholesome and obscured-unspecified matter?
Answer: No.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish unwholesome and non-obscured-neutral form?
Answer:
One may possess the four great elements and non-obscured neutral matter, but not unwholesome matter; or one may possess both unwholesome matter and non-obscured neutral matter.
What is it to possess the four great elements and non-obscured neutral form, yet not possess unwholesome form?
The answer is:

one who is in the mother’s womb or within the stages of the egg and membrane; or one born in the desire realm who abides in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*), such that they lack the non-informative (*avijñapti*) expression of unwholesome body and speech, or have lost the informative (*vijñapti*) expression previously possessed; or one who abides in a state that is neither moral discipline nor non-discipline, such that they lack the non-informative expression of unwholesome body and speech, or have lost the informative expression previously possessed.

If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), this is called accomplishing the four great elements (mahābhūta) as well as non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) matter, but not unwholesome (akuśala) matter.
How does one accomplish the four great elements as well as both unwholesome and non-obscured neutral matter?
Answer:

One born in the desire realm who abides in the state of moral discipline (śīla) possesses the informative intimation (vijñapti) of unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, as well as the non-loss of previously existing informative intimations;

likewise, one who abides neither in the state of moral discipline nor in the state of non-discipline possesses the informative intimation of unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, as well as the non-loss of previously existing informative intimations. This is called the accomplishment of the four great elements (mahābhūta) and unwholesome or non-obscured-neutral matter (rūpa).
If one accomplishes unwholesome or non-obscured neutral matter, does that person accomplish the four great elements? Answer: Yes.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish the obscured-unspecified and the non-obscured-unspecified forms?
Answer:

One may accomplish the four great elements and the non-obscured-unspecified form but not the obscured-unspecified form; or one may accomplish both the obscured-unspecified and the non-obscured-unspecified forms.
What is it to accomplish the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter, but not obscured-neutral matter?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) who possesses no manifest bodily or vocal intimation (*avijñapti*) that is obscured-neutral; this is called accomplishing the four great elements and non-obscured-neutral matter, but not obscured-neutral matter.
How does one achieve the four great elements as well as both obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter?
The answer is:

one who is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and possesses the informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of body and speech that is obscured-unspecified; this is called achieving the four great elements as well as both obscured-unspecified and non-obscured-unspecified matter.
If one accomplishes both obscured-neutral and non-obscured-neutral matter, does that person accomplish the four great elements?
Answer: It is so;
thus the pair is concluded.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, or non-obscured-unspecified matter? Answer: No.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish wholesome, unwholesome, and non-obscured-neutral matter?
Answer:

One may accomplish the four great elements and non-obscured-neutral matter but not wholesome or unwholesome matter; or accomplish wholesome and non-obscured-neutral matter but not unwholesome matter; or accomplish unwholesome and non-obscured-neutral matter but not wholesome matter; or accomplish wholesome, unwholesome, and non-obscured-neutral matter.
What is it to be endowed with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter, but not with wholesome or unwholesome matter?
The answer is:

an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) dwelling in the mother’s womb during the stages of the embryo and the thickening of the membranes; or one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state that is neither disciplined nor undisciplined, and for whom there is no informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of wholesome or unwholesome bodily or vocal action, or whose previously existing informative intimation has been lost. This is called being endowed with the four great elements and non-obscured neutral matter, but not with wholesome or unwholesome matter.
What is it to be endowed with the four great elements and with wholesome and non-obscured-neutral matter, but not with unwholesome matter?
The answer is:

an undefiled person dwelling in the mother’s womb during the stages of the kalala and arbuda; or one born in the desire realm who abides in the precepts, such that there is no manifest expression of unwholesome bodily or vocal action, or any previously existing manifest expression has been lost.

Furthermore, in a state that is neither characterized by restraint nor non-restraint, there is wholesome informative action (*vijñapti*) of body and speech, and one does not lose the original informative action; whereas there is unwholesome non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of body and speech, and one loses the original informative action.

If one is born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), this is called being endowed with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and wholesome and non-obscured-neutral matter (*anivṛtāvyākṛtarūpa*), but not unwholesome matter.
How is it that one accomplishes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*) as well as non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter, yet not wholesome matter?
The answer is:

if one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in a state lacking moral discipline (*aśīla*), such that there is no manifest intimation (*vijñapti*) of wholesome bodily or vocal action, or if there was previously existing manifest intimation that has been lost; [then one accomplishes these].

Furthermore, in a state that is neither characterized by restraint nor non-restraint, there is an unwholesome bodily or vocal informative act (*vijñapti*) or an original informative act that has not been lost; yet, there is no wholesome bodily or vocal non-informative act (*avijñapti*), or any original informative act that has already been lost. This is called being endowed with the four great elements and unwholesome as well as non-obscured-neutral matter (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*), but not wholesome matter.
How does one accomplish the four great elements as well as wholesome, unwholesome, and non-obscured-neutral matter?
The answer is:

if one is born in the desire realm within the sphere of moral discipline (*śīla*), and possesses unwholesome bodily and vocal informative acts (*vijñapti*) or has not lost the original informative acts already possessed;
In a state that is neither of moral discipline nor non-discipline, there is wholesome bodily and vocal intimation, and the original intimation is not lost;

furthermore, in a state that is neither of moral discipline nor non-discipline, there is wholesome and unwholesome bodily and vocal intimation, and the original intimation is not lost. This is called being endowed with the four great elements and with wholesome, unwholesome, and non-obscured-neutral matter.
If one accomplishes wholesome, unwholesome, or non-obscured neutral matter, does that person accomplish the four great elements? Answer: Yes.
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish wholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified matter?
The answer is:

there are cases where one accomplishes the four great elements and unobscured-unspecified matter, but not wholesome or obscured-unspecified matter; cases where one accomplishes wholesome and unobscured-unspecified matter, but not obscured-unspecified matter; and cases where one accomplishes wholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified matter.
How is it that one accomplishes the four great elements and non-obscured neutral matter, but not wholesome or obscured neutral matter?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person is in the mother’s womb during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana; or when one is born in the desire realm in a state lacking moral discipline, such that there is no manifest wholesome bodily or vocal intimation, or any previously existing manifest intimation has been lost.

Furthermore, in a state that is neither characterized by moral discipline nor non-discipline, where there is no manifest action of body or speech, and any previously existing manifest action has been lost—one is said to be endowed with the four great elements and non-obscured neutral matter, but not with wholesome or obscured neutral matter.
How does one achieve the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and wholesome as well as non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter, yet not [achieve] obscured-neutral matter?
The answer is:

a stainless person (*vimala-pudgala*) dwelling in the mother’s womb during the stages of the membrane and the thickening of the embryo; or, if born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whether abiding in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*), in the state of non-discipline (*aśīla*), or in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, such that there is wholesome informative action (*vijñapti*) of body and speech, or the original informative action has not been lost.

If one born in the form realm possesses the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily and vocal non-informations (avijñapti), this is called being endowed with the four great elements (mahābhūta) as well as wholesome and non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) matter, but not obscured-unspecified matter.
How does one accomplish the four great elements as well as wholesome, obscured-unspecified, and non-obscured-unspecified matter?
The answer is:

one who is born in the form realm and possesses the informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of body and speech that is obscured-unspecified accomplishes the four great elements as well as wholesome, obscured-unspecified, and non-obscured-unspecified matter.
If one accomplishes wholesome, obscured-unspecified, or unobscured-unspecified form, does that person accomplish the four great elements? Answer: Yes.
If one achieves the four great elements, does one achieve unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and non-obscured-unspecified matter?
Answer: No.
(End of the third section.)
If one accomplishes the four great elements, does one also accomplish wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified matter?
Answer: This too does not exist. [End of section on the four great elements.]
If one accomplishes wholesome form, does one also accomplish unwholesome form?
Answer: One may accomplish wholesome form without accomplishing unwholesome form.
What is it to accomplish wholesome form but not unwholesome form?
The answer is:

an undefiled person remaining in the mother’s womb during the stages of the membrane and the thickening of the embryo; or one born in the desire realm who abides in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*), such that there is no manifest intimation (*vijñapti*) of unwholesome bodily or vocal action, and any previously existing manifest intimation has been lost; or one who abides in a state that is neither moral discipline nor non-discipline, such that there is manifest intimation of wholesome bodily or vocal action and no loss of previously existing manifest intimation, while there is no manifest intimation of unwholesome bodily or vocal action and any previously existing manifest intimation has been lost.
If one is born in the form realm;
or if a stainless person (vimala-pudgala) is born in the formless realm—this is called being endowed with wholesome form, but not unwholesome form.
What is meant by being endowed with unwholesome form, but not wholesome form?
Answer: One born in the desire realm in a state of non-restraint possesses no manifest action (*vijñapti*) of wholesome body or speech, and any manifest action previously possessed has been lost;

furthermore, one in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint possesses manifest action of unwholesome body or speech, and any manifest action previously possessed is not lost, yet possesses no manifest action of wholesome body or speech, and any manifest action previously possessed has been lost. This is called "accomplishing unwholesome form, but not wholesome form."
How does one accomplish wholesome and unwholesome form?
The answer is:

being born in the desire realm in a state of moral discipline (*śīla*), one possesses unwholesome bodily and vocal informative acts (*vijñapti*) that are either currently manifest or were previously manifest and have not been lost.
In a state that is neither of moral discipline nor non-discipline, there is wholesome bodily and vocal intimation, and the original intimation is not lost;

furthermore, in a state that is neither of moral discipline nor non-discipline, there is wholesome and unwholesome bodily and vocal intimation, and the original intimation is not lost—this is called the accomplishment of wholesome and unwholesome form.
What is meant by not accomplishing wholesome or unwholesome form?
The answer is:

ordinary persons dwelling in the mother’s womb during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana; or those born in the desire realm who abide in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, such that they possess no informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of wholesome or unwholesome bodily or vocal action, or have lost the informative intimation they previously possessed; and ordinary persons born in the formless realm—these are said to not accomplish wholesome or unwholesome form.
If one accomplishes wholesome form, does one also accomplish obscured-neutral form? Answer: Yes.
If one accomplishes obscured-unspecified form (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*), does that person accomplish wholesome form (*kuśala-rūpa*)?
Is it possible to accomplish wholesome form without accomplishing obscured-unspecified form?
Answer: Yes.

There is: when a person free from defilements (*vimala*) dwells in the mother’s womb during the stages of the membrane and the thickening of the embryo; or when one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) abides in a state of neither discipline nor non-discipline, yet possesses wholesome informative acts (*vijñapti*) of body and speech, or does not lose those informative acts previously possessed;
or when one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) possesses non-informative acts (*avijñapti*) of body and speech that are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*);
or when a person free from defilements is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If one accomplishes wholesome form, does one also accomplish non-obscured neutral form?
Answer:
One may accomplish wholesome form without accomplishing non-obscured neutral form.
How is it that one accomplishes wholesome form (*kuśala-rūpa*) but not non-obscured neutral form (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*)? Answer:
When a stainless person (*vimala-pudgala*) is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called accomplishing wholesome form but not non-obscured neutral form.
How does one accomplish non-obscured neutral form (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*) while not accomplishing wholesome form (*kuśala-rūpa*)?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is in the mother’s womb during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana; or when born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in a state lacking moral discipline (*aśīla*), such that there is no manifest expression (*vijñapti*) of wholesome bodily or vocal action, or if there was previously existing manifest expression, it has already been lost.

Furthermore, in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, where there is no informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of wholesome bodily or vocal action, or where an originally existing informative intimation has been lost—this is called "accomplishing unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter, but not wholesome matter."
How does one accomplish wholesome form and non-obscured neutral form?
The answer is:

an undefiled person while remaining within the fetal membrane in the mother’s womb; or, having been born into the desire realm, whether abiding in the state of moral discipline, in the state of immorality, or in a state that is neither moral nor immoral, possessing wholesome informative acts of body and speech, or not losing informative acts previously possessed.
If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu), this is called being endowed with wholesome form (kuśalarūpa) and non-obscured neutral form (anivṛtāvyākṛtarūpa).
What is it to not be endowed with wholesome form and non-obscured neutral form?
Answer: An ordinary person born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is said to be non-possessed of wholesome form and non-obscured neutral form.
If one is possessed of wholesome form, is one also possessed of unwholesome and obscured neutral form?
Answer: This also does not exist.
If one is endowed with wholesome form, is one also endowed with unwholesome and non-obscured neutral form?
Answer:

One may possess wholesome form but not unwholesome or non-obscured neutral form; or possess non-obscured neutral form but not unwholesome form; or possess both unwholesome and non-obscured neutral form.
How does one accomplish wholesome form (*rūpa*) but not unwholesome or non-obscured neutral form?
Answer: When a stainless person (*vimala-pudgala*) is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called accomplishing wholesome form but not unwholesome or non-obscured neutral form.
How does one accomplish wholesome form (*rūpa*) and non-obscured neutral form (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*), but not unwholesome form?
The answer is:

A stainless person (*vimala-pudgala*) while in the mother’s womb during the stages of the embryo and the thickening membrane; or, if born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), abiding in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*), such that there is no manifest intimation (*vijñapti*) of unwholesome bodily or vocal action, or any previously existing manifest intimation has been lost; furthermore, abiding in a state that is neither moral discipline nor non-discipline, such that there is manifest intimation of wholesome bodily or vocal action, and any previously existing manifest intimation is not lost, while there is no manifest intimation of unwholesome bodily or vocal action, or any previously existing manifest intimation has been lost.

If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), this is called being endowed with wholesome form (*kuśalarūpa*) and non-obscured neutral form (*anivṛtāvyākṛtarūpa*), but not unwholesome form (*akuśalarūpa*).
How is one endowed with wholesome form, as well as both unwholesome and non-obscured neutral form?
Answer:

One born in the desire realm who abides in the state of moral discipline possesses informative acts (*vijñapti*) of unwholesome body and speech, as well as the non-loss of previously existing informative acts;
one who does not abide in the state of moral discipline possesses informative acts of wholesome body and speech, as well as the non-loss of previously existing informative acts.

Furthermore, in a state that is neither the restraint of the precepts nor the non-restraint of the precepts, when there is wholesome or unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), or when there is original intimation that has not been lost—this is called being endowed with wholesome form as well as unwholesome and non-obscured neutral form.
If one accomplishes unwholesome or non-obscured neutral form, does one also accomplish wholesome form?
Answer: One may accomplish it, or one may not.
How is it accomplished?
The answer is:
that which was explained above is what is called accomplishment.
What is it that is not accomplished?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm in a state lacking moral discipline, who possesses no manifest expression of wholesome bodily or vocal action, or whose previously existing manifest expression has been lost.

Furthermore, in a state that is neither the realm of precepts nor the realm of non-precepts, there is no informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of unwholesome bodily or vocal action, nor is there any original informative intimation that has not been lost; yet there is informative intimation of wholesome bodily or vocal action, which was originally present but has now been lost—this is called "non-attainment."
If one accomplishes wholesome form (*kuśala-rūpa*), does one also accomplish obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) form? Answer:

One may accomplish wholesome form without accomplishing obscured-unspecified or unobscured-unspecified form; or accomplish unobscured-unspecified form without accomplishing obscured-unspecified form; or accomplish both obscured-unspecified and unobscured-unspecified form.
What is it to accomplish wholesome form (*kuśala-rūpa*) while not accomplishing obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) or unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) form?
The answer is:

when a stainless person (*vimala-pudgala*) is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called accomplishing wholesome form while not accomplishing obscured-unspecified or unobscured-unspecified form.
What is it to possess wholesome form (*śubha-rūpa*) and non-obscured neutral form (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*), yet not possess obscured neutral form (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*)?
The answer is:

an undefiled person (*vimala-pudgala*) while remaining within the fetal membrane in the mother’s womb; or, if born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whether abiding in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*), in the state of immorality (*aśīla*), or in a state that is neither moral nor immoral, such that they possess wholesome informative acts (*vijñapti*) of body and speech, or have not lost the original informative acts they previously possessed.

If one is born in the form realm and possesses obscured bodily and vocal non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), this is called being endowed with wholesome form and non-obscured neutral form, but not obscured neutral form.
How does one accomplish wholesome form (*śubha-rūpa*) as well as obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) forms?
The answer is:

one who is born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and possesses the informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of body and speech that is obscured-unspecified accomplishes wholesome form as well as obscured-unspecified and unobscured-unspecified forms.
If one accomplishes both obscured-neutral and unobscured-neutral matter, does that person accomplish wholesome matter?
Answer: It is so;
thus the pair is concluded.
If one accomplishes wholesome form, does one also accomplish unwholesome form, obscured-unspecified form, and non-obscured-unspecified form?
Answer:
This too is not the case. [The section on] wholesome form is concluded.
If one accomplishes unwholesome matter, does one also accomplish obscured-unspecified matter?
Answer: This is not the case.
If one accomplishes unwholesome form, does one accomplish non-obscured neutral form?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes unwholesome form, one accomplishes non-obscured neutral form.
Is there one who accomplishes non-obscured neutral form but not unwholesome form?
Answer: Yes. For example:

one dwelling in the mother’s womb or within the layers of the egg-membrane; or one born in the desire realm who abides in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*), yet lacks the non-informative (*avijñapti*) aspect of unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, or has lost the informative (*vijñapti*) aspect that was previously present; or one who abides in a state that is neither moral discipline nor non-discipline, yet lacks the non-informative aspect of unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, or has lost the informative aspect that was previously present.
If one is born in the form realm and possesses unwholesome matter, does that person also possess obscured-unspecified and non-obscured-unspecified matter?
Answer: Yes.
This concludes the section on the unwholesome.
If one is endowed with obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter, is one also endowed with non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter?
Answer: Yes.
Thus, if one possesses obscured-neutral matter (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*), one possesses non-obscured-neutral matter (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa*).
Is it possible to possess non-obscured-neutral matter without possessing obscured-neutral matter?
Answer: There are.
For one born in the desire realm or the form realm, there are unmanifest (avijñapti) bodily and vocal actions that are obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
By which samādhi are the four great elements extinguished?
Answer: Either based on the four [great elements] or based on the future.
Derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) is either based on the four or based on the future.
Contact accompanied by resistance is with both vitarka and vicāra, and it may rely on either the first dhyāna or the *anāgamya* stage.
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) may rely on three stages or the *anāgamya* stage.
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) may rely on two stages or the *anāgamya* stage.
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) subsist on the edible food of physical mass (*kabaṣikāhāra*) and depend on the future [realm].

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), the edible food of contact (*sparśāhāra*), the edible food of mental volition (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*), and the edible food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) either depend on the seven [realms] or depend on the future [realm].
When the four great elements have been exhausted without remainder, what fruit should be said to be produced?
The answer is:

the fruit of Arhatship; or, in certain cases, the fruit of Anāgāmin or the fruit of Arhatship produced by the form derived from the primary elements (*upādāya-rūpa*), by resistance (*sapratigha*), by contact (*sparśa*), by vitarka and vicāra, or by the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*); or, in certain cases, the fruit of Anāgāmin or the fruit of Arhatship produced by the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), or by the food of morsels (*kabaṣikāhāra*); or, in certain cases, the fruit of Arhatship produced by the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), by the food of contact, the food of mental volition (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*), or the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).

The first chapter, the *Abhidharma-viśuddha-indriya-varga*, is hereby completed. In the Sanskrit original it consists of three hundred and ninety-two *ślokas*; in the Qin translation it comprises five thousand eight hundred and eighty-nine words.
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagranthaka-śāstra*, Fascicle 18;
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagranthaka-śāstra*, Fascicle 19.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra and Zhu Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty.

Section Two: The Second Chapter on Conditions (*Pratyaya-vārga*) within the Four Great Divisions (*Catur-mahā-varga*). Regarding those four great elements (*mahābhūta*), how many conditions do they condition?
By how many conditions do the four great elements serve as conditions for derived matter?
By how many conditions does derived matter serve as a condition for that [same] derived matter?
By how many conditions does derived matter serve as a condition for the four great elements?
How many conditions do the four great elements serve as conditions for the mind and mental factors?
How many conditions do the mind and mental factors serve as conditions for those same mind and mental factors?
How many conditions do the mind and mental factors serve as conditions for the four great elements?
By how many conditions do the four great elements condition the eye-base?
By how many conditions does the eye-base condition that same eye-base?
By how many conditions does the eye-base condition the four great elements?
How many conditions do the four great elements (mahābhūta) serve as conditions for the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana)?
How many conditions does the sphere of mental objects serve as a condition for that same sphere of mental objects?
Having finished [examining] how many conditions the sphere of mental objects serves as a condition for the four great elements?
By how many conditions are the four great elements (mahābhūta) and the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya) conditioned? By how many conditions are the eye-faculty and the four great elements conditioned?
And by how many conditions are the four great elements, up to and including the faculty of ignorance (a-jñātāvīndriya), conditioned?
Regarding the faculty of ignorance (*ajñendriya*), how many conditions serve as conditions for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)?

Having finished [discussing] the conditions for the faculties, for what reason do the four great elements arise together, abide together, and perish together, yet are not associated (*asamprayukta*) with one another; whereas the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) arise together, abide together, and perish together, and are thus associated?
Can past primary elements (mahābhūta) produce past matter (rūpa), or future and present matter?
Can future primary elements produce future matter, or past and present matter?
Is it the case that present primary elements (mahābhūta) produce present derived matter (upādāyarūpa), as well as past and future derived matter?
If one is possessed of past primary elements, is one also possessed of past derived matter?
If one achieves past derived matter (bhautika-rūpa), does one achieve the past primary elements (mahābhūta)?
If one achieves the past primary elements, does one achieve the future primary elements?
If one achieves the four great elements of the future, does one achieve the four great elements of the past?
If one achieves the four great elements of the past, does one achieve the derived matter of the future?
If one accomplishes future derived matter (bhautika-rūpa), does one also accomplish past primary elements (mahābhūta)?
If one accomplishes past primary elements, does one also accomplish present primary elements?
If one achieves the present four great elements, does one achieve the past four great elements?
If one achieves the past four great elements, does one achieve the derived matter of the present?
If one achieves present derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), does one achieve past primary elements (*mahābhūta*)? [End of section on past primary elements.
If one achieves past derived matter, does one achieve future primary elements?
If one achieves the future four great elements, does one achieve past derived matter?
And if one achieves past derived matter, does one achieve future derived matter?
If one accomplishes future derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), does one accomplish past derived matter?
If one accomplishes past derived matter, does one accomplish present primary elements (mahābhūta)?
If one accomplishes the present four great elements, does that person accomplish past derived matter?
If one accomplishes past derived matter, does that person accomplish present derived matter?
If one achieves present derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), does one achieve past derived matter? [End of section on past derived matter.
If one achieves future primary elements (mahābhūta), does one achieve future derived matter?
If one accomplishes future derived matter (bhautika-rūpa), does one accomplish the four great elements (mahābhūta) of the future?
If one accomplishes the four great elements of the future, does one accomplish the four great elements of the present?
If one accomplishes the four great elements of the present, does one also accomplish the four great elements of the future?
And if one accomplishes the four great elements of the future, does one also accomplish derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) of the present?
If one achieves the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) of the present, does one achieve the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the future? [End of section on the future primary elements.
If one achieves the derived matter of the future, does one achieve the primary elements of the present?
If one accomplishes the present four great elements, does one accomplish future derived matter?
If one accomplishes future derived matter, does one accomplish present derived matter?
If one accomplishes present derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), does one also accomplish future derived matter? [End of section on future derived matter.
If one accomplishes the present four great elements (*mahābhūta*), does one also accomplish present derived matter?

If one achieves present derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), does one achieve the present four great elements (mahābhūta)? Having completed the analysis of the three time periods, [regarding] past four great elements:
by how many conditions (pratyaya) are those past four great elements conditioned?
By how many conditions do the past four great elements condition past derived matter?
By how many conditions does past derived matter condition that same past derived matter?
By how many conditions does past derived matter condition the past four great elements?
How many conditions do the past four great elements serve as conditions for the future four great elements?
How many conditions do those future four great elements serve as conditions for other future four great elements?
How many conditions do the future four great elements serve as conditions for the past four great elements?
By how many conditions do the past four great elements condition future derived matter?
By how many conditions does future derived matter condition that same future derived matter?
By how many conditions does future derived matter condition the past four great elements?
How many conditions do the past four great elements serve as conditions for the present four great elements?
How many conditions do the present four great elements serve as conditions for those present four great elements?
How many conditions do the present four great elements serve as conditions for the past four great elements?
By how many conditions do past great elements condition present derived matter?
By how many conditions does present derived matter condition that same present derived matter?
By how many conditions does present derived matter condition past great elements? [End of section on past great elements.]
How many conditions do past derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) serve as conditions for future primary elements (mahābhūta)?
How many conditions do future primary elements serve as conditions for past derived matter?
How many conditions do past derived matter serve as conditions for future derived matter?
By how many conditions do future derived matter and past derived matter act as conditions for one another?
By how many conditions does past derived matter act as a condition for present primary elements?
By how many conditions do present primary elements act as a condition for past derived matter?
By how many conditions do past derived matter and present derived matter act as conditions?
By how many conditions do present derived matter and past derived matter act as conditions? [End of section on past derived matter.
By how many conditions do future primary elements act as conditions for future derived matter?
How many conditions do future derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) and future great elements (mahābhūta) condition?
How many conditions do future great elements and present great elements condition?
How many conditions do present great elements and future great elements condition?
By how many conditions do the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the future serve as conditions for the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) of the present?
By how many conditions does the derived matter of the present serve as a condition for the four great elements of the future? [End of section on the four great elements of the future.
By how many conditions does the derived matter of the future serve as a condition for the four great elements of the present?
By how many conditions do present great elements (mahābhūta) condition future derived matter (upādāya-rūpa)?
By how many conditions does future derived matter condition present derived matter?
By how many conditions does present derived matter condition future derived matter? [End of section on future derived matter.]
By how many conditions do the present four great elements (mahābhūta) condition the present derived matter (upādāya-rūpa)?
By how many conditions does the present derived matter condition the present four great elements? [Thus concludes the section on] the three periods of time.
If one accomplishes the four great elements bound to the desire realm, does one also accomplish the derived matter bound to the desire realm?
If one accomplishes derived matter bound to the desire realm, does that person accomplish the four great elements bound to the desire realm?
And if one accomplishes the four great elements bound to the form realm, does that person accomplish derived matter bound to the form realm?
If one accomplishes derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), does that person accomplish the four great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the realm of form?

As for the four great elements bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), by how many conditions (pratyaya) do they serve as conditions for those [derived matters] bound to the desire realm?
By how many conditions do the four great elements bound to the desire realm serve as conditions for derived matter bound to the desire realm?
By how many conditions does derived matter bound to the desire realm serve as a condition for that same derived matter bound to the desire realm?
Regarding matter derived from the great elements bound to the desire realm: by how many conditions are those great elements bound to the desire realm conditioned?
Regarding the great elements bound to the form realm: by how many conditions are those great elements bound to the form realm conditioned?

By how many conditions are the four great elements bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-mahābhūta) conditioned for derived matter bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-upādāyarūpa)?
By how many conditions is derived matter bound to the realm of form conditioned for that same derived matter bound to the realm of form?
How many conditions do derived matter bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-bhautika) serve as conditions for the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the form realm?
If one accomplishes the primary elements bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), does one also accomplish the primary elements bound to the form realm?
If one achieves the four great elements bound to the realm of form, does one achieve the four great elements bound to the realm of desire?
If one achieves the four great elements bound to the realm of desire, does one achieve the derived matter bound to the realm of form?

If one accomplishes derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), does that person accomplish the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
And if one accomplishes derived matter bound to the desire realm, does that person accomplish the four great elements bound to the realm of form?
If one accomplishes the four great elements bound to the form realm, does one accomplish the derived matter bound to the desire realm?
If one accomplishes the derived matter bound to the desire realm, does one accomplish the derived matter bound to the form realm?
If one accomplishes derived matter bound to the form realm, does one also accomplish derived matter bound to the desire realm?
Regarding the four great elements bound to the desire realm and the four great elements bound to the form realm, how many conditions serve as conditions for one another?
By how many conditions do the four great elements bound to the form realm condition the four great elements bound to the desire realm?
By how many conditions do the four great elements bound to the desire realm condition the derived matter bound to the form realm?
How many conditions do the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) serve as conditions for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
How many conditions do the four great elements bound to the form realm serve as conditions for the derived matter bound to the desire realm?
By how many conditions do the four great elements bound to the form realm serve as conditions for derived matter bound to the desire realm?
By how many conditions does derived matter bound to the desire realm serve as a condition for derived matter bound to the form realm?
By how many conditions do derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) condition derived matter bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Are all those derived matters bound to the desire realm produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the desire realm?
If form is produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm, is that form entirely bound to the desire realm?
Regarding all forms bound to the form realm, is that form entirely produced by the four great elements bound to the form realm?
If a visible form is bound to the realm of form and is derived from the four great elements, is that form entirely bound to the realm of form?
Regarding all forms that are past, are those forms all derived from past great elements?
If visible form is produced by the past four great elements, is that form entirely past?
Regarding all future forms, are those forms entirely produced by future four great elements?
If matter is produced by the four great elements of the future, is all that matter necessarily of the future?
Regarding all matter of the present, is all that matter necessarily produced by the four great elements of the present?
If matter is present and produced by the four great elements, is all that matter present?
What is "earth"?
What is the "earth element"?
What is water? What is the element of water?
What is fire?
What is fire? What is wind? What is the element of wind?
Under which bases (*āyatana*) is earth subsumed, and by how many consciousnesses is it cognized?

Likewise for the element of earth, the element of water, the element of fire, and the element of wind—by how many bases are these four great elements (*mahābhūta*) subsumed, and by how many consciousnesses are they cognized?
I wish to explain fully the meaning of this chapter:
The four great elements are the cause and the predominant condition for those [other] four great elements.
The four great elements are the cause and the predominant condition for derived matter.
Derived matter is the cause and the predominance condition for that derived matter.
Derived matter is the cause and the predominance condition for those four great elements.
The four great elements are the object condition and the predominance condition for mind and mental factors.
Mind and mental factors are the cause, immediate antecedent, object-condition, and predominant condition for those same mind and mental factors.
Mind and mental factors are the cause and predominant condition for the four great elements.
The four great elements are the cause and predominant condition for the eye-base.
The eye-base is the cause and the dominant condition for that same eye-base.
The eye-base has the four great elements as its dominant condition.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body bases, as well as the odor and flavor bases.
The four great elements are the cause and the predominant condition for the sense-base of form.
The sense-base of form is the cause and the predominant condition for that same sense-base of form.
The sense-base of form is the cause and the predominant condition for the four great elements.
The same applies to the spheres of sound and tangibility.
The four great elements are the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*).

For that sphere of mind, the sphere of mind itself is the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The mind-base (manāyatana) has the four great elements as its cause and its predominance-condition (adhipati-paccaya).
The four great elements have the dharma-base (dharmāyatana) as their cause, condition, and predominance-condition.
The dharma-base has that same dharma-base as its cause, immediate-condition (anantara-paccaya), condition, and predominance-condition.
Regarding the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are its cause and predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The four great elements are the cause and predominant condition of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
The eye-faculty is the sole predominant condition for the four great elements.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, male, and female.
The four great elements are the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the mind-faculty.
The mind-faculty is the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition for the four great elements.

The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; likewise the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
For the four great elements and the life-faculty, there is one predominance.
The life-faculty has the four great elements as its one predominant condition.
The four great elements are the conditions for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and they are its predominant condition.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" has the four great elements as its one predominant condition.
The faculty of "I have known" (*ājñātendriya*) and the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) are also thus. This concludes the section on the faculties.
For what reason do the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise, abide, and perish together, yet are not associated (*asaṃprayukta*);
whereas the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika dharma*) arise, abide, and perish together, yet are associated (*saṃprayukta*)?
Answer: As it is said, one may attain the four great elements whether they be large or small, yet these are not mental states or mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Furthermore, while mental states and mental factors share common objects of perception (*ālambana*), the four great elements have no such objects; that which lacks an object cannot be associated (*samprayukta*) with others.
Is there that which is composed of the past four great elements (mahābhūta) and yet consists of past, future, or present form?
Answer: Yes, there is.
Is there that which is derived from the four great elements of the future and is a form of the future?
Answer: Yes;
there is such, but not that which belongs to the past or the present.
Is there that which is currently produced by the four great elements and is currently form?
Answer: There is;
there is none that is past, but there is that which is future.
If one accomplishes the past four great elements, does one also accomplish the past derived matter?
Answer: There is no accomplishment of the past four great elements, yet there is accomplishment of past derived matter.

When a stainless person dwells in the mother’s womb within the thickening layers of the chorion and amnion; or if they are born in the desire realm, whether in a state of moral discipline, a state of non-discipline, or a state that is neither disciplined nor undisciplined, and their original bodily and vocal informative acts (*vijñapti*) are not lost; or if they are born in the form realm; or if they are a learner (*śaikṣa*) born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes the past four great elements, does one also accomplish the future four great elements?
Answer:
There is no one who accomplishes the past four great elements and yet does not also accomplish the future four great elements.
If one accomplishes the past four great elements (*mahābhūta*), does one also accomplish future derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)? Answer:

There is no one who accomplishes the past four great elements, yet there is one who accomplishes future derived matter: namely, a stainless person (*vimala-pudgala*) abiding in the mother’s womb during the stages of the membrane and the thickening of the embryo; or one born in the desire realm who has attained a wholesome mind of the form realm; or one born in the form realm; or a stainless person born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes the past four great elements, does one also accomplish the present four great elements?
Answer:
There is no one who accomplishes the past four great elements; there are those who accomplish the present four great elements, namely, those born in the desire realm and the form realm.
If one accomplishes the past four great elements, does one accomplish present derived matter?
Answer:

There is no accomplishment of the past four great elements; there is accomplishment of present derived matter for those born in the desire realm or the form realm. [The section on the past four great elements is concluded.]
If one accomplishes past derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), does that person accomplish future primary elements (mahābhūta)?
Answer: There is no accomplishment of future primary elements, but there is accomplishment of past derived matter.

When a stainless person dwells in the mother’s womb and the fetal membranes gradually thicken, or if they are born into the desire realm—whether in a state of moral discipline, a state of non-discipline, or a state that is neither moral discipline nor non-discipline—their original bodily and vocal informative acts (*vijñapti*) are not lost; this also applies if they are born into the form realm or are a learner (*śaikṣa*) born into the formless realm.
If one accomplishes past derived matter, does one also accomplish future derived matter?
Answer:
One may accomplish past derived matter without accomplishing future derived matter.
How is it that one accomplishes past derived matter but not future derived matter?
Answer: One is born in the desire realm in a state of moral discipline, yet does not attain a wholesome mind of the form realm.

In a state that is neither unvirtuous nor non-unvirtuous, where the original teachings of body and speech have not been lost, this is called accomplishing past derived matter, but not future derived matter.
How is it that one accomplishes future derived matter but not past derived matter?
The answer is:
an Arhat born in the formless realm; this is called accomplishing future derived matter but not past derived matter.
How does one accomplish past derived matter and future derived matter?
The answer is:

an undefiled person who is in the mother’s womb during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana; or one born in the desire realm who attains a wholesome mind of the form realm; or one born in the form realm; or one training in the formless realm—these are said to accomplish past derived matter and future derived matter.
What is meant by not accomplishing past and future derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is in the mother’s womb during the stages of the embryo and the thickening of the membrane; or when one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and abides in a state that is neither disciplined nor undisciplined, such that there was originally no informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of body or speech, or any informative intimation that arose has been lost; or when an ordinary person is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This is called not accomplishing past and future derived matter.
If one accomplishes past derived matter, does one also accomplish present primary elements?
Answer:
One may accomplish past derived matter without accomplishing present primary elements.
How is it that one accomplishes past derived matter but not present primary elements?
Answer: A learner born in the formless realm; this is called accomplishing past derived matter but not present primary elements.
What is it to accomplish the present four great elements (*mahābhūta*) but not the past derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is in the mother’s womb, within the membranes and the thickening layers; or when born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), abiding neither in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*) nor in the state of non-discipline (*aśīla*); and whose body and speech have no prior informative action (*vijñapti*), or if such action existed, it has been lost—this is called accomplishing the present four great elements but not the past derived matter.
How does one accomplish past derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and present primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
The answer is:

an undefiled person (*vimala-pudgala*) while in the mother’s womb during the stages of the embryo and the thickening of the membranes; or, having been born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whether abiding in the state of moral discipline (*śīla*), in the state of non-discipline (*aśīla*), or in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, such that the original informative acts (*vijñapti*) of body and speech have not been lost.
If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), this is called "accomplishing past derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) and present primary elements (mahābhūta).
What is it to not accomplish past derived matter and present primary elements?
Answer: Arhats and ordinary persons born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are said not to possess past derived matter (upādāyarūpa) nor present primary elements (mahābhūta).
If one possesses past derived matter, does that person also possess present derived matter?
Answer: One may accomplish past derived matter but not present derived matter.
How does one accomplish past derived matter but not present derived matter?
Answer: One who is a student (śaikṣa) born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is said to possess past derived matter (bhautika-rūpa), but not present derived matter.
How does one possess present derived matter but not past derived matter?
Answer:

When an ordinary person is in the mother’s womb within the layers of the egg-membrane, or when born in the desire realm neither in a state of moral discipline nor in a state of non-discipline, their body and speech originally lack informative intimation (*vijñapti*), or if such intimation exists it is immediately lost; this is called being accomplished with present derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) but not with past derived matter.
How does one accomplish past derived matter and present derived matter?
The answer is:

an undefiled person who is in the mother’s womb or within the stages of the egg and membrane; or, if born in the desire realm, whether abiding in the state of moral discipline, in the state of non-discipline, or in the state of neither discipline nor non-discipline, such that they have not lost the original informative acts of body and speech.
If one is born in the form realm, this is called being endowed with past derived matter and present derived matter.
What is meant by not being endowed with past derived matter and present derived matter?
Answer:

When Arhats and ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) are born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), this is called "not accomplishing past and present derived matter" (bhautika-rūpa). [End of section on past derived matter.]
If one accomplishes the four great elements of the future, does one accomplish the derived matter of the future?
Answer: There is no accomplishment of the four great elements of the future, but there is accomplishment of the derived matter of the future.

An immaculate person (vimala-pudgala) while dwelling in the mother’s womb, as the layers of the chorion gradually thicken; or one born in the desire realm who attains a wholesome mind of the form realm; or an immaculate person born in the form realm; or one born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes the four great elements of the future, does one also accomplish the four great elements of the present?
Answer:

There is no one who accomplishes the four great elements of the future, but there are those who accomplish the four great elements of the present—namely, those born in the desire realm or the form realm.
If one accomplishes the four great elements of the future, does one accomplish the derived matter of the present?
Answer:

There is no accomplishment of the four great elements of the future, yet there is accomplishment of the derived matter of the present, up to the point of being born in the desire or form realms where the four great elements of the future are completed.
If one accomplishes future derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), does one accomplish the present four great elements (mahābhūta)?
Answer:
One may accomplish future derived matter without accomplishing the present four great elements.
How is it that one achieves future derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) but not present primary elements (*mahābhūta*)? Answer:
When an undefiled person (*vimala-pudgala*) is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called achieving future derived matter but not present primary elements.
What is it to accomplish the present four great elements (*mahābhūta*) but not the future derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)?
The answer is:

an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) dwelling in the mother’s womb during the stages of the embryo and the thickening membrane, or one born in the desire realm who has not attained a wholesome mind of the form realm—this is called accomplishing the present four great elements but not the future derived matter.
How does one accomplish future derived matter and present primary elements?
The answer is:

an undefiled person remaining in the mother’s womb during the stages of the embryo and the thickening of the membranes; or, having been born in the desire realm, attaining a wholesome mind of the form realm; or, being born in the form realm. This is called accomplishing future derived matter and present primary elements.
What is meant by not possessing future derived matter and present primary elements?
The answer is:
an ordinary person born in the formless realm; this is called not possessing future derived matter and present primary elements.
If one accomplishes future derived matter, does one also accomplish present derived matter?
Answer:
One may accomplish future derived matter without accomplishing present derived matter.
What is it to accomplish future derived matter but not present derived matter?
The answer is:
when a stainless person is born into the formless realm, this is called accomplishing future derived matter but not present derived matter.
What is it to achieve present derived matter but not future derived matter?
The answer is:

an ordinary person dwelling in the mother’s womb during the stages of the ovum and the thickening membrane, or one born in the desire realm who has not attained a wholesome mind of the form realm—this is called achieving present derived matter but not achieving future derived matter.
How does one accomplish future and present derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)?
The answer is:

an undefiled person (*anāsrava-pudgala*) who is in the mother’s womb during the stages of the membrane and the thickening of the embryo; or one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who has attained a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); or one born in the form realm. This is called accomplishing future and present derived matter.
What is meant by not accomplishing future and present derived matter?
The answer is:
an ordinary person born in the formless realm; this is called not accomplishing future and present derived matter. [The section on present derived matter is concluded.]
If one accomplishes the present four great elements, does one accomplish the present derived matter?
Answer: It is so.
If one achieves present derived matter (bhautika-rūpa), does one achieve the present four great elements (mahābhūta)?
Answer: It is so.
Thus ends the accomplishment [of dharmas] across the three periods of time.
Past great elements are the cause and the predominance condition for those past great elements.
Past great elements are the cause and the predominance condition for past derived matter.
Past derived matter is the cause and the predominance condition for that past derived matter.
Past derived matter is the cause and the predominant condition for past primary elements.
Past primary elements are the cause and the predominant condition for future primary elements.
