Future primary elements are the cause and the predominant condition for those same future primary elements.
The four great elements of the future are the single dominant condition for the four great elements of the past.
The four great elements of the past are the cause and the dominant condition for the derived matter of the future.
The derived matter of the future is the cause and the dominant condition for that same derived matter of the future.
Future derived matter has the past four great elements as its single predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The past four great elements are the cause and the predominant condition for present four great elements.
Present four great elements are the cause and the predominant condition for those present four great elements.
Present primary elements (mahābhūta) are the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) for past primary elements.
Past primary elements are the cause and the dominant condition for present derived matter (upādāya-rūpa).
Present derived matter is the cause and the dominant condition for that same present derived matter.
Present derived matter has past primary elements as its single predominant condition (adhipati-paccaya). [End of section on past primary elements.
Past derived matter has future primary elements as its cause-condition (hetu-paccaya) and predominant condition.
Future great elements (mahābhūta) are a single dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) for past derived matter (upādāya-rūpa).
Past derived matter is a cause and a dominant condition for future derived matter.
Future derived matter is a single dominant condition for past derived matter.
Past derived matter is the cause and the predominant condition for present primary elements.
Present primary elements are the single predominant condition for past derived matter.
Past derived matter is the cause and the predominant condition for present derived matter.
Present derived matter is the dominant condition for past derived matter. [The section on] past derived matter is concluded.
Future primary elements are the cause and dominant condition for future derived matter.
Future derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) has future primary elements (mahābhūta) as its cause and predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Future primary elements have present primary elements as their sole predominant condition.
Present primary elements have future primary elements as their cause and predominant condition.
The four great elements of the future have one predominance with respect to the derived matter of the present.
The derived matter of the present has [the four great elements] of the future as its cause and its predominance. This concludes the section on the four great elements of the future.
Future derived matter has one predominance with respect to present primary elements.
Present primary elements are both cause and predominance with respect to future derived matter.
Future derived matter has one predominance with respect to present derived matter.
Present derived matter is the cause and the predominant condition for future derived matter. [The section on] future derived matter is concluded.
Present primary elements are the cause and the predominant condition for present derived matter.
Present derived matter has present primary elements as its cause and predominant condition; thus ends the section on the three time periods.
If one possesses the primary elements bound to the desire realm, does one also possess the derived matter bound to the desire realm?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes derived matter bound to the desire realm, does one also accomplish the four great elements bound to the desire realm?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the four great elements bound to the form realm, does one also accomplish the derived matter bound to the form realm?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes the four great elements bound to the realm of form, one accomplishes the derived matter bound to the realm of form.
Is it possible, however, to accomplish derived matter bound to the realm of form without accomplishing the four great elements bound to the realm of form?
Answer: There is.
When one born in the desire realm attains a wholesome mind of the form realm, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm do not manifest.
The four great elements bound to the desire realm serve as the cause and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for those [elements].
The four great elements bound to the desire realm are the cause and the predominant condition for derived matter bound to the desire realm.
Derived matter bound to the desire realm is the cause and the predominant condition for that same derived matter bound to the desire realm.
The derived matter bound to the desire realm has as its causes and predominant conditions the great elements bound to the desire realm.
The great elements bound to the form realm have as their causes and predominant conditions those great elements bound to the form realm.

The four great elements bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-mahābhūta) are the cause and the predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) for derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) bound to the realm of form.
Derived matter bound to the realm of form is the cause and the predominant condition for that same derived matter bound to the realm of form.
Derived matter bound to the form realm has as its causes and predominant conditions the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the form realm.
If one possesses the primary elements bound to the desire realm, does one also possess the primary elements bound to the form realm?
Answer:
One may be endowed with the four great elements bound to the desire realm but not with the four great elements bound to the form realm.
How is one endowed with the four great elements bound to the desire realm but not with the four great elements bound to the form realm?
Answer:

One born in the desire realm for whom the four great elements of the form realm are not present before them—this is called accomplishing the four great elements bound to the desire realm, but not the four great elements bound to the form realm.

What is it to possess the four great elements bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-mahābhūta*) but not the four great elements bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-mahābhūta*)?
The answer is:

one who is born in the form realm, who manifests or does not manifest emanations of the desire realm, and who does not produce speech of the desire realm; this is called possessing the four great elements bound to the form realm but not the four great elements bound to the desire realm.
How does one achieve the four great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm and the form realm?
The answer is:
being born in the desire realm, the four great elements of the form realm manifest before one.

If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and manifests a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) in the desire realm that utters the speech of the desire realm, this is called being endowed with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to both the desire realm and the form realm.
What is it to not be endowed with the four great elements bound to the desire realm and not be endowed with the four great elements bound to the form realm?

Answer: One born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is said to be non-possessed of the four great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and not possessed of the four great elements bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu).
If one is possessed of the four great elements bound to the desire realm, is that person also possessed of the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) bound to the form realm?
Answer:

One may achieve the four great elements bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-mahābhūta) without achieving the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
How does one achieve the four great elements bound to the desire realm without achieving the derived matter bound to the form realm?
Answer:

One who is born in the desire realm but has not attained a wholesome mind of the form realm is said to be endowed with the four great elements bound to the desire realm, but not with the derived matter bound to the form realm.
How is one endowed with the derived matter bound to the form realm, but not with the four great elements bound to the desire realm?
Answer:

One born in the form realm who manifests a transformation-body in the desire realm does not produce speech of the desire realm; this is called accomplishing derived matter bound to the form realm, but not the four great elements bound to the desire realm.
How does one accomplish the four great elements bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who attains a wholesome mind of the form realm, or one born in the form realm who manifests a transformation-body of the desire realm and utters speech of the desire realm; this is called accomplishing the four great elements bound to the desire realm and the derived matter bound to the form realm.
What is it that one does not possess: the four great elements bound to the desire realm, but not the derived matter bound to the form realm?
Answer: One born in the formless realm; this is what is called not possessing the four great elements bound to the desire realm, but not the derived matter bound to the form realm.
If one accomplishes derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) bound to the desire realm, does that person accomplish the four great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the form realm?
Answer:
There are cases where one accomplishes derived matter bound to the desire realm but does not accomplish the four great elements bound to the form realm.
How is it that one accomplishes derived matter bound to the desire realm but not the four great elements bound to the form realm?
The answer is:

being born in the desire realm, when the four great elements of the form realm do not manifest before one; this is called accomplishing derived matter bound to the desire realm but not the four great elements bound to the form realm.
What is it to achieve the four great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the form realm, but not the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) bound to the desire realm?
Answer:

One who is born in the form realm, and who neither manifests a transformation-body (nirmāṇa) of the desire realm nor produces speech of the desire realm—this is called achieving the four great elements bound to the form realm, but not the derived matter bound to the desire realm.
How does one accomplish derived matter bound to the desire realm while possessing the four great elements bound to the form realm?
The answer is:
being born in the desire realm, the four great elements of the form realm manifest before one.

If one is born in the form realm and manifests a transformation body in the desire realm that utters the speech of the desire realm, this is called "accomplishing derived matter bound to the desire realm while possessing the four great elements bound to the form realm.
What is meant by not accomplishing derived matter bound to the desire realm while possessing the four great elements bound to the form realm?
What is it that one does not possess as derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) bound to the desire realm, yet does not lack the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the form realm?
The answer is:
one born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); this is called not possessing derived matter bound to the desire realm while not lacking the four great elements bound to the form realm.
If one accomplishes derived matter bound to the desire realm, does one accomplish derived matter bound to the form realm?
Answer:
One may accomplish derived matter bound to the desire realm without accomplishing derived matter bound to the form realm.
How does one accomplish derived matter bound to the desire realm but not derived matter bound to the form realm?
Answer:

One who is born in the desire realm and has not attained a wholesome mind of the form realm; this is called accomplishing derived matter bound to the desire realm but not derived matter bound to the form realm.
How does one accomplish derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) but not derived matter bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
The answer is:

one who is born in the form realm, whether manifesting a transformation-body (*nirmāṇa*) or not, and does not produce speech of the desire realm—this is called accomplishing derived matter bound to the form realm but not derived matter bound to the desire realm.
How does one accomplish both derived matter bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-nirmāṇarūpa*) and derived matter bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-nirmāṇarūpa*)?
The answer is:

one who is born in the desire realm and attains a wholesome mind of the form realm, or one who is born in the form realm and manifests a transformation-body of the desire realm to speak the language of the desire realm—this is called accomplishing both derived matter bound to the desire realm and derived matter bound to the form realm.
What is it that does not accomplish derived matter bound to the desire realm and does not accomplish derived matter bound to the form realm?
The answer is:
one born in the formless realm; this is called not accomplishing derived matter bound to the desire realm and not accomplishing derived matter bound to the form realm.
The four great elements bound to the desire realm have one [great element] bound to the form realm as their dominant condition.
The four great elements bound to the form realm have one [great element] bound to the desire realm as their dominant condition.
The four great elements bound to the desire realm are a single dominant condition for the derived matter bound to the form realm.
Derived matter bound to the form realm is a single dominant condition for the four great elements bound to the desire realm.
The derived matter bound to the desire realm has the four great elements bound to the form realm as its single predominant condition.
The four great elements bound to the form realm have the derived matter bound to the desire realm as their single predominant condition.
Conditioned matter bound to the desire realm is the single dominant condition for conditioned matter bound to the form realm;
conditioned matter bound to the form realm is likewise the single dominant condition for conditioned matter bound to the desire realm.
Regarding those forms that are bound to the desire realm, are all those forms produced by the four great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm?
Answer:
Some forms are bound to the desire realm, yet those forms are not produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm.
What is the case where matter is bound to the desire realm, yet that matter is not produced by the great elements bound to the desire realm?
Answer: The great elements bound to the desire realm; this is called matter bound to the desire realm that is not produced by the great elements bound to the desire realm.
What is form that is produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm, yet that form is not bound to the desire realm?
Answer:

It refers to all forms that are unbound (not belonging to any realm) and are produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm; this is called form produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm, yet that form is not bound to the desire realm.
What is form that is bound to the desire realm and is produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm?
The answer is:

all forms that are bound to the desire realm and are produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm; this is called form that is bound to the desire realm and is produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm.
What is form that is not bound to the desire realm, yet that form is not created by the four great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm?
The answer is:

forms bound to the form realm that are created by the four great elements bound to the form realm; and forms that are unbound (not belonging to any realm) that are created by the four great elements bound to the form realm. This is called form that is not bound to the desire realm, yet that form is not created by the four great elements bound to the desire realm.
Regarding all forms that are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), are all those forms produced by the four great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the realm of form?
Answer:
Some forms are bound to the realm of form, yet those forms are not produced by the four great elements bound to the realm of form.
What is that matter which is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), yet that matter is not produced by the great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the realm of form? Answer:
The great elements bound to the realm of form—this is called matter bound to the realm of form that is not produced by the great elements bound to the realm of form.

What is meant by "matter that is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) being produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the realm of form, yet that matter itself is not bound to the realm of form"?
The answer is:

all matter that is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*) is produced by the four great elements bound to the realm of form; this is called "matter that is bound to the realm of form being produced by the four great elements bound to the realm of form, yet that matter itself is not bound to the realm of form."
What is matter that is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and which is produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the realm of form? Answer:

All matter that is bound to the realm of form and produced by the four great elements bound to the realm of form—this is called matter that is bound to the realm of form and produced by the four great elements bound to the realm of form.
What is form that is not bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), yet that form is produced by the great elements (mahābhūta) that are not bound to the realm of form?
The answer is:

forms bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) produced by the great elements bound to the desire realm; and forms that are unbound (anupādhiśeṣa) produced by the great elements bound to the desire realm. This is called form that is not bound to the realm of form, yet that form is produced by the great elements that are not bound to the realm of form.
Regarding all forms that are past, are all those forms produced by the past four great elements?
Answer: Some forms that are past are not produced by the past four great elements.
What is form that is past, yet that form is not produced by past great elements?
Answer: Past great elements; this is called form that is past, yet that form is not produced by past great elements.
What is meant by "matter is produced by the past four great elements, yet that matter is not past"?
The answer is:
all matter that is future or present and is produced by the past four great elements—this is called "matter produced by the past four great elements, yet that matter is not past."
What is form that is past, and that past form is derived from the four great elements of the past?
The answer is:
all forms that are past and are derived from the four great elements of the past; this is called form that is past, and that past form is derived from the four great elements of the past.
What is form that is not past, yet that form is not created by the four great elements (mahābhūta) of the past?
The answer is:

forms of the future and present created by the four great elements of the future and present; and forms of the future created by the four great elements of the future. This is called form that is not past, yet that form is not created by the four great elements of the past.
Regarding all forms that are future, are all those forms produced by the four great elements of the future?
Answer: It is so;
all forms that are future are produced by the four great elements of the future, and all such forms are indeed future.
Is there any form that is future, yet not produced by the four great elements of the future?
Answer: There is;
[there are] forms of the future produced by the four great elements of the future, as well as those produced by the four great elements of the past and present.
Regarding all forms that are present, are all those forms produced by the present four great elements?
The answer is:
there may be forms that are present, yet those forms are not produced by the present four great elements.
What is meant by "matter is present, yet that matter is not produced by present primary elements"?
The answer is:

when present primary elements produce various matters that are present but were produced by past primary elements; this is called "matter is present, yet that matter is not produced by present primary elements."
What is meant by "matter is produced from the four great elements of the present, yet that matter is not of the present"?
The answer is:

all matter that is produced from the four great elements of the future and the present; this is called "matter produced from the four great elements of the present, yet that matter is not of the present."
What is form that is present and that form is produced from the present four great elements? Answer:
All forms that are present and are produced from the present four great elements—this is called form that is present and that form is produced from the present four great elements.
What is meant by "matter that is not present" and "that matter is not produced from the four great elements of the present"?
The answer is:

all matter of the past and future is produced from the four great elements of the past and future; all matter of the future is produced from the four great elements of the future. This is called matter that is not present and that matter is not produced from the four great elements of the present.

Regarding a disciple of the Blessed One who has realized the Truths (dṛṣṭisampanna) but whose craving for sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) is not yet exhausted: they possess the bodily and vocal moral discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Of what four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is that form composed?
Answer: It is bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).

When one born in the desire realm enters the first dhyāna with outflows, or enters the second, third, or fourth dhyānas with outflows, those various bodily and vocal precepts—of what four great elements (mahābhūta) are those forms produced?
Answer: It is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

When one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) enters the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna, or enters the untainted second, third, or fourth dhyānas, by what four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are those bodily and vocal precepts (*śīla*) of theirs produced?
Answer: They are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

When one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) enters the first dhyāna with outflows (*sāsrava*), or enters the second, third, or fourth dhyānas with outflows, those bodily and vocal moral restraints (*śīla*)—what four great elements (*mahābhūta*) do those forms (*rūpa*) arise from?
Answer: They are bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

When one born in the realm of form enters the first *dhyāna* by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*), or enters the second, third, or fourth *dhyānas* by means of the untainted—what are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitute those bodily and vocal moral restraints (*śīla-saṃvara*)?
Answer: It is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

When a disciple of the Blessed One is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they possess various untainted (*anāsrava*) bodily and vocal moral disciplines (*śīla-saṃvara*); by what four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are those forms produced?
Answer: It is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
When one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm, one first acquires the four great elements; of those four great elements, what are the causes?
Answer: It is bound to the desire realm.
When one passes away from the formless realm and is first born into the form realm, one obtains the four great elements; what are the causes of those four great elements?
Answer: It is bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).

When one passes away from the realm of form and is first born into the desire realm (kāmadhātu), one acquires the four great elements (mahābhūta). Of those four great elements, what are they caused by?
Answer: It is bound to the desire realm.
When one born in the desire realm manifests a transformation-body in the form realm and produces speech of the form realm, by what four great elements is that form produced?
Answer: It is bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
When one born in the realm of form manifests a transformation-body in the realm of desire and utters speech of the realm of desire, by which four great elements (mahābhūta) is that form produced?
Answer: It is bound to the desire realm.
Should it be said that the transformation consists of the four great elements, or does it not consist of the four great elements?
Answer: Regarding a transformation-body (nirmāṇa), should it be said to consist of the four great elements (mahābhūta)?
Should it be said to consist of derived matter (upādāyarūpa) or non-derived matter?
Answer: It should be said that it is derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Should it be said that it possesses mind (*sacittaka*) or is without mind (*acittaka*)?
Answer: It is without mind.
One should ask: whose mind is used to speak?
Answer: A transformation being speaks with the mind.
Regarding the intermediate state (antarābhava), should it be said to consist of the four great elements or not?
Answer: Regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), should it be said to consist of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Should it be said to consist of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) or non-derived matter (*anupādāyarūpa*)?
Answer: It should be said that it is derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Should it be said that it possesses mind (*sacitta*) or is without mind (*acitta*)?
Answer: One should say that there is a mind.
But whose mind should one say is being used to speak?
Answer: It should be said that one speaks with words using one's own mind.
What phenomenon does the world name this?
Answer: It is the name for a number of occurrences.
What phenomenon is called a kalpa?
Answer: [These are] the names for the number of months, fortnights, seasons, springs, and years.
What dharma is named "the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the mind"?
Answer: "Time" (*kāla*) is a designation for a brief duration.
Are there any phenomena that arise from four conditions?
Answer: Yes, they arise.
Do all minds and mental factors arise from three conditions?
Answer: It arises.
Do the two attainments—the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation—arise through conditions?
Answer: Yes, they arise.
With the exception of the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation, do all other formations dissociated from mind and matter arise from a single condition?
Answer: It does not arise.
How, then, can dharmas be associated with causes?
Answer: All minds and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*).
What are the phenomena that are dissociated from causes (*viprayuktahetu*)?
Answer: Form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.
What are those dharmas that have associated causes and dissociated causes?
Answer: That mind and mental factors are associated with causes in some respects and dissociated from causes in others.
What kind of dharma is neither associated with causes nor dissociated from causes?
Answer:
Those minds and mental factors are neither slightly dissociated from their causes nor slightly non-dissociated from their causes.
What is a dharma that serves as a common object-condition (*sālambana-pratyaya*)?
Answer: All groups of mental consciousness are associated with the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta) as their common objects of perception (ālambana).
What, then, are phenomena that are not common objects of perception?
Answer: The various groups of the five consciousnesses take as their objects form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind that are associated with them.
What is a dharma that is both a common object-condition and a non-common object-condition?
Answer:

The various groups of the five consciousnesses, together with the corresponding groups of mental consciousness, take as their objects the mind and mental factors that correspond to them, as well as matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from the mind.
What is a dharma that is neither a common object-condition nor a non-common object-condition?
Answer: Form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.

"There is the perception of formlessness."
What is meant by "the perception of formlessness"? The answer is:

when this body is about to die or has already died; when it is about to be cast into a cemetery or has already been cast into a cemetery; when it is about to be buried in the earth or has already been buried in the earth; when it is about to be devoured by various kinds of worms or has already been devoured by various kinds of worms; when it is about to be scattered in various places or has already been scattered in various places—one does not contemplate this body, nor does one see those various worms.

In this way, when this body is about to die, has died; is about to be cast into a cemetery, has been cast into a cemetery; is about to be piled with firewood, has been piled with firewood; is about to be burned by fire, has been burned by fire; and is about to be extinguished, has been extinguished—one does not contemplate this body nor does one see the fire.

Just as a mass of snow, or congealed butter, or clarified butter, when placed upon a fire, will melt away once it has been placed there, and will be extinguished once it has melted—so too, he does not contemplate this body, nor does he perceive the fire.
In this way, there are those who possess the perception of the formless and those who possess form but lack perception; are all such persons completely exhausted of craving for form?
Answer: Yes.

It is so. All those who possess form and are non-percipient have exhausted their craving for form; however, is it possible that one has exhausted craving for form yet is not among those who possess form and are non-percipient?
The answer is: Yes.
If one has exhausted craving for form but does not enter meditative absorption, are all those who do not possess form or non-perception ones whose craving for form is not yet exhausted?
Answer: Yes.
It is so. For all those who have not yet exhausted craving for form, they all lack both form and perception; is there anyone who lacks both form and perception yet has not exhausted craving for form?
Answer: There are those who have exhausted craving for form but do not enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Regarding the four stations of consciousness and the seven stations of consciousness: does the inclusion of the four stations of consciousness encompass the seven stations of consciousness?
Answer: Sometimes there are four but not seven.
What are the four that are not seven?
The answer is:

the form, feeling, perception, and formations of the hells; the form, feeling, perception, and formations of animals, hungry ghosts, and the gods of the Fruit of the Body (*bṛhatphala*); and the feeling, perception, and formations of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these are called the four that are not seven.
What are the seven that are not four?
The answer is:

the minds of humans, the gods of the desire realm, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Ākāśānantyāyatana, the Vijñānānantyāyatana, and the Ākiṃcanyāyatana; these are called the seven that are not four.
What are the four sets of seven?
The answer is:

the form, feeling, perception, and formations of humans and the gods of the desire realm; the form, feeling, perception, and formations of the Brahmakāyika, Ābhāsvara, and Śubhakṛtsna heavens; and the feeling, perception, and formations of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness. These are called the four sets of seven.
What is neither fourfold nor sevenfold?
The answer is:

the mind of hell-beings, the minds of animals, hungry ghosts, the fruit-realm beings, and the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these are called neither fourfold nor sevenfold.
Regarding the four stations of consciousness and the nine abodes of sentient beings: do the four stations of consciousness encompass the nine abodes of sentient beings?
The answer is:
they may be four but not nine.
What are the four that are not nine?
The answer is:

the form, sensation, perception, and formations of hell; and the form, sensation, perception, and formations of animals, hungry ghosts, and non-percipient beings that are not included within the fruit of retribution—these are called the four that are not nine.
What are the nine that are not four?
The answer is:

the minds of humans, gods of the desire realm, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the beings of the non-percipient realm, and the minds of the formless realm—these are called the nine that are not four.
What are the four groups of nine?
The answer is:

the form, feeling, perception, and formations of humans and the gods of the desire realm; the form, feeling, perception, and formations of the Brahmakāyika, Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and Asaṃjñisattva gods; and the feeling, perception, and formations of the formless realm. These are called the four groups of nine.
What is meant by "neither four nor nine"?
The answer is:
the mind of hell-beings, the minds of animals, hungry ghosts, and the fruit-minds not included among the beings of non-perception—these are called "neither four nor nine."

Regarding the seven stations of consciousness and the nine abodes of sentient beings: do the seven stations of consciousness encompass the nine abodes of sentient beings, or do the nine abodes of sentient beings encompass the seven stations of consciousness?
Answer: Nine and seven, not seven and nine.
What is not included?
Answer: There are two places:
the beings in the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

This concludes the third chapter on "Seeing the Truths" (*Dṛṣṭivarga*), consisting of one hundred and sixty-nine *śloka*s in the Sanskrit original and two thousand nine hundred and twenty words in the Qin translation.

4. In the fourth chapter on Internal Formations (*adhyātma-abhisamskāra-varga*) within the *Abhidharma-mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the section on the Four Great Elements: Regarding those internal great elements, by how many conditions do they condition internal great elements and non-internal great elements?
Regarding the non-internal great elements (*mahābhūta*), how many conditions do those non-internal great elements serve as conditions for other non-internal great elements?

Regarding associated factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*), how many conditions do those associated factors serve as conditions for associated factors and dissociated factors (*viprayuktadharma*)? How many conditions do associated factors serve as conditions for dissociated factors?
Regarding dissociated factors as causes: how many conditions do those dissociated causal factors serve as conditions for other dissociated causal factors and for associated causal factors?
Regarding co-arising factors: how many conditions do those co-arising factors serve as conditions for other co-arising factors and for non-object-conditions (anālambana) factors?
Regarding non-object-conditioned phenomena (*anālambana-dharma*), how many conditions do those non-object-conditioned phenomena act as conditions for other non-object-conditioned phenomena?

Regarding material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), how many conditions do those material phenomena act as conditions for [other] material phenomena? [Regarding] material and immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*), [how many conditions do they act as conditions for] immaterial phenomena?
How many conditions do those formless phenomena serve as conditions for formless phenomena and for form phenomena?
The same applies to the visible and the invisible, and to the resistant and the non-resistant.
Regarding outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), how many conditions do they serve as conditions for outflowing phenomena and for outflow-free phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*)?
Regarding untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), by how many conditions do those untainted phenomena condition other untainted phenomena and tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*)?
Regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), by how many conditions do those conditioned phenomena condition conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
Regarding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*): how many conditions do those unconditioned phenomena serve as conditions for other unconditioned phenomena and conditioned phenomena?
As for that which is bound by its own fetters (*saṃyojana*) and undergoes existence in hell, it acquires the various faculties (*indriya*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
By how many conditions are those sense-faculties and the four great elements conditioned by that mind and its mental factors?
By how many conditions are that mind and its mental factors conditioned by those sense-faculties and the four great elements?

Regarding those sense-faculties and the four great elements acquired by one who is bound by their own bonds and is reborn among animals, hungry ghosts, devas, or humans—by how many conditions are those sense-faculties and the four great elements conditioned by that mind and its mental factors?
By how many conditions do those minds and mental factors condition those faculties and the four great elements?

When one is born in the desire realm and enters the tainted first dhyāna, or even enters the tainted state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, those faculties grow and increase, and the four great elements augment those faculties. By how many conditions do those four great elements condition those minds and mental factors?
By how many conditions are those minds and mental factors conditioned by those faculties and those four great elements?

When one is born in the desire realm and enters the untainted first dhyāna, or the untainted states up to the sphere of nothingness, those faculties and four great elements increase; by how many conditions are those faculties and four great elements conditioned by those minds and mental factors?
By how many conditions are those minds and mental factors conditioned by those faculties and the four great elements?

When one born in the form realm enters the first dhyāna with outflows, or even enters the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with outflows, those faculties and four great elements are augmented. By how many conditions are those faculties and four great elements conditioned by those minds and mental factors?
By how many conditions are those minds and mental factors conditioned by those faculties and the four great elements?

When one born in the form realm enters the untainted first dhyāna, or up to the untainted state of entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, those faculties and four great elements are augmented. By how many conditions are those faculties and four great elements conditioned by those minds and mental factors?
By how many conditions are those minds and mental factors conditioned by those faculties and the four great elements?
What is the meaning of "internal"?
What is the meaning of "not internal"?
What is the meaning of "feeling" (vedanā)?
What is the meaning of "non-feeling"?
What is the meaning of "fetter" (saṃyojana)?
What is the meaning of "non-bondage"?
What is the meaning of "basis for views"?
What is the meaning of "non-basis for views"?
Regarding all phenomena that are internal, are those phenomena comprised within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*)?
Conversely, if phenomena are comprised within the internal bases, are those phenomena internal?

Regarding all phenomena that are external, are those phenomena comprised within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*)? Conversely, if phenomena are comprised within the external bases, are those phenomena external?
Regarding the two types of feeling and the three types of feeling: do the two types of feeling subsume the three types of feeling, or do the three types of feeling subsume the two types of feeling?

Regarding the two types of feeling, the four types of feeling, the five types of feeling, the six types of feeling, the eighteen types of feeling, the thirty-six types of feeling, and the one hundred and eight types of feeling: do the two types of feeling subsume the one hundred and eight types of feeling, or do the one hundred and eight types of feeling subsume the two types of feeling?

Up to thirty-six types of feeling and one hundred and eight types of feeling: do the thirty-six types of feeling subsume the one hundred and eight types of feeling, or do the one hundred and eight types of feeling subsume the thirty-six?

When one proceeds toward the fruit of *srotāpanna* by means of the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) and realizes that path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), how many applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are cultivated as present, and how many are cultivated for the future? How many right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), paths (*mārgāṅga*), dhyānas, immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), knowledges (*jñāna*), and samādhis are cultivated as present, and how many are cultivated for the future? Furthermore, when proceeding toward the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, the supernormal powers of flying, divine hearing, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, clairvoyance, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) by means of the path of non-obstruction, [how many are cultivated as present and how many for the future]?

When cultivating that path, how many applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are cultivated as being present before one, and how many are cultivated for the future? How many right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), how many bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), how many faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), how many factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), how many factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), how many dhyānas, how many meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), how many formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), how many liberations (*vimokṣa*), how many spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), how many spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and how many knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated? How many concentrations (*samādhi*) are cultivated as being present before one, and how many are cultivated for the future?
I wish to explain fully the meaning of this chapter.
The internal four great elements are the cause and the predominant condition for those internal four great elements.
The internal four great elements are the cause and the predominant condition for the non-internal four great elements.
The non-internal great elements are not the cause or the predominance condition for those non-internal great elements.
The non-internal great elements are the cause and the predominance condition for the internal great elements.
For associated phenomena, those associated phenomena are the cause, the immediate condition, the object condition, and the predominance condition.
Factors associated with causes are related to factors dissociated from causes by way of cause, sequence, and predominance, but not by way of object.
Factors dissociated from causes are related to those same factors dissociated from causes by way of cause and predominance.
Conditioned by a dissociated dharma, a conjoined dharma is related as cause, object-condition, and predominance, but not as sequence.
Conditioned by a co-object-conditioned dharma, that co-object-conditioned dharma is related as cause, sequence, object-condition, and predominance.
Regarding dharmas that have common objects: they are causes, immediate antecedents, and predominant conditions for dharmas without objects, but they do not have [those] as their objects.
Regarding dharmas without objects: those dharmas without objects are their causes and predominant conditions.

Non-object-conditioned phenomena (anālambana-dharma) are causes, objects, and predominant conditions for co-object-conditioned phenomena (sālambana-dharma), but there is no sequence-condition (anantara-pratyaya).
Material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) are causes, objects, and predominant conditions for those same material phenomena.
Form-phenomena (rūpa-dharma) are the cause, condition, and predominant condition for formless phenomena (arūpa-dharma), but they do not constitute a sequence-condition (anantara-pratyaya).
Formless phenomena are the cause, sequence-condition, condition, and predominant condition for those same formless phenomena.

Non-material phenomena (arūpadharma) are the cause and the predominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) for material phenomena (rūpadharma), but they are neither an object-condition (ālambanapratyaya) nor a sequential condition (samanantarapratyaya).
The same applies to visible and invisible phenomena, as well as to those with resistance (sapratigha) and those without resistance (apratigha).
Contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) are the cause, immediate antecedent, object-condition, and predominant condition for those same contaminated phenomena.
Contaminated phenomena are the immediate antecedent, object-condition, and predominant condition for uncontaminated phenomena (anāsrava-dharma), but they are not their cause.

Regarding untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*): those untainted phenomena are caused by this [cause]; they are obtained through immediate succession; they exist because of these conditions; and they continue through sovereign influence (*adhipati*).
Untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are, with respect to tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), conditions of sequence, object, and predominance, but not causes.
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are, with respect to those same conditioned phenomena, causes, conditions of sequence, objects, and predominant conditions.
Conditioned phenomena do not exist in unconditioned phenomena;
unconditioned phenomena do not exist in those unconditioned phenomena.
Unconditioned phenomena are conditions and predominant conditions for conditioned phenomena.

Those who are bound by their own fetters undergo existence in hell; they obtain the sense faculties and the four great elements. Those faculties and those four great elements exercise a single predominant influence over the mind and mental factors;
those mind and mental factors exercise a single predominant influence over those faculties and four great elements.

Regarding those who are bound by their own fetters and undergo existence as animals, hungry ghosts, devas, or humans: those obtain the sense faculties (indriya) and the four great elements (mahābhūta). Those sense faculties and four great elements have a single predominance over the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma);
and those minds and mental factors have a single predominance over those sense faculties and four great elements.

When one born in the desire realm enters the first dhyāna with outflows, or even enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with outflows, those faculties grow and the four great elements increase. Those faculties and those four great elements have the mind and mental factors as their single predominant condition;
those mind and mental factors have those faculties and four great elements as their single predominant condition.

When one born in the desire realm enters the untainted first dhyāna, or enters up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti), those faculties increase and the four great elements (mahābhūta) flourish;

those faculties and those four great elements have the mind and mental factors as their single sovereign condition, and those mind and mental factors have those faculties and four great elements as their single sovereign condition.

When one born in the realm of form enters the first dhyāna with outflows, or even enters the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with outflows, those faculties increase and the four great elements are augmented. Those faculties and those four great elements have a single predominance over that mind and its mental factors;
that mind and its mental factors have a single predominance over those faculties and the four great elements.

When one born in the Form Realm enters the untainted first dhyāna, and so on up to entering the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, those faculties increase and the four great elements are augmented. Those faculties and those four great elements have the mind and mental factors as their single dominant condition;
those mind and mental factors have those faculties and four great elements as their single dominant condition.
What dharma is internal?
The answer is:
that which is designated as one's own enumeration.
What is the meaning of "not internal"?
The answer is:
it refers to that which is not counted as oneself.
What is the meaning of "feeling" (vedanā)?
The answer is:
it is a designation for the category of phenomena associated with outflows (sāsrava-dharma).
What is the meaning of "not being grasped"?
Answer: It is a designation for the category of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What is the meaning of "bond" (*saṃyojana*)?
The answer is:
it is a designation for the category of phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
What is the meaning of "without fetters" (*asaṃyojana*)?
Answer: It is a designation for the category of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
What is the meaning of "view-standpoint" (*diṭṭhigata*)?
The answer is:
it is a designation for the category of tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
What is the meaning of "not being seen"?
Answer: It is a designation for the category of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
Regarding all phenomena that are internal, are those phenomena subsumed under the internal sense-bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*)?
The answer is:
there are some phenomena that are internal, yet those phenomena are not subsumed under the internal sense-bases.
What is meant by "the dharma is internal, yet that dharma is not included within the internal bases"?
The answer is:

as it has been said, when one dwells in the contemplation of internal feelings and internal dharmas, this is called "the dharma is internal, yet that dharma is not included within the internal bases."
What is the case where a phenomenon is included within the internal sense-base (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), yet that phenomenon is not internal?
The answer is:
as it has been taught, when one dwells contemplating the external body and the external mind, this is called a phenomenon included within the internal sense-base that is nonetheless not internal.
What is the case where a phenomenon is internal and that phenomenon is included within the internal bases (*āyatana*)?
The answer is:
as it has been taught, when one dwells contemplating the mind in the internal body and the internal mind, this is called a phenomenon that is internal and included within the internal bases.
What is the case where a phenomenon is not internal, yet that phenomenon is not included within the internal bases?
The answer is:

as it has been said, when one dwells in the contemplation of external feelings and external phenomena, this is called a phenomenon that is not internal, yet that phenomenon is not included within the internal bases.
If a phenomenon is external to the [internal] phenomena, is that phenomenon subsumed under the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*)?
Answer: There are phenomena that are external to the [internal] phenomena, yet those phenomena are not subsumed under the external bases.
What is meant by "external phenomena" that are not included within the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*)?
The answer is:

as it has been taught, when one dwells in the contemplation of the body externally and the mind externally, these are called "external phenomena" that are not included within the external sense bases.
What is the case where a phenomenon is included within the external sense-base (*dharmāyatana*), yet that phenomenon is not external?
The answer is:

as it has been said, when one dwells in the contemplation of internal feelings and internal phenomena regarding the phenomena, this is called a phenomenon included within the external sense-base that is nonetheless not external.
What is meant by "external phenomena" being included within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*)?
The answer is:
as it has been taught, when one dwells in the contemplation of external feelings and external phenomena, this is called "external phenomena" being included within the external bases.
What is the phenomenon that is not external and yet is not included within the external bases?
The answer is:

as it has been said, when one dwells observing the mind with respect to the internal body and the internal mind, this is called the phenomenon that is not external and is not included within the external bases.
Regarding the two types of feeling and the three types of feeling: do the two types of feeling subsume the three types of feeling, or do the three types of feeling subsume the two types of feeling?
Answer: They subsume one another according to their respective categories.

Regarding the two types of feeling, the four types of feeling, and the five or six types of feeling: do the two types of feeling subsume the six types of feeling, or do the six types of feeling subsume the two types of feeling?
Answer: They subsume one another according to their respective categories.

Regarding the two types of feeling and the eighteen types of feeling: do the two types of feeling subsume the eighteen types of feeling, or do the eighteen types of feeling subsume the two types of feeling?
Answer: The two subsume the eighteen, but the eighteen do not subsume the two.
What is not included?
The answer is:

the faculty of suffering that is with-outflows (*sāsrava*), the faculty of pleasure associated with resistance (*sapratigha*), and the faculty of equanimity that is outflow-free (*anāsrava*) sensation.
The same applies to the thirty-six pains and the one hundred and eight pains.
This extends even to the six pains and the eighteen pains: do the six subsume the eighteen, or do the eighteen subsume the six?
Answer: The six encompass the eighteen, but the eighteen do not encompass the six.
What is it that is not encompassed?

Answer: The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*); the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is associated with the resistant (*sapratigha*); the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is the untainted (*anāsrava*) feeling (*vedanā*).
The same applies to the thirty-six feelings and the one hundred and eight feelings.
The eighteen types of painful feeling and the thirty-six types of painful feeling are also like this.

Regarding the thirty-six types of painful feeling and the one hundred and eight types of painful feeling: do the thirty-six encompass the one hundred and eight, or do the one hundred and eight encompass the thirty-six?

Answer: They are mutually inclusive according to their respective seeds. When one proceeds toward the realization of the fruit of *srotāpanna* by means of the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*), at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness) is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* (right efforts) as future; four *ṛddhipādas* (bases of power) as future; five *indriyas* (faculties) as future; five *balas* (powers) as future; six *bodhyaṅgas* (limbs of enlightenment) as future; eight *mārgāṅgas* (path factors) as future. There is no *dhyāna*, no *samāpatti*, no *ārūpyasamāpatti*, no *vimokṣas*, no *abhibhvāyatanas*, no *kṛtsnāyatanas*, no *jñānas*, and none as future. One *samādhi* is cultivated as future. This concludes the section on the track of the way (*mārga-pada*).

When one proceeds toward the realization of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* by means of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), if one attains realization by skipping stages due to the further exhaustion of desire, then at the time of cultivating that path: One *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness) is cultivated as present, and four are cultivated as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* (right efforts) are cultivated as future; four *ṛddhipādas* (bases of power) are cultivated as future; five *indriyas* (faculties) are cultivated as future; five *balas* (powers) are cultivated as future; six *bodhyaṅgas* (factors of enlightenment) are cultivated as future; eight *mārgāṅgas* (limbs of the path) are cultivated as future. There is no *dhyāna*, no *samāpatti*, no *ārūpyasamāpatti*, no *vimokṣas*, no *abhibhvāyatanas*, no *kṛtsnāyatanas*, and no *jñānas* cultivated as future; one *samādhi* is cultivated as future.

If one has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and, by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), takes up the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, then at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* as future; four *ṛddhipādas* as future; five *indriyas* as future; five *balas* as future; no *bodhyaṅgas* as future [but] six as future; no *mārgāṅgas* as future [but] eight as future; no *dhyānas*, no *samāpattis*, no *ārūpyasamāpattis*, no *vimokṣas*, no *abhibhvāyatanas*, and no *kṛtsnāyatanas*; one *jñāna* as future and seven as future; and no *samādhis* as future [but] three as future.

If one has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and, by means of the untainted path, takes up the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, then at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* as future; four *ṛddhipādas* as future; five *indriyas* as future; five *balas* as future; six *bodhyaṅgas* as future (excluding *prīti*); eight *mārgāṅgas* as future; no *dhyānas*, no *samāpattis*, no *ārūpyasamāpattis*, no *vimokṣas*, no *aṣṭavimokṣāyatanas*, and no *daśakṛtsnāyatanas*;
two knowledges (*jñāna*)—the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge—as future; and three *samādhis* as future. This concludes the section on the *sakṛdāgāmin*.

By means of the path of non-obstruction, one realizes the fruit of *anāgāmin*. If one realizes this fruit by transcending stages through the exhaustion of sensual desire, then at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* as future; four *ṛddhipādas* as future; five *indriyas* as future; five *balas* as future; six *bodhyaṅgas* as future; eight *mārgāṅgas* as future. There is no *dhyāna*, no *samāpatti*, no *ārūpya-samāpatti*, no *vimokṣa*, no *abhibhvāyatana*, and no *kṛtsnāyatana*. There is no *jñāna* as future, nor is there any [other] as future; one *samādhi* is cultivated as future.

If one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* based on the first *dhyāna*, when cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* as future; four *ṛddhipādas* as future; five *indriyas* as future; five *balas* as future; seven *bodhyaṅgas* as future; eight *mārgāṅgas* as future; one *dhyāna* as future; there is no *samādhi*, no formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), no liberations (*vimokṣa*), no eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and no ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*); no knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated as future; and one *samādhi* is cultivated as future.

If one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* based on the intermediate stage of the first *dhyāna*, then at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four in the future; four *samyakprahāṇas* in the future; four *ṛddhipādas* in the future; five *indriyas* in the future; five *balas* in the future; six *bodhyaṅgas* in the future; seven *mārgāṅgas* in the future; no *dhyānas* in the future; no *samāpattis*, no *ārūpyasamāpattis*, no *vimokṣas*, no eight *abhibhvāyatanas*, and no ten *kṛtsnāyatanas*; no *jñānas* in the future; and one *samādhi* in the future.

If one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* based on the second *dhyāna*, when cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* (the *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated as present; four future *smṛtyupasthānas*; four *samyakprahāṇas* in the future; four *ṛddhipādas* in the future; five faculties (*indriya*) in the future; five powers (*bala*) in the future; seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) in the future; eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) in the future; one *dhyāna* in the future; two [limbs] of the first *dhyāna* in the future. There is no *samādhi* without equal, no formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), no liberations (*vimokṣa*), no eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), no ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and no knowledges (*jñāna*). There is one *samādhi* in the future.

If one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* based on the third dhyāna, when cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* as future; four *ṛddhipādas* as future; five *indriyas* as future; five *balas* as future; six *bodhyaṅgas* as future; seven *mārgāṅgas*—excluding *samyaksaṃkalpa*—as future; one *dhyāna* as future; three *ārūpyasamāpattis* are absent; there are no *vimokṣas*, no *abhibhvāyatanas*, and no *kṛtsnāyatanas*; no *jñānas* are cultivated as future; and one *samādhi* is cultivated as future.

If one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* based on the four *dhyānas*, then at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* are cultivated as future; four *ṛddhipādas* are cultivated as future; five *indriyas* are cultivated as future; five *balas* are cultivated as future; six *bodhyaṅgas* are cultivated as future; seven *mārgāṅgas* are cultivated as future; one *dhyāna* is cultivated as future and four as future; there is no *samāpatti*, no *ārūpya-samāpatti*, no *vimokṣa*, no eight *abhibhvāyatanas*, no ten *kṛtsnāyatanas*, and no *jñāna*; and one *samādhi* is cultivated as future, which is the transcendent [path] leading to the exhaustion of the non-returner.

If one has attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* and, by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), takes up the fruit of *anāgāmin*, then at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* are cultivated as future; four *ṛddhipādas* are cultivated as future; five *indriyas* are cultivated as future; five *balas* are cultivated as future; no *bodhyaṅgas* are cultivated as future, but six are cultivated as future; no *mārgāṅgas* are cultivated as future, but eight are cultivated as future; there are no *dhyānas*, no *samāpattis*, no *ārūpyasamāpattis*, no *vimokṣas*, no *abhibhvāyatanas*, and no *kṛtsnāyatanas*; one *jñāna* is cultivated as future—namely, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)—and seven others; no *samādhis* are cultivated as future, but three are cultivated as future.

If one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* and, by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), takes up the fruit of *anāgāmin*, then at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* as future; four *ṛddhipādas* as future; five *indriyas* as future; five *balas* as future; six *bodhyaṅgas* as future; eight *mārgāṅgas* as future. There are no *dhyānas*, no *samāpattis*, no *ārūpyasamāpattis*, no *vimokṣas*, no *abhibhvāyatanas*, and no *kṛtsnāyatanas*. Two *jñānas* are cultivated as future and seven [others] as future; one *samādhi* is cultivated as future and three [others] as future. This concludes the section on the *anāgāmin*.

By means of the supernormal power of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), if an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) relies upon the first dhyāna to cultivate the path of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): when cultivating that path, they cultivate one application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in the present—namely, the body (*kāya*)—and four in the future; four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) in the future; four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) in the future; five faculties (*indriya*) in the future; five powers (*bala*) in the future; no factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) in the future; no factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) in the future; one dhyāna in the future; no meditative attainments of equality (*samāpatti*) in the future, but four in the future; no formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) in the future; no liberations (*vimokṣa*) in the future, but two in the future; no spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) in the future, but four in the future; no spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) in the future; one knowledge (*jñāna*) in the future; no samādhis in the future; and three inclinations toward the goal (*niyāma*) in the future.

If a person free from defilements, relying on the first *dhyāna*, cultivates the path of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), then at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* are cultivated as future; four *ṛddhipādas* are cultivated as future; five *indriyas* are cultivated as future; five *balas* are cultivated as future; no *bodhyaṅgas* are cultivated as future, but seven [are cultivated] as future; no *mārgāṅgas* are cultivated as future, but eight [are cultivated] as future; one *dhyāna* is cultivated as future; no *samāpattis* are cultivated as future, but four [are cultivated] as future; no formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are cultivated as future; no liberations (*vimokṣa*) are cultivated as future, but two [are cultivated] as future; no eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are cultivated as future, but the four branches of the four *dhyānas* [are cultivated]; no ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are cultivated as future; one knowledge (*jñāna*) is cultivated as future and seven [are cultivated] as future; no samādhis are cultivated as future, but three [are cultivated] as future.

If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), relying on the second *dhyāna*, cultivates the path of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): when cultivating that path, one *smṛtyupasthāna* is present and four are future; four *samyakprahāṇas* are future; four *ṛddhipādas* are future; five faculties (*indriya*) are future; five powers (*bala*) are future; there are none of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) future; none of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are future; one *dhyāna* is future; none of the *samādhis* are future; none of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are future; two liberations (*vimokṣa*)—the first and the second—are future; none of the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)—eight perceptions, four views, and four colors—are future; none of the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are future; one knowledge (*jñāna*) is future; and none of the concentrations (*samādhi*) are future.

If a person free from defilement (vimala) relies on the second dhyāna to cultivate the path of the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), then at the time of cultivating that path: one application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is cultivated as present and four as future; four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) are cultivated as future; four bases of psychic power are cultivated as future; five faculties (indriya) are cultivated as future; five powers (bala) are cultivated as future; no factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are cultivated as future, but seven are cultivated as future; no factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are cultivated as future, but eight are cultivated as future; one dhyāna is cultivated as future and two as future; no attainments of equality (samāpatti) are cultivated as future, but four are cultivated as future; no formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) are cultivated as future; no liberations (vimokṣa) are cultivated as future, but two are cultivated as future; no spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are cultivated as future, but four sets of four views are cultivated as future; no spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are cultivated as future; one knowledge (jñāna) is cultivated as future and seven are cultivated as future; no samādhis are cultivated as future, but three are cultivated as future.

If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), relying on the third dhyāna, cultivates the path of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): while cultivating that path, one present application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated, and four future ones; four future right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*); four future bases of psychic power; five future faculties (*indriya*); five future powers (*bala*); no future factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); no future factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*); one future dhyāna; no future meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); three future liberations (*vimokṣa*), excluding that of joy (*prīti*); no future formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); no future liberations (*vimokṣa*); no future spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); no future spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*); one future knowledge (*jñāna*), which is the single conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); and no future samādhis.

If a person free from defilements relies on the third dhyāna to cultivate the path of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), then at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* are cultivated as future; four *ṛddhipādas* are cultivated as future; five *indriyas* are cultivated as future; five *balas* are cultivated as future; no *bodhyaṅgas* are cultivated as future, but seven are cultivated as future; no *mārgāṅgas* are cultivated as future, but eight are cultivated as future; one *dhyāna* is cultivated as future and three as future; no *samāpattis*, no *vimokṣas*, no *abhibhvāyatanas*, and no *kṛtsnāyatanas* are cultivated; one *jñāna* is cultivated as future and seven as future; and no *samādhis* are cultivated as future, but three are cultivated as future.

If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), relying on the four dhyānas, cultivates the path of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): when cultivating that path, one *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness) is present and four are future; four *samyakprahāṇas* (right efforts) are future; four *ṛddhipādas* are future; five *indriyas* (faculties) are future; five *balas* (powers) are future; no *bodhyaṅgas* (limbs of enlightenment) are future; no *mārgāṅgas* (limbs of the path) are future; one *dhyāna* is future; no *samāpattis* (equanimities) are future; three *ārūpyasamāpattis* (formless attainments) are future; no *vimokṣas* (liberations) are future; one *vimokṣa* is future; eight *abhibhvāyatanas* (bases of mastery) are future; four *abhibhvāyatanas* are future; ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities) are future; eight *kṛtsnāyatanas* are future; one *jñāna* (knowledge) is future; one *jñāna* is future; no *samādhis* (concentrations) are future; no *samādhis* are future.

If a person free from defilements, relying on the fourth dhyāna, cultivates the path of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), then at the time of cultivating that path: one foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated as present and four as future; four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are cultivated as future; four bases of psychic power are cultivated as future; five faculties (*indriya*) are cultivated as future; five powers (*bala*) are cultivated as future; no factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are cultivated as future, but seven are cultivated as future; no factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are cultivated as future, but eight are cultivated as future; one dhyāna is cultivated as future and four as future; no "equal" states (*samāpatti*) are cultivated as future, but three are cultivated as future; no formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are cultivated as future; no liberations (*vimokṣa*) are cultivated as future, but one—the pure liberation—is cultivated as future; no spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are cultivated as future, but four of the four form-spheres are cultivated as future; no spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are cultivated as future, but eight are cultivated as future; one knowledge (*jñāna*) is cultivated as future and seven are cultivated as future; no samādhis are cultivated as future, but three are cultivated as future. This concludes the bases of psychic power.
The divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of one's own past lives, and the power of clairvoyance are also like this.

By means of the path of non-obstruction, one realizes the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*). If, relying on the future *samādhi* with directed thought and sustained evaluation (*savitarka-savicāra*), one attains Arhatship, then at the time of cultivating that path: One *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness) is cultivated as present and four as future; Four *samyakprahāṇas* (right efforts) as future; Four *ṛddhipādas* (bases of power) as future; Five *indriyas* (faculties) as future; Five *balas* (powers) as future; Six *bodhyaṅgas* (limbs of enlightenment) as future; Eight *mārgāṅgas* (path factors) as future; No *dhyānas* (meditative absorptions) are cultivated, though four are future; No *samāpattis* (equanimities) are cultivated, though none are future; No *ārūpya-samāpattis* (formless attainments) are cultivated, though three are future; No *vimokṣas* (liberations) are cultivated, though three are future; No *abhibhvāyatanas* (bases of mastery) or *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities) are cultivated; Two *jñānas* (knowledges) are cultivated as future and six as future; four are not yet realized; One *samādhi* (concentration) is cultivated as future and three as future.

If one attains Arhatship based on the first dhyāna, at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness) is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇa* (right efforts) as future; four *ṛddhipāda* (bases of power) as future; five *indriya* (faculties) as future; five *bala* (powers) as future; seven *bodhyaṅga* (factors of enlightenment) as future; eight *mārgāṅga* (limbs of the path) as future; one *dhyāna* as future and four as future; no *samāpatti* (equanimity) as future; no formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) as future, but three as future; no *vimokṣa* (liberations) as future, but three as future; no *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery) or *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities); two *jñāna* (knowledges) as future and six as future; and one *samādhi* (concentration) as future and three as future.

If one attains Arhatship by relying on the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* as future; four *ṛddhipādas* as future; five *indriyas* as future; five *balas* as future; six *bodhyaṅgas* as future; seven *mārgāṅgas* as future; no *dhyānas* as future; no *samāpattis* as future; no *ārūpyasamāpattis* as future; no *vimokṣas* as future; no *abhibhvāyatanas* or *kṛtsnāyatanas*; two *jñānas* as future and six as future; one *samādhi* as future and three as future, with three applications toward one.

If one relies on the second dhyāna to attain the path of Arhatship, when cultivating that path: one application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is cultivated as present and four as future; four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) as future; four bases of power (ṛddhipāda) as future; five faculties (indriya) as future; five powers (bala) as future; seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) as future; eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) as future; one dhyāna as future and four as future; no "equal" [attainments] as future and none as future; no formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti) as future and three as future; no liberations (vimokṣa) as future and three as future; no eight stages of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) and no ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana); two knowledges (jñāna) as future and six as future; and one samādhi as future and three as future.

If one attains Arhatship based on the third or fourth dhyāna, when cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness) is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇa* (right efforts) as future; four *ṛddhipāda* (bases of power) as future; five *indriya* (faculties) as future; five *bala* (powers) as future; six *bodhyaṅga* (limbs of enlightenment) as future; seven *mārgāṅga* (path factors) as future; one *dhyāna* as future and four as future; no *samādhi* (equanimity) as future; no formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) as future, but three as future; no *vimokṣa* (liberations) as future, but three as future; no eight *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery) nor ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities); two *jñāna* (knowledges) as future and six as future; and one *samādhi* (concentration) as future and three as future.

If one attains Arhatship by relying on the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), then at the time of cultivating that path: one *smṛtyupasthāna* is cultivated as present and four as future; four *samyakprahāṇas* as future; four *ṛddhipādas* as future; five *indriyas* as future; five *balas* as future; six *bodhyaṅgas* as future; seven *bodhipākṣika-dharmas* as future (excluding the *śīla-saṃvara*); four *mārgāṅgas* as future (excluding *śīla-saṃvara*); no *dhyānas* as future; no *samādhis* as future; one *ārūpya-samāpatti* as future; three *vimokṣas* as future; no *abhibhvāyatanas* or *kṛtsnāyatanas*; two *jñānas* as future; and one *samādhi* as future.

The fourth chapter, "On Internal Fabrication," is completed. In the Sanskrit original, it consists of three hundred and fifty-three *ślokas*; in the Qin translation, it comprises four thousand five hundred and twenty-three words.
The fifth major section, "The Four Great Elements" (*Caturmahābhūta-khaṇḍa*), is completed. This was recited on the third day.

The Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-one.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra.
The Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Fu Qin dynasty [states]:
