"The twenty-two faculties exist; contact, initial mind, and so forth, are the primary causes and conditions for the arising [of consciousness]."
Chapter One: The Chapter on Faculties (Indriya-varga) of the Abhidharma. The Twenty-two Faculties:

the faculty of the eye, the faculty of the ear, the faculty of the nose, the faculty of the tongue, the faculty of the body, the faculty of the mind; the male faculty, the female faculty, the life-faculty; the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, the faculty of equanimity; the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom; the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
Of these twenty-two faculties, how many are of the learner (*śaikṣa*), how many are of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither of the learner nor the non-learner?
Are all those faculties that belong to the learner necessarily possessed by a person who is a learner?
If they are the faculties of a person in training (śaikṣa), are they the training-faculties (śaikṣendriya)?
Are all faculties that are beyond training (aśaikṣa) the non-training faculties (aśaikṣendriya) of a person beyond training?
And if they are the faculties of a person beyond training, are they the non-training faculties?
If the faculties are neither of the learner nor of the non-learner, are those faculties the faculties of a person who is neither of the learner nor of the non-learner?
Conversely, if a person is neither of the learner nor of the non-learner, are their faculties neither of the learner nor of the non-learner?
Among these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are wholesome (*kuśala*) and how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*)?
How many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), how many have retribution (*savipāka*), and how many are without retribution (*avipāka*)?
How many are to be abandoned by the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*), how many are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aheya*)?

How many are abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*), the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*), or the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*), and how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)? How many are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
How many are seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and how many are not seen (*adṛṣṭa*)?

How many are with vitarka and vicāra (*savitarka-savicāra*), how many are without vitarka but with vicāra (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), and how many are without vitarka and without vicāra (*avitarkāvicāra*)?

How many are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), how many with the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), how many with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), how many with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and how many with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?

How many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?

How many are associated with causes? How many are dissociated from causes? How many are both associated with and dissociated from causes? And how many are neither associated with nor dissociated from causes?

How many are common objective conditions (*sādhāraṇālambana-nimitta*), how many are uncommon objective conditions (*asādhāraṇālambana-nimitta*), how many are both common and uncommon objective conditions, and how many are neither uncommon nor non-uncommon objective conditions?
Regarding these faculties (*indriya*), are those faculties belonging to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?
Conversely, if the faculties belong to an ordinary person, are those faculties included within this dharma?

How many faculties are subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and how many faculties are subsumed under the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)?

How many bases (*dhātu*), how many entrances (*āyatana*), and how many aggregates (*skandha*) are subsumed under the wholesome roots? How many bases, how many entrances, and how many aggregates are subsumed under the unwholesome roots? How many bases, how many entrances, and how many aggregates are subsumed under the obscured indeterminate roots? How many bases, how many entrances, and how many aggregates are subsumed under the non-obscured indeterminate roots?

How many bases (āyatana), how many elements (dhātu), and how many aggregates (skandha) are comprised by the factors that are faculties (indriya)? How many bases, how many elements, and how many aggregates are comprised by the factors that are not faculties? How many bases, how many elements, and how many aggregates are comprised by the factors that are both faculties and non-faculties?

Is there that which, conditioned by a faculty (*indriya*), arises as a faculty? Is there that which, conditioned by a faculty, arises as a non-faculty? Is there that which, conditioned by a faculty, arises both as a faculty and as a non-faculty?
Is there that which, conditioned by a non-faculty, arises as a non-faculty? Is there that which, conditioned by a non-faculty, arises as a faculty?
Can that which is not a faculty arise conditioned by what is not a faculty?

Can that which is a faculty arise conditioned by what is both a faculty and not a faculty? Can that which is not a faculty arise conditioned by what is both a faculty and not a faculty? Can that which is both a faculty and not a faculty arise conditioned by what is both a faculty and not a faculty?

Is it possible that, conditioned by the eye-faculty, the eye-faculty arises? Is it possible that, conditioned by the eye-faculty, [any faculty] up to the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (ājñātāvīndriya) arises?

Is it possible that, conditioned by the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown," the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" arises? Is it possible that, conditioned by the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown," [any faculty] from the eye-faculty up to the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñendriya) arises?
Regarding the eye-faculty: by how many conditions is that eye-faculty conditioned?
From the eye-faculty up to the faculty of final knowledge (aññātāvindriya), by how many conditions are they conditioned?
Regarding the faculty of final knowledge: by how many conditions is that faculty of final knowledge conditioned?

Regarding the faculty of ignorance (*aññā-indriya*), how many conditions serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-paccaya*) for the faculties from the eye-faculty (*cakkhu-indriya*) up to the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvī-indriya*)?
I wish to explain the meaning of this chapter in full detail.
The twenty-two faculties are: [The list of twenty-two faculties follows.]

The eye faculty, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties; the male faculty, the female faculty, and the life faculty; the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
Among these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are of the learner (*śaikṣa*), how many are of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither of the learner nor the non-learner?
The answer is:
two are of the learner, one is of the non-learner, ten are neither of the learner nor the non-learner, and nine are to be analyzed.
The mind-faculty (manas-indriya) is either that of one in training (śaikṣa), or that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), or neither that of one in training nor that of one beyond training.
What is that of one in training?
The answer is:
The mental states associated with the faculty of mind that are attended to by one in training—this is called "in training.
What is "beyond training" (aśaikṣa)?
The answer is:
That which is associated with the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) as it is attended to by the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is called "beyond training.
What is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training? Answer:
Those mental objects associated with the faculty of mind that are accompanied by outflows (āsrava) are called neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, joy, equanimity, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
If the faculties are those of one in training (śaikṣa), are they the faculties of a person who is still in the state of training? Answer:
Some faculties belong to one in training, yet those faculties do not belong to a person who is still in the state of training.
What are the faculties that are of the learner (śaikṣa) but whose possessor is not a student of the householder (śaikṣa)? Answer:

Those faculties which belong to the learner but are not possessed by one who is a student of the householder; these are called the faculties that are of the learner but whose possessor is not a student of the householder.
What are the faculties of one in training (śaikṣa) that are not themselves faculties of one in training? Answer:

Those faculties which are neither of one in training nor of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), yet are accomplished by one in training—these are called the faculties of one in training that are not themselves faculties of one in training.
What are the faculties of one in training? Are those faculties the faculties of one who is a trainee?
Answer: Yes.
Those who possess the faculties of training (śaikṣa-indriya) are called "those with the faculties of training" and "those belonging to the stage of training.
What are those who do not possess the faculties of training and do not belong to the stage of training?
The answer is:

The faculties of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-indriya) and those faculties that are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-indriya) are not possessed by one who is a master of training (śaikṣa). These are called the faculties that are not of training, yet those faculties do not belong to a master of training.
Are all faculties of one beyond training possessed by one who is not a master of training?
Answer: There are cases where a faculty is that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), yet that faculty does not belong to one who is a non-learner (aśaikṣa).
What is the case where a faculty is that of one beyond training, yet that faculty does not belong to one who is a non-learner?

Answer: Those faculties of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) that are not possessed by one who is a member of the family of those beyond training—these are called "faculties of the stage of no-more-learning" that do not belong to one who is a member of the family of those beyond training.
What are the faculties of one who is a member of the family of those beyond training that do not belong to one who is of the stage of no-more-learning?
Answer: Those faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa) which are accomplished by one who is a non-learner (aśaikṣa)—these are called the faculties of a non-learner.
Since those faculties are not themselves non-learner [faculties], how can they be the faculties of a non-learner belonging to one who is a non-learner?
Answer:

Those faculties of the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) that are accomplished by one in the stage of no-more-learning—these are called "faculties of the stage of no-more-learning belonging to one in the stage of no-more-learning.
What are those that are neither faculties of the stage of no-more-learning nor belong to one in the stage of no-more-learning?

Answer: The faculty of training (*śaikṣa-indriya*) and those faculties that are neither of training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-indriya*) are not possessed by one who is not a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*). This is called: "it is not a faculty of a non-learner, yet that faculty does not belong to one who is not a non-learner."
If the faculties are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, are those faculties the faculties of one who is neither a learner nor a non-learner?
Answer: It is so;
those faculties which belong to one who is neither a learner nor a non-learner are indeed the faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Regarding those faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, are they not accomplished by one who is neither a learner nor a non-learner? Answer:
There are certain faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner which are not accomplished by one who is neither a learner nor a non-learner.
Among these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
The answer is:
eight are wholesome, eight are indeterminate, and six are to be analyzed.
The mind-faculty is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
The answer is:
When wholesome mental factors are associated with the various faculties of mind, this is called "wholesome.
What is "unwholesome"?
The answer is:
When unwholesome mental factors arise in association with the faculty of mind, this is called the unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate?
The answer is:
When the mind associated with the faculty of mind is accompanied by indeterminate mental factors, this is called the indeterminate.
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, and equanimity.
The faculty of grief is either wholesome or unwholesome.
What is wholesome?
The answer is:
If wholesome mental factors are associated with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), this is called wholesome.
What is unwholesome?
The answer is:
When unwholesome mental factors are associated with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), this is called "unwholesome.
Among these twenty-two faculties, how many have retribution (*savipāka*) and how many are without retribution (*avipāka*)?
Answer: One is with retribution, eleven are without retribution, and ten should be analyzed individually.
The faculty of mind (manas) is either with retribution or without retribution.
What is that which has retribution?
The answer is:
the unwholesome and the wholesome-with-outflows mental faculties (*manas-indriya*); these are said to have retribution.
What is that which has no retribution?
The answer is:
the indeterminate and untainted mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
This is called "without retribution.
The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of joy, and the faculty of equanimity are likewise.
The faculty of pain is either with retribution or without retribution.
What is retribution?
The answer is:
unwholesome states and wholesome states associated with the faculty of pain; these are called retribution.
What is that which has no retribution?
The answer is:
the indeterminate faculty of suffering; this is called that which has no retribution.
Regarding the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom: those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) have retribution;
those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are said to be without retribution.

Among these twenty-two faculties, how many are abandoned by the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
Answer: Nine are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), three are not abandoned, and ten should be distinguished.
As for the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*), it is either abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), abandoned by cultivation, or not abandoned.
What is meant by "abandoned through the vision of the truths" (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*)?
The answer is:
those faculties of mind (*manas-indriya*) which are abandoned through the patience (*kṣānti*) of one who practices with firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) or firm dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
What is abandoned through the vision of the truths?
The eighty-eight proclivities associated with the mental faculty—these are said to be abandoned through the vision of the truths.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: All those things to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that have been seen by those in training (*śaikṣa*).
What are those things to be abandoned by cultivation?
The ten proclivities (daśa-anuśaya) are associated with the mental faculty (manas), and the defiled mental faculty is also outflow-tainted (sāsrava);
these are said to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya). What is not abandoned? Answer:
The untainted faculty of mind is called "not to be abandoned.
The faculty of equanimity is also like this.
The faculty of pleasure is either abandoned by seeing the truths, or abandoned by cultivation, or not abandoned at all.
How is it abandoned through the vision of the truths?
The answer is:

all faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) are abandoned by the forbearances (*kṣānti*) of those who practice through firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who practice through the dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
What is abandoned through the vision of the truths?
The answer is:
those twenty-eight proclivities associated with the faculty of pleasure; these are said to be abandoned through the vision of the truths.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
The answer is:
those factors abandoned through cultivation that pertain to the trainees who have seen the path.
What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

The five latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), as well as the undefiled yet outflowing (*anāsrava-sāsrava*) faculty of pleasure—these are said to be abandoned through cultivation.
What is not abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
Answer: The untainted faculty of pleasure (*anāsrava-sukhendriya*) is called "not to be abandoned" (*aprahātavya*).
The faculty of joy (*prīti-indriya*) is either abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-prahātavya*), abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or not to be abandoned.
What is abandoned through the vision of the truths? Answer:
All faculties of joy that are abandoned by the patience associated with the practice of those who possess firm faith and firm dharma.
What is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*)?
The fifty-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), these are said to be abandoned through the vision of the truths.
What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
The answer is:
For those in training who have seen the tracks, [defilements] are abandoned through cultivation.
What are those abandoned through cultivation?
The six latent tendencies (anuśaya) are associated with the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), as are the undefiled yet out-flowing (anāsrava-sāsrava) faculty of joy;
these are said to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya). What is not abandoned?
The answer is:
The untainted faculty of joy (*anāsrava-prīti-indriya*) is called "not to be abandoned.
As for the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya-indriya*), it is either abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*) or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
How is it abandoned through the vision of the truths? The answer is:
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) that is abandoned through the patience (*kṣānti*) of those who practice by way of firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) or firm dharma (*dharmānusārin*)—
which among these is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*)?
Those sixteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the faculty of sorrow are said to be abandoned through the vision of the truths.
What is abandonment through cultivation?
The answer is:
those things abandoned through cultivation that pertain to the learner who has seen the track.
What is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
The two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), as well as the undefiled faculty of sorrow—these are said to be abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, when they are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), are abandoned by cultivation.
All that is untainted (anāsrava) is not to be abandoned.

Among these twenty-two faculties (indriya), how many are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), how many by the vision of origin (samudaya), cessation (nirodha), and the path (mārga), how many by cultivation (bhāvanā), and how many are not to be abandoned?
Answer: Nine are abandoned through contemplation; three are not abandoned; ten should be distinguished.

As for the faculty of mind (*manas*), it is either abandoned through the vision of suffering, or abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, or abandoned through contemplation, or it is not abandoned.
What is abandoned through the vision of suffering?
The answer is:
those faculties of mind that are abandoned by the patience associated with the practice of firm faith and the practice of firm dharma.
What is abandoned through the vision of suffering?

Twenty-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) associated with the mental faculty (manas) are abandoned through the vision of suffering; nineteen underlying tendencies are abandoned through the vision of origin; nineteen underlying tendencies are abandoned through the vision of cessation; twenty-two underlying tendencies associated with the mental faculty are abandoned through the vision of the path. These are called those abandoned through the vision of the truths.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
The answer is:
all faculties of mind that belong to those in training who have seen the path and are abandoned through cultivation.
What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?

The ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the mental faculty (*manas*), as well as the undefiled yet outflowing (*sāsrava*) mental faculty—these are said to be abandoned through cultivation.
What is not abandoned (*aheya*)?
Answer: The untainted faculty of mind (anāsrava-manas-indriya) is called "uninterrupted.
The faculty of protection (ārakṣa-indriya) is likewise.

The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is either abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), or abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, or through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or it is not abandoned.
What is abandoned through the vision of suffering? Answer:
The various pleasure faculties (*sukhendriya*) are abandoned through the patience of those who practice with firm faith and firm Dharma.
Which are abandoned by the vision of suffering?

Nine underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the pleasure faculties are abandoned by the vision of origination; six underlying tendencies are abandoned by the vision of cessation; and six underlying tendencies are abandoned by the vision of the path. Seven underlying tendencies associated with the pleasure faculties—these are said to be abandoned by the vision of the truths.
What is abandonment through cultivation?
The answer is:
those factors abandoned through cultivation that pertain to the learner who has seen the tracks.
What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

The five underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), as well as the undefiled yet outflowing (*anāsrava-sāsrava*) faculty of pleasure—these are said to be abandoned through cultivation.
What is not abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
Answer: The untainted faculty of pleasure (anāsrava-sukhendriya) is called "not to be abandoned" (aprahātavya).

The faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) is either abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), or abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, or through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya), or it is not to be abandoned.
How is it abandoned through the vision of suffering?
The answer is:

all faculties of joy (*somanassindriya*) are abandoned by means of the patience (*kṣānti*) associated with those who practice through firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who practice through the dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
What is abandoned through the vision of suffering?

Seventeen latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the faculty of joy (*somanasyendriya*) are abandoned through the vision of origination; eleven are abandoned through the vision of cessation; eleven are abandoned through the vision of the path; and thirteen latent tendencies associated with the faculty of joy are abandoned through the vision of the truths. This is called abandonment through the vision of the truths.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
The answer is:
those things belonging to the trainees who have seen the path and are abandoned through cultivation.
What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

The six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), as well as the undefiled yet outflowing (*sāsrava*) faculty of joy—these are said to be abandoned through cultivation.
What is not abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
Answer: The untainted faculty of joy (*anāsrava-prīti-indriya*) is called "not to be abandoned.

The faculty of grief (*daurmanasya-indriya*) is either abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), or abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through the vision of suffering? Answer:
All faculties of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) that are abandoned by the patience (*kṣānti*) of one who practices with firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) or firm Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
What is abandoned through the vision of suffering?

It consists of the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering; the four [underlying tendencies] abandoned through the vision of origin; the four abandoned through the vision of cessation; and the four abandoned through the vision of the path—these are what are called "abandoned through the vision of the truths" (*satyadarśana-heya*).
What is abandonment through cultivation?
The answer is:
it is the abandonment through cultivation by those in training who have seen the tracks.
What is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Those two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), as well as the undefiled faculty of sorrow—these are said to be abandoned through cultivation.
The faculties of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, when they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), are abandoned through cultivation.
All that is untainted (anāsrava) is not to be abandoned.
Among these twenty-two faculties (indriya), how many are seen (dṛṣṭa) and how many are not seen?
The answer is:
One is "view" (*dṛṣṭi*); seventeen are "not view"; four are to be analyzed.
The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is either view or not view. What is view?

Answer: That wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness-body (manovijñānakāya) which is not included within the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) is called "view" (dṛṣṭi).
What, then, is "non-view" (adṛṣṭi)?

Answer: The wholesome wisdom associated with the five groups of consciousness, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), are said to be "not seeing.
As for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), it is sometimes seeing and sometimes not seeing.
What is view?
The answer is:
wisdom subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is called view.
What is meant by "not seeing"?
The answer is:
the eight faculties subsumed under the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) are called "not seeing."
The faculty of "already-known" (ājñātendriya) is also like this.
As for the faculty of "not-yet-known" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), it is sometimes seen and sometimes not seen.
In what way is it seen?

Answer: The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not included [in the faculty of wisdom]; rather, it is the wisdom included within the faculty of "I do not know" (*ajānanendriya*) that is called "view.
What, then, is "non-view"?

Answer: The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) subsumes eight faculties; the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are called "not seeing.
Among these twenty-two faculties, how many are with vitarka and with vicāra, how many are without vitarka but with vicāra, and how many are without vitarka and without vicāra?
Answer: Two [faculties] possess both vitarka and vicāra; eight possess neither vitarka nor vicāra; twelve are to be distinguished.
As for the faculty of mind (manas), it may possess both vitarka and vicāra, or possess vicāra without vitarka, or possess neither vitarka nor vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and vicāra"?
The answer is:
those mental states associated with the faculty of mind (manas) that are attended by a mind possessing vitarka and vicāra; this is called "with vitarka and vicāra."
What is "without vitarka but with vicāra"?
The answer is:
that which is associated with the mental faculty (manas-indriya) among the mental factors (caitta) when the mind is without vitarka but with vicāra; this is called "without vitarka but with vicāra."
What is meant by "without vitarka and without vicāra"?
The answer is:

that which is associated with the mental faculty (manas-indriya) among the mental factors (caitta) when the mind is without vitarka and without vicāra—this is called "without vitarka and without vicāra."

The faculty of guarding, the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known," are likewise so.
The faculty of pleasure is either with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is meant by "with vitarka and vicāra"?
The answer is:
when the mind that possesses vitarka and vicāra is associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) regarding its objects of thought, this is called "with vitarka and vicāra."
What is "without vitarka and without vicāra"?
The answer is:
that which is associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) within a state of mind that is without vitarka and without vicāra; this is called "without vitarka and without vicāra."
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is likewise.

The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy, and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are partially associated with nine faculties; the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) are partially associated with six faculties.

Regarding these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
The answer is:
four are bound to the desire realm, three are unbound, and fifteen are to be analyzed.
The eye-faculty is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
What is bound to the desire realm?
The answer is:
The various eye-faculties produced by the four great elements bound to the desire realm are called "bound to the desire realm.
What is meant by "bound to the form realm"?
The answer is:
The various eye-faculties produced by the four great elements bound to the realm of form are said to be "bound to the realm of form.
The ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties are likewise.
As for the mind faculty, it may be bound to the realm of desire, bound to the realm of form, bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is meant by "bound to the realm of desire" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
The answer is:
those mental factors associated with the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) that are attended to by a mind bound to the realm of desire; this is called being bound to the realm of desire.
What is meant by "bound to the realm of form" (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
The answer is:
those mental factors associated with the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) that are attended to by a mind bound to the realm of form; this is called being bound to the realm of form.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
The answer is:
those mental factors associated with the faculty of mind (manas) that are attended by a mind bound to the formless realm; this is called being bound to the formless realm.
What is meant by "unbound"?
The answer is:
that which is associated with the mental faculty (manas-indriya) as it is attended to by an untainted mind (anāsrava-citta); this is called "unbound."
The faculties of guarding, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are also like this.
The life-faculty is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm.
What is meant by "bound to the desire realm"?
The answer is:
the life-force bound to the desire realm is what is called being bound to the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the realm of form?
The answer is:
the life-force bound to the realm of form is what is called being bound to the realm of form.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
The answer is:
the life-force bound to the formless realm is what is called "bound to the formless realm."
The faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is either bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), or bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), or unbound (apratisaṃyukta).
What is bound to the desire realm? Answer:
When the mental factors associated with the desire realm take up various faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their objects, this is called "bound to the desire realm.
What is "bound to the form realm"?
The answer is:
When the mind associated with the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) attends to and is conjoined with the various faculties of pleasure (sukhendriya), this is called "bound to the form realm.
What is "unbound" (apratisaṃyukta)?
The answer is:
When an untainted (anāsrava) mental state is associated with any of the faculties of pleasure (sukhendriya), this is called "unbound" (apratisaṃyukta).
The same applies to the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
Among these twenty-two faculties, how many are associated with causes (hetu)?
Answer: Fourteen.
How many are dissociated from causes?
Answer: Eight.
How many causes are associated, and how many causes are dissociated?
Answer: Those fourteen [factors] are associated with minor causes and dissociated from minor causes.
How many are dissociated from causes but not dissociated from the absence of causes?
Answer: Those fourteen [factors] are not associated with minor causes, yet those minor causes are not non-associated.
Among these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many share the characteristic of being object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
Answer: Thirteen [mental factors] are partially included.
How many do not share the same object, yet take it as their object?
Answer: One [of the three] and thirteen [of the eighteen] are partially included.
How many have common objects as their conditions (*sādhāraṇālambana-pratyaya*), and how many have uncommon objects as their conditions (*asādhāraṇālambana-pratyaya*)?
Answer: Thirteen.
How many have uncommon object-conditions (*asādhāraṇālambana-pratyaya*) and do not have non-uncommon object-conditions?
Answer: Eight.
Regarding these factors, those faculties do not belong to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
The faculties of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) do not belong to this dharma.
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) comprises seven faculties;
the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) comprises five faculties, with a partial inclusion of three faculties.
The aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) does not include the sense faculties.
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) includes the six sense faculties, with a partial inclusion of three faculties.
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) includes one sense faculty, with a partial inclusion of three faculties.
The roots of goodness subsume eight bases (*dhātu*), two entrances (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*).
The unwholesome roots subsume eight bases, two entrances, and two aggregates.
The obscured-unspecified roots subsume six bases, two entrances, and two aggregates.
The non-obscured neutral roots comprise thirteen bases (*dhātu*), seven entrances (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*).
The factors that possess roots comprise thirteen bases, seven entrances, and four aggregates.
The factors that lack roots comprise six bases, six entrances, and three aggregates.
The factors of faculties and non-faculties comprise eighteen bases (*dhātus*), twelve spheres (*āyatanas*), and five aggregates (*skandhas*).
Is it possible for a faculty to arise conditioned by a faculty?
Answer: Yes.
It arises. Does it arise somewhat by means of a root, or without a root? Answer:
Regarding birth:
can that which is born have as its condition both a faculty and a non-faculty?
Answer: Yes.
It arises. Does it arise without a root by depending on that which is not a root?
Answer: No.
It arises. Does it arise based on roots that are not themselves rooted?
Answer: Yes.
It arises. Does it arise based on that which is not a root, or does it arise based on that which is not a root? Answer: It arises based on that which is not a root.
It arises.
To what extent does it arise based on a faculty (indriya) or a non-faculty? Answer:
It arises.
Does it arise by depending on both the faculty (*indriya*) and the non-faculty?
Answer: It does.
It is born.
Does it arise from a root or a non-root? Or does it arise from both a root and a non-root? The answer is: [it arises from a root].
It arises.
Does it arise conditioned by the eye-faculty?
Answer: Yes.
Is it born?
Is it perhaps born dependent upon the eye-faculty, up to and including the faculty of ignorance?
Answer: Yes.
It arises.
Does it arise from the faculty of ignorance as its condition?
Answer: Yes.
It arises. Does it arise by depending on the faculty of ignorance (ajñendriya), or even up to the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya)?
Answer: Yes.
The section on "Arising of Arisings" is concluded.
As for the eye-faculty, it is the cause and the predominant condition (*adhipati*) for that same eye-faculty;
it is the sole predominant condition for the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-faculties, the male-faculty, the female-faculty, the life-faculty, and the faculty of suffering.
The others [are] conditions and predominants.
The same applies to the faculties of ear, nose, and tongue.
As for the body faculty, it is the cause and the predominant condition for that very body faculty.
The male faculty and female faculty are also [conditioned by] cause and predominance;
the life faculty, the pain faculty, and the faculties of eye, ear, nose, and tongue are [conditioned by] one [type], predominance;
the remainder are [conditioned by] object and predominance. This concludes the section on the body.
The mind-faculty (manendriya) is the cause, immediate antecedent, object-condition, and predominant condition for that same mind-faculty.
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is the cause and predominant condition for the eight faculties, the five faculties of sensation, and the male, female, and life faculties.
The suffering-faculty (duḥkhendriya) is the cause, immediate antecedent, and predominant condition [for itself], but it has no object-condition.
The others [are related] by way of cause, sequence, object-condition, and predominance.
The same applies to the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of joy, the faculty of equanimity, and the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The female faculty is the cause and the predominant condition for that female faculty;
it is the single predominant condition for the male faculty, the life faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue;
and it is the cause and the predominant condition for the body faculty.
The others [are] conditions and predominants.
The male faculty is also like this.
As for the life-faculty, it is the cause and the predominant condition for that same life-faculty.
The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya), the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, and the male and female faculties have one predominance [over them].
For the others, they are conditions and predominances.
As for the faculty of suffering, it is the cause and predominance of that same faculty of suffering; it has no conditionality and no immediate succession.
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) has eight [conditions]: cause and predominance; being untainted (anāsrava), it has object and predominance.
The pleasure-faculty (sukhendriya) has cause, object, and predominance, but no immediate succession (anantara).
The remaining [faculties] have cause, immediate succession, object, and predominance.
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) has that faculty of grief as its cause, its immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and its predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
the faculty of life (*jīvitendriya*) has eight causes and the predominant condition;

the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has the cause, the immediate condition, and the predominant condition; [the faculty of equanimity] has no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) when it is untainted (*anāsrava*); [the faculties of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom] have the object-condition and the predominant condition.
The others [are related] by way of cause, sequence, condition, and predominance.

As for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), it is related to that same faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" by way of cause, sequence, condition, and predominance;
it is also related to the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) by way of cause, sequence, condition, and predominance.
The faculty of ignorance has [ignorance] as its cause, condition, and predominance, but no immediate succession;
it has the eight faculties including the life-faculty and the single faculty of suffering as its predominance;
and it has the faculty of grief as its condition and predominance.
The others [are related] by way of cause, immediate succession, condition, and predominance.
As for the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*), it is related to that same faculty of one who has already known by way of cause, immediate succession, condition, and predominance;
it is also related to the faculty of final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) by way of cause, immediate succession, condition, and predominance.
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the eight [faculties] have predominance over the suffering-faculty (duḥkhendriya);
the grief-faculty (daurmanasyendriya) and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) are conditions and predominant;
the remaining [faculties] are causes, immediate antecedents, conditions, and predominant.
Regarding the faculty of ignorance (ajñendriya), that faculty of ignorance is its cause, its sequential condition (samanantara-pratyaya), and its predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya);
it is the predominant condition for eight faculties and one instance of the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya);

and for the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya), the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), and the faculty of perfect knowledge (ājñendriya), it is both the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the predominant condition.
The remainder [are] cause, immediate, object, and predominant conditions.

The twenty-seventh chapter, "The Chapter on the Twenty-two Faculties," ends here. In the Sanskrit original it consists of three hundred fourteen *ślokas*; in the Qin translation it consists of four thousand forty-two words.

2. In the *Bhavāgrya* chapter of the *Abhidharma-mūla-skandha*, second section on *bhava*: When one undergoes existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhava*), how many faculties (*indriya*) are initially acquired?
When one undergoes existence in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu-bhava*), how many faculties are initially acquired?
Is there any mental object associated with the desire realm that one fully understands as belonging to the desire realm, yet also fully understands as belonging to the form and formless realms?
Is there any mental object associated with the form realm that one fully understands as belonging to the form realm, yet also fully understands as belonging to the desire and formless realms?
Are there any phenomena associated with the formless realm that, when attended to by the mind, allow one to clearly comprehend the formless realm as well as the desire and form realms?
When clearly comprehending the desire realm, how many faculties (*indriya*) does one clearly comprehend?
When one clearly understands the realm of form and the formless realm, how many faculties (indriya) does one clearly understand?
How many faculties clearly understand the desire realm?
And how many faculties clearly understand the realms of form and the formless?
How many faculties (indriya) lead to the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala)?
How many faculties lead to the attainment of the fruits of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returning (anāgāmin), and arhatship?

Regarding those faculties that lead to the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry—once the fruit of stream-entry has been attained—should it be said that these faculties are possessed (samanvāgata) or should it be said that they are not possessed?

Regarding the faculties by which one attains the fruits of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat—once the fruit of arhatship has been attained, should these faculties be said to be possessed or not possessed?
Regarding those faculties by which one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*: by the cessation of which fetters (*saṃyojana*) are those faculties bound, and in which fruit are those faculties included?

Regarding those faculties by which one attains the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*: by the cessation of which fetters are those faculties bound, and in which fruit are these faculties included?

When the faculties (*indriya*) are abandoned upon attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), by the cessation of which fetters (*saṃyojana*) are those faculties [abandoned], and in which fruit are these faculties included?

When the faculties are abandoned upon attaining the fruits of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and arhat (*arhat*), by the cessation of which fetters are those faculties [abandoned], and in which fruit are these faculties included?

When one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna* and acquires various faculties, by the cessation of which fetters (*saṃyojana*) are those faculties acquired, and in which fruit are those faculties included?

When one attains the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat*, and acquires various faculties, by the cessation of which fetters are those faculties acquired, and in which fruit are those faculties included?
Regarding the faculties perfected by a *srotāpanna*: by the cessation of which fetters (*saṃyojana*) are those faculties [perfected], and under which fruit (*phala*) are those faculties subsumed?

Regarding the faculties perfected by a *sakṛdāgāmin*, an *anāgāmin*, and an *arhat*: by the cessation of which fetters are those faculties [perfected], and under which fruit are those faculties subsumed?

Regarding those faculties through which the fetters of a *srotāpanna* are extinguished: by the extinction of which fetters are these faculties extinguished, and by which fruit are these faculties subsumed?

Regarding those faculties through which the fetters of a *sakṛdāgāmin* and an *anāgāmin* are extinguished: by the extinction of which fetters are these faculties extinguished, and by which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Regarding those faculties included within the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala), by the cessation of which fetters (saṃyojana) are these faculties [attained]?
Regarding those faculties included within the fruits of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), and arhat (arhattva), by the cessation of which fetters are these faculties [attained]?
Regarding the various knowledges of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), are they the untainted knowledge of suffering (*anāsrava-duḥkha-jñāna*)?
Conversely, if they are the untainted knowledge of suffering, are they the knowledge of suffering?
Regarding the various knowledges of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the path (*mārga-jñāna*), are they the untainted knowledge of the path (*anāsrava-mārga-jñāna*)?
If this path is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), is it path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*)?
Are those untainted faculties (*indriya*) that have objects belonging to the desire realm associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?
If those untainted faculties are associated with the knowledge of phenomena, do those faculties have objects belonging to the desire realm?
Are those untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) that have objects belonging to the form and formless realms associated with the knowledge of what is not yet known (*ajñāta-ājñāna-jñāna*)?
Conversely, are those untainted faculties that are associated with the knowledge of what is not yet known necessarily those whose objects belong to the form and formless realms?
Regarding dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), should it be called dharma-knowledge?

Regarding subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna), knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna): should they be said to be with vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka but with vicāra, or without both vitarka and vicāra?

Should it be said that the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)?

Should it be said that they have objects belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), objects belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), objects belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or objects that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
The same applies to the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*).

Regarding "liberation through equal-mindedness" (*sāmayikī-vimukti*), should it be said that one attains the faculties of training (*śaikṣendriya*) or the faculties of no-more-training (*aśaikṣendriya*)?
Regarding "liberation free from doubt" (*akopyā vimukti*), should it be said that one attains the faculties of training or the faculties of no-more-training?
When all fetters are exhausted, should it be said that one has attained the faculty of training (śaikṣendriya) or the faculty of no-more-training (aśaikṣendriya)?

When the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) is realized by means of the path of non-obstruction (ānantaryamārga), should this path be said to be associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)?

Regarding the knowledge of the unknown, the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path: should they be said to be with vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka and with vicāra, or without vitarka and without vicāra?

Should it be said that they are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), or with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), or with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)? Should it be said that they have objects belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or objects belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or objects that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*)?

When one realizes the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat* by means of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), should this path be said to be associated with dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)?

Or is it associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), or knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)? Furthermore, should it be said to be with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), or without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*)?
Should it be said that it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?

Or with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)? Should it be said that its objects are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), bound to the form or formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
Through the severance and arising of how many faculties (indriya) should one say that the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) is attained?
Through the severance and arising of how many faculties should one say that the fruits of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), and arhatship (arhat-phala) are attained?
I wish to explain in full the meaning of this chapter.
When one undergoes birth in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), how many faculties (*indriya*) are initially acquired?
The answer is:
In the case of birth from eggs, birth from a womb, and birth by coalescence, there are two [faculties]:

the body faculty and the life faculty. In the case of apparitional birth, there may be six, seven, or eight: six for those without sexual organs, seven for those with one set of sexual organs, and eight for those with both sets of sexual organs.
Regarding the existence of the form realm (rūpadhātu), how many faculties (indriya) are initially acquired?
The answer is: six.
When one undergoes existence in the formless realm, how many faculties are initially acquired?
Answer: One.
Is it the case that when mental factors bound to the desire realm are being attended to, one clearly understands the desire realm?
Answer: One does not clearly understand it.
Does one clearly understand the realm of form and the formless realm?
Answer: One does not clearly understand them.
Is it the case that when one contemplates phenomena associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) with a mind bound to the form realm, one clearly understands the form realm?
Answer: One clearly understands it.
"Is he one who thoroughly understands the desire realm?
He replied, "He does."
"Is the formless realm fully understood?
He replied,
"It is not fully understood."
Is there a mind associated with the formless realm that, when attending to phenomena, clearly understands the formless realm?
Answer: It does so understand.
"Is the desire realm fully understood?
He replied,
"It is not fully understood."
"Is the realm of form thoroughly understood?
He replied,
"It is thoroughly understood."
If one thoroughly understands the desire realm, how many faculties (*indriya*) does one thoroughly understand?
The answer is:
four—the male faculty, the female faculty, the faculty of sorrow, and the faculty of suffering.
If one clearly understands the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), how many faculties (*indriya*) does one clearly understand?
Answer: Five, namely the five sensory faculties.
If one fully understands the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), how many faculties (indriya) does one understand?
The answer is:
eight—the five [feeling] faculties, the mind faculty (manas), the life faculty (jīvita), and the equanimity faculty (upekṣā).
How many faculties (*indriya*) clearly comprehend the desire realm?
The answer is:

for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), seven—the five [sensual] faculties, the mind faculty, and the faculty of equanimity; for those free from defilement (*vimala*), eight, with the addition of the faculty of "I have known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
How many faculties clearly comprehend the form realm?
The answer is:
for ordinary persons, seven; for those free from defilement, ten, adding the faculties of pleasure and joy.
How many faculties clearly comprehend the formless realm?
The answer is:
eleven, with the addition of the faculty of "I do not know."
How many faculties (indriya) take up the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala)?
The answer is:

nine—the faculty of mind (manas), the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya), the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), and the five faculties [of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom] (pañcendriyāṇi).
How many faculties (indriya) take one to the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala)? Answer:
If one attains realization by skipping stages through the exhaustion of the two types of desire, nine [faculties] are involved.
If one has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, there are seven faculties for attaining the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* by means of the mundane path and eight by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*) path.
How many faculties are required to attain the fruit of *anāgāmin*?
Answer: If one who has exhausted desire for the realm of form attains realization by skipping stages, there are nine;
if one who has attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* by means of the worldly path, there are seven, or eight if by the untainted path.
How many faculties (indriya) take up the fruit of arhatship?
The answer is:
eleven; their enumeration is entirely as stated above.

Regarding the faculties for attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*): once the fruit of stream-entry has been attained, should it be said that these faculties are accomplished or not accomplished?
The answer is:
they are not accomplished in the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*), but they are accomplished in the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

Regarding the faculties by which one attains the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*: once the fruit of *arhat* has been attained, should it be said that these faculties are possessed or not possessed?
Answer: It is not accomplished in the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), but it is accomplished in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
When the faculties take up the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), by the cessation of which fetters (*saṃyojana*) are these faculties [established]?
Answer: They are either bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), or bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or they have no specific location.
Regarding those faculties by which one attains the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) or non-returner (*anāgāmin*): what fetters (*saṃyojana*) are extinguished by these faculties?
Answer: They may be bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form or formless realms, or they may have no location.
When the faculties take up the fruit of arhatship, by which fetters bound to what [realm] are those faculties extinguished?
Answer: It is either bound to the formless realm or it has no location.
As for the faculties that take up the fruit of stream-entry, by which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: The fruit of *srotāpanna* may have no fixed location.
If the various faculties take up the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, by which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin may sometimes have no fixed location.
When the various faculties take up the fruit of the Anāgāmin, by which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: The fruit of anāgāmin may have no fixed location.
When the faculties take up the fruit of arhatship, by which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: The fruit of arhatship may have no fixed location.
When one attains the fruit of srotāpanna and discards the faculties, by the cessation of which fetters are these faculties abandoned?
Answer: They are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form or formless realms, or they have no locus.
When one abandons the faculties upon attaining the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, or *anāgāmin*, by which fetters (*saṃyojana*) are those faculties extinguished?
Answer:
They are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form or formless realms, or they have no fixed location.
When one abandons the faculties upon attaining the fruit of arhatship, by the cessation of which fetters are these faculties abandoned?
Answer: They may be bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), or bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or they may have no fixed location.
When one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) and abandons the faculties (*indriya*), to which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: There is no fixed location.
When one abandons the faculties upon attaining the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, under which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: For one who has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, there may be no [specific] locus.
When one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* and abandons the faculties [of the former stage], to which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin may sometimes have no fixed location.
When one attains the fruit of Arhatship and discards the faculties [of the lower stages], to which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: For one who has attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*, there may be no specific location.
When one attains the various faculties upon realizing the fruit of *srotāpanna*, by the cessation of which fetters (*saṃyojana*) are these faculties bound?
Answer: There is no fixed location.
When one attains the fruits of Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat, and acquires the various faculties (indriya), by what fetters (saṃyojana) are these faculties bound, and what must be extinguished?
Answer: There is no fixed location.
When one attains the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), various faculties (indriya) are acquired; under which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: It is the fruit of srotāpanna.
When one attains the fruits of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat, and acquires the various faculties, by which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: The fruit of Arhatship.
When a Srotāpanna accomplishes the faculties, by the cessation of which fetters do these faculties arise?
Answer: Either bound to the desire realm or belonging to no specific location.
When a Sakṛdāgāmin accomplishes these faculties, by what fetters is this faculty bound, and what is extinguished?
Answer: They are either bound to the desire realm or have no fixed location.
Regarding the faculties accomplished by an Anāgāmin, to which fetters do these faculties belong that are being extinguished?
Answer: They are either bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), or bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), or they have no fixed location.
When an Arhat accomplishes the faculties (indriya), by the cessation of which fetters (saṃyojana) are these faculties bound?
Answer: There is no fixed location.
When a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) accomplishes the various faculties (indriya), under which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: It is either the fruit of *srotāpanna* or it has no fixed location.
As for the faculties accomplished by those who have attained the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*, under which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: The fruit of arhatship may have no specific locus.
Regarding the faculties by which the fetters of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) are extinguished—by what bond are these faculties themselves bound, such that they are extinguished?
Answer: They are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding those faculties through which the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) are extinguished—by what are these faculties bound, such that the fetters are extinguished?
Answer: They are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding those faculties for which the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of an *anāgāmin* have been extinguished—by what are these faculties bound, such that their fetters are extinguished?
Answer: They may be bound to the realm of form or the formless realm.
As for those faculties through which the fetters of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) are extinguished, by which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: There is no fixed location.
When the fetters of a sakṛdāgāmin or an anāgāmin are extinguished through these faculties, by which fruit are these faculties subsumed?
Answer: There is no specific location.
These faculties are subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala); to what fetters (saṃyojana) do these faculties belong for their cessation?
Answer: There is no fixed location.
These faculties are subsumed under the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*. To which fetters (*saṃyojana*) do these faculties lead to the cessation?
Answer: There is no such place.
Is the knowledge of suffering regarding all sufferings the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) of suffering?
Answer: It is so;
the knowledge of suffering regarding all sufferings is the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of suffering.
Is there, however, any untainted knowledge of suffering that is not the knowledge of suffering?
Answer: Yes, it is the knowledge of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-jñāna*).
Is that knowledge of the origin of suffering the untainted knowledge of the origin (*anāsrava-samudaya-jñāna*)?
Answer: It is so;
that which is the knowledge of cultivation (bhāvanājñāna) is indeed the untainted knowledge of cultivation (anāsrava-bhāvanājñāna).
Is there, however, any untainted knowledge of cultivation that is not the knowledge of cultivation?
Answer: Yes;
it is the knowledge of the suffering that has been cultivated.
Is all knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) necessarily the untainted knowledge of exhaustion (anāsrava-kṣayajñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one has exhausted the knowledge of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna), is that the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
Are all path-knowledges (mārga-jñāna) that same untainted knowledge of the path (anāsrava-mārga-jñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If it is untainted knowledge regarding the Path, is that the knowledge of the Path?
Answer: It is so.
If uncontaminated faculties have objects associated with the desire realm, are these faculties associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?

Answer: There are untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) that have objects belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-ālambana), yet these faculties are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).
How is it that an untainted faculty can have an object belonging to the desire realm while not being associated with the knowledge of phenomena?
The answer is:

the faculties associated with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti), the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna), the patience regarding the origin of suffering (samudaya-dharma-kṣānti), and the knowledge of the origin of suffering (samudaya-dharma-jñāna)—these are called the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) that have objects bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta). These faculties are not associated with the knowledge of the dharma (dharma-jñāna).

What are the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), yet have objects that are not bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-saṃprayukta*)? Answer:

Those faculties that have the cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*) as their object and are associated with the knowledge of phenomena; these are called the untainted faculties associated with the knowledge of phenomena whose objects are not bound to the realm of desire.
What are the untainted faculties that have objects belonging to the desire realm and are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
The answer is:

those faculties that have suffering as their object or have origination as their object and are associated with the knowledge of phenomena; these are called the untainted faculties that have objects belonging to the desire realm and are associated with the knowledge of phenomena.

What are the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) that do not have objects conditioned by the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-ālambana*) and are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?

Answer: The faculties associated with the patience regarding the unknown suffering (*duḥkhe ’jñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the unknown suffering (*duḥkhe ’jñāna*); the faculties associated with the patience regarding the unknown origin (*samudaye ’jñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the unknown origin (*samudaye ’jñāna*); the faculties associated with the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñāna-kṣānti*); the faculties associated with the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñāna*), the patience regarding the unknown cessation (*nirodhe ’jñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*), and the knowledge of the unknown cessation (*nirodhe ’jñāna*); and the faculties associated with the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārge dharmajñāna-kṣānti*). These are called the untainted faculties that do not have objects conditioned by the desire realm and are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena.

If those untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) have objects (ālambana) bound to the form and formless realms, are those faculties associated with the knowledge of what is not yet known (ajñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna)? Answer:
Some untainted faculties have objects bound to the form and formless realms, yet those faculties are not associated with the knowledge of what is not yet known.

What are the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) that have objects belonging to the form and formless realms (rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta-ālambana), yet those faculties are not associated with the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna)? Answer:

The faculties associated with the patience regarding the knowledge of the unknown concerning suffering (duḥkhe 'nājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-kṣānti); the faculties associated with the knowledge of the unknown concerning suffering (duḥkhe 'nājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna); and the patience regarding the knowledge of the unknown concerning origination (samudaye 'nājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-kṣānti) and the faculties associated with the knowledge of the unknown concerning origination (samudaye 'nājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna)—these are called the untainted faculties that have objects belonging to the form and formless realms, yet those faculties are not associated with the knowledge of the unknown.
What are the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) associated with the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñāta-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) whose objects are not bound to the form or formless realms? Answer:

Those faculties that take cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*) as their object and are associated with the knowledge of the unknown—these are called the untainted faculties associated with the knowledge of the unknown whose objects are not bound to the form or formless realms.

What are the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) that have as their object the factors bound to the form and formless realms (rūpārūpya-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta), and which are associated with the knowledge of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna)? Answer:

Those faculties that have suffering (duḥkha) or its origin (samudaya) as their object and are associated with the knowledge of the unknown—these are called the untainted faculties that have as their object the factors bound to the form and formless realms and are associated with the knowledge of the unknown.

What are the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) that do not have the form and formless realms as their objects, and whose corresponding faculties are not associated with the knowledge of the unknown (*ajñātājñāna-indriya*)?

Answer: The faculties associated with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*); the faculties associated with the patience regarding the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*); the faculties associated with the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*), the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), and the patience regarding the unknown regarding cessation (*nirodha-ajñātājñāna-kṣānti*); the faculties associated with the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation (*nirodha-ajñātājñāna*); the faculties associated with the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*); and the patience regarding the unknown regarding the path (*mārga-ajñātājñāna-kṣānti*). These are called the untainted faculties whose corresponding faculties do not have the form and formless realms as their objects, and which are not associated with the knowledge of the unknown.
Should it be said that dharma-knowledge is dharma-knowledge? The answer is: dharma-knowledge should be said to be dharma-knowledge;

or it is the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, or the knowledge of the path; or it is with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra, or without vitarka and without vicāra; or it is associated with the faculty of pleasure, or the faculty of joy, or the faculty of equanimity; or it is associated with emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; or it has objects conditioned by the desire realm, or objects not so conditioned—thus dharma-knowledge is exhausted.

Should it be said that the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*) is the knowledge of the unknown? The answer is: the knowledge of the unknown should be said to be the knowledge of the unknown;

or it is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), or the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). It is either with initial application and sustained application (*savitarka-savicāra*), or without initial application but with sustained application (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), or without initial application and without sustained application (*avitarka-avicāra*). It is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); or it is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), or wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). It has as its object that which is bound to the realm of form or the formless realm, or that which is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*). Thus is the knowledge of the unknown exhausted.
Regarding "liberation through equanimity" (sāmayikī vimukti), should it be said that one attains the faculties of a learner (śaikṣa-indriya) or the faculties of one beyond learning (aśaikṣa-indriya)?
Answer: Regarding liberation through equanimity, it should be said that one attains both the faculties of a learner and the faculties of one beyond learning.

Regarding the liberation through the absence of doubt (*aniyata-vimukti*), should it be said that one attains the faculties of training (*śaikṣendriya*) or the faculties beyond training (*aśaikṣendriya*)? Answer:
If one first attains the absence of doubt, it should be said that one attains both the faculties of training and the faculties beyond training.
If an Arhat who has attained equanimity-liberation (sāmayikī vimukti) has attained freedom from doubt, should it be said that he has attained the faculties of one beyond training (aśaikṣendriya)?
Since all fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted, should it be said that he has attained the faculties of one in training (śaikṣendriya) or the faculties of one beyond training?
Answer: When all fetters are exhausted, it should be said that one has attained the faculty of training (*śaikṣendriya*) and the faculty of no-more-training (*aśaikṣendriya*).

By means of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*), one realizes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*); this path should be said to be associated with patience (*kṣānti*), associated with both applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*). It should be said that its object is not bound, as the track of the path is completed.

When one realizes the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* by means of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), if this realization is attained by transcending stages through the complete exhaustion of double the [remaining] desires, this path should be said to be associated with patience (*kṣānti*), associated with both applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), associated with the guarding of the faculties (*indriya-rakṣā*) and associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*), and should be said to have unconditioned objects (*aniyata-ālambana*).

If one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) takes up the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) by means of the mundane path (laukikamārga), this path should be said to be associated with conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), should be said to be accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, associated with the guarding of the faculties (indriyārakṣā), and should be said to have objects (ālambana) bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
