If one has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and, by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, this path should be said to be associated with either the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), or the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). It should be said to be accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*). It should be said to be associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), or with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), or wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). It should be said to have as its object that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or that which is not so bound (*apratisaṃyukta*). This concludes the section on the "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

When one realizes the fruit of *anāgāmin* by means of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), if one realizes it by transcending stages through the exhaustion of sensual desire, this path should be said to be associated with patience (*kṣānti*), and may be either with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), or without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*); it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and is associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*).

If one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* and then takes up the fruit of *anāgāmin* by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), this path should be said to be associated with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), should be said to possess both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), should be said to be associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and should be said to have objects pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

If one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* and, by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), takes up the fruit of *anāgāmin*, this path should be said to be associated with either the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), or the knowledges of origin, cessation, and the path (*samudaya-nirodha-mārgajñāna*). It should be said to possess both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). It should be said to be associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), or associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). It should be said to have as its object that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or that which is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*). [The section on the *anāgāmin* concludes.]

One realizes the fruit of Arhatship by means of the path of non-obstruction. If one realizes the fruit of Arhatship by relying on the future *samādhi* with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), this path is either associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), or with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), or with the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, or the path. It should be said to be with applied thought and sustained thought; it should be said to be associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), or with emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; and it has as its object that which is bound to the formless realm or that which is unbound.

If one attains the fruit of Arhatship by relying on the first dhyāna, this path is either associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), or the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; it should be said to possess both vitarka and vicāra; it should be said to be associated with the faculty of joy (prītīndriya); or it is associated with emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), or wishlessness (apraṇihita); and its object is either bound to the formless realm or unbound.

If one attains the fruit of Arhatship by relying on the intermediate dhyāna, this path is either associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), or the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. It should be said to be without vitarka and with vicāra; it should be said to be associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya); or it is associated with emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; or it has as its object that which is bound to the formless realm or that which is unbound.

If one attains the fruit of arhatship by relying on the second dhyāna, this path is either associated with dharma-knowledge, unknown-knowledge, or the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; it should be said to be without vitarka and without vicāra; it should be said to be associated with the faculty of joy (prīti-indriya); or it is associated with emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; or it has as its object that which is bound to the formless realm, or that which is unbound.

If one attains the fruit of Arhatship based on the third dhyāna, this path is either associated with dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, or the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; it should be said to be without applied thought and without sustained thought; it should be said to be associated with the faculty of pleasure; or it is associated with emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; or it has as its object that which is bound to the formless realm, or it has as its object that which is unbound.

If one attains the fruit of arhatship by relying on the fourth dhyāna, this path is either associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), or the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; it should be said to be without vitarka and without vicāra; it should be said to be associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya); or it is associated with emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; or it has as its object that which is bound to the formless realm, or it has as its object that which is unbound.

If one attains the fruit of Arhatship by relying on the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), this path should be said to be associated with either the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñāta-ājñāna-jñāna*) or the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; it should be said to be without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*); it should be said to be associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), or with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (*śūnyatā-animitta-apraṇihita*); and it should be said to have as its object that which is bound to the formless realm or that which is unbound. This concludes the section on the True Person (*āryapudgala*).
How many faculties (*indriya*) cease and arise when one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*)?
The answer is:

not all faculties cease; seven cease and arise, one ceases but does not arise (the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"), and one arises but does not cease (the faculty of "having known"). It should be said that one thus attains the fruit of stream-entry.
How many faculties must cease and arise for one to be said to attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*?
The answer is:

if one attains realization by transcending the stages through the exhaustion of double-desire (*dviguṇa-kāma*), the faculties do not all cease; seven cease and arise, one ceases but does not arise, and one arises but does not cease—at this point, one should be said to attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.

If one has attained the fruit of srotāpanna and, by means of the mundane path, takes up the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, such that the faculties are not entirely extinguished but seven have been exhausted and seven have arisen, it should be said that one has attained the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin.

If one has attained the fruit of Srotāpanna and, by means of the untainted path, takes up the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin, such that the faculties are not entirely extinguished but eight have been exhausted and arisen as "already known," it should be said that one has attained the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin.
How many faculties must cease and arise for one to be said to attain the fruit of *anāgāmin*? Answer:

If one attains realization by transcending the stages through the exhaustion of sensual desire, the faculties do not all cease. Seven cease and arise, one ceases but does not arise, and one arises but does not cease; in this case, one should be said to attain the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

If one has attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* and, by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), takes up the fruit of *anāgāmin*, such that the dhyānas do not manifest and the four faculties—sorrow, suffering, masculinity, and femininity—are all extinguished, then with the cessation of these seven, it should be said that one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

If dhyāna manifests before one, the four faculties are all extinguished; six have ceased and five have arisen; one is extinguished and does not arise; and one arises and does not cease—this should be called attaining the fruit of anāgāmin.

If one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* and, by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), takes up the fruit of *anāgāmin*, such that the dhyānas do not manifest before him, then four faculties are entirely extinguished and eight cessations arise; this should be called the attainment of the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

If dhyāna manifests before one, the four faculties are all extinguished; seven cease and five faculties—mind, knowledge, and equanimity—arise; one faculty ceases and does not arise; and one faculty arises and does not cease, whether it be pleasure or joy; this should be called attaining the fruit of anāgāmin.
How many faculties (*indriya*) cease and how many arise when one is said to attain the fruit of Arhatship?
The answer is:

If one attains the fruit of Arhatship by relying on the future *samādhi* with directed thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), then one faculty entirely ceases—namely, life; seven cease and arise; one ceases and does not arise—namely, the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātāvī*); and one arises and does not cease—namely, the faculty of "not yet known" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmī*). In this case, one is said to attain the fruit of Arhatship.
The same applies to the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

If one attains the fruit of arhatship by relying on the first dhyāna, two faculties are both extinguished: the life-faculty and the faculty of protection; six are extinguished and arise; one is extinguished but does not arise; one arises but is not exhausted; and one is both exhausted and arises. This should be called the attainment of the fruit of arhatship.
The second and third dhyānas are likewise thus. This concludes the twenty-eighth chapter on the faculty of pleasure in the third dhyāna.
In the Sanskrit original, there are three hundred and twenty-eight ślokas; in the Qin language, there are four thousand two hundred and seventy-two words.
3. Chapter on Contact (Phassa-vagga), Root Section (Mūla-khaṇḍa), Chapter Thirty-six: Contact. Contact:

contact through resistance (paṭigha-samphassa), contact through designation (adhivacana-samphassa), contact of clarity (ñāṇa-samphassa), contact of ignorance (aññāṇa-samphassa), contact that is neither clarity nor ignorance, contact of craving (taṇhā-samphassa), contact of aversion (paṭigha-samphassa), contact of pleasant feeling (sukhā-vedanā-samphassa), contact of painful feeling (dukkhā-vedanā-samphassa), contact of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkham-asukhā-vedanā-samphassa), contact of the eye, contact of the ear, contact of the nose, contact of the tongue, contact of the body, and contact of the mind.
What is the contact of resistance (*sapratigha-sparśa*), and so on, up to what is the contact of the mind (*manaḥ-sparśa*)?
How many contacts are subsumed under the contact of resistance, and so on, up to how many contacts are subsumed under the contact of the mind?
With how many faculties is contact with resistance (*sapratigha-sparśa*) associated, and so on, up to: with how many faculties is mental contact (*manas-sparśa*) associated?
Are all these faculties the causes of contact with resistance, and is contact with resistance associated with these faculties?

If a faculty is both resistant (*sapratigha*) and associated with contact (*sparśa*), is that faculty likewise a cause for contact that is resistant, and so on, up to being a cause for mental contact (*manas-sparśa*)?
Furthermore, regarding those who possess this type of eye-faculty, do they also possess this type of body-faculty?
If one achieves this kind of body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), does one achieve this kind of eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*)?
The same applies to the ear, nose, and tongue faculties.
How many faculties are achieved in the hells?

How many faculties (indriya) do animals, hungry ghosts, those who have severed the roots of goodness, those of wrong determination, those of right determination, those of no fixed determination, those of Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, Uttarakuru, the bodies of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, the intermediate state (antarābhava), the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), those of firm faith (śraddhādhimukta), those of firm dharma (dharmānusārin), those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), those with bodily realization (kāyasākṣin), those liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta), and those liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) possess?
When the faculty of the eye attains the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), how many faculties attain the knowledge of abandonment?
... up to when the faculty of wisdom attains the knowledge of abandonment, how many faculties attain the knowledge of abandonment?
When the faculty of the eye attains the realization of exhaustion (*kṣayaprativedha*), how many faculties attain the realization of exhaustion?
Up until the time when the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) attains the realization of exhaustion (*kṣayābhisamaya*), how many faculties attain the realization of exhaustion?
I wish to explain the meaning of this chapter in full detail.
There are sixteen types of contact (*sparśa*):

There is contact-pleasure through resistance, contact-pleasure through designation, contact-pleasure through clarity, contact-pleasure through ignorance, contact-pleasure that is neither clarity nor ignorance, contact-pleasure of craving, contact-pleasure of aversion, contact-pleasure of pleasant feeling, contact-pleasure of painful feeling, contact-pleasure of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, contact-pleasure of the eye, contact-pleasure of the ear, contact-pleasure of the nose, contact-pleasure of the tongue, contact-pleasure of the body, and contact-pleasure of the mind.
What is contact with resistance?
The answer is:
contact associated with the five groups of consciousness.
What is the contact of designation (adhivacana-saṃsparśa)?
The answer is:
the contact associated with the group of mental consciousness (mano-vijñāna-kāya).
What is clear contact?
The answer is:
untainted contact.
What is contact associated with ignorance?
The answer is:
defiled contact.
What is contact that is neither with ignorance nor without ignorance? Answer:
It is contact that is undefiled yet tainted (sāsrava).
What is the contact of craving?
The answer is:
contact associated with desire.
What is the contact of aversion?
The answer is:
contact associated with ill-will.
What is meant by "contact associated with pleasant feeling"?
The answer is:
contact associated with pleasant feeling.
What is meant by painful contact?
The answer is:
contact associated with pain.
What is meant by the contact that is neither painful nor pleasant?
The answer is:
contact associated with feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.
What is meant by "eye-contact-pleasure"?
The answer is:
contact associated with the aggregate of eye-consciousness.
The same applies to the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
What is meant by mental contact?
The answer is:
Contact associated with the body of mental consciousness (*manovijñānakāya*) includes contact through resistance (*pratigha-sparśa*),
which subsumes six types of contact and partially enters into seven types of contact.
Contact through designation (*adhivacana-sparśa*) subsumes three types of contact and partially enters into seven types of contact.
Clear contact (vidyā-sparśa) includes clear contact and partially includes four types of contact.
Ignorant contact (avidyā-sparśa) includes three types of contact and partially includes eleven types of contact.
Neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance encompasses the contact of neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance, which is included within a portion of the eleven types of contact.
The contact of craving encompasses the contact of craving, which is included within a portion of the eleven types of contact.
The contact of aversion includes the contact of aversion, with eleven contacts partially included therein.
The contact of pleasant feeling includes the contact of pleasant feeling, with twelve contacts partially included therein.
Painful contact is subsumed under painful contact; eleven contacts enter into it only partially.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact is subsumed under neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact; thirteen contacts enter into it only partially.
Eye-contact (cakṣu-saṃsparśa) includes eye-contact itself and a portion of eight contacts.
The same applies to ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact.
Mental contact (mano-saṃsparśa) includes three types of contact and a portion of seven contacts.
Contact through resistance (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) is associated with one faculty and partially enters into eight faculties.
Contact through designation (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) is associated with five faculties and partially enters into eight faculties.
Contact associated with knowledge (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*) is associated with three faculties and partially enters into nine faculties.
Contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*) is partially associated with six faculties.
Contact associated with neither-knowledge-nor-ignorance (*naivavidyā-nāvidyā-saṃsparśa*) is partially associated with eleven faculties.
The contact of affection (*rāga-saṃsparśa*) is associated with four faculties and partially associated with [the remaining] faculties.
The contact of aversion (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) is associated with four faculties and partially associated with [the remaining] faculties.
The contact of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā-saṃsparśa*) is associated with two faculties and partially associated with nine faculties.
Painful contact associated with pleasure is associated with two faculties and partially enters six faculties.
Contact that is neither painful nor pleasant is associated with one faculty and partially enters nine faculties.
Visual contact (*cakṣuḥ-saṃsparśa*) is associated with nine faculties (*indriya*) in part.
The same applies to auditory contact, olfactory contact, gustatory contact, and tactile contact.
Mental contact (*manaḥ-saṃsparśa*) is associated with five faculties and eight faculties in part.
If the various faculties have contact with resistance as their cause, are those faculties associated with that contact with resistance?
Answer: It is so;
whichever faculties are associated with contact with resistance, those faculties have contact with resistance as their cause.
Is there a faculty that has contact with resistance as its cause, yet this faculty is not associated with contact with resistance?
Answer: Yes.
There are faculties that have contact with resistance as their cause, but are associated with other types of contact.

If a faculty has as its cause contact through resistance (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) that arises as a result of maturation (*vipāka*) and is without an object (*anālambana*), and so on up to contact through the mind (*manaḥ-saṃsparśa*), it is likewise.
Excluding these two types of contact, if various faculties have as their cause contact through clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), are these faculties associated with contact through clarity?
Answer: It is so.
The various faculties are associated with contact through clear sensation.
Is that faculty caused by contact associated with clear knowledge?
He replied: "It is so."
If the various faculties have as their cause a contact that is neither ignorance nor non-ignorance, are these faculties associated with that contact which is neither ignorance nor non-ignorance?
Answer: It is so;
those faculties that are associated with a contact that is neither ignorance nor non-ignorance have as their cause a contact that is neither ignorance nor non-ignorance.
Is there a faculty that has as its cause neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance-contact, yet this faculty is not associated with neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance-contact?
Answer: Yes;
there are those faculties which have as their cause neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance-contact and are born of retribution, being without an object-condition (*anālambana*).
If one possesses this particular type of eye faculty, does one also possess this particular type of body faculty?
Answer: One may possess this particular type of eye faculty without possessing this particular type of body faculty.
How is it that one may achieve this kind of eye faculty but not this kind of body faculty?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who has not obtained the eye faculty, or who, having obtained it, has lost it, yet obtains the divine eye (divyacakṣus); this is called achieving this kind of eye faculty but not this kind of body faculty.
What is it that constitutes the accomplishment of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) of this kind, but not the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) of this kind?
The answer is:

one who is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and does not obtain the eye-faculty, or having obtained it, loses it, and does not obtain the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); this is called the accomplishment of the body-faculty of this kind, but not the eye-faculty of this kind.
What is meant by "possessing this kind of eye-faculty and this kind of body-faculty"?
The answer is:

one who is born in the desire realm and has acquired the eye-faculty without losing it, or one who is born in the form realm; this is called possessing this kind of eye-faculty and this kind of body-faculty.
What is it that does not possess this kind of eye faculty and does not possess this kind of body faculty?
The answer is:
one born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); this is called not possessing this kind of eye faculty and not possessing this kind of body faculty.
The faculty of hearing is also like this.
If one possesses this type of nose faculty, does one also possess that type of body faculty?
The answer is:
Thus, if one possesses the nose faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) by way of this seed, one also possesses the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) by way of that seed.
Is it possible that one possesses the body faculty by way of this seed, yet does not possess the nose faculty by way of this same seed?
Answer: There are.
For example, one born in the desire realm who does not obtain the nose faculty, or who obtains it but then loses it.
The same applies to the tongue faculty.
How many faculties (*indriya*) are possessed by those in the hells? Answer:
At most, nineteen; at least, eight.
Among animals, at most there are nineteen, and at least thirteen.
It is the same for hungry ghosts.
For those who have severed their roots of goodness, at most there are thirteen, and at least eight.
In the case of the wrongly fixed [faculties], they are at most nineteen and at least eight.
In the case of the rightly fixed [faculties], they are at most nineteen and at least eleven.
In the case of the unfixed [faculties], they are at most nineteen and at least eight.
It is the same for Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, and Pūrvavideha.
In Uttarakuru, at most there are eighteen, and at least thirteen.
The bodies of the Four Great Kings are at most nineteen and at least seventeen.
It is the same for the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
In the Brahma and Parīttābha heavens, there are at most sixteen and at least fifteen.
It is the same for the Ābhāsvara heaven.
In the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, there are at most sixteen and at least fourteen.
The Fruit-Body Devas number at most sixteen and at least thirteen.
The Intermediate State beings number at most nineteen and at least thirteen.
In the formless realm, if at maximum there are eleven, at minimum there are eight.
For those of steadfast faith and steadfast dharma, if at maximum there are nineteen, at minimum there are thirteen.
For those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), at most there are nineteen, and at least eleven.

For those who have realized through the body (kāyasākṣin), those liberated through wisdom (prajñāvimukta), and those liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), at most there are eighteen, and at least eleven.

When the faculty of the eye attains the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), it reaches the exhaustion of craving for form (*rūparāga-kṣaya*); at that time, five faculties attain the knowledge of abandonment.
It is the same for the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

When the mental faculty (*manas*) attains the knowledge of abandonment, it reaches the exhaustion of craving for the formless (*ārūpyarāga-kṣaya*); at that time, eight faculties attain the knowledge of abandonment.
The life-faculty and the faculties of guarding are likewise; so too are the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

When the male faculty and female faculty attain the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*), they reach the exhaustion of sensual desire; at that time, four faculties attain the knowledge of abandonment.
The faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) are likewise.

When the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) attains the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the *Śubhakṛtsna* realm; at that moment, that very faculty of pleasure attains the knowledge of abandonment.

When the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) attains the knowledge of abandonment, one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the Ābhāsvara realm; at that moment, that very faculty of joy attains the knowledge of abandonment.

When the faculty of the eye is fully realized, one reaches the exhaustion of craving for forms; when the five faculties are fully realized, one attains arhatship through the full realization of nineteen faculties.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
When the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) is fully realized, nineteen faculties are fully realized, including the attainment of Arhatship.

The same applies to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the faculties of faith (*śraddhendriya*), vigor (*vīryendriya*), mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

When the male faculty and female faculty are fully realized, one reaches the exhaustion of sensual desire; four faculties are fully realized, and upon attaining arhatship, nineteen faculties are fully realized.
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) are likewise.

When the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is fully realized, one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the Realm of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*); at that very moment, having fully realized the exhaustion of that faculty of pleasure, one attains arhatship through the full realization of nineteen faculties.

When one realizes the exhaustion of the faculty of gladness (*somanassindriya*), one reaches the exhaustion of craving for the Ābhāsvara realm; that very realization of the exhaustion of the faculty of gladness constitutes the realization of the exhaustion of nineteen faculties upon attaining Arhatship.

The Abhidharma Chapter on Contact (Sparśa), the twenty-ninth, is concluded. In the Sanskrit original, it consists of one hundred and forty-one ślokas; in the Qin language, this amounts to one thousand nine hundred and one words.
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-one;
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-two.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra and Zhu Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty.

Chapter Four: The Section on the Root of the Initial Mind (Ādi-citta-varga-mūla-khaṇḍa). Regarding the fourth section on the initial mind: Should it be said that all sentient beings have an initial arising of the mind, an initial abiding of the mind, and an initial ceasing of the mind?
Regarding those minds with desire and those minds without desire—should these minds be said to arise, abide, and cease for the first time?

Regarding those with anger and those without anger; those with delusion and those without delusion; those that are defiled and those that are undefiled; those that are distracted and those that are undistracted; those that are indolent and those that are not indolent; those that are small and those that are great; those that are cultivated and those that are uncultivated; those with samādhi and those without samādhi; and regarding all minds that are unliberated and all minds that are liberated—should these minds be said to arise, abide, and perish for the first time?
Should it be said that life-force turns together with the mind or does not turn together with the mind?
Should it be said that it turns in accordance [with the mind], or should it be said that it abides from its initial arising?
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
The life-force of human beings is exhausted like the water of a small river;
for all sentient beings, their lifespan is constant—how, then, is it brought to an end?

When entering the meditative attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), should one say that the formations of lifespan (*āyur-saṃskāra*) are reversed or not reversed upon entry?
In the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), how many faculties (*indriya*) cease, and what bound (*saṃyojana*) mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) cease?
Upon arising from the non-conception samādhi, how many faculties manifest, and what bound mind and mental factors manifest?
When entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), how many faculties (*indriya*) cease, and which bound mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) cease?
Upon arising from the samādhi of cessation, how many faculties manifest, and which bound mind and mental factors manifest?
When one is born among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), how many faculties (*indriya*) cease, and what bound states of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) cease?
How many faculties manifest, and what bound states of mind and mental factors manifest?
When beings in the realm of non-perception pass away, how many faculties cease? Which bound mind and mental factors cease?
How many faculties manifest? Which bound mind and mental factors manifest?
Regarding non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), should it be said that they are born with perception (*saṃjñā*) or that they are born without perception?
Furthermore, the Blessed One has said:
"Those beings are born with perception; when they pass away from that place, that perception ceases."
When those sentient beings pass away from that place, they do not cease to exist; where, then, does this perception cease?
Should this perception be said to be wholesome or indeterminate?
By how many latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is this perception driven, and by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) is it bound?
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"All sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment."
What do the beings in the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) consume as food?
How many faculties (*indriya*) are subsumed under the faculty of the eye, and so on, up to how many are subsumed under the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*)?

How many faculties are subsumed under the power of faith (*śraddhābala*), and so on, up to the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*); the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisaṃbodhyaṅga*), and so on, up to the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣāsaṃbodhyaṅga*); right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and so on, up to right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*); the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), and so on, up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); and how many faculties are subsumed under the samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)?
With how many faculties is the mind-faculty associated, and so on, up to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?

With how many faculties are the power of faith through to the power of wisdom; the awakening factor of mindfulness through to the awakening factor of equanimity; right view through to right concentration; the knowledge of phenomena through to the knowledge of the path; and the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness associated?
When one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the desire realm, how many faculties cease, and what bound states of mind and mental factors cease?
How many faculties manifest, and what bound states of mind and mental factors manifest?

When one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm; when one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm; when one passes away from the form realm and is reborn in the form realm; when one passes away from the form realm and is reborn in the desire realm; when one passes away from the form realm and is reborn in the formless realm; when one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm; when one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm; and when one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm—in each of these cases, how many faculties (*indriya*) cease, and what bound (*saṃyojana*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) cease?
How many faculties (*indriya*) manifest? What bound (*saṃyojana*) mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) manifest?
At the parinirvāṇa of an Arhat, how many faculties are the last to cease?
I pray that you will fully expound the meaning of this chapter.
"Should it be said that for all sentient beings, the mind first arises, the mind first abides, and the mind first ceases?
He replied: "It is so."
Regarding those minds with desire and those minds without desire, should it be said that these minds first arise, first abide, and first cease?
He replied: "It is so."

Regarding states with hatred and without hatred, with delusion and without delusion, with defilement and without defilement, with distraction and without distraction, with sloth and without sloth, small and great, uncultivated and cultivated, undetermined and determined, and minds that are not liberated versus minds that are liberated—should these minds be said to arise, abide, and cease for the first time?
The answer is:
It is so. Should it be said that life-span revolves together with the mind, or does it not revolve together with the mind?
Answer: It should be said that life does not turn along with the mind.
Should it be said that it turns in accordance [with the mind] at the very moment of its initial arising and abiding?
Answer:

Sentient beings of the desire realm who have not entered the concentration of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*) or the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) follow the cycle of rebirth; however, those who have entered the concentration of non-conception, the concentration of cessation, or who are born among the devas of the form and formless realms, should be said to abide from the very moment of their birth.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"The life of a human being is consumed and exhausted like a small river;
the lifespan of all sentient beings is constant, yet that lifespan eventually comes to an end."
How is it known that their lifespan has ended?
The answer is:
at the end of an eon, at the end of a kalpa, or upon entering the samādhi of non-conception or the samādhi of cessation.
Should the formations of lifespan be said to be "conforming" (*anuloma*) or "abiding" (*sthiti*)?
Answer: They should be said to be abiding.
When entering the samādhi of non-conception, how many faculties cease?
Answer: Seven.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors bound that cease?
Answer: They are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
When emerging from the samādhi of non-conception, how many faculties are present?
Answer: Seven.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors bound that manifest?
Answer: They are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
When entering the samādhi of cessation, how many faculties (indriya) are extinguished?
Answer: Seven.
What are the mental states and mental factors that are bound to which realm? Answer:
Those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
When emerging from the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), how many faculties (indriya) are present?
The answer is:
either seven—the five [sensory] faculties, the mind faculty (manas), and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣā)—or eight, with the addition of the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya).
There are seven types of tainted (sāsrava) minds and eight types of untainted (anāsrava) minds.
To which realm are the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) bound when they manifest? Answer:
Whether bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) or unbound,
when one is born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), how many faculties (*indriya*) are exhausted? Answer:
85. Regarding the protection of the life-force of feeling and perception:
by the cessation of what bound mind and mental factors do they come to an end? Answer:
Regarding those bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-vyavasthita),
how many faculties (indriya) are present? Answer:
8. To what fetters (saṃyojana) are the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) bound when they manifest? Answer:
Regarding those bound to the realm of form:
when beings in the state of non-perception pass away, how many faculties are exhausted?
Answer: [The following].
8. What fetters are exhausted when the mind and mental factors cease? Answer:
Regarding those bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-vyavakṛṣṭa),
how many faculties (indriya) are present? Answer:
There are eight, nine, or ten [fetters].
Eight for those without sexual organs; nine for those with one sexual organ, adding female or male; ten for those with both sexual organs.
With which fetters (saṃyojana) bound do the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika) manifest?
Answer: It is bound to the desire realm.
Regarding non-percipient beings, should it be said that they are born with perception or born without perception?
Answer: It should be said that for beings in the state of non-perception, perception arises.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
One thinks, "That sentient being has passed away from that place," which constitutes the cessation of perception.
Is it not the case that "that sentient being has passed away from that place" also constitutes the non-cessation [of perception]?
The answer is: No.
When that perception ceases, those sentient beings pass away from that place; it is not that they remain without having ceased.
Where does that perception cease?
The answer is:
One abides in that and eliminates that perception.
Should this perception be called wholesome or indeterminate?
The answer is:
This perception is either wholesome or indeterminate.
By how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) is this perception influenced? Answer:
Regarding the outflow-tainted objects of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are they bound? Answer:
Sixth.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"All sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment."
What is the nutriment of the Heaven of Non-conception?
The answer is:
it is the consciousness of mental attention.
The eye faculty includes the eye faculty.
The ear, nose, and tongue faculties are likewise.
The body faculty includes three faculties.
The faculty of mind (manendriya) includes the faculty of mind itself and partially includes three faculties.

The same applies to the faculties of pleasure (sukhendriya), joy (saumanasyendriya), equanimity (upekṣendriya), faith (śraddhendriya), diligence (vīryendriya), mindfulness (smṛtīndriya), concentration (samādhīndriya), and wisdom (prajñendriya).
The female faculty includes the female faculty and a portion of the body faculty.
The male faculty includes the male faculty and a portion of the body faculty.
The life faculty includes the life faculty.
The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) is subsumed by the faculty of suffering;
the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya) is subsumed by the faculty of grief;
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) is subsumed by the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," with nine faculties partially included therein.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and the faculty of "one who knows" are also like this.
The power of faith subsumes one faculty and partially enters into three faculties;
the powers of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are also like this.

The awakening factor of mindfulness partially enters into four faculties; the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena, energy, rapture, and concentration are likewise. The awakening factors of tranquility and equanimity do not include any faculties.

Right view, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*): these are subsumed under a portion of four faculties.
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) is subsumed under a portion of three faculties.
Conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) is subsumed under one faculty (*indriya*) and a portion [of others].
The knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, are subsumed under four faculties and a portion [of others].
The mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is associated with ten faculties, five faiths, and five feelings, and is subsumed under three faculties and a portion [of others].
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are associated with nine faculties, with a partial entry [into each].

The faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) are associated with six faculties, with a partial entry [into each], and five faculties plus the mental faculty (*manas*).
The faculty of faith is associated with four faculties and partially enters into nine faculties.
The same applies to the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is associated with nine faculties and partially enters into them.
The faculty of "I have known" and the faculty of "I have fully known" are also like this.
The power of faith is associated with four faculties and partially enters into nine faculties.
The powers of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are also like this.
The awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is associated with eleven faculties (*indriya*) to a small degree.
The same applies to the awakening factors of phenomena (*dharma*), energy (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*).
The awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is associated with nine faculties to a small degree.

The enlightenment factor of equanimity (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the enlightenment factor of vigilance (*apramāda-saṃbodhyaṅga*) are associated with three faculties and partially enter into nine faculties.

Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are associated with eleven faculties and partially enter [into them].
The knowledge of others' minds is associated with ten faculties, entering slightly.
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is associated with two faculties, entering slightly with eight faculties.
The knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, are associated with eleven faculties, entering slightly.
Regarding birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how many faculties (*indriya*) are exhausted?

The answer is: either four, or nine, or eight, or thirteen, or nine, or fourteen, or ten, or fifteen. For one with a desire-realm-bound indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) who dies gradually, four are exhausted; for one with a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*), nine. For one without sexual organs who dies simultaneously with an indeterminate mind, eight are exhausted; for one with a wholesome mind, thirteen. For one with one set of sexual organs who dies simultaneously with an indeterminate mind, nine are exhausted; for one with a wholesome mind, fourteen. For one with both sets of sexual organs who dies simultaneously with an indeterminate mind, ten are exhausted; for one with a wholesome mind, fifteen.
What are the mental states and mental factors bound to that which are exhausted? Answer:
Those bound to the desire realm.
How many faculties are present?
The answer is:
either eight, nine, or ten. For those without sexual organs, there are eight; for those with one sexual organ, there are nine; for those with two sexual organs, there are ten.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors that manifest bound?
Answer: They are bound to the desire realm.
When one is born in the form realm from the desire realm, how many faculties (*indriya*) are exhausted?

The answer is: either four, or nine, or fourteen. If death occurs gradually with a neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) bound to the desire realm, four are exhausted; if with a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*), nine are exhausted. If death occurs instantaneously with a neutral mind, nine are exhausted; if with a wholesome mind, fourteen are exhausted.
To what realm are those minds and mental factors bound that are extinguished?
Answer: They are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
How many faculties are present?
The answer is:
eight.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors bound that manifest?
Answer: They are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
When one born in the desire realm passes away into the formless realm, how many faculties (*indriya*) are exhausted?

The answer is: either four, or nine, or fourteen. When passing away gradually with a neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) bound to the desire realm, four are exhausted; with a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*), nine. When passing away instantaneously with a neutral mind, nine are exhausted; with a wholesome mind, fourteen.
What are the mental states and mental factors that are bound to which realm?
Answer: Those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
How many faculties are present?
Answer: Three.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors bound that manifest?
Answer: They are bound to the formless realm; this concludes the section on the desire realm.
When one is born in the form realm from the form realm, how many faculties (*indriya*) are exhausted?
The answer is:
either eight or thirteen; if death occurs with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), eight are exhausted; if with a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*), thirteen are exhausted.
What are the mental states and mental factors that are bound to?
Answer: Those bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
How many faculties are present?
Answer: Eight.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors bound that manifest?
Answer: They are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
When one is born in the form realm and dies in the desire realm, how many faculties (*indriya*) are exhausted?
The answer is:
either eight or thirteen; if death occurs with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), eight are exhausted; if with a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*), thirteen are exhausted.
To what are the mind and mental factors bound that are extinguished?
Answer: Those bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
How many faculties are present?
The answer is:
either eight, nine, or ten. Those without sexual organs have eight; those with one sexual organ have nine; and those with two sexual organs have ten.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors that manifest bound?
Answer: They are bound to the desire realm.
When one is born in the form realm and passes away from the state bound to the formless realm, how many faculties (*indriya*) are exhausted?
The answer is:
either eight or thirteen; if death occurs with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), eight are exhausted; if with a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*), twelve are exhausted.
To what realm are the minds and mental factors that have ceased bound?
Answer: To the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
How many faculties are present?
Answer: Three.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors bound that manifest?
Answer: They are bound to the formless realm; this concludes the section on the form realm.
When one is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), how many faculties (indriya) are exhausted? Answer:
Either three or eight; three if the mind is neutral (avyākṛta), and eight if the mind is wholesome (kuśala).
What are the mental states and mental factors bound to that which are exhausted? Answer:
Those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
How many faculties are present?
The answer is:
three.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors bound that manifest?
Answer: They are bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
When one is born in the desire realm from the formless realm, how many faculties (*indriya*) are exhausted?
The answer is:
either three or eight; three if the mind is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and eight if the mind is wholesome (*kuśala*).
To what realm are the minds and mental factors that have ceased bound?
The answer is:
they are bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
How many faculties are present?
The answer is:
either eight, nine, or ten. For those without sexual organs, there are eight; for those with one sexual organ, there are nine; and for those with two sexual organs, there are ten.
What kind of fettered mind and mental factors manifest?
Answer: Those fettered to the desire realm.
When one is born from the formless realm into the form realm, how many faculties (*indriya*) are exhausted?
The answer is:
either three or eight; three in the case of an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), and eight in the case of a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*).
What are the mental states and mental factors bound to that which are exhausted? Answer:
Those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
How many faculties are present?
Answer: Eight.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors that manifest bound?
Answer: They are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Regarding the Arhat’s parinirvāṇa, how many faculties (indriya) are extinguished last?
The answer is:

either four, or nine, or eight, or three. In the desire realm, there are four for gradual parinirvāṇa and nine for simultaneous [parinirvāṇa]; in the form realm, there are eight; and in the formless realm, there are three.

The thirtieth chapter, "The Initial Mind," of the Abhidharma is completed. The Sanskrit text consists of two hundred and sixty-nine ślokas; in the Qin language, this is two thousand two hundred and twenty-one words.

Chapter Five: The Chapter on the Initial Arousing of the Thought of Enlightenment (*Prathamacittotpāda-varga*). From the *Abhidharma-mūla-prakaraṇa*, the fifth chapter, "The Initial Arousing of the Thought of Enlightenment": Are those phenomena that arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind associated with that mind?
If a phenomenon is associated with the mind, does that phenomenon arise, persist, and cease together with the mind?
And for those phenomena that arise, persist, and cease together with the mind, do they share the same object as the mind?
If various phenomena arise with the mind sharing a single object, do those phenomena arise, abide, and cease together with that mind?
If various phenomena arise with the mind—meaning they do not arise without the mind—do those phenomena arise such that the mind arises together with them, meaning it does not arise without them?
When that dharma abides in exhaustion and the mind abides together in exhaustion, is it not the case that the mind is not being employed?
How is it that the faculty of the eye is not cultivated, and how are the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind not cultivated?
How does one cultivate the faculty of the eye? How does one cultivate the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?
If one who has not yet accomplished the faculties of a trainee attains the faculties of a trainee, are they all those who have realized the fruit by skipping stages?
If one attains realization by skipping stages, are all such persons non-attainers of the faculties of training who then attain the faculties of training?
If they are non-attainers of the faculties of training who then attain the faculties of training, are they all in the immediate succession of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)?

Regarding the sequence of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*): are all those who do not yet possess the faculties of one in training (*śaikṣendriya*) and who attain the faculties of one in training [included]?
Furthermore, regarding those who discard untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) and attain untainted faculties: are they all [attaining] the fruit from a previous fruit?
If one abandons all the fruits and the causes of the fruits, does one abandon the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and obtain the untainted faculties?
If one abandons the untainted faculties and obtains the untainted faculties, do all those untainted faculties completely cease, and do the untainted faculties manifest before one?

If one brings forth the untainted faculty of exhaustion (*kṣayajñānendriya*) while the untainted faculty of cessation (*nirodhajñānendriya*) is present before them, do they all abandon the untainted faculties and acquire the untainted faculties?
Regarding all the faculties of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), do they all cultivate the truths that were previously uncultivated?
If one does not cultivate the Truths but cultivates existence, are all those [factors] the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
When the initial knowledge of exhaustion arises, are all those [factors] in the sequence of the path of non-obstruction?
If there is a sequence following the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), is that entirely subsequent knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?
When the initial knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) arises, is that entirely subsequent to the knowledge of exhaustion?
And if there is a sequence following the knowledge of exhaustion, is that entirely the knowledge of non-arising?

Just as that which takes the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) as its object takes the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) as its object, and just as that which takes the knowledge of exhaustion as its object takes the path of non-obstruction as its object, does that which takes the knowledge of exhaustion as its object also take the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) as its object?

Regarding the knowledge of non-arising that takes [the Truth of Suffering] as its object, and the knowledge of exhaustion that takes it as its object: should the knowledge of exhaustion be called "knowledge of exhaustion"?

Should it be called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharma-jñāna*), "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*), "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracitta-jñāna*), "knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-jñāna*), "knowledge of origin" (*samudaya-jñāna*), "knowledge of exhaustion" (*nirodha-jñāna*), or "knowledge of the path" (*mārga-jñāna*)? Should it be said to be with initial application and sustained application (*savitarka-savicāra*), without initial application but with sustained application (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), or without initial application and without sustained application (*avitarka-avicāra*)?
Should it be said that [this state] is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*);

and should it be said that its objects are connected to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-ālambana*), connected to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-ālambana*), or unconnected (*apratisaṃyukta-ālambana*)?
The same applies to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and the noble right view (*aśaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Regarding all phenomena associated with the noble right view: are those phenomena also associated with the noble right intention (*aśaikṣī samyaksaṃkalpa*)?
If various dharmas are associated with the *aśaikṣa* right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), are those dharmas also associated with the *aśaikṣa* right view (*samyak-dṛṣṭi*)?

If various dharmas are associated with the *aśaikṣa* right view, are those dharmas also associated with the *aśaikṣa* right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), right liberation (*samyak-vimukti*), and right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*)?
If various phenomena are associated with the post-learner (aśaikṣa) right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), are those phenomena also associated with the post-learner right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
If various phenomena are associated with the post-learner [factors] up to and including right liberation (*samyagvimukti*), are those phenomena also associated with the post-learner right knowledge?

If various phenomena are associated with the post-learned (*aśaikṣa*) universal knowledge (*sarvatraga-jñāna*), are those phenomena associated with post-learned universal liberation (*aśaikṣa-sarvatraga-vimukti*)?
I pray that you will fully expound the meaning of this chapter.
Are those phenomena associated with the mind that arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with it?
Answer: It is so;
those dharmas that are associated with the mind arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with that mind.
Is there any dharma that arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the mind, yet is not associated with the mind?
Answer: Yes.
There are dharmas that turn together with the mind—namely, matter that turns with the mind (*cittānuvartin-rūpa*) and formations dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Regarding those dharmas that arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind, do they all share the same object as the mind?
The answer is:
Yes. All phenomena that share a single object with the mind arise, abide, and cease together with that mind.
Are there any phenomena that arise, abide, and cease together with the mind, yet those phenomena do not share the same object as the mind?
Answer: Yes.

There are the mental transformations of form (*rūpa*) and the mental transformations of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*); these phenomena arise together with the mind and do not exist without the mind.

When those phenomena arise, they arise together with the mind; it is not that they do not depend on the mind. When those phenomena abide and cease, do they abide and cease together with the mind; is it not that they do not depend on the mind? Answer:

For sentient beings of the desire and form realms who have not entered the *asaṃjñi-samāpatti* (attainment of non-perception) or the *nirodha-samāpatti* (attainment of cessation), their faculties and the four great elements arise together with the mind when those phenomena arise; they abide and cease together with the mind when those phenomena abide and cease; it is not that they do not depend on the mind. However, when they enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they do not depend on the mind.
What is meant by "not cultivating the faculty of the eye"?
The answer is:

when craving for the faculty of the eye is not yet exhausted, greed is not yet exhausted, attachment is not yet exhausted, and thirst is not yet exhausted; furthermore, when one does not cultivate and rely upon that path which exhausts craving for form through the unimpeded path—in this way, one does not cultivate the faculty of the eye.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
What is meant by not cultivating the faculty of the mind? Answer:

If craving for the mind-faculty (*manendriya*) is not yet exhausted, greed is not yet exhausted, attachment is not yet exhausted, and thirst is not yet exhausted; furthermore, if one does not cultivate or rely upon that path by which craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*) is exhausted through the path of non-obstruction (*anantaryamārga*), in this way the mind-faculty is not cultivated.
How does one cultivate the faculty of the eye?
The answer is:

by the exhaustion of craving for the faculty of the eye, the exhaustion of greed, the exhaustion of conceit, and the exhaustion of thirst; furthermore, by means of the path of non-obstruction, one exhausts craving for forms, and cultivates that path with tranquility—in this way, one cultivates the faculty of the eye.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
How does one cultivate the faculty of the mind?
The answer is:

The faculty of mind is exhausted of craving, exhausted of greed, exhausted of conceit, and exhausted of thirst; furthermore, by means of the path of non-obstruction, one exhausts the craving for the formless realm, cultivating that path with tranquility—in this way, one cultivates the faculty of mind.
If one who was not previously established in the faculty of training (śaikṣendriya) attains the faculty of training, are they all those who have attained realization by skipping stages (vīthilābha)?
The answer is:
Yes; all those who have attained realization by skipping stages are those who, not having been previously established in the faculty of training, attain the faculty of training.
Is it possible that one who was not previously accomplished in the faculties of training (śaikṣendriya) attains the faculties of training, yet does not do so by skipping stages (atikrānta-samāpatti)?
Answer: Yes;
this occurs in the case of a falling away from the fruit of Arhatship.

If one who was not previously accomplished in the faculty of training attains the faculty of training, is all such a person in the immediate succession of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*)?
Answer: It is so;
all those in the immediate succession of the supreme mundane dharma are ones who, not having previously accomplished the faculty of training, attain the faculty of training.

Is there one who, not having previously accomplished the faculties of training (śaikṣendriya), attains the faculties of training, yet for whom this is not the sequence immediately following the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma)?
Answer: Yes;
it is the case of one who falls away from the fruit of arhatship.
If one abandons untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and acquires untainted faculties, are they all instances of "abiding in the fruit" (*phala-phalastha*)?
Answer: Yes;
all those who abide in the fruit abandon untainted faculties and acquire untainted faculties.
Is there a case where one abandons an untainted faculty (anāsrava-indriya) and acquires an untainted faculty, yet this is neither a fruit nor that which arises from a fruit?
The answer is:

Yes. For instance, when the path of cultivation consisting of the knowledge of what is not yet known (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna) manifests; or when an Arhat who has attained liberation through equanimity (sāmayikī vimuktiḥ) attains the state of being free from doubt (akopya-dharman); or when one abandons an untainted faculty and acquires an untainted faculty.
When all those untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) have ceased, do the untainted faculties manifest? Answer:

There are cases where one abandons untainted faculties and acquires untainted faculties, yet those [abandoned] untainted faculties have not entirely ceased, even though untainted faculties are now manifesting.
What is meant by "discarding an untainted faculty (anāsrava-indriya) and obtaining an untainted faculty, yet not exhausting the untainted faculties while the untainted faculties are present"?
The answer is:

when one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or *anāgāmin* via the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), or when an *arhat* falls back from the fruit of *arhatship*, or an *anāgāmin* or *sakṛdāgāmin* falls back from their respective fruits—this is called discarding an untainted faculty and obtaining an untainted faculty, wherein one does not exhaust the untainted faculties while the untainted faculties are present.

What is meant by "the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are exhausted, the untainted faculties manifest before one, yet one does not abandon the untainted faculties to obtain the untainted faculties"?
The answer is:

as when the untainted faculties previously obtained are exhausted and manifest before one; this is called the exhaustion of the untainted faculties, the manifestation of the untainted faculties, wherein one does not abandon the untainted faculties to obtain the untainted faculties.
What is meant by "discarding an untainted faculty (anāsrava-indriya) and obtaining an untainted faculty, wherein that untainted faculty is exhausted and an untainted faculty manifests"?
The answer is:

when the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—namely, the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*)—manifests; when one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or *anāgāmin* through the untainted path; when one attains the fruit of *arhat*; and when an *arhat* of "liberation through equanimity" (*samayavimukta*) attains "liberation beyond doubt" (*akopyadharman*). This is called discarding an untainted faculty and obtaining an untainted faculty, wherein that untainted faculty is exhausted and an untainted faculty manifests.
What is it to neither discard the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) nor fail to acquire them, neither exhaust the untainted faculties, yet have the untainted faculties manifest before one?
Answer: It is the exclusion of all such aforementioned cases.
Regarding all instances of the faculty of "I do not yet know" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), is it the case that they are all not cultivated as the cultivation of the truths?
The answer is:
there are instances of the faculty of "I do not yet know" that are not such that they are not cultivated as the cultivation of the truths.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) such that it is not the case that there is no cultivation of the truths?
The answer is:

all instances of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," whether past or future, are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" such that it is not the case that there is no cultivation of the truths.
What is it that is not cultivated through the cultivation of the truths (*satya-bhāvanā*), yet exists as something for which there is no faculty of "I do not yet know" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
The answer is:

those dharmas that are rootless (*amūlaka*) exist as things cultivated through the cultivation of the truths; this is what is meant by "not cultivated through the cultivation of the truths, yet existing as something for which there is no faculty of 'I do not yet know'."
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) such that there is cultivation of truths not yet cultivated?
The answer is:

those faculties of "I shall come to know the unknown" for which there is cultivation of truths not yet cultivated; this is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" such that there is cultivation of truths not yet cultivated.
What is it that is neither the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) nor the cultivation of the truths through non-cultivation?
Answer: It is everything except for those aforementioned matters.
When the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) first arises, is it always preceded by the path of non-obstruction (ānantaryamārga)?
Answer: It is so.
If one establishes the sequence of the path of non-obstruction, is all of that the knowledge of exhaustion?
Answer: It is so.
When the initial knowledge of non-arising arises, is it followed in succession by all instances of the knowledge of exhaustion?
Answer: It is so.
If one asks whether all that follows the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna),
the answer is:
it may be the knowledge of exhaustion, or the knowledge of non-arising, or the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi).
If a path of non-obstruction takes certain factors as its object, does that path of non-obstruction take the knowledge of exhaustion as its object?
The answer is:

If a path of non-obstruction takes those specific types [of factors] as its object, it takes the knowledge of exhaustion as its object; if a path of non-obstruction does not take those specific types as its object, it does not take the knowledge of exhaustion as its object.
If one takes the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows as an object, does one take the knowledge of non-arising as an object?
Answer: It is so.
If one takes non-arising knowledge as its object, does it take the knowledge of exhaustion as its object?
Answer: It is so.
Should the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) be called "knowledge of exhaustion"? The answer is: the knowledge of exhaustion should be called "knowledge of exhaustion";

or it is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna), the knowledge of origin (samudayajñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), or the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); it is either with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra, or without vitarka and without vicāra; it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), or the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), or the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya); it is associated with emptiness (śūnyatā), wishlessness (apranihita), or signlessness (animitta); it has objects conditioned by the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), or objects conditioned by the form or formless realms (rūpa-ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), or objects that are unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta).
The knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is also like this.
Should the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) be called the right view of one beyond training?
The answer is: Yes.

The right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) should be described as the right view of one beyond training; or it is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), or the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. It is either with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka but with vicāra, or without both vitarka and vicāra. It is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), or the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). It is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), or signlessness (*animitta*). It has as its object that which is bound to the desire realm, or that which is bound to the form or formless realms, or that which is unbound. This concludes the section on the right view of one beyond training.

Regarding those phenomena that are associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi), are they also associated with the right intention (samyaksaṃkalpa) of one beyond training?
Answer: Some are associated with right view but not with right intention.
What is right view that is not associated with right intention?
The answer is:

those factors associated with right view that are either associated with right intention or are factors associated with right view but not associated with right intention; these are called right view that is not right intention.
What is meant by "equanimity of intention" (samyak-saṃkalpa) that is not "right view" (samyag-dṛṣṭi)?
The answer is:

those factors associated with equanimity of intention that are associated with right view, as well as all factors associated with equanimity of intention that are not associated with right view—these are called "equanimity of intention" that is not "right view."
What is right view and right intention?
The answer is:
with the exception of right intention associated with right view, all other factors associated with both right view and right intention are called right view and right intention.
What is that which is neither right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) nor right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*)? Answer:

Right intention not associated with right view, right view not associated with right intention, and all other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called that which is neither right view nor right intention.
Regarding all phenomena associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi), are they also associated with the right effort (samyakpradhāna) of one beyond training?
Answer: Some are associated with right view but not with right effort.
What is right view that is not right effort?
The answer is:
that which is associated with right view but is not right effort; this is called right view that is not right effort.
What is right effort that is not right view?
The answer is:
those factors associated with right effort that are dissociated from all forms of right view; this is called right effort that is not right view.
What is meant by "right view accompanied by right effort"?
The answer is:
with the exception of right effort itself, all factors associated with right view are called "right view accompanied by right effort."
What is that which is neither right view nor right effort?
The answer is:

right effort not associated with right view, as well as all other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind; these are called that which is neither right view nor right effort.
The same applies to right mindfulness, right concentration, and right liberation.
Those dharmas that are associated with the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are not necessarily the right knowledge of one beyond training.

Furthermore, those dharmas that are associated with the right knowledge of one beyond training are not necessarily the right view of one beyond training. [End of the section on the right view of one beyond training.]
Regarding those dharmas that are associated with the *aśaikṣa* (beyond-training) right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), are they also associated with the *aśaikṣa* right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*)?
Answer: Some are associated with right intention but not with right effort.
What is right intention that is not right effort?
The answer is:
that which is associated with right intention but is not right effort; this is called right intention that is not right effort.
What is right effort that is not right intention?
The answer is:
right intention and those factors associated with right effort but dissociated from right intention—this is called right effort that is not right intention.
What is meant by "right intention" (samyak-saṃkalpa) and "right effort" (samyak-vyāyāma)?
The answer is:
with the exception of right effort itself, all factors associated with right intention are called "right intention" and "right effort."
What is neither right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) nor right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*)?
The answer is:

that which is not associated with right intention, namely all other minds (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*). These are called neither right intention nor right effort.
The same applies to equanimity of mindfulness (*samānasmṛti*), equanimity of concentration (*samānasamādhi*), and equanimity of liberation (*samānavimukti*).

Regarding those phenomena associated with the equanimity of intention (*samānacetanā*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), are they also the equanimity of knowledge (*samānajñāna*) of one beyond training?
Answer: Yes.
Or, there is right intention that is not right knowledge.
What is right intention that is not right knowledge?
The answer is:

Those factors associated with equanimity (upekkhā-saṃsaṭṭha) that are not associated with equanimity-knowledge (upekkhā-ñāṇa), and those factors associated with equanimity that are not associated with equanimity-knowledge—these are called "associated with equanimity but not equanimity-knowledge.
What is "equanimity-knowledge but not associated with equanimity"?
Answer:

Equanimity-knowledge associated with equanimity-intention, and those factors associated with equanimity-knowledge that are not associated with equanimity-intention—these are called "equanimity-knowledge but not equanimity-intention."
What is meant by "equal intention and equal knowledge"?
The answer is:
excluding the equal knowledge that is associated with equal intention, all other phenomena associated with both equal intention and equal knowledge are called "equal intention and equal knowledge."
What is that which is neither *samādhi* nor *prajñā*?
The answer is:

*prajñā* not associated with *samādhi*, *samādhi* not associated with *prajñā*, and all other minds (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*). This is called that which is neither *samādhi* nor *prajñā*. [The section on *samādhi* is concluded.]

Regarding those phenomena that are associated with the equanimity of post-learner (*aśaikṣa*) skillful means (*upāya*), are they also associated with the equanimity of post-learner mindfulness (*smṛti*)?
Answer: Some are associated with the equanimity of skillful means but not with the equanimity of mindfulness.
