What is meant by "equal application of effort" (samyak-pradhāna) that is not "equal mindfulness" (samyak-smṛti)?
The answer is:
equal mindfulness; this is called "equal application of effort" that is not "equal mindfulness."
What is right mindfulness that is not right effort?
The answer is:
right effort is what is called right mindfulness that is not right effort.
What is meant by "right effort associated with right mindfulness"?
The answer is:
excluding right mindfulness itself, all factors associated with right effort are called "right effort associated with right mindfulness."
What is "neither right effort nor right mindfulness"?
The answer is:
all other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—these are called "neither right effort."
The same applies to equanimity of mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti*), equanimity of concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity of liberation (*vimukti*).
Regarding all phenomena associated with the equanimity of post-learner skillful means (*aśaikṣa-upāya*), are they also associated with the equanimity of post-learner knowledge (*aśaikṣa-jñāna*)?
Answer: Sometimes there is equal application (samyak-prayoga) that is not equal knowledge (samyag-jñāna).
What is meant by equal application that is not equal knowledge?
Answer: There are cases where there is equal application (samyak-prayoga) but not equal knowledge (samyag-jñāna).
What is meant by "equal application but not equal knowledge"?

Answer: Regarding conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*), those factors that are associated with conventional knowledge but not associated with conventional skillful means (*samvṛtyupāya*), these are called conventional skillful means but not conventional knowledge.
What is conventional knowledge but not conventional skillful means?
Answer: When conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is associated with conventional skillful means (upāya), this is called conventional knowledge that is not conventional skillful means.
What is conventional skillful means that is conventional knowledge?
Answer:
With the exception of right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*), all factors associated with right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) are called both right effort and right knowledge.
What are those that are neither right effort nor right knowledge?
Answer:

It refers to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) that is not associated with correct application (*samyak-prayoga*), as well as all other minds, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind. This is called "that which is neither correct application nor conventional knowledge. [The section on conventional knowledge is concluded.]
The same applies to the gates of equanimity and equanimity-concentration.
Regarding all phenomena associated with the equanimity-liberation of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), are they associated with the equanimity-knowledge (aśaikṣa-samādhi-jñāna) of one beyond training?
The answer is: Yes.
Or, there may be equal liberation that is not equal knowledge.
What is equal liberation that is not equal knowledge?
The answer is:

Regarding conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*): those factors that are associated with conventional knowledge but not associated with equanimity-liberation (*upekṣā-vimukti*)—these are called "equanimity-liberation but not conventional knowledge.
What is conventional knowledge but not equanimity-liberation?

Answer: When conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) is associated with equanimity and is accompanied by equanimous liberation, this is called "conventional knowledge that is not equanimous liberation.
What is "equanimous liberation that is conventional knowledge"?
Answer:

With the exception of the factors associated with equanimity-liberation (upekkhā-vimokkha) and the various factors associated with equanimity-knowledge (upekkhā-ñāṇa), these are called both equanimity-liberation and equanimity-knowledge.
What are those that are neither equanimity-liberation nor equanimity-knowledge?
Answer:

It refers to conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) that is not associated with equal liberation (sāmānya-vimukti), as well as all other minds (citta), mental factors (caitasika), matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra). These are called those that are neither equal liberation nor conventional knowledge.

The thirty-first chapter, "On the Initial Arousing of the Mind," concludes. In the Sanskrit original, it consists of two hundred and forty-two ślokas; in the Qin language (Chinese), it comprises three thousand nine hundred and forty-two words.
6. The Chapter on the Fish-Egg (Matsyāṇḍa) in the Abhidharma-mūla-skandha, the Sixth Chapter on the Fish-Egg, concerning the Twenty-two Faculties (Indriyas):

the faculty of the eye, the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the male faculty, the female faculty, and the life faculty; the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; the faculty of faith, the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
If one is endowed with the faculty of the eye, how many of these twenty-two faculties does one possess and how many does one not possess?

Continue in this manner until: if one is endowed with the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), how many of these twenty-two faculties does one possess and how many does one not possess? [End of section on possession.]
If one possesses the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), among these twenty-two faculties, how many are possessed in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?

If one possesses [the faculties] up to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), among these twenty-two faculties, how many are possessed in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present? [This concludes the section on possession across the three times.]
If one does not possess the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), how many of these twenty-two faculties does one possess and how many does one not possess?

If one does not possess them up to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), how many of these twenty-two faculties does one possess and how many does one not possess? [End of section on non-possession.]
If one does not possess the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), how many of these twenty-two faculties does one possess in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?

If one does not possess [any] up to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), how many of these twenty-two faculties does one possess in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present? [Thus concludes the section on non-possession across the three periods of time.]
If the faculties are wholesome, are those faculties rooted in wholesome roots?
Conversely, if the faculties are rooted in wholesome roots, are those faculties wholesome?
If the faculties are unwholesome, are those faculties rooted in unwholesome roots?
If the various faculties have unwholesome roots as their cause, are those faculties unwholesome?
If the various faculties are indeterminate, do those faculties have indeterminate roots as their cause?
If the various faculties have indeterminate roots as their cause, are those faculties indeterminate?

Are there faculties that are not based on the roots of the wholesome, nor based on the roots of the unwholesome, nor based on the roots of the indeterminate, yet those faculties are not without a basis?
I wish to expound fully the meaning of this chapter. The twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) are:

the eye faculty, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties; the male faculty, the female faculty, and the life faculty; the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
If one is endowed with the eye faculty, one is necessarily endowed with five faculties, adding the lower [faculties] to the eye; as for the others, one may or may not be endowed with them.
The same applies to the ear, nose, and tongue faculties.
If one possesses the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), one necessarily possesses four faculties: the body, life, mind, and equanimity; as for the others, they may or may not be possessed.
If one possesses the mind faculty (*manendriya*), one necessarily possesses three faculties: the mind, life, and equanimity; as for the others, they may or may not be possessed.
The same applies to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the faculty of guarding (*anāgāmin-indriya*).
If one possesses either the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) or the female faculty (*strīndriya*), one necessarily possesses eight faculties; as for the others, they may or may not be possessed.
If one possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one necessarily possesses four faculties; as for the others, they may or may not be possessed.
If one possesses the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), one necessarily possesses seven faculties; as for the others, they may or may not be possessed.
If one accomplishes the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily accomplishes five faculties; as for the others, they may or may not be accomplished.

If one accomplishes the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), one necessarily does not accomplish one faculty, one necessarily accomplishes eight faculties; as for the others, they may or may not be accomplished.
If one is endowed with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), one is necessarily endowed with eight faculties; as for the others, they may or may not be present.

The same applies to the faculties of energy (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), with the addition of the faculties of mind (*manas*), life-force (*jīvita*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

If one possesses the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), one necessarily does not possess two faculties—the faculty of "already-known" (ājñendriya) and the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātāvīndriya)—but necessarily possesses thirteen faculties: the five beginning with faith (śraddhā), plus the mind (manas), suffering (duḥkha), body (kāya), life (jīvita), equanimity (upekṣā), pleasure (sukha), joy (saumanasya), and the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know. As for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them.

If one possesses the faculty of "having already known" (ājñātendriya), one necessarily does not possess two faculties—the faculty of "not yet known" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the faculty of "knowing" (jñānendriya)—and necessarily possesses eleven faculties, excluding the aforementioned two, namely sorrow (daurmanasya) and suffering (duḥkha); as for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them.

If one is endowed with the faculty of "I-do-not-know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), one necessarily does not possess three faculties—the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya), the faculty of "having known" (ājñātāvīndriya), and the faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya)—but necessarily possesses eleven faculties; as for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them. [The section on possession is concluded.]

If one possesses the eye faculty, one necessarily does not possess eight faculties—both past and future—but necessarily possesses two faculties—past and future—and three faculties—present; as for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, and tongue.

If one possesses the faculty of the body, one necessarily does not possess eight faculties—both past and future—but necessarily possesses two faculties—past and future—and two present ones; as for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them.

If one possesses the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties—both past and future—but necessarily possesses two faculties—past and future—and one present faculty; as for the remaining ones, they may or may not be possessed.
The same applies to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the faculty of guarding (*anāgāmī-indriya*).

If one possesses either the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) or the female faculty (*strīndriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties of the past or future; one necessarily possesses five faculties of the past or future and three of the present; as for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them.

If one is endowed with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties—both past and future; one necessarily possesses two faculties—past and future—one future faculty, and one present faculty; as for the remaining faculties, they may or may not be possessed.

If one possesses the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties of the past or future, but necessarily possesses five faculties of the past or future and two of the present; as for the remaining ones, one may or may not possess them.

If one is endowed with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties of the past or future; one necessarily possesses two faculties of the past or future, two of the future, and one of the present; as for the remaining ones, they may or may not be possessed.

If one possesses the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties—both past and future; one necessarily does not possess one faculty—past, future, and present; one necessarily possesses four faculties—past and future; two faculties—past, future, and present; and two faculties—present. As for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them.

If one is endowed with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties of the past or future, but necessarily possesses seven faculties of the past or future, one of the present, and as for the remainder, they may or may not be possessed.
The same applies to the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

If one possesses the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties of the past or future; one necessarily does not possess two faculties of the past, future, or present; one necessarily possesses seven faculties of the past, future, and present; three of the past and future; one of the future and present; and two of the present; as for the remaining ones, they may or may not be possessed.

If one possesses the faculty of "having already known" (ājñātāvīndriya), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties of the past or future; one necessarily does not possess two faculties of the past, future, or present; one necessarily possesses seven faculties of the past and future, three of the future, and one of the present; as for the remaining faculties, they may or may not be possessed.

If one possesses the faculty of ignorance (*ajñendriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties of the past or future; one necessarily does not possess three faculties of the past, future, or present; one necessarily possesses seven faculties of the past and future, three of the future, and one of the present; as for the remaining [faculties], they may or may not be possessed. This concludes the analysis of possession across the three periods of time.
If one does not possess the eye faculty, one necessarily does not possess one faculty, necessarily possesses three faculties, and may or may not possess the remaining ones.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, and tongue.

If one does not possess the faculty of the body, one necessarily does not possess ten faculties, necessarily possesses eight faculties, and for the remaining faculties, possession may or may not occur.
The faculty of mind (*manas*), the life-faculty (*jīvita*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*) are necessarily possessed.

If one does not possess either the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) or the female faculty (*strīndriya*), one necessarily does not possess one faculty, necessarily possesses three faculties, and for the remaining ones, possession may or may not occur.

If one does not possess the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one necessarily does not possess nine faculties, necessarily possesses eight faculties, and as for the remaining ones, they may or may not be possessed.

If one does not possess the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), one necessarily does not possess five faculties, necessarily possesses eight faculties, and for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them.

If one does not possess the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties; one necessarily possesses eight faculties; as for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them.

If one does not possess the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), one necessarily does not possess one faculty, necessarily possesses eight faculties, and for the remaining faculties, possession may or may not occur.

If one does not achieve the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), one will certainly not achieve eight faculties; one will certainly achieve eight faculties, while for the remaining ones, one may or may not achieve them.
The same applies to the faculties of energy (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
If one does not possess the faculty of "I-do-not-yet-know," one necessarily does not possess one faculty, necessarily possesses three faculties, and may or may not possess the remaining ones.
The faculties of "already-known" (*ājñātendriya*) and "one who has known" (*ājñātavindriya*) are likewise not established.

Having concluded that they are not established, if one does not possess the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), one necessarily does not possess one faculty among those of the past, future, or present; one necessarily does not possess seven faculties of the past or future; one necessarily possesses two faculties of the past or future and one of the present; and for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, and tongue.

If one does not possess the faculty of the body, one necessarily does not possess ten faculties—past, future, and present—and necessarily does not possess one faculty—past and future; one necessarily possesses five faculties—past and future—and two faculties—past, future, and present—one of which is present; as for the remaining faculties, one may or may not possess them.
The faculty of mind, the life-faculty, and the faculty of equanimity are necessarily accomplished.

If one does not accomplish the male faculty or the female faculty, one necessarily does not accomplish one root in the past, future, or present; one necessarily does not accomplish seven roots in the past or future; one necessarily accomplishes two roots in the past and future and one in the present; as for the remaining roots, they may or may not be accomplished.

If one does not possess the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one necessarily does not possess nine faculties—past, future, and present—and necessarily does not possess six faculties—past and future; one necessarily possesses seven faculties—past and future—and one present faculty, while for the remaining faculties, possession may or may not occur.

If one does not possess the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), one necessarily does not possess the five faculties of the past, future, and present; one necessarily does not possess the six faculties of the past and future; one necessarily possesses seven faculties of the past and future and one of the present; as for the remainder, one may or may not possess them.

If one does not possess the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily does not possess eight faculties—past, future, and present—and necessarily does not possess six faculties—past and future; one necessarily possesses seven faculties—past and future—and one present faculty; as for the remaining ones, they may or may not be possessed.

If one does not possess the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), one necessarily does not possess one faculty of the past, future, or present; one necessarily does not possess eight faculties of the past or future; one necessarily possesses seven faculties of the past and future and one of the present; as for the remainder, one may or may not possess them.

If one does not achieve the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), one will necessarily not achieve eight faculties—both past and future—and necessarily not achieve eight faculties—past and future; one will necessarily achieve four faculties—past and future—and two faculties—both past, future, and present; and two faculties—present. As for the remaining faculties, one may or may not achieve them.
The same applies to the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

If one does not possess the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), one necessarily does not possess one faculty of the past, future, or present; one necessarily does not possess eight faculties of the past or future; one necessarily possesses two faculties of the past or future and one of the present; and as for the remaining [faculties], one may or may not possess them.

The faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*) and the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātavindriya*) are likewise not accomplished across the three periods of time. [The section on] non-accomplishment is concluded.
Regarding the faculties that are wholesome (*kuśala*), are those faculties caused by wholesome roots?
Answer: Yes.
Thus, when the faculties are wholesome, those faculties have wholesome roots as their cause.
Is it possible that there are faculties which have wholesome roots as their cause, yet those faculties themselves are not wholesome?
The answer is: Yes.
There are; they are the roots of non-defined maturation that arise from wholesome roots.
Regarding those faculties that are unwholesome, are those faculties caused by unwholesome roots?
Answer: Yes.
In this way, those faculties that are unwholesome have their cause in the roots of the unwholesome.
Is there any faculty that has its cause in the roots of the unwholesome, yet is itself not unwholesome?
Answer: Yes, there are.

These are the unwholesome roots that have retribution as their indeterminate roots, specifically those roots associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the realm of desire.
As for those roots that are indeterminate, are those roots caused by indeterminate roots?
Answer: There are cases where a faculty is indeterminate, yet that faculty does not have an indeterminate root as its cause.
What is meant by a faculty being indeterminate while that faculty does not have an indeterminate root as its cause?
Answer: Those indeterminate faculties that lack an object-condition are called "faculties that are indeterminate, yet those faculties do not have an indeterminate root as their cause.
What are the faculties that have an indeterminate root as their cause, yet those faculties are not themselves indeterminate?
Answer: Unwholesome roots are called roots whose cause is the unwholesome root, yet those roots themselves are not indeterminate.
What are roots that are indeterminate and whose cause is the indeterminate root?

Answer: When a root is indeterminate (avyākṛta) and has an indeterminate fundamental root as its object, this is called a root that is indeterminate and whose cause is an indeterminate fundamental root.
What is a root that is not indeterminate and whose cause is not an indeterminate fundamental root?
Answer: A wholesome root is called a root that is not indeterminate, yet that root does not have an indeterminate root as its cause.

Is there a root that does not have a wholesome root as its cause, does not have an unwholesome root as its cause, and does not have an indeterminate root as its cause, yet that root is not itself without a cause?
Answer: There are.
Namely, those roots that lack an object-condition (anālambana), which have matter (rūpa) and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra) as their causes.

This concludes the thirty-second chapter, "On Fish Eggs" (Matsyāṇḍa-varga). In the Sanskrit original it consists of one hundred seventy-three ślokas; in the Qin language, it comprises three thousand three hundred forty-two words.
