What are the faculties that have the cessation of seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), while having the path of subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) as their cause of abandonment?
The answer is:

those faculties that are abandoned by the path of subsequent knowledge of origination and have the cessation of seeing as their object-condition; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by the path of subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and have the path of subsequent knowledge of origination as their cause of abandonment and the cessation of seeing as their object-condition; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by the path of subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) and have the path of subsequent knowledge of origination as their cause of abandonment and the cessation of seeing as their object-condition.
What are the faculties that have cessation through seeing (*darśana-heya*) as their object and are caused by that which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)? Answer:
Those faculties that are abandoned through cultivation and have cessation through seeing as their object.
What are the faculties that have cessation through seeing (*darśana-heya*) as their object and have non-abandonment (*aheya*) as their cause? Answer:
All faculties that are non-abandoned and have as their objects the four truths and the eight cessations [to be abandoned] through the seeing of cessation.

What are the faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*) and have as their object that which is to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-prahātavya*)?

those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and have as their object that which is to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*), which are themselves caused by what is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and have as their object that which is to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering.

What are the faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna-prahātavya*) and have as their object the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna-prahātavya*)? Answer:

Those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and have as their object the knowledge of the dharma of origination; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of origination and have as their cause the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and as their object the knowledge of the dharma of origination.

What are the faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) and have as their object that which is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*)? Answer:

Those faculties abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering that have as their object that which is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origin; furthermore, those faculties abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origin that have as their cause that which is abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and have as their object that which is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origin.

What are the faculties that are abandoned through the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna-prahātavya*) and have as their object the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna-prahātavya*)? Answer:

What are the faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) and have as their object that which is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvayajñāna*)?
The answer is:

those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and have as their object that which is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of cessation; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*), are caused by what is abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, and have as their object that which is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of cessation.

What are the faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*) and have as their object the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*)? Answer:

Those faculties which are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and have as their object the knowledge of the dharma of the path; furthermore, those faculties which are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*), are caused by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, and have as their object the knowledge of the dharma of the path; furthermore, those faculties which are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of the path, are caused by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, and have as their object the knowledge of the dharma of the path.

What are the faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) and have as their object that which is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*)? Answer:

Those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and have as their object that which is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), are caused by what is abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, and have as their object that which is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path.

What are the faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), have as their object that which is abandoned by reflection (*vicāra-prahātavya*), and are themselves abandoned by reflection?
The answer is:

What are the faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya), have as their object that which is not to be abandoned (aprahātavyālambana), and for which the cause is abandonment by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering? Answer:

Those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (nirodha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya) and abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya), whose cause is abandonment by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, and which have as their object that which is not to be abandoned.
What are the faculties that have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*) as their cause and are without objects? Answer:
Those faculties that are without objects and have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment as their cause.
If the various faculties have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*) as their object, do those faculties have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment as their cause?

Answer: Some faculties that have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment as their object have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment as their cause; some have origination-dharma-knowledge-abandonment (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*) as their cause; some have cultivation-abandonment (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) as their cause; and some have no abandonment as their cause (*aprahātavya*).

What are the faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna-prahātavya), have as their object the dharma of suffering abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, and for which the cause is abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering? Answer:

All faculties abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering that take as their object the dharma of suffering abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering; furthermore, all faculties abandoned by the knowledge of the origin of suffering (samudaya-dharmajñāna-prahātavya) that have as their cause the dharma of suffering abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and take as their object the dharma of suffering abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering.

What are the faculties that have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment as their object and are caused by cultivation-abandonment?
Answer: Those faculties that are abandoned by cultivation and have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment as their object.
What are the faculties that have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment as their object and have non-abandonment as their cause?
Answer: Those faculties that are of the nature of non-abandonment and have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment as their object.

If the faculties have as their cause the abandonment through the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*), do those faculties have as their object the abandonment through the subsequent knowledge of suffering?

What are the faculties that are abandoned through the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāta-jñāna-prahātavya*), conditioned by what is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*)?
The answer is:

those faculties that are abandoned through the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering and are conditioned by what is abandoned through the vision of cessation; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned through the knowledge of the unknown regarding origination (*samudaya-ajñāta-jñāna-prahātavya*), which have as their cause what is abandoned through the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering and are conditioned by what is abandoned through the vision of cessation; and furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned through the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation (*nirodha-ajñāta-jñāna-prahātavya*), which have as their cause what is abandoned through the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering and are conditioned by what is abandoned through the vision of cessation.

What are the faculties that, having the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering (*duḥkha-ajñāna*) as their cause for abandonment, have the vision of the path (*darśana-mārga*) as their object for abandonment?
The answer is:

those faculties that have the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering as their cause for abandonment and have the vision of the path as their object for abandonment; furthermore, those faculties that have the knowledge of the unknown regarding origination (*samudaya-ajñāna*) as their cause for abandonment, have the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering as their cause for abandonment, and have the vision of the path as their object for abandonment; furthermore, those faculties that have the knowledge of the unknown regarding the path (*mārga-ajñāna*) as their cause for abandonment, have the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering as their cause for abandonment, and have the vision of the path as their object for abandonment.
What are the faculties that have suffering as their cause, are abandoned by the knowledge of the unknown (anvaya-jñāna), and have reflection (bhāvanā) as their condition?
The answer is:

those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering and have reflection as their condition; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the unknown regarding origination (samudaya) and have suffering as their cause, are abandoned by the knowledge of the unknown, and have reflection as their condition; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by reflection and have suffering as their cause, are abandoned by the knowledge of the unknown, and have reflection as their condition.
What are the faculties that have the cessation-of-the-unknown-of-suffering (duḥkha-ajñāta-jñāna-prahātavya) as their cause, and for which the unceasing (aprahātavya) is the object-condition? Answer:

All faculties that are abandoned by the cessation-of-the-unknown-of-suffering, abandoned by the path-of-the-unknown (mārga-ajñāta-jñāna), and have the cessation-of-the-unknown-of-suffering as their cause, for which the unceasing is the object-condition.

If the various faculties have suffering-not-yet-known-intuition-cultivation (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti) as their object-condition, do those faculties have the abandonment through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) as their cause?

Answer: Some faculties that have suffering-not-yet-known-intuition-cultivation as their object-condition have the abandonment through the vision of suffering as their cause; some have the abandonment through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) as their cause; some have the abandonment through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya) as their cause; and some have no [such] cause.

What are the faculties that, being abandoned through the knowledge of the suffering-to-be-known (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna), have as their cause those things abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya)? Answer:

Those faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering which take as their object the knowledge of the suffering-to-be-known; furthermore, those faculties abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) which have as their cause those things abandoned through the vision of suffering and take as their object the knowledge of the suffering-to-be-known.

What are the faculties that have suffering as their object through the path of the knowledge of the unknown (duḥkha-ajñāna-anvaya-jñāna-bhāvanā), and for which the path of the knowledge of origination (samudaya-darśana) is the cause?
The answer is:

those faculties that are abandoned by the path of the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering and have the path of the knowledge of origination as their cause; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by the path of the knowledge of suffering and for which the path of the knowledge of origination is the cause and the path of the knowledge of the unknown regarding suffering is the object.

What are the faculties that have suffering as their object through the knowledge of the unknown (duḥkha-ajñāna), are abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), and have cultivation as their cause? Answer:
Those faculties that are abandoned by cultivation and have suffering as their object through the knowledge of the unknown.

What are the faculties that have suffering as their object through the path of "knowledge of the unknown" (*anvaya-jñāna*) and are abandoned by the path of "knowledge of the unknown," while having non-abandonment as their cause? Answer:
All faculties that are non-abandoned, which take as their object suffering through the path of "knowledge of the unknown"—this concludes the eight [faculties] regarding the knowledge of suffering.

As with the faculties abandoned through the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*) which take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), so it is for those abandoned through the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvayajñāna*).

If various faculties have as their cause that which is abandoned through the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), do those faculties take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*)?

Answer: Some faculties have their cause (*hetu*) in the abandonment through the knowledge of the destruction of outflows (*kṣayadharma-jñāna*), while their object (*ālambana*) is abandoned through the vision of the destruction of outflows, or they have no object, or they are not objects at all.
How is it that a faculty has its cause in the abandonment through the knowledge of the destruction of outflows and its object is abandoned through the vision of the destruction of outflows?
Answer: All faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the cessation of outflows (kṣayajñāna) take as their object that which is abandoned by the vision of the cessation of outflows.
How is it that a faculty has its cause abandoned by the knowledge of the cessation of outflows, yet takes as its object that which is not abandoned?
Answer: All faculties that are abandoned by the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (kṣayajñāna) take as their object that which is not abandoned.
How is it that a faculty, being caused by the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, has no object?
Answer: Are there faculties that have no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and are abandoned by the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*kṣayajñāna*)?

Furthermore, if there are faculties whose object-condition is abandoned by the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena, are those faculties abandoned by the vision of the destruction [of the outflows] (*kṣayadarśana*)?
Answer:

Some faculties have the cessation-dharma-knowledge (kṣayajñāna) as their object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), while being caused by the abandonment through the vision of cessation (kṣayadarśana-prahātavya), caused by the abandonment through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya), caused by the abandonment through the vision of origin (samudayadarśana-prahātavya), caused by the abandonment through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya), or caused by no abandonment (aprahātavya).

What are the faculties that have the exhaustion-dharma-knowledge (kṣayadharmanirvedhabhāgīya) as their object-condition and are abandoned by the vision of exhaustion (kṣayadarśana-prahātavya), while having as their cause that which is abandoned by the vision of exhaustion? Answer:
All faculties that are abandoned by the vision of exhaustion and have the exhaustion-dharma-knowledge as their object-condition.

What are the faculties that, having the exhaustion of phenomena as their object (*ālambana*) and being abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), have as their cause those things abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*)?
The answer is:

first, those faculties abandoned by the vision of suffering which have the exhaustion of phenomena as their object; second, those faculties abandoned by the vision of origination (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) which have as their cause those things abandoned by the vision of suffering and have the exhaustion of phenomena as their object; and third, those faculties abandoned by the vision of suffering which have the exhaustion of phenomena as their object.

What are the faculties that have cessation as their object (*ālambana*), are abandoned by the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), and have as their cause those things abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*)?
The answer is:

those faculties which are abandoned by the vision of origin and have cessation as their object; furthermore, those faculties which are abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), have as their cause those things abandoned by the vision of origin, and have cessation as their object; furthermore, those faculties which are abandoned by the vision of cessation, have as their cause those things abandoned by the vision of origin, and have cessation as their object.
What are the faculties that have cessation through the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) as their object-condition and are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*)? Answer:
Those faculties that are abandoned by cultivation and have cessation through the knowledge of phenomena as their object-condition.

What are the faculties that have cessation through the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), are abandoned by the knowledge of exhaustion, yet have non-abandonment as their cause?
Answer: Those faculties that are themselves non-abandoned and have cessation through the knowledge of exhaustion as their object-condition.

If the faculties have their cause abandoned through the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (kṣayajñāna), do those faculties have their object abandoned through the vision of the destruction of the outflows? Answer:

Some faculties have their cause abandoned through the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, while their objects are abandoned through the vision of the destruction of the outflows, or their objects are not abandoned at all.

What are the faculties that have their cause in the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (kṣayajñāna), are abandoned by the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, and have as their object that which is abandoned by the vision of the destruction of the outflows? Answer:

They are those faculties whose cause is the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, which are abandoned by the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, and which take as their object that which is abandoned by the vision of the destruction of the outflows.
What are the faculties that have their cause in the abandonment through the knowledge of the exhaustion of the unknown (kṣayā-jñāna) and take as their object that which is not to be abandoned?
Answer: All faculties that have their cause in the abandonment through the knowledge of the exhaustion of the unknown take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.

If the various faculties have as their object that which is abandoned by the knowledge of the exhaustion of the unknown (ājñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), do those faculties have as their cause that which is abandoned by the vision of the exhaustion [of suffering] (kṣaya-darśana)? Answer:

Some faculties have as their object that which is abandoned by the knowledge of the exhaustion of the unknown, while having as their cause that which is abandoned by the vision of the exhaustion, or abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana), or abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana), or abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā), or abandoned by no [cause].
What are the faculties that, having the cessation through unknown knowledge as their object, have as their cause those things abandoned by the vision of cessation? Answer:
Those faculties abandoned by the vision of cessation which have as their object the cessation through unknown knowledge.

What are the faculties that, having as their object the abandonment through the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation (*nirodha-ajñāna-aparijñā-prahātavya*), have as their cause the abandonment through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)?
The answer is:

those faculties which are abandoned through the vision of suffering and have as their object the abandonment through the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation; furthermore, those faculties which are abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), have as their cause the abandonment through the vision of suffering, and have as their object the abandonment through the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation; furthermore, those faculties which are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), have as their cause the abandonment through the vision of suffering, and have as their object the abandonment through the knowledge of the unknown regarding cessation.

What are the faculties that have cessation as their object through the knowledge of the unknown (ajñātam-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna), are abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), and have the vision of the origin as their cause?
The answer is:

those faculties that are abandoned by the vision of the origin, which have cessation as their object through the knowledge of the unknown; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), have the vision of the origin as their cause, and have cessation as their object through the knowledge of the unknown; furthermore, those faculties that are abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya), have the vision of the origin as their cause, and have cessation as their object through the knowledge of the unknown.
What are the faculties that have cessation as their object through the knowledge of the unknown (ajñātijñāna) and are abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya)? Answer:
Those faculties which are abandoned by cultivation and have cessation as their object through the knowledge of the unknown.

What are the faculties that have cessation through the knowledge of the unknown (*ajñāta-ājñāsyāmī-jñāna*) as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), while having non-abandonment (*aprahāṇa*) as their cause? Answer:
Those faculties that are non-abandoned and have cessation through the knowledge of the unknown as their object-condition.

The same applies as above regarding those abandoned through the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) which take as their object what is abandoned through the vision of the path (darśana-mārga), and those abandoned through the subsequent knowledge of the path (anvaya-jñāna) which take as their object what is abandoned through the vision of the path.
The thirty-third chapter, the Section on Conditions (Pratyaya-varga) within the Chapter on Faculties (Indriya-grantha) of the Abhidharma, is completed.
The sixth chapter, the Indriya-varga, is completed.
The preface to this scripture states:
"That person forgot the *Pratītyasamutpāda* chapter; therefore, that text is missing."
Recently, the Kasmirian śramaṇa Dharmapriya memorized it; while passing through Mijian, Saṃghadeva translated this chapter, which contains the complete text of the eight *granthas*.
Fabei remarked:
"The *Aṣṭagrantha* is merely the core body [of the Abhidharma], while there are separately the six *Pādas*, which comprise approximately one million words.
Fabei has recited two of these *Pādas*, but they have not yet been translated; it would be well to produce them, for my regret is truly profound."
Recorded on the nineteenth day of the first month in the fifteenth year of the Jianyuan era of the Qin dynasty at the Zhengguan Buddhist Monastery in Yangzhou.
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-four;
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-five.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Fu Qin dynasty, together with Zhu Fonian.

Section Seven: Concentration (Samādhi-khaṇḍa). This section contains thirty-eight chapters in total. 1. Attainment in the Past (Atīta-prāpti) 2. Conditionality (Pratyaya) 3. Liberation (Vimukti) 4. Non-returner (Anāgāmin) 5. Single-Practice Contemplation (Ekāyana-darśana), following after.

1. Chapter on Attainment in the Past (*Atītapratilambhādhikaraṇa*), the first part of the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda*. If one attains a dharma of the past, does that attainment itself belong to the past?
If one attains the past, does one attain past dharmas?

Or [future and present dharmas; wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas; dharmas bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; dharmas of the learner, the non-learner, and those of neither the learner nor the non-learner; dharmas abandoned through seeing the truths and those abandoned through cultivation]?
If one attains a state that is non-interrupted (*anantarya*), does that attainment itself remain non-interrupted?
Conversely, if an attainment remains non-interrupted, is that which is attained a non-interrupted dharma?
When wholesome formless states (*arūpa*) arise, are they concomitant with a wholesome mind?
If they are associated with a wholesome mind, are those dharmas wholesome, formless?

Are they unwholesome or indeterminate; bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee; abandoned by vision of the truths, abandoned by cultivation, or not abandoned?
If a dharma is an unconditioned formless phenomenon (*arūpa*), is it concomitant with an uninterrupted mind (*anivṛta-citta*)?
Conversely, if it is concomitant with an uninterrupted mind, is that dharma an uninterrupted unconditioned formless phenomenon?
Are all factors of the first *dhyāna* fivefold?
Are all the four types of the second dhyāna, all the five types of the third dhyāna, and all the four types of the fourth dhyāna likewise?
Regarding the first dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*), when one enters it, should it be called "relishing," and when one emerges from it, should it be called "relishing"?

Regarding the states associated with attachment (*āsvādana*), up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*): should it be said that they are associated with attachment both upon entering and upon arising?
And as for all those first dhyānas associated with attachment, are they all obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)?
If something is obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), is it necessarily the first dhyāna associated with attachment (*āsvādanā-saṃprayukta*)?
And are all states from those associated with attachment up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) necessarily obscured-indeterminate?
If they are obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), are they all associated with relishing (āsvādana) up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)?
Is it possible to enter the second dhyāna without having entered the first dhyāna?
Is it possible that one does not enter the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaṃjñāsaṃjñāyatana*) and yet enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Is it possible that one does not enter the first dhyāna and yet is born in the first dhyāna?
Is it possible that one does not enter [the stages] up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and yet is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
If one attains the first dhyāna but not the second, where will they be reborn at the end of life?
If they attain up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception but not the sphere of nothingness, where will they be reborn at the end of life?

How does one enter into loving-kindness (*maitrī*) through mental attention? How does one enter into compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) through mental attention?
By the cessation of which fetters and bonds is loving-kindness purified? By the cessation of which fetters and bonds are compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity purified?
What fetters bound by what are extinguished through the first dhyāna, up to the pure state, and even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?

What fetters bound by what are extinguished through the first liberation up to the eighth liberation; the first base of mastery up to the eighth base of mastery; the first totality up to the tenth totality; from the knowledge of phenomena up to the knowledge of the path; and through emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness? What fetters bound by what are extinguished?
What is the pure retribution received for loving-kindness? What is the pure retribution received for compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?
What is the pure retribution received for the reward of the first dhyāna?
And so on, up to: what is the pure retribution received for the reward of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?

Regarding the first liberation through to the eighth liberation, the first base of mastery through to the eighth base of mastery, and the first universal base through to the tenth universal base—what kind of retribution is received for the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, and their respective fruits?
I wish to explain fully the meaning of this chapter.
If one attains past dharmas, does that person possess the past? Answer:
It may be past, future, or present.
If it is attained as past, does that attainment pertain to past phenomena?
Answer: Yes.
Whether it be past, future, present, or unconditioned— having concluded with the past—
if one attains a future dharma, does that attainment itself belong to the future?
Answer: It may be past, future, or present.
If it is acquired as future, does that acquisition itself acquire a future dharma?
Answer: It may be past, future, present, or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
If one attains a present dharma, does that attainment itself belong to the present?
Answer: It may be past, future, or present.
If it is attained as present, does that attainment itself pertain to a present dharma?
Answer: It may be past, future, present, or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Having attained wholesome dharmas, does one possess those wholesome [dharmas]?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains the wholesome, does that person attain wholesome dharmas?
Answer: It is so.
If one acquires unwholesome dharmas, does one thereby acquire the unwholesome?
Answer: It is so.
If one acquires the unwholesome, does one acquire unwholesome dharmas?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains an indeterminate dharma, does that person possess that indeterminate [dharma]?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains the indeterminate, does one attain indeterminate dharmas?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains a dharma bound to the desire realm, does that attainment itself belong to the desire realm?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains that which is bound to the desire realm, does one thereby attain dharmas bound to the desire realm?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains a dharma bound to the realm of form, does that attainment itself belong to the realm of form?
Answer: It is so.
If one obtains that which is bound to the form realm, does one obtain dharmas bound to the form realm?
Answer: It is either bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or not bound.
If one acquires a dharma bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), is that acquisition itself bound to the formless realm?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains that which is bound to the formless realm, does one thereby attain dharmas bound to the formless realm?
Answer: It is either bound to the formless realm or not bound.
If one attains the dharmas of a learner (śaikṣa), is that attainment itself a learner’s attainment?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains the state of a learner (śaikṣa), does that person attain the dharmas of a learner?
Answer: It is either training (śaikṣa) or neither-training-nor-non-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
If one attains a dharma of non-training (aśaikṣa), does that attainment itself belong to non-training?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), does one thereby attain the dharmas of no-more-learning?
Answer: It is either that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) or that which is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
If one attains a dharma that is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training, does that attainment itself belong to the category of neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training?
Answer: It may be that which is in training (*śaikṣa*), that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or that which is neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
If one attains that which is neither in training nor beyond training, does one thereby attain dharmas that are neither in training nor beyond training?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains the abandonment of dharmas through the vision of the truths, does that [attainment] itself abandon through the vision of the truths?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains that which is abandoned by seeing the truths, does that person possess those dharmas abandoned by seeing the truths?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains a dharma that is abandoned through cultivation, is that attainment itself abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: It is so.
If one attains that which is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), does one thereby attain the dharmas abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: It is either abandoned through contemplation or not abandoned.
If one attains a state that is not abandoned, does that attainment itself remain un-abandoned?
Answer: It is either abandoned through contemplation or not abandoned.
If it is not abandoned, does that acquisition itself constitute an unconditioned dharma?
Answer: It is so;
they have been fully attained.
When various wholesome formless phenomena arise, are they concomitant with a wholesome mind?
Answer:
Certain phenomena arise as wholesome formless states, co-arising with a wholesome mind, co-arising with an unwholesome mind, or co-arising with a neutral mind.
What are the phenomena that arise as wholesome formless states co-arising with a wholesome mind?
Answer: Those phenomena that are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being wholesome—these are called phenomena that are wholesome immaterial states arising together with a wholesome mind.
What are phenomena that are wholesome immaterial states arising together with an unwholesome mind?

Answer: For example, when an unwholesome mind either regresses or arises, wholesome dharmas are produced; this is called "the arising of wholesome formless dharmas concomitant with an unwholesome mind.
What is the arising of wholesome formless dharmas concomitant with that indeterminate mind?

Answer: For example, when an indeterminate mind either regresses or arises, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of wholesome dharmas arises; this is called "wholesome formless dharmas arising together with an indeterminate mind.
Now, if various dharmas arise together with a wholesome mind, are those dharmas wholesome formless [dharmas]?
Answer: Certain phenomena arise together with a wholesome mind: wholesome formless states and indeterminate formless states.
What are the phenomena that arise together with a wholesome mind as wholesome formless states?
Answer: Those phenomena that are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being wholesome—these are called wholesome formless states arising together with a wholesome mind.
What are the indeterminate formless states arising together with a wholesome mind?
Answer: Just as the acquisition (*prāpti*) of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas arises when the wholesome mind (*kuśalacitta*) progresses;

just as while abiding in a wholesome mind, the roots of the indeterminate increase, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are augmented, become supple, excellent, and full, and the various acquisitions, birth, aging, and impermanence (*anityatā*) of those dharmas arise—this is called the indeterminate formless state that arises simultaneously with a wholesome mind. This concludes the section on the wholesome.
When various unwholesome non-material phenomena arise, are they concomitant with an unwholesome mind?
The answer is:
some unwholesome non-material phenomena that arise are concomitant with an unwholesome mind, while others are concomitant with an indeterminate mind.
What are the phenomena that are unwholesome, formless, and arise together with an unwholesome mind? Answer:
Those phenomena which are associated with that mind and coexist with it as unwholesome; these are called the phenomena that are unwholesome, formless, and arise together with an unwholesome mind.
What is the case where unwholesome formless states arise together with an indeterminate mind? Answer:

For example, when an indeterminate mind either regresses or arises, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of unwholesome dharmas arises; this is called the case where unwholesome formless states arise together with an indeterminate mind.
If various phenomena arise together with an unwholesome mind, are those phenomena unwholesome immaterial factors? Answer:
Some phenomena that arise together with an unwholesome mind are unwholesome immaterial factors, wholesome immaterial factors, or indeterminate immaterial factors.
What are the dharmas that arise together with an unwholesome mind as unwholesome formless states (*arūpa*)? Answer:
Those dharmas which are associated with that mind and coexist with it as unwholesome; these are called the dharmas that arise together with an unwholesome mind as unwholesome formless states.
What are the wholesome formless states that arise simultaneously with an unwholesome mind?
The answer is:

for example, when an unwholesome mind either regresses or arises, and the acquisition of wholesome dharmas occurs; these are called the wholesome formless states that arise simultaneously with an unwholesome mind.
What are the indeterminate formless states that arise simultaneously with an unwholesome mind?
The answer is:
for example, when an unwholesome mind either regresses or arises, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of indeterminate dharmas arises.

Just as when one dwells in an unwholesome mind, the roots of the indeterminate increase and flourish, and the four great elements are augmented, softened, beautified, and satiated; so too are the acquisitions (*prāpti*), arising, aging, and impermanence of those phenomena. This is called the phenomenon that arises simultaneously with an unwholesome mind and is an indeterminate non-material form (*arūpa*). Thus ends the section on the unwholesome.
When various dharmas that are indeterminate and formless arise, are they accompanied by an indeterminate mind? Answer:
Some dharmas that are indeterminate and formless arise accompanied by an indeterminate mind, some accompanied by a wholesome mind, and some accompanied by an unwholesome mind.
What are the factors that are indeterminate (avyākṛta), non-material (arūpin), and arise together with an indeterminate mind? Answer:

Those factors which are associated with that mind and coexist with it as indeterminate; these are called the factors that are indeterminate, non-material, and arise together with an indeterminate mind.
What is the case where an indeterminate formless dharma arises together with a wholesome mind?
The answer is:
as when an indeterminate dharma is acquired during the advancement of a wholesome mind.

Just as when one abides in a wholesome mind, the roots of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) increase and flourish, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are augmented, become supple, beautiful, and full; and the various acquisitions (*prāpti*), birth, aging, and impermanence of those phenomena arise—this is called the arising of indeterminate formless phenomena concomitant with a wholesome mind.
How is it that an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) formless dharma arises together with an unwholesome mind? Answer:
For example, when an unwholesome mind either regresses or arises, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of indeterminate dharmas arises.

Just as when one abides in an unwholesome mind, the roots of the indeterminate increase and flourish, and the four great elements are augmented, become supple, excellent, and full; so too do the acquisitions (*prāpti*), birth, aging, and impermanence of those phenomena arise. This is called the arising of an indeterminate, formless phenomenon concomitant with an unwholesome mind.
If various dharmas arise simultaneously with an indeterminate mind, are those dharmas indeterminate and formless? Answer:
Some dharmas that arise simultaneously with an indeterminate mind are indeterminate and formless, some are wholesome and formless, and some are unwholesome and formless.
What are the non-material (arūpa) factors that arise simultaneously with a neutral mind and are themselves neutral?
The answer is:

those factors which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being neutral; these are called the non-material factors that arise simultaneously with a neutral mind and are themselves neutral.
What are the wholesome formless states that arise simultaneously with a neutral mind? Answer:

When a neutral mind either regresses or arises, and the acquisition (*prāpti*) of wholesome dharmas arises, these are called the wholesome formless states that arise simultaneously with a neutral mind.
What are the unwholesome formless states that arise simultaneously with an indeterminate state of mind? Answer:

For example, when an indeterminate mind either regresses or arises, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of unwholesome dharmas arises; these are called the unwholesome formless states that arise simultaneously with an indeterminate state of mind. This concludes the section on the indeterminate.
When various phenomena belonging to the desire realm arise as formless, are they concomitant with a mind belonging to the desire realm?
The answer is:

some phenomena belonging to the desire realm that arise as formless are concomitant with a mind belonging to the desire realm, concomitant with a mind belonging to the form realm, concomitant with a mind belonging to the formless realm, or concomitant with a mind that is unconditioned (unbound).
What are the phenomena that are non-material (arūpa) and bound to the desire realm, which arise together with a mind bound to the desire realm?
Answer:

Those phenomena that are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being bound to the desire realm—these are called the phenomena that are non-material and bound to the desire realm, which arise together with a mind bound to the desire realm.
What is the case where a dharma bound to the desire realm arises together with a mind bound to the form realm?
Answer:
For example, when a mind bound to the form realm arises or progresses toward higher stages, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of dharmas bound to the desire realm arises.

Just as when one abides in a mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-citta*), the faculties bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-indriya*) are nourished and increased, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are augmented, becoming supple, beautiful, and full; and the acquisitions (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), and impermanence (*anityatā*) of these phenomena arise—this is called a phenomenon bound to the desire realm that arises while being accompanied by a mind bound to the form realm.
What is the phenomenon that, being bound to the desire realm and arising as formless, co-exists with a mind bound to the formless realm?
The answer is:

for example, when a mind bound to the formless realm abides, it causes the faculties bound to the desire realm to grow and flourish, and the four great elements to increase, become supple, beautiful, and full; these phenomena, including their various acquisitions (*prāpti*), birth, aging, and impermanence, are called phenomena that, being bound to the desire realm and arising as formless, co-exist with a mind bound to the formless realm.
What is the case where a dharma bound to the desire realm arises together with a mind that is not bound?
Answer: It is as when a mind that is not bound undergoes advancement (*viśeṣagamana*), and the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a dharma bound to the desire realm arises.

Just as when the mind is not bound [to the formless realm], the faculties bound to the desire realm are increased and nourished, the four great elements are augmented, becoming supple, beautiful, and full; and the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) of these phenomena—namely birth, aging, and impermanence—this is called the arising of formless phenomena bound to the desire realm together with a mind that is not bound.
If various phenomena arise together with a mind bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), are those phenomena immaterial (*arūpa*) factors bound to the desire realm?
Answer:

Some phenomena that arise together with a mind bound to the desire realm are immaterial factors bound to the desire realm, immaterial factors bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), immaterial factors bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or immaterial factors that are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
What are the dharmas that arise together with a mind bound to the desire realm as formless states (ārūpya) bound to the desire realm?
The answer is:

those dharmas which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being bound to the desire realm; these are called the dharmas that arise together with a mind bound to the desire realm as formless states bound to the desire realm.
What is the dharma that arises together with a mind bound to the desire realm and is a formless state (ārūpya) bound to the form realm? Answer:

For example, when a mind bound to the desire realm undergoes retrogression or rebirth, the acquisition (prāpti) of dharmas bound to the form realm arises; this is called the dharma that arises together with a mind bound to the desire realm and is a formless state bound to the form realm.
What is the formless [dharma] bound to the formless realm that arises simultaneously with a mind bound to the desire realm?
Answer:

It is when, through the falling away from or the rebirth into a mind bound to the desire realm, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a dharma bound to the formless realm arises; this is called the formless [dharma] bound to the formless realm that arises simultaneously with a mind bound to the desire realm.
What is the phenomenon that arises together with a mind bound to the desire realm, yet is a non-bound formless state? Answer:

It is as when, through the falling away from a mind bound to the desire realm, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a non-bound phenomenon arises; this is called the phenomenon that arises together with a mind bound to the desire realm, yet is a non-bound formless state. [End of section on the desire realm.]
When various phenomena belonging to the form realm arise as non-material (immaterial), are they concomitant with a mind belonging to the form realm?
The answer is:

some phenomena belonging to the form realm arise as non-material, being concomitant with a mind belonging to the form realm, a mind belonging to the desire realm, a mind belonging to the formless realm, or a mind that is unconditioned (not bound to any realm).
What are the phenomena that are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), are non-material (*arūpin*), and arise together with a mind bound to the form realm? Answer:

Those phenomena which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being bound to the form realm—these are called the phenomena that are bound to the form realm, are non-material, and arise together with a mind bound to the form realm.
What is the case where a dharma that is a non-material phenomenon (arūpadharma) belonging to the form realm arises together with a mind belonging to the desire realm? Answer:

It is when, through the falling away from or the arising [of a state] of a mind belonging to the desire realm, the acquisition (prāpti) of a dharma belonging to the form realm arises; this is called a dharma that is a non-material phenomenon belonging to the form realm arising together with a mind belonging to the desire realm.
What are the phenomena that, being bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and being immaterial (*arūpin*), arise together with a mind bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)? Answer:

For example, when a mind bound to the formless realm abides, it causes the faculties (*indriya*) bound to the form realm to grow and increase; the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are augmented, becoming supple, beautiful, and full. These phenomena—the acquisitions (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), and impermanence (*anityatā*)—are what are called phenomena that, being bound to the form realm and being immaterial, arise together with a mind bound to the formless realm.
What is the case where a dharma bound to the form realm arises together with a mind that is not bound?
Answer: It is as when, through the advancement of a mind that is not bound, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a dharma bound to the form realm arises.

Just as when the mind is not bound [to the form realm], the faculties bound to the form realm are increased and nourished, the four great elements are augmented, becoming supple, excellent, and full, and these factors—including their acquisitions, birth, aging, and impermanence—are called "form-realm-bound formless phenomena arising together with a mind that is not bound."
If various phenomena arise together with a mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), are those phenomena formless factors (*arūpa*) bound to the form realm?
Answer:

Some phenomena that arise together with a mind bound to the form realm are formless factors bound to the form realm; some are formless factors bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); some are formless factors bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); and some are unbound formless factors (*apratisaṃyukta*).
What are the dharmas that arise together with a mind bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-citta) and are formless (arūpa) factors bound to the form realm? Answer:

Those dharmas which are associated with that mind and those which coexist with it and are bound to the form realm—these are called the dharmas that arise together with a mind bound to the form realm and are formless factors bound to the form realm.
What are the dharmas bound to the form realm that arise together with a mind bound to the form realm, yet are themselves bound to the desire realm?
Answer:
For example, when a mind bound to the form realm is progressing toward higher attainment, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of dharmas bound to the desire realm arises.

Just as when a mind bound to the form realm causes the faculties bound to the desire realm to grow and increase, and the four great elements to become augmented, supple, beautiful, and full, the various acquisitions (*prāpti*), birth, aging, and impermanence of these factors—this is called the non-material [factors] bound to the desire realm that arise simultaneously with a mind bound to the form realm.
What are the formless factors bound to the form realm that arise simultaneously with a mind bound to the form realm?
Answer:

For example, when a mind bound to the form realm undergoes retrogression or is reborn, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of factors bound to the formless realm arises; these are called the formless factors bound to the form realm that arise simultaneously with a mind bound to the form realm.
What is the dharma that arises together with a mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-citta*) yet is a non-bound formless state (*apratisaṃyukta-ārūpya*)? Answer:

For example, when a mind bound to the form realm undergoes either decline or advancement, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a non-bound dharma arises; this is called the dharma that arises together with a mind bound to the form realm yet is a non-bound formless state. This concludes the section on the form realm.
Regarding those phenomena that arise as formless and are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), do they coexist with a mind bound to the formless realm? Answer:

Some phenomena that arise as formless and are bound to the formless realm coexist with a mind bound to the formless realm, some coexist with a mind bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), some coexist with a mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and some coexist with a mind that is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
What are the phenomena that are bound to the formless realm, are formless, and arise together with a mind bound to the formless realm?
Answer:

Those phenomena which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being bound to the formless realm—these are called the phenomena that are bound to the formless realm, are formless, and arise together with a mind bound to the formless realm.
What is the case where a dharma bound to the formless realm arises as a non-material phenomenon concomitant with a mind bound to the desire realm?
Answer:

It is when, through the falling away from or the arising of a mind bound to the desire realm, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a dharma bound to the formless realm arises; this is called a dharma bound to the formless realm arising as a non-material phenomenon concomitant with a mind bound to the desire realm.
What is the case where a dharma bound to the formless realm arises as a non-material phenomenon concomitant with a mind bound to the form realm?
Answer:

It is when, upon the falling away from or the rebirth into a mind bound to the form realm, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a dharma bound to the formless realm arises; this is called a dharma bound to the formless realm arising as a non-material phenomenon concomitant with a mind bound to the form realm.
What is the case where a dharma bound to the formless realm arises as a non-material phenomenon concomitant with a mind that is not bound? Answer:

It is when, through the progressive advancement of a mind that is not bound, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a dharma bound to the formless realm arises; this is called a dharma bound to the formless realm arising as a non-material phenomenon concomitant with a mind that is not bound.
If various phenomena arise together with a mind bound to the formless realm, are those phenomena formless and bound to the formless realm?
The answer is:

some phenomena that arise together with a mind bound to the formless realm are formless and bound to the formless realm; some are formless and bound to the desire realm; some are formless and bound to the form realm; and some are formless and unbound.
What are the formless factors that arise simultaneously with a mind bound to the formless realm? Answer:

Those factors which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being bound to the formless realm—these are called the formless factors that arise simultaneously with a mind bound to the formless realm.
What are the formless phenomena that arise together with a mind bound to the formless realm and are themselves bound to the desire realm?
The answer is:

for example, when a mind bound to the formless realm abides, it causes the faculties bound to the desire realm to grow and increase; the four great elements are augmented, becoming supple, excellent, and full. These phenomena—the various acquisitions (*prāpti*), birth, aging, and impermanence—are called the formless phenomena that arise together with a mind bound to the formless realm and are themselves bound to the desire realm.
What is the formless (arūpa) dharma that arises simultaneously with a mind bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-baddha-citta) and is itself bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-baddha)? Answer:

For example, when a mind bound to the formless realm abides, it causes the faculties (indriya) bound to the form realm to grow and increase, and the four great elements (mahābhūta) to become augmented, supple, excellent, and full. These dharmas—the acquisitions (prāpti), birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and impermanence (anityatā)—are called the formless dharmas that arise simultaneously with a mind bound to the formless realm and are themselves bound to the form realm.
What are the non-bound formless states that arise together with a mind bound to the formless realm? Answer:

For example, when a mind bound to the formless realm undergoes retrogression or advancement, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-bound dharmas arises; these are called the non-bound formless states that arise together with a mind bound to the formless realm. [End of section on formless states.]
Regarding those phenomena that arise as the formless aggregates of one in training (*śaikṣa*), do they arise together with a mind of one in training? Answer:

Some phenomena that arise as the formless aggregates of one in training arise together with a mind of one in training, while others arise together with a mind that is neither of one in training nor of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What are the phenomena that arise as unconditioned (ārūpya) and are concomitant with a mind that is in training (śaikṣa)? Answer:

Those phenomena which are associated with that mind and coexist with it while being in training; these are called the phenomena that arise as unconditioned and are concomitant with a mind that is in training.
What is the case where a dharma that is a learner’s immaterial attainment arises together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer:

For example, when a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner undergoes either retrogression or advancement, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a learner’s dharma arises; this is called a dharma that is a learner’s immaterial attainment arising together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
If various phenomena arise together with a mind that is in training (*śaikṣa*), are those phenomena formless states (*ārūpya*) of one in training?
The answer is:
some phenomena arising together with a mind in training are formless states of one in training, while others are formless states that are neither in training nor beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What are the dharmas that arise together with a mind of training (śaikṣa) as unconditioned formless states (ārūpya)? Answer:
Those dharmas which are associated with that mind and coexist with it as states of training; these are called the dharmas that arise together with a mind of training as unconditioned formless states.
What is the non-learner, non-non-learner formless state that arises together with a learner’s mind?
The answer is:
as when a learner’s mind progresses and the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a non-learner, non-non-learner dharma arises.

Just as when the mind of one in training abides, the faculties that are neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training increase and flourish; the four great elements increase, become supple, beautiful, and fully nourished, and reach their full development; and those various phenomena undergo birth, aging, and impermanence—this is called the phenomenon that arises together with the mind of one in training, which is a non-trainee/non-beyond-training formless state.
When various dharmas that are *aśaikṣa* (beyond training) and formless arise, are they concomitant with an *aśaikṣa* mind? Answer:
Some *aśaikṣa* formless dharmas arise concomitant with an *aśaikṣa* mind, while others arise concomitant with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What are the dharmas that are unlearned (aśaikṣa), non-material (arūpin), and arise together with an unlearned mind? Answer:
Those dharmas which are associated with that mind and coexist with it as unlearned; these are called the dharmas that are unlearned, non-material, and arise together with an unlearned mind.
What is the case where an unlearned (aśaikṣa) formless dharma arises together with a mind that is neither-learned-nor-unlearned? Answer:

For example, when a mind that is neither-learned-nor-unlearned undergoes either decline or advancement, the acquisition (prāpti) of an unlearned dharma arises; this is called an unlearned formless dharma arising together with a mind that is neither-learned-nor-unlearned.
If various dharmas arise together with a mind that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), are those dharmas also formless (*arūpa*) and beyond training?
The answer is:
some dharmas that arise together with a mind beyond training are both formless and beyond training, while others are formless but neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What are the dharmas that arise simultaneously with an *aśaikṣa* mind as *aśaikṣa* formless states (*ārūpya*)? Answer:
Those dharmas which are associated with that mind and coexist with it as *aśaikṣa*; these are called the dharmas that arise simultaneously with an *aśaikṣa* mind as *aśaikṣa* formless states.
What are the non-learner (aśaikṣa) mental states that arise simultaneously with a dharma that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa) formless state? Answer:
It is as when, through the progressive advancement of a non-learner mind, the acquisition (prāpti) of a dharma that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner arises.

Just as when the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) dwells in the faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are increased, strengthened, softened, beautified, and nourished; and the acquisitions (*prāpti*), birth, aging, and impermanence of these factors—this is called the factor that arises together with the mind of one beyond training, which is a non-material phenomenon (*arūpa-dharma*) that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner. This concludes the section on the mind of one beyond training.
When various phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner arise as formless (*arūpa*), are they accompanied by a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer:

Some phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner arise as formless and are accompanied by a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner—namely, those that are with-outflows (*sāsrava*); some are accompanied by a learner’s (*śaikṣa*) mind; and some are accompanied by a non-learner’s (*aśaikṣa*) mind.
What are the phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner formless states arising together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer:

Those phenomena which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being neither-learner-nor-non-learner; these are called the phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner formless states arising together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What are the non-learner and non-non-learner formless states that arise together with a learner’s mind? Answer:
As when a learner’s mind advances, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-learner and non-non-learner dharmas arises.

When the mind of one in training abides, the faculties that are neither of one in training nor of one beyond training—namely, the five material faculties, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, and the faculties of pain and grief—increase; the four great elements increase, becoming supple, beautiful, and full; and these factors, including their acquisitions, as well as birth, aging, and impermanence, arise together with the mind of one in training. This is called the arising of non-material phenomena that are neither of one in training nor of one beyond training, occurring in conjunction with the mind of one in training.
What are the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, which are formless, and arise together with a non-learner mind? Answer:
For example, when a non-learner mind advances, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner arises.

Just as when the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) abides in the faculties that are neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), the four great elements (mahābhūta) are increased, strengthened, softened, beautified, and nourished; and the acquisitions (prāpti), birth, aging, and impermanence of those factors—this is called the arising of factors that are neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training and formless (arūpa), which are concomitant with the mind of one beyond training.
If various phenomena arise together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, are those phenomena non-learner-nor-non-learner immaterial factors?
Answer:

Some phenomena that arise together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner are non-learner-nor-non-learner immaterial factors; some are learner immaterial factors; and some are non-learner immaterial factors.
What are the dharmas that arise together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, yet are themselves non-learner-non-non-learner immaterial factors (*arūpa*)?
Answer:

Those dharmas which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being neither-learner-nor-non-learner; these are called the dharmas that arise together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, yet are themselves non-learner-non-non-learner immaterial factors.
What are the non-learner and non-non-learner dharmas that arise simultaneously with a mind that is neither learner nor non-learner?
Answer:

For example, when a mind that is neither learner nor non-learner undergoes either decline or progress, and the acquisition (*prāpti*) of learner dharmas arises; these are called the non-learner and non-non-learner dharmas that arise simultaneously with a mind that is neither learner nor non-learner.
What is the non-learner (aśaikṣa) formless [attainment] that arises simultaneously with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer:

It is when, through the regression or the advancement of a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, the acquisition (prāpti) of a non-learner dharma arises; this is called the non-learner formless [attainment] arising simultaneously with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner. This concludes the section on the neither-learner-nor-non-learner.

Regarding those dharmas that are formless (*arūpin*) and abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), do they arise simultaneously with a mind abandoned through the vision of the truths? Answer:

Some formless dharmas abandoned through the vision of the truths arise simultaneously with a mind abandoned through the vision of the truths, while others arise simultaneously with a mind abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

What are those phenomena that are formless (*ārūpya*), abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), and arise together with a mind abandoned through the vision of the truths? Answer:

Those phenomena which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being abandoned through the vision of the truths—these are called phenomena that are formless, abandoned through the vision of the truths, and arise together with a mind abandoned through the vision of the truths.
What is the case where a dharma abandoned by seeing the truths (dṛṣṭiheya) arises as a non-material phenomenon (ārūpya) concomitant with a mind abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya)? Answer:

It is when, upon the falling away from or the arising of a mind abandoned by cultivation, the acquisition (prāpti) of a dharma abandoned by seeing the truths arises; this is called a dharma abandoned by seeing the truths arising as a non-material phenomenon concomitant with a mind abandoned by cultivation.

If various phenomena arise together with a mind that is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), are those phenomena formless (*arūpa*) and abandoned through the vision of the truths?
Answer:

Some phenomena that arise together with a mind abandoned through the vision of the truths are formless and abandoned through the vision of the truths; others are formless and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What are the non-material phenomena (*arūpa*) that are abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) and arise together with a mind abandoned by seeing the truths? Answer:

Those phenomena which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, and are abandoned by seeing the truths—these are called the non-material phenomena abandoned by seeing the truths that arise together with a mind abandoned by seeing the truths.
What is the formless [state] that arises together with a mind abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-prahātavya*), yet is itself abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)? Answer:
It is when, upon the falling away from or the arising of a mind abandoned by seeing the truths, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a dharma abandoned by cultivation arises.

Just as when the mind abandoned by seeing the truths (dṛṣṭi-heya) abides, the faculties abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) grow and increase; the four great elements (mahābhūta) are augmented, becoming supple, beautiful, and full; and there arise the acquisitions (prāpti), birth, aging, and impermanence of those factors—this is called the formless state abandoned by cultivation that arises simultaneously with the mind abandoned by seeing the truths. This concludes the section on abandoning by seeing the truths.
When various dharmas that are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) arise as formless (*arūpin*), are they associated with a mind abandoned by cultivation?
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-five;
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-six.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīr together with Zhu Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty.
Section on Determination (Viniścaya-khaṇḍa), Chapter One: Past Attainments (Atīta-prāpti-varga), Part Two. He replied:

Or, there are formless states (*ārūpya*) that arise through the abandonment by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which are associated with a mind abandoned by cultivation, a mind abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), or a mind not to be abandoned (*aheya*).
What are those formless states that arise through the abandonment by cultivation and are associated with a mind abandoned by cultivation?
Answer:

Those phenomena that are associated with that mind and coexist with it, and which are abandoned through cultivation—these are called phenomena abandoned through cultivation that arise together with a mind abandoned through cultivation.
What is the arising of formless states abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) together with a mind abandoned by seeing the truths (darśana-heya)? Answer:
It is as when, upon the falling away from or the arising of a mind abandoned by seeing the truths, the acquisition (prāpti) of formless states abandoned by cultivation arises.

Just as when the mind abandoned by seeing the truths (dṛṣṭiheya) abides, the faculties abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya) increase and grow; the four great elements (mahābhūta) increase, becoming supple, beautiful, and full; and the various acquisitions (prāpti), birth, aging, and impermanence of those factors arise—this is called the arising of formless factors abandoned by cultivation together with the mind abandoned by seeing the truths.
What is the arising of a formless state abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) accompanied by a mind not abandoned (*aheya*)?
Answer: It is as when the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a formless state abandoned through cultivation arises through the advancement (*viśeṣagamana*) of a mind not abandoned.

Just as when one dwells with a mind that is not subject to abandonment, one cultivates and increases the faculties subject to abandonment; the four great elements increase, becoming supple, beautiful, and full; and the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) of those phenomena—namely birth, aging, and impermanence—arise. This is called the arising of formless states subject to abandonment through mental cultivation, concomitant with a mind that is not subject to abandonment.
If various phenomena arise together with a mind that is abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), are those phenomena formless states (arūpa) abandoned by cultivation? Answer:

Some phenomena arising together with a mind abandoned by cultivation are formless states abandoned by cultivation, formless states abandoned by seeing the truths (darśana-heya), or formless states not to be abandoned (aheya).
What are the formless states (*ārūpya*) that arise together with a mind to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)? Answer:

Those dharmas which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, and are themselves to be abandoned by cultivation—these are called the formless states that arise together with a mind to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the immateriality (ārūpya) abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya) that arises simultaneously with the mind abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya)? Answer:

For example, when a mind abandoned by cultivation either regresses or arises, the acquisition (prāpti) of dharmas abandoned by insight arises; this is called the immateriality abandoned by insight that arises simultaneously with the mind abandoned by cultivation.
What is the non-manifest (avijñapti) form that arises simultaneously with a mind to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), yet is itself not to be abandoned? Answer:

It is when, upon the regression or the advancement of a mind to be abandoned by cultivation, the acquisition (prāpti) of a dharma that is not to be abandoned arises. This concludes the section on the non-manifest form arising simultaneously with a mind to be abandoned by cultivation.
When various phenomena that are uninterrupted (*aprahīṇa*) and formless (*arūpin*) arise, are they associated with an uninterrupted mind? Answer:

Some phenomena that are uninterrupted and formless arise associated with an uninterrupted mind; some are associated with a mind to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). How do phenomena that are uninterrupted and formless arise associated with an uninterrupted mind?

Answer: Those dharmas that are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being uninterrupted—these are called "dharmas that arise as uninterrupted formless states and are accompanied by an uninterrupted mind.
What are those dharmas that arise as uninterrupted formless states and are accompanied by a mind to be abandoned through cultivation?
Answer:

For example, when the mind of abandonment through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) either regresses or progresses, the acquisition (prāpti) of dharmas that are not subject to abandonment arises; this is called the arising of a formless dharma not subject to abandonment together with a mind abandoned through cultivation.
If various phenomena arise simultaneously with a mind that is uninterrupted, are those phenomena also uninterrupted and formless?
The answer is:
some phenomena that arise simultaneously with an uninterrupted mind are both uninterrupted and formless, while others are formless and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
What are the phenomena that arise together with a non-abandoned mind and are themselves non-abandoned immaterial states?
The answer is:

those phenomena which are associated with that mind and coexist with it, being non-abandoned; these are called the phenomena that arise together with a non-abandoned mind and are themselves non-abandoned immaterial states.
What is the formless [dharma] that arises together with a mind that is not to be abandoned, yet is to be abandoned through cultivation?
The answer is:
as when the attainment (*prāpti*) of a dharma to be abandoned through cultivation arises in a superior progression from a mind that is not to be abandoned.

Just as when one dwells with a mind that is not abandoned, one contemplates the severing of the roots [of unwholesomeness] and causes them to grow and increase; the four great elements (mahābhūta) are augmented, becoming supple, beautiful, and full, and those factors (dharma) undergo acquisition, birth, aging, and impermanence—this is called a factor arising together with a mind that is not abandoned.
Having finished the contemplation on the abandonment of the formless and the non-abandonment [of the form realm], one asks:
Are all [factors] of the first dhyāna of five kinds?
The answer is: No.
The non-defiled has five types; the defiled does not have five types.
What [types] are absent?
The answer is:
It is also free from joy and pleasure.
Are all second dhyānas of these four kinds?
Answer: No.
The non-defiled are of four kinds; the defiled are not of four kinds.
What is missing?
The answer is:
Is it internal faith?
Are all [factors] of the third dhyāna fivefold?
Answer: No.
