How is it that one accomplishes past emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and future signlessness (*animitta*), but not the past or present? The answer is:

if the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) has been exhausted but not lost, and furthermore, one has attained the concentration of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*) which has neither been exhausted nor—if it was exhausted—lost, yet it does not manifest before one; this is called accomplishing past emptiness and future signlessness, but not the past or present.
How is it that one accomplishes past emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and past and future signlessness (*animitta*), but not the present?
The answer is:

if the samādhis of emptiness and signlessness have been exhausted but are not lost, and furthermore, that signless samādhi does not manifest before one, this is called accomplishing past emptiness and past and future signlessness, but not the present.
How is it that one accomplishes past emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and future and present signlessness (*animitta*), but not the past?
The answer is:

if the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) has been exhausted but not lost, and furthermore that concentration of signlessness is present before one, yet has not been exhausted—or even if it was exhausted, it has been lost—this is called accomplishing past emptiness and future and present signlessness, but not the past.
How does one accomplish past emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as well as past, future, and present signlessness (*animitta*)?
The answer is:

if the samādhis of emptiness and signlessness have been exhausted [in the past] but not lost, and furthermore that signless samādhi manifests in the present, this is called accomplishing past emptiness as well as past, future, and present signlessness.
If one accomplishes the signless (animitta) of the past, future, and present, does one accomplish the emptiness (śūnyatā) of the past?

Answer: If it has been exhausted and not lost, then one accomplishes it; if it has not been exhausted, or if having been exhausted it is lost, then one does not accomplish emptiness and the signless. [End of Section 7.]

The same applies to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). First, past emptiness, past wishlessness, and past signlessness are one; second, future [emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness]; third, present [emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness]; fourth, past and present [emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness]; fifth, future and present [emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness]; sixth, past and future [emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness]; seventh, past, future, and present signlessness. Thus ends the sevenfold signlessness.
If one cultivates the samādhi of emptiness, does one also cultivate the wishless?
The answer is:
it may be emptiness but not the wishless.
What is emptiness that is not wishlessness?
The answer is:
when the originally attained samādhi of emptiness manifests before one, this is called emptiness that is not wishlessness.
What is meant by "the wishless but not the empty"?
The answer is:

when the previously attained wishless samādhi manifests before one, or when the previously unattained wishless samādhi manifests before one, and at that time one does not cultivate the empty samādhi—this is called "the wishless but not the empty."
What is the emptiness-concentration of wishlessness?
The answer is:
when the emptiness-samādhi, which was previously unattained, manifests before one, at that time one cultivates the wishlessness-samādhi.
If one has not previously attained the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) and it now manifests before one, one cultivates the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) at that time;

if one has not previously attained the signless (*animitta*), or if one has not previously attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and it now manifests before one, one cultivates both the emptiness and wishless samādhis at that time—this is called "emptiness and wishlessness."
What is it that is neither the emptiness nor the wishlessness [samādhi]?
The answer is:

when either the signless samādhi previously attained or not previously attained manifests before one; or when either conventional knowledge previously attained or not previously attained manifests before one—at such times, one is not cultivating the samādhis of emptiness and wishlessness.

When all ordinary persons enter the concentration of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*), the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*), or the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) with a defiled or neutral mind, they do not cultivate the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) nor the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*); this is called "neither emptiness nor wishlessness."
If one cultivates the emptiness samādhi, does one cultivate the signless [samādhi] as well?
Answer: It may be that one cultivates emptiness but not the signless.
What is meant by "emptiness is not signlessness"?
The answer is:

when the previously attained emptiness-samādhi manifests before one, or when the previously unattained emptiness-samādhi manifests before one, one cannot at that time cultivate the signlessness-samādhi.

If one who has not previously attained the wishless samādhi brings it into manifestation, and at that time cultivates the emptiness samādhi rather than the signless, this is called "emptiness but not signless."
What is meant by "signless but not empty"?
The answer is:

when the signless samādhi previously attained manifests before one, or when the signless samādhi not previously attained manifests before one, and at that time one cannot cultivate the emptiness samādhi—this is called "signless but not empty."
What is the emptiness of signlessness?
The answer is:
when the emptiness samādhi has not yet been attained and is brought before one, at that time one cultivates the signlessness samādhi.
If one has not previously attained the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*) and it now manifests before one, at that time one cultivates the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*);

if one has not previously attained the wishless [samādhi] (*apraṇihita*), or if one has not previously attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and it now manifests before one, at that time one cultivates both the emptiness and signless samādhis—this is called the cultivation of emptiness and the signless.
What is meant by neither cultivating emptiness nor cultivating signlessness?
The answer is:

when either the wishlessness samādhi previously attained or not previously attained manifests before one; or when either mundane wisdom previously attained or not previously attained manifests before one—at such times, one cannot cultivate the samādhis of emptiness and signlessness.

When all ordinary persons enter the signless samādhi, the cessation samādhi, or the realm of non-perception with a defiled or neutral mind, they are neither cultivating the emptiness samādhi nor the signless [samādhi]; this is called "neither empty nor signless."
If one cultivates the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*), does one cultivate the signless (*animitta*)?
The answer is:
there are cases where one cultivates wishlessness but not the signless.
What is meant by "the wishless is not the signless"?
The answer is:

when the wishless samādhi previously attained manifests before one, or when the wishless samādhi not previously attained manifests before one, one is unable at that time to cultivate the signless samādhi.

If one has not previously attained the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi) and it now manifests before one, and at that time one cultivates the wishlessness samādhi (apranihita-samādhi) but not the signlessness samādhi (animitta-samādhi), this is called "wishlessness but not signlessness."
What is the case of being signless (animitta) but not wishless (apranihita)?
The answer is:

when the signless samādhi previously attained manifests before one, or when the signless samādhi not previously attained manifests before one, and at that time one does not cultivate the wishless samādhi—this is called being signless but not wishless.
What is the wishless and signless?
The answer is:
when the wishless samādhi, which was previously unattained, manifests before one, at that time one cultivates the signless samādhi.
If one has not previously attained the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*) such that it manifests before one, then at this time one cultivates the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*);

if one has not previously attained emptiness (*śūnyatā*), or if one has not previously attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) such that it manifests before one, then at this time one cultivates both the wishless and the signless samādhis—this is called the cultivation of the wishless and the signless.
What is meant by "not cultivating the wishless and the signless"? Answer:

When the emptiness samādhi previously attained manifests before one; or when mundane knowledge previously attained—or mundane knowledge not previously attained—manifests before one, at that time one cannot cultivate the wishless and signless samādhis.

When all ordinary persons enter the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*), the cessation samādhi (*nirodha-samādhi*), or the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-deva*) with a defiled or neutral mind, they are neither cultivating the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) nor the signless; this is called "neither wishless nor signless."
Is there any fetter that is extinguished through emptiness, yet not through wishlessness or signlessness?
Answer: It is not extinguished.
Is cessation without aspiration neither emptiness nor signlessness?
The answer is:
it is cessation.

Are all fetters and habitual tendencies abandoned through the Truth of Cessation, abandoned through the Truth of the Path, abandoned through the Wishless, and abandoned through the Signless, yet not abandoned through the Empty or the Wishless?
Answer: They are abandoned through Cessation.

Are all fetters severed by the Truth of Cessation, severed through signlessness (*animitta*), and extinguished through emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), yet not through signlessness?
Answer: They are extinguished.
Are the various fetters abandoned through the truth of suffering, through emptiness, through wishlessness, through cessation, through emptiness, or through signlessness, yet not through wishlessness?
Answer: They are not abandoned.
Is that which is wishless and signless not empty when it ceases?
The answer is:
it does not cease.
"Are emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness extinguished?
He replied: "They are extinguished."

Regarding the fetters that are extinguished through the path of training, the path of vision, and the path of cultivation: is there any fetter that is extinguished by neither emptiness, nor the wishless, nor the signless?
Answer: Yes, it is extinguished;
namely, those fetters extinguished by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
What is meant by "attaining realization by leaping over stages" through mental reflection?
The answer is:
impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
To what realm are the mental states associated with the practice of skipping stages and attaining realization?
The answer is:
those bound to the desire realm.
Should the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) be said to be the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna)?
The answer is:
the knowledge of exhaustion is either the application of mindfulness to the body, or it is the applications of mindfulness to sensation (vedanā), mind (citta), and phenomena (dharma).
The knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is also like this.
What is the distinction between the bliss of the various untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyānas and the various factors of enlightenment consisting of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
The answer is:
There is no difference.
What is the distinction between the various untainted pleasures of the second dhyāna and the various factors of enlightenment consisting of tranquility?
The answer is:
There is no difference.
When one arises from samādhi, does that arise from conditions?
The answer is: Yes.
Or, there is the arising of samādhi that is not through an object-condition (*ālambana*).
What is the arising of samādhi that is not through an object-condition?
The answer is:

It is as if there is one who, with various perceptions and mental applications, enters the first dhyāna; yet, that which is mentally applied as perception enters the second dhyāna. This is called arising from samādhi without its corresponding object.
What is dependent origination that is not meditative concentration?
The answer is:

for example, there is someone who, with various perceptions and mental applications, enters the first dhyāna; if, according to that concentration, he has other two types of perceptions and mental applications, this is called dependent origination that is not meditative concentration.
What is the condition for the emergence from samādhi?
The answer is:

Suppose there is one who enters the first dhyāna with various thoughts and mental objects; when that mind shifts its mental objects to other, second-order thoughts and enters the second dhyāna, this is called the condition for the emergence from samādhi.
What is meant by "neither arising from samādhi nor from an object"?
The answer is:

suppose there is someone who, with various thoughts and mental applications, enters the first dhyāna; if he dwells for a long time in that concentration, this is called neither arising from samādhi nor from an object.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"That which is called the samādhi of perception is the limit of what can be taught.
If a disciple of the Blessed One is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, by depending on what do they attain the fruit of arhatship?
Answer: It is the untainted (anāsrava) sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Furthermore, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:
"I recall, worthy friends!

While I was on Vulture Peak, by the side of the *Tikṣṇarasā* (Butter Essence) Pond, having entered the concentration of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*), there were many great elephants with their trunks raised, trumpeting; I heard the sound."
Did the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana hear the sound while remaining in meditative absorption, or did he hear it after arising from it?
He replied:
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana heard the sound after arising from absorption, not while remaining in it.
Regarding all those that are indeterminate, are they all truly instances of ignorance and expressions of ignorance?
Answer: It is so;
all those that are indeterminate are indeed truly instances of ignorance and expressions of ignorance.
Is it not the case that there are instances where ignorance is indeed ignorance, yet that statement is not indeterminate?
The answer is:
Yes, there are; namely, those of wrong determination (*mithyā-niyata*).
"Are all those meditative concentrations (samādhi) truly the words of clear knowledge (vidyā-vākya)?
He replied: "It is so."
All that is true knowledge (*vidyā*), true illumination (*abhijñā*), and true speech (*vāc*) is necessarily concentration (*samādhi*).
Is there any concentration that is not true knowledge, true illumination, and true speech?
Answer: Yes.
There is; namely, those of wrong determination (*mithyā-niyata*).
As for all those of indeterminate determination (*aniyata*), are they all non-possessors of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Yes.
In this way, all those who are indeterminate do not achieve the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Is there anyone who does not achieve the factors of enlightenment but is not indeterminate?
Answer: Yes.
There is the state of wrong determination (*mithyā-samyaktva-niyata*). Are all those states of determination necessarily endowed with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: No.

It is so. All those who have accomplished the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are necessarily concentrated (samāhita). Is there, however, any concentration that does not involve the accomplishment of the factors of enlightenment?
The answer is: Yes.
There is: namely, those of wrong determination.
If one accomplishes the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), does that person accomplish the outflow-free dharmas (anāsravadharma)?
Answer: Yes.
Thus, those who have accomplished the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) have accomplished the untainted dharmas (anāsravadharma).
Is it possible to accomplish the untainted dharmas without having accomplished the factors of enlightenment?
The answer is: Yes.
There is: namely, the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
If one does not accomplish the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), does that person not accomplish the untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*)?
Answer: Yes.
There is no one who does not accomplish the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), yet there are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who do not accomplish the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
If one attains the factors of enlightenment, does one thereby attain the untainted dharmas?
Answer: It is so;
if one attains the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), one attains the untainted dharmas (anāsravadharma).
Is it possible to attain untainted dharmas that are not factors of enlightenment?
The answer is:
There are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
If one abandons the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), does one thereby abandon the untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*)?
Answer: There is no discarding of untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*), nor is there any complete abandonment of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
If one regresses from the factors of enlightenment, does one regress from the untainted dharmas?
Answer: There is no falling back from the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), nor is there any exhaustion or falling back from the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
If they are not exhausted, does that mean one does not know them?
The answer is:
It is so; those who do not know [it] do not exhaust it.
Is it possible that one does not exhaust it, yet is not ignorant of it?
Answer: Yes, there are knowledges that are "known" but not "knowledge of exhaustion.
Are all those exhaustions known by that knowledge?
Answer: It is so;
one knows all that is exhausted.
Is there anything known that is not exhausted?
Answer: There is.

Regarding all those who know what is already known through the knowledge of non-interruption (*anantarya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), there are those for whom the eye had previously not seen forms in this life, yet later they manifest the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Based upon what do they manifest the divine eye?
The answer is:
It is just as there is one whose nature naturally knows past lives; having previously seen forms with the eye in another birth, he distinguishes the divine eye based upon that.
It is the same for sounds with the ear.

For what reason do ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), when they fall away, regain the fetters abandoned through the vision of the truths (satyadarśana-prahātavya) as well as those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya), whereas the disciples of the World-Honored One (śrāvaka) do not regain those abandoned through cultivation?
Answer:

When an ordinary person uses a particular path to extinguish the fetters abandoned through the vision of the truths, if they fall away from that path, they regain those fetters which were abandoned through cultivation by means of that same path.
Among the disciples of the Blessed One, those who have used a certain path to extinguish the fetters abandoned through seeing the truths (dṛṣṭiheya) do not fall away from that path;
however, regarding the path they have used to extinguish the fetters abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanāheya), they may either fall away or not fall away from it.

The path by which that Blessed One’s disciples abandon the fetters through the vision of the truths and through cultivation—that path abandons the fetters through cultivation, and from that path they do not fall back.
For what reason does one fall back from the fruit of arhatship, but not from the fruit of stream-entry?

Answer: The dharmas abandoned through the vision of the truths (darśana-heya) are without substitution; those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) involve substitution. Therein, there is the perception of purity and the perception of impurity. That perception of purity does not accord with what is intended by the mind, nor does it accord with the non-perception of purity when one falls away. Among them, there is not a single dharma that is "I" or "mine. All those who grasp at "I" or "mine" fall away from right view.
For what reason do the fruits of Anāgāmin and Sakṛdāgāmin undergo retrogression, whereas the fruit of Srotāpanna does not?
The answer is:
the dharmas abandoned through the vision of the truths (darśana-heya) are not subject to retrogression, while those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) are subject to retrogression.

He possesses both the perception of purity and the perception of impurity; he does not conform to his own mental inclinations, nor does he conform to the perception of impurity, and thus he falls away. He does not hold that there is even a single dharma which is "mine" or "I," yet he falls away from the view of self and non-self regarding all those things he grasps.

Regarding the various acquisitions of the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) that are lost upon falling away from the fruit of Arhatship: should it be said that these are acquired as previously acquired, or should it be said that they are acquired as not previously acquired?
Answer: It should be said that they are acquired as previously acquired.

Regarding the fruits of *anāgāmin* and *sakṛdāgāmin*, and the various attainments of the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) that are lost upon falling away from these fruits: should it be said that they are attained as previously acquired, or should it be said that they are attained as not previously acquired?
Answer: It should be said that they are obtained by means of what was previously obtained.

When one passes away from the formless realm and is born into the desire realm, regarding the acquisitions (prāpti) of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), great elements (mahābhūta), wholesome roots, unwholesome roots, neutral roots, fetters (saṃyojana), bonds (bandhana), latent tendencies (anuśaya), outflows (mala), and entanglements (paryavasthāna)—should it be said that these are obtained by means of what was previously obtained, or should it be said that they are obtained by means of what was not previously obtained?

Answer: Regarding the wholesome or the defiled, one should say they are "attained by what was previously attained. Regarding the retribution-born, one should say they are "attained by what was not previously attained.

When one dies in the formless realm and is born in the form realm, regarding the various attainments of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), great elements (*mahābhūta*), wholesome roots, neutral roots, fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), stains (*mala*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), should one say they are "attained by what was previously attained," or should one say they are "attained by what was not previously attained"?

Answer: Regarding the wholesome, if it is defiled, one should say it is "attained by what was previously attained"; regarding retribution, one should say it is "attained by what was not previously attained.

When one dies in the form realm and is born in the desire realm, among all those attainments—namely, the bases, the elements, the aggregates, the four great elements, the roots of goodness, the roots of unwholesomeness, the indeterminate roots, and the fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, stains, and entanglements—one should say they are "attained by what was previously attained," or should one say they are "attained by what was not previously attained"?

Answer: Regarding the wholesome, if it is defiled, one should say it is "attained by what was previously attained"; regarding the retribution, one should say it is "attained by what was not previously attained.

If one relies on the first dhyāna to cultivate the supernormal power of the realization of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñānasākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*) through the path of cultivation, how far can that reach?
Answer: It is Brahmā.
If one relies on the first dhyāna to cultivate the supernormal power of the knowledge of clairaudience (*dibbasota-ñāṇa-abhiññā*), to what extent can that [power] enable the ears to hear sounds?
Answer: It is bound to the Brahma-heaven.
If one cultivates the path through the supernormal power of knowing others' minds based on the first dhyāna, to what level of bondage is that knowledge of others' mental states limited?
Answer: It is bound to the Brahma-heaven.

If one, relying on the first dhyāna, cultivates the path through the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*), to what extent can they recollect their own past lives? To what are they bound?
Answer: It is bound to the Brahma-heaven.
If one relies on the first dhyāna to attain the supernormal power of clear vision through the cultivation of the path, to what realm would that eye, which is thus capable of seeing forms, be bound?
Answer: It is bound to the Brahma-heaven, the second [heaven] of Ābhāsvara, the third of Śubhakṛtsna, and the fourth of Bṛhatphala.

If one attains the fruit of Arhatship through the contemplation of suffering-as-suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā), to what is that mind which contemplates suffering-as-suffering bound when one attains the fruit of Arhatship?
Answer: It is bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
The same applies to its cultivation (vāsanā).

If one attains the fruit of arhatship through the total exhaustion of whatever is intended by the mind, to what realm is that intended mental activity bound which leads to the attainment of the fruit of arhatship?
The answer is:
it may be bound to the desire realm, or to the form realm, or to the formless realm.

If one contemplates the path with the mind and thereby attains the fruit of arhatship, to which realm are those formations bound that constitute the path contemplated by the mind for the attainment of arhatship?
The answer is:
they are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form or formless realms.
The fifth chapter, the *Ekottaravarga*, of the *Abhidharma* concludes.
The seventh section, the *Samādhivarga*, concludes.
*Abhidharmāṣṭaskandhaśāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-Eight.
The Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-nine.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kapiśa during the Fu Qin dynasty.

Translated together with Zhu Fonian. Section 8: The Chapter on Seeing (Dṛṣṭi-khaṇḍa). The eighth chapter on seeing consists of: the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), desire, perception, knowledge of conditions, and views; the verse section follows later.

1. Chapter on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Smṛtyupasthāna-varga). Chapter One on the Foundations of Mindfulness. There are four foundations of mindfulness: the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body as body;

the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings as feelings; the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the mind as mind; and the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of phenomena as phenomena.
If one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as the body, does one also cultivate [the foundation of mindfulness of] feelings?
If one cultivates [the foundation of mindfulness of] feelings, does one also cultivate the body?
If one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as the body, does one also cultivate the mind?
If one cultivates the mind, does one cultivate the body?
If one cultivates the application of mindfulness to the body as the body, does one cultivate the dharma?
If one cultivates the dharma, does one cultivate the body?
If one cultivates the application of mindfulness by contemplating feelings as feelings, does one cultivate the mind?
If one cultivates the mind, does one cultivate feelings?
If one cultivates the application of mindfulness by contemplating feelings as feelings, does one cultivate phenomena?
If one cultivates the cultivation of phenomena (dharma), does one cultivate suffering (vedanā)?
If one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating mind (citta-cittānupassanā-sati-paṭṭhāna), does one cultivate phenomena?
If one cultivates phenomena, does one cultivate the mind?

Regarding the application of mindfulness that contemplates the body as body, should it be described as knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), or the knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
Should it be said that it possesses vitarka and vicāra? Or should it be said that it is without vitarka but with vicāra? Or should it be said that it is without both vitarka and vicāra?

Should it be said that it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), or the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya)? Or should it be said that it is associated with emptiness (śūnyatā), wishlessness (apranihita), or signlessness (animitta)?
Should it be said that they have objects associated with the desire realm, objects associated with the form and formless realms, or objects that are unassociated?
The same applies to the foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"When one experiences a pleasant feeling, one knows, 'I experience a pleasant feeling.
Should this knowledge be called dharma-knowledge?"
Should it be said that this extends even to the knowledge of the path?

When experiencing a painful feeling, one knows "I am experiencing a painful feeling"; when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one knows "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Should this knowledge be called the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), or should it be said to extend even to the knowledge of the path?

Regarding the pleasant body, the painful body, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant body; the pleasant mind, the painful mind, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant mind; the pleasant nutriment, the painful nutriment, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant nutriment; and the pleasant non-nutriment, the painful non-nutriment, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant non-nutriment—one relies on the dullness of pleasure, the dullness of pain, and the dullness of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant; one relies on the renunciation of pleasure, the renunciation of pain, and the renunciation of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant. When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation, one knows that it is the renunciation of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Should this knowledge of sensation be called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharma-jñāna*), or should it be called even up to "knowledge of the path" (*mārga-jñāna*)?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"When one has a mind with desire, one knows as it truly is that one has a mind with desire.
Should this knowledge be called dharma-knowledge, or should it be called, up to and including, path-knowledge?

He knows, as it truly is, when there is no desire but there is ill will; when there is no ill will but there is delusion; when there is no delusion but there is defilement; when there is no defilement but there is distraction; when there is no distraction but there is indolence; when there is no indolence, whether it be slight or great; whether there is cultivation or lack of cultivation; whether there is concentration or lack of concentration; he knows, as it truly is, when the mind is liberated and when the mind is not liberated; and he knows, as it truly is, when the unliberated mind becomes liberated.
Should this knowledge be called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*), or should it be called even up to "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*)?
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:

"When the eye is conditioned by forms, internal fetters arise. That bhikṣu truly knows that those internal fetters exist; he knows as it really is that when those internal fetters do not exist, they are absent. Likewise, he knows as it really is when unarisen internal fetters arise, when arisen ones are extinguished, and when extinguished ones do not arise again."
Should this knowledge be called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*), or should it be called up to "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*)?
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

When the mind takes phenomena as its object and internal sensual desire arises, that bhikṣu, regarding that internal sensual desire as it truly is, knows as it really is: "I have this internal sensual desire. Regarding internal sensual desire that is not present, he knows as it really is: "I do not have this internal sensual desire. Likewise, he knows as it really is when unarisen internal sensual desire arises, when arisen internal sensual desire is extinguished, and when extinguished internal sensual desire does not arise again.
Should this knowledge be called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*), or should it be called up to "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*)?

It is the same for ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, and doubt. When the internal awakening factor of mindfulness arises, that bhikṣu truly possesses that internal awakening factor of mindfulness; he knows as it really is that he has this internal awakening factor of mindfulness. When he does not truly possess the internal awakening factor of mindfulness, he knows as it really is that he lacks this internal awakening factor of mindfulness. Likewise, he knows as it really is when the unarisen internal awakening factor of mindfulness arises, when the arisen one remains, and when it is not forgotten, does not decline, but is further expanded, cultivated, and brought to fulfillment through thorough reflection. He knows all this as it really is.
Should this wisdom be called "dharma-knowledge," or should it be called "path-knowledge," and so forth?
The same applies to the awakening-factors of dharma, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"He observes for himself that lust, hatred, and delusion are prevalent within him.
In what way are lust, hatred, and delusion prevalent?"
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"He observes for himself that lust, hatred, and delusion have become thin.
In what way have lust, hatred, and delusion become thin?"
What is the pain at the time of death?
To what extent does the pain at the time of death extend?
By which sense-base (*āyatana*) is the pain at the time of death subsumed, and by how many consciousnesses is it cognized?
Should it be said that an Arhat attains parinirvāṇa with a wholesome mind, or should it be said that he attains parinirvāṇa with an indeterminate mind?
For what reason did the Buddha, the World-Honored One, first attain parinirvāṇa after his two chief disciples, and only thereafter the Buddha, the World-Honored One himself?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"The Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa by entering the immovable samādhi.
Does the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa while remaining in meditative absorption, or does he enter parinirvāṇa after arising from it?
There are four types of existence:
existence at the time of the basis, existence at death, intermediate existence, and existence at birth.
What is existence at the time of the basis?
What is death-existence?
What is intermediate existence?
What is birth-existence?
Is everything that exists within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) comprised of the five aggregates?
Conversely, is everything that consists of the five aggregates comprised of the realm of desire?
Furthermore, regarding the gods of the realm of form who possess perception (rūpadhātu-saṃjñin), is everything among them comprised of the five aggregates?
If there are those with the five aggregates, are they all gods of the form realm who possess perception?
Are all gods of the form realm who lack perception necessarily those with the two aggregates?
If there are those with the two aggregates, are they all gods of the form realm who lack perception?
Are all those who exist in the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu) possessed of the four modes of conduct?
Conversely, are all those who possess the four modes of conduct necessarily in the formless realms?
Furthermore, can there be five modes of conduct, four, three, two, or even one mode of conduct?
I wish to expound fully the meaning of this chapter.
There are four foundations of mindfulness:

the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body as body; the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings; the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the mind; and the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of phenomena as phenomena.
If one cultivates the application of mindfulness by contemplating the body as the body, does that person also cultivate [the application of mindfulness of] sensation?
Answer: There are cases where there is the body but not sensation.
What is meant by "the body, but not sensation"?
The answer is:
when the established mindfulness of the body as the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) manifests before one, this is called "the body, but not sensation."
What is meant by "feeling is not the body"?
The answer is:

when the application of mindfulness to feelings as feelings that was previously acquired manifests in the present; or, when the application of mindfulness to feelings as feelings that was not previously acquired manifests in the present, one does not at that time cultivate the application of mindfulness to the body as the body manifesting in the present.

If one has not originally attained the mind or not originally attained the dharmas, and at this time attains the application of mindfulness by contemplating feelings as feelings rather than as the body, this is called "feeling is not the body."
What is bodily pain?
The answer is:

when one who previously had not attained the body attains it at this time, or when one who previously had not attained pain attains it at this time, or when one who previously had not attained the mind or dharmas attains them at this time, one cultivates the application of mindfulness by contemplating pain within the body; this is called bodily pain.
What is neither body nor sensation?
The answer is:
the mind originally acquired and the dharmas originally acquired.

If, when the mindfulness of mental objects regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been attained, it manifests before one; or if at that time the mindfulness of bodily feelings regarding feelings (*kāyavedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*) has not been attained;

or during all defiled or neutral states of mind, or when entering the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or being born in the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*); in these cases, one is neither practicing the mindfulness of the body regarding the body nor the mindfulness of feelings—this is called "neither body nor feeling."
If one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as the body, does that person also cultivate the mind?
Answer: There are cases where one cultivates the body but not the mind.
What is meant by "the body, not the mind"?
The answer is:
when the established mindfulness of the body regarding the body (*kāye kāyānupaśyanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) manifests before one, this is called "the body, not the mind."
What is meant by "the mind but not the body"?
The answer is:

when the present manifestation of the mindfulness of mental objects regarding the mind (*cittānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*)—whether previously attained or not previously attained—is present, one does not at that time cultivate the mindfulness of bodily objects regarding the body (*kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*).

If one has not originally attained sensation and has not originally attained mental phenomena (*dharma*), yet at this time attains the cultivation of the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) rather than to the body, this is called "mind but not body.
What is meant by "body and mind"?
The answer is:
If one has not previously attained the body, one attains the mind at this time;
if one has not previously attained the mind, one attains the body at this time.

If one has not originally attained sensation and has not originally attained mental phenomena, yet at this time attains the cultivation of the mindfulness of the body and mind—the application of mindfulness to the mind—this is called "body and mind.
What is "neither body nor mind"?
The answer is:

When one has already attained the contemplation of sensation (*vedanā*) and the contemplation of phenomena (*dharma*), and the present manifestation of the mindfulness of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) regarding phenomena that were previously unattained occurs, one cannot at that time cultivate the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) or the mindfulness of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, when all defiled minds (*kliṣṭacitta*) or neutral minds (*avyākṛtacitta*) enter the *asaṃjñi-samādhi*, the *nirodha-samādhi*, or the state of the *asaṃjñi-devas*, one is not cultivating the mindfulness of the body nor the mindfulness of the mind; this is called "neither body nor mind."
If one cultivates the application of mindfulness by observing the body as the body, does that person also cultivate the dharma?
The answer is:
sometimes it is the body, but not the dharma.
What is the body that is not the Dharma?
The answer is:
when the mindfulness of the body regarding the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) that was originally attained manifests before one, this is called the body that is not the Dharma.
What is the case where the dharma is not the body?
The answer is:

when the established mindfulness of mental objects regarding dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) has already been attained and is present before one; or when the previously unattained mindfulness of mental objects regarding dharmas is present before one, yet at that time, one does not cultivate the established mindfulness of the body regarding the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

If one has not previously attained [the perception of] pain and has not previously attained [the perception of] mind, and at this time attains the application of mindfulness by contemplating phenomena within phenomena rather than the body, this is called "phenomena, not the body.
What are bodily phenomena?
The answer is:
If one has not originally obtained the body, one obtains this dharma at this time;
if one has not originally obtained the dharma, one obtains this body at this time.

If one has fundamentally not attained [the perception of] pain and fundamentally not attained [the perception of] mind, yet at this time attains the application of mindfulness by contemplating the phenomena within the body, this is called "body-phenomena.
What is neither body nor phenomenon?
Answer:

When one who has previously attained the mindfulness of sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) or the mindfulness of mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*) brings them to presence, one does not at that time cultivate the mindfulness of body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*) or the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, when all defiled minds or neutral minds (*avyākṛta-citta*), or when entering the *asaṃjñi-samādhi*, the *nirodha-samādhi*, or being born in the Heaven of No Perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), one does not cultivate the mindfulness of body nor the mindfulness of phenomena. This is called "neither body nor phenomenon."
If one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating feelings as feelings, does that person cultivate the mind?
Answer: There are cases where one cultivates feelings but not the mind.
What is the case where there is feeling but no mind?
The answer is:
when the mindfulness of the body (kāyānupaśyanā-smṛtyupasthāna) that was previously attained manifests in the present, this is called "feeling but no mind."
What is meant by "mind but not sensation"?
The answer is:
when the application of mindfulness to the mind (cittānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna), which was previously attained, is present before one; this is called "mind but not sensation."
What is the painful mind?
The answer is:
when one has not previously attained the painful [feeling], one attains it at this time; this is the mind.
If one has not previously attained the mind, one attains it at this time;

if one has not previously attained the body or the dharmas, one attains them at this time and cultivates the application of mindfulness to the mind by means of the painful feeling. This is called the application of mindfulness to the mind through painful feeling.
What is neither feeling nor mind?
The answer is:
that which was originally obtained as body and that which was originally obtained as phenomena (dharma).

If one has not previously attained the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and it now manifests before one, one cannot at that time cultivate the applications of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā*) or to the mind (*citta*).

Furthermore, when the mind is entirely defiled or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), or when one enters the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or is born in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), one is neither cultivating the application of mindfulness to feelings nor to the mind; this is called "neither feeling nor mind."
If one cultivates the application of mindfulness by contemplating feelings as feelings, does that person also cultivate dharmas?
Answer: It may be feelings, but not dharmas.
What is the application of mindfulness to feelings that is not the Dharma? Answer:
When the application of mindfulness to feelings already previously attained manifests in the present, this is called the application of mindfulness to feelings that is not the Dharma.
What is the dharma that is not feeling?
The answer is:
when the present manifestation of the mindfulness of mental objects regarding dharmas (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna), which was previously attained, occurs before one.

If, when the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dhammānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna) has not yet been attained, it manifests in the present moment, one cannot at that time cultivate the application of mindfulness to feelings (vedanānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna); this is called "phenomena, but not feelings."
What is the phenomenon of sensation?
The answer is:
that which was originally not obtained as sensation is at that time obtained as a phenomenon.
Originally not having attained the Dharma, one now attains the perception of suffering;

originally not having attained the body and originally not having attained the mind, one now cultivates the application of mindfulness to the phenomena of suffering. This is called the phenomenon of suffering.
What is neither the contemplation of feeling nor the contemplation of phenomena?
The answer is:

when one who has previously attained the contemplation of the body and previously attained the contemplation of the mind brings the present mindfulness of the mind to manifestation, at that time one does not cultivate the contemplations of feeling or phenomena.

When all defiled minds, indeterminate minds, or when entering the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or being born in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), one does not cultivate the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*). This is called "neither feeling nor dharma."
If one cultivates the application of mindfulness by contemplating the mind, does that person cultivate the factors of dharma?
The answer is:
sometimes it is the mind, but not the dharmas.
What is the mind that is not the dharma?
The answer is:
when the present manifestation of the original attainment of the mindfulness of mental objects (cittānupaśyanā-smṛtyupasthāna) occurs, this is called the mind that is not the dharma.
What is the dharma that is not the mind?
The answer is:
when the present manifestation of the established mindfulness of mental objects regarding dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that one has previously attained occurs;

If, when the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) that was not previously attained manifests before one, one cannot at that time cultivate the application of mindfulness to the mind (citta-smṛtyupasthāna), this is called "phenomena, but not mind."
What are mental phenomena?
The answer is:
when one has not yet attained the mind, at that time one attains the phenomena.
If one has not previously attained the Dharma, at that time one attains the mind;

if one has not previously attained the body or the sensations, one attains at this time the application of mindfulness by contemplating the mind and mental phenomena (*cittadhammānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*). This is called "mind and phenomena" (*cittadhamma*).
What is neither mind nor dharma?
The answer is:

when one who has previously attained the body-contemplation or the feeling-contemplation brings that present mindfulness of objects (ānāpānasati) to the fore, at that time one does not cultivate the mindfulness of objects consisting of the contemplation of mind or dharmas.

When all defiled minds, indeterminate minds, or when entering the meditative absorption of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), one does not cultivate the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) nor to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). This is called "neither mind nor phenomena."
Regarding the application of mindfulness to the body as body (*kāye kāyānupaśyanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), should it be called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*)? Answer:

The application of mindfulness to the body as body may be knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*), or knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). It may be accompanied by both initial and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), or without initial thought but with sustained thought (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), or without both initial and sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*). It may be associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). It may be associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or wishlessness (*apranihita*). Its object may be bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Regarding the application of mindfulness through the contemplation of feelings (*vedanā-anupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*), should it be called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dhamma-ñāṇa*)? Answer:

The application of mindfulness through the contemplation of feelings may be knowledge of phenomena, knowledge of the unknown (*anājñāta-ājñāsyāmī-ñāṇa*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-ñāṇa*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-ñāṇa*), knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin, or knowledge of the path. It may be accompanied by initial and sustained application of thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), or without initial application but with sustained application (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), or without both initial and sustained application (*avitarka-avicāra*). It may be associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). It may be associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or wishlessness (*apranihita*). Its objects may be bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), bound to the form or formless realms (*rūpa-arūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
The application of mindfulness as the observation of mind upon mind is also like this.
Regarding the application of mindfulness as the observation of phenomena upon phenomena, should it be called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*)?
The answer is: No.

In the application of mindfulness by contemplating phenomena as phenomena (*dhammānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*), there may be the knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñāta-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-ñāṇa*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-ñāṇa*), or the knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. It may be accompanied by both initial and sustained mental application (*savitakka-savicāra*), or without initial but with sustained application (*avitakka-vicāramatta*), or without both initial and sustained application (*avitakka-avicāra*). It may be associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*), the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*); or it may be associated with emptiness (*suññata*), the wishless (*appaṇihita*), or the signless (*animitta*). Its objects may be bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), bound to the form or formless realms (*rūpa-arūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"When one experiences a pleasant feeling, one knows, 'I experience a pleasant feeling.
There are four knowledges:"
Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and path-knowledge (mārga-jñāna).
When experiencing a painful feeling, one knows "I am experiencing a painful feeling"—this is one type of conventional knowledge.
When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one knows "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"—these are four types of knowledge:
Dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), and path-knowledge (mārgajñāna).
Regarding the body of pleasure, the body of suffering, and the body of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure: the mind of suffering is one type of conventional knowledge;
the mind of pleasure and the mind of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure are four types of knowledge: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge.
The taste of suffering, the taste of pleasure, and the taste of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure that is without nutriment (anāhāra) are each one single knowledge (ñāṇa).
The absence of nutriment in pleasure and the absence of nutriment in neither-suffering-nor-pleasure are four knowledges:
dharma-knowledge (dhamma-ñāṇa), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-ñāṇa), conventional knowledge (sammuti-ñāṇa), and path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa).
There is attachment based on pleasure, attachment based on pain, and attachment based on neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Regarding the renunciation of pain, there is one type of clear knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
Regarding the renunciation of pleasure and the renunciation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, there are four types of clear knowledge:
Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"One knows as it truly is a mind with desire as a mind with desire"—this is one instance of conventional knowledge.
In the absence of desire, there are four knowledges:
knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
In the presence of ill-will, there is one: conventional knowledge.
In the absence of ill-will, there are three knowledges:
knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
In the presence of delusion, there is one: conventional knowledge.
In the absence of delusion, there are four knowledges:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge.
When accompanied by defilement, there is one: conventional knowledge.
It is undefiled and consists of four knowledges:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the knowledge of the unknown (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
It is undisturbed.
There are four knowledges:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the knowledge of the unknown (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
There is confusion regarding one, namely conventional knowledge.
When there is indolence, there is one type of knowledge: conventional knowledge (*sammuti-ñāṇa*).
When there is no indolence, there are four knowledges:
knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-ñāṇa*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-ñāṇa*), conventional knowledge, and knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*).
Fewer: one type of knowledge, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
More: four types of knowledge:
dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*).
It is not cultivated by one kind of knowledge: conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
It is cultivated by four kinds of knowledge:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge.
Indeterminate: one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Determinate: four types of knowledge:
dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), and path-knowledge (mārgajñāna).
Liberation is one: conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*).
Liberations are four knowledges:
dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:

"Visual consciousness arises conditioned by forms, giving rise to internal fetters. When a bhikṣu truly possesses these internal fetters, he knows as it really is that he has these internal fetters; this is the first kind of knowledge."
When there are no internal fetters that are unreal, one knows them as they truly are; this involves four knowledges:
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
When internal fetters that have not yet arisen do arise, one knows them as they truly are; this involves only conventional knowledge.
That birth has already ceased and what has ceased does not arise—this too he knows as it truly is, through four knowledges:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the knowledge of the unknown (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
The same applies to sounds for the ear, tangibles for the body, and mental objects for the mind.

When the nose conditions odors to give rise to internal fetters, that bhikṣu, having those internal fetters, knows them as they truly are: "I have these internal fetters"—this is the first kind of knowledge.
When there are no internal fetters that are unreal, one knows them as they truly are; this involves three knowledges:
dharma-knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge.
When internal fetters that have not yet arisen do arise, one knows this as it truly is; this is one [type of] conventional knowledge.
That which arises and then ceases, having ceased does not arise—this too is known as it truly is through three knowledges:
dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), and path-knowledge (mārgajñāna).
It is the same for the tongue and tastes, sensual desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-worry, and doubt; they likewise arise [and cease].

Regarding the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness internally: that bhikṣu truly possesses the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness internally; he knows as it really is that he possesses this factor of enlightenment of mindfulness internally. There are four knowledges:
knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

When there is no internal factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, he knows as it truly is that there is no internal factor of enlightenment of mindfulness; this is one kind of clear knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

Likewise, when the internal factor of enlightenment of mindfulness has not yet arisen, he knows as it truly is how it arises; when it has arisen, he knows as it truly is how it remains, is not forgotten, does not decline, is cultivated through reflection, and is brought to increase, expansion, and fulfillment. This too is one kind of clear knowledge.
The four knowledges are:
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
The same applies to the factors of enlightenment consisting of: the factor of dharma, diligence, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"He observes for himself that lust, hatred, and delusion are prevalent within him.
In what way are lust, hatred, and delusion prevalent?"
The answer is:
When desire, hatred, and delusion are slight, they become moderate; when moderate, they then increase further; in this way, desire, hatred, and delusion flourish.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
He observes for himself that lust, hatred, and delusion are thin.
How are lust, hatred, and delusion thin?
The answer is:
When lust, hatred, and delusion increase, they then become middling and finally slight; in this way, lust, hatred, and delusion become thin.
What is the pain at the time of death?
The answer is:
Question: When all the joints ache, and when the life-force is exhausted, at which point does death occur, and where is the pain felt?
Answer: [As follows:]
The joints ache;
at the time of death when life is exhausted, the pain is subsumed under one entrance, the entrance of the smooth and slippery (spraṣṭavya). It is cognized by two consciousnesses:
[the body-consciousness and the mental consciousness].
Regarding body-consciousness and mind-consciousness, when the limbs ache, does body-consciousness arise first and mind-consciousness afterwards?
Should it be said that an Arhat enters parinirvāṇa with a wholesome mind or with an indeterminate mind?
Answer: An Arhat enters parinirvāṇa with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*).
For what reason did the Buddha, the World-Honored One, enter parinirvāṇa after his two foremost disciples, rather than before them?
The answer is:
That venerable one has performed uninterrupted practice throughout the long night and thus receives its retribution; let it not be empty, fruitless, or without retribution.
Furthermore, it is the constant law of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, that his two foremost disciples enter parinirvāṇa first, and only thereafter does the Buddha, the World-Honored One, do so.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"The Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa by entering the immovable samādhi.
Does the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa while remaining in meditative absorption, or does he enter parinirvāṇa after arising from it?
Answer: The Tathāgata’s arising of parinirvāṇa is not an entry into meditative concentration.
There are four modes of existence (bhava):

There are the existence at the time of the root (*mūlabhava*), the existence at the time of death (*maraṇabhava*), the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), and the existence at the time of birth (*upapattibhava*). What is the existence at the time of the root?
The answer is:
The five aggregates at the juncture of death and birth, encompassing all that exists within this interval, are called "existence at the time of the origin" (*pūrvakālabhava*).
What is "existence at the moment of death" (*maraṇabhava*)?
The answer is:
The five aggregates at the moment of death are called "existence at death" (maranabhava).
What is "intermediate existence" (antarābhava)?
The answer is:
Within this, there are the five aggregates; this is called "intermediate existence" (antarābhava).
What is "birth existence" (upapattibhava)?
The answer is:
The arising of the five aggregates is called "birth-existence" (jāti-bhava).
Are all those that are "existence-in-desire" (kāma-bhava) necessarily of the five modes of existence (pañca-gati)?
Answer: No.
Or, there may be that existence which is not of the five aggregates.
What is that existence which is not of the five aggregates?
The answer is:

Sentient beings of the desire realm who do not abide in their own minds yet enter the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—these various states of existence are called "desire-existence" (*kāma-bhava*), yet those existences are not of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
What is existence that consists of the five aggregates but is not desire-existence?
Answer:

It refers to the existence of the gods who possess perception in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) who abide in their own minds and do not enter the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);

as well as the existence of the non-perceiving gods (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) in the form realm who have not yet attained non-perception. These are called the five types of existence that belong to the form realm but are not the desire realm existence (*kāmadhātu-bhava*).
What is meant by "desire-existence" (kāmadhātu-bhava) having five modes of existence?
The answer is:

when sentient beings of the desire realm abide in their own minds and do not enter the attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) or the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), these various states of being are called desire-existence with its five modes of existence.
What is it that is not the realm of desire, yet that existence is not of the five modes?
The answer is:
the gods of the form realm who possess perception, whose minds do not abide [in the lower realms], and who have entered the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation.

Those existences that are the non-percipient beings of the form realm who have attained the state of non-perception, as well as those existences in the formless realm—these are called existences that are not sensual existences and yet are not fivefold existences.
Regarding all those in the form realm who possess perception, do they all possess the five aggregates?
Answer: Some in the form realm who possess perception do not possess the five aggregates.
What is meant by "there are beings in the form realm with perception whose existence does not consist of the five aggregates"?
The answer is:

those beings in the form realm who possess perception, yet whose minds do not abide in themselves as they enter the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) or the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti)—this is called "beings in the form realm with perception whose existence does not consist of the five aggregates."
What are those who possess the five aggregates yet are neither in the form realm nor among the gods of the perception-sphere? Answer:
Sentient beings of the desire realm who abide in their own minds, and who have not entered the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation; all such states of existence.

If one in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) among the non-percipient gods (*asaṃjñisattva*) does not attain the state of non-perception, this is called "having five aggregates but not being in the realm of form with perception.
What is meant by "being in the realm of form with perception and having five aggregates"?
The answer is:

Those gods of the realm of form who possess perception dwell in their own minds; they do not enter the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation. These are the gods of the realm of form with perception, and in them there are five types of existence.
What are those non-material realms with perception where those beings do not possess the five aggregates?
The answer is:

the various states of existence of sentient beings in the desire realm whose minds are not self-abiding as they enter the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation; the various states of existence of those who have attained non-perception in the non-perceiving heavens of the form realm; and the states of existence in the formless realm. These are called the non-material realms with perception where those beings do not possess the five aggregates.
Regarding all those in the form realm who belong to the Heaven of Non-perception, do they all possess both types of formations?
Answer: Some in the form realm who belong to the Heaven of Non-perception do not possess both types of formations.
What is meant by "there is form-existence (rūpabhava) in the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva), yet that existence is not of the two types of formations"?
The answer is:

when one in the Heaven of Non-perception within the Form Realm does not attain the state of non-perception, this is called "there is form-existence in the Heaven of Non-perception, yet that existence is not of the two types of formations."
What are those who possess the two types of practice but do not belong to the form realm or the heaven of non-perception?
The answer is:

sentient beings of the desire realm who, with a mind that does not abide [in itself], enter the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation; and those in various states of existence within the heaven of perception in the form realm who, with a mind that does not abide [in itself], enter the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation. These are called those who possess the two types of practice but do not belong to the form realm or the heaven of non-perception.
What is meant by "there are two modes of existence for those in the form realm who are in the Heaven of Non-perception"?
The answer is:

when one attains the state of non-perception within the heavens of the form realm, this is called "there being two modes of existence for those in the form realm who are in the Heaven of Non-perception."
What is meant by "there are beings who are non-material and without perception, yet they do not possess the two types of meditative attainments"?
The answer is:

sentient beings of the desire realm who abide in their own minds, but have not entered the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation; all such states of existence [fall under this category].

If one is a being in the realm of form who dwells in the perception of heaven with a mind of its own accord, yet does not enter the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation—this constitutes existence in the formless realm;
this is called non-material existence, wherein the beings of the heaven of non-perception do not possess those two types of formations.
Are all those who exist in the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu) exhausted by the four modes of activity (caturākāra)?
Answer: It is so;
all those who possess the four modes of activity are exhausted within the existence of the formless realms.
Is there anything in the formless realm that exists yet is not among the four modes of conduct?
Answer: There is;
namely, sentient beings in the formless realm whose minds do not abide in themselves.
Question: Are there any beings who possess the five aggregates? Answer: Yes;
there are those in the desire realm who abide in their own minds, yet have not entered the meditative attainment of non-conception or the meditative attainment of cessation. These are such beings.
The gods of the realm of form who possess perception abide in their own minds; they do not enter the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation, nor do they exist as such.
Furthermore, the gods of the realm of form who are non-percipient do not attain non-perception.
Is there any instance of the four modes of conduct?
The answer is:
Yes; for example, when sentient beings in the formless realm abide in their own minds.
Is there any instance of three courses of action?
Answer: There is no such instance of three courses of action.
Are there two types of existence?
Answer: Yes;
there are those who, as sentient beings of the desire realm, do not abide in their own minds when entering the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation.

The various states of existence (*bhava*) of the gods of the realm of form who possess perception, whose minds do not abide of their own accord, and who have entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);
and the various states of existence of the gods of the realm of form who lack perception and have attained the state of being without perception (*asaṃjñika*).
Is there perhaps a single category?
He replied: There is;
it consists of the various existences of sentient beings in the formless realm whose minds do not abide in themselves.

The thirty-ninth chapter, "The Foundations of Mindfulness" (Smṛtyupasthāna), of the Abhidharma is completed. It consists of three hundred and fifteen *ślokas* in the Sanskrit original, and four thousand six hundred and twenty-two words in the Qin translation.

2. In the second chapter on Desire within the *Dṛṣṭi-kāṇḍa* of the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda*, it is asked: If one abandons existence in the desire realm and takes up existence in the desire realm, are all those [beings] who exhaust the phenomena bound to the desire realm such that the phenomena bound to the desire realm manifest before them?

If all phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have been exhausted and phenomena bound to the desire realm are manifest before one, have they all abandoned existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhava*) and taken up existence in the desire realm?

Or, if they have abandoned existence in the desire realm and taken up existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu-bhava*), have they all exhausted phenomena bound to the desire realm and do phenomena bound to the form realm manifest before them?

If one has exhausted all phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and phenomena bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) manifest before them, have they all abandoned existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhava*) and taken up existence in the form realm?

Or, if they have abandoned existence in the desire realm and taken up existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-bhava*), have they all exhausted all phenomena bound to the desire realm and do phenomena bound to the formless realm manifest before them?

If all phenomena bound to the desire realm are exhausted and phenomena bound to the formless realm manifest before one, does that person abandon existence in the desire realm and take up existence in the formless realm?

If one abandons existence in the form realm and takes up existence in the form realm, does all that [existence] consist of the exhaustion of phenomena bound to the form realm, and do phenomena bound to the form realm manifest?

Conversely, if all phenomena bound to the form realm are exhausted and phenomena bound to the form realm manifest, does all that [existence] consist of abandoning existence in the form realm and taking up existence in the form realm?

If one abandons existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu-bhava*) and takes up existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhava*), are all those [beings] exhausting the factors bound to the form realm (*rūpāvacara-dharma*) and bringing forth the factors bound to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-dharma*)?

Conversely, if they exhaust the factors bound to the form realm and bring forth the factors bound to the desire realm, do they all abandon existence in the form realm and take up existence in the desire realm?

If one abandons existence in the form realm to undergo existence in the formless realm, are all those [beings] exhausting the phenomena bound to the form realm such that the phenomena bound to the formless realm manifest? Conversely, if they exhaust the phenomena bound to the form realm and the phenomena bound to the formless realm manifest, do they all abandon existence in the form realm to undergo existence in the formless realm?
If one abandons existence with feeling belonging to the formless realm, does all that which is bound to the formless realm cease, and do the factors bound to the formless realm manifest?

If all phenomena bound to the formless realm are exhausted, and phenomena bound to the formless realm manifest before one, are they all abandoned as existence in the formless realm and as the appropriation of existence in the formless realm?

If one abandons existence with formless-sphere feeling and takes up existence with desire-sphere feeling, does all that which is bound to the formless sphere cease, and do all phenomena bound to the desire sphere manifest?

If one has completely exhausted the phenomena associated with the formless realm and the phenomena associated with the desire realm manifest before them, does that person abandon existence in the formless realm and receive existence in the desire realm?

If one abandons existence with form in the formless realm and takes up existence with form in the form realm, does all that which is bound to the formless realm cease, and do phenomena bound to the form realm manifest?

If all factors bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are exhausted and factors bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) manifest before one, have they all abandoned existence in the formless realm and received existence in the form realm?
For what reason are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm not those by which one is bound in the form and formless realms?
For what reason are the latent tendencies of the form realm not those by which one is bound in the desire and formless realms?
For what reason are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm not those by which one is bound in the desire and form realms?
For what reason are the latent tendencies of the desire realm that are not universal (*sarvatraga*) not those by which one is bound in all instances within the desire realm?
For what reason are the pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) not all those by which the form realm is proclived?
