For what reason are the pervasive proclivities of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) not all those by which the formless realm is proclived?
The ten perceptions:

the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of impurity, the perception of the contemplation of food, the perception of the unattractiveness of all worlds, the perception of death, the perception of abandonment, the perception of the absence of lust, and the perception of exhaustion.
If one cultivates the perception of impermanence, is that which is intended by the mind the perception of impermanence?
Conversely, if that which is intended by the mind is the perception of impermanence, does one cultivate the perception of impermanence?
This applies likewise up to the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saṃjñā*).
When one perceives a thought of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*), is that which is attended to by the mind a thought of sensual desire?
And if that which is attended to by the mind is a thought of sensual desire, does one perceive that thought of sensual desire?
The same applies to thoughts of ill will and harmfulness.
When one is experiencing a thought of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-vitarka*), is that thought of renunciation what the mind is attending to?
And if the mind is attending to a thought of renunciation, is that thought of renunciation what is being experienced at that time?
The same applies to non-ill will and non-harming thoughts.
Regarding all phenomena that have ignorance as their cause: do those phenomena have ignorance as their condition?
Conversely, if phenomena have ignorance as their condition, do those phenomena have ignorance as their cause?
If all phenomena have ignorance as their cause, do those phenomena have clarity as their condition?
Conversely, if phenomena have clarity as their condition, do those phenomena have ignorance as their cause?
If all phenomena have ignorance as their cause, do those phenomena have clarity as their condition?
If a phenomenon has ignorance as its condition, does that phenomenon have ignorance as its cause?
If various phenomena have clarity as their cause, do those phenomena have ignorance as their condition?
If a phenomenon has ignorance as its condition, does that phenomenon have clarity as its cause?
If all phenomena have ignorance as their cause, are those phenomena unwholesome?
Conversely, if phenomena are unwholesome, do they have ignorance as their cause?
If all phenomena have clear knowledge as their cause, are those phenomena wholesome?
If a phenomenon is wholesome, is that phenomenon caused by clear knowledge (*vidyā*)?
Is there perhaps a phenomenon that is neither caused by clear knowledge nor caused by ignorance (*avidyā*), yet that phenomenon is not such that it has no cause?
I wish to explain fully the meaning of this chapter:

If one abandons existence in the desire realm and takes up existence in the desire realm, are all those [beings] who exhaust the phenomena bound to the desire realm such that the phenomena bound to the desire realm manifest before them?
The answer is: It is so.

If one abandons existence in the desire realm and takes up existence in the desire realm, all those [beings] exhaust the phenomena bound to the desire realm, and the phenomena bound to the desire realm manifest before them.

Is there a case where one has completely exhausted the phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*), and phenomena bound to the desire realm are present before them, yet they have neither abandoned existence in the desire realm nor are they receiving existence in the desire realm?
The answer is:
Yes. For example, when one has not yet reached the end of life, one exhausts the phenomena bound to the desire realm while phenomena bound to the desire realm are present before them.

If one abandons existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhava*) and takes up existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu-bhava*), does all that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) cease, and do all that which is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) manifest?
Answer: It is so;
if one abandons existence in the desire realm and takes up existence in the form realm, all that which is bound to the desire realm ceases, and all that which is bound to the form realm manifests.

Is there a case where one exhausts the phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*), and phenomena bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) manifest before them, yet that person neither abandons existence in the desire realm nor takes up existence in the form realm?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one has not yet died, one exhausts the phenomena bound to the desire realm while phenomena bound to the form realm manifest before them.

If one abandons existence in the desire realm and takes up existence in the formless realm, does all that which is bound to the desire realm cease, and do all that which is bound to the formless realm manifest?
Answer: It is so.

If all phenomena bound to the desire realm are exhausted and phenomena bound to the formless realm manifest before one, does that person abandon existence in the desire realm and take up existence in the formless realm?
Answer: It is so.

If one abandons existence in the form realm and takes up existence in the form realm, are all those [beings] entirely exhausting the factors bound to the form realm, and do the factors bound to the form realm manifest before them?
Answer: It is so;

if one abandons existence in the form realm and takes up existence in the form realm, all those [beings] have exhausted the factors bound to the form realm, yet factors bound to the form realm manifest before them.

Is it possible that one has exhausted the factors bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*), yet factors bound to the realm of form manifest before them, such that they have neither abandoned existence in the realm of form nor are they taking up existence in the realm of form?
Answer: Yes, there is.
For example, as long as one has not yet died, one may exhaust the factors bound to the realm of form while factors bound to the realm of form continue to manifest.

If one abandons existence in the form realm and takes up existence in the desire realm, are all those bound phenomena of the form realm extinguished, and do the bound phenomena of the desire realm manifest?
Answer: It is so;

if one abandons existence in the form realm and takes up existence in the desire realm, all those bound phenomena of the form realm are extinguished, and the bound phenomena of the desire realm manifest.

Is there a case where one exhausts the factors bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*), while factors bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) manifest before them, yet he neither abandons existence in the form realm nor takes up existence in the desire realm?
Answer: There is.
For example, as long as one has not yet died, one may exhaust the factors bound to the form realm while factors bound to the desire realm manifest before them.

If one abandons existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu-bhava*) and takes up existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-bhava*), does all that which is bound to the form realm cease, and do all phenomena bound to the formless realm manifest?
Answer: It is so;
if one abandons existence in the form realm and takes up existence in the formless realm, all that which is bound to the form realm ceases, and all phenomena bound to the formless realm manifest.

Is it possible that one exhausts the phenomena bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*), while phenomena bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) manifest before them, yet he does not abandon existence in the form realm nor take up existence in the formless realm?
The answer is:
Yes. For example, as long as one has not yet died, one may exhaust the phenomena bound to the form realm while phenomena bound to the formless realm manifest before them.
If one abandons existence with feeling belonging to the formless realm, does all that which is bound to the formless realm become exhausted, and do the dharmas bound to the formless realm manifest?
Answer: It is so.

If one abandons existence in the formless realm and takes up existence in the formless realm, all those phenomena bound to the formless realm are exhausted, and phenomena bound to the formless realm manifest before one.

Is it possible that one has exhausted all phenomena bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*), yet a phenomenon bound to the formless realm manifests before them, such that they have not abandoned existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*) nor have they taken up existence in the formless realm?
Answer: Yes.
For example, as long as one has not yet died, all dharmas bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are exhausted, and dharmas bound to the formless realm manifest before one.

If one abandons existence in the formless realm and takes up existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are all those exhausted dharmas bound to the formless realm, and do dharmas bound to the desire realm manifest before one?
Answer: It is so.

Suppose one exhausts all phenomena bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) and brings forth phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) into the present; does that person abandon existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*) and take up existence in the desire realm (*kāmabhava*)?
Answer: It is so.

If one abandons existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and takes up existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), does all that which is bound to the formless realm cease, and do phenomena bound to the form realm manifest?
Answer: It is so.

If one abandons existence in the formless realm and takes up existence in the realm of form, all those factors bound to the formless realm are exhausted, and factors bound to the realm of form manifest.

Is it possible that one has completely exhausted the factors bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*), yet factors bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) manifest before them, such that they have not abandoned existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*) but have not yet taken up existence in the form realm (*rūpabhava*)?
Answer: It is possible.
For example, as long as one has not yet died, one may completely exhaust the factors bound to the formless realm while factors bound to the form realm manifest before them.
For what reason are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm not those by which one is bound in the form and formless realms?
The answer is:
because that would entail a collapse of the realms; for if there were no craving or ignorance regarding the desire realm, [those higher realms] would not exist.
For what reason are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) not those by which one is bound in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Answer: Because that would entail a confusion of realms; moreover, they are not conditions for this [desire realm].
For what reason are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) not those by which one is bound in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The answer is:
because the realms would then be confused; there is neither craving nor ignorance regarding the form realm [in the formless realm].
For what reason are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm not those by which one is bound in the desire realm or the form realm?
The answer is:
because that would result in the destruction of the realms; furthermore, they are not conditions for these [lower realms].
For what reason are the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the desire realm not themselves objects of all [proclivities] within the desire realm?
Answer: Although they pervade all existence, they are not the conditions for these [other proclivities].
For what reason is it that the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) do not cause all things within the form realm to be conditioned by them?
Answer: Although they pervade all existence, they are not the conditions for these [objects].
For what reason are the pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the formless realm not pervasive throughout the entire formless realm?
Answer: Although they pervade all existence (*bhava*), they do not take that [formless realm] as their object (*ālambana*).
The ten perceptions:

the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of impurity, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds, the perception of death, the perception of cessation, the perception of the absence of lust, and the perception of exhaustion.
If one cultivates the perception of impermanence, is that perception of impermanence what is intended by the mind?
The answer is:
there are cases where one cultivates the perception of impermanence, yet it is not what is intended by the mind as the perception of impermanence.
What is the cultivation of the perception of impermanence that is not a mental recollection of the perception of impermanence?
The answer is:

it is like cultivating the perception of impermanence through other conditions; this is called the cultivation of the perception of impermanence that is not a mental recollection of the perception of impermanence.
What is meant by "the mind attends to the perception of impermanence, yet one does not cultivate the perception of impermanence"?
The answer is:

it is like other instances where the mind attends to the perception of impermanence; this is called "the mind attends to the perception of impermanence, yet one does not cultivate the perception of impermanence."
How does one cultivate the perception of impermanence such that the mind is mindful of the perception of impermanence?
The answer is:

when one cultivates the perception of impermanence by taking the perception of impermanence as its object, this is called cultivating the perception of impermanence such that the mind is mindful of the perception of impermanence.
What is it that is neither the cultivation of the perception of impermanence nor the mental attention directed toward the perception of impermanence?
Answer: It is everything except for those aforementioned matters.
This continues up to the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saṃjñā*), which is also like this.
If one experiences a thought of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*), is that which the mind attends to a thought of sensual desire?
Answer: Yes.
Or, when one perceives a thought of sensual desire, that thought of sensual desire is not what is being attended to by the mind.
How is it that when one perceives a thought of sensual desire, that thought of sensual desire is not what is being attended to by the mind? Answer:

It is like when one perceives a thought of sensual desire through other conditions; this is called perceiving a thought of sensual desire while that thought of sensual desire is not what is being attended to by the mind.
What is it to have a thought of sensual desire attended to by the mind while one is not perceiving a thought of sensual desire?

Answer: It is like when other thoughts are present in the mind while one is experiencing a thought of sensual desire; this is called "the thought of sensual desire being present in the mind, yet it is not the time of experiencing that thought of sensual desire.
What is the case where it is the time of experiencing a thought of sensual desire, yet the thought of sensual desire is not present in the mind?

Answer: It is just as when one perceives a thought of sensual desire while that thought of sensual desire is present; this is called "perceiving a thought of sensual desire at the time of its presence" and "that which is intended by the mind is a thought of sensual desire.
What is it to not perceive a thought of sensual desire at the time of its presence and for that which is intended by the mind not to be a thought of sensual desire?
Answer: With the exception of those aforementioned matters,
the same applies to thoughts of ill will and harmfulness.
If one perceives the perception of renunciation, is that which is perceived by the mind the perception of renunciation?
Answer: Sometimes, when one perceives the perception of renunciation, that which is perceived by the mind is not the perception of renunciation.
What is it that when one experiences the awakening of the thought of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṃkappa*), that thought of renunciation is not what the mind is attending to? Answer:

It is, for example, when one experiences the awakening of the thought of renunciation due to other conditions; this is called experiencing the awakening of the thought of renunciation while that thought of renunciation is not what the mind is attending to.
What is the case where one attends to an escape-contemplation with the mind, yet it is not an escape-contemplation at the time of that contemplation?
The answer is:

it is just as when one attends to other escape-contemplations with the mind; this is called attending to an escape-contemplation with the mind while it is not an escape-contemplation at the time of that contemplation.
What is the case when one is mindful of the awakening-factor of renunciation (*nekkhamma-sambojjhaṅga*)?
The answer is:

just as when one is mindful of the awakening-factor of renunciation by taking the awakening-factor of renunciation as its object, this is called being mindful of the awakening-factor of renunciation when one is mindful of the awakening-factor of renunciation.
What is it that, when one is experiencing a thought of non-emancipation (*anairyāṇika-vitarka*), that thought of non-emancipation is not what the mind is attending to?
Answer: It is all cases other than those mentioned above.
The same applies to non-ill will and non-harming thoughts.
Regarding those phenomena that have ignorance as their cause, do those phenomena have ignorance as their condition?
Answer: Yes.
In this way, those phenomena that arise with ignorance as their cause have ignorance as their condition.
Is there any phenomenon that has ignorance as its condition but does not have ignorance as its cause?
The answer is: Yes.
There are [such formations], namely all other non-obscured neutral formations and wholesome formations, excluding those that are the retribution of ignorance.
Are all phenomena that have clarity (*vidyā*) as their cause also conditioned by clarity?
Answer: It is so;
those dharmas that have clarity as their cause also have clarity as their condition.
Is there perhaps a dharma that has clarity as its condition but does not have clarity as its cause?
Answer: Yes;
this refers to the case where there are contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) at the outset.
If various phenomena have ignorance as their cause, do those phenomena take clarity (*vidyā*) as their condition?
The answer is: It is so;
those phenomena that have ignorance as their cause have clarity as their condition.
Is there any phenomenon that has clarity as its condition but does not have ignorance as its cause?
Answer: Yes;
with the exception of the retribution of ignorance (*avidyā-vipāka*), all other non-obscured neutral formations (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-saṃskāra*) as well as wholesome formations (*kuśala-saṃskāra*).
If a dharma has clarity (*vidyā*) as its cause, does that dharma have ignorance as its condition (*pratyaya*)?
Answer: It is so;
those dharmas that have ignorance as their condition do not have clarity as their cause.
Is there any dharma that has ignorance as its condition but does not have clarity as its cause?
Answer: Yes;
this refers to the first clarification regarding conditioned phenomena that are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Are all phenomena that have ignorance as their cause unwholesome?
Answer: It is so;
those phenomena that are unwholesome have ignorance as their cause.
Is there any phenomenon that has ignorance as its cause but is not unwholesome?
Answer: Yes;
there are defiled formations that are the retribution of ignorance.
Are those phenomena virtuous which have clarity as their cause?
Answer: It is so;
those phenomena that arise from clarity are wholesome.
Is there any phenomenon that is wholesome yet does not arise from clarity?
Answer: Yes;
for example, wholesome *sāsrava* (outflowing) formations are illuminated by knowledge (*vidyā*).
Is there any phenomenon that is neither caused by knowledge nor caused by ignorance, yet is not the case that it has no cause?
Answer: There are.

Excluding those formations that are the retribution of ignorance (*avidyā-vipāka*), all other non-obscured neutral (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*) formations, as well as wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) formations, are "initially manifest.

This concludes the fortieth chapter, the *Kāmadhātu-varga*, of the *Abhidharma*; it consists of one hundred and eighty-six *śloka* verses in the Sanskrit original, and two thousand nine hundred and fifty-six words in the Qin translation.
Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-nine.

Composed by Kātyāyanīputra.

Chapter Three: The Section on Perception (Saṃjñā-varga). Chapter Ten: The Section on Views (Dṛṣṭi-grantha). The Ten Perceptions:

the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of impurity, the perception of reflecting on food, the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds, the perception of death, the perception of cessation, the perception of the absence of lust, and the perception of exhaustion.
If various phenomena arise from the perception of impermanence, are those phenomena associated with the perception of impermanence?
Conversely, if various phenomena are associated with the perception of impermanence, do those phenomena arise from the perception of impermanence?
This applies even up to the perception of exhaustion (*nirodha-saṃjñā*).
Regarding all phenomena arising from the perception of impermanence (*anicca-saṃjñā*): are those phenomena the same object as that perception of impermanence?
Conversely, if all phenomena share the same object as the perception of impermanence, do those phenomena arise from the perception of impermanence?
This applies likewise up to the perception of cessation (*nirodhasaṃjñā*).
Is there any dharma that is analyzed by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) which is neither abandoned, nor cultivated, nor realized?
Is there any dharma that is analyzed by the knowledge of phenomena which is neither abandoned nor cultivated, yet is realized?
Is there any dharma that is discerned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), is not abandoned, is cultivated, and is realized?
Is there any dharma that is discerned by the knowledge of phenomena, is abandoned, is cultivated, and is realized?
Is there any dharma that is discerned by the knowledge of phenomena, is abandoned, is not cultivated, and is realized?
Are there any phenomena that are abandoned through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-vibhaṅga*), yet are neither cultivated nor realized?

Are there any phenomena that arise simultaneously with a phenomenon that has no object-condition (*anālambana*) as its cause, or with a phenomenon that has no object-condition as its object-condition?

Is there anything that possesses an image (*sanimitta*) which is not non-existent and not without image—namely, other forms, other feelings, other perceptions, other consciousnesses, and their associated factors—is it correct to say that such a phenomenon is a cause for those [other] phenomena, or is it correct to say it is a condition?
Furthermore, should it be said that this is a condition (*pratyaya*), or should it be said that it is not a cause (*hetu*)?
Should that phenomenon (*dharma*) be said to be wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
By how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is that phenomenon driven, and by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) is it bound?
If a phenomenon arises together with the mind and cannot exist without the mind, is it the case that when such a mind arises, that phenomenon likewise arises?
And when the mind ceases, does that phenomenon likewise cease?
As that mind attains [its state], does that dharma likewise attain it?
As that mind abandons [its state], does that dharma likewise abandon it?
As that mind receives retribution, does that dharma likewise receive it?
By how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is feeling associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta-vedanā*) driven?
By how many underlying tendencies is feeling not associated with views (*adṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta-vedanā*) driven?
By how many underlying tendencies is feeling associated with doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃprayukta-vedanā*) driven?
How many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bind the feeling (*vedanā*) that is dissociated from doubt?
How many bases (*dhātu*), how many sense-spheres (*āyatana*), and how many aggregates (*skandha*) are included within that which is produced through the path-conditioned arising?

Excluding the mental factors associated with the mind, how many bases, how many sense-spheres, and how many aggregates are included among the remaining phenomena—namely, those perceptions and feelings (*saṃjñā-vedanā*) produced by eye-contact and so forth? Excluding the mental factors dissociated from the mind, how many bases, how many sense-spheres, and how many aggregates are included among the remaining phenomena—namely, those perceptions and feelings produced by ear-contact and so forth? How many bases, how many sense-spheres, and how many aggregates are included among all other remaining phenomena?

Regarding the perceptions and feelings produced by the contact of the nose, tongue, and body—excluding those associated with the mind—and the perceptions and feelings produced by the contact of the mind—excluding those dissociated from the mind—as well as all other remaining phenomena: how many *dhātus*, how many *āyatanas*, and how many *skandhas* do they comprise?
The meaning of this chapter shall now be fully expounded.
There are ten perceptions:

the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of impurity, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds, the perception of death, the perception of relinquishment, the perception of the absence of lust, and the perception of exhaustion.
If various phenomena arise from the perception of impermanence, are those phenomena associated with the perception of impermanence?
Answer: There are some phenomena that arise from the perception of impermanence, yet those phenomena are not associated with the perception of impermanence.
What is meant by "a phenomenon arises from the perception of impermanence, yet that phenomenon is not associated with the perception of impermanence"?
The answer is:

for example, when the perception of impermanence has necessarily ceased beforehand and other perceptions have necessarily arisen beforehand, those perceptions and their associated phenomena—this is called a phenomenon arising from the perception of impermanence, yet that phenomenon is not associated with the perception of impermanence.
What is the case where a phenomenon is associated with the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), yet that phenomenon does not arise from the perception of impermanence?
The answer is:

for example, when other perceptions have necessarily ceased beforehand and the perception of impermanence has necessarily arisen beforehand, those phenomena associated with that perception—this is called a phenomenon associated with the perception of impermanence that does not arise from the perception of impermanence.
What is meant by "a phenomenon arises with the perception of impermanence, and that phenomenon is associated with the perception of impermanence"?
The answer is:

just as when the perception of impermanence is about to cease and the perception of impermanence is about to arise, all phenomena associated with that perception—this is called a phenomenon arising with the perception of impermanence and being associated with that perception of impermanence.
What is the case where a phenomenon does not arise from the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), yet that phenomenon is associated with the perception of impermanence?
The answer is:

it is like other perceptions that must necessarily cease beforehand, or like other perceptions that must necessarily arise beforehand; those perceptions and their associated phenomena—this is called a phenomenon that does not arise from the perception of impermanence, yet that phenomenon is associated with the perception of impermanence.
This applies even up to the perception of exhaustion (*nirodha-saṃjñā*).
When the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*) arises toward various phenomena, does that perception of impermanence have those phenomena as its single object?
Answer: No.
There may be a phenomenon that arises from the perception of impermanence, yet that phenomenon does not share the same object as the perception of impermanence.
How is it that a phenomenon arises from the perception of impermanence, yet that phenomenon does not share the same object as the perception of impermanence?
Answer:

It is like the perception of impermanence which must necessarily cease first, while another perception must necessarily arise next; because there is that other condition, this is called the arising of the perception of the impermanence of phenomena from a condition that is not the perception of the impermanence of those same phenomena.
What is meant by "the perception of the impermanence of phenomena has a single object, yet that phenomenon does not arise from the perception of impermanence"? Answer:

It is as when other perceptions must necessarily cease first and the perception of impermanence must necessarily arise next; since that [perception of impermanence] takes that [preceding phenomenon] as its object, this is called "the perception of the impermanence of phenomena has a single object, yet that phenomenon does not arise from the perception of impermanence."
How is it that when the perception of the impermanence of phenomena arises, that perception of the impermanence of phenomena has a single object? Answer:

Just as the perception of impermanence must necessarily cease first and the perception of impermanence must necessarily arise next, that [arising] has this [ceasing] as its object; this is called the perception of the impermanence of phenomena arising with that perception of the impermanence of phenomena as its single object.
What is the case where a phenomenon does not arise from the perception of impermanence, yet that phenomenon shares the same object as the perception of impermanence?
The answer is:

it is like other perceptions that must necessarily cease beforehand, or like other perceptions that must necessarily arise beforehand; these have other objects, and this is called a phenomenon that does not arise from the perception of impermanence, yet shares the same object as that perception of impermanence.
This applies even up to the perception of extinction (*nirodha-saṃjñā*).
Is there any dharma that is analyzed by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna-vikalpa*) which is neither abandoned, nor cultivated, nor realized?
Answer: Yes.
There are: space and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Is there any dharma that is distinguished by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), yet is neither abandoned, nor cultivated, nor realized?
Answer: Yes.
There is: the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Is there any dharma that is abandoned by the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna-vikalpa*), yet is cultivated and realized?
Answer: Yes.
There are; namely, untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Is there any phenomenon that is abandoned through the discernment of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna-pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and realized through cultivation (*bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā*)?
Answer: Yes.
Yes; it refers to wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
Is there any phenomenon that is abandoned through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), yet is neither cultivated nor realized?
Answer: Yes.
There are [such things], namely the divine eye and the divine ear.
Is there any dharma that is analyzed by the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), abandoned, not cultivated, and not realized?
Answer: Yes.
There are such [factors], namely all other indeterminate conditioned factors and unwholesome factors, excluding the divine eye and the divine ear.
Is there any factor that has no object-condition (anālambana), yet arises simultaneously with a factor that has an object-condition, by way of being its cause through the object-condition?
Answer: Yes.

Those associated with the various groups of the five consciousnesses, those associated with the various groups of the mental consciousness, as well as form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind—the acquisitions (*prāpti*), birth, aging, and impermanence that arise in dependence upon those dharmas—these are called "dharmas that have no object-condition, which have no object-condition as their cause, and which arise together with the object-condition."

There is that which possesses an image, and there is that dharma; it is not the case that this dharma does not exist. Therefore, there is that which possesses an image, and it is neither non-existent nor devoid of an image.
Yet, there is that dharma, and it is not the case that this dharma does not exist. Therefore, it is neither non-existent nor devoid of an image.

Other than matter, that dharma is not matter; other than feeling, that dharma is not feeling; other than perception, that dharma is not perception; other than consciousness, that dharma is not consciousness; other than those associated dharmas, that dharma is not associated. Therefore, regarding those dissociated dharmas, should it be said that one dharma is a cause for another dharma, or should it be said that it is a condition?
Or should it be said that they are conditions?
Should it be said that they are not causes?
The answer is:
Regarding a later birth in relation to a prior birth, one should say it is a cause and one should say it is a condition;
regarding a prior birth in relation to a later birth, one should say it is a condition, but one should not say it is a cause.
Should that dharma be said to be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
Answer: Those phenomena should be described as wholesome when among the wholesome, as unwholesome when among the unwholesome, and as indeterminate when among the indeterminate.
By how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are those phenomena influenced?
Answer: [They are] the objects of the outflows within the three realms.
How many fetters bind them?
Answer: Nine.
All phenomena arise together with the mind and do not exist without the mind; as that mind arises, do those phenomena likewise arise?
Answer: The preceding mind arises first, and subsequently that dharma [arises].
If that mind is exhausted, is that dharma likewise exhausted?
Answer: First the mind is exhausted, and subsequently that dharma [is exhausted].
Is it the case that as that mind is attained, so too is that dharma?
The answer is:
First the mind is attained, and afterwards those dharmas.
If that mind is abandoned, are those dharmas likewise abandoned?
Answer: First one abandons the phenomena, and subsequently one abandons that mind.
If that mind receives retribution, does that phenomenon do so as well?
Answer: It may be so, or it may not.
Regarding the feelings associated with views, by how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are they influenced?
Answer: It has both outflow-conditions (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and is also seen as having non-outflow-conditions (*anāsrava-ālambana*), namely, the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with it.
As for the sensations (*vedanā*) dissociated from views, by how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are they driven?
Answer: With the exception of the views that take the untainted as their object and the ignorance associated with them, all other [factors] are [so].
As for the feelings associated with doubt, by how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are they influenced?

Answer: [The latent dispositions] abandoned through seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) have outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), as do those associated with doubt (*vicikitsā*) that have non-outflowing objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*), as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with them.
Regarding the sensations (*vedanā*) not associated with doubt, by how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are they influenced?

Answer: With the exception of the doubt-free objects of the untainted (anāsrava) and the ignorance associated with them, all other [defilements] are abandoned through the vision of the truths (satyadarśana-prahātavya).
As for those conditioned by the path (mārga), they are comprised within the eighteen bases (dhātu), the twelve sense-bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha).

Excluding the mental concomitants (citta-saṃprayukta-dharma) such as perception and feeling produced by eye-contact and so forth, and excluding the non-mental concomitants (citta-viprayukta-dharma) such as perception and feeling produced by ear-contact and so forth, all remaining phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen bases (āyatana), the twelve sense-fields (dhātu), and the five aggregates (skandha).

The perceptions and feelings arising from the contact of the nose, tongue, and body, excluding those mental factors associated with the mind; and the perceptions and feelings arising from the contact of the mind, excluding those factors dissociated from the mind—all other such phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen bases (*dhātus*), the twelve spheres (*āyatanas*), and the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

The *Abhidharma-saṃjñā-varga*, Chapter Forty-one, is completed. In the Sanskrit original it consists of one hundred four *ślokas*; in the Qin [translation] it consists of one thousand six hundred twenty-two words. **Chapter Four:

The Section on the Time of Knowledge (*Jñānakāla-varga*)** In the *Abhidharma-darśana-grantha*, the fourth section, the Section on the Time of Knowledge: Regarding those aggregates that exist at the time of knowledge, are those aggregates abandoned?
If a category is abandoned, is that category known?
If one is weary of a category, is one free from desire for that category?
If one is free from desire for a category, is one weary of that category?
If a collection is subject to revulsion, is that collection cultivated with revulsion?
Conversely, if a collection is cultivated with revulsion, is that collection subject to revulsion?
If a collection is free from desire, is that collection cultivated with revulsion?
If one cultivates revulsion toward a certain aggregate, is there no desire for that aggregate?
If a phenomenon is the cause of various phenomena, or if it is a phenomenon at a certain time, should that phenomenon not be called a cause?

If a phenomenon is the immediate, the object-condition, or the predominant condition of various phenomena, or if it is such a phenomenon at a certain time, should that phenomenon not be called an immediate, object, or predominant condition?
Are all mental contacts (manas-saṃsparśa) equally threefold contacts?
And if they are equally threefold contacts, are they all mental contacts?
Are all instances of conceit (māna) acts of conceiting?
If one generates conceit, is that conceit?
Are all forms of conceit mental predominance?
And if something is mental predominance, is it conceit?
Are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) non-guarded?
If they are non-guarded, are they those conditioned phenomena?
Are all conditioned phenomena guarded by them?
If one establishes a protection, does one practice that [protection]?
If a collection is not obtained, is that collection not accomplished?
If a collection is not accomplished, is that collection not obtained?
If one attains a particular aggregate (*khandha*), does one accomplish that aggregate?
Conversely, if one accomplishes a particular aggregate, does one attain that aggregate?

Excluding the Noble Truth of Suffering and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), how many bases (*āyatana*), how many spheres (*dhātu*), and how many aggregates (*skandha*) do all other remaining phenomena comprise?
The same applies to the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Excluding the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), how many bases (*dhātu*), how many spheres (*āyatana*), and how many aggregates (*skandha*) do all remaining phenomena comprise?
The same applies to the path (*mārga*).

Excluding the form-aggregate (*rūpa-dharma*) and the dharma-base (*dharma-āyatana*), how many bases (*dhātu*), how many bases (*āyatana*), and how many aggregates (*skandha*) do all remaining dharmas comprise?

Regarding those that are non-material (*arūpin*), visible (*sanidarśana*) or invisible (*anidarśana*), resistant (*sapratigha*) or non-resistant (*apratigha*), with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*), conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), past, future, or present, wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), bound to the form or formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), trainee (*śaikṣa*), non-trainee (*aśaikṣa*), or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee (*naivaśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa*); excluding the dharmas to be abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or those not to be abandoned (*aheya*), as well as the dharma-base—how many bases, how many bases, and how many aggregates do all these remaining dharmas comprise?
Excluding the dharmas that have arisen and those dharmas that will certainly not arise, how many *dhātus*, how many *āyatanas*, and how many *skandhas* do all other remaining dharmas comprise?

Excluding unarisen form and formless [dharmas], visible and invisible, resistant and non-resistant, outflowing and non-outflowing, conditioned and unconditioned, past, future, and present, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, those bound to the desire realm and those bound to the form and formless realms, those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither in nor beyond training; excluding the dharmas abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and those not to be abandoned, as well as all dharmas that will certainly not arise—how many *dhātus*, how many *āyatanas*, and how many *skandhas* do all other remaining dharmas comprise?
Is it possible for a single *dhātu*, a single *āyatana*, or a single *skandha* to encompass all phenomena?
I pray that you will fully expound the meaning of this chapter.
Furthermore, when a collection of knowledge is abandoned, is that collection [of defilements] also abandoned?
Answer: There are cases where one accumulates knowledge, yet that accumulation is not severed.
What is meant by accumulating knowledge while that accumulation is not severed?

Answer: When one employs the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path, yet does not thereby eliminate defilements, this is called "knowing a collection [of aggregates] while that collection is not severed.
What is meant by "the collection is severed, yet that collection is not known"?

Answer: By means of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), the patience regarding origination (*samudaya-kṣānti*), the patience regarding cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*), and the patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*), one abandons the defilements; this is called "the abandonment of the aggregate, yet non-cognition of that aggregate.
What is "cognition of the aggregate and the abandonment of that aggregate"?

Answer: By means of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path, one abandons defilements; this is called "knowing the aggregate and abandoning that aggregate.
What is meant by "not knowing the aggregate and not abandoning that aggregate"?

Answer: Because one does not abandon the defilements through the patiences regarding suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, this is called a "heap" that is characterized by non-wisdom and whose heap is not abandoned.
Are all those heaps subject to revulsion, and are those heaps free from desire?
Answer: There are some aggregates that one feels weary of, yet one does not lack desire for those same aggregates.
What are these aggregates that one feels weary of, yet for which one does not lack desire?
Answer:

When one does not abandon defilements through the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), the patience regarding origin (*samudaya-kṣānti*), the knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), or the knowledge regarding origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), this is called "a group that is weary of that group, yet that group is not free from desire.
What is a group that is free from desire toward that group, yet that group is not weary?

Answer: By means of the patience of the path of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna-mārga-kṣānti*) and by means of the knowledge of the path of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna-mārga-jñāna*), one abandons defilements; this is called a collection that is free from desire, yet that collection is not characterized by revulsion.
What is a collection that is characterized by revulsion, yet that collection is free from desire?
Answer:

By means of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and the patience regarding origination (*samudaya-kṣānti*), and by means of the knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge regarding origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), one abandons defilements; this is called "disgust toward a certain aggregate and non-desire for that aggregate.
What is "neither disgust toward a certain aggregate nor non-desire for that aggregate"?

Answer: Because one does not abandon defilements through the patience regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna-kṣānti*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), this is called "the aggregates are not subject to revulsion, yet those aggregates are not free from desire.
Are all aggregates subject to revulsion, and are those aggregates cultivated as revulsion?
Answer: It is so;
when one is weary of a certain aggregate, one cultivates weariness toward that aggregate.
Is there any aggregate for which one cultivates weariness, yet that aggregate is not itself wearisome?
Answer: Yes;
it is by means of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) that one abandons defilements.
Regarding those aggregates that are free from desire, are those aggregates cultivated with revulsion?
Answer: There may be a category that is free from desire, yet that category is not cultivated through revulsion.
What is the category that is free from desire but is not cultivated through revulsion?

Answer: When one eliminates defilements through the patience of the path of exhaustion and the patience of the path, this is called a "group characterized by freedom from desire," yet that group does not involve the cultivation of revulsion.
What is a "group characterized by the cultivation of revulsion" that is not a "group characterized by freedom from desire"?
Answer:

When one does not abandon defilements through the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), the patience regarding origination (*samudaya-kṣānti*), the knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), or the knowledge regarding origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), this is called "cultivating revulsion toward that aggregate, yet not being free from desire for that aggregate.
What is "being free from desire for that aggregate while cultivating revulsion toward that aggregate"?
Answer:

By means of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and the patience regarding the origin (*samudaya-kṣānti*), and by means of the knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge regarding the origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge regarding the path (*mārga-jñāna*), one abandons defilements; this is called "the aggregate that is free from desire, and that aggregate is cultivated with revulsion.
What is the aggregate that is not free from desire, and that aggregate is not cultivated with revulsion?

Answer: Because the patience of the path of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*) does not sever the defilements (*kleśa*), this is called a "group" (*rāśi*) that is not free from desire, and that group is not cultivated through revulsion (*nirveda*).
If a phenomenon is the cause of various phenomena, or at some time those phenomena [arise] from it, should that phenomenon not be said to be a cause?
Answer: No.
If a dharma is the sequence of various dharmas, or if at some time that dharma exists, should that dharma not be said to be the sequence?
Answer: If that dharma has not yet arisen.

If a dharma is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) or the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for various dharmas, or at times for that very dharma, should it not be said that this dharma is the object-condition or the dominant condition?
Answer: No.
Are all those mental contacts (*manas-saṃsparśa*) equally of the three types?
Answer: It is so;
all mental contacts (*manas-saṃsparśa*) are those three kinds of contact.
Is there any kind of the threefold contact that is not a mental contact?
Answer: There is;
it is contact associated with the five groups of consciousness.
The Blessed One has also said:
"Monks! There is the maintenance of mind, the maintenance of phenomena, and the maintenance of ignorance.
Does ignorance, feeling, contact, and sensation exist as something acquired, as something unacquired, or as something both acquired and unacquired?"
Are all forms of conceit (*māna*) of the nature of self?
Answer: It is so;
all forms of conceit are of the nature of self.
Is there perhaps conceit that is not self-conceit?
Answer: Yes, there is; namely, views.
The Blessed One also said:
"Monks, I am my own master; for me, monks, I am my own master."
Are all forms of conceit characterized by such predominance and intensity? Answer:
Yes, all forms of conceit are characterized by such predominance and intensity.
Is there that which is exceedingly intense yet is not pride?
Answer: Yes;
with the exception of pride itself, when any other defilements manifest.
The World-Honored One has also said:
"O Bhikṣus!
If one increases [defilements], one is bound by Māra; if one does not increase them, one is liberated from Pāpīyān."
Are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) not non-restraint? Answer:
Some conditioned phenomena are not non-restraint.
What is meant by "practicing that which is not non-guarding"?
The answer is:
guarding the body and guarding speech; this is called practicing that which is not non-guarding.
What is that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint?
Answer: The faculties that are not restraint; this is called that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
What is conduct that is non-guarded?
The answer is:
bodily non-guarding and verbal non-guarding; this is called conduct that is non-guarded.
What is that which is neither conduct nor non-guarding?
The answer is:
guarding of the faculties; this is called that which is neither conduct nor non-guarding.
Are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) guarded? Answer:
Some conditioned phenomena are not guarded.
What is meant by practicing that which is non-protection?
The answer is:
not protecting the body and not protecting speech; this is called practicing that which is non-protection.
What is the guarding against those unwholesome courses of action?
The answer is:
guarding the sense faculties; this is called guarding against those unwholesome courses of action.
What is the practice of that protection?
The answer is:
bodily protection and verbal protection; this is called the practice of that protection.
What is that which is neither a course of action nor a restraint? Answer:
A faculty that is not a restraint; this is called that which is neither a course of action nor a restraint.
If a collection is not obtained, is that collection not accomplished?
Answer: It is so;
if a collection is not obtained, that collection is not accomplished.
Is there a collection that is not accomplished, yet for which that collection is not non-acquired?
Answer: There is;
namely, when a collection is acquired and then immediately lost.
If one acquires a collection, does one accomplish that collection?
Answer: It is so;
if one accomplishes it, one acquires that collection.
Is it possible that one has acquired a collection, yet that collection is not accomplished?
Answer: Yes;
for instance, if one acquires a collection and then immediately loses it.
Excluding the Noble Truth of Suffering and the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), all remaining phenomena are subsumed under two bases, held by one consciousness-element, and included in one aggregate.
It is the same for Origination.
Excluding the Noble Truth of Cessation and the dharma-base, all remaining phenomena are subsumed under seventeen bases, held by eleven elements, and included in two aggregates.
The Path is also like this.

Excluding the form-aggregate (*rūpa-dharma*) and the dharma-base (*dharma-āyatana*), all remaining dharmas are subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Excluding the formless dharmas (*arūpa-dharma*) and the dharma-base, all remaining dharmas are subsumed under ten elements, ten bases, and one aggregate.

Excluding visible phenomena (*sanidarśana-dharma*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), all remaining phenomena are subsumed under sixteen bases (*āyatana*), ten elements (*dhātu*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding invisible phenomena (*anidarśana-dharma*) and the sphere of mental objects, all remaining phenomena are subsumed under one base, one element, and one aggregate.

Excluding the resistant dharmas (*sapratigha-dharma*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), all remaining dharmas are subsumed under seven bases (*āyatana*), held by one consciousness-base (*vijñānāyatana*), and included in one aggregate (*skandha*).
Excluding the non-resistant dharmas (*apratigha-dharma*) and the dharma-base, all remaining dharmas are subsumed under ten bases, held by ten bases, and included in one aggregate.
Excluding the tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), all remaining dharmas are subsumed under two aggregates (*skandha*), one element (*dhātu*), and one base (*āyatana*).
Excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas and the dharma-base, all remaining dharmas are subsumed under seventeen elements, eleven bases, and two aggregates.

Excluding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), there is no collection of all phenomena; this is an empty discourse. Excluding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) and the sphere of mental objects, the remaining phenomena are subsumed within seventeen bases (*āyatana*), eleven elements (*dhātu*), and two aggregates (*skandha*), namely, form (*rūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Excluding past and present phenomena (*dharma*) as well as the *dharmāyatana*, all remaining phenomena are subsumed under seventeen bases (*āyatana*), eleven elements (*dhātu*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding future phenomena and the *dharmāyatana*, all remaining phenomena are subsumed under seventeen bases, eleven elements, and two aggregates.

Excluding wholesome and unwholesome dharmas as well as the dharma-āyatana, all remaining dharmas are subsumed under seventeen bases (dhātus), eleven elements (āyatanas), and two aggregates (skandhas).
Excluding indeterminate dharmas and the dharma-āyatana, all remaining dharmas are subsumed under nine bases, three elements, and two aggregates.

Excluding the factors associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), all remaining factors are subsumed under thirteen bases (*āyatana*), nine elements (*dhātu*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).

Excluding the factors associated with the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the factors of those in training and those beyond training (*śaikṣa-aśaikṣa-dharma*), and the sphere of phenomena, all remaining factors are subsumed under seventeen bases, eleven elements, and two aggregates.
Except for the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner and the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), all other dharmas are comprised within two aggregates, one element, and one base.

Except for the dharmas abandoned by seeing the truths, the dharmas not to be abandoned, and the dharma-base, all other dharmas are comprised within seventeen elements, eleven bases, and two aggregates.

Excluding the factors abandoned through contemplation (*cintā-heya*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), all remaining factors are subsumed under two aggregates, one element, and one sphere.
Excluding the factors that have arisen and those factors that will necessarily not arise, all remaining factors are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.

Excluding unarisen phenomena and those phenomena that will necessarily not arise, and excluding all phenomena as being a mere empty discourse without aggregation; excluding material phenomena and those phenomena that will necessarily not arise, all remaining phenomena are subsumed within eight bases (*āyatana*), two elements (*dhātu*), four sense-bases (*āyatana*), and the aggregates (*skandha*).

Excluding formless phenomena (*ārūpya-dharma*) and those phenomena that are necessarily non-arising, all remaining phenomena are subsumed under eleven bases (*āyatana*), eleven elements (*dhātu*), and one aggregate (*skandha*).

Excluding visible phenomena (*sanidarśana-dharma*) and those phenomena that are necessarily non-arising, all remaining phenomena are subsumed under seventeen bases, eleven elements, and five aggregates.

Excluding the invisible dharmas and those dharmas that will necessarily not arise, all other remaining dharmas are subsumed under one aggregate, maintained by one [element], and included in one skandha.

Excluding the resistant dharmas and those dharmas that will necessarily not arise, all other remaining dharmas are subsumed under eight [elements], maintained by two [elements], and included in five skandhas.

Excluding non-obstructive phenomena (*apratigha-dharma*) and all phenomena that are necessarily non-arising, all remaining phenomena are subsumed under ten bases (*āyatana*), ten elements (*dhātu*), and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Excluding contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and all phenomena that are necessarily non-arising, all remaining phenomena are subsumed under three bases, two elements, and five aggregates.

Excluding the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and those dharmas that will certainly not arise, all other remaining dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen bases (*āyatana*), the twelve supports (*dhātu*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).

Excluding the conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and those dharmas that will certainly not arise, there is nothing remaining but an empty discourse regarding the non-aggregation of all dharmas. Excluding the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and those dharmas that will certainly not arise, all other remaining dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen bases, the twelve supports, and the five aggregates.

Excluding past and present phenomena, as well as those phenomena that will necessarily not arise, all remaining phenomena are comprised within the eighteen bases (*āyatana*), the twelve elements (*dhātu*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).

Excluding future phenomena, as well as those phenomena that will necessarily not arise—this being a mere empty discourse since no such collection of phenomena exists—all remaining phenomena are comprised within the eighteen bases, the twelve elements, and the five aggregates. Excluding wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, as well as those phenomena that will necessarily not arise, all remaining phenomena are comprised within the eighteen bases, the twelve elements, and the five aggregates.

Excluding indeterminate dharmas and those dharmas that will certainly not arise, all other remaining dharmas are subsumed under ten bases (āyatana), four elements (dhātu), and five aggregates (skandha).
Excluding dharmas bound to the desire realm and those dharmas that will certainly not arise, all other remaining dharmas are subsumed under fourteen bases, ten elements, and five aggregates.

Excluding those factors bound to the realms of form and formlessness, the factors of those in training and those beyond training, and all factors that will never arise, the remaining factors are subsumed within the eighteen bases (*āyatana*), the twelve elements (*dhātu*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).

Except for the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner and those dharmas that will certainly not arise, all other dharmas are subsumed under three aggregates (*skandha*), contained within two bases (*āyatana*), and included in five constituents (*dhātu*).

Except for the dharmas abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), the dharmas that are not to be abandoned, and those dharmas that will certainly not arise, all other dharmas are subsumed under eighteen elements (*dhātu*), contained within twelve bases (*āyatana*), and included in five constituents (*skandha*).

Excluding the dharmas abandoned through contemplation (*cintāmayī-prahātavya*) and those dharmas that will never arise, all other remaining dharmas are subsumed under three aggregates (*skandha*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five constituents (*dhātu*).
Is there any single base, single entrance, or single constituent that subsumes all dharmas?
Answer: There is.
One *dharmadhātu* comprises one *āyatana*, namely the *manāyatana*, and one *skandha*, namely the *rūpaskandha*.

This concludes the fourth chapter, the *Jñānavarga*, of the *Abhidharma*; it consists of one hundred and seventy-eight *śloka*s in the Sanskrit original, and two thousand three hundred and forty-one words in the Qin translation.
Wrong views sever purity; there is neither cause nor wisdom-vision.
The power of wisdom lacks diligence, yet they claim it is the cause of the seven types of persons.
The four primary conditions are non-existent; there is no cause, whether from oneself or from another.
"I am the creator," "the created is without cause," "this," "that," "I"—these are the six views;
Desire-pleasures, the various dhyānas, emptiness, existence, non-existence, and non-wind;
"I am the creator" is also accompanied by conceit; Whether already attained or yet to be attained.
Therefore, this Chapter on Views is taught.
That is to say, this view—namely, that there is no giving, no merit, and no teaching—is a false view abandoned through the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The view that there is no fruit or retribution for good or evil deeds is a false view abandoned through the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
"There is no present life and no future life; there is no father and no mother"—this wrong view is abandoned by the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
"There are no Arhats in the world who have attained the Dharma through realization"—this wrong view is abandoned by the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
The view that there are no peerless dharmas is abandoned by the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The view that one does not attain any destination in this world or the next, but dwells having personally realized and accomplished it through one's own wisdom, is abandoned by the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
This so-called view— that one lives here in this life, while elsewhere there is annihilation, destruction, and non-existence after death—
is subsumed under the extreme view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), and is to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

This view holds that when this human body composed of the four great elements meets its end, at that time the earth-element of the body returns to earth, the water-element of the body returns to water, the fire-element of the body returns to fire, the wind-element of the body returns to wind, and the space-element of the body—when the five men carry the corpse away to be discarded in the cemetery—is left behind as a mere trace, while the faculties return to the void.
This is included within the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and constitutes the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), which is abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
This view is as follows: "The bones are the color of white doves; I transform into ash, or if there is fire, it is my objective support (*ālambana*)."
This is not [correct] view; it is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
If there is a view of self regarding conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*), this is a false view abandoned through the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*);
if there is a view of self regarding unconditioned phenomena without outflows (*anāsrava-saṃskāra*), this is a false view abandoned through the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
This so-called view holds that the greedy praise giving while the wise praise receiving;
it slanders the Dharma of wisdom—this is a false view, abandoned by the Truth of the Path.
This so-called view is empty and false speech.
This is folly, not wisdom.
Those who make such a claim—that there is life here and yet no death elsewhere, where one is cut off and destroyed—hold a view of eternalism subsumed under the extreme views;
it is to be abandoned by the vision of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
This view—that sentient beings become defiled without cause and without condition—is a false view;
it is abandoned through the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
This so-called view—that sentient beings are purified without cause and without condition—is a false view; it is abandoned by the Truth of the Path.
This view—that sentient beings lack wisdom and insight because they are without cause and without condition—is wrong view; it is abandoned through the Truth of the Origin [of Suffering].
This so-called view—that sentient beings possess wisdom and vision without cause or condition—is a false view; it is abandoned through the Truth of the Path.

This view is as follows: there is no power and no diligence; there is neither power nor diligence; there is no self-agency, no agency by another, and no human agency; it is not self-made, not made by another, and not made by a person; yet there is the power of a person, the diligence of a person, and the exertion of a person. All sentient beings, all insects, and all spirits have no power, no sovereignty, no diligence, and no exertion; they possess only the retribution of their actions. Sentient beings experience suffering and pleasure without cause and without condition.
Regarding the sixfold set of six, if one slanders the contaminated power of diligence, this wrong view is abandoned through the Truth of Origination;
if one slanders the uncontaminated power of diligence, this wrong view is abandoned through the Truth of the Path.

This is the view they hold: "Committing acts of killing, teaching others to kill; committing acts of cutting, teaching others to cut; boiling, teaching others to boil; causing grief, distress, beating one’s breast, and lamentation with a distracted mind; harming sentient beings; taking what is not given; sexual misconduct; false speech; drinking alcohol; breaking through walls, destroying storehouses, stealing gold, and violating the wives of others; harming villages, harming cities, and harming sentient beings—one who does such things as these commits no evil.

Whether using a sword or a wheel, if one were to cut, sever, beat, and strike every single insect on this earth until all are gathered into one mass of flesh within a single day, there would be no evil, nor would there be any karmic retribution for evil.

Likewise, whether one comes from the left bank of the Ganges to perform meritorious deeds, give alms, and preach the Dharma, or from the right bank of the Ganges to cut, sever, beat, and strike, there is neither merit nor evil."

To say that giving, the perfection of precepts, and joyful speech regarding wealth bring no merit by reason of those causes and conditions, and bring no karmic fruit by reason of those causes and conditions—
this is a false view, which is abandoned through the Truth of the Origin [of Suffering].

This refers to the view that there are seven classes of beings who neither act nor cause others to act, neither transform nor cause others to transform; they exist as a real, stable, and eternal collection, established in their respective positions without moving or interfering with one another, whether in merit or demerit, or in suffering or pleasure.

What are they? They are the seven so-called "person-bodies" (*pudgala-kāya*): the earth-body, water-body, fire-body, wind-body, suffering, pleasure, and life. These seven are not made by a maker nor transformed by a transformer; they exist as a real, stable, and permanent collection. They stand firm, do not move, and are mutually independent. Whether it be merit or demerit, pleasure or pain, or the pleasure and pain of a person—these do not interfere with worldly affairs. Within these seven bodies, one passes away without harming life. This doctrine of non-action asserts that whether there is harm or killing, it does not reach the end of life, yet it reaches the end of life.
This extreme view is subsumed under the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) and is to be abandoned through the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
That which is called this view arises from four hundred thousand gates of birth, sixty hundred thousand great eons,
six hundred and three types of practice and half-practice, sixty-two paths of progress, sixty-two dust-holders,
sixty-two intermediate eons, one hundred and twenty faculties, one hundred and thirty-six great hells, and forty...
There are nine hundred thousand families of brahmins, four million nine hundred thousand villages of naked ascetics,
and four million nine hundred thousand dragon realms; therein he enters the sixfold birth and the eight stages of the noble ones (aṣṭāryapudgala),

the seven courses of perception, the seven courses of non-perception, the seven courses of the Nirgranthas, the seven courses of the asuras and the seven courses of those who are not asuras, and the seven heavens.
Seven instances of anger, seven humans, seven non-humans; seven springs and seven hundred springs; seven precipices and seven hundred precipices;

seven mountains and seven hundred mountains; seven dreams and seven hundred dreams—this is called eighty-four hundred thousand great kalpas, during which both the foolish and the wise come and go, passing through them until the end of suffering is reached.

He does not say: "By means of this fruit of the precepts and pure conduct, I shall not practice what is immature, but shall practice what is mature; what is already mature I shall further mature, and what is already doubled I shall double again; thus, having advanced beyond suffering and pleasure, I shall never regress."

It is like a ball of thread: when one holds the thread and lets it unwind, so too do the ignorant and the wise, through eighty-four hundred thousand great kalpas of coming and going, exhaust the limit of suffering; there is no agent, yet there is the condition for action.
This is the misapprehension of precepts and vows, which is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering.
It refers to this view held by certain people: that whatever has been experienced by them, all of that is caused solely by past actions, and there is no present action or condition for such action.
This is the theft of precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
This view holds that whatever this person experiences, all of it is caused by the transformation of wealth and conditioned by non-action (*akriyā*).
This is the "theft of precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
As for this view— that whatever a person experiences here is all without cause and without condition—
this is "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which is abandoned through the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).

This view, namely: "I am the creator of suffering and pleasure, and there is no other creator or causal condition for their creation"—this is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
This view, namely: "Another is the creator of suffering and pleasure, and there is no other creator or causal condition for their creation."
This clinging to precepts and observances is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering.
That is to say, this view— namely, that "I am the agent," "another is the agent," or that "suffering and pleasure arise without being made or through the conditions of making"—
this clinging to precepts and observances is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering.

This view holds that the suffering and pleasure experienced by sentient beings are neither self-created nor created by another, neither created by oneself nor caused to be created by instructing others; they arise without cause and without condition.
This wrong view is abandoned through the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*).
That is to say, this view holds: "That is the self; that is the world; I am that eternal dharma, an unchanging dharma."
This extreme view is subsumed under the view of eternalism and is abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
That is to say, this view holds that "this self truly exists.
This extreme view is subsumed under the view of eternalism and is abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering.
This so-called view— that "in reality, this self does not exist"—
is subsumed under the extreme view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) and is abandoned through the realization of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
This so-called view— that "I perceive my eye, and form is where I abide"— [is likewise abandoned].
This view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering.
This so-called view is: "I perceive what is not-self as 'my eye'; I abide in the collection of form (rūpaskandha), which is the cause [of my existence].
This view of a self is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering.
This so-called view is the view of self in what is not-self: "The self is form; it dwells in the eye, with the various sensory bases as its cause.
This view of a self in the body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned by the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

This so-called view is: "This is my self; whether speaking, perceiving, acting, instructing, or causing others to act, it is born and reborn, performing various good and evil deeds and receiving their retribution."
This extreme view is subsumed under the view of eternalism and is abandoned through the realization of the Truth of Suffering.
This so-called view holds that purity and liberation consist in the enjoyment of the five sensual pleasures, mistakenly regarding these defiled phenomena as supreme.
This is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

This view holds that "this is purification, this is liberation, this is deliverance from desire," up to the point of attaining and dwelling in the fourth dhyāna through the condition of non-action (*akriyā*) and action (*kriyā*).

This is the theft of precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). Regarding this view: "I am superior" arises as overweening pride (*abhimāna*) based on the view of emptiness;

"I am equal" arises as pride (*māna*) based on the view of emptiness; "I am inferior" arises as slight pride (*ūnamāna*) based on the view of emptiness. "Those who are superior to me" arise as slight pride based on that view; "those who are equal to me" arise as pride based on that view; "those who are inferior to me" arise as overweening pride based on that view. "There is no one superior to me" arises as overweening pride based on that view; "there is no one equal to me" arises as overweening pride based on that view; "there is no one inferior to me" arises as slight pride based on that view. Regarding this view: there is no wind, no rain, and no shooting stars; pregnancy occurs without conception; rivers do not flow; fire does not burn; the sun and moon neither rise nor set; and there is no abiding place for defilement or purity.
This is an extreme view subsumed under the view of annihilationism; it is abandoned through the realization of the Truth of Suffering.
That is to say, this view holds:
"I am the creator of sentient beings, and others are also creators."
In each and every instance, there is no seeing; one does not perceive this as an arrow.
Regarding the statement "sentient beings are created by me": because [the self] acts, creates, and transforms, it is said that "sentient beings are created by me."
There is also that which is created by another; it is made by another, fashioned by another, and transformed by another, hence it is said, "there is also that which is created by another.

There is no seer in each and every thing, and each and every thing is not the arrow of all; because one sees them as neither looking, nor gazing, nor perceiving, it is said, "there is no seer in each and every thing."
One should not contemplate this as the arrow; rather, one should contemplate the conditions for this arrow.
If contact gives rise to feeling, it is neither created by me nor created by another.
Regarding the instruction to "contemplate the conditions of this arrow": this arrow refers to views (*dṛṣṭi*).

This arrow gives rise to distinct birth, distinct aging, distinct illness, and distinct death. One contemplates this arrow of views as perception; therefore, it is called "contemplating the conditions of the arrow."

Regarding "if one touches upon the arising of feeling," "arising" refers to its basis; because one trains in and becomes attached to the touch of these various views, it is said, "if one touches upon the arising of feeling."
